Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Khuddakanikāye

In the Khuddaka Nikāya

Khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathā

Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

Buddhaṃ [M 0.0001][P 0.0011][V 0.0001] saraṇaṃ gacchāmi;

Dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi;

Saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmīti.

I go to the Buddha for refuge; I go to the Dhamma for refuge; I go to the Saṅgha for refuge.

Ayaṃ saraṇagamananiddeso khuddakānaṃ ādi.

This is the explanation of going for refuge, the beginning of the Minor Texts.

Imassa dāni atthaṃ paramatthajotikāya khuddakaṭṭhakathāya vivarituṃ vibhajituṃ uttānīkātuṃ idaṃ vuccati –

Now, to explain, analyze, and make plain the meaning of this with the Paramatthajotikā, the commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha, this is said:

Uttamaṃ [V 0.0002] vandaneyyānaṃ, vanditvā ratanattayaṃ;

Khuddakānaṃ karissāmi, kesañci atthavaṇṇanaṃ.

Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, foremost of the venerable, I shall compose an explanation of the meaning of some of the Minor Texts.

Khuddakānaṃ gambhīrattā, kiñcāpi atidukkarā;

Vaṇṇanā mādisenesā, abodhantena sāsanaṃ.

Although, due to the profundity of the Minor Texts, this explanation is exceedingly difficult for one like me, who does not understand the Teaching,

Ajjāpi tu abbocchinno, pubbācariyanicchayo;

Tatheva ca ṭhitaṃ yasmā, navaṅgaṃ satthusāsanaṃ.

Yet, even today, the judgment of the ancient teachers stands unbroken; and since the ninefold Teaching of the Master stands just so,

Tasmāhaṃ kātumicchāmi, atthasaṃvaṇṇanaṃ imaṃ;

Sāsanañceva nissāya, porāṇañca vinicchayaṃ.

Therefore, relying on both the Teaching and the ancient judgment, I wish to compose this explanation of the meaning.

Saddhammabahumānena, nāttukkaṃsanakamyatā;

Nāññesaṃ vambhanatthāya, taṃ suṇātha samāhitāti.

Out of great respect for the True Dhamma, not from a desire for self-exaltation, nor for the purpose of disparaging others—listen to it with a concentrated mind.

Khuddakavavatthānaṃ

The Determination of the Minor Texts

Tattha [M 0.0002] “khuddakānaṃ karissāmi, kesañci atthavaṇṇana”nti vuttattā khuddakāni tāva vavatthapetvā pacchā atthavaṇṇanaṃ karissāmi. Khuddakāni nāma khuddakanikāyassa ekadeso, khuddakanikāyo nāma pañcannaṃ nikāyānaṃ ekadeso. Pañca nikāyā nāma –

Therein, since it was said, “I shall compose an explanation of the meaning of some of the Minor Texts,” having first determined the Minor Texts, I will afterwards compose the explanation of the meaning. The Minor Texts are a portion of the Khuddaka Nikāya; the Khuddaka Nikāya is a portion of the five Nikāyas. The five Nikāyas are:

Dīghamajjhimasaṃyutta, aṅguttarikakhuddakā;

Nikāyā pañca gambhīrā, dhammato atthato cime.

The Dīgha, Majjhima, Saṃyutta, Aṅguttara, and Khuddaka—these five Nikāyas are profound both in text and in meaning.

Tattha [P 0.0012] brahmajālasuttādīni catuttiṃsa suttāni dīghanikāyo. Mūlapariyāyasuttādīni diyaḍḍhasataṃ dve ca suttāni majjhimanikāyo. Oghataraṇasuttādīni satta suttasahassāni satta ca suttasatāni dvāsaṭṭhi ca suttāni saṃyuttanikāyo. Cittapariyādānasuttādīni nava suttasahassāni pañca ca suttasatāni sattapaññāsañca suttāni aṅguttaranikāyo. Khuddakapāṭho, dhammapadaṃ, udānaṃ, itivuttakaṃ, suttanipāto, vimānavatthu, petavatthu, theragāthā, therīgāthā, jātakaṃ, niddeso, paṭisambhidā[V 0.0003], apadānaṃ, buddhavaṃso, cariyāpiṭakaṃ, vinayābhidhammapiṭakāni, ṭhapetvā vā cattāro nikāye avasesaṃ buddhavacanaṃ khuddakanikāyo.

Therein, the thirty-four suttas beginning with the Brahmajāla Sutta are the Dīgha Nikāya. The one hundred and fifty-two suttas beginning with the Mūlapariyāya Sutta are the Majjhima Nikāya. The seven thousand seven hundred and sixty-two suttas beginning with the Oghataraṇa Sutta are the Saṃyutta Nikāya. The nine thousand five hundred and fifty-seven suttas beginning with the Cittapariyādāna Sutta are the Aṅguttara Nikāya. The Khuddakapāṭha, Dhammapada, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Suttanipāta, Vimānavatthu, Petavatthu, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, Jātaka, Niddesa, Paṭisambhidā, Apadāna, Buddhavaṃsa, Cariyāpiṭaka, and the Vinaya and Abhidhamma Piṭakas; or, setting aside the four Nikāyas, the remaining word of the Buddha is the Khuddaka Nikāya.

Kasmā panesa khuddakanikāyoti vuccati? Bahūnaṃ khuddakānaṃ dhammakkhandhānaṃ samūhato nivāsato ca. Samūhanivāsā hi “nikāyo”ti vuccanti. “Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ ekanikāyampi samanupassāmi evaṃ cittaṃ, yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave, tiracchānagatā pāṇā (saṃ. ni. 3.100). Poṇikanikāyo, cikkhallikanikāyo”ti evamādīni cettha sādhakāni sāsanato lokato ca. Ayamassa khuddakanikāyassa ekadeso. Imāni suttantapiṭakapariyāpannāni atthato vivarituṃ vibhajituṃ uttānīkātuñca adhippetāni khuddakāni, tesampi khuddakānaṃ saraṇasikkhāpadadvattiṃsākārakumārapañhamaṅgalasutta- ratanasuttatirokuṭṭanidhikaṇḍamettasuttānaṃ vasena navappabhedo khuddakapāṭho ādi ācariyaparamparāya vācanāmaggaṃ āropitavasena na bhagavatā vuttavasena. Bhagavatā hi vuttavasena –

Now, why is this called the Khuddaka Nikāya? Because it is a collection (samūha) and a dwelling place (nivāsa) of many minor (khuddaka) sections of the Dhamma. For collections and dwelling places are called “nikāya.” “Bhikkhus, I do not see any other single group (ekanikāya) so variegated as the animals of the animal realm.” “The dwelling of the Poṇikas (poṇikanikāyo), the dwelling of the Cikkhallikas (cikkhallikanikāyo)”—such examples from both the Teaching and the world are evidence here. This Khuddakapāṭha is a portion of the Khuddaka Nikāya. These Minor Texts, which are included in the Suttanta Piṭaka, are intended to be explained, analyzed, and clarified in meaning. Among these Minor Texts, the Khuddakapāṭha—which has nine divisions, namely: the Refuges, the Precepts, the Thirty-two Parts, the Youth’s Questions, the Maṅgala Sutta, the Ratana Sutta, the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta, the Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta, and the Metta Sutta—is the first by way of its placement on the path of recitation by the lineage of teachers, not by way of its being spoken by the Blessed One. For, by way of what was spoken by the Blessed One:

“Anekajātisaṃsāraṃ, sandhāvissaṃ anibbisaṃ;

Gahakāraṃ gavesanto, dukkhā jāti punappunaṃ.

Through the round of countless births I have run, seeking but not finding the house-builder. Painful is birth again and again.

“Gahakāraka [M 0.0003][P 0.0013] diṭṭhosi, puna gehaṃ na kāhasi;

Sabbā te phāsukā bhaggā, gahakūṭaṃ visaṅkhataṃ;

Visaṅkhāragataṃ cittaṃ, taṇhānaṃ khayamajjhagā”ti. (dha. pa. 153-154) –

O house-builder, you are seen! You shall not build a house again. All your rafters are broken, the ridge-pole is dismantled. The mind, gone to the unconditioned, has attained the destruction of craving.

Idaṃ gāthādvayaṃ sabbassāpi buddhavacanassa ādi. Tañca manasāva vuttavasena, na vacībhedaṃ katvā vuttavasena. Vacībhedaṃ pana katvā vuttavasena –

This pair of verses is the beginning of the entire word of the Buddha. And that is the beginning by way of being spoken by the mind alone, not by way of being spoken after breaking into speech. But by way of being spoken after breaking into speech:

“Yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā,

Ātāpino jhāyato brāhmaṇassa;

Athassa kaṅkhā vapayanti sabbā,

Yato pajānāti sahetudhamma”nti. (udā. 1; mahāva. 1) –

When, indeed, phenomena appear to the ardent, meditating brahmin, then all his doubts vanish, since he understands the conditioned phenomenon together with its cause.

Ayaṃ gāthā ādi. Tasmā yvāyaṃ navappabhedo khuddakapāṭho imesaṃ khuddakānaṃ ādi, tassa ādito pabhuti atthasaṃvaṇṇanaṃ ārabhissāmi.

This verse is the beginning. Therefore, this Khuddakapāṭha with its nine divisions is the beginning of these Minor Texts. I shall begin the explanation of its meaning from the very start.

Nidānasodhanaṃ

The Purification of the Introduction

Tassa [V 0.0004] cāyamādi “buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī”ti. Tassāyaṃ atthavaṇṇanāya mātikā –

And its beginning is this: 'I go to the Buddha for refuge, I go to the Dhamma for refuge, I go to the Saṅgha for refuge.' This is the mātikā for its explanation of the meaning:

“Kena kattha kadā kasmā, bhāsitaṃ saraṇattayaṃ;

Kasmā cidhādito vutta, mavuttamapi ādito.

By whom, where, when, and for what reason was the Threefold Refuge spoken? And why is it stated at the beginning here, though not spoken at the beginning by the Tathāgata?

“Nidānasodhanaṃ katvā, evamettha tato paraṃ;

Buddhaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ, gamakañca vibhāvaye.

Having purified the introduction here, then thereafter, one should explain the going for refuge to the Buddha and the one who goes for refuge.

“Bhedābhedaṃ phalañcāpi, gamanīyañca dīpaye;

Dhammaṃ saraṇamiccādi, dvayepesa nayo mato.

One should explain the distinction between the breaking and non-breaking of the refuge, and also the fruit, and the act of going for refuge. This same method is to be understood for the two refuges beginning with 'I go to the Dhamma for refuge'.

“Anupubbavavatthāne, kāraṇañca viniddise;

Saraṇattayametañca, upamāhi pakāsaye”ti.

In the gradual arrangement, one should also point out the reason; and one should illuminate this Threefold Refuge with similes.

Tattha paṭhamagāthāya tāva idaṃ saraṇattayaṃ kena bhāsitaṃ, kattha bhāsitaṃ, kadā bhāsitaṃ, kasmā bhāsitaṃ [P 0.0014] avuttamapicādito tathāgatena kasmā idhādito vuttanti pañca pañhā.

Herein, regarding the first verse, there are first these five questions: By whom was this Threefold Refuge spoken? Where was it spoken? When was it spoken? For what reason was it spoken? And, although not spoken at the beginning by the Tathāgata, why is it stated at the beginning here?

Tesaṃ [M 0.0004] vissajjanā kena bhāsitanti bhagavatā bhāsitaṃ, na sāvakehi, na isīhi, na devatāhi. Katthāti bārāṇasiyaṃ isipatane migadāye. Kadāti āyasmante yase saddhiṃ sahāyakehi arahattaṃ patte ekasaṭṭhiyā arahantesu bahujanahitāya loke dhammadesanaṃ karontesu. Kasmāti pabbajjatthañca upasampadatthañca. Yathāha –

The answers to these are: Regarding 'By whom was it spoken?': It was spoken by the Blessed One, not by disciples, not by seers, not by deities. Regarding 'Where?': At Isipatana in the Deer Park at Bārāṇasī. Regarding 'When?': When the Venerable Yasa, together with his companions, had attained Arahantship, and the sixty-one Arahants were teaching the Dhamma in the world for the welfare of the many. Regarding 'For what reason?': For the purpose of the going forth and for the purpose of the higher ordination. As it is said:

“Evañca pana, bhikkhave, pabbājetabbo upasampādetabbo. Paṭhamaṃ kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādāpetvā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ kārāpetvā bhikkhūnaṃ pāde vandāpetvā ukkuṭikaṃ nisīdāpetvā añjaliṃ paggaṇhāpetvā ‘evaṃ vadehī’ti vattabbo ‘buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī’”ti (mahāva. 34).

“And thus, monks, one should be given the going forth and the higher ordination. First, having had their hair and beard shaved off, having had them put on saffron robes, having had the upper robe arranged over one shoulder, having them pay homage at the feet of the monks, having them sit in the squatting position, having them raise their hands in añjali, they should be told, ‘Say thus: “I go to the Buddha for refuge, I go to the Dhamma for refuge, I go to the Sangha for refuge.”’”

Kasmā [V 0.0005] cidhādito vuttanti idañca navaṅgaṃ satthusāsanaṃ tīhi piṭakehi saṅgaṇhitvā vācanāmaggaṃ āropentehi pubbācariyehi yasmā iminā maggena devamanussā upāsakabhāvena vā pabbajitabhāvena vā sāsanaṃ otaranti, tasmā sāsanotārassa maggabhūtattā idha khuddakapāṭhe ādito vuttanti ñātabbaṃ.

Regarding 'And why is it stated at the beginning here?', it should be known that it was stated at the beginning here in the Khuddakapāṭha by the ancient teachers—who compiled the nine-limbed Dispensation of the Teacher into the three Piṭakas and established the path of recitation—because by this path gods and humans enter the Dispensation, either as lay followers or as those who have gone forth. Therefore, because it is the very path for entering the Dispensation, it is stated at the beginning.

Kataṃ nidānasodhanaṃ.

The purification of the introduction is completed.

1. Saraṇattayavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Three Refuges

Buddhavibhāvanā

Exposition of the Buddha

Idāni [V 0.0006] yaṃ vuttaṃ “buddhaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ, gamakañca vibhāvaye”ti, tattha sabbadhammesu appaṭihatañāṇanimittānuttaravimokkhādhigamaparibhāvitaṃ khandhasantānamupādāya, paññattito sabbaññutaññāṇapadaṭṭhānaṃ vā saccābhisambodhimupādāya paññattito sattaviseso buddho. Yathāha –

Now, concerning what was said, ‘I shall explain the going for refuge to the Buddha, and the Guide,’ therein, the Buddha is a special being, conceptually, on account of the continuum of aggregates imbued with the attainment of unsurpassed liberation, which is the object of unobstructed knowledge regarding all phenomena; or, conceptually, on account of the full awakening to the truths, which has omniscient knowledge as its proximate cause. As it is said:

“Buddhoti [M 0.0005] yo so bhagavā sayambhū anācariyako pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu sāmaṃ saccāni abhisambujjhi, tattha ca sabbaññutaṃ patto, balesu ca vasībhāva”nti (mahāni. 192; cūḷani. pārāyanatthutigāthāniddesa 97; paṭi. ma. 1.161).

“‘Buddha’ is that Blessed One who, being self-arisen and without a teacher, by himself thoroughly awakened to the truths concerning phenomena unheard of before, and therein attained omniscience and attained mastery over the powers.”

Ayaṃ tāva atthato buddhavibhāvanā.

This, then, is the exposition of the Buddha in terms of meaning.

Byañjanato pana “bujjhitāti buddho, bodhetāti buddho”ti evamādinā nayena veditabbo. Vuttañcetaṃ –

In terms of designation, however, it should be understood by the method beginning with “one who has understood is a Buddha, one who causes to understand is a Buddha.” And this has been said:

“Buddhoti kenaṭṭhena buddho? Bujjhitā saccānīti buddho, bodhetā pajāyāti buddho, sabbaññutāya buddho, sabbadassāvitāya buddho, anaññaneyyatāya buddho, vikasitāya [P 0.0015] buddho, khīṇāsavasaṅkhātena buddho, nirupakkilesasaṅkhātena buddho, ekantavītarāgoti buddho, ekantavītadosoti buddho, ekantavītamohoti buddho, ekantanikkilesoti buddho, ekāyanamaggaṃ gatoti buddho, eko anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddhoti buddho, abuddhivihatattā buddhipaṭilābhā buddho. Buddhoti netaṃ nāmaṃ mātarā kataṃ, na pitarā kataṃ, na bhātarā kataṃ, na bhaginiyā kataṃ, na mittāmaccehi kataṃ, na ñātisālohitehi kataṃ, na samaṇabrāhmaṇehi kataṃ, na devatāhi kataṃ, vimokkhantikametaṃ buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ bodhiyā mūle saha sabbaññutaññāṇassa paṭilābhā sacchikā [V 0.0007] paññatti yadidaṃ buddho”ti (mahāni. 192; cūḷani. pārāyanatthutigāthāniddesa 97; paṭi. ma. 1.162).

“‘By what meaning is he called “Buddha”? He is called “Buddha” because he has understood the truths. He is called “Buddha” because he causes the populace to understand. He is called “Buddha” on account of his omniscience. He is called “Buddha” on account of his all-seeing nature. He is called “Buddha” on account of not being led by another. He is called “Buddha” on account of being fully blossomed. He is called “Buddha” because he is designated as one whose taints are destroyed. He is called “Buddha” because he is designated as one without defilements. He is called “Buddha” as one entirely free from passion. He is called “Buddha” as one entirely free from aversion. He is called “Buddha” as one entirely free from delusion. He is called “Buddha” as one entirely without defilements. He is called “Buddha” as one who has gone on the one-way path. He is called “Buddha” as the one who alone has thoroughly awakened to the unsurpassed, perfect, and full awakening. He is called “Buddha” on account of having destroyed non-understanding and having attained understanding. This name “Buddha” was not given by his mother, nor by his father, nor by his brother, nor by his sister, nor by his friends and companions, nor by his relatives and kinsmen, nor by ascetics and brahmins, nor by deities. This is a realized designation for the Blessed Buddhas, finalized at the point of liberation at the foot of the Bodhi tree, together with the attainment of omniscient knowledge—that is, “Buddha”.’”

Ettha ca yathā loke avagantā avagatoti vuccati, evaṃ bujjhitā saccānīti buddho. Yathā paṇṇasosā vātā paṇṇasusāti vuccanti, evaṃ bodhetā pajāyāti buddho. Sabbaññutāya buddhoti sabbadhammabujjhanasamatthāya buddhiyā buddhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Sabbadassāvitāya buddhoti sabbadhammabodhanasamatthāya buddhiyā buddhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Anaññaneyyatāya buddhoti aññena abodhito sayameva buddhattā buddhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Vikasitāya buddhoti nānāguṇavikasanato padumamiva vikasanaṭṭhena buddhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Khīṇāsavasaṅkhātena buddhoti evamādīhi cittasaṅkocakaradhammapahānato [M 0.0006] niddākkhayavibuddho puriso viya sabbakilesaniddākkhayavibuddhattā buddhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Ekāyanamaggaṃ gatoti buddhoti buddhiyatthānaṃ gamanatthapariyāyato yathā maggaṃ gatopi puriso gatoti vuccati, evaṃ ekāyanamaggaṃ gatattāpi buddhoti vuccatīti dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Eko anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddhoti buddhoti na parehi buddhattā buddho, kintu sayameva anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddhattā buddhoti vuttaṃ hoti[P 0.0016]. Abuddhivihatattā buddhipaṭilābhā buddhoti buddhi buddhaṃ bodhoti pariyāyavacanametaṃ. Tattha yathā nīlarattaguṇayogato “nīlo paṭo, ratto paṭo”ti vuccati, evaṃ buddhiguṇayogato buddhoti ñāpetuṃ vuttaṃ hoti. Tato paraṃ buddhoti netaṃ nāmanti evamādi atthamanugatā ayaṃ paññattīti bodhanatthaṃ vuttanti evarūpena nayena sabbesaṃ padānaṃ buddhasaddassa sādhanasamattho attho veditabbo.

Herein, just as in the world one who goes is called ‘gone,’ so he is called Buddha because he has understood the truths. Just as winds that cause leaves to dry are called ‘leaf-dryers,’ so he is called Buddha because he causes the populace to understand. ‘He is called Buddha on account of his omniscience’ means he is called Buddha on account of the wisdom capable of understanding all phenomena. ‘He is called Buddha on account of his all-seeing nature’ means he is called Buddha on account of the wisdom capable of making known all phenomena. ‘He is called Buddha on account of not being led by another’ means he is called Buddha because he understood by himself, not being made to understand by another. ‘He is called Buddha on account of being fully blossomed’ means he is called Buddha in the sense of blossoming like a lotus, due to the unfolding of various qualities. By the phrases beginning with ‘He is called Buddha because he is designated as one whose taints are destroyed,’ it is meant that, through abandoning states that constrict the mind, he is called Buddha because he is awakened from the destruction of the sleep of all defilements, like a man awakened from the destruction of sleep. ‘He is called Buddha as one who has gone on the one-way path’ was said to show that, by way of the figurative meaning of ‘going’ among the meanings of ‘buddha,’ just as a man who has gone on a path is also called ‘gone,’ so too, he is called Buddha because of having gone on the one-way path. ‘He is called Buddha as the one who alone has thoroughly awakened to the unsurpassed, perfect, and full awakening’ means he is not called Buddha because of being made to understand by others, but rather he is called Buddha because he himself has thoroughly awakened to the unsurpassed, perfect, and full awakening. The phrase ‘He is called Buddha on account of having destroyed non-understanding and having attained understanding’—that is, wisdom, the awakened one, awakening—is a figurative expression. Herein, just as a cloth is called ‘blue cloth’ or ‘red cloth’ due to its connection with the quality of blue or red, so it is said to make known that he is called Buddha due to his connection with the qualities of a Buddha. After that, the statement beginning with ‘This name “Buddha” is not...’ was said to make known that this is a designation that follows its meaning. By such a method, the complete meaning, capable of establishing the word ‘Buddha,’ should be understood from all these terms.

Ayaṃ byañjanatopi buddhavibhāvanā.

This is the exposition of the Buddha in terms of designation as well.

Saraṇagamanagamakavibhāvanā

Exposition of the Going for Refuge and of the One Who Goes

Idāni saraṇagamanādīsu hiṃsatīti saraṇaṃ, saraṇagatānaṃ teneva saraṇagamanena bhayaṃ santāsaṃ dukkhaṃ duggatiṃ parikkilesaṃ hiṃsati vidhamati nīharati nirodhetīti attho. Atha vā hite pavattanena ahitā ca nivattanena sattānaṃ bhayaṃ hiṃsatīti buddho, bhavakantārā uttaraṇena assāsadānena ca dhammo, appakānampi kārānaṃ vipulaphalapaṭilābhakaraṇena saṅgho. Tasmā imināpi pariyāyena taṃ ratanattayaṃ saraṇaṃ. Tappasādataggarutāhi vihataviddhaṃsitakileso tapparāyaṇatākārappavatto aparappaccayo vā cittuppādo saraṇagamanaṃ. Taṃsamaṅgī satto taṃ saraṇaṃ gacchati, vuttappakārena cittuppādena “esa me saraṇaṃ, esa me parāyaṇa”nti evametaṃ upetīti attho[V 0.0008]. Upento ca “ete mayaṃ, bhante, bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāma, dhammañca, upāsake no bhagavā dhāretū”ti tapussabhallikādayo [M 0.0007] viya samādānena vā, “satthā me, bhante, bhagavā, sāvakohamasmī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.154) mahākassapādayo viya sissabhāvūpagamanena vā, “evaṃ vutte brahmāyu brāhmaṇo uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā yena bhagavā tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā tikkhattuṃ udānaṃ udānesi ‘namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa. Namo tassa…pe… sammāsambuddhassā’”ti [P 0.0017] (ma. ni. 2.388) brahmāyuādayo viya tappoṇattena vā, kammaṭṭhānānuyogino viya attasanniyyātanena vā, ariyapuggalā viya saraṇagamanupakkilesasamucchedena vāti anekappakāraṃ visayato kiccato ca upeti.

Now, in 'going for refuge' and so on, the meaning should be understood thus: Because it destroys (hiṃsati), it is called refuge (saraṇaṃ). For those who have gone for refuge, by that very going for refuge, it destroys, dispels, removes, and causes to cease fear, terror, suffering, a woeful state, and mental afflictions; this is the meaning. Alternatively, the Buddha is a refuge because he destroys the fear of beings by promoting their welfare and turning them away from what is not their welfare. The Dhamma is a refuge by enabling one to cross the wilderness of existence and by giving solace. The Saṅgha is a refuge by causing the attainment of abundant fruit even from small offerings. Therefore, in this way too, that Triple Gem is a refuge. Going for refuge is the arising of a thought which has its defilements struck down and destroyed through faith and reverence for that Triple Gem, which proceeds in the manner of having that as its ultimate resort, and which is independent of another cause. A being endowed with that goes to that refuge. This is the meaning: by means of a thought of the kind described, one approaches it thus, 'This is my refuge, this is my ultimate resort.' And one who approaches does so either by undertaking, like Tapussa and Bhallika and others, saying, 'Venerable sir, we go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma. May the Blessed One regard us as lay followers'; or by approaching the state of a disciple, like Mahākassapa and others, saying, 'Venerable sir, the Blessed One is my teacher; I am a disciple'; or by being inclined towards that, like Brahmāyu and others, as when the brahmin Brahmāyu, when this was said, rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined hands towards the Blessed One, and three times uttered this inspired utterance: “Homage to that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One!…”; or by self-surrender, like those devoted to a meditation subject; or by the eradication of the corruptions of going for refuge, like the noble persons. Thus one approaches it in many ways, with respect to the object and with respect to the function.

Ayaṃ saraṇagamanassa gamakassa ca vibhāvanā.

This is the exposition of the going for refuge and of the one who goes.

Bhedābhedaphaladīpanā

Elucidation of Breaking, Non-Breaking, and Fruit

Idāni “bhedābhedaṃ phalañcāpi, gamanīyañca dīpaye”ti vuttānaṃ bhedādīnaṃ ayaṃ dīpanā, evaṃ saraṇagatassa puggalassa duvidho saraṇagamanabhedo – sāvajjo ca anavajjo ca. Anavajjo kālakiriyāya, sāvajjo aññasatthari vuttappakārappavattiyā, tasmiñca vuttappakāraviparītappavattiyā. So duvidhopi puthujjanānameva. Buddhaguṇesu aññāṇasaṃsayamicchāñāṇappavattiyā anādarādippavattiyā ca tesaṃ saraṇaṃ saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ hoti. Ariyapuggalā pana abhinnasaraṇā ceva asaṃkiliṭṭhasaraṇā ca honti. Yathāha “aṭṭhānametaṃ, bhikkhave, anavakāso, yaṃ diṭṭhisampanno puggalo aññaṃ satthāraṃ uddiseyyā”ti (a. ni. 1.276; ma. ni. 3.128; vibha. 809). Puthujjanā tu yāvadeva saraṇabhedaṃ na pāpuṇanti, tāvadeva abhinnasaraṇā. Sāvajjova nesaṃ saraṇabhedo, saṃkileso ca aniṭṭhaphalado hoti. Anavajjo avipākattā aphalo, abhedo pana phalato iṭṭhameva phalaṃ deti.

Now, this is the explanation of 'breaking' and so on, which were mentioned in the line 'one should explain breaking and non-breaking, and also the fruit, and the object of going.' Thus, for a person who has gone for refuge, the breaking of the going for refuge is twofold: that with fault and that without fault. That without fault is by reason of death. That with fault is due to conduct of the aforementioned kind towards another teacher, and due to conduct contrary to the aforementioned kind towards that Triple Gem. Both these two kinds exist only for worldlings. Their refuge becomes corrupted through the occurrence of ignorance, doubt, and wrong knowledge regarding the qualities of the Buddha, and through the occurrence of disrespect and so on. But noble persons have an unbroken refuge and an uncorrupted refuge. As it is said: 'It is impossible, monks, it cannot happen, that a person accomplished in view would point to another as teacher.' Worldlings, however, have an unbroken refuge only for as long as they do not reach a breaking of the refuge. Their breaking of refuge which is with fault is a defilement and yields an undesirable fruit. That without fault, being without result, is fruitless. But non-breaking, with respect to fruit, gives only a desirable fruit.

Yathāha –

As it is said:

“Yekeci [M 0.0008] buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gatāse, na te gamissanti apāyabhūmiṃ;

Pahāya mānusaṃ dehaṃ, devakāyaṃ paripūressantī”ti. (dī. ni. 2.332; saṃ. ni. 1.37);

“Whoever has gone to the Buddha for refuge, they will not go to a plane of misery; having abandoned the human body, they will fill the host of devas.”

Tatra [V 0.0009] ca ye saraṇagamanupakkilesasamucchedena saraṇaṃ gatā, te apāyaṃ na gamissanti. Itare pana saraṇagamanena na gamissantīti evaṃ gāthāya adhippāyo veditabbo.

And in that verse, those who have gone for refuge by eradicating the corruptions of going for refuge—they will not go to a plane of misery. As for the others, however, it is not simply by going for refuge that they will avoid going to a plane of misery. In this way, the intention of the verse should be understood.

Ayaṃ tāva bhedābhedaphaladīpanā.

This, for now, is the elucidation of breaking, non-breaking, and fruit.

Gamanīyadīpanā

An Exposition of the Object of Going

Gamanīyadīpanāyaṃ codako āha – “buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī”ti ettha yo buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchati, esa buddhaṃ vā gaccheyya saraṇaṃ vā, ubhayathāpi ca ekassa vacanaṃ niratthakaṃ. Kasmā? Gamanakiriyāya kammadvayābhāvato. Na hettha “ajaṃ gāmaṃ netī”tiādīsu viya dvikammakattaṃ akkharacintakā icchanti.

In this Exposition of the Object of Going, a questioner says: "In the phrase 'I go to the Buddha for refuge,' as for the one who goes to the Buddha for refuge, he might go to the Buddha, or he might go to refuge. In either case, one of the words is meaningless. Why? Because the action of going does not have two objects. For here, grammarians do not accept a double-object construction as in such cases as 'he leads the goat to the village.'"

“Gacchateva pubbaṃ [P 0.0018] disaṃ, gacchati pacchimaṃ disa”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.159; 3.87) viya sātthakamevāti ce? Na, buddhasaraṇānaṃ samānādhikaraṇabhāvassānadhippetato. Etesañhi samānādhikaraṇabhāve adhippete paṭihatacittopi buddhaṃ upasaṅkamanto buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gato siyā. Yañhi taṃ buddhoti visesitaṃ saraṇaṃ, tamevesa gatoti. “Etaṃ kho saraṇaṃ khemaṃ, etaṃ saraṇamuttama”nti (dha. pa. 192) vacanato samānādhikaraṇattamevāti ce? Na, tattheva tabbhāvato. Tattheva hi gāthāpade etaṃ buddhādiratanattayaṃ saraṇagatānaṃ bhayaharaṇattasaṅkhāte saraṇabhāve abyabhicaraṇato “khemamuttamañca saraṇa”nti ayaṃ samānādhikaraṇabhāvo adhippeto, aññattha tu gamisambandhe sati saraṇagamanassa appasiddhito anadhippetoti asādhakametaṃ. “Etaṃ [M 0.0009] saraṇamāgamma, sabbadukkhā pamuccatī”ti ettha gamisambandhepi saraṇagamanapasiddhito samānādhikaraṇattamevāti ce? Na pubbe vuttadosappasaṅgato. Tatrāpi hi samānādhikaraṇabhāve sati etaṃ buddhadhammasaṅghasaraṇaṃ paṭihatacittopi āgamma sabbadukkhā pamucceyyāti evaṃ pubbe vuttadosappasaṅgo eva siyā, na ca no dosena atthi atthoti asādhakametaṃ. Yathā “mamañhi, ānanda, kalyāṇamittaṃ āgamma jātidhammā sattā jātiyā parimuccantī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.129) ettha bhagavato kalyāṇamittassa ānubhāvena parimuccamānā sattā “kalyāṇamittaṃ āgamma parimuccantī”ti vuttā. Evamidhāpi buddhadhammasaṅghassa saraṇassānubhāvena muccamāno “etaṃ saraṇamāgamma, sabbadukkhā pamuccatī”ti vuttoti evamettha adhippāyo veditabbo.

If it is said: "Just as in such cases as 'One goes to the eastern direction, one goes to the western direction,' it is indeed meaningful," this is not so, because a coreferential relationship between 'Buddha' and 'refuge' is not intended. For if a coreferential relationship between them were intended, even one with a hostile mind who approached the Buddha would have gone to the Buddha for refuge. For it is to that very refuge, specified as 'Buddha,' that this one has gone. If it is said: "Because of the statement, 'This refuge is safe, this is the supreme refuge,' it must be a coreferential construction," this is not so, because that is its nature only in that specific context. For only in that verse is this coreferential relationship intended, because this Triple Gem of the Buddha and so on is unfailing in its capacity as a refuge, which is characterized as the removal of fear for those who have gone for refuge; thus it is called the 'safe and supreme refuge.' Elsewhere, however, when there is a connection with the verb 'to go,' this is not intended, because the 'going for refuge' is not established. Therefore, this is not a valid argument. If it is said: "But in the line, 'Having come to this refuge, one is freed from all suffering,' since the 'going for refuge' is established even with the connection to 'going,' it must be a coreferential construction," this is not so, due to the arising of the fault previously stated. For in that case too, if there were a coreferential relationship, then even one with a hostile mind, having come to this refuge of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, would be freed from all suffering. Thus, the fault previously stated would indeed arise, and we have no use for a fault; therefore, this is not a valid argument. Just as in the statement, 'For, Ānanda, by relying on me as a good friend, beings subject to birth are freed from birth,' beings who are being freed by the power of the Blessed One as a good friend are said to be 'freed by relying on the good friend.' Similarly here, one who is being freed by the power of the refuge of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha is said to be 'freed by having come to this refuge.' Thus, the intended meaning here should be understood in this way.

Evaṃ sabbathāpi na buddhassa gamanīyattaṃ yujjati, na saraṇassa, na ubhayesaṃ, icchitabbañca [V 0.0010] gacchāmīti niddiṭṭhassa gamakassa gamanīyaṃ, tato vattabbā ettha yuttīti. Vuccate –

Thus, in every way, it is not suitable for the Buddha to be the object of going, nor for the refuge, nor for both. And an object of going is required for the goer indicated by 'I go.' Therefore, the reasoning to be stated here is suitable. It is said:

Buddhoyevettha gamanīyo, gamanākāradassanatthaṃ tu taṃ saraṇavacanaṃ, buddhaṃ saraṇanti gacchāmi. Esa me saraṇaṃ, esa me parāyaṇaṃ, aghassa, tātā, hitassa ca vidhātāti [P 0.0019] iminā adhippāyena etaṃ gacchāmi bhajāmi sevāmi payirupāsāmi, evaṃ vā jānāmi bujjhāmīti. Yesañhi dhātūnaṃ gatiattho buddhipi tesaṃ atthoti. Iti-saddassa appayogā ayuttamiti ce? Taṃ na. Tattha siyā – yadi cettha evamattho bhaveyya, tato “aniccaṃ rūpaṃ aniccaṃ rūpanti yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”ti evamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.55, 85) viya iti-saddo payutto siyā, na ca payutto, tasmā ayuttametanti. Tañca na, kasmā? Tadatthasambhavā. “Yo ca buddhañca dhammañca saṅghañca saraṇaṃ gato”ti evamādīsu (dha. pa. 190) viya idhāpi iti-saddassa attho sambhavati, na ca vijjamānatthasambhavā iti-saddā sabbattha payujjanti, appayuttassāpettha payuttassa viya iti-saddassa attho viññātabbo aññesu ca evaṃjātikesu, tasmā adoso eva soti. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tīhi saraṇagamanehi pabbajja”ntiādīsu (mahāva. 34) saraṇasseva gamanīyato yaṃ vuttaṃ “gamanākāradassanatthaṃ tu saraṇavacana”nti, taṃ na yuttamiti ce. Taṃ [M 0.0010] nāyuttaṃ. Kasmā? Tadatthasambhavā eva. Tatrāpi hi tassa attho sambhavati, yato pubbasadisameva appayuttopi payutto viya veditabbo. Itarathā hi pubbe vuttadosappasaṅgo eva siyā, tasmā yathānusiṭṭhameva gahetabbaṃ.

Here, the Buddha alone is the object of going. The term 'refuge,' however, serves to indicate the manner of going: "I go to the Buddha, [regarding him] as refuge." This means one goes with the intention: 'He is my refuge, he is my ultimate recourse, the destroyer of suffering and the provider of welfare.' It is with this intention that I go to him, resort to him, serve him, and attend upon him; or, alternatively, that I know and understand him thus. For indeed, those verbal roots that have the meaning of 'going' also have the meaning of 'understanding'. If it is said, "This is inappropriate because the word 'iti' is not used," that is not so. On this point, one might argue: "If this meaning were intended here, the word 'iti' would have been used, as in such cases as 'He understands as it really is: "Impermanent is form"' and so on. But it is not used; therefore, this is inappropriate." But that is not so. Why? Because that meaning is possible. Just as in such cases as 'One who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha,' here too the meaning of the word 'iti' is possible. And 'iti' words are not used everywhere just because their meaning is present. Here, even though the 'iti' word is not used, its meaning should be understood as if it were used, and similarly in other such cases. Therefore, this is indeed without fault. If it is said: "In such cases as 'Monks, I allow ordination by means of the three goings for refuge,' the refuge itself is the object of going; therefore, what was stated—'the word "refuge" is for showing the manner of going'—is not appropriate," that is not inappropriate. Why? Because that meaning is indeed possible. For there too its meaning is possible, since, just as before, even though it is not used, it should be understood as if it were used. Otherwise, the fault previously stated would indeed arise. Therefore, it should be taken just as has been instructed.

Ayaṃ gamanīyadīpanā.

This is the Exposition of the Object of Going.

Dhammasaṅghasaraṇavibhāvanā

The Elucidation of the Refuge in the Dhamma and the Saṅgha

Idāni yaṃ vuttaṃ “dhammaṃ saraṇamiccādi, dvayepesa nayo mato”ti ettha vuccate – yvāyaṃ “buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī”ti ettha atthavaṇṇanānayo vutto, “dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī”ti etasmimpi padadvaye esova veditabbo. Tatrāpi hi dhammasaṅghānaṃ atthato byañjanato ca vibhāvanamattameva asadisaṃ, sesaṃ vuttasadisameva. Yato yadevettha asadisaṃ, taṃ vuccate – maggaphalanibbānāni dhammoti eke. Bhāvitamaggānaṃ sacchikatanibbānānañca apāyesu apatanabhāvena dhāraṇato paramassāsavidhānato ca maggavirāgā eva imasmiṃ atthe dhammoti amhākaṃ khanti, aggappasādasuttañceva sādhakaṃ. Vuttañcettha “yāvatā, bhikkhave, dhammā saṅkhatā[V 0.0011], ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”ti evamādi [P 0.0020] (a. ni. 4.34; itivu. 90).

Now, regarding what was said: “Taking refuge in the Dhamma, etc., this method is to be understood in both cases”—herein it is stated: Just as the method of explaining the meaning was stated in the case of “I go for refuge to the Buddha,” so too this very method should be understood in this pair of phrases, “I go for refuge to the Dhamma” and “I go for refuge to the Saṅgha.” For in these cases too, only the elucidation of the Dhamma and the Saṅgha by way of meaning and by way of phrasing is dissimilar; the remainder is just like what has been said. Since there is something dissimilar here, that is stated: Some say that the Dhamma is the path, the fruits, and Nibbāna. It is our preferred view that in this sense, the Dhamma is precisely the Path and Dispassion, because it sustains those who have developed the path and realized Nibbāna by means of their not falling into the lower realms, and because it provides the highest solace. And the Aggappasāda Sutta is the proof. For it was said herein: “Bhikkhus, inasmuch as there are conditioned things, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared the foremost among them,” and so on.

Catubbidhaariyamaggasamaṅgīnaṃ catusāmaññaphalasamadhivāsitakhandhasantānānañca puggalānaṃ samūho diṭṭhisīlasaṅghātena saṃhatattā saṅgho. Vuttañcetaṃ bhagavatā –

The Saṅgha is the assembly of individuals endowed with the fourfold noble path and whose continuities of aggregates are permeated by the four fruits of asceticism, on account of their being united by the cohesion of view and virtue. This was spoken by the Blessed One:

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, ānanda, ye vo mayā dhammā abhiññā desitā, seyyathidaṃ, cattāro satipaṭṭhānā, cattāro sammappadhānā, cattāro iddhipādā, pañcindriyāni, pañca balāni, satta bojjhaṅgā, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo, passasi no tvaṃ, ānanda, imesu dhammesu dvepi bhikkhū nānāvāde”ti (ma. ni. 3.43).

“What do you think, Ānanda, regarding the teachings I have directly known and taught—namely, the four establishments of mindfulness, the four right exertions, the four bases of spiritual power, the five spiritual faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path—do you see, Ānanda, even two bhikkhus who hold differing views about these teachings?”

Ayañhi paramatthasaṅgho saraṇanti gamanīyo. Sutte ca “āhuneyyo pāhuneyyo dakkhiṇeyyo añjalikaraṇīyo anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassā”ti [M 0.0011] (itivu. 90; a. ni. 4.34, 181) vutto. Etaṃ pana saraṇaṃ gatassa aññasmimpi bhikkhusaṅghe vā bhikkhunisaṅghe vā buddhappamukhe vā saṅghe sammutisaṅghe vā catuvaggādibhede ekapuggalepi vā bhagavantaṃ uddissa pabbajite vandanādikiriyāya saraṇagamanaṃ neva bhijjati na saṃkilissati, ayamettha viseso. Vuttāvasesantu imassa dutiyassa ca saraṇagamanassa bhedābhedādividhānaṃ pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva “dhammaṃ saraṇamiccādi, dvayepesa nayo mato”ti etassa vaṇṇanā.

For this Sangha in the ultimate sense is to be approached as a refuge. And in the Sutta, it is spoken of as: “Worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.” Moreover, for one who has gone to this refuge, when performing acts of veneration and so on towards another community of monks or community of nuns, or a Sangha with the Buddha at its head, or a conventional Sangha, or a group distinguished as a quorum of four, etc., or even a single individual, or one who has gone forth with dedication to the Blessed One, the going for refuge is neither broken nor defiled. This is the distinction herein. But as for the remainder, the procedure regarding the breaking and non-breaking, etc., of this second going for refuge should be understood by the very method stated previously. This, for now, is the explanation of the phrase: “Regarding the pair beginning with ‘I go to the Dhamma for refuge,’ this method is to be understood.”

Anupubbavavatthānakāraṇaniddeso

Exposition of the Reason for the Sequential Arrangement

Idāni anupubbavavatthāne, kāraṇañca viniddiseti ettha etesu ca tīsu saraṇavacanesu sabbasattānaṃ aggoti katvā paṭhamaṃ buddho, tappabhavato tadupadesitato ca anantaraṃ dhammo, tassa dhammassa ādhārakato tadāsevanato ca ante saṅgho. Sabbasattānaṃ vā hite niyojakoti katvā paṭhamaṃ buddho, tappabhavato sabbasattahitattā anantaraṃ dhammo, hitādhigamāya paṭipanno adhigatahito cāti katvā ante saṅgho saraṇabhāvena vavatthapetvā pakāsitoti evaṃ anupubbavavatthāne kāraṇañca viniddise.

Now, regarding the text, 'In the sequential arrangement, one should also point out the reason': Among these three refuges, having considered, 'He is the highest of all beings,' first the Buddha is revealed. Because it originates from him and is taught by him, next after him the Dhamma is spoken of. Because it is the support of that Dhamma and because of its cultivation, at the end the Sangha is spoken of. Alternatively, having considered, 'He engages all beings in their welfare,' first the Buddha is spoken of. Because it originates from him and is for the welfare of all beings, next the Dhamma is spoken of. And having considered, 'One who has practiced for the attainment of welfare has attained welfare,' at the end the Sangha is revealed, having been determined as a refuge. In this way, in the sequential arrangement, the reason should also be pointed out.

Upamāpakāsanā

Illustration by Similes

Idāni [V 0.0012] yampi vuttaṃ “saraṇattayametañca, upamāhi pakāsaye”ti[P 0.0021], tampi vuccate – ettha pana puṇṇacando viya buddho, candakiraṇanikaro viya tena desito dhammo, puṇṇacandakiraṇasamuppāditapīṇito loko viya saṅgho. Bālasūriyo viya buddho, tassa rasmijālamiva vuttappakāro dhammo, tena vihatandhakāro loko viya saṅgho. Vanadāhakapuriso viya buddho, vanadahanaggi viya kilesavanadahano dhammo, daḍḍhavanattā khettabhūto viya bhūmibhāgo daḍḍhakilesattā puññakkhettabhūto saṅgho. Mahāmegho viya buddho, salilavuṭṭhi viya dhammo, vuṭṭhinipātūpasamitareṇu viya janapado upasamitakilesareṇu saṅgho. Susārathi [M 0.0012] viya buddho, assājānīyavinayūpāyo viya dhammo, suvinītassājānīyasamūho viya saṅgho. Sabbadiṭṭhisalluddharaṇato sallakatto viya buddho, salluddharaṇūpāyo viya dhammo, samuddhaṭasallo viya jano samuddhaṭadiṭṭhisallo saṅgho. Mohapaṭalasamuppāṭanato vā sālākiyo viya buddho, paṭalasamuppāṭanupāyo viya dhammo, samuppāṭitapaṭalo vippasannalocano viya jano samuppāṭitamohapaṭalo vippasannañāṇalocano saṅgho. Sānusayakilesabyādhiharaṇasamatthatāya vā kusalo vejjo viya buddho, sammā payuttabhesajjamiva dhammo, bhesajjapayogena samupasantabyādhi viya janasamudāyo samupasantakilesabyādhānusayo saṅgho.

Now, as for what was said: 'This threefold refuge, one should illustrate with similes,' that too is spoken of. Here, the Buddha is like the full moon; the Dhamma taught by him is like the multitude of its rays; and the Sangha is like the world, gladdened by the arising of the full moon's rays. The Buddha is like the morning sun; the Dhamma of the aforementioned kind is like the net of its rays; and the Sangha is like the world, its darkness dispelled by him. The Buddha is like a man who sets fire to a forest; the Dhamma, which burns the forest of defilements, is like the forest-burning fire; and the Sangha, having its defilements burnt, is a field of merit, like a piece of land that has become a field because the forest was burnt. The Buddha is like a great cloud; the Dhamma is like a shower of water; and the Sangha, with the dust of its defilements settled, is like a country where the dust is settled by the falling rain. The Buddha is like a good charioteer; the Dhamma is like the means for training thoroughbred horses; and the Sangha is like a group of well-trained thoroughbreds. Because he extracts the dart of all wrong views, the Buddha is like a surgeon; the Dhamma is like the means for extracting the dart; and the Sangha, having had the dart of wrong view extracted, is like a person who has had a dart extracted. Or, because he removes the film of delusion, the Buddha is like a cataract surgeon; the Dhamma is like the means for removing the film; and the Sangha, having had the film of delusion removed and possessing the clear eye of wisdom, is like a person who has had a film removed and has very clear eyes. Or, because of his ability to remove the disease of defilements together with their underlying tendencies, the Buddha is like a skilled physician; the Dhamma is like well-applied medicine; and the Sangha, with the disease of defilements and their underlying tendencies pacified, is like a community of people whose disease has been pacified by the application of medicine.

Atha vā sudesako viya buddho, sumaggo viya khemantabhūmi viya ca dhammo, maggappaṭipanno khemantabhūmippatto viya saṅgho. Sunāviko viya buddho, nāvā viya dhammo, pārappatto sampattiko viya jano saṅgho. Himavā viya buddho, tappabhavosadhamiva dhammo, osadhūpabhogena nirāmayo viya jano saṅgho. Dhanado viya buddho, dhanaṃ viya dhammo, yathādhippāyaṃ laddhadhano viya jano sammāladdhaariyadhano saṅgho. Nidhidassanako viya [P 0.0022] buddho, nidhi viya dhammo, nidhippatto viya jano saṅgho.

Or, the Buddha is like a good guide; the Dhamma is like a good path and a place of safety; and the Sangha is like one who, having entered the path, has reached the place of safety. The Buddha is like a good ship's captain; the Dhamma is like a boat; and the Sangha is like a person who has reached the far shore and is prosperous. The Buddha is like the Himālaya mountain; the Dhamma is like the medicinal herbs originating from it; and the Sangha is like a person free from disease through using the medicine. The Buddha is like a giver of wealth; the Dhamma is like wealth; and the Sangha, who has rightly obtained the noble wealth, is like a person who has obtained wealth according to their wish. The Buddha is like one who shows a treasure; the Dhamma is like the treasure; and the Sangha is like a person who has reached the treasure.

Apica abhayado viya vīrapuriso buddho, abhayamiva dhammo, sampattābhayo viya jano accantasabbabhayo saṅgho. Assāsako viya buddho, assāso viya dhammo, assatthajano viya saṅgho. Sumitto viya buddho, hitūpadeso viya dhammo, hitūpayogena pattasadattho viya jano saṅgho. Dhanākaro viya buddho, dhanasāro viya dhammo, dhanasārūpabhogo viya jano saṅgho. Rājakumāranhāpako viya buddho, sīsanhānasalilaṃ viya dhammo, sunhātarājakumāravaggo viya saddhammasalilasunhāto saṅgho. Alaṅkārakārako viya buddho, alaṅkāro viya dhammo, alaṅkatarājaputtagaṇo [V 0.0013] viya saddhammālaṅkato saṅgho. Candanarukkho viya buddho, tappabhavagandho viya dhammo, candanupabhogena santapariḷāho viya jano saddhammūpabhogena santapariḷāho saṅgho. Dāyajjasampadānako viya pitā buddho, dāyajjaṃ viya dhammo, dāyajjaharo puttavaggo viya saddhammadāyajjaharo saṅgho. Vikasitapadumaṃ [M 0.0013] viya buddho, tappabhavamadhu viya dhammo, tadupabhogībhamaragaṇo viya saṅgho. Evaṃ saraṇattayametañca, upamāhi pakāsaye.

Furthermore, the Buddha is like a heroic man, a giver of fearlessness; the Dhamma is like fearlessness; and the Sangha, completely free from all fear, is like a person who has attained fearlessness. The Buddha is like a comforter; the Dhamma is like comfort; and the Sangha is like people who have been comforted. The Buddha is like a good friend; the Dhamma is like beneficial advice; and the Sangha is like a person who has attained their true purpose through the application of what is beneficial. The Buddha is like a creator of wealth; the Dhamma is like the essence of wealth; and the Sangha is like a person who enjoys the essence of wealth. The Buddha is like one who bathes a prince; the Dhamma is like water for washing the head; and the Sangha, having been well-bathed with the water of the good Dhamma, is like a group of well-bathed princes. The Buddha is like a decorator; the Dhamma is like an ornament; and the Sangha, adorned with the ornament of the good Dhamma, is like a group of adorned princes. The Buddha is like a sandalwood tree; the Dhamma is like the fragrance originating from it; and the Sangha, with its fever pacified by using the good Dhamma, is like a person whose fever is pacified by using sandalwood. The Buddha is like a father who bestows the inheritance; the Dhamma is like an inheritance; and the Sangha, heirs to the inheritance of the good Dhamma, are like a group of sons who are heirs to the inheritance. The Buddha is like a blossomed lotus; the Dhamma is like the honey originating from it; and the Sangha is like a swarm of bees enjoying it. Thus, one should illustrate this Triple Refuge with similes.

Ettāvatā ca yā pubbe “kena kattha kadā kasmā, bhāsitaṃ saraṇattaya”ntiādīhi catūhi gāthāhi atthavaṇṇanāya mātikā nikkhittā, sā atthato pakāsitā hotīti.

Thus far, the mātikā for the explanation of the meaning, which was previously set down by the four verses beginning with, 'By whom, where, when, why was the Triple Refuge spoken?'—that has been explained in terms of its meaning.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha.

Saraṇattayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Triple Refuge is concluded.

2. Sikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Training Rules

Sikkhāpadapāṭhamātikā

The Mātikā to the Text of the Training Rules

Evaṃ [V 0.0014] saraṇagamanehi sāsanotāraṃ dassetvā sāsanaṃ otiṇṇena upāsakena vā pabbajitena vā yesu sikkhāpadesu paṭhamaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ, tāni dassetuṃ nikkhittassa sikkhāpadapāṭhassa idāni vaṇṇanatthaṃ ayaṃ mātikā –

Having thus shown the entry into the Dispensation by means of taking refuge, this mātikā is now for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the text of the training rules that has been laid down, in order to show those training rules in which a lay follower or one who has gone forth, having entered the Dispensation, should first train—

“Yena [P 0.0023] yattha yadā yasmā, vuttānetāni taṃ nayaṃ;

Vatvā katvā vavatthānaṃ, sādhāraṇavisesato.

“By whom, where, when, for what reason these were spoken—that method; having stated and having made a determination, by way of what is common and specific.

“Pakatiyā ca yaṃ vajjaṃ, vajjaṃ paṇṇattiyā ca yaṃ;

Vavatthapetvā taṃ katvā, padānaṃ byañjanatthato.

“What is an offense by nature and what is an offense by prescription; having distinguished and established that, by the letter and meaning of the terms.

“Sādhāraṇānaṃ sabbesaṃ, sādhāraṇavibhāvanaṃ;

Atha pañcasu pubbesu, visesatthappakāsato.

“Of all that are common, the explanation of what is common; then, in the first five, from the explanation of the special meaning.

“Pāṇātipātapabhuti-hekatānānatādito;

Ārammaṇādānabhedā, mahāsāvajjato tathā.

“Beginning with the destruction of life, from singularity, diversity, and so on; from the object, the undertaking, and the breaking; and likewise from great blameworthiness.

“Payogaṅgasamuṭṭhānā, vedanāmūlakammato;

Viramato ca phalato, viññātabbo vinicchayo.

“The judgment should be known from effort, factor, and origin; from action rooted in feeling; from abstaining; and from the result.

“Yojetabbaṃ [M 0.0014] tato yuttaṃ, pacchimesvapi pañcasu;

Āveṇikañca vattabbaṃ, ñeyyā hīnāditāpi cā”ti.

“Then, what is appropriate should be applied to the latter five as well; the unique teaching should also be stated, and the state of being inferior and so on should be known.”

Tattha etāni pāṇātipātāveramaṇītiādīni dasa sikkhāpadāni bhagavatā eva vuttāni, na [V 0.0015] sāvakādīhi. Tāni ca sāvatthiyaṃ vuttāni jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme āyasmantaṃ rāhulaṃ pabbājetvā kapilavatthuto sāvatthiṃ anuppattena sāmaṇerānaṃ sikkhāpadavavatthāpanatthaṃ. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ –

Therein, these ten training rules, beginning with 'abstaining from the destruction of life,' were spoken by the Blessed One alone, not by disciples and others. And they were spoken in Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika, for the purpose of establishing the training rules for novices, by the Blessed One who had arrived in Sāvatthī from Kapilavatthu after giving the going forth to the Venerable Rāhula. For this has been said—

“Atha kho bhagavā kapilavatthusmiṃ yathābhirantaṃ viharitvā yena sāvatthi tena cārikaṃ pakkāmi. Anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno yena sāvatthi tadavasari. Tatra sudaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tena kho pana samayena …pe… atha kho sāmaṇerānaṃ etadahosi – ‘kati nu kho amhākaṃ sikkhāpadāni, kattha ca amhehi sikkhitabba’”nti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sāmaṇerānaṃ dasa sikkhāpadāni, tesu ca sāmaṇerehi sikkhituṃ[P 0.0024], pāṇātipātāveramaṇī…pe… jātarūparajatapaṭiggahaṇā veramaṇī”ti (mahāva. 105).

“Then the Blessed One, having dwelt in Kapilavatthu as long as he pleased, set out on a journey toward Sāvatthī. Wandering on tour in due course, he arrived at Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One dwelt in Jeta’s Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika. Now at that time… then it occurred to the novices: ‘How many training rules do we have, and in what should we train?’ They informed the Blessed One of this matter. ‘Monks, I allow ten training rules for novices, and I allow the novices to train in them: abstaining from the destruction of life… abstaining from accepting gold and silver.’”

Tānetāni “samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesū”ti (dī. ni. 1.193; ma. ni. 2.24; vibha. 508) suttānusārena saraṇagamanesu ca dassitapāṭhānusārena “pāṇātipātā veramaṇisikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmī”ti evaṃ vācanāmaggaṃ āropitānīti veditabbāni. Evaṃ tāva “yena yattha yadā yasmā, vuttānetāni taṃ nayaṃ vatvā”ti so nayo daṭṭhabbo.

These are to be understood as having been established in the verbal formula as follows: in accordance with the Suttas, such as, ‘Having undertaken them, one trains in the training rules,’ and in accordance with the text shown in the context of taking refuge, such as, ‘I undertake the training rule of abstaining from the destruction of life.’ Thus, for now, that method—namely, ‘By whom, where, when, for what reason these were spoken, having stated that method’—is to be understood.

Sādhāraṇavisesavavatthānaṃ

The Determination of What is Common and What is Specific

Ettha ca ādito dve catutthapañcamāni upāsakānaṃ sāmaṇerānañca sādhāraṇāni niccasīlavasena. Uposathasīlavasena pana upāsakānaṃ sattamaṭṭhamaṃ cekaṃ aṅgaṃ katvā sabbapacchimavajjāni sabbānipi sāmaṇerehi sādhāraṇāni, pacchimaṃ pana sāmaṇerānameva visesabhūtanti evaṃ sādhāraṇavisesato vavatthānaṃ kātabbaṃ. Purimāni cettha pañca ekantaakusalacittasamuṭṭhānattā pāṇātipātādīnaṃ pakativajjato veramaṇiyā, sesāni [M 0.0015] paṇṇattivajjatoti evaṃ pakatiyā ca yaṃ vajjaṃ, vajjaṃ paṇṇattiyā ca yaṃ, taṃ vavatthapetabbaṃ.

And here, from the beginning, the first two, and the fourth and fifth precepts are common to lay devotees and novices by way of perpetual morality. But by way of the Uposatha precepts, for lay devotees, having made the seventh and eighth into one factor, all precepts except the very last are common with novices; the last precept, however, is a special one for novices only. Thus, a determination should be made according to what is common and what is specific. And here, the first five are abstentions from natural offenses, such as killing, because they arise from a purely unwholesome mind; the remaining are abstentions from offenses by convention. Thus, what is an offense by nature and what is an offense by convention should be distinguished.

Sādhāraṇavibhāvanā

The Common Elucidation

Yasmā cettha “veramaṇisikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmī”ti etāni sabbasādhāraṇāni padāni, tasmā etesaṃ padānaṃ byañjanato ca atthato ca ayaṃ sādhāraṇavibhāvanā veditabbā –

And since, here, these terms 'veramaṇisikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi' ('I undertake the training precept of abstention') are common to all, therefore this common elucidation of these terms should be understood both by way of expression and by way of meaning:

Tattha [V 0.0016] byañjanato tāva veraṃ maṇatīti veramaṇī, veraṃ pajahati, vinodeti, byantīkaroti, anabhāvaṃ gametīti attho. Viramati vā etāya karaṇabhūtāya veramhā puggaloti, vikārassa vekāraṃ katvā veramaṇī. Teneva cettha “veramaṇisikkhāpadaṃ viramaṇisikkhāpada”nti dvidhā sajjhāyaṃ karonti. Sikkhitabbāti sikkhā, pajjate anenāti padaṃ. Sikkhāya padaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ, sikkhāya adhigamūpāyoti attho. Atha vā mūlaṃ nissayo patiṭṭhāti vuttaṃ hoti. Veramaṇī eva sikkhāpadaṃ veramaṇisikkhāpadaṃ, viramaṇisikkhāpadaṃ vā dutiyena nayena. Sammā ādiyāmi samādiyāmi, avītikkamanādhippāyena akhaṇḍakāritāya acchiddakāritāya asabalakāritāya ca ādiyāmīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Herein, firstly, by way of expression: it dispels the enemy (vera), which is the unwholesome, thus it is veramaṇī; the meaning is that it abandons, dispels, brings to an end, and leads to the non-existence of that enemy. Alternatively, a person abstains (viramati) from the enemy by means of this, thus, by changing 'vi' to 've', it becomes veramaṇī. For that very reason, they recite it in two ways: 'veramaṇisikkhāpadaṃ' and 'viramaṇisikkhāpadaṃ'. Because it is to be trained in (sikkhitabbā), it is sikkhā (training). Because one attains (pajjate) by means of this (anena), it is padaṃ (cause). Sikkhāya padaṃ is sikkhāpadaṃ; the meaning is 'the means for attaining the training'. Alternatively, it is said to mean root, support, and foundation. Abstention (veramaṇī) itself is the training precept (sikkhāpadaṃ), hence veramaṇisikkhāpadaṃ; or, by the second method, viramaṇisikkhāpadaṃ. I undertake well (sammā ādiyāmi), thus samādiyāmi. This means: I undertake with the intention of not transgressing, and with the quality of making it unbroken, without holes, and without blemishes.

Atthato pana veramaṇīti kāmāvacarakusalacittasampayuttā virati, sā [P 0.0025] pāṇātipātā viramantassa “yā tasmiṃ samaye pāṇātipātā ārati virati paṭivirati veramaṇī akiriyā akaraṇaṃ anajjhāpatti velāanatikkamo setughāto”ti evamādinā (vibha. 704) nayena vibhaṅge vuttā. Kāmañcesā veramaṇī nāma lokuttarāpi atthi, idha pana samādiyāmīti vuttattā samādānavasena pavattārahā, tasmā sā na hotīti kāmāvacarakusalacittasampayuttā viratīti vuttā.

But by way of meaning, veramaṇī is the abstinence associated with wholesome sense-sphere consciousness. For one who abstains from killing living beings, it is spoken of in the Vibhaṅga in this way: 'Whatever at that time is the refraining from killing living beings, the abstaining, the abstention, the avoidance, the non-action, the non-doing, the non-offense, the non-transgression of the boundary, the destruction of the cause,' and so on. Although this so-called veramaṇī also exists as supramundane, here, because it is said, 'I undertake,' it is the abstinence that is fit to arise by way of undertaking. Therefore, that supramundane abstinence is not what is meant here, and so it is said to be 'the abstinence associated with wholesome sense-sphere consciousness'.

Sikkhāti tisso sikkhā adhisīlasikkhā, adhicittasikkhā, adhipaññāsikkhāti. Imasmiṃ panatthe sampattaviratisīlaṃ lokikā vipassanā rūpārūpajhānāni ariyamaggo ca sikkhāti adhippetā. Yathāha –

As for sikkhā (training), there are three trainings: the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom. But in this context, 'training' is intended to mean the virtue of attained abstinence, mundane insight, the form and formless absorptions, and the noble path. As it is said:

“Katame dhammā sikkhā? Yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti, somanassasahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ…pe… tasmiṃ samaye [M 0.0016] phasso hoti…pe… avikkhepo hoti, ime dhammā sikkhā.

"What are the qualities of training? At the time when a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen, accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge... at that time there is contact... there is non-distraction. These qualities are training.

“Katame dhammā sikkhā? Yasmiṃ samaye rūpūpapattiyā maggaṃ bhāveti vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ…pe… pañcamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati…pe… avikkhepo hoti, ime dhammā sikkhā.

"What are the qualities of training? At the time when one develops the path for rebirth in the Form Realm, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome qualities... having attained the first absorption... the fifth absorption, one abides... there is non-distraction. These qualities are training.

“Katame dhammā sikkhā? Yasmiṃ samaye arūpapattiyā…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasahagataṃ…pe… avikkhepo hoti, ime dhammā sikkhā.

"What are the qualities of training? At the time when one develops the path for rebirth in the formless realm... associated with the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception... there is non-distraction. These qualities are training.

“Katame [V 0.0017] dhammā sikkhā? Yasmiṃ samaye lokuttaraṃ jhānaṃ bhāveti niyyānikaṃ…pe… avikkhepo hoti, ime dhammā sikkhā”ti (vibha. 712-713).

"What are the qualities of training? At the time when one develops the supramundane absorption that leads to release... there is non-distraction. These qualities are training." (Vibhaṅga 712-713).

Etāsu sikkhāsu yāya kāyaci sikkhāya padaṃ adhigamūpāyo, atha vā mūlaṃ nissayo patiṭṭhāti sikkhāpadaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ – “sīlaṃ nissāya sīle patiṭṭhāya satta bojjhaṅge bhāvento bahulīkaronto”ti evamādi (saṃ. ni. 5.182). Evamettha sādhāraṇānaṃ padānaṃ sādhāraṇā byañjanato atthato ca vibhāvanā kātabbā.

For any of these trainings, that which is the cause (padaṃ), the means of attainment—or alternatively, the root, support, and foundation—is a training precept (sikkhāpadaṃ). For it has been said: 'Relying on virtue, established in virtue, one develops and cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment,' and so on (Saṃ. Ni. 5.182). Thus, here, the common elucidation of the common terms should be made both by way of expression and by way of meaning.

Purimapañcasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Former Five Training Rules

Idāni yaṃ vuttaṃ – “atha pañcasu pubbesu, visesatthappakāsato…pe… viññātabbo vinicchayo”ti[P 0.0026], tatthetaṃ vuccati – pāṇātipātoti ettha tāva pāṇoti jīvitindriyappaṭibaddhā khandhasantati, taṃ vā upādāya paññatto satto. Tasmiṃ pana pāṇe pāṇasaññino tassa pāṇassa jīvitindriyupacchedakaupakkamasamuṭṭhāpikā kāyavacīdvārānaṃ aññataradvārappavattā vadhakacetanā pāṇātipāto. Adinnādānanti ettha adinnanti parapariggahitaṃ, yattha paro yathākāmakāritaṃ āpajjanto adaṇḍāraho anupavajjo ca hoti, tasmiṃ parapariggahite parapariggahitasaññino tadādāyakaupakkamasamuṭṭhāpikā kāyavacīdvārānaṃ aññataradvārappavattā eva theyyacetanā adinnādānaṃ. Abrahmacariyanti aseṭṭhacariyaṃ, dvayaṃdvayasamāpattimethunappaṭisevanā kāyadvārappavattā asaddhammappaṭisevanaṭṭhānavītikkamacetanā abrahmacariyaṃ[M 0.0017]. Musāvādoti ettha musāti visaṃvādanapurekkhārassa atthabhañjanako vacīpayogo kāyapayogo vā, visaṃvādanādhippāyena panassa paravisaṃvādakakāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā kāyavacīdvārānameva aññataradvārappavattā micchācetanā musāvādo. Surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānanti ettha pana surāti pañca surā – piṭṭhasurā, pūvasurā, odanasurā, kiṇṇapakkhittā, sambhārasaṃyuttā cāti. Merayampi pupphāsavo, phalāsavo, guḷāsavo, madhvāsavo, sambhārasaṃyutto cāti pañcavidhaṃ. Majjanti tadubhayameva madaniyaṭṭhena majjaṃ, yaṃ vā panaññampi kiñci atthi madaniyaṃ, yena pītena matto hoti pamatto, idaṃ vuccati majjaṃ. Pamādaṭṭhānanti yāya cetanāya taṃ pivati ajjhoharati, sā cetanā madappamādahetuto pamādaṭṭhānanti vuccati, yato ajjhoharaṇādhippāyena kāyadvārappavattā surāmerayamajjānaṃ ajjhoharaṇacetanā “surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhāna”nti [P 0.0027] veditabbā. Evaṃ tāvettha pāṇātipātappabhutīhi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Now, regarding what was said—"Now, as to the five previous ones... the analysis should be understood"—herein, this is said: In the phrase 'destruction of life' (pāṇātipāta), firstly, 'life' (pāṇa) refers to the continuum of aggregates connected with the life faculty, or alternatively, a being designated in dependence on that. With respect to that life, when one perceives it as life, the volition to kill, arising from an endeavor that severs the life faculty of that life and occurring through either the body door or the speech door, is the destruction of life. In the phrase 'taking what is not given' (adinnādāna), 'what is not given' (adinna) refers to what is possessed by another, concerning which the other person, acting as they wish, is not liable to punishment and is blameless. With respect to that which is possessed by another, when one perceives it as such, the thievish volition, arising from an endeavor to take it and occurring through either the body door or the speech door, is the taking of what is not given. 'Unchastity' (abrahmacariya) is un-noble conduct. The unwholesome volition to transgress, arising through the body door, which consists of indulging in the unrighteous practice of sexual intercourse, the congress of two by two, is called unchastity. In the phrase 'false speech' (musāvāda), 'false' (musā) refers to a verbal or bodily action that destroys the benefit of another, undertaken with the intention of deceiving. The wrong volition, arising from a bodily or verbal action intended to deceive another and occurring through either the body door or the speech door, is false speech. In the phrase 'intoxicants which are the basis for heedlessness' (surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhāna), 'liquor' (surā) is of five kinds: liquor made from flour, liquor made from cakes, liquor made from rice, liquor with yeast added, and liquor mixed with ingredients. 'Fermented drink' (meraya) is also of five kinds: flower extract, fruit extract, molasses extract, honey extract, and extract mixed with ingredients. 'Intoxicant' (majja) refers to both of these, because of their intoxicating nature, or any other intoxicating substance that, when drunk, makes one intoxicated and heedless; this is called an intoxicant. 'Basis for heedlessness' (pamādaṭṭhāna) refers to the volition with which one drinks or consumes it; that volition, being the cause of intoxication and heedlessness, is called the basis for heedlessness. Wherefore, the volition to consume liquor, fermented drinks, and intoxicants, which arises through the body door with the intention of consuming, should be understood as 'the basis for heedlessness due to liquor, fermented drinks, and intoxicants'. Thus, in this way, the analysis should be understood regarding the destruction of life and so on.

Ekatānānatādivinicchayaṃ

The Analysis of Oneness, Manifoldness, and So On

Ekatānānatāditoti [V 0.0018] ettha āha – kiṃ pana vajjhavadhakappayogacetanādīnaṃ ekatāya pāṇātipātassa aññassa vā adinnādānādino ekattaṃ, nānatāya nānattaṃ hoti, udāhu noti. Kasmā panetaṃ vuccati? Yadi tāva ekatāya ekattaṃ, atha yadā ekaṃ vajjhaṃ bahū vadhakā vadhenti, eko vā vadhako bahuke vajjhe vadheti, ekena vā sāhatthikādinā payogena bahū vajjhā vadhīyanti, ekā vā cetanā bahūnaṃ vajjhānaṃ jīvitindriyupacchedakapayogaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, tadā ekena pāṇātipātena bhavitabbaṃ. Yadi pana nānatāya nānattaṃ. Atha yadā eko vadhako ekassatthāya ekaṃ payogaṃ karonto bahū vajjhe vadheti, bahū vā vadhakā devadattayaññadattasomadattādīnaṃ bahūnamatthāya bahū payoge karontā ekameva devadattaṃ yaññadattaṃ somadattaṃ vā vadhenti, bahūhi vā sāhatthikādīhi payogehi eko vajjho vadhīyati. Bahū vā cetanā ekasseva vajjhassa jīvitindriyupacchedakapayogaṃ samuṭṭhāpenti, tadā bahūhi pāṇātipātehi bhavitabbaṃ. Ubhayampi cetamayuttaṃ. Atha neva etesaṃ vajjhādīnaṃ ekatāya ekattaṃ, nānatāya nānattaṃ, aññatheva tu ekattaṃ nānattañca hoti, taṃ vattabbaṃ pāṇātipātassa, evaṃ sesānampīti.

Here, concerning oneness, manifoldness, and so on, it is asked: Is it that by the oneness of the victim, killer, endeavor, volition, and so on, there is oneness of the destruction of life or of the taking of what is not given, etc., and by their manifoldness there is manifoldness, or not? And why is this said? If, firstly, by oneness there is oneness, then when many killers kill one victim, or one killer kills many victims, or many victims are killed by one endeavor such as by one's own hand, or one volition instigates an endeavor that severs the life faculty of many victims, then there should be one act of destruction of life. If, however, by manifoldness there is manifoldness, then when one killer, making one endeavor for the sake of one victim, kills many victims; or many killers, making many endeavors for the sake of many victims such as Devadatta, Yaññadatta, and Somadatta, kill only one Devadatta, Yaññadatta, or Somadatta; or one victim is killed by many endeavors such as by one's own hand; or many volitions instigate an endeavor that severs the life faculty of just one victim, then there should be many acts of destruction of life. And both of these are unsuitable. Therefore, it is neither that by the oneness of these victims and so on there is oneness, nor by their manifoldness there is manifoldness. Rather, oneness and manifoldness occur in another way. This should be stated regarding the destruction of life, and likewise for the rest.

Vuccate [M 0.0018] – tattha tāva pāṇātipātassa na vajjhavadhakādīnaṃ paccekamekatāya ekatā, nānatāya nānatā, kintu vajjhavadhakādīnaṃ yuganandhamekatāya ekatā, dvinnampi tu tesaṃ, tato aññatarassa vā nānatāya nānatā. Tathā hi bahūsu vadhakesu bahūhi sarakkhepādīhi ekena vā opātakhaṇanādinā payogena bahū vajjhe vadhentesupi bahū pāṇātipātā honti. Ekasmiṃ vadhake ekena, bahūhi vā payogehi tappayogasamuṭṭhāpikāya ca ekāya, bahūhi vā cetanāhi bahū vajjhe vadhentepi bahū pāṇātipātā honti, bahūsu ca vadhakesu yathāvuttappakārehi bahūhi, ekena vā payogena ekaṃ vajjhaṃ vadhentesupi bahū pāṇātipātā honti. Esa nayo adinnādānādīsupīti. Evamettha ekatānānatāditopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

It is said: Here, firstly, in the case of the destruction of life, there is not oneness by the individual oneness of the victim, killer, and so on, nor manifoldness by their individual manifoldness. Rather, there is oneness by the oneness of their pairing—the victim, killer, and so on; but there is manifoldness by the manifoldness of two of them, or of either one of them. For instance, when many killers kill many victims with many endeavors such as shooting arrows, or with one endeavor such as digging a pitfall, there are many acts of destruction of life. This same principle should be known for the taking of what is not given, and so on. Thus, herein, the analysis should be understood in terms of oneness, manifoldness, and so on.

Ārammaṇatoti [P 0.0028] pāṇātipāto cettha jīvitindriyārammaṇo. Adinnādānaabrahmacariyasurāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānāni rūpadhammesu rūpāyatanādiaññatarasaṅkhārārammaṇāni. Musāvādo yassa musā bhaṇati, tamārabhitvā pavattanato sattārammaṇo. Abrahmacariyampi sattārammaṇanti eke. Adinnādānañca yadā satto haritabbo hoti, tadā sattārammaṇanti. Api cettha saṅkhāravaseneva sattārammaṇaṃ, na paṇṇattivasenāti. Evamettha ārammaṇatopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Regarding the Object: Herein, the destruction of life has the life faculty as its object. The taking of what is not given, unchastity, and intoxicants which are the basis for heedlessness, have as their object a conditioned phenomenon among material phenomena, such as the form base or another. False speech has a being as its object because it occurs with reference to the one about whom one speaks falsely. Some say unchastity also has a being as its object. And the taking of what is not given, when a being is to be stolen, then has a being as its object. However, herein, it has a being as its object only by way of conditioned phenomena, not by way of designation. Thus, herein, the analysis should be understood in terms of the object.

Ādānatoti [V 0.0019] pāṇātipātāveramaṇisikkhāpadādīni cetāni sāmaṇerena bhikkhusantike samādinnāneva samādinnāni honti, upāsakena pana attanā samādiyantenāpi samādinnāni honti, parassa santike samādiyantenāpi. Ekajjhaṃ samādinnānipi samādinnāni honti, paccekaṃ samādinnānipi. Kintu nānaṃ ekajjhaṃ samādiyato ekāyeva virati, ekāva cetanā hoti, kiccavasena panetāsaṃ pañcavidhattaṃ viññāyati. Paccekaṃ samādiyato pana pañceva viratiyo, pañca ca cetanā hontīti veditabbā. Evamettha ādānatopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Regarding 'by way of undertaking': The determination should be understood thus: These training rules, beginning with the training rule of abstaining from killing living beings, when undertaken by a novice in the presence of a bhikkhu, are then considered properly undertaken. But for a lay follower, they are considered properly undertaken even when undertaken by oneself, and also when undertaken in the presence of another. They are considered properly undertaken whether undertaken all together or undertaken individually. However, for one who undertakes them all together, there is only one abstinence and only one volition; but by way of function, their fivefold nature is known. But for one who undertakes them individually, it should be known that there are five abstinences and five volitions. Thus, here, the determination to be known is also by way of undertaking.

Bhedatoti sāmaṇerānañcettha ekasmiṃ bhinne sabbānipi bhinnāni honti. Pārājikaṭṭhāniyāni hi tāni tesaṃ, yaṃ taṃ vītikkantaṃ hoti, teneva kammabaddho. Gahaṭṭhānaṃ pana ekasmiṃ bhinne ekameva bhinnaṃ hoti, yato [M 0.0019] tesaṃ taṃsamādāneneva puna pañcaṅgikattaṃ sīlassa sampajjati. Apare panāhu – “visuṃ visuṃ samādinnesu ekasmiṃ bhinne ekameva bhinnaṃ hoti, ‘pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ sīlaṃ samādiyāmī’ti evaṃ pana ekato samādinnesu ekasmiṃ bhinne sesānipi sabbāni bhinnāni honti. Kasmā? Samādinnassa abhinnattā, yaṃ taṃ vītikkantaṃ, teneva kammabaddho”ti. Evamettha bhedatopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Regarding 'by way of breach': For novices here, if one is breached, all are breached. Indeed, for them, these are grounds for a pārājika offense. By whichever precept is transgressed, by that very one is one bound by kamma. For householders, however, if one is breached, only that one is breached, because for them the five-factored nature of the virtue is perfected again only by undertaking that broken precept again. But other teachers say: 'When undertaken separately, if one is breached, only that one is breached. But when undertaken together thus, "I undertake the virtue endowed with five factors," if one is breached, the remaining ones are also breached. Why? Because of the indivisibility of the undertaking. By whichever precept is transgressed, by that very one is one bound by kamma.' Thus, here, the determination to be known is also by way of breach.

Mahāsāvajjatoti guṇavirahitesu tiracchānagatādīsu pāṇesu khuddake pāṇe pāṇātipāto appasāvajjo, mahāsarīre mahāsāvajjo. Kasmā? Payogamahantatāya. Payogasamattepi vatthumahantatāya. Guṇavantesu pana manussādīsu appaguṇe pāṇātipāto appasāvajjo, mahāguṇe mahāsāvajjo[P 0.0029]. Sarīraguṇānantu samabhāve sati kilesānaṃ upakkamānañca mudutāya appasāvajjatā, tibbatāya mahāsāvajjatā ca veditabbā. Esa nayo sesesupi. Api cettha surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānameva mahāsāvajjaṃ, na tathā pāṇātipātādayo. Kasmā? Manussabhūtassāpi ummattakabhāvasaṃvattanena ariyadhammantarāyakaraṇatoti. Evamettha mahāsāvajjatopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Regarding 'greatly blameworthy': Among beings devoid of virtue, such as animals, the act of killing a small being has little blame, while killing a large-bodied one has great blame. Why? Because of the greatness of the effort. Even when the effort is equal, it is greatly blameworthy because of the greatness of the object. But among virtuous beings, such as humans, the act of killing a being of little virtue has little blame, while killing one of great virtue has great blame. When there is an equality of body and virtue, the state of having little blame should be known due to the mildness of the defilements and the undertakings, and the state of having great blame due to their intensity. This same method should be known in the remaining precepts as well. Moreover, here, only the training rule concerning the basis for heedlessness from liquor, spirits, and intoxicants is greatly blameworthy; the acts beginning with killing are not so. Why? Because it leads even a human being to a state of madness and because it creates an obstacle to the noble Dhamma. Thus, here, the determination to be known is also by way of great blameworthiness.

Payogatoti ettha ca pāṇātipātassa sāhatthiko, āṇattiko, nissaggiyo, thāvaro, vijjāmayo, iddhimayoti chappayogā. Tattha kāyena vā kāyappaṭibaddhena vā paharaṇaṃ sāhatthiko payogo, so uddissānuddissabhedato duvidho hoti. Tattha uddissake yaṃ uddissa paharati, tasseva maraṇena kammunā bajjhati. “Yo koci maratū”ti evaṃ anuddissake pahārapaccayā yassa kassaci maraṇena. Ubhayathāpi ca paharitamatte vā maratu, pacchā vā teneva [V 0.0020] rogena, paharitakkhaṇe eva kammunā bajjhati. Maraṇādhippāyena ca pahāraṃ datvā tena amatassa puna aññena cittena pahāre dinne pacchāpi yadi paṭhamapahāreneva marati, tadā eva kammunā baddho hoti. Atha dutiyapahārena, natthi pāṇātipāto. Ubhayehi matepi paṭhamapahāreneva kammunā baddho, ubhayehipi amate nevatthi pāṇātipāto. Esa nayo bahukehipi [M 0.0020] ekassa pahāre dinne. Tatrāpi hi yassa pahārena marati, tasseva kammabaddho hoti.

Regarding 'by way of application': Here, for the act of killing, there are six applications: by one's own hand, by command, by missile, by a stationary trap, by knowledge, and by psychic power. Among these, striking with one's own body or with something connected to the body is the application by one's own hand. This is twofold, by the distinction of specified and unspecified. In the specified case, when one strikes aiming at a certain being, one is bound by kamma only by the death of that very one. In the unspecified case, striking with the thought 'May someone or other die,' one is bound by kamma by the death of whomever dies as a result of the blow. And in both cases, whether one dies just upon being struck or dies later from that very injury, one is bound by kamma at the very moment of striking. And having given a blow with the intention to kill, and the victim not dying from it, if another blow is given later with a different mind, should the victim die from the first blow, one is then bound by kamma. Then, by the second blow, the act of killing does not occur. Even if the victim dies from both, one is bound by kamma by the first blow. If the victim does not die from either, there is no act of killing at all. This is the method also when many people strike one being. For there too, by whose blow the victim dies, only that person is bound by kamma.

Adhiṭṭhahitvā pana āṇāpanaṃ āṇattiko payogo. Tatthapi sāhatthike payoge vuttanayeneva kammabaddho anussaritabbo. Chabbidho cettha niyamo veditabbo –

But having determined, the giving of a command is the application by command. There too, the binding by kamma should be recalled according to the method stated for the application by one's own hand. And here a sixfold determination should be known:

“Vatthu kālo ca okāso, āvudhaṃ iriyāpatho;

Kiriyāvisesoti ime, cha āṇattiniyāmakā”ti. (pāci. aṭṭha. 2.174);

"The object, the time, and the place, the weapon, the posture, and the specific action—these six are the determinants of a command."

Tattha [P 0.0030] vatthūti māretabbo pāṇo. Kāloti pubbaṇhasāyanhādikālo ca, yobbanathāvariyādikālo ca. Okāsoti gāmo vā nigamo vā vanaṃ vā racchā vā siṅghāṭakaṃ vāti evamādi. Āvudhanti asi vā usu vā satti vāti evamādi. Iriyāpathoti māretabbassa mārakassa ca ṭhānaṃ vā nisajjā vāti evamādi.

Here, 'object' is the living being to be killed. 'Time' is time such as forenoon and afternoon, and also the time of life such as youth and maturity. 'Place' means a village, a town, a forest, a road, a crossroads, and so on. 'Weapon' means a sword, an arrow, a spear, and so on. 'Posture' means the standing or sitting, and so on, of both the one to be killed and the killer.
