Kiriyāvisesoti vijjhanaṃ vā chedanaṃ vā bhedanaṃ vā saṅkhamuṇḍikaṃ vāti evamādi. Yadi hi vatthuṃ visaṃvādetvā “yaṃ mārehī”ti āṇatto, tato aññaṃ māreti, āṇāpakassa natthi kammabaddho. Atha vatthuṃ avisaṃvādetvā māreti, āṇāpakassa āṇattikkhaṇe āṇattassa māraṇakkhaṇeti ubhayesampi kammabaddho. Esa nayo kālādīsupi.

'Specific action' means piercing, or cutting, or splitting, or a blow that makes the head like a polished conch shell, and so on. Indeed, if, having misrepresented the object, the one commanded kills another than the one intended in the command, 'Kill so-and-so,' for the one who gave the command, there is no binding by kamma. But if one kills without misrepresenting the object, the one who gave the command is bound by kamma at the moment of commanding, and the one commanded is bound at the moment of killing; thus, for both of them, there is binding by kamma. This is the method for time and the others as well.

Māraṇatthantu kāyena vā kāyappaṭibaddhena vā paharaṇanissajjanaṃ nissaggiyo payogo. Sopi uddissānuddissabhedato duvidho eva, kammabaddho cettha pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

Now, for the purpose of killing, releasing a weapon with the body or with something connected to the body is the application by missile. That too is of two kinds, by the distinction of specified and unspecified. And here, the binding by kamma should be known only by the method stated previously.

Māraṇatthameva opātakhaṇanaṃ, apassenaupanikkhipanaṃ, bhesajjavisayantādippayojanaṃ vā thāvaro payogo. Sopi uddissānuddissabhedato duvidho, yato tatthapi pubbe vuttanayeneva kammabaddho veditabbo. Ayantu viseso – mūlaṭṭhena opātādīsu paresaṃ mūlena vā mudhā vā dinnesupi yadi tappaccayā koci marati, mūlaṭṭhasseva kammabaddho. Yadipi ca tena aññena vā [V 0.0021] tattha opāte vināsetvā bhūmisame katepi paṃsudhovakā vā paṃsuṃ gaṇhantā, mūlakhaṇakā vā mūlāni khaṇantā āvāṭaṃ karonti[M 0.0021], deve vā vassante kaddamo jāyati, tattha ca koci otaritvā vā laggitvā vā marati, mūlaṭṭhasseva kammabaddho. Yadi pana yena laddhaṃ, so añño vā taṃ vitthaṭataraṃ gambhīrataraṃ vā karoti, tappaccayāva koci marati, ubhayesampi kammabaddho. Yathā tu mūlāni mūlehi saṃsandanti, tathā tatra thale kate muccati. Evaṃ apassenādīsupi yāva tesaṃ pavatti, tāva yathāsambhavaṃ kammabaddho veditabbo.

For the purpose of killing only, the digging of a pit, the placing of a trap-door, or the employing of medicine, poison, contraptions, and the like is the stationary application. That too is twofold, by way of the distinction between specified and unspecified, since therein also the binding by kamma should be understood in the manner already stated. This, however, is the distinction: in the case of a pit and so on, even if it is given to others to do for a price or for free, if someone dies because of it, for the original instigator only is there binding by kamma. And even if that person or another, having destroyed that pit, makes the ground level, if dust-washers taking dust, or root-diggers digging roots, make a hole, or if the sky rains and mud is created, and someone, having fallen in or gotten stuck therein, dies, for the original instigator only is there binding by kamma. But if the one who acquired it, or another, makes it wider or deeper, and as a result of that someone dies, for both is there binding by kamma. However, just as roots are joined by roots, so too, when a mound is made there, one is freed. Thus, in the case of a trap-door and so on, as long as they are in operation, the binding by kamma should be understood according to how it may occur.

Māraṇatthaṃ pana vijjāparijappanaṃ vijjāmayo payogo. Dāṭhāvudhādīnaṃ dāṭhākoṭanādimiva māraṇatthaṃ kammavipākajiddhivikārakaraṇaṃ iddhimayo payogoti. Adinnādānassa tu theyyapasayhapaṭicchannaparikappakusāvahāravasappavattā [P 0.0031] sāhatthikāṇattikādayo payogā, tesampi vuttānusāreneva pabhedo veditabbo. Abrahmacariyādīnaṃ tiṇṇampi sāhatthiko eva payogo labbhatīti. Evamettha payogatopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

For the purpose of killing, however, the muttering of spells is the application consisting of knowledge. Like the striking of the fang of Dāṭhāvudha and others, the performance of a special psychic power born of kamma-result for the purpose of killing is the application consisting of psychic power. As for taking what is not given, the applications are those such as by one's own hand and by command, which proceed by way of theft, force, concealment, scheming, and fraudulent conveyance. Their distinction, too, should be understood in accordance with what has been stated. For the three precepts of unchastity and so on, only the application by one's own hand is found. Thus, the determination should be understood from the perspective of application also.

Aṅgatoti ettha ca pāṇātipātassa pañca aṅgāni bhavanti – pāṇo ca hoti, pāṇasaññī ca, vadhakacittañca paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hoti, vāyamati, tena ca maratīti. Adinnādānassāpi pañceva – parapariggahitañca hoti, parapariggahitasaññī ca, theyyacittañca paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hoti, vāyamati, tena ca ādātabbaṃ ādānaṃ gacchatīti. Abrahmacariyassa pana cattāri aṅgāni bhavanti – ajjhācariyavatthu ca hoti, tattha ca sevanacittaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hoti, sevanapaccayā payogañca samāpajjati, sādiyati cāti, tathā paresaṃ dvinnampi. Tattha musāvādassa tāva musā ca hoti taṃ vatthu, visaṃvādanacittañca paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hoti, tajjo ca vāyāmo, paravisaṃvādanañca viññāpayamānā viññatti pavattatīti cattāri aṅgāni veditabbāni. Surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānassa pana surādīnañca aññataraṃ hoti madanīyapātukamyatācittañca paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hoti, tajjañca vāyāmaṃ āpajjati, pīte ca pavisatīti imāni cattāri aṅgānīti. Evamettha aṅgatopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Regarding the factors: Herein, for taking life, there are five factors: there is a living being, one perceives it as a living being, the intention to kill is present, one makes an effort, and by that effort, it dies. For taking what is not given, there are also five: it is the possession of another, one perceives it as the possession of another, the intention to steal is present, one makes an effort, and by that effort, the object to be taken is taken. For unchastity, however, there are four factors: there is an object of transgression, the intention to engage is present therein, one undertakes the effort for the purpose of engagement, and one consents to it. Similarly, for the other two precepts, there are four factors. Therein, for false speech, first: the matter is untrue, the intention to deceive is present, there is an effort born of that, and a communication occurs which causes another to be deceived—these four factors should be understood. For the partaking of intoxicants which are a basis for heedlessness, there are these four factors: one of the intoxicants such as liquor is present, the desire to drink the intoxicant is present, one undertakes the effort born of that, and when drunk, it enters the body. Thus, the determination should be understood from the perspective of the factors also.

Samuṭṭhānatoti pāṇātipātaadinnādānamusāvādā cettha kāyacittato, vācācittato, kāyavācācittato cāti tisamuṭṭhānā honti. Abrahmacariyaṃ kāyacittavasena ekasamuṭṭhānameva. Surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānaṃ kāyato ca, kāyacittato cāti dvisamuṭṭhānanti. Evamettha samuṭṭhānatopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Regarding the origin: Herein, taking life, taking what is not given, and false speech have three origins: from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. Unchastity has only one origin: by way of body and mind. The partaking of intoxicants which are a basis for heedlessness has two origins: from the body, and from body and mind. Thus, the determination should be understood from the perspective of the origin also.

Vedanātoti [V 0.0022][M 0.0022] ettha ca pāṇātipāto dukkhavedanāsampayuttova. Adinnādānaṃ tīsu vedanāsu aññataravedanāsampayuttaṃ, tathā musāvādo. Itarāni dve sukhāya vā adukkhamasukhāya vā vedanāya sampayuttānīti. Evamettha vedanātopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Regarding feeling: Herein, taking life is associated only with painful feeling. Taking what is not given is associated with any one of the three feelings; likewise for false speech. The other two are associated with either pleasant feeling or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Thus, the determination should be understood from the perspective of feeling also.

Mūlatoti pāṇātipāto cettha dosamohamūlo. Adinnādānamusāvādā [P 0.0032] lobhamohamūlā vā dosamohamūlā vā. Itarāni dve lobhamohamūlānīti. Evamettha mūlatopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Regarding the root: Herein, taking life is rooted in aversion and delusion. Taking what is not given and false speech are rooted in either greed and delusion or aversion and delusion. The other two are rooted in greed and delusion. Thus, the determination should be understood from the perspective of the root also.

Kammatoti pāṇātipātaadinnādānaabrahmacariyāni cettha kāyakammameva kammapathappattāneva ca, musāvādo vacīkammameva. Yo pana atthabhañjako, so kammapathappatto. Itaro kammameva. Surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānaṃ kāyakammamevāti. Evamettha kammatopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Regarding action: Herein, taking life, taking what is not given, and unchastity are bodily actions and also constitute a course of action. False speech is solely verbal action. But that false speech which is destructive of another's welfare, that constitutes a course of action. The other is merely action. The partaking of intoxicants which are a basis for heedlessness is solely a bodily action. Thus, the determination should be understood from the perspective of action also.

Viramatoti ettha āha “pāṇātipātādīhi viramanto kuto viramatī”ti? Vuccate – samādānavasena tāva viramanto attano vā paresaṃ vā pāṇātipātādiakusalato viramati. Kimārabhitvā? Yato viramati, tadeva. Sampattavasenāpi viramanto vuttappakārākusalatova. Kimārabhitvā? Pāṇātipātādīnaṃ vuttārammaṇāneva. Keci pana bhaṇanti “surāmerayamajjasaṅkhāte saṅkhāre ārabhitvā surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā viramati, sattasaṅkhāresu yaṃ pana avaharitabbaṃ bhañjitabbañca, taṃ ārabhitvā adinnādānā musāvādā ca, satteyevārabhitvā pāṇātipātā abrahmacariyā cā”ti. Tadaññe “evaṃ sante ‘aññaṃ cintento aññaṃ kareyya, yañca pajahati, taṃ na jāneyyā’ti evaṃdiṭṭhikā hutvā anicchamānā yadeva pajahati, taṃ attano pāṇātipātādiakusalamevārabhitvā viramatī”ti vadanti. Tadayuttaṃ. Kasmā? Tassa paccuppannābhāvato bahiddhābhāvato ca. Sikkhāpadānañhi vibhaṅgapāṭhe “pañcannaṃ sikkhāpadānaṃ kati kusalā…pe… kati araṇā”ti pucchitvā “kusalāyeva, siyā sukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā”ti (vibha. 716) evaṃ pavattamāne vissajjane “paccuppannārammaṇā”ti ca “bahiddhārammaṇā”ti ca evaṃ paccuppannabahiddhārammaṇattaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ attano pāṇātipātādiakusalaṃ ārabhitvā viramantassa na yujjati. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ – “aññaṃ [M 0.0023] cintento aññaṃ kareyya, yañca pajahati, taṃ na jāneyyā”ti. Tattha vuccate – na kiccasādhanavasena pavattento aññaṃ cintento [P 0.0033] aññaṃ karotīti vā, yañca pajahati, taṃ na jānātīti vā vuccati.

Regarding abstaining: Here, the questioner asks, 'When one abstains from taking life and so forth, from what does one abstain?' The answer is given: Firstly, by way of undertaking, one who abstains, abstains from the unwholesome act of taking life, etc., whether one's own or others'. Taking what as object? The very thing from which one abstains. Also, when abstaining by way of actual encounter, one abstains from the unwholesome act of the kind described. Taking what as object? The aforementioned objects of taking life and so forth. Some, however, say: 'Taking as object the conditioned things designated as liquor and intoxicants, one abstains from the occasion for heedlessness which is liquor and intoxicants. As for that which is to be stolen or destroyed through speech, taking that as object, one abstains from taking what is not given and from false speech. And taking living beings themselves as object, one abstains from taking life and from sexual misconduct.' To this, others say: 'If that were so, one would be thinking of one thing and doing another, and would not know what one is abandoning.' Not wishing to fall into such a view, they argue that one abstains by taking as object the very thing one abandons, namely one's own unwholesome act of taking life, etc. That is incorrect. Why? Because its object would not be present and not be external. For in the text of the Vibhaṅga on the training rules, having asked, 'Of the five training rules, how many are wholesome... how many are objects?' and in the answer that proceeds, 'They are only wholesome; they may be associated with pleasant feeling,' it is stated that they have 'present objects' and 'external objects.' This does not apply to one who abstains by taking one's own unwholesome act of taking life, etc., as object. As for what was said—'One thinks of one thing but does another, and abandons something without knowing it'—to this it is replied: It is not said that one who proceeds by way of accomplishing a task 'thinks of one thing and does another,' or that one 'abandons something without knowing it.'

“Ārabhitvāna [V 0.0023] amataṃ, jahanto sabbapāpake;

Nidassanañcettha bhave, maggaṭṭhoriyapuggalo”ti.

The noble person standing on the path, who abandons all evil by taking the Deathless as object, should be an example here.

Evamettha viramatopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Thus, the determination here should also be understood by way of abstaining.

Phalatoti sabbe eva cete pāṇātipātādayo duggatiphalanibbattakā honti, sugatiyañca aniṭṭhākantāmanāpavipākanibbattakā honti, samparāye diṭṭhadhamme eva ca avesārajjādiphalanibbattakā. Apica “yo sabbalahuso pāṇātipātassa vipāko manussabhūtassa appāyukasaṃvattaniko hotī”ti (a. ni. 8.40) evamādinā nayenettha phalatopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Regarding the result: All these acts, beginning with taking life, produce results in the woeful states; and in a happy state, they produce results that are undesirable, unpleasing, and disagreeable; and in the next life and in this very life, they produce results such as lack of confidence and so on. Moreover, the determination here should also be understood by way of the result, by the method beginning with: 'The lightest result of taking life, for one who has become a human being, is that it is conducive to a short life' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.40).

Api cettha pāṇātipātādiveramaṇīnampi samuṭṭhānavedanāmūlakammaphalato viññātabbo vinicchayo. Tatthāyaṃ viññāpanā – sabbā eva cetā veramaṇiyo catūhi samuṭṭhahanti kāyato, kāyacittato, vācācittato, kāyavācācittato cāti. Sabbā eva ca sukhavedanāsampayuttā vā, adukkhamasukhavedanāsampayuttā vā, alobhādosamūlā vā alobhādosāmohamūlā vā. Catassopi cettha kāyakammaṃ, musāvādāveramaṇī vacīkammaṃ, maggakkhaṇe ca cittatova samuṭṭhahanti, sabbāpi manokammaṃ.

Furthermore, the analysis of the abstinences from killing, etc., should be understood by way of their origin, feeling, root, kamma, and result. Herein is the explanation: All these abstinences arise from four origins: from the body; from body and mind; from speech and mind; and from body, speech, and mind. And all are associated either with pleasant feeling or with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; and are rooted either in non-greed and non-hatred, or in non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion. Herein, four are bodily kamma, and the abstinence from false speech is verbal kamma. But at the moment of the path, they arise from mind only, and all are mental kamma.

Pāṇātipātā veramaṇiyā cettha aṅgapaccaṅgasampannatā ārohapariṇāhasampattitā javasampattitā suppatiṭṭhitapādatā cārutā mudutā sucitā sūratā mahabbalatā vissatthavacanatā lokapiyatā nelatā abhejjaparisatā acchambhitā duppadhaṃsitā parūpakkamena amaraṇatā anantaparivāratā surūpatā susaṇṭhānatā appābādhatā asokitā piyehi manāpehi saddhiṃ avippayogatā dīghāyukatāti evamādīni phalāni.

Herein, from the abstinence from killing living beings, [come] such results as these: completeness of major and minor limbs, perfection of stature and girth, swiftness, well-planted feet, charm, gentleness, purity, courage, great strength, trustworthy speech, being beloved by the world, faultlessness, having an undivided retinue, fearlessness, being difficult to assail, not dying through the attack of others, having an infinite retinue, beauty of form, fine physique, few ailments, freedom from sorrow, not being separated from those who are dear and beloved, and long life.

Adinnādānā veramaṇiyā mahaddhanatā pahūtadhanadhaññatā anantabhogatā anuppannabhoguppattitā uppannabhogathāvaratā icchitānaṃ bhogānaṃ khippappaṭilābhitā rājacorudakaggiappiyadāyādehi asādhāraṇabhogatā [M 0.0024][P 0.0034] asādhāraṇadhanappaṭilābhitā lokuttamatā natthikabhāvassa ajānanatā sukhavihāritāti evamādīni.

From the abstinence from taking what is not given, [come] such results as these: great wealth, abundant money and grain, infinite possessions, the arising of possessions not yet arisen, the stability of possessions that have arisen, the swift attainment of desired possessions, possessions not shared with kings, thieves, water, fire, or unloved heirs, the attainment of exceptional wealth, worldly superiority, not knowing what it is to have nothing, and living in happiness.

Abrahmacariyā veramaṇiyā vigatapaccatthikatā sabbajanapiyatā annapānavatthasayanādīnaṃ lābhitā [V 0.0024] sukhasayanatā sukhappaṭibujjhanatā apāyabhayavinimuttatā itthibhāvappaṭilābhassa vā napuṃsakabhāvappaṭilābhassa vā abhabbatā akkodhanatā paccakkhakāritā apatitakkhandhatā anadhomukhatā itthipurisānaṃ aññamaññapiyatā paripuṇṇindriyatā paripuṇṇalakkhaṇatā nirāsaṅkatā appossukkatā sukhavihāritā akutobhayatā piyavippayogābhāvatāti evamādīni.

From the abstinence from sexual misconduct, [come] such results as these: having no enemies, being dear to all people, easily gaining food, drink, clothing, and lodging, sleeping in comfort, waking in comfort, being free from the fear of the woeful states, being incapable of rebirth as a woman or a eunuch, being without anger, acting directly, not having stooped shoulders, not being downcast, mutual affection between men and women, completeness of faculties, completeness of characteristics, being free from apprehension, being untroubled, living in happiness, being fearless from any quarter, and the absence of separation from loved ones.

Musāvādā veramaṇiyā vippasannindriyatā vissaṭṭhamadhurabhāṇitā samasitasuddhadantatā nātithūlatā nātikisatā nātirassatā nātidīghatā sukhasamphassatā uppalagandhamukhatā sussūsakaparijanatā ādeyyavacanatā kamaluppalasadisamudulohitatanujivhatā anuddhatatā acapalatāti evamādīni.

From the abstinence from false speech, [come] such results as these: exceptionally clear faculties, clear and sweet speech, evenly set and pure teeth, being neither too stout nor too lean, neither too short nor too tall, having a pleasant touch, a mouth fragrant like a blue lotus, a retinue eager to listen, speech that is acceptable, a tongue like a lotus—soft, red, and thin—and being neither restless nor fickle.

Surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā veramaṇiyā atītānāgatapaccuppannesu sabbakiccakaraṇīyesu khippaṃ paṭijānanatā sadā upaṭṭhitasatitā anummattakatā ñāṇavantatā analasatā ajaḷatā anelamūgatā amattatā appamattatā asammohatā acchambhitā asārambhitā anussaṅkitā saccavāditā apisuṇāpharusāsamphapalāpavāditā rattindivamatanditatā kataññutā kataveditā amaccharitā cāgavantatā sīlavantatā ujutā akkodhanatā hirimanatā ottappitā ujudiṭṭhikatā mahāpaññatā medhāvitā paṇḍitatā atthānatthakusalatāti evamādīni phalāni. Evamettha pāṇātipātādiveramaṇīnaṃ samuṭṭhānavedanāmūlakammaphalatopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

From abstaining from liquor and intoxicants, which are a cause of heedlessness, [come] these and other such results: quickness in understanding all duties of the past, future, and present; always having established mindfulness; sanity; being endowed with knowledge; diligence; not being dull; not being mute; not being intoxicated; heedfulness; non-bewilderment; fearlessness; being without hostility; not being an object of suspicion; truthfulness; not speaking slanderous, harsh, or frivolous speech; tirelessness day and night; gratitude; acknowledging what has been done; not being stingy; generosity; virtue; uprightness; being without anger; moral shame; moral dread; right view; great wisdom; penetrating wisdom; sagacity; and skill in what is beneficial and not beneficial. Thus, herein, the analysis concerning the abstinences from taking life and so forth should also be known by way of origin, feeling, root, kamma, and result.

Pacchimapañcasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Latter Five Training Rules

Idāni yaṃ vuttaṃ –

Now, as was said:

“Yojetabbaṃ tato yuttaṃ, pacchimesvapi pañcasu;

Āveṇikañca vattabbaṃ, ñeyyā hīnāditāpi cā”ti.

“What is suitable from that should be applied also to the latter five; what is unique should also be stated; and inferiority and so forth should also be known.”

Tassāyaṃ [M 0.0025] atthavaṇṇanā – etissā purimapañcasikkhāpadavaṇṇanāya [P 0.0035] yaṃ yujjati, taṃ tato gahetvā pacchimesvapi pañcasu sikkhāpadesu yojetabbaṃ. Tatthāyaṃ yojanā – yatheva hi purimasikkhāpadesu ārammaṇato ca surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānaṃ rūpāyatanādiaññatarasaṅkhārārammaṇaṃ, tathā idha vikālabhojanaṃ. Etena nayena sabbesaṃ ārammaṇabhedo veditabbo. Ādānato ca yathā purimāni sāmaṇerena vā upāsakena vā samādiyantena samādinnāni honti, tathā etānipi. Aṅgatopi [V 0.0025] yathā tattha pāṇātipātādīnaṃ aṅgabhedo vutto, evamidhāpi vikālabhojanassa cattāri aṅgāni – vikālo, yāvakālikaṃ, ajjhoharaṇaṃ, anummattakatāti. Etenānusārena sesānampi aṅgavibhāgo veditabbo. Yathā ca tattha samuṭṭhānato surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānaṃ kāyato ca kāyacittato cāti dvisamuṭṭhānaṃ, evamidha vikālabhojanaṃ. Etena nayena sabbesaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Yathā ca tattha vedanāto adinnādānaṃ tīsu vedanāsu aññataravedanāsampayuttaṃ, tathā idha vikālabhojanaṃ. Etena nayena sabbesaṃ vedanāsampayogo veditabbo. Yathā ca tattha abrahmacariyaṃ lobhamohamūlaṃ, evamidha vikālabhojanaṃ. Aparāni ca dve etena nayena sabbesaṃ mūlabhedo veditabbo. Yathā ca tattha pāṇātipātādayo kāyakammaṃ, evamidhāpi vikālabhojanādīni. Jātarūparajatappaṭiggahaṇaṃ pana kāyakammaṃ vā siyā vacīkammaṃ vā kāyadvārādīhi pavattisabbhāvapariyāyena, na kammapathavasena. Viramatoti yathā ca tattha viramanto attano vā paresaṃ vā pāṇātipātādiakusalato viramati, evamidhāpi vikālabhojanādiakusalato, kusalatopi vā ekato. Yathā ca purimā pañca veramaṇiyo catusamuṭṭhānā kāyato, kāyacittato, vācācittato, kāyavācācittato cāti, sabbā sukhavedanāsampayuttā vā adukkhamasukhavedanāsampayuttā vā, alobhādosamūlā vā alobhādosāmohamūlā vā, sabbā ca nānappakāraiṭṭhaphalanibbattakā, tathā idhāpīti.

This is its explanation of the meaning: Whatever is suitable in the explanation of the former five precepts, that should be taken from there and applied also to the latter five precepts. Herein, this is the application: Just as in the former precepts, from the perspective of the object, abstaining from liquor and intoxicants, a cause of heedlessness, has as its object some conditioned thing such as the form base, so too here does eating at the wrong time. By this method, the distinction of objects for all of them should be understood. From the perspective of undertaking, just as the former are undertaken by one who is a novice or a lay follower, so too are these. From the perspective of factors, just as the distinction of factors for taking life and so forth was stated there, so too here eating at the wrong time has four factors: the wrong time, what is allowable for a limited time, the act of consuming, and not being insane. Following this guideline, the division of factors for the rest should also be understood. And just as there, from the perspective of origin, abstaining from liquor and intoxicants has a twofold origin—from the body and from the body-and-mind—so too here does eating at the wrong time. By this method, the origin of all of them should be known. And just as there, from the perspective of feeling, taking what is not given is associated with one of the three feelings, so too here is eating at the wrong time. By this method, the association with feeling for all of them should be understood. And just as there unchastity is rooted in greed and delusion, so too here is eating at the wrong time. For the remaining two also, the distinction of roots for all of them should be understood by this method. And just as there taking life and so forth are bodily actions, so too here are eating at the wrong time and so forth. The acceptance of gold and silver, however, may be a bodily action or a verbal action by way of its natural mode of occurrence through the body-door and so forth, not by way of the path of action. Regarding 'abstains,' just as there one who abstains does so from the unwholesome act of taking life, etc., for oneself or for others, so too here one abstains from the unwholesome act of eating at the wrong time, etc., or in one respect from what is wholesome. And just as the former five abstinences have four origins—from the body, from the body-and-mind, from speech-and-mind, and from body-speech-and-mind—and all are associated with pleasant feeling or with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, are rooted in non-greed and non-hatred or in non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion, and all produce various desirable results, so too is it here.

“Yojetabbaṃ tato yuttaṃ, pacchimesvapi pañcasu;

Āveṇikañca vattabbaṃ, ñeyyā hīnāditāpi cā”ti. –

“What is suitable from that should be applied also to the latter five; what is unique should also be stated; and inferiority and so forth should also be known.”

Ettha pana [P 0.0036] vikālabhojananti majjhanhikavītikkame bhojanaṃ. Etañhi anuññātakāle vītikkante bhojanaṃ, tasmā “vikālabhojana”nti vuccati[M 0.0026], tato vikālabhojanā. Naccagītavāditavisūkadassananti ettha naccaṃ nāma yaṃkiñci naccaṃ, gītanti yaṃkiñci gītaṃ, vāditanti yaṃkiñci vāditaṃ. Visūkadassananti kilesuppattipaccayato kusalapakkhabhindanena visūkānaṃ dassanaṃ, visūkabhūtaṃ vā dassanaṃ visūkadassanaṃ. Naccā ca gītā ca vāditā ca visūkadassanā ca naccagītavāditavisūkadassanā. Visūkadassanañcettha brahmajāle vuttanayeneva gahetabbaṃ. Vuttañhi tattha –

Herein, 'eating at the wrong time' (vikālabhojana) means eating after midday has passed. Since this is eating when the permitted time has passed, it is therefore called 'eating at the wrong time'; hence, from eating at the wrong time. In the phrase 'seeing dancing, singing, instrumental music, and shows' (naccagītavāditavisūkadassana), 'dancing' means any kind of dancing, 'singing' means any kind of singing, and 'instrumental music' means any kind of instrumental music. 'Seeing shows' (visūkadassana) means seeing things that are contrary (visūka) by breaking down the wholesome side, being a condition for the arising of defilements; or it is seeing what has become a show. Dancing, and singing, and instrumental music, and seeing shows are 'dancing, singing, instrumental music, and seeing shows.' And 'seeing shows' herein should be understood according to the method stated in the Brahmajāla Sutta. For it was stated there:

“Yathā vā paneke bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā saddhādeyyāni bhojanāni bhuñjitvā te evarūpaṃ visūkadassanamanuyuttā viharanti, seyyathidaṃ, naccaṃ gītaṃ vāditaṃ pekkhaṃ akkhānaṃ pāṇissaraṃ vetālaṃ kumbhathūṇaṃ sobhanakaṃ caṇḍālaṃ vaṃsaṃ dhovanaṃ hatthiyuddhaṃ assayuddhaṃ [V 0.0026] mahiṃsayuddhaṃ usabhayuddhaṃ ajayuddhaṃ meṇḍayuddhaṃ kukkuṭayuddhaṃ vaṭṭakayuddhaṃ daṇḍayuddhaṃ muṭṭhiyuddhaṃ nibbuddhaṃ uyyodhikaṃ balaggaṃ senābyūhaṃ anīkadassanaṃ iti vā, iti evarūpā visūkadassanā paṭivirato samaṇo gotamo”ti (dī. ni. 1.12).

“Or, just as some venerable ascetics and brahmins, having eaten food given in faith, dwell engaged in viewing such unseemly shows as these—that is to say: dancing, singing, instrumental music, theatrical shows, recitations, hand-clapping, ballads, drumming, magic shows, acrobatic feats, bamboo-pole feats, bone-washing rituals, elephant fights, horse fights, buffalo fights, bull fights, goat fights, ram fights, cock fights, quail fights, stick-fighting, boxing, wrestling, mock-fights, troop musters, troop formations, and military reviews—the ascetic Gotama abstains from viewing such unseemly shows.”

Atha vā yathāvuttenatthena naccagītavāditāni eva visūkāni naccagītavāditavisūkāni, tesaṃ dassanaṃ naccagītavāditavisūkadassanaṃ, tasmā naccagītavāditavisūkadassanā. “Dassanasavanā”ti vattabbe yathā “so ca hoti micchādiṭṭhiko viparītadassano”ti evamādīsu (a. ni. 1.308) acakkhudvārappavattampi visayaggahaṇaṃ “dassana”nti vuccati, evaṃ savanampi “dassana”ntveva vuttaṃ. Dassanakamyatāya upasaṅkamitvā passato eva cettha vītikkamo hoti. Ṭhitanisinnasayanokāse pana āgataṃ gacchantassa vā āpāthagataṃ passato siyā saṃkileso, na vītikkamo. Dhammūpasaṃhitampi cettha gītaṃ na vaṭṭati, gītūpasaṃhito pana dhammo [P 0.0037] vaṭṭatīti veditabbo.

Alternatively, by the meaning already stated: dancing, singing, and instrumental music are themselves causes for the growth of defilements (visūkāni). Seeing these causes for the growth of defilements is naccagītavāditavisūkadassanaṃ. Therefore, one abstains from naccagītavāditavisūkadassanā. Where it should be said “seeing and hearing,” just as in instances such as, “he is one of wrong view, a person with distorted views,” even the apprehension of an object not occurring through the eye-door is called “seeing”; in the same way, hearing is also spoken of as “seeing.” And here, a transgression occurs only for one who approaches with the desire to see and then looks. But for one who sees what has come into a place of standing, sitting, or lying down, or for one who is walking and sees what has come into range, there may be defilement, but there would not be a transgression. And here, it is not allowable to recite even a song connected with the Dhamma; but it is allowable to hear the Dhamma that is connected with a song. Thus it should be understood.

Mālādīni dhāraṇādīhi yathāsaṅkhyaṃ yojetabbāni. Tattha mālāti yaṃkiñci pupphajātaṃ. Vilepananti yaṃkiñci vilepanatthaṃ pisitvā paṭiyattaṃ. Avasesaṃ sabbampi vāsacuṇṇadhūpanādikaṃ gandhajātaṃ gandho. Taṃ sabbampi maṇḍanavibhūsanatthaṃ na vaṭṭati, bhesajjatthantu vaṭṭati, pūjanatthañca abhihaṭaṃ sādiyato na kenaci pariyāyena na vaṭṭati. Uccāsayananti pamāṇātikkantaṃ vuccati. Mahāsayananti akappiyasayanaṃ akappiyattharaṇañca. Tadubhayampi sādiyato [M 0.0027] na kenaci pariyāyena vaṭṭati. Jātarūpanti suvaṇṇaṃ. Rajatanti kahāpaṇo, lohamāsakadārumāsakajatumāsakādi yaṃ yaṃ tattha tattha vohāraṃ gacchati, tadubhayampi jātarūparajataṃ. Tassa yena kenaci pakārena sādiyanaṃ paṭiggaho nāma, so na yena kenaci pariyāyena vaṭṭatīti evaṃ āveṇikaṃ vattabbaṃ.

Garlands and other items should be applied respectively according to their categories of wearing and so forth. Therein, ‘garland’ (mālā) is any kind of flower. ‘Ointment’ (vilepana) is any substance ground and prepared for the purpose of anointing. All the rest—any kind of scent, such as scented powders, incense, and the like—is ‘scent’ (gandha). All of that is not allowable for the purpose of adornment and beautification, but for medicinal purposes, it is allowable. And for one who delights in what is brought for the purpose of veneration, it is not that it is unallowable in any way; it is indeed allowable. ‘High seat’ (uccāsayana) is said to be that which exceeds the standard measure. ‘Great seat’ (mahāsayana) is an improper bed and an improper covering. For one who delights in both of these, it is not allowable in any way. ‘Gold’ (jātarūpa) is gold. ‘Silver’ (rajata) is a coin; whatever coin—such as a copper māsaka, a wooden māsaka, or a lac māsaka—is used for trade in various places, both of these are ‘gold and silver’ (jātarūparajata). For that person, delighting in it in any way whatsoever is called ‘acceptance’ (paṭiggaha); that is not allowable in any way. Thus, what is distinct from the previous precepts should be stated.

Dasapi cetāni sikkhāpadāni hīnena chandena cittavīriyavīmaṃsāhi vā samādinnāni hīnāni, majjhimehi majjhimāni, paṇītehi paṇītāni. Taṇhādiṭṭhimānehi vā upakkiliṭṭhāni hīnāni, anupakkiliṭṭhāni majjhimāni, tattha tattha paññāya anuggahitāni paṇītāni. Ñāṇavippayuttena vā kusalacittena samādinnāni hīnāni, sasaṅkhārikañāṇasampayuttena majjhimāni, asaṅkhārikena paṇītānīti evaṃ ñeyyā hīnāditāpi cāti.

These ten training rules, when undertaken with inferior desire, or with inferior mind, effort, and wisdom, are inferior; with middling ones, they are middling; with excellent ones, they are excellent. Or, when defiled by craving, views, or conceit, they are inferior; when undefiled, they are middling; when supported by wisdom in each case, they are excellent. Or, when undertaken with a wholesome mind dissociated from knowledge, they are inferior; when undertaken with wholesome consciousness that is prompted and associated with knowledge, they are middling; when undertaken with unprompted wholesome consciousness, they are excellent. Thus, the state of being inferior and so forth should also be known.

Ettāvatā [V 0.0027] ca yā pubbe “yena yattha yadā yasmā”tiādīhi chahi gāthāhi sikkhāpadapāṭhassa vaṇṇanatthaṃ mātikā nikkhittā, sā atthato pakāsitā hotīti.

And thus far, the matrix (mātikā) that was previously set forth with the six verses beginning with ‘by whom, where, when, from what’ and so forth, for the purpose of explaining the text of the training rules, has been clarified in terms of its meaning.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha,

Sikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rules is concluded.

3. Dvattiṃsākāravaṇṇanā

3. The Description of the Thirty-Two Parts

Padasambandhavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Connection of Terms

Idāni [V 0.0028] yadidaṃ evaṃ dasahi sikkhāpadehi parisuddhapayogassa sīle patiṭṭhitassa kulaputtassa āsayaparisuddhatthaṃ [P 0.0038] cittabhāvanatthañca aññatra buddhuppādā appavattapubbaṃ sabbatitthiyānaṃ avisayabhūtaṃ tesu tesu suttantesu –

Now, that which—never before arisen except with the arising of a Buddha, beyond the reach of all other sects, and found in various discourses—is for the sake of purifying the intention and developing the mind of a son of good family established in virtue, with his practice purified by these ten training rules—

“Ekadhammo, bhikkhave, bhāvito bahulīkato mahato saṃvegāya saṃvattati. Mahato atthāya saṃvattati. Mahato yogakkhemāya saṃvattati. Mahato satisampajaññāya saṃvattati. Ñāṇadassanappaṭilābhāya saṃvattati. Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāya saṃvattati. Vijjāvimuttiphalasacchikiriyāya saṃvattati. Katamo [M 0.0028] ekadhammo? Kāyagatā sati. Amataṃ te, bhikkhave, na paribhuñjanti, ye kāyagatāsatiṃ na paribhuñjanti. Amataṃ te, bhikkhave, paribhuñjanti, ye kāyagatāsatiṃ paribhuñjanti. Amataṃ tesaṃ, bhikkhave, aparibhuttaṃ paribhuttaṃ, parihīnaṃ aparihīnaṃ, viraddhaṃ āraddhaṃ, yesaṃ kāyagatā sati āraddhā”ti. (A. ni. 1.564-570) –

“Monks, there is one thing that, when developed and cultivated, leads to a great sense of urgency, leads to great benefit, leads to great security from the yokes, leads to great mindfulness and clear comprehension, leads to the attainment of knowledge and vision, leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life, and leads to the realization of the fruit of true knowledge and liberation. What is that one thing? Mindfulness directed to the body. Monks, those who do not partake of mindfulness directed to the body do not partake of the Deathless. Monks, those who partake of mindfulness directed to the body partake of the Deathless. Monks, for those by whom mindfulness directed to the body is partaken of, for them the Deathless is partaken of. For those by whom it is not partaken of, for them the Deathless is not partaken of. For those for whom it has declined, for them the Deathless has declined. For those for whom it has not declined, for them the Deathless has not declined. For those for whom it is missed, for them the Deathless is missed. For those by whom it is undertaken, for them the Deathless is undertaken.”

Evaṃ bhagavatā anekākārena pasaṃsitvā –

Thus, the Blessed One having praised it in various ways—

“Kathaṃ bhāvitā, bhikkhave, kāyagatāsati kathaṃ bahulīkatā mahabbalā hoti mahānisaṃsā? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu araññagato vā”ti (ma. ni. 3.154) –

“Monks, how is mindfulness directed to the body developed, how is it cultivated, so that it is of great power and great benefit? Here, monks, a monk gone to the forest—”

Ādinā nayena ānāpānapabbaṃ iriyāpathapabbaṃ catusampajaññapabbaṃ paṭikūlamanasikārapabbaṃ dhātumanasikārapabbaṃ nava sivathikapabbānīti imesaṃ cuddasannaṃ pabbānaṃ vasena kāyagatāsatikammaṭṭhānaṃ niddiṭṭhaṃ. Tassa bhāvanāniddeso anuppatto. Tattha yasmā iriyāpathapabbaṃ catusampajaññapabbaṃ dhātumanasikārapabbanti imāni tīṇi vipassanāvasena vuttāni. Nava sivathikapabbāni vipassanāñāṇesuyeva ādīnavānupassanāvasena vuttāni. Yāpi cettha uddhumātakādīsu samādhibhāvanā [V 0.0029] iccheyya, sā visuddhimagge vitthārato asubhabhāvanāniddese pakāsitā eva. Ānāpānapabbaṃ pana paṭikūlamanasikārapabbañceti imānettha dve samādhivasena vuttāni. Tesu ānāpānapabbaṃ ānāpānassativasena visuṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃyeva. Yaṃ panetaṃ –

Following this method, the section on mindfulness of breathing, the section on postures, the section on fourfold clear comprehension, the section on contemplation of repulsiveness, the section on contemplation of elements, and the nine charnel ground sections—these fourteen sections have been specified as the meditation subject of mindfulness of the body. The exposition of their development has now come. Here, the section on postures, the section on fourfold clear comprehension, and the section on contemplation of elements are spoken of in relation to insight. The nine charnel ground sections are spoken of in relation to the insight knowledges through contemplation of danger. If one should wish to develop concentration through the bloated corpse and so forth here, that has already been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga’s exposition on the development of the foul. However, the section on mindfulness of breathing and the section on contemplation of repulsiveness are spoken of here in relation to concentration. Among these, the section on mindfulness of breathing is a distinct meditation subject as mindfulness of breathing. But that which—

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu imameva kāyaṃ uddhaṃ pādatalā adho kesamatthakā tacapariyantaṃ pūraṃ nānappakārassa asucino paccavekkhati ‘atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā, lomā…pe… mutta”nti (ma. ni. 3.154).

“Furthermore, monks, a monk reflects on this very body, upwards from the soles of the feet and downwards from the crown of the head, enclosed by skin and full of various kinds of impurities, thus: ‘In this body there are head hairs, body hairs… urine.’”

Evaṃ tattha tattha matthaluṅgaṃ aṭṭhimiñjena saṅgahetvā desitaṃ kāyagatāsatikoṭṭhāsabhāvanāpariyāyaṃ dvattiṃsākārakammaṭṭhānaṃ āraddhaṃ, tassāyaṃ atthavaṇṇanā –

Thus, the meditation subject of the thirty-two parts—the method for developing the constituents of mindfulness directed to the body, which was taught in various places by including the brain under the term ‘bone marrow’—is now undertaken. This is its explanation of meaning—

Tattha atthīti saṃvijjanti. Imasminti yvāyaṃ uddhaṃ pādatalā adho kesamatthakā tacapariyanto pūro nānappakārassa asucinoti vuccati, tasmiṃ[M 0.0029]. Kāyeti sarīre. Sarīrañhi asucisañcayato, kucchitānaṃ vā kesādīnañceva cakkhurogādīnañca rogasatānaṃ āyabhūtato kāyoti vuccati. Kesā…pe… muttanti ete kesādayo dvattiṃsākārā, tattha “atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā atthi lomā”ti evaṃ sambandho veditabbo[P 0.0039]. Tena kiṃ kathitaṃ hoti? Imasmiṃ pādatalā paṭṭhāya upari, kesamatthakā paṭṭhāya heṭṭhā, tacato paṭṭhāya paritoti ettake byāmamatte kaḷevare sabbākārenāpi vicinanto na koci kiñci muttaṃ vā maṇiṃ vā veḷuriyaṃ vā agaruṃ vā candanaṃ vā kuṅkumaṃ vā kappūraṃ vā vāsacuṇṇādiṃ vā aṇumattampi sucibhāvaṃ passati, atha kho paramaduggandhajegucchaṃ assirikadassanaṃ nānappakāraṃ kesalomādibhedaṃ asucimeva passatīti.

Herein, ‘there is’ means ‘they exist.’ ‘In this’ refers to that which is called ‘full of various kinds of impurities, upwards from the soles of the feet and downwards from the crown of the head, bounded by the skin’; in that. ‘In the body’ means in the physical form. For the physical form is called ‘kāya’ because it is a collection of impurities, or because it is a repository for repulsive things such as hair, and for hundreds of diseases such as eye diseases. ‘Hairs… down to urine’—these are the thirty-two aspects beginning with hair. Herein, the connection should be understood thus: ‘In this body, there are hairs; there are body hairs,’ and so on. What is stated by this? That when one investigates this fathom-long corpse—upwards from the soles of the feet, downwards from the crown of the head, and all around from the skin inwards—in every way, one does not see even a minute particle of purity, such as a pearl, a gem, lapis lazuli, aloeswood, sandalwood, saffron, camphor, or scented powder. Instead, one sees only what is impure: extremely foul-smelling, repulsive, unlovely to behold, and of various kinds, distinguished as head hair, body hair, and so on.

Ayaṃ tāvettha padasambandhato vaṇṇanā.

This, first of all, is the explanation herein by way of the connection of the terms.

Asubhabhāvanā

Meditation on Foulness

Asubhabhāvanāvasena panassa evaṃ vaṇṇanā veditabbā – evametasmiṃ pāṇātipātāveramaṇisikkhāpadādibhede sīle patiṭṭhitena payogasuddhena ādikammikena kulaputtena āsayasuddhiyā adhigamanatthaṃ dvattiṃsākārakammaṭṭhānabhāvanānuyogamanuyuñjitukāmena paṭhamaṃ tāvassa āvāsakulalābhagaṇakammaddhānañātigantharogaiddhipalibodhena kittipalibodhena vā saha dasa palibodhā [V 0.0030] honti. Athānena āvāsakulalābhagaṇañātikittīsu saṅgappahānena, kammaddhānaganthesu abyāpārena, rogassa tikicchāyāti evaṃ te dasa palibodhā upacchinditabbā, athānena upacchinnapalibodhena anupacchinnanekkhammābhilāsena koṭippattasallekhavuttitaṃ pariggahetvā khuddānukhuddakampi vinayācāraṃ appajahantena āgamādhigamasamannāgato tato aññataraṅgasamannāgato vā kammaṭṭhānadāyako ācariyo vinayānurūpena vidhinā upagantabbo, vattasampadāya ca ārādhitacittassa tassa attano adhippāyo nivedetabbo. Tena tassa nimittajjhāsayacariyādhimuttibhedaṃ ñatvā yadi etaṃ kammaṭṭhānamanurūpaṃ, atha [M 0.0030] yasmiṃ vihāre attanā vasati, yadi tasmiṃyeva sopi vasitukāmo hoti, tato saṅkhepato kammaṭṭhānaṃ dātabbaṃ. Atha aññatra [P 0.0040] vasitukāmo hoti, tato pahātabbapariggahetabbādikathanavasena sapurekkhāraṃ rāgacaritānukulādikathanavasena sappabhedaṃ vitthārena kathetabbaṃ. Tena taṃ sapurekkhāraṃ sappabhedaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggahetvā ācariyaṃ āpucchitvā yāni tāni –

Now, by way of the meditation on foulness, its explanation should be understood thus: A clansman established in virtue—distinguished by such things as the training rule of abstaining from taking life—who is pure in endeavor and a beginner, wishing to undertake the practice of developing the meditation subject of the thirty-two aspects for the sake of purity of disposition and for the sake of attainment, should know that for him there are, first of all, ten impediments. These are the impediments of dwelling, supporters, gain, a group, new undertakings, travel, relatives, scriptures, illness, and supernormal power, or together with the impediment of fame. Then, these ten impediments should be cut off by him: by abandoning attachment in the cases of the dwelling, supporters, gain, the group, relatives, and fame; by non-involvement in new undertakings, travel, and scriptures; and by treatment for illness. Then, having cut off the impediments, with an uninterrupted aspiration for renunciation, having undertaken a life of austerity that has reached the ultimate, not abandoning even the minor and lesser points of Vinaya conduct, being endowed with learning and attainment or endowed with some other such quality, a teacher who is a giver of a meditation subject should be approached according to the proper procedure in line with the Vinaya. And having pleased his mind by being accomplished in the duties, one's own intention should be declared to him. That teacher, having known the distinctions of his sign, disposition, conduct, and inclination, if this meditation subject is suitable, and if the practitioner wishes to live in the very same monastery where he himself lives, then the meditation subject should be given in brief. But if he wishes to live elsewhere, then it should be taught in detail, with its preliminaries, by way of explaining what is to be abandoned and what is to be undertaken, and with its divisions, by way of explaining what is suitable for one of a lustful temperament and so on. Having learned that meditation subject with its preliminaries and its divisions from him, and having taken leave of the teacher, [he should avoid] those [places] which are:

“Mahāvāsaṃ navāvāsaṃ, jarāvāsañca panthaniṃ;

Soṇḍiṃ paṇṇañca pupphañca, phalaṃ patthitameva ca.

“A large monastery, a new monastery, a dilapidated monastery, and one on a main road; one with a pond, one dependent on vegetables, one on flowers, one on fruit, and one that is much sought after.

“Nagaraṃ dārunā khettaṃ, visabhāgena paṭṭanaṃ;

Paccantasīmāsappāyaṃ, yattha mitto na labbhati.

“A monastery near a city, one near a forest of timber, and one near a field; one with incompatible persons, and one near a port; one on the border, an unsuitable one, and one where a friend is not to be found.

“Aṭṭhārasetāni ṭhānāni, iti viññāya paṇḍito;

Ārakā parivajjeyya, maggaṃ sappaṭibhayaṃ yathā”ti. (visuddhi. 1.52) –

“These eighteen places, the wise person, having understood thus, should avoid from afar, just as one avoids a dangerous path.”

Evaṃ aṭṭhārasa senāsanāni parivajjetabbānīti vuccanti. Tāni vajjetvā, yaṃ taṃ –

Thus, it is said that these eighteen kinds of lodgings are to be avoided. Having avoided them, that which is—

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, senāsanaṃ pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, senāsanaṃ nātidūraṃ hoti, naccāsannaṃ, gamanāgamanasampannaṃ, divā appākiṇṇaṃ, rattiṃ appasaddaṃ appanigghosaṃ appaḍaṃsamakasavātātapasarīsapasamphassaṃ. Tasmiṃ kho pana senāsane viharantassa appakasirena uppajjanti cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārā. Tasmiṃ kho pana senāsane therā bhikkhū viharanti bahussutā āgatāgamā dhammadharā vinayadharā mātikādharā, te kālena kālaṃ upasaṅkamitvā paripucchati paripañhati ‘idaṃ, bhante, kathaṃ, imassa ko attho’ti? Tassa, te āyasmanto [V 0.0031] avivaṭañceva vivaranti, anuttānīkatañca uttāniṃ karonti, anekavihitesu ca kaṅkhāṭhāniyesu dhammesu kaṅkhaṃ paṭivinodenti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, senāsanaṃ pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ hotī”ti (a. ni. 10.11). –

“And how, Bhikkhus, is a lodging endowed with five factors? Here, Bhikkhus, a lodging is not too far, not too near, convenient for coming and going, not crowded by day, with little sound and little noise by night, free from the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things. While dwelling in that lodging, robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick arise without difficulty. In that lodging, elder bhikkhus dwell—very learned, who have mastered the traditions, upholders of the Dhamma, upholders of the Vinaya, upholders of the Mātikā. From time to time, one approaches them and asks and inquires: ‘Venerable sirs, how is this? What is the meaning of this?’ Those venerable ones then reveal what is unrevealed, make clear what is not clear, and dispel doubt regarding the many kinds of doctrines that occasion doubt. It is in this way, Bhikkhus, that a lodging is endowed with five factors.”

Evaṃ pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ senāsanaṃ vuttaṃ. Tathārūpaṃ senāsanaṃ upagamma katasabbakiccena kāmesu ādīnavaṃ, nekkhamme ca ānisaṃsaṃ paccavekkhitvā buddhasubuddhatāya [M 0.0031] dhammasudhammatāya [P 0.0041] saṅghasuppaṭipannatāya ca anussaraṇena cittaṃ pasādetvā yaṃ taṃ –

Thus, a lodging endowed with five factors has been described. Having approached such a lodging, and being one who has completed all his duties, having reflected on the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation, and having gladdened the mind by recollecting the Buddha's state of being well-awakened, the Dhamma's state of being well-taught, and the Sangha's state of practicing well, that which is—

“Vacasā manasā ceva, vaṇṇasaṇṭhānato disā;

Okāsato paricchedā, sattadhuggahaṇaṃ vidū”ti. –

“By word and by mind, by color and form, by direction, by location and by delimitation—the wise know the sevenfold grasping.”

Evaṃ sattavidhaṃ uggahakosallaṃ; anupubbato, nātisīghato, nātisaṇikato, vikkhepappaṭibāhanato, paṇṇattisamatikkamato, anupubbamuñcanato, appanāto, tayo ca suttantāti evaṃ dasavidhaṃ manasikārakosallañca vuttaṃ. Taṃ apariccajantena dvattiṃsākārabhāvanā ārabhitabbā. Evañhi ārabhato sabbākārena dvattiṃsākārabhāvanā sampajjati no aññathā.

Thus, the sevenfold skill in grasping has been spoken of. And thus the tenfold skill in advertence has also been spoken of: in sequence, not too fast, not too slow, by warding off distraction, by transcending designation, by sequentially releasing, by way of absorption, and the three suttas. Not abandoning this, one should undertake the development of the thirty-two aspects. For one who undertakes it thus, the development of the thirty-two aspects succeeds in every way, and not otherwise.

Tattha āditova tacapañcakaṃ tāva gahetvā api tepiṭakena “kesā lomā”tiādinā nayena anulomato, tasmiṃ paguṇībhūte “taco dantā”ti evamādinā nayena paṭilomato, tasmimpi paguṇībhūte tadubhayanayeneva anulomappaṭilomato bahi visaṭavitakkavicchedanatthaṃ pāḷipaguṇībhāvatthañca vacasā koṭṭhāsasabhāvapariggahatthaṃ manasā ca addhamāsaṃ bhāvetabbaṃ. Vacasā hissa bhāvanā bahi visaṭavitakke vicchinditvā manasā bhāvanāya pāḷipaguṇatāya ca paccayo hoti, manasā bhāvanā asubhavaṇṇalakkhaṇānaṃ aññataravasena pariggahassa, atha teneva nayena vakkapañcakaṃ addhamāsaṃ, tato tadubhayamaddhamāsaṃ, tato papphāsapañcakamaddhamāsaṃ, tato taṃ pañcakattayampi addhamāsaṃ, atha ante avuttampi matthaluṅgaṃ pathavīdhātuākārehi saddhiṃ ekato bhāvanatthaṃ idha pakkhipitvā matthaluṅgapañcakaṃ addhamāsaṃ, tato pañcakacatukkampi addhamāsaṃ, atha medachakkamaddhamāsaṃ, tato medachakkena saha pañcakacatukkampi addhamāsaṃ, atha muttachakkamaddhamāsaṃ, tato sabbameva dvattiṃsākāramaddhamāsanti evaṃ cha māse vaṇṇasaṇṭhānadisokāsaparicchedato vavatthapentena bhāvetabbaṃ. Etaṃ majjhimapaññaṃ puggalaṃ sandhāya [P 0.0042] vuttaṃ. Mandapaññena tu yāvajīvaṃ bhāvetabbaṃ tikkhapaññassa na cireneva bhāvanā sampajjatīti.

Herein, first, having taken up the skin-pentad, even a monk who knows the Tipiṭaka should develop it for half a month—by the method beginning 'head-hairs, body-hairs,' and so on, in forward order; when that becomes familiar, then by the method beginning 'skin, teeth,' and so on, in reverse order; when that too becomes familiar, then by both methods, in forward and reverse order. It should be developed verbally for the purpose of cutting off thoughts scattered externally and for becoming familiar with the Pāli text, and mentally for the purpose of grasping the nature of the parts. For his verbal development, having cut off thoughts scattered externally, becomes a condition for mental development and for proficiency in the Pāli. Mental development is a condition for grasping by way of one of the characteristics of foulness, such as color. Then, in the same way, the kidney-pentad should be developed for half a month; then both of those together for half a month; then the lung-pentad for half a month; then all three of those pentads together for half a month. Next, the brain, though mentioned at the end, is included here for the purpose of developing it together with the parts of the earth element, and the brain-pentad should be developed for half a month; then all four pentads for half a month. After that, the fat-hexad for half a month; then the four pentads together with the fat-hexad for half a month. Then the urine-hexad for half a month; finally, all thirty-two aspects for half a month. Thus, for six months, it should be developed by one who determines them by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation. This is said with reference to a person of middling intelligence. But one of dull intelligence should develop it for life, while for one of sharp intelligence, the development is accomplished without delay.

Etthāha [V 0.0032][M 0.0032] – “kathaṃ panāyamimaṃ dvattiṃsākāraṃ vaṇṇādito vavatthapetī”ti? Ayañhi “atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā”ti evamādinā nayena tacapañcakādivibhāgato dvattiṃsākāraṃ bhāvento kesā tāva vaṇṇato kāḷakāti vavatthapeti, yādisakā vānena diṭṭhā honti. Saṇṭhānato dīghavaṭṭalikā tulādaṇḍamivāti vavatthapeti. Disato pana yasmā imasmiṃ kāye nābhito uddhaṃ uparimā disā adho heṭṭhimāti vuccati, tasmā imassa kāyassa uparimāya disāya jātāti vavatthapeti. Okāsato nalāṭantakaṇṇacūḷikagalavāṭakaparicchinne sīsacamme jātāti. Tattha yathā vammikamatthake jātāni kuṇṭhatiṇāni na jānanti “mayaṃ vammikamatthake jātānī”ti; napi vammikamatthako jānāti “mayi kuṇṭhatiṇāni jātānī”ti; evameva na kesā jānanti “mayaṃ sīsacamme jātā”ti, napi sīsacammaṃ jānāti “mayi kesā jātā”ti. Ābhogapaccavekkhaṇavirahitā hi ete dhammā acetanā abyākatā suññā paramaduggandhajegucchappaṭikūlā, na satto na puggaloti vavatthapeti. Paricchedatoti duvidho paricchedo sabhāgavisabhāgavasena. Tattha kesā heṭṭhā patiṭṭhitacammatalena tattha vīhaggamattaṃ pavisitvā patiṭṭhitena attano mūlatalena ca upari ākāsena tiriyaṃ aññamaññena paricchinnāti evaṃ sabhāgaparicchedato, kesā na avasesaekatiṃsākārā. Avasesā ekatiṃsā na kesāti evaṃ visabhāgaparicchedato ca vavatthapeti. Evaṃ tāva kese vaṇṇādito vavatthapeti.

Here it is said: "But how does one determine these thirty-two bodily parts by way of color and so on?" Indeed, one who develops these thirty-two bodily parts by way of the division of the skin-pentad and so on, beginning with "There are in this body head-hairs," first determines the head-hairs by color as black, such as have been seen. By shape, they are determined as long and cylindrical, like the beam of a balance. By direction, since in this body the part above the navel is called the upper direction and the part below the lower direction, it is determined that they grow in the upper direction of this body. By location, they are determined as growing on the skin of the head, bounded by the edge of the forehead, the tips of the ears, the crown, and the nape of the neck. Therein, just as stunted grass growing on an anthill does not know, "We grow on an anthill," nor does the anthill know, "Stunted grass grows on me," so too, the head-hairs do not know, "We grow on the skin of the head," nor does the skin of the head know, "Head-hairs grow on me." For these phenomena are devoid of reflection and deliberation, non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, utterly foul, disgusting, and repulsive. It is determined that they are neither a being nor a person. As for delimitation, there are two kinds of delimitation: homogeneous and heterogeneous. Herein, the head-hairs are delimited below by the surface of the skin in which they are established and by their own root-base, which is established therein having penetrated to the extent of a grain of rice; they are delimited above by space, and horizontally by one another—thus by homogeneous delimitation. The head-hairs are not the remaining thirty-one parts, and the remaining thirty-one parts are not the head-hairs—thus by heterogeneous delimitation. In this way, first, the head-hairs are determined by way of color and so on.

Avasesesu lomā vaṇṇato yebhuyyena nīlavaṇṇāti vavatthapeti, yādisakā vānena diṭṭhā honti. Saṇṭhānato oṇatacāpasaṇṭhānā, upari vaṅkatālahīrasaṇṭhānā vā, disato dvīsu disāsu jātā, okāsato hatthatalapādatale ṭhapetvā yebhuyyena avasesasarīracamme [P 0.0043] jātāti.

Among the remaining parts, the body-hairs are determined by color as being for the most part dark, or of whatever sort have been seen by him. By shape, they have the shape of a bent bow, or the shape of a palmyra fiber curved at the tip. By direction, they grow in the two directions. By location, excluding the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet, they grow for the most part on the skin of the remaining body.

Tattha yathā purāṇagāmaṭṭhāne jātāni dabbatiṇāni na jānanti “mayaṃ purāṇagāmaṭṭhāne jātānī”ti, na ca purāṇagāmaṭṭhānaṃ jānāti “mayi dabbatiṇāni jātānī”ti, evameva na lomā jānanti “mayaṃ sarīracamme jātā”ti, napi sarīracammaṃ jānāti “mayi lomā jātā”ti. Ābhogapaccavekkhaṇavirahitā hi ete dhammā acetanā abyākatā suññā [M 0.0033] paramaduggandhajegucchapaṭikūlā, na satto na puggaloti vavatthapeti. Paricchedato heṭṭhā patiṭṭhitacammatalena tattha likkhāmattaṃ pavisitvā patiṭṭhitena attano mūlena ca upari ākāsena tiriyaṃ aññamaññena paricchinnāti vavatthapeti. Ayametesaṃ sabhāgaparicchedo, visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadiso evāti evaṃ lome vaṇṇādito vavatthapeti.

Therein, just as the dabba grass growing on an old village site does not know, 'We grow on an old village site,' nor does the old village site know, 'Dabba grass grows on me,' even so, the body-hairs do not know, 'We grow on the skin of the body,' nor does the skin of the body know, 'Body-hairs grow on me.' For these phenomena are devoid of reflection and deliberation, non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, utterly foul-smelling, disgusting, and repulsive. One determines that they are neither a being nor a person. As for delimitation, one determines that they are delimited below by the surface of the skin in which they are established and by their own root, which is established therein having penetrated to the extent of a nit; above by space; and horizontally by one another. This is their homogeneous delimitation. The heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like that of the head-hairs. Thus one determines the body-hairs by way of color and so on.

Tato paraṃ nakhā yassa paripuṇṇā, tassa vīsati. Te sabbepi vaṇṇato maṃsavinimuttokāse [V 0.0033] setā, maṃsasambandhe tambavaṇṇāti vavatthapeti. Saṇṭhānato yathāsakapatiṭṭhitokāsasaṇṭhānā, yebhuyyena madhukaphalaṭṭhikasaṇṭhānā, macchasakalikasaṇṭhānā vāti vavatthapeti. Disato dvīsu disāsu jātā, okāsato aṅgulīnaṃ aggesu patiṭṭhitāti.

Next, the nails. For one for whom they are complete, there are twenty. One determines that by color, they are all white in the area free from flesh, and of a reddish color where connected to the flesh. One determines that by shape, they have the shape of the place where each is established, and for the most part have the shape of a madhuka fruit seed, or the shape of a fish scale. By direction, they grow in the two directions. By location, they are situated at the tips of the fingers and toes.

Tattha yathā nāma gāmadārakehi daṇḍakaggesu madhukaphalaṭṭhikā ṭhapitā na jānanti “mayaṃ daṇḍakaggesu ṭhapitā”ti, napi daṇḍakā jānanti “amhesu madhukaphalaṭṭhikā ṭhapitā”ti; evameva nakhā na jānanti “mayaṃ aṅgulīnaṃ aggesu patiṭṭhitā”ti, napi aṅguliyo jānanti “amhākaṃ aggesu nakhā patiṭṭhitā”ti. Ābhogapaccavekkhaṇavirahitā hi ete dhammā acetanā…pe… na puggaloti vavatthapeti. Paricchedato heṭṭhā mūle ca aṅgulimaṃsena, tattha patiṭṭhitatalena vā upari agge ca ākāsena, ubhatopassesu aṅgulīnaṃ ubhatokoṭicammena paricchinnāti vavatthapeti. Ayametesaṃ sabhāgaparicchedo, visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadiso evāti evaṃ nakhe vaṇṇādito vavatthapeti.

Therein, just as madhuka fruit seeds placed by village children on the tips of sticks do not know, 'We are placed on the tips of sticks,' nor do the sticks know, 'Madhuka fruit seeds are placed on us'; so too, the nails do not know, 'We are situated at the tips of the fingers and toes,' nor do the fingers and toes know, 'Nails are situated at our tips.' Indeed, these phenomena are devoid of advertence and reviewing, are without consciousness... (etc.)... not a person: thus one determines. As for delimitation: one determines that they are delimited below at the base by the flesh of the fingers and toes or by the surface established there; above at the tip by space; and on both sides by the skin at both ends of the fingers and toes. This is their homogeneous delimitation. As for the heterogeneous delimitation, it is just like that of the hair. Thus one determines the nails from the perspective of color and so on.

Tato paraṃ dantā yassa paripuṇṇā, tassa dvattiṃsa. Te sabbepi vaṇṇato setavaṇṇāti vavatthapeti. Yassa samasaṇṭhitā honti, tassa kharapattacchinnasaṅkhapaṭalamiva samaganthitasetakusumamakuḷamālā [P 0.0044] viya ca khāyanti. Yassa visamasaṇṭhitā, tassa jiṇṇaāsanasālāpīṭhakapaṭipāṭi viya nānāsaṇṭhānāti saṇṭhānato vavatthapeti. Tesañhi ubhayadantapantipariyosānesu heṭṭhato uparito ca dve dve katvā aṭṭha dantā catukoṭikā catumūlikā āsandikasaṇṭhānā, tesaṃ orato teneva [M 0.0034] kamena sanniviṭṭhā aṭṭha dantā tikoṭikā timūlikā siṅghāṭakasaṇṭhānā. Tesampi orato teneva kamena heṭṭhato uparito ca ekamekaṃ katvā cattāro dantā dvikoṭikā dvimūlikā yānakūpatthambhinīsaṇṭhānā. Tesampi orato teneva kamena sanniviṭṭhā cattāro dāṭhādantā ekakoṭikā ekamūlikā mallikāmakuḷasaṇṭhānā. Tato ubhayadantapantivemajjhe heṭṭhā cattāro upari cattāro katvā aṭṭha dantā ekakoṭikā ekamūlikā tumbabījasaṇṭhānā. Disato uparimāya disāya jātā. Okāsato uparimā uparimahanukaṭṭhike adhokoṭikā, heṭṭhimā heṭṭhimahanukaṭṭhike uddhaṃkoṭikā hutvā patiṭṭhitāti.

After that, the teeth. For one for whom they are complete, there are thirty-two. One determines that, by color, all of them are white. For one whose teeth are evenly arranged, they appear like a slab of conch shell cut by a saw and like a garland of evenly strung, white jasmine buds. For one whose teeth are unevenly arranged, they have various shapes, like the row of seats in an old, dilapidated rest house; thus one determines them by shape. Indeed, among them, at the ends of both rows of teeth, there are eight teeth, two each below and above, that have four points and four roots and are shaped like a long-legged chair. Inward from these, arranged in the same sequence, are eight teeth that have three points and three roots and are shaped like a three-way crossroads. Inward from these as well, arranged in the same sequence, are four teeth, two below and two above, that have two points and two roots and are shaped like a chariot prop. Inward from these as well, arranged in the same sequence, are four canine teeth that have one point and one root and are shaped like a jasmine bud. Then, in the middle of both rows of teeth, there are eight teeth, four below and four above, that have one point and one root and are shaped like a gourd seed. By direction, they arise in the upper region of the body. By location, the upper teeth are situated in the upper jawbone with their points facing downwards, while the lower teeth are situated in the lower jawbone with their points facing upwards.

Tattha yathā navakammikapurisena heṭṭhā silātale patiṭṭhāpitā uparimatale pavesitā thambhā na jānanti “mayaṃ heṭṭhāsilātale patiṭṭhāpitā, uparimatale pavesitā”ti, na heṭṭhāsilātalaṃ jānāti “mayi thambhā patiṭṭhāpitā”ti, na uparimatalaṃ jānāti “mayi thambhā paviṭṭhā”ti; evameva dantā na jānanti “mayaṃ heṭṭhāhanukaṭṭhike patiṭṭhitā, uparimahanukaṭṭhike paviṭṭhā”ti, nāpi [V 0.0034] heṭṭhāhanukaṭṭhikaṃ jānāti “mayi dantā patiṭṭhitā”ti, na uparimahanukaṭṭhikaṃ jānāti “mayi dantā paviṭṭhā”ti. Ābhogapaccavekkhaṇavirahitā hi ete dhammā…pe… na puggaloti. Paricchedato heṭṭhā hanukaṭṭhikūpena hanukaṭṭhikaṃ pavisitvā patiṭṭhitena attano mūlatalena ca upari ākāsena tiriyaṃ aññamaññena paricchinnāti vavatthapeti. Ayametesaṃ sabhāgaparicchedo, visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadiso evāti evaṃ dante vaṇṇādito vavatthapeti[P 0.0045].

Therein, just as pillars established by a new worker on the lower stone floor and inserted into the upper floor do not know, 'We are established on the lower stone floor and inserted into the upper floor,' nor does the lower stone floor know, 'Pillars are established on me,' nor does the upper floor know, 'Pillars have been inserted into me'; so too, the teeth do not know, 'We are established in the lower jawbone and have entered the upper jawbone,' nor does the lower jawbone know, 'Teeth are established in me,' nor does the upper jawbone know, 'Teeth have entered me.' Indeed, these phenomena are devoid of advertence and reviewing... (etc.)... not a person. As for delimitation: one determines that they are delimited below by the socket of the jawbone and by their own root-surface which has entered and become established in the jawbone; above by space; and horizontally by one another. This is their homogeneous delimitation. As for the heterogeneous delimitation, it is just like that of the hair. Thus one determines the teeth from the perspective of color and so on.

Tato paraṃ antosarīre nānākuṇapasañcayappaṭicchādakaṃ taco vaṇṇato setoti vavatthapeti. So hi yadipi chavirāgarañjitattā kāḷakodātādivaṇṇavasena nānāvaṇṇo viya dissati, tathāpi sabhāgavaṇṇena seto eva. So panassa setabhāvo aggijālābhighātapaharaṇapahārādīhi viddhaṃsitāya chaviyā pākaṭo hoti. Saṇṭhānato saṅkhepena kañcukasaṇṭhāno, vitthārena nānāsaṇṭhānoti. Tathā hi pādaṅgulittaco kosakārakakosasaṇṭhāno, piṭṭhipādattaco puṭabaddhūpāhanasaṇṭhāno, jaṅghattaco bhattapuṭakatālapaṇṇasaṇṭhāno[M 0.0035], ūruttaco taṇḍulabharitadīghatthavikasaṇṭhāno, ānisadattaco udakapūritapaṭaparissāvanasaṇṭhāno, piṭṭhittaco phalakonaddhacammasaṇṭhāno, kucchittaco vīṇādoṇikonaddhacammasaṇṭhāno, urattaco yebhuyyena caturassasaṇṭhāno, dvibāhuttaco tūṇīronaddhacammasaṇṭhāno, piṭṭhihatthattaco khurakosasaṇṭhāno phaṇakatthavikasaṇṭhāno vā, hatthaṅgulittaco kuñcikākosasaṇṭhāno, gīvattaco galakañcukasaṇṭhāno, mukhattaco chiddāvachiddakimikulāvakasaṇṭhāno, sīsattaco pattatthavikasaṇṭhānoti.

After that, one determines that the skin, which covers the various accumulations of impurities within the body, is white by color. For although it appears multicolored—by way of colors such as black, white, and so on—due to being colored by the passion for the complexion, it is nevertheless white by its own natural color. This whiteness of it becomes apparent in a complexion that has been destroyed by the striking of fire-flames, blows, attacks, and so on. By shape, it is briefly shaped like a tunic; in detail, it has various shapes. Thus: the skin on the toes is shaped like a silkworm's cocoon; the skin on the back of the foot is shaped like a shoe bound over the instep; the skin on the shin is shaped like a palm-leaf container with wrapped rice; the skin on the thigh is shaped like a long sack filled with rice; the skin on the buttocks is shaped like a cloth water-strainer filled with water; the skin on the back is shaped like a hide stretched over a plank; the skin on the belly is shaped like a hide stretched over the body of a lute; the skin on the chest is for the most part square-shaped; the skin on the two arms is shaped like a leather covering for a quiver; the skin on the back of the hand is shaped like a razor case or a comb case; the skin on the fingers is shaped like a key case; the skin on the neck is shaped like the neck-part of a tunic; the skin on the face is shaped like a worm's nest riddled with holes; and the skin on the head is shaped like a bowl-bag.

Tacapariggaṇhakena ca yogāvacarena uttaroṭṭhato paṭṭhāya tacassa maṃsassa ca antarena cittaṃ pesentena paṭhamaṃ tāva mukhattaco vavatthapetabbo, tato sīsattaco, atha bahigīvattaco, tato anulomena paṭilomena ca dakkhiṇahatthattaco. Atha teneva kamena vāmahatthattaco, tato piṭṭhittaco, atha ānisadattaco, tato anulomena paṭilomena ca dakkhiṇapādattaco, atha vāmapādattaco, tato vatthiudarahadayaabbhantaragīvattaco, tato heṭṭhimahanukattaco, atha adharoṭṭhattaco. Evaṃ yāva puna upari oṭṭhattacoti[P 0.0046]. Disato dvīsu disāsu jāto. Okāsato sakalasarīraṃ pariyonandhitvā ṭhitoti.

And by the meditator who comprehends the skin, sending the mind between the skin and the flesh, starting from the upper lip, first the skin of the face should be determined; then the skin of the head; then the outer skin of the neck; then, both forwards and backwards, the skin of the right arm. Then, in the same way, the skin of the left arm; then the skin of the back; then the skin of the buttocks; then, both forwards and backwards, the skin of the right leg; then the skin of the left leg; then the skin of the bladder, abdomen, heart, and inner neck; then the skin of the lower jaw; then the skin of the lower lip. Thus, it should be determined again up to the skin of the upper lip. In terms of direction, it arises in two directions. In terms of location, it stands having enveloped the entire body.

Tattha yathā allacammapariyonaddhāya peḷāya na allacammaṃ jānāti “mayā peḷā pariyonaddhā”ti, napi peḷā jānāti “ahaṃ allacammena pariyonaddhā”ti; evameva na taco jānāti “mayā idaṃ cātumahābhūtikaṃ sarīraṃ onaddha”nti, napi idaṃ cātumahābhūtikaṃ sarīraṃ jānāti [V 0.0035] “ahaṃ tacena onaddha”nti. Ābhogapaccavekkhaṇavirahitā hi ete dhammā…pe… na puggaloti. Kevalaṃ tu –

Therein, just as in the case of a box enveloped with wet leather, the wet leather does not know, 'By me the box is enveloped,' nor does the box know, 'I am enveloped by wet leather'; in the same way, the skin does not know, 'By me this body composed of the four great elements is enveloped,' nor does this body composed of the four great elements know, 'I am enveloped by the skin.' For these phenomena are devoid of directing the mind and reviewing... [etc.]... not a person. It is merely that—

“Allacammapaṭicchanno, navadvāro mahāvaṇo;

Samantato paggharati, asucipūtigandhiyo”ti.

Covered with wet skin, a great wound with nine doors; from all around the impure oozes, and it is putrid-smelling.

Paricchedato heṭṭhā maṃsena tattha patiṭṭhitatalena vā upari chaviyā paricchinnoti vavatthapeti. Ayametassa sabhāgaparicchedo, visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadiso evāti evaṃ tacaṃ vaṇṇādito vavatthapeti.

In terms of delimitation, one determines thus: below, it is delimited by the flesh or by the surface established thereon; above, it is delimited by the epidermis. This is its delimitation by similar nature; the delimitation by dissimilar nature, however, is just like that of the hair. Thus, one determines the skin by its color and other characteristics.

Tato [M 0.0036] paraṃ sarīre navapesisatappabhedaṃ maṃsaṃ vaṇṇato rattaṃ pālibhaddakapupphasannibhanti vavatthapeti. Saṇṭhānato nānāsaṇṭhānanti. Tathā hi tattha jaṅghamaṃsaṃ tālapattapuṭabhattasaṇṭhānaṃ, avikasitaketakīmakuḷasaṇṭhānantipi keci. Ūrumaṃsaṃ sudhāpisananisadapotakasaṇṭhānaṃ, ānisadamaṃsaṃ uddhanakoṭisaṇṭhānaṃ, piṭṭhimaṃsaṃ tālaguḷapaṭalasaṇṭhānaṃ, phāsukadvayamaṃsaṃ vaṃsamayakoṭṭhakucchipadesamhi tanumattikālepasaṇṭhānaṃ, thanamaṃsaṃ vaṭṭetvā avakkhittaddhamattikāpiṇḍasaṇṭhānaṃ, dvebāhumaṃsaṃ naṅguṭṭhasīsapāde chetvā niccammaṃ katvā ṭhapitamahāmūsikasaṇṭhānaṃ, maṃsasūnakasaṇṭhānantipi eke. Gaṇḍamaṃsaṃ gaṇḍappadese ṭhapitakarañjabījasaṇṭhānaṃ, maṇḍūkasaṇṭhānantipi eke. Jivhāmaṃsaṃ nuhīpattasaṇṭhānaṃ, nāsāmaṃsaṃ omukhanikkhittapaṇṇakosasaṇṭhānaṃ, 0.akkhikūpamaṃsaṃ addhapakkaudumbarasaṇṭhānaṃ, sīsamaṃsaṃ pattapacanakaṭāhatanulepasaṇṭhānanti[P 0.0047]. Maṃsapariggaṇhakena ca yogāvacarena etāneva oḷārikamaṃsāni saṇṭhānato vavatthapetabbāni. Evañhi vavatthāpayato sukhumāni maṃsāni ñāṇassa āpāthaṃ āgacchantīti. Disato dvīsu disāsu jātaṃ. Okāsato sādhikāni tīṇi aṭṭhisatāni anulimpitvā ṭhitanti.

Next, one determines the flesh in the body, which is divided into nine hundred pieces, as being red in color, resembling the coral tree flower. In shape, it is of various forms. Indeed, therein the flesh of the calf is shaped like a food-parcel wrapped in a palm leaf; some say it is also shaped like an unopened screwpine bud. The thigh flesh is shaped like a grinding stone for lime plaster. The buttock flesh is shaped like the top of a stove. The back flesh is shaped like a palm-sugar slab. The flesh of the two ribs is shaped like a thin plaster of mud on the belly-region of a bamboo granary. The breast flesh is shaped like a rounded lump of wet clay that has been thrown down. The flesh of the two arms is shaped like a large rat placed there after its tail, head, and feet have been cut off and its skin removed; some also say it is shaped like a piece of meat on a stake. The cheek flesh is shaped like a karañja seed placed in the cheek area; some also say it is shaped like a frog. The tongue flesh is shaped like a spurge leaf. The nose flesh is shaped like a leaf-cone placed with its opening downwards. The flesh of the eye-socket is shaped like a half-ripe fig. The head flesh is shaped like a thin plaster on a bowl-baking pot. And by the meditator who comprehends the flesh, these very coarse pieces of flesh should be determined by their shapes. For when one determines thus, the finer pieces of flesh come into the range of knowledge. In terms of direction, it arises in two directions. In terms of location, it stands having plastered over more than three hundred bones.

Tattha yathā thūlamattikānulittāya bhittiyā na thūlamattikā jānāti “mayā bhitti anulittā”ti, napi bhitti jānāti “ahaṃ thūlamattikāya anulittā”ti, evamevaṃ na navapesisatappabhedaṃ maṃsaṃ jānāti “mayā aṭṭhisatattayaṃ anulitta”nti, napi aṭṭhisatattayaṃ jānāti “ahaṃ navapesisatappabhedena maṃsena anulitta”nti. Ābhogapaccavekkhaṇavirahitā hi ete dhammā…pe… na puggaloti. Kevalaṃ tu –

Therein, just as in the case of a wall plastered with coarse clay, the coarse clay does not know, 'By me the wall is plastered,' nor does the wall know, 'I am plastered by coarse clay'; even so, the flesh divided into nine hundred pieces does not know, 'By me the collection of three hundred bones is plastered,' nor does the collection of three hundred bones know, 'I am plastered by the flesh divided into nine hundred pieces.' For these phenomena are devoid of directing the mind and reviewing... [etc.]... not a person. It is merely that—

“Navapesisatā [V 0.0036] maṃsā, anulittā kaḷevaraṃ;

Nānākimikulākiṇṇaṃ, mīḷhaṭṭhānaṃva pūtika”nti.

The nine hundred pieces of flesh plaster the body, which, swarming with various kinds of worms, is putrid, like a place of filth.

Paricchedato heṭṭhā aṭṭhisaṅghāṭena tattha patiṭṭhitatalena vā upari tacena tiriyaṃ aññamaññena paricchinnanti vavatthapeti. Ayametassa sabhāgaparicchedo, visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadiso evāti evaṃ maṃsaṃ vaṇṇādito vavatthapeti.

In terms of delimitation, one determines thus: below, it is delimited by the framework of bones or by the surface established thereon; above, by the skin; and horizontally, by each other. This is its delimitation by similar nature; the delimitation by dissimilar nature, however, is just like that of the hair. Thus, one determines the flesh by its color and other characteristics.

Tato paraṃ sarīre navasatappabhedā nhārū vaṇṇato setāti vavatthapeti, madhuvaṇṇātipi eke. Saṇṭhānato nānāsaṇṭhānāti. Tathā [M 0.0037] hi tattha mahantā mahantā nhārū kandalamakuḷasaṇṭhānā, tato sukhumatarā sūkaravāgurarajjusaṇṭhānā, tato aṇukatarā pūtilatāsaṇṭhānā, tato aṇukatarā sīhaḷamahāvīṇātantisaṇṭhānā, tato aṇukatarā thūlasuttakasaṇṭhānā, hatthapiṭṭhipādapiṭṭhīsu nhārū sakuṇapādasaṇṭhānā, sīse nhārū gāmadārakānaṃ sīse [P 0.0048] ṭhapitaviraḷataradukūlasaṇṭhānā, piṭṭhiyā nhārū temetvā ātape pasāritamacchajālasaṇṭhānā, avasesā imasmiṃ sarīre taṃtaṃaṅgapaccaṅgānugatā nhārū sarīre paṭimukkajālakañcukasaṇṭhānāti. Disato dvīsu disāsu jātā. Tesu ca dakkhiṇakaṇṇacūḷikato paṭṭhāya pañca kaṇḍaranāmakā mahānhārū purato ca pacchato ca vinandhamānā vāmapassaṃ gatā, vāmakaṇṇacūḷikato paṭṭhāya pañca purato ca pacchato ca vinandhamānā dakkhiṇapassaṃ gatā, dakkhiṇagalavāṭakato paṭṭhāya pañca purato ca pacchato ca vinandhamānā vāmapassaṃ gatā, vāmagalavāṭakato paṭṭhāya pañca purato ca pacchato ca vinandhamānā dakkhiṇapassaṃ gatā, dakkhiṇahatthaṃ vinandhamānā purato ca pacchato ca pañca pañcāti dasa kaṇḍaranāmakā eva mahānhārū āruḷhā. Tathā vāmahatthaṃ, dakkhiṇapādaṃ, vāmapādañcāti evamete saṭṭhi mahānhārū sarīradhārakā sarīraniyāmakātipi vavatthapeti. Okāsato sakalasarīre aṭṭhicammānaṃ aṭṭhimaṃsānañca antare aṭṭhīni ābandhamānā ṭhitāti.

Next, in the body, one determines that the nine hundred kinds of sinews are white by way of color; some also say they are honey-colored. By way of shape, they are of various shapes. Indeed, among them, the very large sinews have the shape of jasmine buds; those finer than them have the shape of a rope for a pig-trap; those finer still have the shape of a pūtilatā creeper; those finer still have the shape of the great lute-string of the Sinhalese; those finer yet have the shape of a coarse thread. The sinews on the back of the hands and the back of the feet have the shape of a bird’s feet. The sinews on the head have the shape of a very loosely woven white cloth placed on the head of village boys. The sinews on the back have the shape of a fishing net that has been wetted and spread out in the sun. The remaining sinews in this body, following those various major and minor limbs, have the shape of a mesh coat put on the body. By way of direction, they arise in two directions. And among them, starting from the tip of the right ear, five great sinews named kaṇḍara, interlacing both in front and behind, go to the left side. Starting from the tip of the left ear, five, interlacing both in front and behind, go to the right side. Starting from the right side of the neck, five, interlacing both in front and behind, go to the left side. Starting from the left side of the neck, five, interlacing both in front and behind, go to the right side. Interlacing the right arm, five in front and five behind, thus ten great sinews named kaṇḍara ascend. Similarly for the left arm, the right foot, and the left foot. Thus, one also determines that these sixty great sinews are supporters of the body and definers of the body. By way of location, one determines that they are situated throughout the entire body between the bones and skin and between the bones and flesh, binding the bones.

Tattha yathā vallisantānabaddhesu kuṭṭadārūsu na vallisantānā jānanti “amhehi kuṭṭadārūni ābaddhānī”ti, napi kuṭṭadārūni jānanti “mayaṃ vallisantānehi ābaddhānī”ti; evameva na nhārū jānanti “amhehi tīṇi aṭṭhisatāni ābaddhānī”ti, napi tīṇi aṭṭhisatāni jānanti “mayaṃ nhārūhi ābaddhānī”ti. Ābhogapaccavekkhaṇavirahitā hi ete dhammā…pe… na puggaloti. Kevalaṃ tu –

Therein, just as in the case of wall-timbers bound with a series of creepers, the series of creepers do not know, “We have bound the wall-timbers,” nor do the wall-timbers know, “We are bound by the series of creepers”; in the very same way, the sinews do not know, “We have bound the three hundred bones,” nor do the three hundred bones know, “We are bound by the sinews.” For these phenomena are devoid of advertence and reflection... not a person. Merely, however—

“Navanhārusatā [V 0.0037] honti, byāmamatte kaḷevare;

Bandhanti aṭṭhisaṅghāṭaṃ, agāramiva valliyo”ti.

“There are nine hundred sinews in a body of a fathom’s measure; they bind the collection of bones, like creepers an abode.”

Paricchedato heṭṭhā tīhi aṭṭhisatehi tattha patiṭṭhitatalehi vā upari tacamaṃsehi tiriyaṃ aññamaññena paricchinnāti vavatthapeti. Ayametesaṃ sabhāgaparicchedo, visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadiso evāti evaṃ nhārū vaṇṇādito [P 0.0049] vavatthapeti.

By way of delimitation, one determines that they are delimited below by the three hundred bones or the surfaces established thereon, above by the skin and flesh, and transversely by one another. This is their delimitation by what is homogeneous; but the delimitation by what is heterogeneous is just like that of the head hairs. Thus one determines the sinews by way of color, etc.
