And when the bladder is full of urine, beings have the impulse, 'We shall urinate.' Therein, just as the cesspool water situated in the sealed earthen pot does not know, 'I am situated in the sealed earthen pot,' nor does the sealed earthen pot know, 'Cesspool water is situated in me'; even so, the urine does not know, 'I am situated in the bladder,' nor does the bladder know, 'Urine is situated in me.' For these phenomena are devoid of advertence and reflection... not a person. By way of delimitation, one determines that it is delimited by the interior of the bladder and by the part that is urine. This is its homogeneous delimitation; its heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like the hair. In this way, one determines urine by way of color and so forth. In this way, this practitioner determines these thirty-two aspects by way of color and so forth.

Tassevaṃ imaṃ dvattiṃsākāraṃ vaṇṇādivasena vavatthapentassa taṃ taṃ bhāvanānuyogaṃ āgamma kesādayo paguṇā honti, koṭṭhāsabhāvena upaṭṭhahanti. Tato pabhuti seyyathāpi nāma cakkhumato purisassa dvattiṃsavaṇṇānaṃ pupphānaṃ ekasuttaganthitaṃ mālaṃ olokentassa sabbapupphāni apubbāpariyamiva pākaṭāni honti; evameva “atthi imasmiṃ kāye [M 0.0056] kesā”ti imaṃ kāyaṃ satiyā olokentassa sabbe te dhammā apubbāpariyamiva pākaṭā honti. Kesesu āvajjitesu [V 0.0053] asaṇṭhahamānāva sati yāva muttaṃ, tāva pavattati. Tato pabhuti tassa āhiṇḍantā manussatiracchānādayo ca sattākāraṃ vijahitvā koṭṭhāsarāsivaseneva upaṭṭhahanti, tehi ca ajjhohariyamānaṃ pānabhojanādi koṭṭhāsarāsimhi pakkhippamānamiva upaṭṭhātīti.

For one who thus defines these thirty-two parts by way of color and so on, depending on that particular application to meditation, the hair of the head and other parts become familiar and present themselves as portions. From then on, just as for a man with eyesight looking at a garland of flowers of thirty-two colors strung on a single thread, all the flowers become manifest as if without before or after; even so, for one looking at this body with mindfulness, thinking, 'In this body there is hair of the head,' all those phenomena become manifest as if without before or after. When attention is directed to the hair of the head, mindfulness, without wavering, proceeds as far as the urine. From then on, wandering humans, animals, and so on, appear to that person having abandoned the aspect of a 'being' and only by way of a heap of parts. And drink, food, and so on, being consumed by them, appears as if being put into that heap of parts.

Etthāha “athānena tato paraṃ kiṃ kātabba”nti? Vuccate – tadeva nimittaṃ āsevitabbaṃ bhāvetabbaṃ bahulīkātabbaṃ suvavatthitaṃ vavatthapetabbaṃ. Kathaṃ panāyaṃ taṃ nimittaṃ āsevati bhāveti bahulīkaroti suvavatthitaṃ vavatthapetīti? Ayañhi taṃ kesādīnaṃ koṭṭhāsabhāvena upaṭṭhānanimittaṃ āsevati, satiyā alliyati bhajati upagacchati, satigabbhaṃ gaṇhāpeti. Tattha laddhaṃ vā satiṃ vaḍḍhento taṃ bhāvetīti vuccati. Bahulīkarotīti punappunaṃ satisampayuttaṃ vitakkavicārabbhāhataṃ karoti. Suvavatthitaṃ vavatthapetīti yathā suṭṭhu vavatthitaṃ hoti, na puna antaradhānaṃ gacchati, tathā taṃ satiyā vavatthapeti, upadhāreti upanibandhati.

Here a questioner asks: 'Then what should be done by this person after that?' It is said: that very sign should be resorted to, developed, made much of, and well-defined. But how does this person resort to, develop, make much of, and well-define that sign? This person resorts to that sign of the appearance of hair of the head, etc., as parts; with mindfulness one adheres to it, associates with it, approaches it, and makes mindfulness its core. Therein, by increasing the mindfulness that has been gained, it is said that one 'develops' it. 'Making much of it' means one repeatedly brings it about, impelled by thought and examination associated with mindfulness. 'Well-defining it' means that one defines it with mindfulness in such a way that it becomes well-defined and does not disappear again; one sustains it, one fastens it.

Atha vā yaṃ [P 0.0070] pubbe anupubbato, nātisīghato, nātisaṇikato, vikkhepappahānato, paṇṇattisamatikkamanato, anupubbamuñcanato, lakkhaṇato, tayo ca suttantāti evaṃ dasavidhaṃ manasikārakosallaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha anupubbato manasikaronto āsevati, nātisīghato nātisaṇikato ca manasikaronto bhāveti, vikkhepappahānato manasikaronto bahulī karoti, paṇṇattisamatikkamanādito manasikaronto suvavatthitaṃ vavatthapetīti veditabbo.

Alternatively, there is the tenfold skill in attention that was previously mentioned: by way of gradualness, not too fast, not too slow, by abandoning distraction, by transcending concepts, by gradual relinquishment, by way of characteristic, and the three suttantas. Therein, one who attends by way of gradualness 'resorts to it.' One who attends not too fast and not too slow 'develops it.' One who attends by abandoning distraction 'makes much of it.' It should be understood that one who attends by way of transcending concepts and so on 'well-defines it.'

Etthāha “kathaṃ panāyaṃ anupubbādivasena ete dhamme manasi karotī”ti? Vuccate – ayañhi kese manasi karitvā tadanantaraṃ lome manasi karoti, na nakhe. Tathā lome manasi karitvā tadanantaraṃ nakhe manasi karoti, na dante. Esa nayo sabbattha. Kasmā? Uppaṭipāṭiyā hi manasikaronto seyyathāpi nāma akusalo puriso dvattiṃsapadaṃ nisseṇiṃ uppaṭipāṭiyā ārohanto kilantakāyo tato nisseṇito [M 0.0057] papatati, na ārohanaṃ sampādeti; evameva bhāvanāsampattivasena adhigantabbassa assādassa anadhigamanato kilantacitto dvattiṃsākārabhāvanāto papatati, na bhāvanaṃ sampādetīti.

Here a questioner asks: 'But how does this person attend to these phenomena by way of gradualness and so on?' It is said: This person, having attended to the hair of the head, immediately after attends to the hair of the body, not the nails. Similarly, having attended to the hair of the body, immediately after one attends to the nails, not the teeth. This is the method in all cases. Why? Because one who attends out of order is like an unskilled person who, climbing a ladder with thirty-two rungs out of order, becomes weary in body, falls from that ladder, and does not accomplish the ascent. Even so, due to not attaining the satisfaction that should be attained through the accomplishment of the development, the mind becomes weary, one falls away from the development of the thirty-two parts, and does not accomplish the development.

Anupubbato manasikarontopi ca kesā lomāti nātisīghatopi manasi karoti. Atisīghato hi manasikaronto seyyathāpi nāma addhānaṃ gacchanto puriso samavisamarukkhathalaninnadvedhāpathādīni magganimittāni upalakkhetuṃ na sakkoti, tato na maggakusalo hoti, addhānañca parikkhayaṃ neti; evameva vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādīni dvattiṃsākāranimittāni [V 0.0054] upalakkhetuṃ na sakkoti, tato na dvattiṃsākāre kusalo hoti, kammaṭṭhānañca parikkhayaṃ neti.

And one who attends by way of gradualness also attends to 'hair of the head, hair of the body,' and so on, not too quickly. For one who attends too quickly is like a person traveling a long road who is not able to observe the signs of the path—such as level and uneven ground, trees, highlands, lowlands, and forked paths; therefore, one is not skilled in the thirty-two parts and brings the meditation subject to ruin.

Yathā ca nātisīghato, evaṃ nātisaṇikatopi manasi karoti. Atisaṇikato hi manasikaronto seyyathāpi nāma puriso addhānamaggaṃ paṭipanno antarāmagge rukkhapabbatataḷākādīsu vilambamāno icchitappadesaṃ apāpuṇanto antarāmaggeyeva sīhabyagghādīhi anayabyasanaṃ pāpuṇāti; evameva dvattiṃsākārabhāvanāsampadaṃ apāpuṇanto [P 0.0071] bhāvanāvicchedena antarāyeva kāmavitakkādīhi anayabyasanaṃ pāpuṇāti.

And just as one attends not too quickly, so too one attends not too slowly. For one who attends too slowly is like a person who, having set out on a long road, lingers along the way among trees, mountains, ponds, and so on, and not reaching the desired destination, meets with misfortune and ruin from lions, tigers, and so on, right on the path. Even so, not reaching the accomplishment of the development of the thirty-two parts, one meets with misfortune and ruin from sensual thoughts and so on, right in the middle of it, due to the interruption of the development.

Nātisaṇikato manasikarontopi ca vikkhepappahānatopi manasi karoti. Vikkhepappahānato nāma yathā aññesu navakammādīsu cittaṃ na vikkhipati, tathā manasi karoti. Bahiddhā vikkhepamānacitto hi kesādīsveva asamāhitacetovitakko bhāvanāsampadaṃ apāpuṇitvā antarāva anayabyasanaṃ āpajjati takkasilāgamane bodhisattassa sahāyakā viya. Avikkhipamānacitto pana kesādīsveva samāhitacetovitakko bhāvanāsampadaṃ pāpuṇāti bodhisatto viya takkasilarajjasampadanti. Tassevaṃ vikkhepappahānato manasikaroto adhikāracariyādhimuttīnaṃ vasena te dhammā asubhato vā vaṇṇato vā suññato vā upaṭṭhahanti.

And one who attends not too slowly also attends by abandoning distraction. 'Abandoning distraction' means that one attends in such a way that the mind is not distracted by other things like new work, and so on. For one whose mind is distracted externally, with thoughts and mind unconcentrated on the hair of the head and other parts, not having reached the accomplishment of the development, meets with misfortune and ruin midway, like the Bodhisatta's companions on the way to Takkasilā. But one with an undistracted mind, with thoughts and mind concentrated on the hair of the head and other parts, reaches the accomplishment of the development, like the Bodhisatta reaching the royal fortune of Takkasilā. For one who thus attends by abandoning distraction, according to one's disposition, conduct, and inclination, those phenomena appear either as foul, or by way of color, or as empty.

Atha paṇṇattisamatikkamanato te dhamme manasi karoti. Paṇṇattisamatikkamanatoti kesā lomāti evamādivohāraṃ samatikkamitvā vissajjetvā yathūpaṭṭhitānaṃ asubhādīnaṃyeva vasena manasi karoti. Kathaṃ[M 0.0058]? Yathā araññanivāsūpagatā manussā aparicitabhūmibhāgattā udakaṭṭhānasañjānanatthaṃ sākhābhaṅgādinimittaṃ katvā tadanusārena gantvā udakaṃ paribhuñjanti, yadā pana paricitabhūmibhāgā honti, atha taṃ nimittaṃ vissajjetvā amanasikatvāva udakaṭṭhānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā udakaṃ paribhuñjanti, evamevāyaṃ kesā lomātiādinā taṃtaṃvohārassa vasena paṭhamaṃ te dhamme manasākāsi, tesu dhammesu asubhādīnaṃ aññataravasena upaṭṭhahantesu taṃ vohāraṃ samatikkamitvā vissajjetvā asubhāditova manasi karoti.

Then he attends to those things by way of transcending the concept. 'By way of transcending the concept' means that having transcended and abandoned the conventional expression 'hair of the head, body hair,' and so on, he attends only by way of the foulness, etc., as it has appeared. How? Just as people who have gone to live in the forest, being unfamiliar with the area of land, make a sign, such as the breaking of a branch, for the purpose of knowing the water-drawing place, and having gone following that, they use the water; but when they become familiar with the area of land, then, having abandoned that sign and without attending to it at all, they approach the water-drawing place and use the water. Just so, this person at first attended to those things by way of this or that conventional expression, such as 'hair of the head, body hair'; but when, in those things, one or another aspect of foulness, etc., appears, having transcended and abandoned that conventional expression, he attends only by way of foulness and so on.

Etthāha “kathaṃ panassa ete dhammā asubhādito upaṭṭhahanti, kathaṃ vaṇṇato, kathaṃ suññato vā, kathañcāyamete asubhato manasi karoti, kathaṃ vaṇṇato, kathaṃ suññato vā”ti? Kesā tāvassa vaṇṇasaṇṭhānagandhāsayokāsavasena pañcadhā asubhato upaṭṭhahanti, pañcadhā eva ayamete asubhato manasi karoti. Seyyathidaṃ – kesā nāmete vaṇṇato asubhā [P 0.0072] paramappaṭikūlajegucchā[V 0.0055]. Tathā hi manussā divā pānabhojane patitaṃ kesavaṇṇaṃ vākaṃ vā suttaṃ vā disvā kesasaññāya manoramampi pānabhojanaṃ chaḍḍenti vā jigucchanti vā. Saṇṭhānatopi asubhā. Tathā hi rattiṃ pānabhojane patitaṃ kesasaṇṭhānaṃ vākaṃ vā suttaṃ vā phusitvā kesasaññāya manoramampi pānabhojanaṃ chaḍḍenti vā jigucchanti vā. Gandhatopi asubhā. Tathā hi telamakkhanapupphadhūmādisaṅkhārehi virahitānaṃ kesānaṃ gandho paramajeguccho hoti, aggīsu pakkhittassa kesassa gandhaṃ ghāyitvā sattā nāsikaṃ pidhenti, mukhampi vikujjenti. Āsayatopi asubhā. Tathā hi nānāvidhena manussāsucinissandena saṅkāraṭṭhāne taṇḍuleyyakādīni viya pittasemhapubbalohitanissandena te ācitā vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ gamitāti. Okāsatopi asubhā. Tathā hi saṅkāraṭṭhāne viya taṇḍuleyyakādīni paramajegucche lomādiekatiṃsakuṇaparāsimatthake manussānaṃ sīsapaliveṭhake allacamme jātāti. Esa nayo lomādīsu. Evaṃ tāva ayamete dhamme asubhato upaṭṭhahante asubhato manasi karoti.

Here, a questioner asks: 'But how do these things appear to him by way of foulness, etc.? How by way of color? Or how by way of voidness? And how does this person attend to these things as foul? How by way of color? Or how by way of voidness?' To him, for a start, the hairs of the head appear as foul in five ways: by way of color, shape, smell, habitat, and location. And this person attends to them as foul in just these five ways. As follows: These things called hairs of the head are foul by way of color, extremely repulsive and disgusting. For indeed, when people see during the day a strand of bark or a thread the color of a hair fallen into their drink and food, with the perception of 'hair,' they either discard or are disgusted by even a delightful drink and food. They are also foul by way of shape. For indeed, when at night they touch a strand of bark or a thread with the shape of a hair fallen into their drink and food, with the perception of 'hair,' they either discard or are disgusted by even a delightful drink and food. They are also foul by way of smell. For indeed, the smell of hairs devoid of preparations such as anointing with oil, wearing flowers, and using incense is extremely disgusting. Having smelled the odor of a hair thrown into a fire, beings cover their noses and also contort their mouths. They are also foul by way of habitat. For indeed, like pot-herbs and so on in a refuse heap nourished by various human impure discharges, so too are these hairs accumulated by the discharge of bile, phlegm, pus, and blood, and are brought to growth, development, and abundance. They are also foul by way of location. For indeed, like pot-herbs and so on in a refuse heap, they grow on the moist skin that wraps the human head, on top of the extremely disgusting heap of the thirty-one foul parts, such as body hair and so on. This is the method for body hair and so on. Thus, for a start, this person attends to these things as foul as they appear to him as foul.

Yadi panassa vaṇṇato upaṭṭhahanti, atha kesā nīlakasiṇavasena upaṭṭhahanti. Tathā lomā dantā odātakasiṇavasenāti. Esa nayo sabbattha[M 0.0059]. Taṃtaṃkasiṇavaseneva ayamete manasi karoti, evaṃ vaṇṇato upaṭṭhahante vaṇṇato manasi karoti. Yadi panassa suññato upaṭṭhahanti, atha kesā ghanavinibbhogavavatthānena ojaṭṭhamakasamūhavasena upaṭṭhahanti. Tathā lomādayo, yathā upaṭṭhahanti. Ayamete tatheva manasi karoti. Evaṃ suññato upaṭṭhahante suññato manasi karoti.

But if they appear to him by way of color, then the hairs of the head appear by way of the blue kasiṇa. Similarly, the body hairs appear by way of the blue kasiṇa, and the teeth by way of the white kasiṇa. This is the method in all cases. This person attends to them only by way of this or that kasiṇa. Thus, when they appear by way of color, he attends by way of color. But if they appear to him by way of voidness, then the hairs of the head appear by way of the group with nutriment as the eighth, through the determination of the analysis of the solid. Similarly, the body hairs and so on appear. As they appear, this person attends to them in just that way. Thus, when they appear by way of voidness, he attends by way of voidness.

Evaṃ manasikaronto ayamete dhamme anupubbamuñcanato manasi karoti. Anupubbamuñcanatoti asubhādīnaṃ aññataravasena upaṭṭhite kese muñcitvā lome manasikaronto seyyathāpi nāma jalūkā naṅguṭṭhena gahitappadese sāpekkhāva hutvā tuṇḍena aññaṃ padesaṃ gaṇhāti, gahite ca tasmiṃ itaraṃ muñcati, evameva kesesu sāpekkhova hutvā lome manasi karoti, lomesu ca patiṭṭhite manasikāre [P 0.0073] kese muñcati. Esa nayo sabbattha. Evaṃ hissa anupubbamuñcanato manasikaroto asubhādīsu aññataravasena te dhammā upaṭṭhahantā anavasesato upaṭṭhahanti, pākaṭatarūpaṭṭhānā ca honti.

Attending in this way, this person attends to these things by way of successively releasing them. 'By way of successively releasing' means that while releasing the hairs of the head that have appeared by way of one or another aspect of foulness, etc., he attends to the body hairs. Just as a leech, while still having a hold on the place grasped with its tail, grasps another place with its mouth, and when that is grasped, it releases the other; just so, while still having a hold on the hairs of the head, he attends to the body hairs, and when attention is established on the body hairs, he releases the hairs of the head. This is the method in all cases. Indeed, for one who attends in this way by successively releasing, those things, appearing by way of one or another aspect of foulness, etc., appear without remainder, and their appearance becomes clearer.

Atha yassa te dhammā asubhato upaṭṭhahanti, pākaṭatarūpaṭṭhānā ca honti, tassa seyyathāpi nāma makkaṭo dvattiṃsatālake tālavane byādhena paripātiyamāno ekarukkhepi asaṇṭhahanto paridhāvitvā yadā nivatto hoti kilanto, atha ekameva ghanatālapaṇṇapariveṭhitaṃ tālasuciṃ [V 0.0056] nissāya tiṭṭhati; evameva cittamakkaṭo dvattiṃsakoṭṭhāsake imasmiṃ kāye teneva yoginā paripātiyamāno ekakoṭṭhāsakepi asaṇṭhahanto paridhāvitvā yadā anekārammaṇavidhāvane abhilāsābhāvena nivatto hoti kilanto. Atha yvāssa kesādīsu dhammo paguṇataro caritānurūpataro vā, yattha vā pubbe katādhikāro hoti, taṃ nissāya upacāravasena tiṭṭhati. Atha tameva nimittaṃ punappunaṃ takkāhataṃ vitakkāhataṃ karitvā yathākkamaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ uppādeti, tattha patiṭṭhāya vipassanamārabhitvā ariyabhūmiṃ pāpuṇāti.

Then, for the one to whom those things appear as foul and their appearance becomes clearer, it is as if a monkey in a palm grove with thirty-two palm trees, being pursued by a hunter, runs about without settling on even one tree, and when it becomes tired and stops, it then stays, relying on a single palm-sprout thickly wrapped with palm leaves. Just so, the monkey of the mind, in this body with its thirty-two parts, being pursued by that same yogi, runs about without settling on even one part, and when, due to the absence of desire in running after many objects, it becomes tired and stops; then, whichever thing among the hairs of the head, etc., is more familiar to him, or more suitable to his temperament, or where he has made a foundation in the past, relying on that, his mind becomes steady by way of access. Then, having repeatedly struck that same sign with applied and sustained thought, he sequentially arouses the first jhāna. Having established himself therein and having undertaken insight, he reaches the noble plane.

Yassa pana te dhammā vaṇṇato upaṭṭhahanti, tassāpi seyyathāpi nāma makkaṭo…pe… atha yvāssa kesādīsu dhammo paguṇataro caritānurūpataro [M 0.0060] vā, yattha vā pubbe katādhikāro hoti, taṃ nissāya upacāravasena tiṭṭhati. Atha tameva nimittaṃ punappunaṃ takkāhataṃ vitakkāhataṃ karitvā yathākkamaṃ nīlakasiṇavasena pītakasiṇavasena vā pañcapi rūpāvacarajjhānāni uppādeti, tesañca yattha katthaci patiṭṭhāya vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā ariyabhūmiṃ pāpuṇāti.

For a certain person, however, these phenomena appear by way of color. For him, it is as if a monkey… and so on… Then, for him, among the parts beginning with the hair of the head, whichever phenomenon is more familiar, or more suited to his temperament, or in which he has previously made a resolution, relying on that, he becomes established by way of access [concentration]. Then, having repeatedly struck that very sign with thought and struck it with initial application, he successively generates the five fine-material jhānas by way of the blue kasiṇa or by way of the yellow kasiṇa. And having established himself in any one of those [jhānas], and having undertaken insight, he reaches the noble plane.

Yassa pana te dhammā suññato upaṭṭhahanti, so lakkhaṇato manasi karoti, lakkhaṇato manasikaronto tattha catudhātuvavatthānavasena upacārajjhānaṃ pāpuṇāti. Atha manasikaronto te dhamme aniccadukkhānattasuttattayavasena manasi karoti[P 0.0074]. Ayamassa vipassanānayo. So imaṃ vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā yathākkamañca paṭipajjitvā ariyabhūmiṃ pāpuṇātīti.

For a certain person, however, these phenomena appear by way of being void of self. That person attends by way of characteristics. Attending by way of characteristics, in those thirty-two parts, he reaches access jhāna by way of the determination of the four elements. Then, while attending, he attends to those phenomena by way of the sutta method of impermanence, suffering, and non-self. This is his method of insight. That person, having undertaken this insight and having practiced in due order, reaches the noble plane.

Ettāvatā ca yaṃ vuttaṃ – “kathaṃ panāyaṃ anupubbādivasena ete dhamme manasi karotī”ti, taṃ byākataṃ hoti. Yañcāpi vuttaṃ – “bhāvanāvasena panassa evaṃ vaṇṇanā veditabbā”ti, tassattho pakāsito hotīti.

And by this much, that which was said—'But how does this person attend to these phenomena by way of gradual succession, etc.?'—that has been explained. And also that which was said—'But by way of development, this explanation should be understood thus'—its meaning has been clarified.

Pakiṇṇakanayo

The Miscellaneous Method

Idāni imasmiṃyeva dvattiṃsākāre vaṇṇanāparicayapāṭavatthaṃ ayaṃ pakiṇṇakanayo veditabbo –

Now, for the sake of proficiency in the explanation of these very thirty-two parts, this miscellaneous method should be understood:

“Nimittato lakkhaṇato, dhātuto suññatopi ca;

Khandhādito ca viññeyyo, dvattiṃsākāranicchayo”ti.

By way of sign, by way of characteristic, by way of element, and also by way of being void; and by way of the aggregates, etc., the determination of the thirty-two parts should be known.

Tattha [V 0.0057] nimittatoti evaṃ vuttappakāre imasmiṃ dvattiṃsākāre saṭṭhisataṃ nimittāni honti, yesaṃ vasena yogāvacaro dvattiṃsākāraṃ koṭṭhāsato pariggaṇhāti. Seyyathidaṃ – kesassa vaṇṇanimittaṃ, saṇṭhānanimittaṃ, disānimittaṃ, okāsanimittaṃ, paricchedanimittanti pañca nimittāni honti. Evaṃ lomādīsu.

Therein, 'by way of sign' means: in this thirty-two-part [meditation] of the aforesaid kind, there are one hundred and sixty signs, by means of which a yogāvacara comprehends the thirty-two parts by way of sections. That is to say: for the hair of the head, there is the sign of color, the sign of shape, the sign of direction, the sign of location, and the sign of delimitation—thus there are five signs. Likewise for the body hair, etc.

Lakkhaṇatoti dvattiṃsākāre aṭṭhavīsatisataṃ lakkhaṇāni honti, yesaṃ vasena yogāvacaro dvattiṃsākāraṃ lakkhaṇato manasi karoti[M 0.0061]. Seyyathidaṃ – kesassa thaddhalakkhaṇaṃ, ābandhanalakkhaṇaṃ, uṇhattalakkhaṇaṃ, samudīraṇalakkhaṇanti cattāri lakkhaṇāni honti. Evaṃ lomādīsu.

'By way of characteristic' means: in the thirty-two parts, there are one hundred and twenty-eight characteristics, by means of which a yogāvacara attends to the thirty-two parts by way of characteristics. That is to say: for the hair of the head, there is the characteristic of hardness, the characteristic of binding, the characteristic of heat, and the characteristic of movement—thus there are four characteristics. Likewise for the body hair, etc.

Dhātutoti dvattiṃsākāre “chadhāturo, bhikkhave, ayaṃ purisapuggalo”ti (ma. ni. 3.343-344) ettha vuttāsu dhātūsu aṭṭhavīsatisataṃ dhātuyo honti, yāsaṃ vasena yogāvacaro dvattiṃsākāraṃ dhātuto pariggaṇhāti. Seyyathidaṃ – yā kese thaddhatā, sā pathavīdhātu; yā ābandhanatā, sā āpodhātu; yā paripācanatā, sā tejodhātu; yā vitthambhanatā, sā vāyodhātūti catasso dhātuyo honti. Evaṃ lomādīsu.

'By way of element' means: in the thirty-two parts, in reference to the elements mentioned where it is said, 'Monks, this person is the six elements,' there are one hundred and twenty-eight elements, by means of which a yogāvacara comprehends the thirty-two parts by way of element. That is to say: whatever hardness is in the hair of the head, that is the earth element; whatever binding is, that is the water element; whatever maturing is, that is the fire element; whatever supporting is, that is the air element—thus there are four elements. Likewise for the body hair, etc.

Suññatoti dvattiṃsākāre aṭṭhavīsatisataṃ suññatā honti, yāsaṃ vasena yogāvacaro dvattiṃsākāraṃ suññato vipassati. Seyyathidaṃ – kese tāva pathavīdhātu [P 0.0075] āpodhātvādīhi suññā, tathā āpodhātvādayo pathavīdhātvādīhīti catasso suññatā honti. Evaṃ lomādīsu.

'By way of voidness' means: in the thirty-two parts, there are one hundred and twenty-eight voidnesses, by means of which a yogāvacara sees with insight the thirty-two parts as void. That is to say: in the hair of the head, firstly, the earth element is void of the water element, etc.; likewise, the water element, etc., are void of the earth element, etc.—thus there are four voidnesses. Likewise for the body hair, etc.

Khandhāditoti dvattiṃsākāre kesādīsu khandhādivasena saṅgayhamānesu “kesā kati khandhā honti, kati āyatanāni, kati dhātuyo, kati saccāni, kati satipaṭṭhānānī”ti evamādinā nayena vinicchayo veditabbo. Evañcassa vijānato tiṇakaṭṭhasamūho viya kāyo khāyati. Yathāha –

'By way of the aggregates, etc.' means: in the thirty-two parts, when the parts beginning with the hair of the head are being classified by way of the aggregates, etc., the determination should be known by the method beginning thus: 'The hair of the head—how many aggregates are they? How many sense bases? How many elements? How many truths? How many foundations of mindfulness?' And for one knowing thus, the body appears like a heap of grass and sticks. As it is said:

“Natthi satto naro poso, puggalo nūpalabbhati;

Suññabhūto ayaṃ kāyo, tiṇakaṭṭhasamūpamo”ti.

There is no being, no man, no male; a person is not found. This body has become void, like a heap of grass and sticks.

Athassa yā sā –

Then, for him, that which is:

“Suññāgāraṃ paviṭṭhassa, santacittassa tādino;

Amānusī rati hoti, sammā dhammaṃ vipassato”ti. –

For one who has entered a secluded dwelling, whose mind is tranquil, who is steadfast, and who sees the Dhamma rightly, there arises a superhuman delight.

Evaṃ [V 0.0058] amānusī rati vuttā, sā adūratarā hoti. Tato yaṃ taṃ –

Thus the superhuman delight is spoken of; it is not very far. Then, that which is:

“Yato yato sammasati, khandhānaṃ udayabbayaṃ;

Labhatī pītipāmojjaṃ, amataṃ taṃ vijānata”nti. (dha. pa. 373-374) –

Whenever one comprehends the arising and passing away of the aggregates, one obtains joy and gladness; that is the Deathless for those who know.

Evaṃ [M 0.0062] vipassanāmayaṃ pītipāmojjāmataṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃ anubhavanto na cireneva ariyajanasevitaṃ ajarāmaraṃ nibbānāmataṃ sacchikarotīti.

Thus is spoken the deathless joy and gladness consisting of insight. Experiencing that, before long one realizes the ageless and deathless Nibbāna, the deathless state frequented by the noble ones.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha,

Dvattiṃsākāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Thirty-Two Parts is concluded.

4. Kumārapañhavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Questions of the Young Man

Aṭṭhuppatti

The Occasion of Arising

Idāni [V 0.0059] ekaṃ nāma kinti evamādīnaṃ kumārapañhānaṃ atthavaṇṇanākkamo anuppatto. Tesaṃ aṭṭhuppattiṃ idha nikkhepappayojanañca vatvā vaṇṇanaṃ karissāma –

Now the turn has come for explaining the meaning of the questions of the young man, such as 'What is one?'. Having stated their occasion of arising and the purpose of their inclusion here, we shall proceed with the explanation.

Aṭṭhuppatti tāva nesaṃ sopāko nāma bhagavato mahāsāvako ahosi. Tenāyasmatā jātiyā sattavasseneva aññā ārādhitā, tassa bhagavā pañhabyākaraṇena upasampadaṃ anuññātukāmo attanā adhippetatthānaṃ pañhānaṃ byākaraṇasamatthataṃ [P 0.0076] passanto “ekaṃ nāma ki”nti evamādinā pañhe pucchi. So byākāsi. Tena ca byākaraṇena bhagavato cittaṃ ārādhesi. Sāva tassāyasmato upasampadā ahosi.

Firstly, as to their occasion of arising: There was a great disciple of the Blessed One named Sopāka. By that venerable one, at the mere age of seven from birth, final knowledge was attained. The Blessed One, wishing to grant him higher ordination by way of answering questions, seeing his ability to answer the questions which had the meaning intended by himself, asked questions beginning with 'What is one?' and so on. He answered. And by that answer, he pleased the mind of the Blessed One. That itself was that venerable one's higher ordination.

Ayaṃ tesaṃ aṭṭhuppatti.

This is their occasion of arising.

Nikkhepappayojanaṃ

The Purpose of Inclusion

Yasmā pana saraṇagamanehi buddhadhammasaṅghānussativasena cittabhāvanā, sikkhāpadehi sīlabhāvanā, dvattiṃsākārena ca kāyabhāvanā pakāsitā, tasmā idāni nānappakārato paññābhāvanāmukhadassanatthaṃ ime pañhabyākaraṇā idha nikkhittā. Yasmā vā sīlapadaṭṭhāno samādhi, samādhipadaṭṭhānā ca paññā; yathāha – “sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño, cittaṃ [M 0.0063] paññañca bhāvaya”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.23, 192), tasmā sikkhāpadehi sīlaṃ dvattiṃsākārena taṃgocaraṃ samādhiñca dassetvā samāhitacittassa nānādhammaparikkhārāya paññāya pabhedadassanatthaṃ idha nikkhittātipi viññātabbā.

Since the development of mind by way of the recollection of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha through the goings for refuge, the development of virtue through the training precepts, and the development of the body through the thirty-two aspects have been explained, therefore these questions and answers are now included here to show an introduction to the development of wisdom in its various aspects. Or, since concentration has virtue as its proximate cause, and wisdom has concentration as its proximate cause—as it is said: 'A wise person, established in virtue, develops the mind and wisdom'—therefore, it should also be understood that after showing virtue through the training precepts and concentration which has the thirty-two aspects as its object, these are included here to reveal the distinctions of wisdom, which has various phenomena as its accessory, for one whose mind is concentrated.

Idaṃ tesaṃ idha nikkhepappayojanaṃ.

This is the purpose for their inclusion here.

Pañhavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Questions

Ekaṃ nāma kintipañhavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Question: 'What is one?'

Idāni [V 0.0060] tesaṃ atthavaṇṇanā hoti – ekaṃ nāma kinti bhagavā yasmiṃ ekadhammasmiṃ bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno anupubbena dukkhassantakaro hoti, yasmiṃ cāyamāyasmā nibbindamāno anupubbena dukkhassantamakāsi, taṃ dhammaṃ sandhāya pañhaṃ pucchati. “Sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā”ti thero puggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya vissajjeti. “Katamā ca, bhikkhave, sammāsati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.8) evamādīni cettha suttāni evaṃ vissajjanayuttisambhave sādhakāni. Ettha yenāhārena sabbe sattā “āhāraṭṭhitikā”ti vuccanti, so āhāro taṃ vā nesaṃ āhāraṭṭhitikattaṃ “ekaṃ nāma ki”nti puṭṭhena therena niddiṭṭhanti veditabbaṃ. Tañhi bhagavatā idha ekanti adhippetaṃ, na tu sāsane loke vā aññaṃ ekaṃ nāma natthīti ñāpetuṃ vuttaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ [P 0.0077] bhagavatā –

Now, the explanation of their meaning is as follows: As for 'What is one?', the Blessed One asks the question with reference to that one phenomenon, by becoming rightly disenchanted with which a monk gradually becomes one who makes an end of suffering, and by becoming disenchanted with which this venerable one gradually made an end of suffering. The elder answers with a teaching based on individuals: 'All beings are sustained by nutriment.' And here, suttas such as 'And what, bhikkhus, is right mindfulness? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body...' are evidence for the suitability of such an answer. Here, it should be understood that the elder, when asked 'What is one?', indicated that nutriment by which all beings are called 'sustained by nutriment,' or their state of being sustained by nutriment. For that was intended by the Blessed One here as 'one'; it was not said to make known that there is no other thing called 'one' in the Dispensation or in the world. For this has been said by the Blessed One—

“Ekadhamme, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammattaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamasmiṃ ekadhamme? Sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā. Imasmiṃ kho, bhikkhave, ekadhamme bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Eko pañho eko uddeso ekaṃ veyyākaraṇa’nti iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vutta”nti (a. ni. 10.27).

“Bhikkhus, in one phenomenon, a bhikkhu, rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly becoming liberated, rightly seeing the limit, having fully comprehended what is right, becomes one who makes an end of suffering in this very life. In what one phenomenon? 'All beings are sustained by nutriment.' Bhikkhus, in this one phenomenon, a bhikkhu, rightly becoming disenchanted... becomes one who makes an end of suffering. That which was said, namely, 'One question, one exposition, one explanation,' was said in reference to this.”

Āhāraṭṭhitikāti cettha yathā “atthi, bhikkhave, subhanimittaṃ. Tattha ayoniso manasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā kāmacchandassa uppādāyā”ti evamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.232) paccayo āhāroti vuccati, evaṃ [M 0.0064] paccayaṃ āhārasaddena gahetvā paccayaṭṭhitikā “āhāraṭṭhitikā”ti vuttā. Cattāro pana āhāre sandhāya – “āhāraṭṭhitikā”ti vuccamāne “asaññasattā devā ahetukā anāhārā aphassakā avedanakā”ti vacanato (vibha. 1017) “sabbe”ti vacanamayuttaṃ bhaveyya.

Here, in the phrase 'sustained by nutriment': Just as in passages such as, 'There is, bhikkhus, the sign of the beautiful. Frequent inappropriate attention to it is the nutriment for the arising of sensual desire that has not yet arisen...' where a condition is called 'nutriment', so too, taking the word 'nutriment' to mean 'condition', those who are sustained by conditions are called 'sustained by nutriment'. However, if 'sustained by nutriment' were said with reference to the four nutriments, then the word 'all' would be unsuitable, according to the statement: 'The non-percipient beings are gods without root-causes, without nutriment, without contact, without feeling'.

Tattha siyā – evampi vuccamāne “katame dhammā sapaccayā? Pañcakkhandhā – rūpakkhandho…pe… viññāṇakkhandho”ti (dha. sa. 1089) vacanato khandhānaṃyeva paccayaṭṭhitikattaṃ yuttaṃ, sattānantu ayuttamevetaṃ vacanaṃ bhaveyyāti. Na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kasmā[V 0.0061]? Sattesu khandhopacārasiddhito. Sattesu hi khandhopacāro siddho. Kasmā? Khandhe upādāya paññāpetabbato. Kathaṃ? Gehe gāmopacāro viya. Seyyathāpi hi gehāni upādāya paññāpetabbattā gāmassa ekasmimpi dvīsu tīsupi vā gehesu daḍḍhesu “gāmo daḍḍho”ti evaṃ gehe gāmopacāro siddho, evameva khandhesu paccayaṭṭhena āhāraṭṭhitikesu [P 0.0078] “sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā”ti ayaṃ upacāro siddhoti veditabbo. Paramatthato ca khandhesu jāyamānesu jīyamānesu mīyamānesu ca “khaṇe khaṇe tvaṃ bhikkhu jāyase ca jīyase ca mīyase cā”ti vadatā bhagavatā tesu sattesu khandhopacāro siddhoti dassito evāti veditabbo. Yato yena paccayākhyena āhārena sabbe sattā tiṭṭhanti, so āhāro taṃ vā nesaṃ āhāraṭṭhitikattaṃ ekanti veditabbaṃ. Āhāro hi āhāraṭṭhitikattaṃ vā aniccatākāraṇato nibbidāṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Atha tesu sabbasattasaññitesu saṅkhāresu aniccatādassanena nibbindamāno anupubbena dukkhassantakaro hoti, paramatthavisuddhiṃ pāpuṇāti. Yathāha –

Here, it might be said: Even when it is stated thus, 'Which phenomena are conditioned? The five aggregates—the form aggregate... the consciousness aggregate', it is fitting that only the aggregates have the state of being sustained by conditions, but for beings, this statement would be inappropriate. However, this should not be seen thus. Why? Because the figurative usage of 'aggregates' is established in relation to beings. Indeed, in relation to beings, the figurative usage of 'aggregates' is established. Why? Because they are designated in dependence on the aggregates. How? Like the figurative usage of 'village' in relation to houses. For just as, because a village is designated in dependence on houses, when one, two, or even three houses are burnt, it is said, 'The village is burnt,' and thus the figurative usage of 'village' in relation to houses is established; in the very same way, when the aggregates are sustained by nutriment in the sense of being a condition, this figurative usage, 'beings are sustained by nutriment,' should be understood as established. And in the ultimate sense, when aggregates are arising, decaying, and dying, the Blessed One, by saying, 'Moment by moment, bhikkhu, you are born, you age, and you die,' has shown that the figurative usage of 'aggregates' in relation to those beings is established; thus it should be understood. Since all beings subsist by that nutriment which is called a condition, that nutriment, or their state of being sustained by nutriment, should be known as 'one'. For nutriment, or the state of being sustained by nutriment, is a basis for disenchantment because of its nature of impermanence. Then, by seeing impermanence in those formations perceived as 'all beings', one who becomes disenchanted gradually becomes an end-maker of suffering and attains ultimate purity. As it is said:

“Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccāti, yadā paññāya passati;

Atha nibbindati dukkhe, esa maggo visuddhiyā”ti. (dha. pa. 277);

“‘All conditioned things are impermanent’—when one sees this with wisdom, one then becomes disenchanted with suffering. This is the path to purification.”

Ettha ca “ekaṃ nāma ki”nti ca “kihā”ti ca duvidho pāṭho, tattha sīhaḷānaṃ kihāti pāṭho. Te hi “ki”nti vattabbe “kihā”ti vadanti. Keci bhaṇanti “ha-iti nipāto, theriyānampi ayameva pāṭho”ti ubhayathāpi pana ekova attho. Yathā ruccati, tathā paṭhitabbaṃ. Yathā pana “sukhena phuṭṭho atha vā dukhena (dha. pa. 83), dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedetī”ti evamādīsu [M 0.0065] katthaci dukhanti ca katthaci dukkhanti ca vuccati, evaṃ katthaci ekanti, katthaci ekkanti vuccati. Idha pana ekaṃ nāmāti ayameva pāṭho.

And here there are two readings: 'ekaṃ nāma kiṃ' and 'kihā'. Among these, the Sinhalese reading is 'kihā'. For when they should say 'kiṃ', they say 'kihā'. Some say, '“ha” is a particle, and this is also the reading of the Therīgāthā.' In either case, however, the meaning is one and the same. It should be recited as one prefers. Just as in passages such as 'touched by happiness or by suffering' (Dhammapada 83), and 'one experiences suffering and displeasure,' sometimes 'dukha' is said and sometimes 'dukkha' is said; similarly, sometimes 'ekaṃ' is said, and sometimes 'ekkaṃ' is said. Here, however, this is the reading: 'ekaṃ nāma'.

Dve nāma kintipañhavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Question: 'What, by name, are two?'

Evaṃ iminā pañhabyākaraṇena āraddhacitto satthā purimanayeneva uttariṃ pañhaṃ pucchati dve nāma kinti? Thero dveti paccanubhāsitvā “nāmañca rūpañcā”ti dhammādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya vissajjeti. Tattha ārammaṇābhimukhaṃ namanato, cittassa ca natihetuto sabbampi [P 0.0079] arūpaṃ “nāma”nti vuccati. Idha pana nibbidāhetuttā sāsavadhammameva adhippetaṃ ruppanaṭṭhena cattāro ca mahābhūtā, sabbañca tadupādāya pavattamānaṃ rūpaṃ “rūpa”nti vuccati, taṃ sabbampi idhādhippetaṃ. Adhippāyavaseneva cettha “dve nāma nāmañca rūpañcā”ti vuttaṃ, na aññesaṃ dvinnamabhāvato. Yathāha –

Thus, with his mind pleased by this answer to the question, the Teacher, in the same way as before, asks a further question: 'What, by name, are two?' The Elder, repeating 'Two,' answers with a teaching founded on the Dhamma: 'Name and form.' Therein, because of its inclining towards an object and because it is the cause for the mind's inclination, all that is immaterial is called 'name'. Here, however, because it is a cause for disenchantment, only phenomena connected with the taints are intended. Because of the meaning of being afflicted, the four great elements and all form that arises in dependence on them are called 'form'; all of that is intended here. And it is only by the power of the intended meaning that it is said here, 'Two, by name, are name and form,' not because of the absence of other pairs. As it is said:

“Dvīsu[V 0.0062], bhikkhave, dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamesu dvīsu? Nāme ca rūpe ca. Imesu kho, bhikkhave, dvīsu dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Dve pañhā, dve uddesā, dve veyyākaraṇānī’ti iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vutta”nti (a. ni. 10.27).

“‘Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is rightly disenchanted with two things... becomes an end-maker of suffering. With which two? With name and with form. Bhikkhus, it is with these two things that a bhikkhu who is rightly disenchanted... becomes an end-maker of suffering. “Two questions, two topics, two explanations”—what was said, was said in reference to this.’” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.27).

Ettha ca nāmarūpamattadassanena attadiṭṭhiṃ pahāya anattānupassanāmukheneva nibbindamāno anupubbena dukkhassantakaro hoti, paramatthavisuddhiṃ pāpuṇātīti veditabbo. Yathāha –

And here it should be understood that by abandoning the view of self through seeing mere name-and-form, and by becoming disenchanted only through the approach of the contemplation of not-self, one gradually becomes an end-maker of suffering and attains ultimate purity. As it is said:

“Sabbe dhammā anattāti, yadā paññāya passati;

Atha nibbindati dukkhe, esa maggo visuddhiyā”ti. (dha. pa. 279);

“‘All phenomena are not-self’—when one sees this with wisdom, one then becomes disenchanted with suffering. This is the path to purification.” (Dhammapada 279);

Tīṇi nāma kintipañhavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Question: 'What, by name, are three?'

Idāni imināpi pañhabyākaraṇena āraddhacitto satthā purimanayeneva uttariṃ pañhaṃ pucchati tīṇi nāma kinti? Thero tīṇīti paccanubhāsitvā puna byākaritabbassa atthassa liṅgānurūpaṃ saṅkhyaṃ dassento “tisso vedanā”ti vissajjeti. Atha vā “yā bhagavatā ‘tisso vedanā’ti vuttā, imāsamatthamahaṃ [M 0.0066] tīṇīti paccemī”ti dassento āhāti evampettha attho veditabbo. Anekamukhā hi desanā paṭisambhidāpabhedena desanāvilāsappattānaṃ. Keci panāhu “tīṇīti adhikapadamida”nti. Purimanayeneva cettha “tisso vedanā”ti vuttaṃ, na aññesaṃ tiṇṇamabhāvato. Yathāha –

Now, with his mind pleased by this explanation as well, the Teacher, in the same way as before, asks a further question: 'What, by name, are three?' The Elder, repeating 'Three,' then answers, 'The three feelings,' showing the number that corresponds to the gender of the meaning to be explained. Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood thus: he speaks to show, 'What was spoken of by the Blessed One as “the three feelings,” I accept that meaning as “three.”' For the teaching has many facets for those who have attained elegance in teaching through the distinctions of the analytical knowledges. Some, however, say, 'This word “tīṇi” is an additional word.' And here, it is said 'the three feelings' in the same way as before, not because of the absence of other triads. As it is said:

“Tīsu, bhikkhave, dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamesu tīsu? Tīsu vedanāsu. Imesu kho, bhikkhave, tīsu dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Tayo pañhā, tayo uddesā, tīṇi veyyākaraṇānī’ti iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ[P 0.0080], idametaṃ paṭicca vutta”nti (a. ni. 10.27).

“‘Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is rightly disenchanted with three things... becomes an end-maker of suffering. With which three? With the three feelings. Bhikkhus, it is with these three things that a bhikkhu who is rightly disenchanted... becomes an end-maker of suffering. “Three questions, three topics, three explanations”—what was said, was said in reference to this.’” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.27).

Ettha ca “yaṃkiñci vedayitaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ dukkhasminti vadāmī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.259) vuttasuttānusārena vā. –

And here, it is in accordance with the sutta that states, “‘Whatever is felt, all that, I say, is included in suffering’” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.259), or...

“Yo [V 0.0063] sukhaṃ dukkhato adda, dukkhamaddakkhi sallato;

Adukkhamasukhaṃ santaṃ, addakkhi naṃ aniccato”ti. (itivu. 53) –

“One who sees pleasure as suffering, suffering as a dart, and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant, which is peaceful, sees that as impermanent.” (Itivuttaka 53)

Evaṃ dukkhadukkhatāvipariṇāmadukkhatāsaṅkhāradukkhatānusārena vā tissannaṃ vedanānaṃ dukkhabhāvadassanena sukhasaññaṃ pahāya dukkhānupassanāmukhena nibbindamāno anupubbena dukkhassantakaro hoti, paramatthavisuddhiṃ pāpuṇātīti veditabbo. Yathāha –

Thus, in accordance with the suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, and the suffering of formations, or by seeing the nature of suffering in the three feelings, that person, having abandoned the perception of pleasure and becoming disenchanted by means of the contemplation of suffering, gradually makes an end of suffering and attains ultimate purity; thus it should be understood. As it is said:

“Sabbe saṅkhārā dukkhāti, yadā paññāya passati;

Atha nibbindati dukkhe, esa maggo visuddhiyā”ti. (dha. pa. 278);

“‘All formations are suffering’—when one sees with wisdom, then one becomes disenchanted with suffering. This is the path to purity.” (Dhammapada 278);

Cattāri nāma kintipañhavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Question: 'What, by name, are four?'

Evaṃ imināpi pañhabyākaraṇena āraddhacitto satthā purimanayeneva uttariṃ pañhaṃ pucchati cattāri nāma kinti? Tattha imassa pañhassa byākaraṇapakkhe katthaci purimanayeneva cattāro āhārā adhippetā. Yathāha –

Thus, with his mind pleased by this explanation as well, the Teacher asks a further question in the same manner as before: “What, by name, are four?” In the explanation of this question, in some cases the four nutriments are intended, in the same way as before. As it is said:

“Catūsu[M 0.0067], bhikkhave, dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamesu catūsu? Catūsu āhāresu. Imesu kho, bhikkhave, catūsu dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Cattāro pañhā cattāro uddesā cattāri veyyākaraṇānī’ti iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vutta”nti (a. ni. 10.27).

“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who rightly becomes disenchanted with four things… makes an end of suffering. In which four? In the four nutriments. Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who rightly becomes disenchanted with these four things… makes an end of suffering. ‘Four questions, four topics, four explanations’—that which was said, was said in reference to this.” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.27).

Katthaci yesu subhāvitacitto anupubbena dukkhassantakaro hoti, tāni cattāri satipaṭṭhānāni. Yathāha kajaṅgalā bhikkhunī –

In some cases, there are four things in which a person with a well-developed mind gradually makes an end of suffering; those are the four foundations of mindfulness. As the nun from Kajaṅgalā said:

“Catūsu, āvuso, dhammesu bhikkhu sammā subhāvitacitto sammā pariyantadassāvī sammattaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro [P 0.0081] hoti. Katamesu catūsu? Catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu. Imesu kho, āvuso, catūsu dhammesu bhikkhu sammā subhāvitacitto…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Cattāro pañhā cattāro uddesā cattāri veyyākaraṇānī’ti iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā, idametaṃ paṭicca vutta”nti (a. ni. 10.28).

“Friend, when a bhikkhu’s mind is well developed in four things, when he rightly sees the limit and has realized peace, he makes an end of suffering in this very life. In which four? In the four foundations of mindfulness. Friend, when a bhikkhu’s mind is well developed in these four things… he makes an end of suffering. ‘Four questions, four summaries, four explanations’—that which was said by the Blessed One, was said in reference to this.”

Idha [V 0.0064] pana yesaṃ catunnaṃ anubodhappaṭivedhato bhavataṇhāchedo hoti, yasmā tāni cattāri ariyasaccāni adhippetāni. Yasmā vā iminā pariyāyena byākataṃ subyākatameva hoti, tasmā thero cattārīti paccanubhāsitvā “ariyasaccānī”ti vissajjeti. Tattha cattārīti gaṇanaparicchedo. Ariyasaccānīti ariyāni saccāni, avitathāni avisaṃvādakānīti attho. Yathāha –

Here, however, since for one who sequentially understands and penetrates these four, the craving for existence is cut off, those four Noble Truths are intended. Or, because an explanation given in this way is indeed well-explained, the Elder, having repeated “four,” clarifies with “Noble Truths.” Herein, “four” is a numerical demarcation. “Noble Truths” means truths that are noble, not unreal, and not deceptive; this is the meaning.

“Imāni kho, bhikkhave, cattāri ariyasaccāni tathāni avitathāni anaññathāni, tasmā ariyasaccānīti vuccantī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1097).

“These four Noble Truths, bhikkhus, are true, not unreal, and not otherwise; therefore they are called ‘Noble Truths.’”

Yasmā vā sadevakena lokena araṇīyato abhigamanīyatoti vuttaṃ hoti, vāyamitabbaṭṭhānasaññite aye vā iriyanato, anaye vā na iriyanato, sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyaariyadhammasamāyogato vā ariyasammatā buddhapaccekabuddhabuddhasāvakā etāni paṭivijjhanti, tasmāpi “ariyasaccānī”ti vuccanti. Yathāha –

Or, because it is said that they are to be known and to be approached by the world with its devas; or, because they produce welfare; or, because they do not produce non-welfare; or, because those considered noble—Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha—penetrate these truths through proper association with the noble Dhamma of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, therefore they are also called ‘Noble Truths.’

“Cattārimāni[M 0.0068], bhikkhave, ariyasaccāni…pe… imāni kho, bhikkhave, cattāri ariyasaccāni, ariyā imāni paṭivijjhanti, tasmā ariyasaccānīti vuccantī”ti.

“These, bhikkhus, are the four Noble Truths… Indeed, bhikkhus, these are the four Noble Truths. The noble ones penetrate these; therefore, they are called ‘Noble Truths.’”

Apica ariyassa bhagavato saccānītipi ariyasaccāni. Yathāha –

Furthermore, they are the truths of the noble Blessed One; for this reason also, they are ‘Noble Truths.’ As it is said:

“Sadevake, bhikkhave…pe… sadevamanussāya tathāgato ariyo, tasmā ariyasaccānīti vuccantī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1098).

“Bhikkhus, in the world with its devas… for devas and humans, the Tathāgata is noble; therefore they are called ‘Noble Truths.’”

Atha vā etesaṃ abhisambuddhattā ariyabhāvasiddhitopi ariyasaccāni. Yathāha –

Or alternatively, because they are fully awakened to, and also because they accomplish the state of a noble one, they are ‘Noble Truths.’ As it is said:

“Imesaṃ kho, bhikkhave, catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ abhisambuddhattā tathāgato arahaṃ sammāsambuddhoti vuccatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1093).

“Bhikkhus, it is because of having fully awakened to these four Noble Truths as they really are that the Tathāgata is called the Arahant, the Perfectly and Fully Awakened One.”

Ayametesaṃ padattho. Etesaṃ pana ariyasaccānaṃ anubodhappaṭivedhato bhavataṇhāchedo [P 0.0082] hoti. Yathāha –

This is the meaning of these terms. For one who sequentially understands and penetrates these Noble Truths, the craving for existence is cut off. As it is said:

“Tayidaṃ[V 0.0065], bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ anubuddhaṃ paṭividdhaṃ…pe… dukkhanirodhagāminipaṭipadā ariyasaccaṃ anubuddhaṃ paṭividdhaṃ, ucchinnā bhavataṇhā, khīṇā bhavanetti, natthi dāni punabbhavo”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1091).

“Bhikkhus, this Noble Truth of suffering has been sequentially understood and penetrated… the Noble Truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering has been sequentially understood and penetrated. The craving for existence is cut off, the guide to existence is destroyed, there is now no further renewed existence.”

Pañca nāma kintipañhavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Question: ‘What, by Name, are the Five?’

Imināpi pañhabyākaraṇena āraddhacitto satthā purimanayeneva uttariṃ pañhaṃ pucchati pañca nāma kinti? Thero pañcāti paccanubhāsitvā “upādānakkhandhā”ti vissajjeti. Tattha pañcāti gaṇanaparicchedo. Upādānajanitā upādānajanakā vā khandhā upādānakkhandhā. Yaṃkiñci rūpaṃ, vedanā, saññā, saṅkhārā, viññāṇañca sāsavā upādāniyā, etesametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Pubbanayeneva cettha “pañcupādānakkhandhā”ti vuttaṃ, na aññesaṃ pañcannamabhāvato. Yathāha –

By this explanation of the question as well, the Teacher, his mind pleased, asked a further question in the same way as before: “What, by name, are the five?” The Elder, repeating “five,” replied: “The aggregates of clinging.” Herein, “five” is a numerical demarcation. The aggregates generated by clinging or generative of clinging are the aggregates of clinging. Whatever form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are connected with the taints and are a basis for clinging—this is a designation for them. Here, as before, it is said “the five aggregates of clinging,” not because other sets of five do not exist. As it is said:

“Pañcasu, bhikkhave, dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamesu pañcasu? Pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu. Imesu kho, bhikkhave, pañcasu dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Pañca pañhā, pañca uddesā[M 0.0069], pañca veyyākaraṇānī’ti iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vutta”nti (a. ni. 10.27).

“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who rightly becomes disenchanted with five things… makes an end of suffering. In which five? In the five aggregates of clinging. Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who rightly becomes disenchanted with these five things… makes an end of suffering. ‘Five questions, five summaries, five explanations’—that which was said, was said in reference to this.”

Ettha ca pañcakkhandhe udayabbayavasena sammasanto vipassanāmataṃ laddhā anupubbena nibbānāmataṃ sacchikaroti. Yathāha –

Here, contemplating the rise and fall of the five aggregates, one gains insight-wisdom and gradually realizes the deathless Nibbāna. As it is said:

“Yato yato sammasati, khandhānaṃ udayabbayaṃ;

Labhatī pītipāmojjaṃ, amataṃ taṃ vijānata”nti. (dha. pa. 374);

“Whenever one discerns the rise and fall of the aggregates, one obtains joy and gladness; that is the deathless state for those who know.”

Cha nāma kintipañhavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Question: ‘What, by Name, are the Six?’

Evaṃ imināpi pañhabyākaraṇena āraddhacitto satthā purimanayeneva uttariṃ pañhaṃ pucchati “cha nāma ki”nti? Thero chaiti paccanubhāsitvā ‘ajjhattikāni āyatanānī’ti vissajjeti. Tattha chaiti gaṇanaparicchedo, ajjhatte niyuttāni, attānaṃ vā adhikatvā pavattāni ajjhattikāni. Āyatanato, āyassa vā tananato, āyatassa vā saṃsāradukkhassa [P 0.0083] nayanato āyatanāni, cakkhusotaghānajivhākāyamanānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Pubbanayena cettha “cha ajjhattikāni āyatanānī”ti vuttaṃ, na aññesaṃ channamabhāvato. Yathāha –

Thus, by this explanation of the question as well, the Teacher, with a pleased mind, asked a further question in the former manner: “What, by name, are the six?” The Elder, repeating “six,” replied: “The internal sense bases.” Herein, “six” is a numerical designation. “Internal” refers to those connected with the inner self, or those that operate with the self as their basis. They are called “bases” because they extend the streams of saṃsāra, or because they lead to the long suffering of saṃsāra—this is a designation for the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. And here, in accordance with the previous method, it is stated as “the six internal sense bases,” not because there is an absence of other groups of six. As it is said:

“Chasu[V 0.0066], bhikkhave, dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamesu chasu? Chasu ajjhattikesu āyatanesu. Imesu kho, bhikkhave, chasu dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Cha pañhā cha uddesā cha veyyākaraṇānī’ti iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vutta”nti (a. ni. 10.27).

“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu rightly becomes disenchanted with six things… he makes an end of suffering. In which six? In the six internal sense bases. Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu rightly becomes disenchanted with these six things… he makes an end of suffering. ‘Six questions, six summaries, six explanations’—this was said with reference to this.”

Ettha ca cha ajjhattikāni āyatanāni, “suñño gāmoti kho, bhikkhave, channetaṃ ajjhattikānaṃ āyatanānaṃ adhivacana”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.238) vacanato suññato pubbuḷakamarīcikādīni viya aciraṭṭhitikato tucchato vañcanato ca samanupassaṃ nibbindamāno anupubbena dukkhassantaṃ katvā maccurājassa adassanaṃ upeti. Yathāha –

Here, the six internal sense bases are called 'the empty village,' as it is said: 'Monks, "empty village" is a designation for these six internal sense bases' (SN 4.238). Seeing them as empty—like a bubble, a mirage, and so on—as not long-lasting, as hollow, and as deceptive, one grows disenchanted. Gradually, by making an end to suffering, one attains the state of not being seen by the King of Death. As it is said:

“Yathā [M 0.0070] pubbuḷakaṃ passe, yathā passe marīcikaṃ;

Evaṃ lokaṃ avekkhantaṃ, maccurājā na passatī”ti. (dha. pa. 170);

“As one would view a bubble, as one would see a mirage, so should one look upon the world; the King of Death does not see one who looks upon it thus.” (Dhp 170)

Satta nāma kintipañhavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Question: ‘What is Seven?’

Imināpi pañhabyākaraṇena āraddhacitto satthā uttariṃ pañhaṃ pucchati satta nāma kinti? Thero kiñcāpi mahāpañhabyākaraṇe satta viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo vuttā, apica kho pana yesu dhammesu subhāvitacitto bhikkhu dukkhassantakaro hoti, te dassento “satta bojjhaṅgā”ti vissajjeti. Ayampi cattho bhagavatā anumato eva. Yathāha –

By this explanation of the question as well, the Teacher, with a pleased mind, asks a further question: “What is ‘seven’?” Although the seven stations of consciousness were mentioned in the great explanation of the question, the Elder, wishing to point out those qualities in which a monk with a well-developed mind makes an end of suffering, replied: “The seven factors of enlightenment.” This meaning, too, was indeed approved by the Blessed One. As it is said:

“Paṇḍitā gahapatayo kajaṅgalikā bhikkhunī, mahāpaññā gahapatayo kajaṅgalikā bhikkhunī, mañcepi tumhe gahapatayo upasaṅkamitvā etamatthaṃ paṭipuccheyyātha, ahampi cetaṃ evameva byākareyyaṃ, yathā taṃ kajaṅgalikāya [P 0.0084] bhikkhuniyā byākata”nti (a. ni. 10.28).

“Householders, the nun of Kajaṅgalā is wise; householders, the nun of Kajaṅgalā is of great wisdom. Householders, if you were to approach me and ask about this matter, I would explain it in the very same way that it was explained by the nun of Kajaṅgalā.” (AN 10.28)

Tāya ca evaṃ byākataṃ –

And by her it was explained thus:

“Sattasu, āvuso, dhammesu bhikkhu sammā subhāvitacitto…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamesu sattasu? Sattasu bojjhaṅgesu. Imesu kho, āvuso, sattasu dhammesu bhikkhu sammā subhāvitacitto…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Satta pañhā [V 0.0067] satta uddesā satta veyyākaraṇānī’ti iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā, idametaṃ paṭicca vutta”nti (a. ni. 10.28).

“Friends, when a monk's mind is well-developed in seven things… he makes an end of suffering in this very life. Which seven? The seven factors of enlightenment. Friends, when a monk's mind is well-developed in these seven things… he makes an end of suffering in this very life. ‘Seven questions, seven summaries, seven explanations’—this was said by the Blessed One with reference to this.” (AN 10.28)

Evamayamattho bhagavatā anumato evāti veditabbo.

Thus, this meaning should be understood as indeed approved by the Blessed One.

Tattha sattāti ūnādhikanivāraṇagaṇanaparicchedo. Bojjhaṅgāti satiādīnaṃ dhammānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ padattho – etāya lokiyalokuttaramaggakkhaṇe uppajjamānāya līnuddhaccapatiṭṭhānāyūhanakāmasukhattakilamathānuyogaucchedasassatābhinivesādi- anekupaddavappaṭipakkhabhūtāya satidhammavicayavīriyapītippassaddhisamādhupekkhāsaṅkhātāya dhammasāmaggiyā ariyasāvako bujjhatīti katvā bodhi, kilesasantānaniddāya uṭṭhahati, cattāri vā ariyasaccāni paṭivijjhati, nibbānameva vā sacchikarotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Yathāha – “satta bojjhaṅge bhāvetvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ [M 0.0071] abhisambuddho”ti. Yathāvuttappakārāya vā etāya dhammasāmaggiyā bujjhatīti katvā ariyasāvakopi bodhi. Iti tassā dhammasāmaggisaṅkhātāya bodhiyā aṅgabhūtattā bojjhaṅgā jhānaṅgamaggaṅgāni viya, tassa vā bodhīti laddhavohārassa ariyasāvakassa aṅgabhūtattāpi bojjhaṅgā senaṅgarathaṅgādayo viya.

Here, 'seven' is a numerical designation that excludes excess and deficiency. 'Factors of enlightenment' (bojjhaṅgā) is a designation for qualities such as mindfulness. The meaning of the word here is this: By this assemblage of qualities—known as mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity—which arises at the moment of the mundane or supramundane path and counteracts various disturbances such as sloth and restlessness, the application of effort that is wrongly established, indulgence in sensual pleasures, the practice of self-mortification, annihilationism, eternalism, and so on—the noble disciple awakens. Thus, it is called 'awakening' (bodhi). It is said that one awakens from the slumber of the continuum of defilements, or one penetrates the four Noble Truths, or one realizes Nibbāna itself. As it is said: “Having developed the seven factors of enlightenment, he awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.” Alternatively, because the noble disciple awakens by means of this assemblage of qualities as described, the noble disciple is also called 'awakening' (bodhi). Therefore, because they are components of that awakening, which is described as an assemblage of qualities—like the factors of jhāna or the factors of the path—they are called 'factors of enlightenment' (bojjhaṅgā). Or, because they are components of the noble disciple who has gained the designation 'awakening'—like the components of an army, a chariot, and so on—they are also called 'factors of enlightenment'.

Apica “bojjhaṅgāti kenaṭṭhena bojjhaṅgā? Bodhāya saṃvattantīti bojjhaṅgā, bujjhantīti bojjhaṅgā, anubujjhantīti bojjhaṅgā, paṭibujjhantīti bojjhaṅgā, sambujjhantīti bojjhaṅgā”ti (paṭi. ma. 2.17) imināpi paṭisambhidāyaṃ vuttena vidhinā bojjhaṅgānaṃ bojjhaṅgaṭṭho veditabbo. Evamime satta bojjhaṅge bhāvento bahulīkaronto na cirasseva ekantanibbidādiguṇapaṭilābhī hoti, tena diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hotīti vuccati[P 0.0085]. Vuttañcetaṃ bhagavatā –

Furthermore, the meaning of 'factors of enlightenment' should be understood according to the method stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: “In what sense are they factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅgā)? Because they conduce to awakening (bodhāya saṃvattantīti), they are factors of enlightenment; because they awaken (bujjhantīti), they are factors of enlightenment; because they understand (anubujjhantīti), they are factors of enlightenment; because they realize (paṭibujjhantīti), they are factors of enlightenment; because they fully awaken (sambujjhantīti), they are factors of enlightenment.” (Paṭi. Ma. 2.17) Thus, one who develops and cultivates these seven factors of enlightenment will, before long, attain the qualities of complete disenchantment and so forth, and thereby is said to make an end of suffering in this very life. And this was spoken by the Blessed One:

“Sattime, bhikkhave, bojjhaṅgā bhāvitā bahulīkatā ekantanibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattantī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.201).

“Monks, these seven factors of enlightenment, when developed and cultivated, lead entirely to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to full awakening, and to Nibbāna.” (SN 5.201)

Aṭṭha nāma kintipañhavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Question: 'What is Eight?'

Evaṃ imināpi pañhabyākaraṇena āraddhacitto satthā uttariṃ pañhaṃ pucchati aṭṭha nāma kinti? Thero kiñcāpi mahāpañhabyākaraṇe aṭṭha lokadhammā vuttā, apica kho pana yesu dhammesu [V 0.0068] subhāvitacitto bhikkhu dukkhassantakaro hoti, te dassento “ariyāni aṭṭha maggaṅgānī”ti avatvā yasmā aṭṭhaṅgavinimutto maggo nāma natthi, aṭṭhaṅgamattameva tu maggo, tasmā tamatthaṃ sādhento desanāvilāsena ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggoti vissajjeti. Bhagavatāpi cāyamattho desanānayo ca anumato eva. Yathāha –

Thus, with his mind pleased by this explanation of the question, the Teacher asks a further question: “What is eight?” Although in the great explanation of the question the Elder had spoken of the eight worldly conditions, wishing to show those states in which a monk with a well-developed mind becomes an end-maker of suffering, without saying, “the eight noble path factors,” he replies, “The Noble Eightfold Path.” He does so because there is no path apart from the eight factors, and the path is nothing but the measure of the eight factors, thus establishing this meaning with the elegance of the teaching. This meaning and this method of teaching were indeed approved by the Blessed One. As it is said:

“Paṇḍitā gahapatayo kajaṅgalikā bhikkhunī…pe… ahampi evameva byākareyyaṃ, yathā taṃ kajaṅgalikāya bhikkhuniyā byākata”nti (a. ni. 10.28).

“Householders, the nun of Kajaṅgalā is wise… I too would explain it in the very same way that it was explained by the nun of Kajaṅgalā.”

Tāya [M 0.0072] ca evaṃ byākataṃ –

And by her it was explained thus:

“Aṭṭhasu, āvuso, dhammesu bhikkhu sammā subhāvitacitto…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Aṭṭha pañhā, aṭṭha uddesā, aṭṭha veyyākaraṇānī’ti iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā, idametaṃ paṭicca vutta”nti (a. ni. 10.28).

“Friends, when a monk's mind is well-developed in eight things… he makes an end of suffering in this very life. ‘Eight questions, eight summaries, eight explanations’—this was said by the Blessed One with reference to this.” (AN 10.28)

Evamayaṃ attho ca desanānayo ca bhagavatā anumato evāti veditabbo.

Thus, this meaning and this method of teaching should be understood as indeed approved by the Blessed One.

Tattha ariyoti nibbānatthikehi abhigantabbo, apica ārakā kilesehi vattanato, ariyabhāvakaraṇato, ariyaphalapaṭilābhato cāpi ariyoti veditabbo. Aṭṭha aṅgāni assāti aṭṭhaṅgiko. Svāyaṃ caturaṅgikā viya senā, pañcaṅgikaṃ viya ca tūriyaṃ aṅgavinibbhogena anupalabbhasabhāvato aṅgamattamevāti veditabbo. Maggati iminā nibbānaṃ, sayaṃ vā maggati, kilese mārento vā gacchatīti maggo.

Herein, 'ariya' (noble) should be understood as that which is to be approached by those who desire Nibbāna. Furthermore, it should be understood as 'ariya' because it proceeds far from the defilements, because it brings about the state of nobility, and also because of the attainment of the noble fruit. 'Aṭṭhaṅgika' means 'having eight factors.' Just like an army with four divisions or a five-part musical ensemble, it should be understood as being merely a collection of factors, because it has no nature that can be found when the factors are separated. It is called 'magga' (path) because by this one seeks Nibbāna, or it seeks Nibbāna itself, or it goes to Nibbāna while destroying the defilements.

Evamaṭṭhappabhedañcimaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bhāvento bhikkhu [P 0.0086] avijjaṃ bhindati, vijjaṃ uppādeti, nibbānaṃ sacchikaroti, tena diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hotīti vuccati. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Thus, it is said that a bhikkhu who develops this eight-factored path with its eightfold division destroys ignorance, gives rise to true knowledge, and realizes Nibbāna; thereby, he becomes an end-maker of suffering in this very life. And this was spoken:

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, sālisūkaṃ vā yavasūkaṃ vā sammā paṇihitaṃ hatthena vā pādena vā akkantaṃ hatthaṃ vā pādaṃ vā bhecchati, lohitaṃ vā uppādessatīti ṭhānametaṃ vijjati. Taṃ kissa hetu? Sammā paṇihitattā, bhikkhave, sūkassa, evameva kho, bhikkhave[V 0.0069], so vata bhikkhu sammā paṇihitāya diṭṭhiyā sammā paṇihitāya maggabhāvanāya avijjaṃ bhecchati, vijjaṃ uppādessati, nibbānaṃ sacchikarissatīti ṭhānametaṃ vijjatī”ti (a. ni. 1.42).

'Just as, monks, an awn of rice or an awn of barley, if rightly placed, when pressed upon by hand or by foot, will pierce the hand or the foot and cause blood to flow—this is possible. For what reason? Because, monks, of the awn being rightly placed. In the very same way, monks, it is possible that a bhikkhu with a rightly established view and a rightly established development of the path will destroy ignorance, give rise to true knowledge, and realize Nibbāna.'

Nava nāma kintipañhavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Question: What is This Called 'Nine'?

Imināpi pañhabyākaraṇena āraddhacitto satthā uttariṃ pañhaṃ pucchati nava nāma kinti? Thero navaiti paccanubhāsitvā “sattāvāsā”ti vissajjeti. Tattha navāti gaṇanaparicchedo. Sattāti jīvitindriyappaṭibaddhe khandhe [M 0.0073] upādāya paññattā pāṇino paṇṇatti vā. Āvāsāti āvasanti etesūti āvāsā, sattānaṃ āvāsā sattāvāsā. Esa desanāmaggo, atthato pana navavidhānaṃ sattānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Yathāha –

Pleased by this answer to the question as well, the Teacher asks a further question: 'What is this called 'nine'?' The Elder, repeating 'nine,' replies: 'The abodes of beings.' Herein, 'nine' is a numerical delimiter. 'Beings' (sattā) are living creatures designated in dependence on the aggregates connected with the life faculty, or it is a designation. 'Abodes' (āvāsā) are so called because beings dwell (āvasanti) in them; the abodes of beings are 'sattāvāsā'. This is the method of the teaching, but in terms of meaning, this is a designation for nine kinds of beings. As it is said:

“Santāvuso, sattā nānattakāyā nānattasaññino, seyyathāpi manussā ekacce ca devā ekacce ca vinipātikā, ayaṃ paṭhamo sattāvāso. Santāvuso, sattā nānattakāyā ekattasaññino, seyyathāpi, devā brahmakāyikā, paṭhamābhinibbattā, ayaṃ dutiyo sattāvāso. Santāvuso, sattā ekattakāyā nānattasaññino, seyyathāpi, devā ābhassarā, ayaṃ tatiyo sattāvāso. Santāvuso, sattā ekattakāyā ekattasaññino, seyyathāpi, devā subhakiṇhā, ayaṃ catuttho sattāvāso. Santāvuso, sattā asaññino appaṭisaṃvedino, seyyathāpi, devā asaññasattā, ayaṃ pañcamo sattāvāso. Santāvuso, sattā sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ…pe… ākāsānañcāyatanūpagā[P 0.0087], ayaṃ chaṭṭho sattāvāso. Santāvuso, sattā…pe… viññāṇañcāyatanūpagā, ayaṃ sattamo sattāvāso. Santāvuso, sattā…pe… ākiñcaññāyatanūpagā, ayaṃ aṭṭhamo sattāvāso. Santāvuso, sattā…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanūpagā, ayaṃ navamo sattāvāso”ti (dī. ni. 3.341).

'Friends, there are beings with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, such as humans, some devas, and some beings in a state of woe. This is the first abode of beings. Friends, there are beings with diverse bodies but unified perception, such as the devas of Brahmā's company, the first to be reborn there. This is the second abode of beings. Friends, there are beings with unified bodies but diverse perceptions, such as the devas of Streaming Radiance. This is the third abode of beings. Friends, there are beings with unified bodies and unified perception, such as the devas of Refulgent Glory. This is the fourth abode of beings. Friends, there are beings without perception and without feeling, such as the non-percipient beings. This is the fifth abode of beings. Friends, there are beings who, having completely transcended perceptions of form… have reached the dimension of infinite space. This is the sixth abode of beings. Friends, there are beings… who have reached the dimension of infinite consciousness. This is the seventh abode of beings. Friends, there are beings… who have reached the dimension of nothingness. This is the eighth abode of beings. Friends, there are beings… who have reached the dimension of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is the ninth abode of beings.'

Purimanayeneva cettha “nava sattāvāsā”ti vuttaṃ, na aññesaṃ navannamabhāvato. Yathāha –

Here, ‘nine abodes of beings’ is stated in the same way as before, not because there are no other groups of nine. As it is said—

“Navasu, bhikkhave, dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamesu navasu? Navasu sattāvāsesu. Imesu kho, bhikkhave, navasu dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Nava pañhā[V 0.0070], nava uddesā, nava veyyākaraṇānī’ti iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vutta”nti (a. ni. 10.27).

'Monks, a bhikkhu who rightly becomes disenchanted with nine things… becomes an end-maker of suffering. With which nine? With the nine abodes of beings. Monks, it is with these nine things that a bhikkhu who rightly becomes disenchanted… becomes an end-maker of suffering. That which was spoken as, ‘Nine questions, nine headings, nine explanations,’ was spoken in reference to this.'

Ettha [M 0.0074] ca “nava dhammā pariññeyyā. Katame nava? Nava sattāvāsā”ti (dī. ni. 3.359) vacanato navasu sattāvāsesu ñātapariññāya dhuvasubhasukhattabhāvadassanaṃ pahāya suddhasaṅkhārapuñjamattadassanena nibbindamāno tīraṇapariññāya aniccānupassanena virajjamāno dukkhānupassanena vimuccamāno anattānupassanena sammā pariyantadassāvī pahānapariññāya sammattamabhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. Tenetaṃ vuttaṃ –

And here, in accordance with the saying: ‘Nine things are to be fully understood. What nine? The nine abodes of beings’ (Dī. Ni. 3.359), with regard to the nine abodes of beings, by the full understanding of what is known (ñātapariññā), one abandons the seeing of a state of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self. By seeing merely a heap of bare formations, one becomes disenchanted. By the full understanding of investigation (tīraṇapariññā), one becomes dispassionate through the contemplation of impermanence, is liberated through the contemplation of suffering, and rightly sees the end through the contemplation of non-self. By the full understanding of abandonment (pahānapariññā), having directly realized the peaceful state, one makes an end of suffering in this very life. Therefore, it was said:

“Navasu, bhikkhave, dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno…pe… diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamesu navasu? Navasu sattāvāsesū”ti (a. ni. 10.27).

“Monks, a bhikkhu who rightly becomes disenchanted with nine things… makes an end of suffering in this very life. Which nine? The nine abodes of beings.” (A. Ni. 10.27)

Dasa nāma kintipañhavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Question: What is This Called 'Ten'?

Evaṃ imināpi pañhabyākaraṇena āraddhacitto satthā uttariṃ pañhaṃ pucchati dasa nāma kinti? Tattha kiñcāpi imassa pañhassa ito aññatra veyyākaraṇesu dasa akusalakammapathā vuttā. Yathāha –

Thus, with this explanation also, the Teacher, his mind pleased, asks a further question: “What is this called ‘ten’?” Here, although in other explanations of this question the ten unwholesome courses of action are spoken of, as it is said:

“Dasasu, bhikkhave, dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamesu dasasu? Dasasu akusalakammapathesu. Imesu kho, bhikkhave, dasasu dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno…pe. [P 0.0088]… dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Dasa pañhā dasa uddesā dasa veyyākaraṇānī’ti iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vutta”nti (a. ni. 10.27).

“Monks, a bhikkhu who rightly becomes disenchanted with ten things… makes an end of suffering in this very life. Which ten? The ten unwholesome courses of action. Monks, a bhikkhu who rightly becomes disenchanted with these ten things… makes an end of suffering in this very life. ‘Ten questions, ten headings, ten explanations’—this was said, and it was said in reference to this.” (A. Ni. 10.27)

Idha pana yasmā ayamāyasmā attānaṃ anupanetvā aññaṃ byākātukāmo, yasmā vā iminā pariyāyena byākataṃ subyākatameva hoti, tasmā yehi dasahi aṅgehi samannāgato arahāti pavuccati, tesaṃ adhigamaṃ dīpento dasahaṅgehi samannāgato arahāti pavuccatīti puggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya vissajjeti. Yato ettha yehi dasahi aṅgehi samannāgato arahāti pavuccati, tāni dasaṅgāni “dasa nāma ki”nti puṭṭhena therena niddiṭṭhānīti veditabbāni. Tāni ca dasa –

But here, since this venerable one, without bringing himself forward, wishes to declare another, or because what is explained in this way is indeed well-explained, therefore, showing the path to their attainment, he answers with a teaching established on the individual, saying, ‘One endowed with ten factors is called an Arahant.’ Since it is said here that one endowed with ten factors is called an Arahant, it should be understood that those ten factors were pointed out by the Elder when asked, ‘What is this called “ten”?’ And those ten are:

“Asekho [V 0.0071] asekhoti, bhante, vuccati, kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, bhikkhu asekho hotīti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu asekhāya [M 0.0075] sammādiṭṭhiyā samannāgato hoti, asekhena sammāsaṅkappena samannāgato hoti, asekhāya sammāvācāya samannāgato hoti, asekhena sammākammantena samannāgato hoti, asekhena sammāājīvena samannāgato hoti, asekhena sammāvāyāmena samannāgato hoti, asekhāya sammāsatiyā samannāgato hoti, asekhena sammāsamādhinā samannāgato hoti, asekhena sammāñāṇena samannāgato hoti, asekhāya sammāvimuttiyā samannāgato hoti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu asekho hotī”ti (a. ni. 10.111). –

“‘One beyond training, one beyond training,’ it is said, venerable sir. To what extent, venerable sir, is a bhikkhu one beyond training?” “Here, monks, a bhikkhu is endowed with the right view of one beyond training, endowed with the right intention of one beyond training, endowed with the right speech of one beyond training, endowed with the right action of one beyond training, endowed with the right livelihood of one beyond training, endowed with the right effort of one beyond training, endowed with the right mindfulness of one beyond training, endowed with the right concentration of one beyond training, endowed with the right knowledge of one beyond training, and endowed with the right liberation of one beyond training. Thus, monks, a bhikkhu is one beyond training.” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.111).

Evamādīsu suttesu vuttanayeneva veditabbānīti.

It should be understood in the same way as stated in such suttas.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha.

Kumārapañhavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Youth's Questions is completed.

5. Maṅgalasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Maṅgala Sutta

Nikkhepappayojanaṃ

The Purpose of its Placement

Idāni [V 0.0072] kumārapañhānantaraṃ nikkhittassa maṅgalasuttassa atthavaṇṇanākkamo anuppatto, tassa idha nikkhepappayojanaṃ vatvā atthavaṇṇanaṃ karissāma. Seyyathidaṃ – idañhi suttaṃ iminā anukkamena bhagavatā avuttampi yvāyaṃ saraṇagamanehi sāsanotāro, sikkhāpadadvattiṃsākārakumārapañhehi [P 0.0089] ca sīlasamādhipaññāppabhedanayo dassito, sabbopesa paramamaṅgalabhūto, yato maṅgalatthikena ettheva abhiyogo kātabbo, so cassa maṅgalabhāvo iminā suttānusārena veditabboti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

5. Now, immediately after the Kumārapañhā (Questions of the Youth), the turn has come for the explanation of the meaning of the Maṅgala Sutta, which was placed here. Having stated the purpose of its placement here, we shall provide the explanation of its meaning. As follows: although this sutta was not spoken by the Blessed One in this sequence, the method with the divisions of virtue, concentration, and wisdom—which has been shown by the goings for refuge that constitute entry into the Dispensation, and by the training rules, the thirty-two aspects, and the Kumārapañhā—all this has become the supreme blessing. Therefore, effort should be made right here by one who desires blessings. And it was stated in order to show that the state of being a blessing of this sutta should be known in accordance with this sutta.

Idamassa idha nikkhepappayojanaṃ.
