This is the purpose of its placement here.

Paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathā

The Account of the First Great Council

Evaṃ [M 0.0076] nikkhittassa panassa atthavaṇṇanatthaṃ ayaṃ mātikā –

Now, for the purpose of explaining the meaning of this sutta thus placed, this is the mātikā (outline):

“Vuttaṃ yena yadā yasmā, cetaṃ vatvā imaṃ vidhiṃ;

Evamiccādipāṭhassa, atthaṃ nānappakārato.

By whom it was spoken, when, and for what reason; having stated this and this method, the meaning of the text beginning with 'Thus' will be explained in various ways.

“Vaṇṇayanto samuṭṭhānaṃ, vatvā yaṃ yattha maṅgalaṃ;

Vavatthapetvā taṃ tassa, maṅgalattaṃ vibhāvaye”ti.

Explaining, having stated the origin and having determined which blessing is in which context, one should clarify its nature as a blessing.

Tattha “vuttaṃ yena yadā yasmā, cetaṃ vatvā imaṃ vidhi”nti ayaṃ tāva addhagāthā yadidaṃ “evaṃ me sutaṃ ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā…pe… bhagavantaṃ gāthāya ajjhabhāsī”ti, idaṃ vacanaṃ sandhāya vuttā. Idañhi anussavavasena vuttaṃ, so ca bhagavā sayambhū anācariyako, tasmā nedaṃ tassa bhagavato vacanaṃ arahato sammāsambuddhassa. Yato vattabbametaṃ “idaṃ vacanaṃ kena vuttaṃ[V 0.0073], kadā, kasmā ca vutta”nti. Vuccate – āyasmatā ānandena vuttaṃ, tañca paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle.

Therein, this half-verse, 'By whom it was spoken, when, and for what reason; having stated this and this method,' was spoken in reference to this statement: 'Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One… addressed the Blessed One with a verse.' For this was spoken by way of oral tradition, and that Blessed One is self-arisen, without a teacher; therefore, this is not the speech of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Since this should be stated: 'By whom was this statement spoken, when, and for what reason was it spoken?' It is said: It was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda, and that was at the time of the First Great Council.

Paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti cesā sabbasuttanidānakosallatthamādito pabhuti evaṃ veditabbā. Dhammacakkappavattanañhi ādiṃ katvā yāva subhaddaparibbājakavinayanā, katabuddhakicce kusinārāyaṃ upavattane mallānaṃ sālavane yamakasālānamantare visākhapuṇṇamadivase paccūsasamaye anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbute, bhagavati lokanāthe bhagavato parinibbāne sannipatitānaṃ sattannaṃ bhikkhusatasahassānaṃ saṅghatthero āyasmā mahākassapo sattāhaparinibbute [P 0.0090] bhagavati subhaddena vuḍḍhapabbajitena “alaṃ, āvuso, mā socittha, mā paridevittha, sumuttā mayaṃ tena mahāsamaṇena, upaddutā ca homa ‘idaṃ vo kappati idaṃ vo na kappatī’ti, idāni pana mayaṃ yaṃ icchissāma taṃ karissāma, yaṃ na icchissāma na taṃ karissāmā”ti (cūḷava. 437; dī. ni. 2.232) vuttavacanamanussaranto “ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjati yaṃ pāpabhikkhū ‘atītasatthukaṃ pāvacana’nti maññamānā pakkhaṃ labhitvā na cirasseva saddhammaṃ antaradhāpeyyuṃ. Yāva ca dhammavinayo tiṭṭhati, tāva anatītasatthukameva pāvacanaṃ hoti. Yathāha bhagavā –

And this First Great Council, for the sake of skill in the introductions of all suttas, should be known thus from the beginning. For when the Blessed One, the Lord of the World—having completed the Buddha's duties, starting from the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma up to the taming of the wanderer Subhadda—had attained Parinibbāna with the Nibbāna-element without residue at dawn on the full-moon day of Visākha, in the Sāla grove of the Mallas at the Upavattana bend of Kusinārā, between the twin Sāla trees; then, among the seven hundred thousand bhikkhus who had assembled at the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One, the Elder of the Saṅgha, the Venerable Mahākassapa, seven days after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, recalled the words spoken by Subhadda, who had ordained in old age: 'Enough, friends, do not grieve, do not lament. We are well freed from that great ascetic. We were oppressed by his saying, “This is allowable for you, this is not allowable for you.” But now we shall do what we wish, and what we do not wish, we shall not do.' Recalling this, he thought: 'There is this possibility that evil bhikkhus, thinking, “The Teacher’s instruction is a thing of the past,” might gain a faction and before long cause the good Dhamma to disappear. And as long as the Dhamma and Vinaya remain, the Teacher’s instruction has not become a thing of the past. As the Blessed One said—

“Yo [M 0.0077] vo, ānanda, mayā dhammo ca vinayo ca desito paññatto, so vo mamaccayena satthā”ti (dī. ni. 2.216).

'Ānanda, the Dhamma and the Vinaya that I have taught and laid down for you all, that will be your Teacher after my passing.'

“Yaṃnūnāhaṃ dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyeyyaṃ, yathayidaṃ sāsanaṃ addhaniyaṃ assa ciraṭṭhitikaṃ”.

'What if I were to chant the Dhamma and the Vinaya, so that this Dispensation might be long-lasting and endure for a long time?'

Yañcāhaṃ bhagavatā –

And I, who was favored by the Blessed One—

“Dhāressasi pana me tvaṃ, kassapa, sāṇāni paṃsukūlāni nibbasanānī”ti vatvā cīvare sādhāraṇaparibhogena ceva –

'Kassapa, will you wear my worn-out, hempen, refuse-rag robes?'—having said this, and by the shared use of the robe—

“Ahaṃ, bhikkhave, yāvade ākaṅkhāmi vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharāmi, kassapopi, bhikkhave, yāvadeva ākaṅkhati vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharatī”ti –

'Monks, just as I wish, secluded from sensual pleasures… I enter and dwell in the first jhāna. Kassapa too, monks, just as he wishes, secluded from sensual pleasures… enters and dwells in the first jhāna.'

Evamādinā [V 0.0074] nayena navānupubbavihārachaḷabhiññāppabhede uttarimanussadhamme attanā samasamaṭṭhapanena ca anuggahito, tassa me kimaññaṃ āṇaṇyaṃ bhavissati? “Nanu maṃ bhagavā rājā viya sakakavacaissariyānuppadānena attano kulavaṃsappatiṭṭhāpakaṃ puttaṃ ‘saddhammavaṃsappatiṭṭhāpako me ayaṃ bhavissatī’ti mantvā iminā asādhāraṇena anuggahena anuggahesī”ti cintayanto dhammavinayasaṅgāyanatthaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ [P 0.0091] ussāhaṃ janesi? Yathāha –

And I was favored by this and other methods, by being placed as equal to himself in the supramundane states distinguished by the nine successive attainments and the six higher knowledges. For me, such a one, what other freedom from debt could there be? 'Did not the Blessed One, just as a king favors a son who establishes his lineage by bestowing the authority of his own royal insignia, favor me with this uncommon favor, thinking, “This one will be the establisher of the lineage of the good Dhamma for me”?' Thinking thus, he generated enthusiasm in the bhikkhus for the chanting of the Dhamma and Vinaya. As it is said:

“Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo bhikkhū āmantesi – ekamidāhaṃ, āvuso, samayaṃ pāvāya kusināraṃ addhānamaggappaṭipanno mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehī”ti (dī. ni. 2.231; cūḷava. 437) sabbaṃ subhaddakaṇḍaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

Then the Venerable Mahākassapa addressed the bhikkhus: 'Friends, on one occasion I was travelling on the long road from Pāvā to Kusinārā with a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, with five hundred bhikkhus.' The entire Subhadda section should be elaborated.

Tato paraṃ āha –

After that, he said:

“Handa mayaṃ, āvuso, dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyeyyāma, pure adhammo dippati, dhammo paṭibāhiyyati, avinayo dippati, vinayo paṭibāhiyyati, pure adhammavādino balavanto honti, dhammavādino dubbalā honti, avinayavādino balavanto honti, vinayavādino dubbalā hontī”ti (cūḷava. 437).

'Come, friends, let us chant the Dhamma and the Vinaya, before the non-Dhamma shines forth and the Dhamma is obstructed, before the non-Vinaya shines forth and the Vinaya is obstructed, before those who speak non-Dhamma become strong and those who speak Dhamma become weak, before those who speak non-Vinaya become strong and those who speak Vinaya become weak.'

Bhikkhū [M 0.0078] āhaṃsu “tena hi, bhante, thero bhikkhū uccinatū”ti. Thero sakalanavaṅgasatthusāsanapariyattidhare puthujjanasotāpannasakadāgāmianāgāmisukkhavipassakakhīṇāsavabhikkhū anekasate anekasahasse ca vajjetvā tipiṭakasabbapariyattippabhedadhare paṭisambhidāppatte mahānubhāve yebhuyyena bhagavatā etadaggaṃ āropite tevijjādibhede khīṇāsavabhikkhūyeva ekūnapañcasate pariggahesi. Ye sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ “atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo ekenūnapañcaarahantasatāni uccinī”ti (cūḷava. 437).

The monks said: "If so, venerable sir, let the Elder select the monks." The Elder, having set aside many hundreds and thousands of monks—worldlings, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and dry-insight Arahants who were bearers of the entire nine-limbed teaching of the Teacher—selected only five hundred Arahants less one. These were bearers of the three Piṭakas, the entire Pariyatti with its divisions; they had attained the analytical knowledges, possessed great power, had for the most part been placed by the Blessed One in the rank of foremost, and had distinctions such as the three knowledges. It was with reference to these that this was said: "Then the Venerable Mahākassapa selected five hundred Arahants less one."

Kissa pana thero ekenūnamakāsīti? Āyasmato ānandattherassa okāsakaraṇatthaṃ. Tena hāyasmatā sahāpi vināpi na sakkā dhammasaṅgīti kātuṃ. So hāyasmā sekho sakaraṇīyo, tasmā saha na sakkā, yasmā panassa kiñci dasabaladesitaṃ suttageyyādikaṃ bhagavato asammukhā paṭiggahitaṃ nāma natthi, tasmā vināpi na sakkā. Yadi evaṃ sekhopi samāno dhammasaṅgītiyā bahūkārattā therena uccinitabbo assa, atha kasmā na uccinitoti? Parūpavādavivajjanato[V 0.0075]. Thero hi āyasmante [P 0.0092] ānande ativiya vissattho ahosi. Tathā hi naṃ sirasmiṃ palitesu jātesupi “na vāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.154) kumārakavādena ovadati. Sakyakulappasuto cāyaṃ āyasmā tathāgatassa bhātā cūḷapitu putto, tatra bhikkhū chandāgamanaṃ viya maññamānā “bahū asekhapaṭisambhidāppatte bhikkhū ṭhapetvā ānandaṃ sekhapaṭisambhidāppattaṃ thero uccinī”ti upavadeyyuṃ. Taṃ parūpavādaṃ parivivajjento “ānandaṃ vinā saṅgīti na sakkā kātuṃ, bhikkhūnaṃyeva anumatiyā gahessāmī”ti na uccini.

Why, then, did the Elder make it one short? To make an opportunity for the Venerable Elder Ānanda. For with that Venerable One, or without him, it was not possible to hold the Dhamma council. That Venerable One was a trainee and still had a task to do; therefore, it was not possible with him. And because there was no discourse, verse, etc., taught by the one with Ten Powers that he had received not in the presence of the Blessed One, it was not possible without him. If so, even though he was a trainee, because of his great service to the Dhamma council, he should have been selected by the Elder. So why was he not selected? To avoid the criticism of others. For the Elder was very intimate with the Venerable Ānanda. Indeed, even when grey hairs had appeared on his head, he would admonish him with the term 'young boy', saying: "This young boy does not know moderation." And this Venerable One was born into the Sakyan clan, the brother of the Tathāgata, the son of his paternal uncle. In that case, the monks, thinking it was like an act of favoritism, might have criticized, saying: "The Elder has set aside many monks who are non-trainees and have attained the analytical knowledges, and has selected Ānanda, who is a trainee and has attained the analytical knowledges." Avoiding that criticism from others, and thinking, "The council cannot be held without Ānanda; I will accept him only with the consent of the monks," he did not select him.

Atha sayameva bhikkhū ānandassatthāya theraṃ yāciṃsu. Yathāha –

Then the monks, of their own accord, requested the Elder for the sake of Ānanda. As it is said:

“Bhikkhū āyasmantaṃ mahākassapaṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘ayaṃ, bhante, āyasmā ānando kiñcāpi sekho, abhabbo chandā dosā mohā bhayā agatiṃ gantuṃ, bahu cānena bhagavato santike dhammo ca vinayo ca pariyatto, tena hi, bhante, thero [M 0.0079] āyasmantampi ānandaṃ uccinatū’ti. Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo āyasmantampi ānandaṃ uccinī”ti (cūḷava. 437).

The monks said this to the Venerable Mahākassapa: "Venerable sir, although this Venerable Ānanda is a trainee, he is incapable of following a wrong course through desire, hate, delusion, or fear. And much Dhamma and Vinaya has been learned by him in the presence of the Blessed One. Therefore, venerable sir, let the Elder also select the Venerable Ānanda." Then the Venerable Mahākassapa also selected the Venerable Ānanda.

Evaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ anumatiyā uccinitena tenāyasmatā saddhiṃ pañcatherasatāni ahesuṃ.

Thus, with that venerable one having been selected with the consent of the monks, there were, together with him, five hundred elders.

Atha kho therānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ etadahosi – “kattha nu kho mayaṃ dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyeyyāmā”ti. Atha kho therānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ etadahosi “rājagahaṃ kho mahāgocaraṃ pahūtasenāsanaṃ, yaṃnūna mayaṃ rājagahe vassaṃ vasantā dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyeyyāma, naññe bhikkhū rājagahe vassaṃ upagaccheyyu”nti. Kasmā pana nesaṃ etadahosi? Idaṃ amhākaṃ thāvarakammaṃ, koci visabhāgapuggalo [P 0.0093] saṅghamajjhaṃ pavisitvā ukkoṭeyyāti. Athāyasmā mahākassapo ñattidutiyena kammena sāvesi. Taṃ saṅgītikkhandhake (cūḷava. 437) vuttanayeneva ñātabbaṃ.

Then this occurred to the elder monks: "Where, indeed, should we chant the Dhamma and the Vinaya?" Then this occurred to the elder monks: "Rājagaha has a great alms-round resort and is endowed with lodgings. What if we, while dwelling for the rains-residence in Rājagaha, were to chant the Dhamma and the Vinaya, and other monks were not to enter the rains-residence in Rājagaha?" And why did this occur to them? "This is our enduring task. Some unsuitable person might enter the midst of the Saṅgha and cause a disruption." Then the Venerable Mahākassapa informed the Saṅgha by means of a formal act preceded by a motion. This should be understood in the same way as it is stated in the Saṅgītikkhandhaka.

Atha tathāgatassa parinibbānato sattasu sādhukīḷanadivasesu sattasu ca dhātupūjādivasesu vītivattesu “aḍḍhamāso atikkanto, idāni gimhānaṃ diyaḍḍho māso seso, upakaṭṭhā vassūpanāyikā”ti mantvā mahākassapatthero “rājagahaṃ, āvuso, gacchāmā”ti upaḍḍhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ gahetvā ekaṃ maggaṃ gato. Anuruddhattheropi upaḍḍhaṃ gahetvā ekaṃ maggaṃ gato, ānandatthero [V 0.0076] pana bhagavato pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto sāvatthiṃ gantvā rājagahaṃ gantukāmo yena sāvatthi, tena cārikaṃ pakkāmi. Ānandattherena gatagataṭṭhāne mahāparidevo ahosi, “bhante ānanda, kuhiṃ satthāraṃ ṭhapetvā āgatosī”ti? Anupubbena sāvatthiṃ anuppatte there bhagavato parinibbānasamaye viya mahāparidevo ahosi.

Then, when seven days of festive honor and seven days of venerating the relics had passed since the Tathāgata’s Parinibbāna, the Elder Mahākassapa, considering, "Half a month has passed, now a month and a half of the hot season remains, and the time for the rains-residence is near," said, "Friends, let us go to Rājagaha." Taking half the community of monks, he went by one road. The Elder Anuruddha also took half and went by one road. The Elder Ānanda, however, taking the Blessed One’s bowl and robe and surrounded by the community of monks, went to Sāvatthī, intending to go to Rājagaha, and so set out on a journey along that route. In every place the Elder Ānanda went, there was great lamentation: "Venerable Ānanda, where have you come from, having left the Teacher behind?" When the Elder arrived in Sāvatthī in due course, there was great lamentation, just as at the time of the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna.

Tatra sudaṃ āyasmā ānando aniccatādipaṭisaṃyuttāya dhammiyā kathāya taṃ mahājanaṃ saññāpetvā jetavanaṃ pavisitvā dasabalena vasitagandhakuṭiyā dvāraṃ vivaritvā mañcapīṭhaṃ nīharitvā papphoṭetvā gandhakuṭiṃ sammajjitvā milātamālākacavaraṃ chaḍḍetvā mañcapīṭhaṃ atiharitvā puna yathāṭhāne ṭhapetvā bhagavato ṭhitakāle karaṇīyaṃ vattaṃ sabbamakāsi. Atha [M 0.0080] thero bhagavato parinibbānato pabhuti ṭhānanisajjabahulattā ussannadhātukaṃ kāyaṃ samassāsetuṃ dutiyadivase khīravirecanaṃ pivitvā vihāreyeva nisīdi, yaṃ sandhāya subhena māṇavena pahitaṃ māṇavakaṃ etadavoca –

There, the Venerable Ānanda, having instructed that great crowd of people with a Dhamma talk connected with impermanence and so on, entered Jetavana. He opened the door of the Perfumed Chamber where the one with Ten Powers had dwelt, took out the bed and chair, dusted them, swept the Perfumed Chamber, discarded the withered flowers and rubbish, brought the bed and chair back in, and placed them again in their proper place. He performed all the duties that were to be done when the Blessed One was present. Then the Elder, in order to soothe his body, whose humors had become aggravated due to much standing and sitting since the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna, on the second day drank a milk-purgative and sat in the monastery. It was with reference to this that he said the following to the young man sent by the youth Subha:

“Akālo kho, māṇavaka, atthi [P 0.0094] me ajja bhesajjamattā pītā, appeva nāma svepi upasaṅkameyyāmā”ti (dī. ni. 1.447).

"It is not the time, young man. A measure of medicine has been drunk by me today. Perhaps we might approach tomorrow."

Dutiyadivase cetakattherena pacchāsamaṇena gantvā subhena māṇavena puṭṭho dīghanikāye subhasuttaṃ nāma dasamaṃ suttamabhāsi.

On the second day, having gone with the Elder Cetaka as his attendant monk, and being questioned by the youth Subha, he spoke the tenth discourse in the Dīgha Nikāya, named the Subha Sutta.

Atha kho thero jetavane vihāre khaṇḍaphullappaṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ kārāpetvā upakaṭṭhāya vassūpanāyikāya rājagahaṃ gato. Tathā mahākassapatthero anuruddhatthero ca sabbaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ gahetvā rājagahameva gatā.

Then the Elder, having caused the repairing of the broken and dilapidated in the Jetavana monastery to be done, went to Rājagaha as the day for entering the rains-residence was approaching. Likewise, the Elder Mahākassapa and the Elder Anuruddha, taking the entire community of bhikkhus, went to Rājagaha itself.

Tena kho pana samayena rājagahe aṭṭhārasa mahāvihārā honti. Te sabbepi chaḍḍitapatitauklāpā ahesuṃ. Bhagavato hi parinibbāne sabbe bhikkhū attano attano pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā vihāre ca pariveṇe ca chaḍḍetvā agamaṃsu. Tattha therā bhagavato vacanapūjanatthaṃ titthiyavādaparimocanatthañca “paṭhamaṃ māsaṃ khaṇḍaphullappaṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ karomā”ti cintesuṃ. Titthiyā hi vadeyyuṃ “samaṇassa gotamassa sāvakā satthari ṭhiteyeva vihāre paṭijaggiṃsu, parinibbute chaḍḍesu”nti. Tesaṃ vādaparimocanatthañca cintesunti vuttaṃ hoti. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Now, at that time, there were eighteen great monasteries in Rājagaha. All of them were full of discarded rubbish and debris. For, on account of the Blessed One's Parinibbāna, all the bhikkhus, having taken their own bowls and robes, had abandoned the monasteries and monastic cells and departed. There, the Elders, for the sake of honoring the Blessed One's word and to be free from the criticism of the sectarians, thought: 'For the first month, let us repair what is broken and dilapidated.' Indeed, the sectarians might say: 'The disciples of the ascetic Gotama maintained the monasteries only while the Teacher was present; when he attained Parinibbāna, they abandoned them.' Thus it is said that they also thought this to be free from their criticism. And this was said:

“Atha kho therānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ etadahosi – bhagavatā kho, āvuso, khaṇḍaphullappaṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ [V 0.0077] vaṇṇitaṃ, handa mayaṃ, āvuso, paṭhamaṃ māsaṃ khaṇḍaphullappaṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ karoma, majjhimaṃ māsaṃ sannipatitvā dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyissāmā”ti (cūḷava. 438).

Then this thought occurred to the Elder bhikkhus: 'Friends, the repairing of the broken and dilapidated has been praised by the Blessed One. Come now, friends, for the first month let us perform the repairing of the broken and dilapidated; in the middle month, having assembled, we shall rehearse the Dhamma and the Vinaya.'

Te dutiyadivase gantvā rājadvāre aṭṭhaṃsu. Ajātasattu rājā āgantvā vanditvā “ahaṃ, bhante, kiṃ karomi, kenattho”ti pavāresi. Therā aṭṭhārasamahāvihārappaṭisaṅkharaṇatthāya hatthakammaṃ paṭivedesuṃ. “Sādhu, bhante”ti rājā hatthakammakārake manusse adāsi. Therā paṭhamaṃ māsaṃ sabbavihāre paṭisaṅkharāpesuṃ.

On the second day, they went and stood at the king's gate. King Ajātasattu approached, paid homage, and invited them, saying: 'Venerable sirs, what shall I do? What is needed?' The Elders informed him of the need for manual labor for the purpose of repairing the eighteen great monasteries. 'Very well, venerable sirs,' the king said, and he gave men who could perform manual labor. For the first month, the Elders had all the monasteries repaired.

Atha [M 0.0081] rañño ārocesuṃ – “niṭṭhitaṃ, mahārāja, vihārappaṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ[P 0.0095], idāni dhammavinayasaṅgahaṃ karomā”ti. “Sādhu, bhante, vissatthā karotha, mayhaṃ āṇācakkaṃ, tumhākaṃ dhammacakkaṃ hotu. Āṇāpetha, bhante, kiṃ karomī”ti? “Dhammasaṅgahaṃ karontānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sannisajjaṭṭhānaṃ mahārājā”ti. “Kattha karomi, bhante”ti? “Vebhārapabbatapasse sattapaṇṇiguhādvāre kātuṃ yuttaṃ mahārājā”ti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti kho, rājā ajātasattu, vissakammunā nimmitasadisaṃ suvibhattabhittithambhasopānaṃ nānāvidhamālākammalatākammavicitraṃ mahāmaṇḍapaṃ kārāpetvā vividhakusumadāmaolambakaviniggalantacāruvitānaṃ ratanavicitramaṇikoṭṭimatalamiva ca naṃ nānāpupphūpahāravicitraṃ supariniṭṭhitabhūmikammaṃ brahmavimānasadisaṃ alaṅkaritvā tasmiṃ mahāmaṇḍape pañcasatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ anagghāni pañcakappiyapaccattharaṇasatāni paññāpetvā dakkhiṇabhāgaṃ nissāya uttarābhimukhaṃ therāsanaṃ, maṇḍapamajjhe puratthābhimukhaṃ buddhassa bhagavato āsanārahaṃ dhammāsanaṃ paññāpetvā dantakhacitaṃ cittabījaniñcettha ṭhapetvā bhikkhusaṅghassa ārocāpesi “niṭṭhitaṃ, bhante, kicca”nti.

Then they informed the king: 'Great king, the repairing of the monasteries is finished. Now we shall perform the rehearsal of the Dhamma and Vinaya.' 'Very well, venerable sirs, proceed without hesitation. Let mine be the wheel of authority, and let yours be the wheel of Dhamma. Command me, venerable sirs, what shall I do?' 'A place for the bhikkhus performing the rehearsal of the Dhamma to assemble, great king.' 'Where shall I make it, venerable sirs?' 'It is suitable to make it at the entrance of the Sattapaṇṇi cave on the slope of Mount Vebhāra, great king.' 'Very well, venerable sirs.' Then King Ajātasattu had a great pavilion constructed, like one created by Vissakamma, with well-divided walls, pillars, and staircases, adorned with various kinds of flower-work and creeper-work. He had that pavilion decorated to be like a mansion of Brahmā, with a beautiful canopy from which various garlands of flowers hung, with its ground-work well-finished and adorned with offerings of various flowers, like a floor inlaid with colorful jewels. In that great pavilion, he had five hundred priceless, suitable coverings spread for the five hundred bhikkhus. Against the southern side, he had the Elder's seat prepared facing north. In the middle of the pavilion, facing east, he had a Dhamma-seat prepared, worthy of the Blessed One, the Buddha. Placing there a decorated fan inlaid with ivory, he had the community of bhikkhus informed: 'Venerable sirs, the task is finished.'

Bhikkhū āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ āhaṃsu “sve, āvuso ānanda, saṅghasannipāto, tvañca sekho sakaraṇīyo, tena te na yuttaṃ sannipātaṃ gantuṃ, appamatto hohī”ti. Atha kho āyasmā ānando “sve sannipāto, na kho pana metaṃ patirūpaṃ, yvāhaṃ sekho samāno sannipātaṃ gaccheyya”nti bahudeva rattiṃ kāyagatāya satiyā vītināmetvā rattiyā paccūsasamaye caṅkamā orohitvā vihāraṃ pavisitvā “nipajjissāmī”ti kāyaṃ āvajjesi. Dve pādā bhūmito muttā, appattañca sīsaṃ bimbohanaṃ, etasmiṃ antare anupādāya [P 0.0096] āsavehi cittaṃ vimucci. Ayañhi āyasmā caṅkamena bahi vītināmetvā visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ asakkonto cintesi “nanu maṃ bhagavā etadavoca – ‘katapuññosi tvaṃ, ānanda, padhānamanuyuñja, khippaṃ hohisi [V 0.0078] anāsavo’ti (dī. ni. 2.207). Buddhānañca kathādoso nāma natthi, mama pana accāraddhaṃ vīriyaṃ, tena me cittaṃ uddhaccāya saṃvattati, handāhaṃ vīriyasamataṃ yojemī”ti caṅkamā orohitvā pādadhovanaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā pāde dhovitvā vihāraṃ pavisitvā mañcake nisīditvā “thokaṃ vissamissāmī”ti kāyaṃ mañcake upanāmesi. Dve pādā [M 0.0082] bhūmito muttā, sīsañca bimbohanamasampattaṃ, etasmiṃ antare anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimucci. Catuiriyāpathavirahitaṃ therassa arahattaṃ. Tena “imasmiṃ sāsane anisinno anipanno aṭṭhito acaṅkamanto ko bhikkhu arahattaṃ patto”ti vutte “ānandatthero”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

The bhikkhus said to the Venerable Ānanda: 'Friend Ānanda, tomorrow is the assembly of the Saṅgha. You are still a learner with a task to be done. Therefore, it is not suitable for you to go to the assembly. Be heedful.' Then the Venerable Ānanda, thinking, 'Tomorrow is the assembly, and it is not proper for me, being a learner, to go to the assembly,' spent the whole night long with mindfulness directed to the body. At dawn, descending from his walking path and entering the monastery, he inclined his body, thinking, 'I will lie down.' His two feet were free from the ground, and his head had not yet reached the pillow; in that interval, his mind was liberated from the taints without clinging. Indeed, this Venerable One, having spent time outside on the walking path, was unable to bring about the special attainment and reflected: 'Did not the Blessed One say this to me: "You have made merit, Ānanda. Apply yourself to the endeavor; you will quickly be without taints"? And there is no fault in the words of the Buddhas. But my energy is over-exerted, and because of that, my mind tends towards restlessness. Come now, I shall apply balanced energy.' Descending from the walking path, standing at the place for washing feet, and washing his feet, he entered the monastery, sat on a couch, and thinking, 'I will rest a little,' he brought his body towards the couch. His two feet were free from the ground, and his head had not yet reached the pillow; in that interval, his mind was liberated from the taints without clinging. The Elder's Arahantship was free from the four postures. Therefore, when it is asked, 'In this Dispensation, which bhikkhu attained Arahantship without sitting, without lying down, without standing, and without walking?' it is right to say, 'The Elder Ānanda.'

Atha therā bhikkhū dutiyadivase bhattakiccaṃ katvā pattacīvaraṃ paṭisāmetvā dhammasabhāyaṃ sannipatitā. Ānandatthero pana attano arahattappattiṃ ñāpetukāmo bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ na gato. Bhikkhū yathāvuḍḍhaṃ attano attano pattāsane nisīdantā ānandattherassa āsanaṃ ṭhapetvā nisinnā. Tattha kehici “etamāsanaṃ kassā”ti vutte ānandassāti. “Ānando pana kuhiṃ gato”ti. Tasmiṃ samaye thero cintesi “idāni mayhaṃ gamanakālo”ti. Tato attano ānubhāvaṃ dassento pathaviyaṃ nimujjitvā attano āsaneyeva attānaṃ dassesi. Ākāsenāgantvā nisīdītipi eke.

Then, on the second day, the elder bhikkhus, having completed their meal duties and put away their bowls and robes, assembled in the Dhamma hall. The Elder Ānanda, however, wishing to make known his attainment of Arahantship, did not go with the bhikkhus. The bhikkhus, sitting down in their respective seats according to seniority, left the Elder Ānanda's seat aside and sat down. When some asked, 'Whose seat is this?' it was said, 'It is Ānanda's.' 'But where has Ānanda gone?' At that moment the Elder thought, 'Now is my time to go.' Then, displaying his spiritual power, he plunged into the earth and showed himself on his very own seat. Some say that he came through the sky and sat down.

Evaṃ nisinne tasmiṃ āyasmante mahākassapatthero bhikkhū āmantesi, “āvuso, kiṃ paṭhamaṃ saṅgāyāma dhammaṃ vā vinayaṃ vā”ti? Bhikkhū āhaṃsu, “bhante mahākassapa, vinayonāmabuddhasāsanassa āyu, vinaye ṭhite sāsanaṃ ṭhitaṃ hoti, tasmā paṭhamaṃ vinayaṃ saṅgāyāmā”ti. “Kaṃ dhuraṃ katvā vinayo saṅgāyitabbo”ti? “Āyasmantaṃ upāli”nti[P 0.0097]. “Kiṃ ānando nappahotī”ti? “No nappahoti, apica kho pana sammāsambuddho dharamānoyeva vinayapariyattiṃ nissāya āyasmantaṃ upāliṃ etadagge ṭhapesi – ‘etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vinayadharānaṃ yadidaṃ upālī’”ti (a. ni. 1.228). Tasmā upālittheraṃ pucchitvā vinayaṃ saṅgāyāmāti. Tato thero vinayaṃ pucchanatthāya attanāva attānaṃ sammanni. Upālittheropi vissajjanatthāya sammanni. Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi –

When he was thus seated, the Venerable Elder Mahākassapa addressed the bhikkhus, 'Friends, what shall we recite first, the Dhamma or the Vinaya?' The bhikkhus said, 'Venerable Mahākassapa, the Vinaya is the very life of the Buddha's Dispensation. When the Vinaya is established, the Dispensation is established. Therefore, let us first recite the Vinaya.' 'Having made whom the leader should the Vinaya be recited?' 'The Venerable Upāli.' 'Is Ānanda not capable?' 'It is not that he is not capable. However, the Sammāsambuddha, while he was still living, with reference to the Vinaya scriptures, placed the Venerable Upāli in the foremost position, saying: "Bhikkhus, foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus who are masters of the Vinaya, is this one, that is, Upāli." Therefore, let us question the Elder Upāli and recite the Vinaya.' Then, the Elder appointed himself for the purpose of questioning on the Vinaya. The Elder Upāli also appointed himself for the purpose of answering. Herein, this is the Pāli:

Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo saṅghaṃ ñāpesi –

Then the Venerable Mahākassapa informed the Saṅgha:

“Suṇātu me, āvuso, saṅgho, yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, ahaṃ upāliṃ vinayaṃ puccheyya”nti.

“Friends, may the Saṅgha hear me. If the time is right for the Saṅgha, I would question Upāli on the Vinaya.”

Āyasmāpi [V 0.0079][M 0.0083] upāli saṅghaṃ ñāpesi –

The Venerable Upāli also informed the Saṅgha:

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, ahaṃ āyasmatā mahākassapena vinayaṃ puṭṭho vissajjeyya”nti.

“Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha hear me. If the time is right for the Saṅgha, I, being questioned on the Vinaya by the Venerable Mahākassapa, would answer.”

Evaṃ attanāva attānaṃ sammannitvā āyasmā, upāli, uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṃsaṃ cīvaraṃ katvā there bhikkhū vanditvā dhammāsane nisīdi dantakhacitaṃ bījaniṃ gahetvā. Tato mahākassapatthero upālittheraṃ paṭhamapārājikaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbaṃ vinayaṃ pucchi, upālitthero vissajjesi. Sabbe pañcasatā bhikkhū paṭhamapārājikasikkhāpadaṃ sanidānaṃ katvā ekato gaṇasajjhāyamakaṃsu. Evaṃ sesānipīti sabbaṃ vinayaṭṭhakathāya gahetabbaṃ. Etena nayena saubhatovibhaṅgaṃ sakhandhakaparivāraṃ sakalaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ saṅgāyitvā upālitthero dantakhacitaṃ bījaniṃ nikkhipitvā dhammāsanā orohitvā vuḍḍhe bhikkhū vanditvā attano pattāsane nisīdi.

Thus having appointed themselves, the Venerable Upāli rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, paid homage to the elder bhikkhus, and, taking an ivory-inlaid fan, sat down on the Dhamma-seat. Then the Elder Mahākassapa questioned the Elder Upāli on the entire Vinaya, beginning with the first Pārājika. The Elder Upāli answered. All five hundred bhikkhus, taking the first Pārājika training rule together with its causal story, performed a group recitation in unison. In this way, the remaining rules should also be understood as per the Vinaya commentary. By this method, having recited the entire Vinaya Piṭaka—the two Vibhaṅgas, together with the Khandhakas and the Parivāra—the Elder Upāli laid down the ivory-inlaid fan, descended from the Dhamma-seat, paid homage to the senior bhikkhus, and sat down in the seat allotted to him.

Vinayaṃ saṅgāyitvā dhammaṃ saṅgāyitukāmo āyasmā mahākassapatthero bhikkhū pucchi – “dhammaṃ saṅgāyantehi kaṃ puggalaṃ dhuraṃ katvā dhammo saṅgāyitabbo”ti? Bhikkhū “ānandattheraṃ dhuraṃ katvā”ti āhaṃsu.

Having recited the Vinaya, the Venerable Elder Mahākassapa, wishing to recite the Dhamma, asked the bhikkhus: 'When reciting the Dhamma, having made which person the leader should the Dhamma be recited?' The bhikkhus replied: 'Having made the Elder Ānanda the leader.'

Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo saṅghaṃ ñāpesi –

Then the Venerable Mahākassapa informed the Saṅgha:

“Suṇātu me, āvuso, saṅgho, yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, ahaṃ ānandaṃ dhammaṃ puccheyya”nti.

“Friends, may the Saṅgha hear me. If the time is right for the Saṅgha, I would question Ānanda on the Dhamma.”

Atha kho āyasmā ānando saṅghaṃ ñāpesi –

Then the Venerable Ānanda informed the Saṅgha:

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, ahaṃ āyasmatā mahākassapena dhammaṃ puṭṭho vissajjeyya”nti.

“Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha hear me. If the time is right for the Saṅgha, I, being questioned on the Dhamma by the Venerable Mahākassapa, would answer.”

Atha kho āyasmā ānando uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṃsaṃ cīvaraṃ katvā there bhikkhū vanditvā dhammāsane nisīdi dantakhacitaṃ bījaniṃ gahetvā. Atha mahākassapatthero ānandattheraṃ dhammaṃ pucchi [V 0.0080] – “brahmajālaṃ, āvuso ānanda, kattha bhāsita”nti? “Antarā ca, bhante, rājagahaṃ antarā ca nāḷandaṃ rājāgārake ambalaṭṭhikāya”nti. “Kaṃ ārabbhā”ti[P 0.0098]? “Suppiyañca paribbājakaṃ brahmadattañca māṇavaka”nti. Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ brahmajālassa nidānampi pucchi, puggalampi pucchi. “Sāmaññaphalaṃ; panāvuso ānanda, kattha bhāsita”nti? “Rājagahe, bhante, jīvakambavane”ti. “Kena saddhi”nti? “Ajātasattunā [M 0.0084] vedehiputtena saddhi”nti. Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ sāmaññaphalassa nidānampi pucchi, puggalampi pucchi. Eteneva upāyena pañcapi nikāye pucchi, puṭṭho puṭṭho āyasmā ānando vissajjesi. Ayaṃ paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti pañcahi therasatehi katā –

Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, paid homage to the elder monks, and, taking an ivory-inlaid fan, sat down on the Dhamma-seat. Then the Elder Mahākassapa questioned the Elder Ānanda on the Dhamma: 'Friend Ānanda, where was the Brahmajāla Sutta spoken?' 'Venerable sir, between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā, in the royal rest-house at Ambalaṭṭhikā.' 'In reference to whom?' 'In reference to Suppiya the wanderer and Brahmadatta the young man.' Then the Venerable Mahākassapa asked the Venerable Ānanda about the causal story of the Brahmajāla and also about the persons involved. 'But the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, friend Ānanda, where was it spoken?' 'In Rājagaha, venerable sir, in Jīvaka's Mango Grove.' 'With whom?' 'With Ajātasattu, son of the Videhī queen.' Then the Venerable Mahākassapa asked the Venerable Ānanda about the causal story of the Sāmaññaphala Sutta and also about the persons involved. By this very method, he questioned him on all five Nikāyas. As each question was asked, the Venerable Ānanda answered. This First Great Council was held by five hundred elders.

“Satehi pañcahi katā, tena pañcasatāti ca;

Thereheva katattā ca, therikāti pavuccatī”ti.

It was held by five hundred, therefore it is called 'The Five Hundred'; and because it was held by the Elders themselves, it is called 'The Council of the Elders' (Therikā).

Imissā paṭhamamahāsaṅgītiyā vattamānāya sabbaṃ dīghanikāyaṃ majjhimanikāyādiñca pucchitvā anupubbena khuddakanikāyaṃ pucchantena āyasmatā mahākassapena “maṅgalasuttaṃ, āvuso ānanda, kattha bhāsita”nti evamādivacanāvasāne “nidānampi pucchi, puggalampi pucchī”ti ettha nidāne pucchite taṃ nidānaṃ vitthāretvā yathā ca bhāsitaṃ, yena ca sutaṃ, yadā ca sutaṃ, yena ca bhāsitaṃ, yattha ca bhāsitaṃ, yassa ca bhāsitaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ kathetukāmena “evaṃ bhāsitaṃ mayā sutaṃ, ekaṃ samayaṃ sutaṃ, bhagavatā bhāsitaṃ, sāvatthiyaṃ bhāsitaṃ, devatāya bhāsita”nti etamatthaṃ dassentena āyasmatā ānandena vuttaṃ “evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme…pe… bhagavantaṃ gāthāya ajjhabhāsī”ti. Evamidaṃ [P 0.0099] āyasmatā ānandena vuttaṃ, tañca pana paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

During this First Great Council, after the entire Dīghanikāya, Majjhimanikāya, and so on had been questioned, the Venerable Mahākassapa, while questioning the Khuddakanikāya in sequence, asked: “Friend Ānanda, where was the Maṅgala Sutta spoken?” At the conclusion of such words, when questioned about the prologue, the Venerable Ānanda, wishing to explain that prologue in detail—how it was spoken, by whom it was heard, when it was heard, by whom it was spoken, where it was spoken, and to whom it was spoken—and to demonstrate this meaning, said: “Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Sāvatthī… (and so on) …addressed the Blessed One in verse.” Thus, this was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda, and it should be understood that this was spoken at the time of the First Great Council.

Idāni “kasmā vutta”nti ettha vuccate – yasmā ayamāyasmā mahākassapattherena nidānaṃ puṭṭho, tasmānena taṃ nidānaṃ ādito pabhuti vitthāretuṃ vuttaṃ. Yasmā vā ānandaṃ dhammāsane nisinnaṃ vasīgaṇaparivutaṃ disvā ekaccānaṃ devatānaṃ cittamuppannaṃ “ayamāyasmā vedehamuni pakatiyāpi sakyakulamanvayo bhagavato dāyādo, bhagavatāpi pañcakkhattuṃ etadagge niddiṭṭho, catūhi acchariyaabbhutadhammehi samannāgato, catunnaṃ parisānaṃ piyo manāpo, idāni maññe bhagavato dhammarajjadāyajjaṃ patvā buddho jāto”ti. Tasmā āyasmā ānando tāsaṃ devatānaṃ cetasā cetoparivitakkamaññāya taṃ abhūtaguṇasambhāvanaṃ anadhivāsento attano sāvakabhāvameva dīpetuṃ āha “evaṃ me sutaṃ ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā [M 0.0085] …pe… ajjhabhāsī”ti. Etthantare pañca arahantasatāni [V 0.0081] anekāni ca devatāsahassāni “sādhu sādhū”ti āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ abhinandiṃsu, mahābhūmicālo ahosi, nānāvidhakusumavassaṃ antalikkhato papati, aññāni ca bahūni acchariyāni pāturahesuṃ, bahūnañca devatānaṃ saṃvego uppajji “yaṃ amhehi bhagavato sammukhā sutaṃ, idāneva taṃ parokkhā jāta”nti. Evamidaṃ āyasmatā ānandena paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle vadantenāpi iminā kāraṇena vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Ettāvatā ca “vuttaṃ yena yadā yasmā, cetaṃ vatvā imaṃ vidhi”nti imissā addhagāthāya attho pakāsito hoti.

Now, regarding the question ‘Why was it said?’, the answer is given here: because this venerable one was questioned by the Elder Mahākassapa about the prologue, he therefore spoke to explain that prologue from the beginning. Or, it was because when some devas saw the Venerable Ānanda seated on the Dhamma-seat, surrounded by a company of masters, a thought arose in their minds: ‘This venerable sage is by nature a descendant of the Sakyan clan, an heir of the Blessed One. The Blessed One himself declared him foremost on five occasions; he is endowed with four amazing and wonderful qualities, and is dear and beloved to the four assemblies. Now, it seems, having attained the inheritance of the Blessed One’s kingdom of Dhamma, he has become a Buddha.’ Therefore, the Venerable Ānanda, perceiving with his own mind the mental reflections of those devas, and not acquiescing to that unfounded praise with non-existent qualities, spoke to reveal his own status as a disciple, saying: ‘Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One… (and so on) …addressed him in verse.’ In that interval, five hundred arahants and many thousands of devas applauded the Venerable Ānanda, exclaiming, ‘Excellent, excellent!’ A great earthquake occurred, a rain of various flowers fell from the sky, and many other marvels appeared. A sense of spiritual urgency arose in many devas, who thought: ‘That which we heard in the very presence of the Blessed One has, just now, become something heard indirectly.’ Thus, it should be understood that this was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda for this reason, even while speaking at the time of the First Great Council. By this much, the meaning of the half-verse—‘By whom, when, and why it was spoken; having said this, this is the method’—is made clear.

Evamiccādipāṭhavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the passage beginning with 'Thus'

1. Idāni “evamiccādipāṭhassa, atthaṃ nānappakārato”ti evamādimātikāya saṅgahitatthappakāsanatthaṃ vuccate – evanti [P 0.0100] ayaṃ saddo upamūpadesasampahaṃsanagarahaṇavacanasampaṭiggahākāranidassanāvadhāraṇādīsu atthesu daṭṭhabbo. Tathā hesa “evaṃ jātena maccena, kattabbaṃ kusalaṃ bahu”nti evamādīsu (dha. pa. 53) upamāyaṃ dissati. “Evaṃ te abhikkamitabbaṃ, evaṃ te paṭikkamitabba”ntiādīsu (a. ni. 4.122) upadese. “Evametaṃ bhagavā, evametaṃ sugatā”ti evamādīsu (a. ni. 3.66) sampahaṃsane. “Evamevaṃ panāyaṃ vasalī yasmiṃ vā tasmiṃ vā tassa muṇḍakassa samaṇakassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsatī”ti evamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.187) garahaṇe. “Evaṃ, bhanteti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosu”nti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 1.1) vacanasampaṭiggahe. “Evaṃ byā kho ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmī”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 1.398) ākāre. “Ehi tvaṃ, māṇavaka, yena samaṇo ānando tenupasaṅkama, upasaṅkamitvā mama vacanena samaṇaṃ ānandaṃ appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ puccha. ‘Subho māṇavo todeyyaputto bhavantaṃ ānandaṃ appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ pucchatī’ti, evañca vadehi sādhu kira bhavaṃ ānando yena subhassa māṇavassa todeyyaputtassa nivesanaṃ, tenupasaṅkamatu anukampaṃ upādāyā”ti evamādīsu (dī. ni. 1.445) nidassane. “Taṃ kiṃ maññatha kālāmā, ime dhammā kusalā vā akusalā vāti? Akusalā, bhante. Sāvajjā vā anavajjā vāti? Sāvajjā, bhante. Viññugarahitā vā viññuppasatthā [M 0.0086] vāti? Viññugarahitā, bhante. Samattā samādinnā ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanti no vā, kathaṃ vo ettha hotīti? Samattā, bhante, samādinnā ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanti, evaṃ no ettha hotī”ti evamādīsu (a. ni. 3.66) avadhāraṇe. Idha pana ākāranidassanāvadhāraṇesu daṭṭhabbo.

1. Now, to explain the meaning collected by the introductory matrix beginning with ‘evamiccādipāṭhassa, atthaṃ nānappakārato’ [‘Of the text starting with evaṃ, the meaning in various ways’], it is said: The word ‘evaṃ’ should be understood in meanings such as simile, instruction, praise, blame, acceptance of speech, manner, indication, and determination. For example, in passages like ‘Thus, by one born as a mortal, much good should be done,’ it is seen as a simile. In ‘Thus should you advance, thus should you retreat,’ it is instruction. In ‘Thus it is, Blessed One; thus it is, Well-Gone One,’ it is praise. In ‘In this very way, this wretch praises the virtues of that shaveling, that wretched ascetic, in any and every way,’ it is blame. In ‘Even so, venerable sir,’ those monks replied to the Blessed One,’ it is acceptance of speech. In ‘Thus, indeed, venerable sir, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One,’ it is manner. In ‘Come, young man, approach the ascetic Ānanda… and speak thus: “The young man Subha, son of Todeyya, asks about your health… and wishes that the venerable Ānanda, out of compassion, would come to his residence,”’ it is indication. In ‘“What do you think, Kālāmas? …Undertaken and practiced, they lead to harm and suffering. That is how it is to us here,”’ it is determination. Here, however, it should be understood in the senses of manner, indication, and determination.

Tattha [V 0.0082] ākāratthena evaṃ-saddena [P 0.0101] etamatthaṃ dīpeti – nānānayanipuṇamanekajjhāsayasamuṭṭhānaṃ atthabyañjanasampannaṃ vividhapāṭihāriyaṃ dhammatthadesanāpaṭivedhagambhīraṃ sabbasattānaṃ sakasakabhāsānurūpato sotapathamāgacchantaṃ tassa bhagavato vacanaṃ sabbappakārena ko samattho viññātuṃ, sabbathāmena pana sotukāmataṃ janetvāpi evaṃ me sutaṃ, mayāpi ekenākārena sutanti.

Among those meanings, by the word ‘evaṃ’ in the sense of manner, it indicates this meaning: The word of that Blessed One—which is subtle through various methods, arises from many intentions, is complete in meaning and phrasing, possesses various marvels, is profound in the Dhamma, its meaning, the teaching, and its penetration, and which reaches the hearing of all beings according to their respective languages—who is able to know it in all its aspects? However, having generated the desire to hear in every way, it is said, ‘Thus have I heard,’ meaning, ‘By me too it has been heard in one manner.’

Nidassanatthena “nāhaṃ sayambhū, na mayā idaṃ sacchikata”nti attānaṃ parimocento “evaṃ me sutaṃ, mayāpi evaṃ suta”nti idāni vattabbaṃ sakalasuttaṃ nidasseti.

In the sense of indication, disclaiming personal authority by stating, ‘I am not self-awakened; this was not realized by me,’ he indicates the entire sutta that is now to be spoken with the words: ‘Thus it was heard by me; by me also it was heard thus.’

Avadhāraṇatthena “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bahussutānaṃ yadidaṃ ānando, gatimantānaṃ, satimantānaṃ, dhitimantānaṃ, upaṭṭhākānaṃ yadidaṃ ānando”ti (a. ni. 1.219-223) evaṃ bhagavatā pasatthabhāvānurūpaṃ attano dhāraṇabalaṃ dassento sattānaṃ sotukamyataṃ janeti “evaṃ me sutaṃ, tañca kho atthato vā byañjanato vā anūnamanadhikaṃ, evameva, na aññathā daṭṭhabba”nti.

In the sense of affirmation, demonstrating his own power of retention befitting the praise given by the Blessed One—‘Bhikkhus, among my bhikkhu disciples who are learned, Ānanda is foremost; among those who are quick-witted, mindful, resolute, and are attendants, Ānanda is foremost’—he generates in beings the desire to listen, saying: ‘Thus it was heard by me, and that, whether in meaning or in phrasing, is not deficient and not excessive; it should be understood as just so, and not otherwise.’

Me-saddo tīsu atthesu dissati. Tathā hissa “gāthābhigītaṃ me abhojaneyya”nti evamādīsu (su. ni. 81) mayāti attho. “Sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetū”ti evamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 4.88) mayhanti attho. “Dhammadāyādā me, bhikkhave, bhavathā”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 1.29) mamāti attho. Idha pana “mayā suta”nti ca “mama suta”nti ca atthadvaye yujjati.

The word ‘me’ is seen in three meanings. For instance, in ‘gāthābhigītaṃ me abhojaneyyaṃ,’ it has the meaning of ‘mayā’ (by me). In ‘Sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetū,’ it has the meaning of ‘mayhaṃ’ (to me). In ‘Dhammadāyādā me, bhikkhave, bhavatha,’ it has the meaning of ‘mama’ (of me). Here, however, it is suitable in both meanings: ‘heard by me’ and ‘my hearing.’

Sutanti ayaṃ sutasaddo saupasaggo anupasaggo ca gamanakhyātarāgābhibhūtūpacitānuyogasotaviññeyyasotadvāraviññātādianekatthappabhedo. Tathā hissa “senāya pasuto”ti evamādīsu gacchantoti [M 0.0087] attho. “Sutadhammassa passato”ti evamādīsu khyātadhammassāti attho. “Avassutā avassutassā”ti evamādīsu (pāci. 657) rāgābhibhūtā rāgābhibhūtassāti attho. “Tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappaka”nti evamādīsu (khu. pā. 7.12) upacitanti attho. “Ye jhānappasutā [P 0.0102] dhīrā”ti evamādīsu (dha. pa. 181) jhānānuyuttāti attho. “Diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ muta”nti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 1.241) sotaviññeyyanti attho. “Sutadharo sutasannicayo”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 1.339) sotadvārānusāraviññātadharoti attho. Idha pana sutanti sotaviññāṇapubbaṅgamāya viññāṇavīthiyā [V 0.0083] upadhāritanti vā upadhāraṇanti vāti attho. Tattha yadā me-saddassa mayāti attho, tadā “evaṃ mayā sutaṃ, sotaviññāṇapubbaṅgamāya viññāṇavīthiyā upadhārita”nti yujjati. Yadā me-saddassa mamāti attho, tadā “evaṃ mama sutaṃ sotaviññāṇapubbaṅgamāya viññāṇavīthiyā upadhāraṇa”nti yujjati.

Regarding the term ‘sutaṃ’, this word ‘suta’, both with and without a prefix, has many different meanings, such as: going, declared, overcome by lust, accumulated, application, knowable by ear-consciousness, and known through the ear-door. For instance, in ‘senāya pasuto,’ it has the meaning of ‘going.’ In ‘sutadhammassa passato,’ it has the meaning of ‘of one whose Dhamma is declared.’ In ‘avassutā avassutassa,’ it has the meaning of ‘a woman overcome by lust, for a man overcome by lust.’ In ‘tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappakaṃ,’ it has the meaning of ‘accumulated.’ In ‘ye jhānappasutā dhīrā,’ it has the meaning of ‘devoted to jhāna.’ In ‘diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ,’ it has the meaning of ‘knowable by ear-consciousness.’ In ‘sutadharo sutasannicayo,’ it has the meaning of ‘one who retains what is known through the ear-door.’ Here, however, ‘sutaṃ’ has the meaning of either ‘ascertained by a cognitive process-series preceded by ear-consciousness’ or ‘the ascertaining.’ Therein, when the word ‘me’ has the meaning of ‘mayā’ (by me), then it is suitable as: ‘Thus it was ascertained by me through a cognitive process-series preceded by ear-consciousness.’ When the word ‘me’ has the meaning of ‘mama’ (of me/my), then it is suitable as: ‘Thus my ascertaining through a cognitive process-series preceded by ear-consciousness.’

Evametesu tīsu padesu evanti sotaviññāṇakiccanidassanaṃ. Meti vuttaviññāṇasamaṅgīpuggalanidassanaṃ. Sutanti assavanabhāvappaṭikkhepato anūnānadhikāviparītaggahaṇanidassanaṃ. Tathā evanti savanādicittānaṃ nānappakārena ārammaṇe pavattabhāvanidassanaṃ. Meti attanidassanaṃ. Sutanti dhammanidassanaṃ.

Thus, in these three terms: 'evaṃ' is an indication of the function of hearing by ear-consciousness. 'Me' is an indication of the person endowed with the consciousness that knows the spoken Dhamma. 'Sutaṃ', by way of rejecting the state of not-hearing, is an indication of grasping without deficiency, excess, or error. Furthermore, 'evaṃ' is an indication of the state of hearing and other consciousnesses arising in various ways in relation to an object. 'Me' is an indication of the self. 'Sutaṃ' is an indication of the Dhamma.

Tathā evanti niddisitabbadhammanidassanaṃ. Meti puggalanidassanaṃ. Sutanti puggalakiccanidassanaṃ.

Furthermore, 'evaṃ' is an indication of the Dhamma to be pointed out. 'Me' is an indication of the person. 'Sutaṃ' is an indication of the person's function.

Tathā evanti vīthicittānaṃ ākārapaññattivasena nānappakāraniddeso. Meti kattāraniddeso. Sutanti visayaniddeso.

Furthermore, the word 'evaṃ' is an indication of various kinds by means of the concept of mode of the cognitive process-series consciousnesses. The word 'me' is an indication of the agent. The word 'sutaṃ' is an indication of the object.

Tathā evanti puggalakiccaniddeso. Sutanti viññāṇakiccaniddeso. Meti ubhayakiccayuttapuggalaniddeso.

Furthermore, the word 'evaṃ' is an indication of the person's function. The word 'sutaṃ' is an indication of the function of consciousness. The word 'me' is an indication of the person connected with both functions.

Tathā evanti bhāvaniddeso. Meti puggalaniddeso. Sutanti tassa kiccaniddeso.

Furthermore, the word 'evaṃ' is an indication of the nature. The word 'me' is an indication of the person. The word 'sutaṃ' is an indication of that person's function.

Tattha evanti ca meti ca sacchikaṭṭhaparamatthavasena avijjamānapaññatti. Sutanti vijjamānapaññatti. Tathā evanti ca meti ca taṃ taṃ upādāya vattabbato [M 0.0088] upādāpaññatti. Sutanti diṭṭhādīni upanidhāya vattabbato upanidhāpaññatti[P 0.0103].

Herein, 'evaṃ' and 'me', by means of ultimate reality which has a meaning to be realized, indicate a non-existent concept. 'Sutaṃ' indicates an existent concept. Furthermore, 'evaṃ' and 'me', because they are spoken of by depending on this or that, indicate a derived concept. 'Sutaṃ', because it is spoken of in reference to what is seen and so on, indicates a concept of comparison.

Ettha ca evanti vacanena asammohaṃ dīpeti, sutanti vacanena sutassa asammosaṃ. Tathā evanti vacanena yonisomanasikāraṃ dīpeti ayoniso manasikaroto nānappakārappaṭivedhābhāvato. Sutanti vacanena avikkhepaṃ dīpeti vikkhittacittassa savanābhāvato. Tathā hi vikkhittacitto puggalo sabbasampattiyā vuccamānopi “na mayā sutaṃ, puna bhaṇathā”ti bhaṇati. Yonisomanasikārena cettha attasammāpaṇidhiṃ pubbe katapuññatañca [V 0.0084] sādheti, avikkhepena saddhammassavanaṃ sappurisūpanissayañca. Evanti ca iminā bhaddakena ākārena pacchimacakkadvayasampattiṃ attano dīpeti, sutanti savanayogena purimacakkadvayasampattiṃ. Tathā āsayasuddhiṃ payogasuddhiñca, tāya ca āsayasuddhiyā adhigamabyattiṃ, payogasuddhiyā āgamabyattiṃ.

And herein, by the word 'evaṃ' he indicates non-delusion, and by the word 'sutaṃ', non-confusion regarding what was heard. Furthermore, by the word 'evaṃ' he indicates wise attention, because for one who attends unwisely there is no penetration of various kinds. By the word 'sutaṃ' he indicates non-distraction, because for one who is distracted there is no act of listening. Indeed, a distracted person, even when spoken to for their complete benefit, says, 'I did not hear; please speak again.' And here, through wise attention, one accomplishes right aspiration for oneself and the state of having made merit in the past; through non-distraction, one accomplishes the hearing of the good Dhamma and reliance on good persons. And by 'evaṃ', in this excellent manner, he indicates his own accomplishment of the latter pair of wheels; by 'sutaṃ', through the connection with hearing, he indicates the accomplishment of the former pair of wheels. Furthermore, he indicates purity of intention and purity of endeavor; and by that purity of intention, proficiency in attainment; by purity of endeavor, proficiency in the scriptures.

Evanti ca iminā nānappakārapaṭivedhadīpakena vacanena attano atthapaṭibhānapaṭisambhidāsampadaṃ dīpeti. Sutanti iminā sotabbabhedapaṭivedhadīpakena dhammaniruttipaṭisambhidāsampadaṃ dīpeti. Evanti ca idaṃ yonisomanasikāradīpakaṃ vacanaṃ bhaṇanto “ete mayā dhammā manasānupekkhitā diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhā”ti ñāpeti. Sutanti idaṃ savanayogadīpakavacanaṃ bhaṇanto “bahū mayā dhammā sutā dhātā vacasā paricitā”ti ñāpeti. Tadubhayenapi atthabyañjanapāripūriṃ dīpento savane ādaraṃ janeti.

And by this word 'evaṃ,' which illuminates the penetration of various kinds, he indicates his own accomplishment in the analytical knowledge of meaning and of spontaneous expression. By this word 'sutaṃ,' which illuminates the penetration of the divisions of what is to be heard, he indicates his accomplishment in the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma and of language. And by uttering this word 'evaṃ,' which illuminates wise attention, he makes it known: 'These teachings have been repeatedly contemplated by my mind and thoroughly penetrated by insight.' By uttering this word 'sutaṃ,' which illuminates the application to listening, he makes it known: 'Many teachings have been heard by me, retained, and familiarized by speech.' Through both, while illuminating the fulfillment of meaning and expression, he generates respect for listening.

Evaṃ me sutanti iminā pana sakalenapi vacanena āyasmā ānando tathāgatappaveditaṃ dhammaṃ attano adahanto asappurisabhūmiṃ, atikkamati, sāvakattaṃ paṭijānanto sappurisabhūmiṃ okkamati. Tathā asaddhammā cittaṃ vuṭṭhāpeti, saddhamme cittaṃ patiṭṭhāpeti. “Kevalaṃ sutamevetaṃ mayā, tasseva tu bhagavato vacanaṃ [P 0.0104] arahato sammāsambuddhassā”ti ca dīpento attānaṃ parimoceti, satthāraṃ apadisati, jinavacanaṃ appeti, dhammanettiṃ patiṭṭhāpeti.

With this entire statement, 'Thus have I heard,' the Venerable Ānanda, not claiming the Dhamma proclaimed by the Tathāgata as his own, transcends the domain of an unworthy person; acknowledging his state as a disciple, he enters the domain of a worthy person. Thus, he raises his mind from the false Dhamma and establishes his mind in the true Dhamma. And by indicating, 'This was merely heard by me; it is indeed the word of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One,' he frees himself, points to the Teacher, attributes it to the word of the Victor, and establishes the guideline of the Dhamma.

Apica “evaṃ me suta”nti attanā uppāditabhāvaṃ appaṭijānanto purimassavanaṃ vivaranto “sammukhā paṭiggahitamidaṃ mayā tassa bhagavato catuvesārajjavisāradassa [M 0.0089] dasabaladharassa āsabhaṭṭhānaṭṭhāyino sīhanādanādino sabbasattuttamassa dhammissarassa dhammarājassa dhammādhipatino dhammadīpassa dhammappaṭisaraṇassa saddhammavaracakkavattino sammāsambuddhassa. Na ettha atthe vā dhamme vā pade vā byañjane vā kaṅkhā vā vimati vā kātabbā”ti sabbadevamanussānaṃ imasmiṃ dhamme assaddhiyaṃ vināseti, saddhāsampadaṃ uppādetīti veditabbo. Hoti cettha –

Moreover, by 'Thus have I heard,' not acknowledging that it was originated by himself but disclosing the prior hearing, he makes it known: 'This was received by me in the presence of that Blessed One—the one skilled in the four kinds of fearlessness, the bearer of the ten powers, standing in the place of a bull, roaring the lion's roar, the supreme among all beings, the lord of the Dhamma, the king of the Dhamma, the sovereign of the Dhamma, the lamp of the Dhamma, the refuge in the Dhamma, the turner of the excellent wheel of the true Dhamma, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Herein, no doubt or uncertainty should be made regarding the meaning, the teaching, the phrase, or the letter.' Thus, he destroys the lack of faith in this Dhamma among all gods and humans and generates the accomplishment of faith—this should be understood. And here there is this:

“Vināsayati assaddhaṃ, saddhaṃ vaḍḍheti sāsane;

Evaṃ me sutamiccevaṃ, vadaṃ gotamasāvako”ti.

He destroys faithlessness, he increases faith in the Dispensation; 'Thus have I heard'—so says the disciple of Gotama.

Ekanti [V 0.0085] gaṇanaparicchedaniddeso. Samayanti paricchinnaniddeso. Ekaṃ samayanti aniyamitaparidīpanaṃ. Tattha samayasaddo –

The word 'ekaṃ' is an indication of enumeration and delimitation. The word 'samayaṃ' is an indication of the delimited. 'Ekaṃ samayaṃ' is an unspecified indication. Herein, the word 'samaya'—

Samavāye khaṇe kāle, samūhe hetudiṭṭhisu;

Paṭilābhe pahāne ca, paṭivedhe ca dissati.

In conjunction, moment, time, assembly, in causes and views; in attainment, abandonment, and in penetration, it is seen.

Tathā hissa “appeva nāma svepi upasaṅkameyyāma kālañca samayañca upādāyā”ti evamādīsu (dī. ni. 1.447) samavāyo attho. “Ekova kho, bhikkhave, khaṇo ca samayo ca brahmacariyavāsāyā”ti evamādīsu (a. ni. 8.29) khaṇo. “Uṇhasamayo pariḷāhasamayo”ti evamādīsu (pāci. 358) kālo. “Mahāsamayo pavanasmi”nti evamādīsu samūho. “Samayopi kho te, bhaddāli, appaṭividdho ahosi, bhagavā kho sāvatthiyaṃ viharati, sopi maṃ jānissati, ‘bhaddāli, nāma bhikkhu satthusāsane [P 0.0105] sikkhāya aparipūrakārī’ti, ayampi kho te bhaddāli samayo appaṭividdho ahosī”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 2.135) hetu. “Tena kho pana samayena uggāhamāno paribbājako samaṇamuṇḍikāputto samayappavādake tindukācīre ekasālake mallikāya ārāme paṭivasatī”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 2.260) diṭṭhi.

Thus, for this word, in passages such as, 'Perhaps tomorrow we may approach, taking into account the time and the conjunction of causes,' the meaning is conjunction. In passages such as, 'Monks, there is just one moment, one occasion for living the holy life,' the meaning is moment. In passages such as, 'The time of heat, the time of scorching,' the meaning is time. In passages such as, 'A great assembly in the forest,' the meaning is assembly. In passages such as, 'The reason too, Bhaddāli, was not penetrated by you. The Blessed One is dwelling at Sāvatthī, and he will know of me, “The monk named Bhaddāli is one who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s Dispensation.” This reason too, Bhaddāli, was not penetrated by you,' the meaning is reason. In passages such as, 'Now at that time the wanderer Uggāhamāna, son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā, was dwelling in Mallikā's park, in the single-halled Tinduka grove where views were debated,' the meaning is view.

“Diṭṭhe dhamme ca yo attho, yo cattho samparāyiko;

Atthābhisamayā dhīro, paṇḍitoti pavuccatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.129) –

“What benefit there is in this very life, and what benefit there is in the life to come; through the realization of the benefit, the steadfast one is called a ‘wise person.’”

Evamādīsu paṭilābho. “Sammā mānābhisamayā antamakāsi dukkhassā”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 1.28) pahānaṃ. “Dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho saṅkhataṭṭho santāpaṭṭho [M 0.0090] vipariṇāmaṭṭho abhisamayaṭṭho”ti evamādīsu (paṭi. ma. 2.8) paṭivedho. Idha panassa kālo attho. Tena ekaṃ samayanti saṃvaccharautumāsaaḍḍhamāsarattidivapubbaṇhamajjhanhikasāyanhapaṭhamamajjhima- pacchimayāmamuhuttādīsu kālakhyesu samayesu ekaṃ samayanti dīpeti.

In such passages, the meaning is attainment. In passages such as, 'Through the complete overcoming of conceit, he made an end of suffering,' the meaning is abandonment. In passages such as, 'Suffering has the meaning of oppression, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of burning, the meaning of change, the meaning of penetration,' the meaning is penetration. Here, however, its meaning is time. Therefore, 'at one time' indicates one time among the times designated by terms such as year, season, month, half-month, night, day, forenoon, midday, afternoon, the first, middle, and last watches of the night, a moment, and so on.

Ye vā ime gabbhokkantisamayo jātisamayo saṃvegasamayo abhinikkhamanasamayo dukkarakārikasamayo māravijayasamayo abhisambodhisamayo diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārasamayo desanāsamayo parinibbānasamayoti evamādayo bhagavato devamanussesu ativiya pakāsā anekakālakhyā eva samayā. Tesu samayesu desanāsamayasaṅkhātaṃ ekaṃ samayanti vuttaṃ hoti. Yo [V 0.0086] cāyaṃ ñāṇakaruṇākiccasamayesu karuṇākiccasamayo, attahitaparahitappaṭipattisamayesu parahitappaṭipattisamayo, sannipatitānaṃ karaṇīyadvayasamayesu dhammīkathāsamayo, desanāpaṭipattisamayesu desanāsamayo, tesupi samayesu yaṃ kiñci sandhāya “ekaṃ samaya”nti vuttaṃ hoti.

Or, there are these times of the Blessed One—such as the time of conception, the time of birth, the time of spiritual urgency, the time of renunciation, the time of undertaking difficult practices, the time of conquering Māra, the time of perfect enlightenment, the time of dwelling in bliss in this very life, the time of teaching, and the time of final Parinibbāna. These and other such times are indeed extremely well-known among gods and humans, being designated as various times. Among these times, 'at one time' refers to one time designated as the time of teaching. And this, which is the time for the function of compassion among the times for the functions of wisdom and compassion; the time for the practice for the welfare of others among the times for the practice for one's own welfare and that of others; the time for a Dhamma talk among the times for the two duties for the assembled; and the time for teaching among the times for teaching and for practice—among these times also, with reference to some one of them, it is said 'at one time'.

Etthāha – atha kasmā yathā abhidhamme [P 0.0106] “yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacara”nti ca ito aññesu suttapadesu “yasmiṃ samaye, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehī”ti ca bhummavacanena niddeso kato, vinaye ca “tena samayena buddho bhagavā”ti karaṇavacanena, tathā akatvā idha “ekaṃ samaya”nti upayogavacananiddeso katoti. Tattha tathā, idha ca aññathā atthasambhavato. Tattha hi abhidhamme ito aññesu suttapadesu ca adhikaraṇattho bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇattho ca sambhavati. Adhikaraṇañhi kālattho samūhattho ca samayo, tattha vuttānaṃ phassādidhammānaṃ khaṇasamavāyahetusaṅkhātassa ca samayassa bhāvena tesaṃ bhāvo lakkhīyati, tasmā tadatthajotanatthaṃ tattha bhummavacananiddeso kato.

Herein, a questioner asks: Why is it that in the Abhidhamma, in the phrase “yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ” (“at the time a sensuous-sphere [consciousness arises]”), and in other Sutta passages apart from this, in the phrase “yasmiṃ samaye, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi” (“at the time, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures”), the indication is made with the locative case; and in the Vinaya, in the phrase “tena samayena buddho bhagavā” (“at that time the Buddha, the Blessed One”), with the instrumental case; yet here, not having done so, the indication “ekaṃ samayaṃ” (“on one occasion”) is made with the accusative case? Because there, it is appropriate in that way, and here, another meaning is appropriate. Indeed, there in the Abhidhamma and in other Sutta passages apart from this, the meaning of location and the meaning of the absolute locative are appropriate. Indeed, the word 'samaya', which has the meaning of time and assembly, is a location. There, the existence of those phenomena such as contact is marked by the state of being of the 'samaya', which is designated as a moment, a conjunction, and a cause. Therefore, to illuminate that meaning, the indication is made there with the locative case.

Vinaye ca hetvattho karaṇattho ca sambhavati. Yo hi so sikkhāpadapaññattisamayo sāriputtādīhipi dubbiññeyyo, tena samayena hetubhūtena karaṇabhūtena ca sikkhāpadāni paññapento sikkhāpadapaññattihetuñca apekkhamāno bhagavā tattha tattha vihāsi, tasmā tadatthajotanatthaṃ tattha karaṇavacananiddeso kato.

In the Vinaya, the meaning of cause and the meaning of instrument are appropriate. Indeed, that occasion for laying down the training rules was difficult to be known even by Sāriputta and others. For the Blessed One dwelt in various places, considering the reason for laying down the training rules and laying them down by means of that occasion, which had become a cause and an instrument. Therefore, to illuminate that meaning, the indication is made there with the instrumental case.

Idha [M 0.0091] pana aññasmiñca evaṃjātike suttantapāṭhe accantasaṃyogattho sambhavati. Yañhi samayaṃ bhagavā imaṃ aññaṃ vā suttantaṃ desesi, accantameva taṃ samayaṃ karuṇāvihārena vihāsi. Tasmā tadatthajotanatthaṃ idha upayogavacananiddeso katoti viññeyyo. Hoti cettha –

Here in this Sutta, however, and in other Sutta passages of this kind, the meaning of continuous connection is appropriate. Indeed, for the entire time that the Blessed One taught this or another Sutta, he dwelt with an abiding in compassion. Therefore, it should be known that to illuminate that meaning, the indication with the accusative case is made here. And there is this summary verse:

“Taṃ taṃ atthamapekkhitvā, bhummena karaṇena ca;

Aññatra samayo vutto, upayogena so idhā”ti.

“Considering each respective meaning, elsewhere the word ‘samaya’ is spoken with the locative and with the instrumental case; here, that word is spoken with the accusative case.”

Bhagavāti guṇavisiṭṭhasattuttamagarugāravādhivacanametaṃ. Yathāha –

This word, ‘Bhagavā,’ is a term of respect and reverence for the supreme being distinguished by virtues. As it is said:

“Bhagavāti [P 0.0107] vacanaṃ seṭṭhaṃ, bhagavāti vacanamuttamaṃ;

Garu gāravayutto so, bhagavā tena vuccatī”ti.

“The word ‘Bhagavā’ is excellent, the word ‘Bhagavā’ is supreme; he is endowed with venerability and reverence, therefore he is called ‘Bhagavā’.”

Catubbidhañhi [V 0.0087] nāmaṃ āvatthikaṃ, liṅgikaṃ, nemittakaṃ, adhiccasamuppannanti. Adhiccasamuppannaṃ nāma “yadicchaka”nti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha vaccho dammo balibaddhoti evamādi āvatthikaṃ, daṇḍī chattī sikhī karīti evamādi liṅgikaṃ, tevijjo chaḷabhiññoti evamādi nemittakaṃ, sirivaḍḍhako dhanavaḍḍhakoti evamādi vacanatthamanapekkhitvā pavattaṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ. Idaṃ pana bhagavāti nāmaṃ guṇanemittakaṃ, na mahāmāyāya, na suddhodanamahārājena, na asītiyā ñātisahassehi kataṃ, na sakkasantusitādīhi devatāvisesehi kataṃ. Yathāha āyasmā sāriputtatthero “bhagavāti netaṃ nāmaṃ mātarā kataṃ…pe… sacchikā paññatti yadidaṃ bhagavā”ti (mahāni. 84).

Indeed, a name is fourfold: circumstantial (āvatthika), based on a sign (liṅgika), based on a cause (nemittaka), and arisen by chance (adhiccasamuppanna). 'Arisen by chance' means 'arbitrary.' Among these, names such as ‘calf,’ ‘tamed one,’ and ‘bullock’ are circumstantial. Names such as ‘staff-bearer,’ ‘umbrella-bearer,’ ‘one with a top-knot,’ and ‘one with a trunk (elephant)’ are based on a sign. Names such as ‘possessor of the threefold knowledge’ and ‘possessor of the six supernormal knowledges’ are based on a cause. Names such as ‘Sirivaḍḍhaka’ and ‘Dhanavaḍḍhaka,’ which arise without regard to the meaning of the word, are arisen by chance. This name, ‘Bhagavā,’ however, is a name based on the cause which is virtue. It was not given by Mahāmāyā, nor by King Suddhodana, nor by the eighty thousand relatives, nor by distinguished deities such as Sakka and Santusita. As the Venerable Sāriputta Thera said: “This name ‘Bhagavā’ was not given by his mother… (etc.)… It is a designation based on direct realization, this which is ‘Bhagavā’.”

Yaṃ guṇanemittakañcetaṃ nāmaṃ, tesaṃ guṇānaṃ pakāsanatthaṃ imaṃ gāthaṃ vadanti –

And since this name is one based on the cause which is virtue, to make those virtues known, they recite this verse:

“Bhagī bhajī bhāgī vibhattavā iti,

Akāsi bhagganti garūti bhāgyavā;

Bahūhi ñāyehi subhāvitattano,

Bhavantago so bhagavāti vuccatī”ti.

“He is endowed with fortunes (bhagī), he is resorted to (bhajī), he is a sharer (bhāgī), and he has analyzed (vibhattavā); he has broken (bhaggaṃ akāsi) the defilements; he is venerable (garu) and fortunate (bhāgyavā); his self is well-developed by many principles; he has gone to the end of existence (bhavantago). Therefore, he is called ‘Bhagavā’.”

Niddesādīsu (mahāni. 84; cūḷani. ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 2) vuttanayeneva cassa attho daṭṭhabbo.

And its meaning should be understood according to the method stated in the Niddesa and other texts.

Ayaṃ pana aparo pariyāyo –

This, however, is another explanation:

“Bhāgyavā bhaggavā yutto, bhagehi ca vibhattavā;

Bhattavā vantagamano, bhavesu bhagavā tato”ti.

“He is fortunate (bhāgyavā), he has broken (bhaggavā) the defilements, he is endowed (yutto) with the fortunes (bhagehi), and he has analyzed (vibhattavā) the dhammas; he has cultivated (bhattavā) the noble states, and has abandoned and gone beyond (vantagamano) the kinds of existence. Therefore, he is ‘Bhagavā’.”

Tattha [M 0.0092] “vaṇṇāgamo vaṇṇavipariyāyo”ti evaṃ niruttilakkhaṇaṃ gahetvā saddanayena vā pisodarādipakkhepalakkhaṇaṃ gahetvā yasmā lokiyalokuttarasukhābhinibbattakaṃ [P 0.0108] dānasīlādipārappattaṃ bhāgyamassa atthi, tasmā bhāgyavāti vattabbe bhagavāti vuccatīti ñātabbaṃ. Yasmā pana lobhadosamohaviparītamanasikāraahirikānottappakodhūpanāhamakkhapalā- issāmacchariyamāyāsāṭheyyathambhasārambhamānātimānamadapamādataṇhāvijjātividhākusalamūladuccarita- saṃkilesamalavisamasaññāvitakkapapañcacatubbidhavipariyesaāsavaganthaoghayogaagatitaṇhupādāna- pañcacetokhilavinibandhanīvaraṇābhinandanachavivādamūlataṇhākāyasattānusaya- aṭṭhamicchattanavataṇhāmūlakadasākusalakammapathadvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigata- aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritappabhedasabbadarathapariḷāhakilesasatasahassāni[V 0.0088], saṅkhepato vā pañca kilesakkhandhaabhisaṅkhāramaccudevaputtamāre abhañji, tasmā bhaggattā etesaṃ parissayānaṃ bhaggavāti vattabbe bhagavāti vuccati. Āha cettha –

Therein, it should be known that by taking the characteristic of etymology as “addition of a letter” or “transposition of a letter,” or by the grammatical method of taking the characteristic of inclusion in the class of words like ‘pisodara,’ because he possesses the fortune (bhāgya) that brings about worldly and supramundane happiness, having reached the perfection of giving, virtue, and so on, therefore, though it should be said ‘Bhāgyavā,’ he is called ‘Bhagavā.’ Furthermore, because he broke greed, hatred, delusion, wrong attention, shamelessness and fearlessness of wrongdoing, anger and hostility, denigration and contempt, envy and stinginess, deceit and craftiness, obstinacy and rivalry, conceit, arrogance, intoxication and negligence, craving and ignorance; the three kinds of unwholesome roots, misconduct, defilements, stains, unwholesome perceptions, thoughts, and proliferations; the four kinds of perversions, cankers, bonds, floods, yokes, wrong courses, and attachments born of craving; the five kinds of mental barrenness, fetters, hindrances, and delights; the six roots of dispute and bodies of craving; the seven latent tendencies; the eight wrongnesses; the nine things rooted in craving; the ten unwholesome courses of action; the sixty-two wrong views; the one hundred and eight forms of craving; and all the hundreds of thousands of defilements which are varieties of conduct, torments, and fevers—or, in brief, the five Māras, namely, the Māra of defilements, the Māra of the aggregates, the Māra of volitional formations, the Māra of death, and the Māra who is a deva’s son—therefore, because of having broken these perils, though it should be said ‘Bhaggavā,’ he is called ‘Bhagavā.’ And it is said in this regard:

“Bhaggarāgo bhaggadoso, bhaggamoho anāsavo;

Bhaggāssa pāpakā dhammā, bhagavā tena vuccatī”ti.

“He has broken lust, broken hatred, broken delusion, and is without cankers; his evil states have been broken, therefore he is called ‘Bhagavā’.”

Bhāgyavatāya cassa satapuññalakkhaṇadharassa rūpakāyasampatti dīpitā hoti, bhaggadosatāya dhammakāyasampatti. Tathā lokiyasarikkhakānaṃ bahumānabhāvo, gahaṭṭhapabbajitehi abhigamanīyatā. Tathā abhigatānañca nesaṃ kāyacittadukkhāpanayane paṭibalabhāvo, āmisadānadhammadānehi upakāritā. Lokiyalokuttarasukhehi ca saṃyojanasamatthatā dīpitā hoti.

By his being fortunate, the perfection of his physical body (rūpakāya), which bears the hundred marks of merit, is revealed. By his having broken the faults, the perfection of his Dhamma body (dhammakāya) is revealed. Likewise, his being highly esteemed by worldly people and his being approachable by householders and renunciants is revealed. Likewise, for those who have approached him, his capability in dispelling their bodily and mental suffering and his helpfulness through the gifts of material things and the Dhamma are revealed. And his ability to connect beings with worldly and supramundane happiness is revealed.

Yasmā ca loke issariyadhammayasasirikāmapayattesu chasu dhammesu bhagasaddo vattati, paramañcassa sakacitte issariyaṃ, aṇimālaghimādikaṃ vā lokiyasammataṃ sabbākāraparipūraṃ [P 0.0109] atthi, tathā lokuttaro dhammo, lokattayabyāpako yathābhuccaguṇādhigato ativiya parisuddho yaso, rūpakāyadassanabyāvaṭajananayanamanappasādajananasamatthā sabbākāraparipūrā sabbaṅgapaccaṅgasirī, yaṃ yaṃ anena icchitaṃ patthitaṃ attahitaṃ parahitaṃ vā, tassa tassa tatheva abhinipphannattā icchitatthanipphattisaññito kāmo, sabbalokagarubhāvappattihetubhūto sammāvāyāmasaṅkhāto payatto ca atthi, tasmā imehi bhagehi yuttattāpi bhagā assa santīti iminā atthena “bhagavā”ti vuccati.

And since in the world the term 'bhaga' applies to six qualities—sovereignty, the Dhamma, fame, glory, desire, and exertion—and he possesses supreme sovereignty in his own mind, and worldly recognized attainments like the powers of becoming minute or light, all fully perfected; and likewise, the supramundane Dhamma; and exceedingly pure fame pervading the three worlds, attained through genuine qualities; and the glory of his physical form, fully perfected in every aspect, complete with all major and minor limbs, capable of generating delight in the eyes and mind of those engaged in seeing it; and whatever he wishes or aspires to, whether for his own welfare or the welfare of others, that very thing is accomplished, thus his desire is known as the fulfillment of what is wished for; and he possesses exertion, known as right effort, which is the cause for attaining a state revered by the entire world; therefore, also because of being endowed with these fortunes, in the sense that 'he possesses fortunes (bhaga),' he is called 'Bhagavā'.

Yasmā [M 0.0093] pana kusalādibhedehi sabbadhamme, khandhāyatanadhātusaccaindriyapaṭiccasamuppādādīhi vā kusalādidhamme, pīḷanasaṅkhatasantāpavipariṇāmaṭṭhena vā dukkhamariyasaccaṃ, āyūhananidānasaṃyogapalibodhaṭṭhena samudayaṃ, nissaraṇavivekāsaṅkhataamataṭṭhena nirodhaṃ, niyyānikahetudassanādhipateyyaṭṭhena maggaṃ vibhattavā, vibhajitvā vivaritvā desitavāti vuttaṃ hoti, tasmā vibhattavāti vattabbe “bhagavā”ti vuccati.

Furthermore, because he analyzed all dhammas by way of divisions such as wholesome, etc.; or wholesome dhammas, etc., by way of aggregates, sense bases, elements, truths, faculties, dependent origination, and so forth; or the Noble Truth of Suffering by the meaning of oppression, the conditioned, affliction, and change; the Noble Truth of the Origin by the meaning of accumulation, cause, connection, and obstruction; the Noble Truth of Cessation by the meaning of escape, seclusion, the unconditioned, and deathlessness; and the Noble Truth of the Path by the meaning of leading out, cause, vision, and dominance—and since it is said, 'He analyzed, explained, and taught'—therefore, when 'Vibhattavā' (the Analyzer) should be said, he is called 'Bhagavā'.

Yasmā ca esa dibbabrahmaariyavihāre kāyacittaupadhiviveke suññatāppaṇihitānimittavimokkhe [V 0.0089] aññe ca lokiyalokuttare uttarimanussadhamme bhaji sevi bahulamakāsi, tasmā bhattavāti vattabbe “bhagavā”ti vuccati.

And because he resorted to, attended to, and frequently practiced the divine abodes, the brahma abodes, the noble abodes, seclusion of body, seclusion of mind, seclusion from defilements, the liberations of emptiness, the desireless, and the signless, and other mundane and supramundane qualities superior to the human state, therefore, when 'Bhattavā' (one who has resorted to) should be said, he is called 'Bhagavā'.

Yasmā pana tīsu bhavesu taṇhāsaṅkhātaṃ gamanaṃ anena vantaṃ, tasmā bhavesu vantagamanoti vattabbe bhavasaddato bhakāraṃ gamanasaddato gakāraṃ vantasaddato vakārañca dīghaṃ katvā ādāya “bhagavā”ti vuccati, yathā loke “mehanassa khassa mālā”ti vattabbe “mekhalā”ti.

Furthermore, because the 'going' known as craving in the three realms of existence has been abandoned by him, therefore, when 'one who has abandoned going in the realms of existence' (bhavesu vantagamano) should be said, by taking the syllable 'bha' from the word 'bhava', the syllable 'ga' from the word 'gamana', and the syllable 'va' from the word 'vanta' and making it long, he is called 'Bhagavā'; just as in the world, when 'mehanassa khassa mālā' should be said, 'mekhalā' is said.

Ettāvatā [P 0.0110] cettha evaṃ me sutanti vacanena yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ desento paccakkhaṃ katvā bhagavato dhammasarīraṃ pakāseti, tena “nayidaṃ atītasatthukaṃ pāvacanaṃ, ayaṃ vo satthā”ti bhagavato adassanena ukkaṇṭhitajanaṃ samassāseti.

By this much, here, with the words 'Thus have I heard,' the Elder Ānanda, while teaching the Dhamma as it was heard and as it was learned, makes the Dhamma-body of the Blessed One directly present and reveals it. Therefore, by this, he consoles the people who are distressed by not seeing the Blessed One, as if saying, 'This teaching is not one whose teacher has passed away; this is your teacher.'

Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavāti vacanena tasmiṃ samaye bhagavato avijjamānabhāvaṃ dassento rūpakāyaparinibbānaṃ dasseti. Tena “evaṃvidhassa imassa ariyadhammassa desetā dasabaladharo vajirasaṅghātakāyo sopi bhagavā parinibbuto, tattha kenaññena jīvite āsā janetabbā”ti jīvitamadamattaṃ janaṃ saṃvejeti, saddhamme cassa ussāhaṃ janeti.

By the words 'At one time, the Blessed One,' he shows the Blessed One's non-existence at the time of recitation, indicating the parinibbāna of the physical body. By this, he arouses a sense of spiritual urgency in people intoxicated with the pride of life, as if to say, 'Even that Blessed One—the teacher of such a noble Dhamma, the bearer of the ten powers, with a body like a diamond core—has attained parinibbāna. In that case, by what other person should a desire for life be generated?' And he generates enthusiasm for the good Dhamma in that person.

Evanti ca bhaṇanto desanāsampattiṃ niddisati, me sutanti sāvakasampattiṃ, ekaṃ samayanti kālasampattiṃ, bhagavāti desakasampattiṃ.

And in saying 'Thus,' he indicates the accomplishment of the teaching; by 'I have heard,' the accomplishment of the disciple; by 'at one time,' the accomplishment of the time; by 'the Blessed One,' the accomplishment of the teacher.

Sāvatthiyaṃ viharatīti ettha sāvatthīti savatthassa isino nivāsaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ nagaraṃ, yathā kākandī mākandīti, evaṃ itthiliṅgavasena sāvatthīti vuccati, evaṃ akkharacintakā. Aṭṭhakathācariyā pana bhaṇanti “yaṃkiñci [M 0.0094] manussānaṃ upabhogaparibhogaṃ sabbamettha atthī”ti sāvatthī. Satthasamāyoge ca “kiṃ bhaṇḍamatthī”ti pucchite “sabbamatthī”ti vacanamupādāya sāvatthī.

Regarding 'He dwells in Sāvatthī': here, 'Sāvatthī' is the city that was the dwelling place of the sage Savattha. Just as with Kākandī and Mākandī, so too it is called 'Sāvatthī' in the feminine gender; thus say the grammarians. The commentary masters, however, say: because 'whatever things for use and enjoyment for humans, all exist here' (sabbam ettha atthi), it is called Sāvatthī.
