And in a caravan gathering, when asked, 'What goods are there?' (kiṃ bhaṇḍam atthi), on account of the reply, 'Everything is here' (sabbam atthi), it is called Sāvatthī.

“Sabbadā sabbūpakaraṇaṃ, sāvatthiyaṃ samohitaṃ;

Tasmā sabbamupādāya, sāvatthīti pavuccati.

'Always, all necessary goods are gathered in Sāvatthī; therefore, on account of 'all' (sabbam), it is called Sāvatthī.'

“Kosalānaṃ puraṃ rammaṃ, dassaneyyaṃ manoramaṃ;

Dasahi saddehi avivittaṃ, annapānasamāyutaṃ.

'The delightful city of the Kosalans, lovely to see and pleasing to the mind; never free from the ten sounds, and endowed with food and drink.'

“Vuḍḍhiṃ [V 0.0090][P 0.0111] vepullataṃ pattaṃ, iddhaṃ phītaṃ manoramaṃ;

Āḷakamandāva devānaṃ, sāvatthipuramuttama”nti. (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.14);

'The excellent city of Sāvatthī has reached growth and expansion; it is prosperous, abundant, and delightful to the mind, like Āḷakamandā of the devas.'

Tassaṃ sāvatthiyaṃ. Samīpatthe bhummavacanaṃ.

In that Sāvatthī. The locative case is used in the sense of 'near'.

Viharatīti avisesena iriyāpathadibbabrahmaariyavihāresu aññataravihārasamaṅgiparidīpanametaṃ. Idha pana ṭhānagamanāsanasayanappabhedesu iriyāpathesu aññatarairiyāpathasamāyogaparidīpanaṃ, tena ṭhitopi gacchantopi nisinnopi sayānopi bhagavā viharaticceva veditabbo. So hi ekaṃ iriyāpathabādhanaṃ aparena iriyāpathena vicchinditvā aparipatantaṃ attabhāvaṃ harati pavatteti. Tasmā viharatīti vuccati.

The word 'viharati' (he dwells), in a general sense, indicates being endowed with one or another of the abodes: the abode of posture, the divine abode, the brahma abode, or the noble abode. Here, however, it indicates engagement in one or another of the postures, namely standing, walking, sitting, and lying down. Therefore, the Blessed One should be understood as 'dwelling' whether he is standing, walking, sitting, or lying down. For he, having cut off the affliction of one posture with another posture, carries on and maintains his individual existence without it collapsing. Therefore, he is said to 'dwell'.

Jetavaneti ettha attano paccatthikajanaṃ jinātīti jeto, raññā vā attano paccatthikajane jite jātoti jeto, maṅgalakamyatāya vā tassa evaṃ nāmameva katantipi jeto. Vanayatīti vanaṃ, attasampadāya sattānaṃ bhattiṃ kāreti, attani sinehaṃ uppādetīti attho. Vanute iti vā vanaṃ, nānāvidhakusumagandhasammodamattakokilādivihaṅgavirutehi mandamālutacalitarukkhasākhāviṭapapupphaphalapallavapalāsehi ca “etha maṃ paribhuñjathā”ti pāṇino yācati viyāti attho. Jetassa vanaṃ jetavanaṃ. Tañhi jetena rājakumārena ropitaṃ saṃvaḍḍhitaṃ paripālitaṃ, so ca tassa sāmī ahosi, tasmā jetavananti vuccati. Tasmiṃ jetavane.

Regarding 'in Jeta's Grove' (Jetavane): here, one who conquers (jināti) his own enemies is a 'Jeta' (conqueror). Or, he was born (jāto) when the king had conquered (jite) his enemies, thus he is 'Jeta'. Or, this name was given to him for the sake of auspiciousness, thus he is 'Jeta'. That which is sought (vanayati) is a 'vana' (grove); the meaning is that by its own abundance, it causes beings to have devotion and fosters affection for itself. Or, it is frequented (vanute), thus it is a 'vana'; the meaning is that with the sounds of cuckoos and other birds, intoxicated by the blended scents of various flowers, and with the branches, boughs, blossoms, fruits, shoots, and leaves of the trees stirred by a gentle breeze, it is as if, though without life, it begs, 'Come, enjoy me.' The grove of Jeta is Jeta's Grove (Jetavana). For it was planted, nurtured, and protected by Prince Jeta, and he was its owner; therefore, it is called Jeta's Grove. In that Jeta's Grove.

Anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāmeti ettha sudatto nāma so gahapati mātāpitūhi katanāmavasena, sabbakāmasamiddhitāya tu vigatamalamaccheratāya karuṇādiguṇasamaṅgitāya ca niccakālaṃ anāthānaṃ piṇḍaṃ [M 0.0095] adāsi, tena anāthapiṇḍikoti [P 0.0112] saṅkhyaṃ gato. Āramanti ettha pāṇino, visesena vā pabbajitāti ārāmo, tassa pupphaphalapallavādisobhanatāya nātidūranāccāsannatādipañcavidhasenāsanaṅgasampattiyā ca tato tato āgamma ramanti abhiramanti anukkaṇṭhitā hutvā nivasantīti attho. Vuttappakārāya vā sampattiyā tattha tattha gatepi attano abbhantaraṃyeva ānetvā rametīti ārāmo. So hi anāthapiṇḍikena gahapatinā jetassa rājakumārassa hatthato aṭṭhārasahiraññakoṭisanthārena kiṇitvā aṭṭhārasahiraññakoṭīhi senāsanaṃ kārāpetvā aṭṭhārasahiraññakoṭīhi vihāramahaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā evaṃ catupaññāsāya hiraññakoṭipariccāgena [V 0.0091] buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa niyyātito, tasmā “anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāmo”ti vuccati. Tasmiṃ anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.

Regarding 'Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park' (Anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme): That householder, named Sudatta by the name given by his parents, came to be reckoned as 'Anāthapiṇḍika' because, due to the fulfillment of all his desires, his freedom from the stain of stinginess, and his endowment with virtues such as compassion, he constantly gave alms (piṇḍa) to the helpless (anātha). It is an 'ārāma' (park) because beings (pāṇino) delight (āramanti) in it, or especially, renunciants (pabbajitā) delight in it. The meaning is that, due to the beauty of its flowers, fruits, and shoots, and its endowment with the fivefold qualities of a dwelling—such as not being too far nor too near—they come from various places, delight, and having become not weary, they dwell there. Or, it is an 'ārāma' because, by means of the aforementioned qualities, even when people have gone to various places, it brings them into its own interior and causes them to delight. Indeed, that park was bought by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika from Prince Jeta for eighteen crores of gold coins by covering the ground with them; he had dwellings built for eighteen crores of gold coins, and he completed the monastery dedication festival for eighteen crores of gold coins. Thus, with a donation of fifty-four crores of gold coins, it was dedicated to the community of monks headed by the Buddha. Therefore, it is called 'Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park'. In that park of Anāthapiṇḍika.

Ettha ca “jetavane”ti vacanaṃ purimasāmiparikittanaṃ, “anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme”ti pacchimasāmiparikittanaṃ. Kimetesaṃ parikittane payojananti? Vuccate – adhikārato tāva “kattha bhāsita”nti pucchāniyāmakaraṇaṃ aññesaṃ puññakāmānaṃ diṭṭhānugatiāpajjane niyojanañca. Tattha hi dvārakoṭṭhakapāsādamāpane bhūmivikkayaladdhā aṭṭhārasa hiraññakoṭiyo anekakoṭiagghanakā rukkhā ca jetassa pariccāgo, catupaññāsa koṭiyo anāthapiṇḍikassa. Yato tesaṃ parikittanena “evaṃ puññakāmā puññāni karontī”ti dassento āyasmā ānando aññepi puññakāme tesaṃ diṭṭhānugatiāpajjane niyojeti. Evamettha puññakāmānaṃ diṭṭhānugatiāpajjane niyojanaṃ payojananti veditabbaṃ.

Here, the phrase 'in Jeta's Grove' is a mention of the former owner, and 'in Anāthapiṇḍika's Park' is a mention of the later owner. What is the purpose in mentioning them? It is said: Firstly, it serves to define the answer to the question, 'Where was it spoken?' and it also serves to encourage other merit-seekers to follow the example they have seen. For there, the gatehouse and mansion, worth the eighteen crores of gold coins received from the sale of the land, and the trees worth many crores, were Jeta's donation; fifty-four crores were Anāthapiṇḍika's. Since by mentioning them, the Venerable Ānanda, showing that 'thus do merit-seekers perform meritorious deeds,' encourages other merit-seekers to follow their example. Thus, it should be understood that the purpose here is the encouragement of merit-seekers to follow the example they have seen.

Etthāha – “yadi tāva bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati, ‘jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme’ti na vattabbaṃ. Atha tattha viharati, ‘sāvatthiya’nti na vattabbaṃ. Na hi sakkā ubhayattha ekaṃ [P 0.0113] samayaṃ viharitu”nti. Vuccate – nanu vuttametaṃ “samīpatthe bhummavacana”nti, yato yathā gaṅgāyamunādīnaṃ samīpe goyūthāni carantāni “gaṅgāya caranti, yamunāya carantī”ti vuccanti, evamidhāpi yadidaṃ sāvatthiyā samīpe jetavanaṃ anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāmo, tattha viharanto vuccati “sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane [M 0.0096] anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme”ti veditabbo. Gocaragāmanidassanatthaṃ hissa sāvatthivacanaṃ, pabbajitānurūpanivāsaṭṭhānanidassanatthaṃ sesavacanaṃ.

Here a questioner says: 'If the Blessed One is dwelling in Sāvatthī, one should not say, "in Jeta's Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍika's Park." And if he is dwelling there, one should not say, "in Sāvatthī." For indeed, it is not possible to dwell in both places at the same time.' It is replied: Has it not been said that this is 'a locative expression in the sense of proximity'? Just as herds of cattle grazing near rivers like the Ganges and Yamunā are said to be 'grazing in the Ganges' or 'grazing in the Yamunā,' so too here, since this Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park, is near Sāvatthī, one dwelling there should be understood to be spoken of as 'dwelling in Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.' Indeed, the mention of Sāvatthī is to indicate his alms-round village, and the remaining words are to indicate a dwelling place suitable for renunciants.

Tattha sāvatthikittanena bhagavato gahaṭṭhānuggahakaraṇaṃ dasseti, jetavanādikittanena pabbajitānuggahakaraṇaṃ. Tathā purimena paccayaggahaṇato attakilamathānuyogavivajjanaṃ, pacchimena vatthukāmappahānato kāmasukhallikānuyogavajjanūpāyadassanaṃ. Purimena ca dhammadesanābhiyogaṃ, pacchimena vivekādhimuttiṃ. Purimena karuṇāya upagamanaṃ, pacchimena ca paññāya apagamanaṃ. Purimena sattānaṃ hitasukhanipphādanādhimuttitaṃ, pacchimena parahitasukhakaraṇe nirupalepataṃ. Purimena dhammikasukhāpariccāganimittaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ, pacchimena uttarimanussadhammānuyoganimittaṃ. Purimena manussānaṃ upakārabahulataṃ, pacchimena devānaṃ. Purimena loke jātassa loke saṃvaḍḍhabhāvaṃ, pacchimena lokena anupalittatanti evamādi.

There, the mention of Sāvatthī shows the Blessed One’s support for householders; the mention of Jetavana and so forth shows his support for renunciants. Likewise, the former shows the avoidance of the practice of self-mortification through the acceptance of requisites; the latter, showing the means of avoiding the practice of indulgence in sensual pleasures through the abandoning of sensual objects. And the former shows his dedication to teaching the Dhamma; the latter, his inclination towards seclusion. The former shows his approaching with compassion; the latter, his departing with wisdom. The former shows his resolve to bring about the welfare and happiness of beings; the latter, his being unstained in bringing about the welfare and happiness of others. The former shows a comfortable abiding, a cause for not abandoning righteous happiness; the latter, a cause for repeatedly engaging in the states of superior men. The former shows his great helpfulness to humans; the latter, to devas. The former shows that one born in the world was well-developed in the world; the latter, his being unstained by the world—and so on.

Athāti avicchedatthe, khoti adhikārantaranidassanatthe nipāto. Tena avicchinneyeva tattha [V 0.0092] bhagavato vihāre idamadhikārantaraṃ udapādīti dasseti. Kiṃ tanti? Aññatarā devatātiādi. Tattha aññatarāti aniyamitaniddeso. Sā hi nāmagottato apākaṭā, tasmā “aññatarā”ti vuttā. Devo eva devatā, itthipurisasādhāraṇametaṃ. Idha pana puriso [P 0.0114] eva, so devaputto kintu, sādhāraṇanāmavasena devatāti vutto.

'Atha' is a particle in the sense of 'uninterrupted'; 'kho' is a particle in the sense of indicating another topic. By this, it shows that while in the Blessed One's dwelling, without interruption, this other topic arose. What is that? It is the passage beginning 'A certain deity.' Therein, 'a certain' (aññatarā) is an indefinite indicator. Indeed, since that deity was not manifest by name and clan, she is called 'a certain one.' A 'deva' is a 'devatā'; this term is common to male and female. Here, however, it is a male, that devaputta, but he is called 'devatā' by way of the common name.

Abhikkantāya rattiyāti ettha abhikkantasaddo khayasundarābhirūpaabbhanumodanādīsu dissati. Tattha “abhikkantā, bhante, ratti, nikkhanto paṭhamo yāmo, ciranisinno bhikkhusaṅgho, uddisatu, bhante, bhagavā bhikkhūnaṃ pātimokkha”nti evamādīsu (cūḷava. 383; a. ni. 8.20) khaye dissati. “Ayaṃ imesaṃ catunnaṃ puggalānaṃ abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro cā”ti evamādīsu (a. ni. 4.100) sundare.

In the phrase 'abhikkantāya rattiyā' (when the night had advanced), the word 'abhikkanta' is seen in senses such as 'passed,' 'beautiful,' 'exceedingly lovely,' 'greatly rejoicing,' and so on. Among these, in passages such as, 'Venerable sir, the night has passed (abhikkantā), the first watch is over, the community of monks has been seated for a long time; venerable sir, may the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha to the monks,' it is seen in the sense of 'passed.' In passages such as, 'This one, among these four persons, is more excellent (abhikkantataro) and more sublime,' it is seen in the sense of 'beautiful' or 'good'.

“Ko me vandati pādāni, iddhiyā yasasā jalaṃ;

Abhikkantena vaṇṇena, sabbā obhāsayaṃ disā”ti. (vi. va. 857); –

'Who is it that worships my feet, shining with power and glory? With an exceedingly lovely complexion (abhikkantena vaṇṇena), illuminating all directions?'

Evamādīsu [M 0.0097] abhirūpe. “Abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama, abhikkantaṃ, bho gotamā”ti evamādīsu (a. ni. 2.16; pārā. 15) abbhanumodane. Idha pana khaye. Tena abhikkantāya rattiyāti parikkhīṇāya rattiyāti vuttaṃ hoti.

In such passages as the preceding, it is seen in the sense of 'exceedingly lovely.' In expressions such as, 'Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!' it is seen in the sense of 'greatly rejoicing' or 'approval.' Here, however, in the phrase under discussion, it is in the sense of 'passed.' Therefore, 'when the night had passed' (abhikkantāya rattiyā) means 'when the night was spent' (parikkhīṇāya rattiyā).

Abhikkantavaṇṇāti ettha abhikkantasaddo abhirūpe, vaṇṇasaddo pana chavithutikulavaggakāraṇasaṇṭhānapamāṇarūpāyatanādīsu dissati. Tattha “suvaṇṇavaṇṇosi bhagavā”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 2.399; su. ni. 553) chaviyaṃ. “Kadā saññūḷhā pana te gahapati ime samaṇassa gotamassa vaṇṇā”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 2.77) thutiyaṃ. “Cattārome, bho gotama, vaṇṇā”ti evamādīsu (dī. ni. 3.115) kulavagge. “Atha kena nu vaṇṇena, gandhathenoti [P 0.0115] vuccatī”ti evamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.234) kāraṇe. “Mahantaṃ hatthirājavaṇṇaṃ abhinimminitvā”ti evamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.138) saṇṭhāne. “Tayo pattassa vaṇṇā”ti evamādīsu pamāṇe. “Vaṇṇo gandho raso ojā”ti evamādīsu rūpāyatane. So idha chaviyaṃ daṭṭhabbo. Tena abhikkantavaṇṇāti abhirūpacchavīti vuttaṃ hoti.

In the phrase “of excellent complexion,” the word “abhikkanta” is in the sense of “exceedingly beautiful.” The word “vaṇṇa,” however, is seen in the senses of skin, praise, lineage, cause, shape, measure, the sense-base of form, and so on. Among these, in phrases such as “The Blessed One is of golden complexion,” it is used in the sense of skin. In phrases such as “When, householder, has this praise of the ascetic Gotama been so established for you?” it is used in the sense of praise. In phrases such as “There are, O Gotama, these four classes,” it is used in the sense of lineage. In phrases such as “Then for what reason is he called ‘scent-thief’?” it is used in the sense of cause. In phrases such as “Having created the form of a great elephant king,” it is used in the sense of shape. In phrases such as “There are three sizes of the bowl,” it is used in the sense of measure. In phrases such as “Form, scent, taste, nutritive essence,” it is used in the sense of the sense-base of form. Here, it should be understood in the sense of skin. Therefore, “of excellent complexion” is said to mean “having exceedingly beautiful skin.”

Kevalakappanti ettha kevalasaddo anavasesayebhuyyaabyāmissānatirekadaḷhatthavisaṃyogādianekattho[V 0.0093]. Tathā hissa “kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariya”nti evamādīsu (pārā. 1) anavasesatā attho. “Kevalakappā ca aṅgamāgadhā pahūtaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ ādāya upasaṅkamissantī”ti evamādīsu (mahāva. 43) yebhuyyatā. “Kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hotī”ti evamādīsu (vibha. 225) abyāmissatā. “Kevalaṃ saddhāmattakaṃ nūna ayamāyasmā”ti evamādīsu (mahāva. 244) anatirekatā. “Āyasmato, bhante, anuruddhassa bāhiyo nāma saddhivihāriko kevalakappaṃ saṅghabhedāya ṭhito”ti evamādīsu (a. ni. 4.243) daḷhatthatā. “Kevalī vusitavā uttamapurisoti vuccatī”ti evamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.57) visaṃyogo. Idha panassa anavasesattamattho adhippeto.

In the term “kevalakappaṃ,” the word “kevala” has many meanings, such as: without remainder, majority, unmixed, not in excess, firm, and separation. For instance, in passages like “the holy life, entirely complete and pure,” it has the meaning of “without remainder.” In phrases like “The majority of the people of Aṅga and Magadha will approach, bringing abundant hard and soft food,” it has the meaning of “majority.” In statements like “Of the unmixed mass of suffering, there is an arising,” it has the meaning of “unmixed.” In expressions like “This venerable one is surely of mere faith,” it has the meaning of “not in excess.” In passages like “Venerable Sir, the co-resident named Bāhiya of the Venerable Anuruddha is firmly intent on causing schism in the Saṅgha,” it has the meaning of “firmness.” In phrases like “One who is separated, who has lived the life, is called the supreme person,” it has the meaning of “separation.” Here, however, its intended meaning is “without remainder.”

Kappasaddo panāyaṃ abhisaddahanavohārakālapaññattichedanavikappalesasamantabhāvādianekattho. Tathā hissa “okappanīyametaṃ [M 0.0098] bhoto gotamassa, yathā taṃ arahato sammāsambuddhassā”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 1.387) abhisaddahanamattho. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pañcahi samaṇakappehi phalaṃ paribhuñjitu”nti evamādīsu (cūḷava. 250) [P 0.0116] vohāro. “Yena sudaṃ niccakappaṃ viharāmī”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 1.387) kālo. “Iccāyasmā kappo”ti evamādīsu (su. ni. 1098; cūḷani. kappamāṇavapucchā 117, kappamāṇavapucchāniddesa 61) paññatti. “Alaṅkato kappitakesamassū”ti evamādīsu (jā. 2.22.1368) chedanaṃ. “Kappati dvaṅgulakappo”ti evamādīsu (cūḷava. 446) vikappo. “Atthi kappo nipajjitu”nti evamādīsu (a. ni. 8.80) leso. “Kevalakappaṃ veḷuvanaṃ obhāsetvā”ti evamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.94) samantabhāvo. Idha panassa samantabhāvo attho adhippeto. Yato kevalakappaṃ jetavananti ettha anavasesaṃ samantato jetavananti evamattho daṭṭhabbo.

Now, this word 'kappa' has many meanings, such as: strong belief, convention, time, designation, cutting, allowance, a hint, and all-aroundness. Indeed, in such phrases as, 'This is credible for Master Gotama, as is fitting for the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One,' it has the meaning of strong belief. In such statements as, 'Monks, I allow the partaking of fruit according to five ascetic conventions,' it has the meaning of convention. In such phrases as, 'Whereby I dwell for all time,' it has the meaning of time. In such expressions as, 'Thus, the Venerable Kappa,' it has the meaning of designation. In such instances as, 'Adorned, with hair and beard cut,' it has the meaning of cutting. In such phrases as, 'The two-finger-breadth allowance is permissible,' it has the meaning of allowance. In such statements as, 'There is a chance to lie down,' it has the meaning of a hint. And in such phrases as, 'Illuminating the Veḷuvana all around,' it has the meaning of all-aroundness. Here, however, the meaning of all-aroundness is intended. Whence, in the phrase 'kevalakappaṃ jetavanaṃ,' the meaning should be understood as 'the Jeta Grove entirely, all around.'

Obhāsetvāti ābhāya pharitvā, candimā viya sūriyo viya ca ekobhāsaṃ ekapajjotaṃ karitvāti attho.

'Having illuminated' means having pervaded with light and, like the moon and the sun, having made a single light, a single radiance—this is the meaning.

Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti bhummatthe karaṇavacanaṃ. Yato yattha bhagavā, tattha upasaṅkamīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Yena vā kāraṇena bhagavā devamanussehi upasaṅkamitabbo, teneva kāraṇena upasaṅkamīti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Kena ca kāraṇena bhagavā upasaṅkamitabbo? Nānappakāraguṇavisesādhigamādhippāyena, sādurasaphalūpabhogādhippāyena dijagaṇehi niccaphalitamahārukkho viya. Upasaṅkamīti ca gatāti vuttaṃ hoti. Upasaṅkamitvāti upasaṅkamanapariyosānadīpanaṃ[V 0.0094]. Atha vā evaṃ gatā tato āsannataraṃ ṭhānaṃ bhagavato samīpasaṅkhātaṃ gantvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvāti bhagavantaṃ vanditvā paṇamitvā namassitvā.

In the phrase 'Where the Blessed One was, there he approached,' this is an instrumental case in the sense of the locative. Herein, the meaning should be understood thus: 'Wherever the Blessed One was, there he approached.' Or, the meaning herein should be understood thus: 'For whatever reason the Blessed One is to be approached by gods and humans, for that very reason he approached.' And for what reason is the Blessed One to be approached? With the intention of attaining various special qualities, just as a great, ever-fruitful tree is approached by flocks of birds with the intention of enjoying sweet-tasting fruits. And 'he approached' is said to mean 'he went.' 'Having approached' indicates the conclusion of the act of approaching. Alternatively, it is said to mean that having gone thus, from there he went to a nearer place, designated as the presence of the Blessed One. 'Having paid homage to the Blessed One' means having venerated, bowed down to, and paid respect to the Blessed One.

Ekamantanti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso ekokāsaṃ ekapassanti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhummatthe vā upayogavacanaṃ. Aṭṭhāsīti [P 0.0117] nisajjādipaṭikkhepo, ṭhānaṃ kappesi, ṭhitā ahosīti attho.

'To one side' is a neuter designation of state; it is said to mean 'in one place, to one side.' Alternatively, it is an accusative case in the sense of the locative. 'Stood' is a rejection of sitting and the like; it establishes the posture of standing. The meaning is, 'she stood.'

Kathaṃ [M 0.0099] ṭhitā pana sā ekamantaṃ ṭhitā ahūti?

But how was it that she, having stood, stood to one side?

“Na pacchato na purato, nāpi āsannadūrato;

Na kacche nopi paṭivāte, na cāpi oṇatuṇṇate;

Ime dose vivajjetvā, ekamantaṃ ṭhitā ahū”ti.

Not behind, not in front, nor too near or too far; not at the side nor upwind, nor on low or high ground. Having avoided these faults, she stood to one side.

Kasmā panāyaṃ aṭṭhāsi eva, na nisīdīti? Lahuṃ nivattitukāmatāya. Devatāyo hi kañcideva atthavasaṃ paṭicca sucipuriso viya vaccaṭṭhānaṃ manussalokaṃ āgacchanti. Pakatiyā pana tāsaṃ yojanasatato pabhuti manussaloko duggandhatāya paṭikūlo hoti, na ettha abhiramanti, tena sā āgatakiccaṃ katvā lahuṃ nivattitukāmatāya na nisīdi. Yassa ca gamanādiiriyāpathaparissamassa vinodanatthaṃ nisīdanti, so devānaṃ parissamo natthi, tasmāpi na nisīdi. Ye ca mahāsāvakā bhagavantaṃ parivāretvā ṭhitā, te patimāneti, tasmāpi na nisīdi. Apica bhagavati gāraveneva na nisīdi. Devatānañhi nisīditukāmānaṃ āsanaṃ nibbattati, taṃ anicchamānā nisajjāya cittampi akatvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi.

Why did this deity stand and not sit down? Due to the desire to return quickly. Indeed, deities come to the human world on account of some purpose, like a man who desires purity going to a latrine. But naturally, to them, the human world, from a hundred yojanas away, is repulsive due to its foul smell; they do not delight in it. Therefore, that deity, having accomplished the task for which she came, did not sit down due to her desire to return quickly. Moreover, the fatigue from postures such as walking, to relieve which people sit, does not exist for deities; for that reason also, she did not sit. And she revered the great disciples who stood surrounding the Blessed One; for that reason also, she did not sit. Furthermore, it was out of reverence for the Blessed One that she did not sit. Indeed, for deities who wish to sit, a seat manifests. Not wishing for it, and not even forming the thought to sit, she stood to one side.

Ekamantaṃ ṭhitā kho sā devatāti evaṃ imehi kāraṇehi ekamantaṃ ṭhitā kho sā devatā. Bhagavantaṃ gāthāya ajjhabhāsīti bhagavantaṃ akkharapadaniyamitaganthitena vacanena abhāsīti attho. Kathaṃ? Bahū devā manussā ca…pe… brūhi maṅgalamuttamanti.

As for the phrase, 'That deity, indeed, stood to one side': for these reasons, that deity, indeed, stood to one side. As for the phrase, 'She addressed the Blessed One with a verse,' the meaning is that she spoke to the Blessed One with speech composed of fixed letters and words. How? 'Many devas and humans... tell us the highest blessing.'

Maṅgalapañhasamuṭṭhānakathā

The Discourse on the Origin of the Question Concerning Blessings

Tattha yasmā “evamiccādipāṭhassa, atthaṃ nānappakārato. Vaṇṇayanto samuṭṭhānaṃ, vatvā”ti mātikā ṭhapitā, tassa ca samuṭṭhānassa ayaṃ vattabbatāya okāso, tasmā maṅgalapañhasamuṭṭhānaṃ tāva vatvā pacchā imesaṃ gāthāpadānamatthaṃ [P 0.0118] vaṇṇayissāmi. Kiñca maṅgalapañhasamuṭṭhānaṃ? Jambudīpe [V 0.0095] kira tattha tattha nagaradvārasanthāgārasabhādīsu mahājano sannipatitvā hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ datvā nānappakāraṃ sītāharaṇādikathaṃ kathāpeti, ekekā kathā catumāsaccayena niṭṭhāti. Tattha ekadivasaṃ maṅgalakathā samuṭṭhāsi “kiṃ nu kho maṅgalaṃ, kiṃ diṭṭhaṃ maṅgalaṃ, sutaṃ maṅgalaṃ, mutaṃ maṅgalaṃ, ko maṅgalaṃ jānātī”ti.

Therein, since the mātikā was established stating, 'Explaining the meaning of the text beginning with “evaṃ” in various ways, having first stated the origin,' and since this is the occasion for that origin to be stated, therefore, I will first state the origin of the question concerning blessings and afterwards explain the meaning of these verse-lines. And what is the origin of the question concerning blessings? It is said that in Jambudīpa, in various places such as city gates, assembly halls, and public forums, a great crowd of people would gather. Having given gold and silver, they would have various kinds of stories told, such as the abduction of Sītā. Each story would conclude after four months. There, one day, a discussion on blessings arose: 'What, indeed, is a blessing? Is what is seen a blessing? Is what is heard a blessing? Is what is sensed a blessing? Who knows what a blessing is?'

Atha [M 0.0100] diṭṭhamaṅgaliko nāmeko puriso āha “ahaṃ maṅgalaṃ jānāmi, diṭṭhaṃ loke maṅgalaṃ diṭṭhaṃ nāma abhimaṅgalasammataṃ rūpaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – idhekacco kālasseva vuṭṭhāya cātakasakuṇaṃ vā passati, beluvalaṭṭhiṃ vā gabbhiniṃ vā kumārake vā alaṅkatapaṭiyatte puṇṇaghaṭe vā allarohitamacchaṃ vā ājaññaṃ vā ājaññarathaṃ vā usabhaṃ vā gāviṃ vā kapilaṃ vā, yaṃ vā panaññampi kiñci evarūpaṃ abhimaṅgalasammataṃ rūpaṃ passati, idaṃ vuccati diṭṭhamaṅgala”nti. Tassa vacanaṃ ekacce aggahesuṃ, ekacce na aggahesuṃ. Ye na aggahesuṃ, te tena saha vivadiṃsu.

Then a man named Diṭṭhamaṅgalika said: 'I know what a blessing is. In the world, what is seen is a blessing. "What is seen" means a form considered a great blessing. For instance: here, someone, having risen early, sees a cātaka bird, or a bamboo staff, or a pregnant woman, or young boys adorned and prepared, or full pots, or a fresh rohita fish, or a thoroughbred horse, or a chariot drawn by thoroughbreds, or a bull, or a cow, or a monkey, or sees any other such form considered a great blessing. This is called a "seen blessing."' Some accepted his words; some did not. Those who did not accept argued with him.

Atha sutamaṅgaliko nāma eko puriso āha – “cakkhunāmetaṃ, bho, sucimpi passati asucimpi, tathā sundarampi, asundarampi, manāpampi, amanāpampi. Yadi tena diṭṭhaṃ maṅgalaṃ siyā, sabbampi maṅgalaṃ siyā. Tasmā na diṭṭhaṃ maṅgalaṃ, apica [P 0.0119] kho pana sutaṃ maṅgalaṃ. Sutaṃ nāma abhimaṅgalasammato saddo. Seyyathidaṃ? Idhekacco kālasseva vuṭṭhāya vaḍḍhāti vā vaḍḍhamānāti vā puṇṇāti vā phussāti vā sumanāti vā sirīti vā sirivaḍḍhāti vā ajja sunakkhattaṃ sumuhuttaṃ sudivasaṃ sumaṅgalanti evarūpaṃ vā yaṃkiñci abhimaṅgalasammataṃ saddaṃ suṇāti, idaṃ vuccati sutamaṅgala”nti. Tassāpi vacanaṃ ekacce aggahesuṃ, ekacce na aggahesuṃ. Ye na aggahesuṃ, te tena saha vivadiṃsu.

Then a man named Sutamaṅgalika said: 'Sirs, with the eye one sees both the pure and the impure, likewise the beautiful and the ugly, the agreeable and the disagreeable. If what is seen were a blessing, then everything seen would be a blessing. Therefore, what is seen is not a blessing. But rather, what is heard is a blessing. "What is heard" means a sound considered a great blessing. For instance? Here, someone, having risen early, hears a sound considered a great blessing, such as "Prosper!" or "Prospering!" or "Full!" or "Phussa!" or "Sumanā!" or "Sirī!" or "Sirivaḍḍha!", or "Today is a good constellation, a good moment, a good day, a good blessing!" or any other such sound. This is called a "heard blessing."' His words, too, some accepted, and some did not. Those who did not accept argued with him.

Atha mutamaṅgaliko nāmeko puriso āha “sotampi hi nāmetaṃ, bho, sādhumpi asādhumpi manāpampi amanāpampi saddaṃ suṇāti. Yadi tena sutaṃ maṅgalaṃ siyā, sabbampi maṅgalaṃ siyā. Tasmā na sutaṃ maṅgalaṃ, apica kho pana mutaṃ maṅgalaṃ. Mutaṃ nāma abhimaṅgalasammataṃ gandharasaphoṭṭhabbaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – idhekacco kālasseva vuṭṭhāya padumagandhādipupphagandhaṃ vā ghāyati, phussadantakaṭṭhaṃ vā khādati, pathaviṃ vā āmasati, haritasassaṃ vā allagomayaṃ vā kacchapaṃ vā tilaṃ vā pupphaṃ vā phalaṃ vā āmasati, phussamattikāya vā sammā limpati, phussasāṭakaṃ vā nivāseti, phussaveṭhanaṃ vā dhāreti. Yaṃ vā panaññampi kiñci evarūpaṃ abhimaṅgalasammataṃ gandhaṃ vā ghāyati, rasaṃ vā sāyati, phoṭṭhabbaṃ [V 0.0096] vā phusati, idaṃ vuccati mutamaṅgala”nti. Tassāpi vacanaṃ ekacce aggahesuṃ, ekacce na aggahesuṃ.

Then a man named Mutamaṅgalika said: 'Sirs, this ear, indeed, hears sounds both good and bad, pleasant and unpleasant. If what is heard were a blessing, then everything heard would be a blessing. Therefore, what is heard is not a blessing. But rather, what is sensed is a blessing. "What is sensed" means a smell, taste, or tangible object considered a great blessing. For instance: here, someone, having risen early, smells the fragrance of flowers such as the lotus; or chews on pleasant tooth-wood; or touches the earth; or touches green crops, fresh cow-dung, a tortoise, sesame, flowers, or fruit; or anoints oneself well with pleasant clay; or wears a pleasant cloth; or wears a pleasant head-wrap. Or whatever else of this kind, one smells a fragrance, tastes a flavor, or touches a tangible object considered a great blessing—this is called a "sensed blessing."' His words, too, some accepted, and some did not.

Tattha [M 0.0101] na diṭṭhamaṅgaliko sutamutamaṅgalike asakkhi ñāpetuṃ, na tesaṃ aññataro itare dve. Tesu ca manussesu ye diṭṭhamaṅgalikassa vacanaṃ gaṇhiṃsu, te “diṭṭhaṃyeva maṅgala”nti gatā. Ye sutamutamaṅgalikānaṃ, te “sutaṃyeva mutaṃyeva maṅgala”nti gatā. Evamayaṃ maṅgalakathā sakalajambudīpe pākaṭā jātā.

Among them, the Diṭṭhamaṅgalika was not able to make the Suta- and Muta-maṅgalikas understand, nor was any one of them able to make the other two understand. And among those people, those who accepted the words of the Diṭṭhamaṅgalika held the view: 'Only what is seen is a blessing.' Those who accepted the words of the Suta- and Muta-maṅgalikas held the view: 'Only what is heard is a blessing, and only what is sensed is a blessing.' Thus this discussion on blessings became well-known throughout all of Jambudīpa.

Atha sakalajambudīpe manussā gumbagumbā [P 0.0120] hutvā “kiṃ nu kho maṅgala”nti maṅgalāni cintayiṃsu. Tesaṃ manussānaṃ ārakkhadevatā taṃ kathaṃ sutvā tatheva maṅgalāni cintayiṃsu. Tāsaṃ devatānaṃ bhummadevatā mittā honti, atha tato sutvā bhummadevatāpi tatheva maṅgalāni cintayiṃsu, tāsaṃ devatānaṃ ākāsaṭṭhadevatā mittā honti, ākāsaṭṭhadevatānaṃ catumahārājikā devatā mittā honti, etenupāyena yāva sudassīdevatānaṃ akaniṭṭhadevatā mittā honti, atha tato sutvā akaniṭṭhadevatāpi tatheva gumbagumbā hutvā maṅgalāni cintayiṃsu. Evaṃ yāva dasasahassacakkavāḷesu sabbattha maṅgalacintā udapādi. Uppannā ca “idaṃ maṅgalaṃ idaṃ maṅgala”nti vinicchayamānāpi appattā eva vinicchayaṃ dvādasa vassāni aṭṭhāsi. Sabbe manussā ca devā ca brahmāno ca ṭhapetvā ariyasāvake diṭṭhasutamutavasena tidhā bhinnā. Ekopi “idameva maṅgala”nti yathābhuccato niṭṭhaṅgato nāhosi, maṅgalakolāhalaṃ loke uppajji.

Then, throughout all of Jambudīpa, humans formed into groups and pondered on blessings, thinking, “What indeed is a blessing?” The guardian deities of those humans, having heard that discussion, likewise pondered on blessings. The earth-deities are friends of those deities; then, having heard it from them, the earth-deities also pondered on blessings in the same way. The sky-dwelling deities are friends of those earth-deities. The Cātumahārājika deities are friends of the sky-dwelling deities. By this method, the chain of friends extended up to the Akaniṭṭha deities, who are friends of the Sudassī deities. Then, having heard it from them, the Akaniṭṭha deities also formed into groups and pondered on blessings in the same way. Thus, throughout the ten thousand world-systems, the thought of blessings arose everywhere. And though this matter arose and they tried to decide, saying, “This is a blessing, this is a blessing,” it stood for twelve years without reaching a decision. All humans, deities, and brahmās—except for the noble disciples—were divided into three factions according to what was seen, heard, or sensed. Not even one was able to reach a conclusion according to reality, saying, “This alone is a blessing.” The uproar concerning blessings arose in the world.

Kolāhalaṃ nāma pañcavidhaṃ kappakolāhalaṃ, cakkavattikolāhalaṃ, buddhakolāhalaṃ, maṅgalakolāhalaṃ, moneyyakolāhalanti. Tattha kāmāvacaradevā muttasirā vikiṇṇakesā rudammukhā assūni hatthehi puñchamānā rattavatthanivatthā ativiya virūpavesadhārino hutvā “vassasatasahassaccayena kappuṭṭhānaṃ hohiti, ayaṃ loko vinassissati, mahāsamuddo sussissati, ayañca mahāpathavī sineru ca pabbatarājā [P 0.0121] uḍḍhayhissati vinassissati, yāva brahmalokā lokavināso bhavissati, mettaṃ mārisā bhāvetha, karuṇaṃ muditaṃ upekkhaṃ mārisā bhāvetha, mātaraṃ upaṭṭhahatha, pitaraṃ upaṭṭhahatha, kule jeṭṭhāpacāyino hotha, jāgaratha mā pamādatthā”ti manussapathe vicaritvā ārocenti. Idaṃ kappakolāhalaṃ nāma.

An uproar, by name, is of five kinds: the eon-uproar, the wheel-turning monarch-uproar, the Buddha-uproar, the blessing-uproar, and the sagehood-uproar. Among these, for the eon-uproar, the deities of the sense-sphere, with heads bare of ornaments, with dishevelled hair, with weeping faces, wiping their tears with their hands, wearing red garments, and having assumed an extremely unsightly appearance, wander in the human world-path and announce: “After one hundred thousand years, the dissolution of the eon will occur! This world will be destroyed, the great ocean will dry up, and this great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, will burn and be destroyed! The destruction of the world will occur up to the Brahma-world! Sirs, develop loving-kindness! Sirs, develop compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity! Attend to your mother, attend to your father! Be respectful to the elders in the family! Be vigilant, do not be heedless!” This is called the eon-uproar.

Kāmāvacaradevāyeva “vassasatassaccayena cakkavattirājā loke uppajjissatī”ti manussapathe [V 0.0097] vicaritvā ārocenti. Idaṃ cakkavattikolāhalaṃ nāma. Suddhāvāsā pana devā brahmābharaṇena alaṅkaritvā brahmaveṭhanaṃ [M 0.0102] sīse katvā pītisomanassajātā buddhaguṇavādino “vassasahassaccayena buddho loke uppajjissatī”ti manussapathe vicaritvā ārocenti. Idaṃ buddhakolāhalaṃ nāma. Suddhāvāsā eva devā devamanussānaṃ cittaṃ ñatvā “dvādasannaṃ vassānaṃ accayena sammāsambuddho maṅgalaṃ kathessatī”ti manussapathe vicaritvā ārocenti. Idaṃ maṅgalakolāhalaṃ nāma. Suddhāvāsā eva devā “sattannaṃ vassānaṃ accayena aññataro bhikkhu bhagavatā saddhiṃ samāgamma moneyyappaṭipadaṃ pucchissatī”ti manussapathe vicaritvā ārocenti. Idaṃ moneyyakolāhalaṃ nāma. Imesu pañcasu kolāhalesu devamanussānaṃ idaṃ maṅgalakolāhalaṃ loke uppajji.

The sense-sphere deities themselves, wandering in the realm of humans, announce: “After one hundred years, a wheel-turning king will arise in the world.” This is called the Wheel-turner uproar. But the deities of the Pure Abodes, having adorned themselves with Brahmā-ornaments, having placed a Brahmā-headdress on their heads, filled with joy and gladness, and speaking of the virtues of the Buddha, wander in the realm of humans and announce: “After one thousand years, a Buddha will arise in the world.” This is called the Buddha uproar. The deities of the Pure Abodes themselves, knowing the minds of deities and humans, wander in the realm of humans and announce: “After twelve years, the Perfectly Enlightened One will teach on blessings.” This is called the blessing uproar. The deities of the Pure Abodes themselves wander in the realm of humans and announce: “After seven years, a certain bhikkhu, having approached the Blessed One, will ask about the practice of sagehood.” This is called the sagehood uproar. Among these five uproars, this blessing uproar arose in the world for deities and humans.

Atha devesu ca manussesu ca vicinitvā vicinitvā maṅgalāni alabhamānesu dvādasannaṃ vassānaṃ accayena tāvatiṃsakāyikā devatā saṅgamma samāgamma evaṃ samacintesuṃ “seyyathāpi nāma gharasāmiko antogharajanānaṃ, gāmasāmiko gāmavāsīnaṃ[P 0.0122], rājā sabbamanussānaṃ, evameva ayaṃ sakko devānamindo amhākaṃ aggo ca seṭṭho ca yadidaṃ puññena tejena issariyena paññāya dvinnaṃ devalokānaṃ adhipati, yaṃnūna mayaṃ sakkaṃ devānamindaṃ etamatthaṃ puccheyyāmā”ti. Tā sakkassa santikaṃ gantvā sakkaṃ devānamindaṃ taṅkhaṇānurūpanivāsanābharaṇasassirikasarīraṃ aḍḍhateyyakoṭiaccharāgaṇaparivutaṃ pāricchattakamūle paṇḍukambalavarāsane nisinnaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ ṭhatvā etadavocuṃ “yagghe, mārisa, jāneyyāsi, etarahi maṅgalapañhā samuṭṭhitā, eke ‘diṭṭhaṃ maṅgala’nti vadanti, eke ‘sutaṃ maṅgala’nti, eke ‘mutaṃ maṅgala’nti, tattha mayañca aññe ca aniṭṭhaṅgatā, sādhu vata no tvaṃ yāthāvato byākarohī”ti. Devarājā pakatiyāpi paññavā “ayaṃ maṅgalakathā kattha paṭhamaṃ samuṭṭhitā”ti āha. “Mayaṃ, deva, cātumahārājikānaṃ assumhā”ti āhaṃsu. Tato cātumahārājikā ākāsaṭṭhadevatānaṃ, ākāsaṭṭhadevatā bhummadevatānaṃ, bhummadevatā manussārakkhadevatānaṃ, manussārakkhadevatā “manussaloke samuṭṭhitā”ti āhaṃsu.

Then, when, after searching again and again among deities and humans, they could not determine what blessings are, after the passing of twelve years, the deities of the Tāvatiṃsa realm gathered and assembled, and deliberated together thus: “Just as the master of a house is for the people within the house, the village headman for the villagers, and the king for all humans, so too this Sakka, lord of the deities, is for us the foremost and the best—that is, by merit, power, sovereignty, and wisdom, he is the lord of the two deva-worlds. What if we were to ask Sakka, the lord of the deities, about this matter?” Having gone to the presence of Sakka, they saw him seated at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree on the excellent Paṇḍukambala seat, his glorious body adorned with garments and ornaments befitting the occasion, surrounded by a retinue of two and a half crores of celestial nymphs. Having paid homage to him, they stood to one side and said this: “Venerable sir, may it please you to know, the question of blessings has now arisen. Some say, ‘The seen is a blessing,’ some say, ‘The heard is a blessing,’ and some say, ‘The sensed is a blessing.’ Therein, we and others have not reached a conclusion. It would be good indeed if you would explain it to us according to reality.” The king of deities, being wise by nature, asked, “Where did this talk of blessings first arise?” They said, “Lord, we heard it from the Cātumahārājikas.” Then the Cātumahārājikas heard it from the sky-dwelling deities, the sky-dwelling deities from the earth-deities, the earth-deities from the human-guardian deities, and the human-guardian deities said, “It arose in the human world.”

Atha devānamindo “sammāsambuddho kattha vasatī”ti pucchi. “Manussaloke devā”ti āhaṃsu. Taṃ bhagavantaṃ koci pucchīti, na koci devāti[M 0.0103]. Kinnu nāma tumhe mārisā aggiṃ chaḍḍetvā khajjopanakaṃ ujjāletha, yena tumhe anavasesamaṅgaladesakaṃ taṃ bhagavantaṃ atikkamitvā maṃ pucchitabbaṃ maññatha, āgacchatha mārisā, taṃ bhagavantaṃ pucchāma, addhā sassirikaṃ pañhaveyyākaraṇaṃ labhissāmāti ekaṃ devaputtaṃ āṇāpesi “taṃ bhagavantaṃ pucchā”ti. So [P 0.0123] devaputto [V 0.0098] taṅkhaṇānurūpena alaṅkārena attānaṃ alaṅkaritvā vijjuriva vijjotamāno devagaṇaparivuto jetavanamahāvihāraṃ gantvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ ṭhatvā maṅgalapañhaṃ pucchanto gāthāya ajjhabhāsi “bahū devā manussā cā”ti.

Then the lord of the deities asked, 'Where does the Perfectly Enlightened One dwell?' They replied, 'In the human world, O Deva.' 'Has anyone asked that Blessed One?' 'No one, O Deva.' 'Why indeed, sirs, do you discard the fire and kindle a firefly, that you think I should be asked, having passed by that Blessed One, the teacher of blessings in their entirety? Come, sirs, let us ask that Blessed One. Surely, we shall obtain a glorious explanation of the question.' Then he commanded a certain devaputta, 'Go and ask that Blessed One.' That devaputta adorned himself with ornaments suitable for the occasion and, shining like lightning, surrounded by a host of devas, went to the Jetavana Great Monastery. He paid homage to the Blessed One, stood to one side, and, wishing to ask the question about blessings, addressed him with the verse beginning: 'Many devas and humans...'

Idaṃ maṅgalapañhasamuṭṭhānaṃ.

This is the origin of the question on blessings.

Bahūdevātigāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Verse Beginning 'Bahū devā'

2. Idāni gāthāpadānaṃ atthavaṇṇanā hoti. Bahūti aniyamitasaṅkhyāniddeso, tena anekasatā anekasahassā anekasatasahassāti vuttaṃ hoti. Dibbantīti devā, pañcahi kāmaguṇehi kīḷanti, attano vā siriyā jotentīti attho. Apica devāti tividhā devā sammutiupapattivisuddhivasena. Yathāha –

Now there is the explanation of the meaning of the words of the verse. 'Many' is an indication of an indefinite number; by this, it is said to mean many hundreds, many thousands, many hundred-thousands. They are called 'devas' because they shine (dibbanti); they sport with the five strands of sensual pleasure, or they shine with their own glory—this is the meaning. Moreover, devas are of three kinds by way of convention, rebirth, and purification. As it is said:

“Devāti tayo devā – sammutidevā, upapattidevā, visuddhidevā. Tattha sammutidevā nāma rājāno deviyo rājakumārā. Upapattidevā nāma cātumahārājike deve upādāya taduttaridevā. Visuddhidevā nāma arahanto vuccantī”ti (cūḷani. dhotakamāṇavapucchāniddesa 32, pārāyanānugītigāthāniddesa 119).

2. 'Devas are of three kinds: devas by convention, devas by rebirth, and devas by purification. Therein, devas by convention are kings, queens, and princes. Devas by rebirth are those beginning with the devas of the Cātumahārājika realm and those above them. Devas by purification are called arahants' (cūḷani. dhotakamāṇavapucchāniddesa 32, pārāyanānugītigāthāniddesa 119).

Tesu idha upapattidevā adhippetā. Manuno apaccāti manussā. Porāṇā pana bhaṇanti – manaso ussannatāya manussā. Te jambudīpakā, aparagoyānakā, uttarakurukā, pubbavidehakāti catubbidhā, idha jambudīpakā adhippetā. Maṅgalanti mahanti imehi sattāti maṅgalāni, iddhiṃ vuddhiñca pāpuṇantīti attho. Acintayunti cintesuṃ ākaṅkhamānāti icchamānā patthayamānā pihayamānā. Sotthānanti sotthibhāvaṃ, sabbesaṃ diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikānaṃ sobhanānaṃ sundarānaṃ kalyāṇānaṃ dhammānamatthitanti vuttaṃ hoti. Brūhīti desehi pakāsehi, ācikkha vivara [M 0.0104] vibhaja [P 0.0124] uttānīkarohi. Maṅgalanti iddhikāraṇaṃ vuddhikāraṇaṃ sabbasampattikāraṇaṃ. Uttamanti visiṭṭhaṃ pavaraṃ sabbalokahitasukhāvahanti ayaṃ gāthāya anupubbapadavaṇṇanā.

Among these, devas by rebirth are intended here. Humans (manussā) are so called because they are the 'offspring of Manu' (Manuno apaccā). The ancients, however, say they are called 'manussā' because of the eminence of their mind (manaso ussannatāya). They are of four kinds: those of Jambudīpa, Aparagoyāna, Uttarakuru, and Pubbavideha; here, those of Jambudīpa are intended. 'Maṅgalāni' (blessings) are so called because 'beings become great (mahanti) through these'; it means they attain prosperity and growth. 'Acintayuṃ' means 'they pondered.' 'Ākaṅkhamānā' means 'desiring, wishing, or longing.' 'Sotthānaṃ' means 'a state of well-being'; it is said to be the existence of all beautiful, good, and wholesome things pertaining to this life and the next. 'Brūhi' means: 'teach, reveal, declare, open up, analyze, make clear.' 'Maṅgalaṃ' is the cause of prosperity, the cause of growth, and the cause of all success. 'Uttamaṃ' means 'distinguished, excellent, bringing welfare and happiness to the whole world.' This is the sequential word-by-word explanation of the verse.

Ayaṃ pana piṇḍattho – so devaputto dasasahassacakkavāḷesu devatā maṅgalapañhaṃ sotukāmatāya imasmiṃ cakkavāḷe sannipatitvā ekavālaggakoṭiokāsamatte dasapi vīsampi tiṃsampi [V 0.0099] cattālīsampi paññāsampi saṭṭhipi sattatipi asītipi sukhumattabhāve nimminitvā sabbadevamārabrahmāno siriyā ca tejasā ca adhiggayha virocamānaṃ paññattavarabuddhāsane nisinnaṃ bhagavantaṃ parivāretvā ṭhitā disvā tasmiñca samaye anāgatānampi sakalajambudīpakānaṃ manussānaṃ cetasā cetoparivitakkamaññāya sabbadevamanussānaṃ vicikicchāsallasamuddharaṇatthaṃ āha –

This, however, is the summary meaning: That devaputta saw the devas from the ten-thousand world-systems. Desiring to hear the question on blessings, they had assembled in this world-system. Having created subtle forms—ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, or even eighty of them in a space the size of a hair-tip's point—they stood surrounding the Blessed One. He was seated on the prepared, excellent Buddha-seat, shining, having surpassed all devas, Māras, and Brahmās with his glory and majesty. At that time, that devaputta, having known with his mind the thoughts in the minds of all the humans of Jambudīpa who had not come, spoke for the purpose of extracting the dart of doubt from all devas and humans:

“Bahū devā manussā ca, maṅgalāni acintayuṃ;

Ākaṅkhamānā sotthānaṃ, brūhi maṅgalamuttama”nti.

“Many devas and humans have pondered on blessings, desiring well-being; declare the highest blessing.”

Tāsaṃ devatānaṃ anumatiyā manussānañca anuggahena mayā puṭṭho samāno yaṃ sabbesameva amhākaṃ ekantahitasukhāvahato uttamaṃ maṅgalaṃ, taṃ no anukampaṃ upādāya brūhi bhagavāti.

With the consent of those devas and for the benefit of humans, being asked by me, O Blessed One, please declare out of compassion for us that supreme blessing which brings certain welfare and happiness to all of us.

Asevanācātigāthāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Verse Beginning with 'Non-Association'

3. Evametaṃ devaputtassa vacanaṃ sutvā bhagavā “asevanā ca bālāna”nti gāthamāha. Tattha asevanāti abhajanā apayirupāsanā. Bālānanti balanti assasantīti bālā, assasitapassasitamattena jīvanti, na paññājīvitenāti adhippāyo. Tesaṃ bālānaṃ. Paṇḍitānanti paṇḍantīti paṇḍitā, sandiṭṭhikasamparāyikesu atthesu ñāṇagatiyā gacchantīti [P 0.0125] adhippāyo. Tesaṃ paṇḍitānaṃ. Sevanāti bhajanā payirupāsanā taṃsahāyatā taṃsampavaṅkatā taṃsamaṅgitā pūjāti sakkāragarukāramānanavandanā. Pūjaneyyānanti pūjārahānaṃ. Etaṃ maṅgalamuttamanti yā ca bālānaṃ asevanā, yā ca paṇḍitānaṃ sevanā, yā ca pūjaneyyānaṃ pūjā, taṃ sabbaṃ sampiṇḍetvā āha “etaṃ maṅgalamuttama”nti. Yaṃ tayā puṭṭhaṃ “brūhi maṅgalamuttama”nti, ettha tāva etaṃ maṅgalamuttamanti gaṇhāhīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ayametissā gāthāya padavaṇṇanā.

3. Having heard these words of the devaputta, the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning, “Not associating with fools.” Herein, ‘non-association’ (asevanā) means not associating (abhajanā), not attending upon (apayirupāsanā). ‘Of fools’ (bālānaṃ): they are ‘fools’ (bālā) because they ‘breathe’ (balanti); they live merely by breathing in and out, not by the life of wisdom—this is the meaning. Of those fools. ‘Of the wise’ (paṇḍitānaṃ): they are ‘wise’ (paṇḍitā) because they ‘proceed’ (paṇḍanti); they proceed with the movement of wisdom in matters pertaining to the here-and-now and to the future life—this is the meaning. Of those wise ones. ‘Association’ (sevanā) means associating (bhajanā), attending upon (payirupāsanā), being a companion to them (taṃsahāyatā), being devoted to them (taṃsampavaṅkatā), being in company with them (taṃsamaṅgitā). ‘Honoring’ (pūjā) means respect (sakkāra), reverence (garukāra), honoring (mānana), and paying homage (vandanā). ‘Of those worthy of honor’ (pūjaneyyānaṃ) means of those who are worthy of honor (pūjārahānaṃ). ‘This is the highest blessing’ (etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ): having combined all of this—the non-association with fools, the association with the wise, and the honoring of those worthy of honor—He said, “This is the highest blessing.” It means: “That which you asked, ‘Declare the highest blessing,’ you should grasp this, for now, as the highest blessing.” This is the explanation of the words of this verse.

Atthavaṇṇanā [M 0.0105] panassā evaṃ veditabbā – evametaṃ devaputtassa vacanaṃ sutvā bhagavā “asevanā ca bālāna”nti imaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha yasmā catubbidhā gāthā pucchitagāthā, apucchitagāthā, sānusandhikagāthā, ananusandhikagāthāti. Tattha “pucchāmi taṃ, gotama, bhūripañña, kathaṅkaro sāvako sādhu hotī”ti (su. ni. 378) ca “kathaṃ nu tvaṃ, mārisa, oghamatarī”ti [V 0.0100] (saṃ. ni. 1.1) ca evamādīsu pucchitena kathitā pucchitagāthā. “Yaṃ pare sukhato āhu, tadariyā āhu dukkhato”ti evamādīsu (su. ni. 767) apucchitena attajjhāsayavasena kathitā apucchitagāthā. Sabbāpi buddhānaṃ gāthā “sanidānāhaṃ, bhikkhave, dhammaṃ desessāmī”ti (a. ni. 3.126; kathā. 806) vacanato sānusandhikagāthā. Ananusandhikagāthā imasmiṃ sāsane natthi. Evametāsu gāthāsu ayaṃ devaputtena pucchitena bhagavatā kathitattā pucchitagāthā. Ayañca yathā cheko puriso kusalo maggassa kusalo amaggassa maggaṃ puṭṭho paṭhamaṃ vijahitabbaṃ ācikkhitvā pacchā gahetabbaṃ ācikkhati “asukasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne dvedhāpatho hoti, tattha vāmaṃ muñcitvā dakkhiṇaṃ gaṇhathā”ti, evaṃ sevitabbāsevitabbesu asevitabbaṃ ācikkhitvā sevitabbaṃ ācikkhati[P 0.0126]. Bhagavā ca maggakusalapurisasadiso. Yathāha –

The explanation of its meaning should be understood thus: Having heard these words of the devaputta, the Blessed One spoke this verse: “Not associating with fools.” Herein, verses are of four kinds: questioned verses, unasked verses, verses with connection, and verses without connection. Among these, verses like “I ask you, Gotama, of vast wisdom, how does a disciple become virtuous?” and “How, sir, did you cross the flood?” are called questioned verses because they are spoken in response to a question. Verses like “What others call happiness, the noble ones call suffering” are called unasked verses because they are spoken spontaneously from one's own inclination. All the verses of the Buddhas are verses with connection, as stated in the words, “Monks, I will teach the Dhamma with its cause.” There are no verses without connection in this Dispensation. Thus, among these verses, this one is a questioned verse because it was spoken by the Blessed One in response to the devaputta's question. And just as a skilled person, who is skilled in the path and skilled in what is not the path, when asked about the path, first points out what should be abandoned and then points out what should be taken—“At such and such a place, the path forks; there, abandon the left and take the right”—so too, regarding those who should be associated with and those who should not, He first explains who should not be associated with and then explains who should be associated with. The Blessed One is like a person skilled in the path. As it is said:

“Puriso maggakusaloti kho, tissa, tathāgatassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ arahato sammāsambuddhassa. So hi kusalo imassa lokassa, kusalo parassa lokassa, kusalo maccudheyyassa, kusalo amaccudheyyassa, kusalo māradheyyassa, kusalo amāradheyyassā”ti.

“‘A person skilled in the path,’ Tissa, is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. For he is skilled regarding this world, skilled regarding the other world, skilled regarding the domain of death, skilled regarding the deathless domain, skilled regarding the domain of Māra, skilled regarding the domain beyond Māra.”

Tasmā paṭhamaṃ asevitabbaṃ ācikkhanto āha – “asevanā ca bālānaṃ, paṇḍitānañca sevanā”ti. Vijahitabbamaggo viya hi paṭhamaṃ bālā na sevitabbā na payirupāsitabbā, tato gahetabbamaggo viya paṇḍitā sevitabbā payirupāsitabbāti. Kasmā pana bhagavatā maṅgalaṃ kathentena paṭhamaṃ bālānamasevanā paṇḍitānañca sevanā kathitāti? Vuccate – yasmā imaṃ diṭṭhādīsu maṅgaladiṭṭhiṃ bālasevanāya devamanussā gaṇhiṃsu, sā ca amaṅgalaṃ, tasmā tesaṃ taṃ idhalokaparalokatthabhañjakaṃ akalyāṇamittasaṃsaggaṃ garahantena ubhayalokatthasādhakañca kalyāṇamittasaṃsaggaṃ [M 0.0106] pasaṃsantena bhagavatā paṭhamaṃ bālānamasevanā paṇḍitānañca sevanā kathitāti.

Therefore, first, explaining who should not be associated with, He said: “Non-association with fools, and association with the wise.” For just as a path to be abandoned, fools should first not be associated with, not be attended upon; then, just as a path to be taken, the wise should be associated with, should be attended upon. But why, when the Blessed One was speaking on blessings, was the non-association with fools and the association with the wise taught first? It is said: Because devas and humans, through association with fools, adopted this view of blessings in things seen and so on, and that is not a blessing. Therefore, condemning that association with bad friends which destroys the benefit for them in this world and the next, and praising that association with good friends which accomplishes the benefit in both worlds, the Blessed One first taught the non-association with fools and the association with the wise.

Tattha bālā nāma ye keci pāṇātipātādiakusalakammapathasamannāgatā sattā, te tīhākārehi jānitabbā. Yathāha “tīṇimāni, bhikkhave, bālassa bālalakkhaṇānī”ti suttaṃ (a. ni. 3.3; ma. ni. 3.246). Apica pūraṇakassapādayo cha satthāro, devadattakokālikakaṭamodakatissakhaṇḍadeviyāputtasamuddadattaciñcamāṇavikādayo atītakāle ca dīghavidassa bhātāti ime aññe [P 0.0127] ca evarūpā sattā bālāti veditabbā.

Therein, ‘fools’ are any beings endowed with unwholesome courses of action beginning with the destruction of life. They are to be known by three characteristics, as He said in the sutta beginning: “Monks, these are the three characteristics of a fool.” Furthermore, the six teachers beginning with Pūraṇa Kassapa; Devadatta, Kokālika, Kaṭamodakatissa, the son of Khaṇḍadevī, Samuddadatta, Ciñcamāṇavikā, and others; and in the past, Dīghavida's brother—these and other such beings are to be understood as ‘fools’.

Te [V 0.0101] aggipadittamiva agāraṃ attanā duggahitena attānañceva attano vacanakārake ca vināsenti. Yathā dīghavidassa bhātā catubuddhantaraṃ saṭṭhiyojanamattena attabhāvena uttāno patito mahāniraye paccati, yathā ca tassa diṭṭhiṃ abhirucanakāni pañca kulasatāni tasseva sahabyataṃ upapannāni mahāniraye paccanti. Vuttañcetaṃ bhagavatā –

They, by means of what is wrongly grasped by them, destroy both themselves and those who act on their words, like a fire a house that is ablaze. Just as Dīghavinaya's brother, for the interval of four Buddhas, having fallen on his back with a body sixty yojanas in extent, is tormented in the great hell; and just as five hundred families who delighted in his view, having attained companionship with him, are tormented in the great hell. And this was said by the Blessed One:

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, naḷāgārā vā tiṇāgārā vā aggi mutto kūṭāgārānipi ḍahati ullittāvalittāni nivātāni phusitaggaḷāni pihitavātapānāni, evameva kho, bhikkhave, yāni kānici bhayāni uppajjanti, sabbāni tāni bālato uppajjanti, no paṇḍitato. Ye keci upaddavā uppajjanti…pe… ye keci upasaggā…pe… no paṇḍitato. Iti kho, bhikkhave, sappaṭibhayo bālo, appaṭibhayo paṇḍito. Saupaddavo bālo, anupaddavo paṇḍito, saupasaggo bālo, anupasaggo paṇḍito”ti (a. ni. 3.1).

‘Just as, bhikkhus, a fire, released from a reed hut or a grass hut, burns down even gabled houses that are plastered inside and out, sheltered from the wind, with bolts fastened and windows closed; even so, bhikkhus, whatever fears arise, all of them arise from the fool, not from the wise one. Whatever calamities arise… whatever troubles arise… all from the fool, not from the wise one. Thus, bhikkhus, the fool is subject to fear, the wise one is free from fear. The fool is subject to calamity, the wise one is free from calamity; the fool is subject to trouble, the wise one is free from trouble.’

Apica pūtimacchasadiso bālo, pūtimacchabandhapattapuṭasadiso hoti tadupasevī, chaḍḍanīyataṃ jigucchanīyatañca pāpuṇāti viññūnaṃ. Vuttañcetaṃ –

Moreover, a fool is like a putrid fish; one who associates with him is like the leaf that wraps a putrid fish. He comes to be discarded and despised by the wise. And this has been said:

“Pūtimacchaṃ kusaggena, yo naro upanayhati;

Kusāpi pūtī vāyanti, evaṃ bālūpasevanā”ti. (jā. 1.15.183; 2.22.1257);

Whatever man wraps a putrid fish with a blade of kusa grass, the kusa grasses also emit a putrid smell; so it is with association with a fool.

Akittipaṇḍito cāpi sakkena devānamindena vare diyyamāne evamāha –

Even the wise Akitti, when offered a boon by Sakka, lord of the devas, spoke thus:

“Bālaṃ [M 0.0107] na passe na suṇe, na ca bālena saṃvase;

Bālenallāpasallāpaṃ, na kare na ca rocaye.

May I not see a fool, may I not hear of one, and may I not associate with a fool. May I not engage in conversation or discussion with a fool, nor find pleasure in it.

“Kinnu te akaraṃ bālo, vada kassapa kāraṇaṃ;

Kena kassapa bālassa, dassanaṃ nābhikaṅkhasi.

What, then, has the fool done to you? Tell the reason, Kassapa. For what reason, Kassapa, do you not desire the sight of a fool?

“Anayaṃ nayati dummedho, adhurāyaṃ niyuñjati;

Dunnayo seyyaso hoti, sammā vutto pakuppati;

Vinayaṃ so na jānāti, sādhu tassa adassana”nti. (jā. 1.13.90-92);

The one of little wisdom leads to what is improper; he engages in a faulty undertaking. Being badly guided, he becomes indolent. When spoken to correctly, he becomes angry. That fool does not know discipline; not seeing him is good.

Evaṃ [V 0.0102][P 0.0128] bhagavā sabbākārena bālūpasevanaṃ garahanto “bālānamasevanā maṅgala”nti vatvā idāni paṇḍitasevanaṃ pasaṃsanto “paṇḍitānañca sevanā maṅgala”nti āha. Tattha paṇḍitā nāma ye keci pāṇātipātāveramaṇiādidasakusalakammapathasamannāgatā sattā, te tīhākārehi jānitabbā. Yathāha “tīṇimāni, bhikkhave, paṇḍitassa paṇḍitalakkhaṇānī”ti (a. ni. 3.3; ma. ni. 3.253) suttaṃ. Apica buddhapaccekabuddhaasītimahāsāvakā aññe ca tathāgatassa sāvakā sunettamahāgovindavidhurasarabhaṅgamahosadhasutasomanimirāja- ayogharakumāraakittipaṇḍitādayo ca paṇḍitāti veditabbā.

Thus, the Blessed One, in every way condemning association with fools, said, “Not associating with fools is a blessing.” Now, praising association with the wise, he said, “And associating with the wise is a blessing.” Herein, the wise are any beings endowed with the ten wholesome courses of action, beginning with abstinence from taking life. They are to be known by three characteristics, as stated in the sutta: “Bhikkhus, these are the three characteristics of a wise one.” Moreover, the wise are to be understood as the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, the eighty great disciples, and other disciples of the Tathāgata, as well as Sunetta, Mahāgovinda, Vidhura, Sarabhaṅga, Mahosadha, Sutasoma, King Nimi, Prince Ayoghara, the wise Akitti, and others.

Te bhaye viya rakkhā andhakāre viya padīpo khuppipāsādidukkhābhibhave viya annapānādippaṭilābho attano vacanakarānaṃ sabbabhayupaddavūpasaggaviddhaṃsanasamatthā honti. Tathā hi tathāgataṃ āgamma asaṅkhyeyyā aparimāṇā devamanussā āsavakkhayaṃ pattā, brahmaloke patiṭṭhitā, devaloke patiṭṭhitā, sugatiloke uppannā, sāriputtatthere cittaṃ pasādetvā catūhi ca paccayehi theraṃ upaṭṭhahitvā asīti kulasahassāni sagge nibbattāni. Tathā mahāmoggallānamahākassapappabhutīsu sabbamahāsāvakesu, sunettassa satthuno sāvakā appekacce brahmaloke uppajjiṃsu, appekacce paranimmitavasavattīnaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ…pe… appekacce gahapatimahāsālānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjiṃsu. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

For those who follow their word, they are like a protector in times of fear, like a lamp in the darkness, and like obtaining food and drink when overcome by the suffering of hunger, thirst, and so on; they are capable of destroying all fear, calamities, and misfortunes. Indeed, on account of the Tathāgata, innumerable and immeasurable devas and humans have attained the destruction of the cankers, have been established in the Brahma-world, established in the deva-world, and have arisen in a happy destination. Having generated confidence in the Elder Sāriputta and having served the Elder with the four requisites, eighty thousand families were reborn in heaven. Likewise, with regard to all the great disciples such as Mahāmoggallāna, Mahākassapa, and others, eighty thousand families who served them were reborn in heaven. Some disciples of the teacher Sunetta arose in the Brahma-world, some arose in the company of the Paranimmitavasavattī devas, and some arose in the company of wealthy householders and brahmins of great wealth. And this has been said:

“Natthi, bhikkhave, paṇḍitato bhayaṃ, natthi paṇḍitato upaddavo, natthi paṇḍitato upasaggo”ti (a. ni. 3.1).

Bhikkhus, from a wise one there is no fear, from a wise one there is no calamity, from a wise one there is no misfortune.

Apica [M 0.0108] tagaramālādigandhasadiso paṇḍito, tagaramālādigandhabandhapaliveṭhanapattasadiso hoti tadupasevī, bhāvanīyataṃ manuññatañca āpajjati viññūnaṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Moreover, the wise one is like a fragrant garland of tagara and other flowers. One who associates with him is like the leaf that wraps the fragrant garland; he comes to be held dear and is pleasing to the discerning. And this has been said:

“Tagarañca [P 0.0129] palāsena, yo naro upanayhati;

Pattāpi surabhī vāyanti, evaṃ dhīrūpasevanā”ti. (itivu. 76; jā. 1.15.184; 2.22.1258);

Whatever man wraps tagara with a palāsa leaf, the leaves also emit a sweet fragrance; so it is with association with the wise.

Akittipaṇḍito cāpi sakkena devānamindena vare diyyamāne evamāha –

Even the wise Akitti, when offered a boon by Sakka, lord of the devas, spoke thus:

“Dhīraṃ [V 0.0103] passe suṇe dhīraṃ, dhīrena saha saṃvase;

Dhīrenallāpasallāpaṃ, taṃ kare tañca rocaye.

May I see the wise, may I hear of the wise, may I associate with the wise. May I engage in conversation and discussion with the wise; may I do that and find pleasure in them.

“Kinnu te akaraṃ dhīro, vada kassapa kāraṇaṃ;

Kena kassapa dhīrassa, dassanaṃ abhikaṅkhasi.

What, then, has the wise one done for you? Tell the reason, Kassapa. For what reason, Kassapa, do you desire the sight of the wise?

“Nayaṃ nayati medhāvī, adhurāyaṃ na yuñjati;

Sunayo seyyaso hoti, sammā vutto na kuppati;

Vinayaṃ so pajānāti, sādhu tena samāgamo”ti. (jā. 1.13.94-96);

The intelligent one leads by the right way; he does not engage in a faulty undertaking. Being well-guided, he becomes progressively more noble. When spoken to correctly, he does not get angry. He understands discipline; association with him is good.

Evaṃ bhagavā sabbākārena paṇḍitasevanaṃ pasaṃsanto “paṇḍitānaṃ sevanā maṅgala”nti vatvā idāni tāya bālānaṃ asevanāya paṇḍitānaṃ sevanāya ca anupubbena pūjaneyyabhāvaṃ upagatānaṃ pūjaṃ pasaṃsanto “pūjā ca pūjaneyyānaṃ maṅgala”nti āha. Tattha pūjaneyyā nāma sabbadosavirahitattā sabbaguṇasamannāgatattā ca buddhā bhagavanto, tato pacchā paccekabuddhā, ariyasāvakā ca. Tesañhi pūjā appakāpi dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya hoti, sumanamālākāramallikādayo cettha nidassanaṃ.

Thus, the Blessed One, in every way praising association with the wise, said, “Association with the wise is a blessing.” Now, praising the honoring of those who have, through such non-association with fools and association with the wise, successively attained a state of being worthy of honor, he said, “And honoring those worthy of honor is a blessing.” Herein, those worthy of honor are the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, on account of being free from all faults and endowed with all virtues; and after them, the Paccekabuddhas and the noble disciples. For a pūjā to them, even if small, is for one’s long-term welfare and happiness. Herein, Sumana the garland-maker, Mallikā, and others are an example.

Tatthekaṃ nidassanamattaṃ bhaṇāma – bhagavā hi ekadivasaṃ pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya rājagahaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Atha kho sumanamālākāro rañño māgadhassa seniyassa bimbisārassa pupphāni gahetvā gacchanto addasa bhagavantaṃ nagaradvāramanuppattaṃ pāsādikaṃ pasādanīyaṃ dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇāsītānubyañjanappaṭimaṇḍitaṃ buddhasiriyā jalantaṃ, disvānassa [P 0.0130] etadahosi “rājā pupphāni gahetvā sataṃ vā sahassaṃ vā dadeyya[M 0.0109], tañca idhalokamattameva sukhaṃ bhaveyya, bhagavato pana pūjā appameyyaasaṅkhyeyyaphalā dīgharattaṃ hitasukhāvahā hoti, handāhaṃ imehi pupphehi bhagavantaṃ pūjemī”ti pasannacitto ekaṃ pupphamuṭṭhiṃ gahetvā bhagavato paṭimukhaṃ khipi, pupphāni ākāsena gantvā bhagavato upari mālāvitānaṃ hutvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Mālākāro tamānubhāvaṃ disvā pasannataracitto puna ekaṃ pupphamuṭṭhiṃ khipi, tānipi gantvā mālākañcuko hutvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Evaṃ aṭṭha pupphamuṭṭhiyo khipi, tāni gantvā pupphakūṭāgāraṃ hutvā aṭṭhaṃsu.

Herein, we shall relate one example: One day, in the morning, the Blessed One, having dressed, took his bowl and robe and entered Rājagaha for alms. Then Sumana the garland-maker, taking flowers for King Bimbisāra of Magadha, who possessed a great army, was going along when he saw the Blessed One who had reached the city gate, serene, inspiring, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor characteristics, blazing with the glory of a Buddha. Having seen him, this thought arose in him: “The king, taking these flowers, might give a hundred or a thousand coins, and that would be happiness only for this world. But an offering to the Blessed One has immeasurable, incalculable fruit, and brings welfare and happiness for a long time. Come now, I shall offer these flowers to the Blessed One!” With a mind of faith, he took one handful of flowers and threw it towards the Blessed One. The flowers, going through the sky, became a floral canopy above the Blessed One and remained there. The garland-maker, seeing that power, with an even more faithful mind, again threw another handful of flowers. Those too, going, became a floral tunic and remained there. In this way, he threw eight handfuls of flowers. They, going, became a gabled pavilion of flowers and remained there.

Bhagavā antokūṭāgāre ahosi, mahājanakāyo sannipati. Bhagavā mālākāraṃ passanto sitaṃ [V 0.0104] pātvākāsi. Ānandatthero “na buddhā ahetū apaccayā sitaṃ pātukarontī”ti sitakāraṇaṃ pucchi. Bhagavā āha “eso, ānanda, mālākāro imissā pūjāya ānubhāvena satasahassakappe devesu ca manussesu ca saṃsaritvā pariyosāne sumanissaro nāma paccekabuddho bhavissatī”ti. Vacanapariyosāne dhammadesanatthaṃ imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi –

The Blessed One was inside the gabled pavilion of flowers, and a great crowd gathered. Seeing the garland-maker, the Blessed One revealed a smile. Venerable Ānanda, knowing that Buddhas do not reveal a smile without a cause or reason, asked the cause of the smile. The Blessed One said, 'Ānanda, this garland-maker, through the power of this offering, having wandered among gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, will finally become a Paccekabuddha named Sumanissara.' At the end of his words, for the purpose of a Dhamma talk, he spoke this verse:

“Tañca kammaṃ kataṃ sādhu, yaṃ katvā nānutappati;

Yassa patīto sumano, vipākaṃ paṭisevatī”ti. (dha. pa. 68);

“That deed is well done which, having done it, one does not regret, and whose result one experiences pleased and joyful.”

Gāthāvasāne caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi. Evaṃ appakāpi tesaṃ pūjā dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya hotīti veditabbā. Sā ca āmisapūjāva, ko pana vādo paṭipattipūjāya? Yato ye kulaputtā saraṇagamanasikkhāpadappaṭiggahaṇena uposathaṅgasamādānena catupārisuddhisīlādīhi ca attano guṇehi bhagavantaṃ pūjenti, ko tesaṃ pūjāphalaṃ vaṇṇayissati? Te hi tathāgataṃ paramāya pūjāya pūjentīti vuttā. Yathāha –

At the end of the verse, the comprehension of the Dhamma arose for eighty-four thousand beings. Thus it should be known that even a small offering made to them brings welfare and happiness for a long time. And that was only an offering of material things; what then is to be said of the offering of practice? For when sons of good family honor the Blessed One with their own virtues—by accepting the refuges and training rules, by undertaking the Uposatha observances, by the fourfold purity of virtue, and so on—who can describe the fruit of their offering? For they are said to honor the Tathāgata with the supreme offering. As it was said:

“Yo kho, ānanda, bhikkhu vā bhikkhunī vā upāsako vā upāsikā vā dhammānudhammappaṭipanno viharati sāmīcippaṭipanno anudhammacārī, so tathāgataṃ sakkaroti garuṃ karoti māneti [P 0.0131] pūjeti apaciyati paramāya pūjāyā”ti (dī. ni. 2.199).

“Whoever, Ānanda, whether a bhikkhu or a bhikkhunī, a male lay follower or a female lay follower, lives practicing in conformity with the Dhamma, practicing correctly, living in accordance with the Dhamma, that person honors, respects, esteems, venerates, and pays homage to the Tathāgata with the supreme offering.”

Etenānusārena paccekabuddhaariyasāvakānampi pūjāya hitasukhāvahatā veditabbā.

In accordance with this principle, it should be understood that offering to Paccekabuddhas and noble disciples also brings welfare and happiness.

Apica [M 0.0110] gahaṭṭhānaṃ kaniṭṭhassa jeṭṭho bhātāpi bhaginīpi pūjaneyyā, puttassa mātāpitaro, kulavadhūnaṃ sāmikasassusasurāti evamettha pūjaneyyā veditabbā. Etesampi hi pūjā kusaladhammasaṅkhātattā āyuādivuḍḍhihetuttā ca maṅgalameva. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Furthermore, among householders, for a younger sibling, an elder brother or sister is worthy of honor; for a child, the parents; and for daughters-in-law, the husband, mother-in-law, and father-in-law. Thus, these should be understood as worthy of honor. For honoring these persons, being reckoned as a wholesome principle and a cause for the increase of longevity and so forth, is indeed an auspicious thing. For this has been said:

“Te matteyyā bhavissanti petteyyā sāmaññā brahmaññā kule jeṭṭhāpacāyino, idaṃ kusalaṃ dhammaṃ samādāya vattissanti, te tesaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ samādānahetu āyunāpi vaḍḍhissanti, vaṇṇenapi vaḍḍhissantī”tiādi (dī. ni. 3.105).

“They will be devoted to their mothers, devoted to their fathers, respectful to ascetics, respectful to brahmins, and will honor the elders in the family. Having undertaken this wholesome Dhamma, they will live accordingly. Because of undertaking these wholesome Dhammas, they will increase in lifespan and also in beauty,” and so forth.

Idāni yasmā “yaṃ yattha maṅgalaṃ. Vavatthapetvā taṃ tassa, maṅgalattaṃ vibhāvaye”ti iti mātikā [V 0.0105] nikkhittā, tasmā idaṃ vuccati – evametissā gāthāya bālānaṃ asevanā, paṇḍitānaṃ sevanā, pūjaneyyānañca pūjāti tīṇi maṅgalāni vuttāni. Tattha bālānaṃ asevanā bālasevanapaccayabhayādiparittāṇena ubhayalokatthahetuttā, paṇḍitānaṃ sevanā pūjaneyyānaṃ pūjā ca tāsaṃ phalavibhūtivaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva nibbānasugatihetuttā maṅgalanti veditabbā. Ito paraṃ tu mātikaṃ adassetvā eva yaṃ yattha maṅgalaṃ, taṃ vavatthapetvā tassa maṅgalattaṃ vibhāvayissāmāti.

Now, since the theme has been set forth, “Whatever is auspicious in any place, having determined that, one should explain its auspiciousness,” therefore this is said: Thus, in this verse, three auspicious things are mentioned—not associating with fools, associating with the wise, and honoring those worthy of honor. Here, not associating with fools is to be known as auspicious because it is the cause of benefit in both worlds by protecting one from the dangers and so forth arising from association with fools. Associating with the wise and honoring those worthy of honor are also to be known as auspicious, as explained in the description of the manifestation of their fruits, because they are causes for a good destination and Nibbāna according to the method already stated. From now on, without setting forth the theme, we will determine whatever is auspicious in any place and explain its auspiciousness.

Niṭṭhitā asevanā ca bālānanti imissā gāthāya atthavaṇṇanā.

Here ends the explanation of the meaning of the verse beginning, ‘Asevanā ca bālānaṃ’.

Patirūpadesavāsocātigāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Verse ‘Dwelling in a Suitable Place’

4. Evaṃ bhagavā “brūhi maṅgalamuttama”nti ekaṃ ajjhesitopi appaṃ yācito bahudāyako uḷārapuriso viya ekāya [P 0.0132] gāthāya tīṇi maṅgalāni vatvā tato uttaripi devatānaṃ sotukāmatāya maṅgalānamatthitāya yesaṃ yesaṃ yaṃ yaṃ anukulaṃ, te te satte tattha tattha maṅgale niyojetukāmatāya ca “patirūpadesavāso cā”tiādīhi gāthāhi punapi anekāni maṅgalāni vattumāraddho. Tattha paṭhamagāthāya tāva patirūpoti anucchaviko. Desoti gāmopi nigamopi nagarampi janapadopi yo koci sattānaṃ nivāso okāso. Vāsoti tattha [M 0.0111] nivāso. Pubbeti purā atītāsu jātīsu. Katapuññatāti upacitakusalatā. Attāti cittaṃ vuccati sakalo vā attabhāvo, sammāpaṇidhīti tassa attano sammā paṇidhānaṃ niyuñjanaṃ, ṭhapananti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti. Ayamettha padavaṇṇanā.

4. Thus, the Blessed One, though requested for one blessing with “Declare the highest blessing,” like a noble man who gives much when asked for little, spoke three blessings in one verse. Then, due to the deities' desire to listen, due to the existence of blessings, and due to the desire to engage those beings in those respective blessings which are suitable for them, He began again to declare many more blessings with verses such as ‘Dwelling in a suitable place,’ and so forth. Therein, in the first verse, firstly: ‘suitable’ means appropriate. ‘Place’ refers to any dwelling or location for beings—be it a village, market town, city, or country. ‘Dwelling’ means living there. ‘Formerly’ means previously, in past lives. ‘Merit made in the past’ means the accumulation of wholesome deeds. ‘Self’ is said to be the mind or the entire personal existence; ‘rightly directing the self’ means the proper directing, engaging, and establishing of that self. This is what is meant. The rest is as explained previously. This is the explanation of the words in this context.

Atthavaṇṇanā pana evaṃ veditabbā – patirūpadesavāso nāma yattha catasso parisā vicaranti, dānādīni puññakiriyavatthūni vattanti, navaṅgaṃ satthu sāsanaṃ dibbati, tattha nivāso sattānaṃ puññakiriyāya paccayattā maṅgalanti vuccati. Sīhaḷadīpapaviṭṭhakevaṭṭādayo cettha nidassanaṃ.

The explanation of the meaning, however, should be understood thus: ‘dwelling in a suitable place’ is where the four assemblies move about, where the grounds for meritorious action such as giving occur, and where the Teacher’s nine-fold dispensation shines. Dwelling there is called a blessing because it is a condition for beings' performance of meritorious action. The fishermen and others who entered the island of Sīhaḷa are an example here.

Aparo nayo – patirūpadesavāso nāma bhagavato bodhimaṇḍappadeso dhammacakkavattitappadeso dvādasayojanāya parisāya majjhe sabbatitthiyamataṃ bhinditvā yamakapāṭihāriyadassitakaṇḍamba rukkhamūlappadeso devorohaṇappadeso, yo vā panaññopi sāvatthirājagahādi [V 0.0106] buddhādhivāsappadeso, tattha nivāso sattānaṃ chaanuttariyappaṭilābhapaccayato maṅgalanti vuccati.

Another method: Dwelling in a suitable place refers to the Bodhimaṇḍa area of the Blessed One; the place where the Wheel of Dhamma was set in motion; the place at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba mango tree where the Twin Miracle was displayed after shattering all heretical views in the midst of an assembly of twelve yojanas; the place of the descent from the deva realm; or any other place such as Sāvatthī, Rājagaha, and so forth, where the Buddha and others resided. Dwelling there is called a blessing because it is a condition for the attainment of the six supreme things by beings.

Aparo nayo (mahāva. 259) – puratthimāya disāya gajaṅgalaṃ nāma nigamo, tassa parena mahāsālā, tato paraṃ paccantimā janapadā, orato majjhe. Dakkhiṇapuratthimāya disāya sallavatī nāma nadī, tato paraṃ paccantimā janapadā, orato majjhe. Dakkhiṇāya disāya [P 0.0133] setakaṇṇikaṃ nāma nigamo, tato paraṃ paccantimā janapadā, orato majjhe. Pacchimāya disāya thūṇaṃ nāma brāhmaṇagāmo, tato paraṃ paccantimā janapadā, orato majjhe. Uttarāya disāya usīraddhajo nāma pabbato, tato paraṃ paccantimā janapadā, orato majjhe. Ayaṃ majjhimadeso āyāmena tīṇi yojanasatāni, vitthārena aḍḍhateyyāni, parikkhepena nava yojanasatāni honti. Eso patirūpadeso nāma.

Another method: To the east is a market-town named Gajaṅgala; beyond that are the great Sāla trees, and beyond that are the border regions, while on this side is the middle country. To the southeast is a river named Sallavatī; beyond that are the border regions, while on this side is the middle country. To the south is a market-town named Setakaṇṇika; beyond that are the border regions, while on this side is the middle country. To the west is a brahmin village named Thūṇa; beyond that are the border regions, while on this side is the middle country. To the north is a mountain named Usīraddhaja; beyond that are the border regions, while on this side is the middle country. This middle country is three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty in width, and nine hundred yojanas in circumference. This is called the suitable place.

Ettha catunnaṃ mahādīpānaṃ dvisahassānaṃ parittadīpānañca issariyādhipaccakārakā cakkavattī uppajjanti, ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ kappasatasahassañca pāramiyo pūretvā sāriputtamoggallānādayo mahāsāvakā uppajjanti, dve asaṅkhyeyyāni kappasatasahassañca pāramiyo pūretvā paccekabuddhā, cattāri aṭṭha soḷasa vā asaṅkhyeyyāni kappasatasahassañca pāramiyo pūretvā [M 0.0112] sammāsambuddhā uppajjanti. Tattha sattā cakkavattirañño ovādaṃ gahetvā pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāya saggaparāyaṇā honti. Tathā paccekabuddhānaṃ ovāde patiṭṭhāya, sammāsambuddhānaṃ pana buddhasāvakānaṃ ovāde patiṭṭhāya saggaparāyaṇā nibbānaparāyaṇā ca honti. Tasmā tattha vāso imāsaṃ sampattīnaṃ paccayato maṅgalanti vuccati.

Here, wheel-turning monarchs, who exercise sovereignty and dominion over the four great continents and the two thousand surrounding small islands, arise. After fulfilling the perfections for one incalculable and one hundred thousand eons, great disciples such as Sāriputta and Moggallāna arise. After fulfilling the perfections for two incalculables and one hundred thousand eons, Paccekabuddhas arise. After fulfilling the perfections for four, eight, or sixteen incalculables and one hundred thousand eons, Sammāsambuddhas arise. There, beings, having accepted the exhortation of a wheel-turning monarch and become established in the five precepts, are bound for heaven. Similarly, being established in the exhortation of Paccekabuddhas, they are bound for heaven. But being established in the exhortation of the Sammāsambuddhas and their disciples, they are bound for heaven and bound for Nibbāna. Therefore, dwelling there is called a blessing because it is a condition for these accomplishments.

Pubbe katapuññatā nāma atītajātiyaṃ buddhapaccekabuddhakhīṇāsave ārabbha upacitakusalatā, sāpi maṅgalaṃ. Kasmā? Buddhapaccekabuddhasammukhato dassetvā buddhānaṃ buddhasāvakānaṃ vā sammukhā sutāya catuppadikāyapi gāthāya pariyosāne arahattaṃ pāpetīti katvā. Yo ca manusso pubbe katādhikāro ussannakusalamūlo hoti, so teneva kusalamūlena vipassanaṃ uppādetvā āsavakkhayaṃ pāpuṇāti yathā rājā mahākappino aggamahesī ca.
