Tena vuttaṃ “pubbe ca katapuññatā maṅgala”nti.

‘Merit made in the past’ refers to the accumulation of wholesome deeds in a past life with respect to Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahants; that too is a blessing. Why? Because having seen Buddhas or Paccekabuddhas face to face, one is led to attain Arahantship at the conclusion of even a four-lined verse heard in the presence of Buddhas or their disciples. And a person who has made a resolution in the past and has abundant wholesome roots, by that very wholesome root, attains the destruction of the taints—just as King Mahākappina and his chief queen did. Therefore it is said, ‘And merit made in the past is a blessing.’

Attasammāpaṇidhi [P 0.0134] nāma idhekacco attānaṃ dussīlaṃ sīle patiṭṭhāpeti, assaddhaṃ saddhāsampadāya patiṭṭhāpeti, macchariṃ cāgasampadāya patiṭṭhāpeti. Ayaṃ vuccati “attasammāpaṇidhī”ti[V 0.0107], eso ca maṅgalaṃ. Kasmā? Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaverappahānavividhānisaṃsādhigamahetutoti.

‘Rightly directing the self’ means that, here, a certain person who is immoral establishes themselves in morality; being faithless, establishes themselves in the accomplishment of faith; being stingy, establishes themselves in the accomplishment of generosity. This is called ‘rightly directing the self,’ and this is a blessing. Why? Because it is a cause for abandoning enmity pertaining to this life and the next, and for attaining various benefits.

Evaṃ imissāpi gāthāya patirūpadesavāso ca, pubbe ca katapuññatā, attasammāpaṇidhī cāti tīṇiyeva maṅgalāni vuttāni. Maṅgalattañca nesaṃ tattha tattha vibhāvitamevāti.

Thus, in this verse as well, just three blessings have been spoken of: dwelling in a suitable place, merit made in the past, and rightly directing the self. And their nature as blessings has already been explained in their respective places.

Niṭṭhitā patirūpadesavāso cāti imissā gāthāya atthavaṇṇanā.

Here ends the explanation of the meaning of the verse beginning ‘Dwelling in a suitable place’.

Bāhusaccañcātigāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Verse Beginning 'Bāhusaccañca'

5. Idāni bāhusaccañcāti ettha bāhusaccanti bahussutabhāvo. Sippanti yaṃ kiñci hatthakosallaṃ. Vinayoti kāyavācācittavinayanaṃ. Susikkhitoti suṭṭhu sikkhito. Subhāsitāti suṭṭhu bhāsitā. Yāti aniyataniddeso. Vācāti girā byappatho. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti. Ayamettha padavaṇṇanā.

Now, in the verse beginning with 'bāhusaccañca', 'bāhusacca' is the state of being one with much learning. 'Sippa' is any kind of manual skill. 'Vinaya' is the means of disciplining the body, speech, and mind. 'Susikkhita' is well-trained. 'Subhāsitā' is well-spoken. The word 'yā' is an indefinite reference. 'Vācā' is utterance, a designation. The rest is in the manner already stated. This is the explanation of the words here.

Atthavaṇṇanā [M 0.0113] pana evaṃ veditabbā – bāhusaccaṃ nāma yaṃ taṃ “sutadharo hoti sutasannicayo”ti (ma. ni. 1.339; a. ni. 4.22) ca “idhekaccassa bahukaṃ sutaṃ hoti, suttaṃ geyyaṃ veyyākaraṇa”nti ca (a. ni. 4.6) evamādinā nayena satthusāsanadharattaṃ vaṇṇitaṃ, taṃ akusalappahānakusalādhigamahetuto anupubbena paramatthasaccasacchikiriyāhetuto ca maṅgalanti vuccati. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

5. The explanation of the meaning, however, should be known thus: That which is called 'extensive learning' is the upholding of the Teacher's Dispensation, described by way of such passages as, 'one is a bearer of what has been heard, a repository of what has been heard,' and, 'Here, someone has heard much: the discourses, the mixed prose and verse, the expositions,' and so on. That extensive learning is called a blessing because it is a cause for abandoning the unwholesome and attaining the wholesome, and because it is a cause for the gradual realization of the ultimate truth. For this was stated by the Blessed One:

“Sutavā ca kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako akusalaṃ pajahati, kusalaṃ bhāveti, sāvajjaṃ pajahati, anavajjaṃ bhāveti, suddhamattānaṃ pariharatī”ti (a. ni. 7.67).

“Bhikkhus, a learned noble disciple, indeed, abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; abandons the blameworthy and develops the blameless; and maintains themselves in purity.”

Aparampi vuttaṃ –

Furthermore, it was said:

“Dhatānaṃ dhammānaṃ atthamupaparikkhati, atthaṃ upaparikkhato dhammā nijjhānaṃ khamanti, dhammanijjhānakkhantiyā sati chando jāyati, chandajāto ussahati, ussahanto tulayati[V 0.0108], tulayanto padahati padahanto kāyena ceva paramatthasaccaṃ sacchikaroti, paññāya ca ativijjha [P 0.0135] passatī”ti (ma. ni. 2.432).

He investigates the meaning of the teachings he has retained. For one who investigates the meaning, the teachings endure contemplation. When the teachings endure contemplation, zeal is born. With zeal born, he makes an effort. Making an effort, he considers. Considering, he strives resolutely. Striving resolutely, he realizes the ultimate truth with the body and sees it by penetrating it with wisdom.

Apica agārikabāhusaccampi yaṃ anavajjaṃ, taṃ ubhayalokahitasukhāvahanato maṅgalanti veditabbaṃ.

Moreover, even the extensive learning of a householder, if it is blameless, should be known as a blessing because it brings benefit and happiness in both worlds.

Sippaṃ nāma agārikasippañca anagārikasippañca. Tattha agārikasippaṃ nāma yaṃ parūparodhavirahitaṃ akusalavivajjitaṃ maṇikārasuvaṇṇakārakammādikaṃ, taṃ idhalokatthāvahanato maṅgalaṃ. Anagārikasippaṃ nāma cīvaravicāraṇasibbanādisamaṇaparikkhārābhisaṅkharaṇaṃ, yaṃ taṃ “idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yāni tāni sabrahmacārīnaṃ uccāvacāni kiṃ karaṇīyāni, tattha dakkho hotī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 3.345; 360; a. ni. 10.17) nayena tattha tattha saṃvaṇṇitaṃ, yaṃ “nāthakaro dhammo”ti ca vuttaṃ, taṃ attano ca paresañca ubhayalokahitasukhāvahanato maṅgalanti veditabbaṃ.

'Skill' refers to both the skill of a householder and the skill of one who has gone forth. Therein, the skill of a householder is that which is free from oppressing others and devoid of the unwholesome, such as the work of gem-cutters, goldsmiths, and so on. That blameless skill is a blessing because it brings benefit in this world. The skill of one who has gone forth is the preparation of a recluse's requisites, such as the making and sewing of robes, which is praised in various places by way of the passage beginning, 'Here, O monks, a monk is skilled in the various duties to be done for his fellow monks.' That skill, which is also called 'a doctrine that creates a refuge,' should be known as a blessing because it brings benefit and happiness in both worlds to oneself and to others.

Vinayo nāma agārikavinayo ca anagārikavinayo ca. Tattha agārikavinayo nāma dasaakusalakammapathaviramaṇaṃ, so tattha susikkhito asaṃkilesāpajjanena ācāraguṇavavatthānena ca ubhayalokahitasukhāvahanato [M 0.0114] maṅgalaṃ. Anagārikavinayo nāma sattāpattikkhandhaanāpajjanaṃ, sopi vuttanayeneva susikkhito, catupārisuddhisīlaṃ vā anagārikavinayo, so yathā tattha patiṭṭhāya arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, evaṃ sikkhanena susikkhito lokiyalokuttarasukhādhigamahetuto maṅgalanti veditabbo.

'Discipline' refers to both the discipline of a householder and the discipline of one who has gone forth. Therein, the discipline of a householder is abstinence from the ten unwholesome courses of action. When one is well-trained in that, it is a blessing because it brings benefit and happiness in both worlds by not leading to defilement and by establishing the virtue of good conduct. The discipline of one who has gone forth is not falling into the seven classes of offenses; when one is well-trained in this in the manner already stated, it is a blessing. Alternatively, the discipline of one who has gone forth is the fourfold purification morality. When one is well-trained by training in such a way that, established in that discipline, one attains Arahantship, it should be known as a blessing because it is a cause for the attainment of worldly and supramundane happiness.

Subhāsitā vācā nāma musāvādādidosavirahitā. Yathāha “catūhi, bhikkhave, aṅgehi samannāgato vācā subhāsitā hotī”ti (su. ni. subhāsitasuttaṃ). Asamphappalāpā vācā eva vā subhāsitā. Yathāha –

What is called 'well-spoken speech' is speech free from faults such as false speech. As it is said: 'O monks, speech endowed with four factors is well-spoken.' Alternatively, speech that is not frivolous talk is itself well-spoken speech. As it is said:

“Subhāsitaṃ uttamamāhu santo,

Dhammaṃ bhaṇe nādhammaṃ taṃ dutiyaṃ;

Piyaṃ bhaṇe nāppiyaṃ taṃ tatiyaṃ,

Saccaṃ bhaṇe nālikaṃ taṃ catuttha”nti. (su. ni. 452);

The virtuous say well-spoken speech is supreme; one should speak Dhamma, not non-Dhamma—that is the second; one should speak what is endearing, not what is unendearing—that is the third; one should speak what is true, not what is false—that is the fourth.

Ayampi [V 0.0109][P 0.0136] ubhayalokahitasukhāvahanato maṅgalanti veditabbā. Yasmā ca ayaṃ vinayapariyāpannā eva, tasmā vinayaggahaṇena etaṃ asaṅgaṇhitvā vinayo saṅgahetabbo. Atha vā kiṃ iminā parissamena paresaṃ dhammadesanādivācā idha subhāsitā vācāti veditabbā. Sā hi yathā patirūpadesavāso, evaṃ sattānaṃ ubhayalokahitasukhanibbānādhigamapaccayato maṅgalanti vuccati. Āha ca –

This too should be known as a blessing because it brings benefit and happiness in both worlds. And since this is already included in 'discipline', it is encompassed by the taking up of 'discipline' without being counted separately. Alternatively, what is the need for this exertion? Here, speech such as teaching the Dhamma to others should be known as 'well-spoken speech'. For just as dwelling in a suitable place is a blessing, so too is this called a blessing because it is a condition for beings to attain the benefit, happiness, and Nibbāna of both worlds. And it is said:

“Yaṃ buddho bhāsati vācaṃ, khemaṃ nibbānapattiyā;

Dukkhassantakiriyāya, sā ve vācānamuttamā”ti. (su. ni. 456);

Whatever speech the Buddha speaks for the secure attainment of Nibbāna, for making an end of suffering—that, indeed, is the supreme of all speech.

Evaṃ imissā gāthāya bāhusaccaṃ, sippaṃ, vinayo susikkhito, subhāsitā vācāti cattāri maṅgalāni vuttāni. Maṅgalattañca nesaṃ tattha tattha vibhāvitamevāti.

Thus, in this verse, four blessings have been stated: extensive learning, skill, discipline well-mastered, and well-spoken speech. And their nature as blessings has been made clear in each respective case.

Niṭṭhitā bāhusaccañcāti imissā gāthāya atthavaṇṇanā.

The explanation of the meaning of this verse beginning with 'Bāhusaccañca' is concluded.

Mātāpituupaṭṭhānantigāthāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Verse on Supporting Mother and Father.

6. Idāni [M 0.0115] mātāpituupaṭṭhānanti ettha mātu ca pitu cāti mātāpitu. Upaṭṭhānanti upaṭṭhahanaṃ. Puttānañca dārānañcāti puttadārassa saṅgaṇhanaṃ saṅgaho. Na ākulā anākulā. Kammāni eva kammantā. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti ayaṃ padavaṇṇanā.

6. Now, in this phrase mātāpituupaṭṭhānaṃ (supporting mother and father): mātu ca pitu ca becomes mātāpitu (mother and father). Upaṭṭhānaṃ means supporting. Puttānañca dārānañca becomes puttadārassa, and saṅgaṇhanaṃ is saṅgaho (supporting). Na ākulā means anākulā (unobstructed). Kammāni eva are kammantā (occupations). The remainder is just as has been explained. This is the explanation of the words.

Atthavaṇṇanā pana evaṃ veditabbā – mātā nāma janikā vuccati, tathā pitā. Upaṭṭhānaṃ nāma pādadhovanasambāhanucchādananhāpanehi catupaccayasampadānena ca upakārakaraṇaṃ. Tattha yasmā mātāpitaro bahūpakārā puttānaṃ atthakāmā anukampakā, ye puttake bahi kīḷitvā paṃsumakkhitasarīrake āgate disvā paṃsuṃ puñchitvā matthakaṃ upasiṅghāyantā paricumbantā ca sinehaṃ uppādenti, vassasatampi mātāpitaro sīsena pariharantā puttā tesaṃ patikāraṃ kātuṃ asamatthā. Yasmā ca te āpādakā posakā imassa lokassa dassetāro, brahmasammatā pubbācariyasammatā, tasmā tesaṃ [P 0.0137] upaṭṭhānaṃ idha pasaṃsaṃ, pecca saggasukhañca āvahati. Tena maṅgalanti vuccati. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

The explanation of the meaning, however, should be understood thus: 'Mother' is called she who gives birth; likewise, 'father' is he who gives birth. 'Supporting' is the rendering of assistance by washing the feet, massaging, anointing, bathing, and by well providing the four requisites. In this regard, because parents are of great help to their children, wish for their welfare, and are compassionate; because when they see their young children, whose bodies are smeared with dust, returning after playing outside, they wipe away the dust, sniff their heads, and kiss them, thereby generating affection; even if children, carrying their parents on their heads for a hundred years, were to serve them, they would be unable to repay the favor. And because they are the originators, the nurturers, the showers of this world, esteemed as Brahmā, and esteemed as the first teachers, therefore supporting them brings praise in this life and the happiness of heaven in the next. For that reason, it is called a blessing. And this was stated by the Blessed One:

“Brahmāti [V 0.0110] mātāpitaro, pubbācariyāti vuccare;

Āhuneyyā ca puttānaṃ, pajāya anukampakā.

'Parents are called Brahmā, and they are called the first teachers; they are worthy of offerings from their children, being compassionate to their offspring.'

“Tasmā hi ne namasseyya, sakkareyya ca paṇḍito;

Annena atha pānena, vatthena sayanena ca;

Ucchādanena nhāpanena, pādānaṃ dhovanena ca.

'Therefore, a wise person should pay homage to them and should also respect them with food and then with drink, with clothing and with lodging, with anointing, with bathing, and with washing of the feet.'

“Tāya naṃ pāricariyāya, mātāpitūsu paṇḍitā;

Idheva naṃ pasaṃsanti, pecca sagge pamodatī”ti. (itivu. 106; jā. 2.20.181-183);

'For that service to mother and father, the wise praise him right here in this life; and after death, he rejoices in heaven.'

Aparo nayo – upaṭṭhānaṃ nāma bharaṇakiccakaraṇakulavaṃsaṭṭhapanādipañcavidhaṃ, taṃ pāpanivāraṇādipañcavidhadiṭṭhadhammikahitasukhahetuto maṅgalanti veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Another method: 'Supporting' is of five kinds, beginning with repaying their support, performing their duties, and establishing the family lineage. That support should be known as a blessing because it is a cause for the fivefold welfare and happiness in this present life, which begins with [the parents'] restraining [the child] from evil. For this was stated by the Blessed One:

“‘Pañcahi kho, gahapatiputta, ṭhānehi puttena puratthimā disā mātāpitaro paccupaṭṭhātabbā bhato ne bharissāmi, kiccaṃ nesaṃ karissāmi[M 0.0116], kulavaṃsaṃ ṭhapessāmi, dāyajjaṃ paṭipajjissāmi, atha vā pana petānaṃ kālakatānaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ anuppadassāmī’ti. Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, pañcahi ṭhānehi puttena puratthimā disā mātāpitaro paccupaṭṭhitā pañcahi ṭhānehi puttaṃ anukampanti, pāpā nivārenti, kalyāṇe nivesenti, sippaṃ sikkhāpenti, patirūpena dārena saṃyojenti, samaye dāyajjaṃ niyyādentī”ti (dī. ni. 3.267).

Householder's son, a son should support his parents, the eastern direction, in five ways: 'Having been supported by them, I will support them. I will do their duties. I will establish the family lineage. I will manage the inheritance. Furthermore, when they have passed away, I will give an offering on their behalf.' Householder's son, when parents are supported by their son in these five ways, they show compassion to their son in five ways: they restrain him from evil, establish him in the good, have him learn a skill, join him with a suitable wife, and at the proper time, hand over the inheritance.

Apica yo mātāpitaro tīsu vatthūsu [P 0.0138] pasāduppādanena, sīlasamādāpanena, pabbajjāya vā upaṭṭhahati, ayaṃ mātāpituupaṭṭhākānaṃ aggo. Tassa taṃ mātāpituupaṭṭhānaṃ mātāpitūhi katassa upakārassa paccupakārabhūtaṃ anekesaṃ diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ samparāyikānañca atthānaṃ padaṭṭhānato maṅgalanti vuccati.

Furthermore, a son who supports his parents by causing them to have faith in the Three Jewels, by causing them to undertake the precepts, or by [supporting their] ordination—this is the foremost among those who support their parents. That support of parents, being a repayment for the help rendered by the parents, is called a blessing because it is the foundation for many benefits both in this present life and in the next.

Puttadārassāti ettha attato jātā puttāpi dhītaropi puttāicceva saṅkhyaṃ gacchanti. Dārāti vīsatiyā bhariyānaṃ yā kāci bhariyā. Puttā ca dārā ca puttadāraṃ, tassa puttadārassa. Saṅgahoti sammānanādīhi upakārakaraṇaṃ. Taṃ susaṃvihitakammantatādidiṭṭhadhammikahitasukhahetuto [V 0.0111] maṅgalanti veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā – “pacchimā disā puttadārā veditabbā”ti ettha uddiṭṭhaṃ puttadāraṃ bhariyāsaddena saṅgaṇhitvā “pañcahi kho, gahapatiputta, ṭhānehi sāmikena pacchimā disā bhariyā paccupaṭṭhātabbā sammānanāya, anavamānanāya, anati cariyāya, issariyavossaggena, alaṅkārānuppadānena. Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, pañcahi ṭhānehi sāmikena pacchimā disā bhariyā paccupaṭṭhitā pañcahi ṭhānehi sāmikaṃ anukampati, susaṃvihitakammantā ca hoti, saṅgahitaparijanā ca, anaticārinī ca, sambhatañca anurakkhati dakkhā ca hoti analasā sabbakiccesū”ti (dī. ni. 3.269).

In the phrase 'puttadārassa,' here, both sons born of oneself and daughters are included in the count of 'puttā' (children). 'Dārā' refers to any one of the twenty kinds of wives. Sons and wives together are 'puttadāra,' and 'puttadārassa' means 'of the sons and wives.' 'Saṅgaho' means rendering assistance through respect and other such acts. This should be understood as a blessing because it is a cause for welfare and happiness in this present life, such as having well-managed work. For this was stated by the Blessed One: 'Wife and children should be known as the western direction.' Here, 'puttadāra' having been specified, and including 'wife' in the term, it is stated: 'Householder's son, a husband should support his wife, the western direction, in five ways: by showing respect, by not showing disrespect, by not being unfaithful, by handing over authority, and by providing adornments. Householder's son, when a wife is thus supported in these five ways by her husband, she shows compassion to her husband in five ways: her duties are well-managed, her retinue is supported, she is not unfaithful, she guards the accumulated wealth, and she is skilled and diligent in all duties.'

Ayaṃ vā aparo nayo – saṅgahoti dhammikāhi dānapiyavācātthacariyāhi saṅgaṇhanaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – uposathadivasesu paribbayadānaṃ, nakkhattadivasesu nakkhattadassāpanaṃ, maṅgaladivasesu maṅgalakaraṇaṃ, diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikesu atthesu ovādānusāsananti. Taṃ vuttanayeneva diṭṭhadhammikahitahetuto [P 0.0139] samparāyikahitahetuto devatāhipi namassanīyabhāvahetuto ca maṅgalanti veditabbaṃ. Yathāha sakko devānamindo –

Or this is another method: 'Supporting' means gathering together through righteous giving, pleasant speech, and beneficial conduct. For example: giving provisions on Uposatha days, showing them the festivities on festival days, performing auspicious rites on auspicious days, and giving advice and instruction on matters pertaining to benefits in this life and the next. This should be known as a blessing for the reasons already stated: because it is a cause for benefit in this life, a cause for benefit in the next life, and a cause for being worthy of reverence even by the devas. As Sakka, the lord of the devas, said:

“Ye [M 0.0117] gahaṭṭhā puññakarā, sīlavanto upāsakā;

Dhammena dāraṃ posenti, te namassāmi mātalī”ti. (saṃ.ni.1.1.264);

Those householders who perform meritorious deeds, are virtuous lay followers, and who righteously support their wives—to them, Mātali, I pay homage.

Anākulā kammantā nāma kālaññutāya patirūpakāritāya analasatāya uṭṭhānavīriyasampadāya, abyasanīyatāya ca kālātikkamanaappatirūpakaraṇasithilakaraṇādiākulabhāvavirahitā kasigorakkhavāṇijjādayo kammantā. Ete attano vā puttadārassa vā dāsakammakarānaṃ vā byattatāya evaṃ payojitā diṭṭheva dhamme dhanadhaññavuddhipaṭilābhahetuto maṅgalanti vuccanti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

'Unobstructed occupations' are occupations such as agriculture, cattle-herding, and trade, which—through timeliness, suitability of action, diligence, endowment with striving and energy, and not being prone to ruin—are free from the state of obstruction, such as acting after the time has passed, doing what is unsuitable, and acting with slackness. When these occupations are skillfully employed for oneself, one's wife and children, or one's servants and workers, they are called a blessing because they are a cause for the increase and acquisition of wealth and grain in this very life. For this was stated by the Blessed One:

“Patirūpakārī dhuravā, uṭṭhātā vindate dhana”nti ca (su. ni. 185; saṃ. ni. 1.246).

One who acts fittingly, is endowed with wisdom, and is diligent, finds wealth.

“Na divā soppasīlena, rattimuṭṭhānadessinā;

Niccaṃ mattena soṇḍena, sakkā āvasituṃ gharaṃ.

It is not possible to maintain a household by being in the habit of sleeping during the day, by hating to rise at night, by being constantly heedless, and by being a drunkard.

“Atisītaṃ [V 0.0112] atiuṇhaṃ, atisāyamidaṃ ahu;

Iti vissaṭṭhakammante, atthā accenti māṇave.

'It is too cold, it is too hot, it is too late in the evening'—for the young man who abandons his work with such excuses, opportunities pass by.

“Yodha sītañca uṇhañca, tiṇā bhiyyo na maññati;

Karaṃ purisakiccāni, so sukhaṃ na vihāyatī”ti. (dī. ni. 3.253);

He who does not regard cold and heat as more than grass, while performing the duties of a man, does not fall away from happiness.

“Bhoge saṃharamānassa, bhamarasseva irīyato;

Bhogā sannicayaṃ yanti, vammikovūpacīyatī”ti. ca evamādi (dī. ni. 3.265);

For one who gathers wealth like a bee, riches accumulate and are built up like an anthill. And so forth.

Evaṃ [P 0.0140] imissā gāthāya mātuupaṭṭhānaṃ, pituupaṭṭhānaṃ, puttadārassa saṅgaho, anākulā ca kammantāti cattāri maṅgalāni vuttāni, puttadārassa saṅgahaṃ vā dvidhā katvā pañca, mātāpituupaṭṭhānaṃ vā ekameva katvā tīṇi. Maṅgalattañca nesaṃ tattha tattha vibhāvitamevāti.

Thus, in this verse, four blessings are spoken of: attending to one's mother, attending to one's father, supporting one's wife and children, and unobstructed occupations. Alternatively, by taking 'support of wife and children' as two, five blessings are spoken of. Or, by taking 'attending to mother and father' as just one, three are spoken of. And their nature as a blessing has been made clear in the respective places.

Niṭṭhitā mātāpituupaṭṭhānanti imissā gāthāya atthavaṇṇanā.

The explanation of the meaning of this verse on 'Attending to Mother and Father' is concluded.

Dānañcātigāthāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Verse Beginning with 'Dānañca'

7. Idāni dānañcāti ettha dīyate imināti dānaṃ, attano santakaṃ parassa paṭipādīyatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Dhammassa cariyā, dhammā vā anapetā cariyā [M 0.0118] dhammacariyā. Ñāyante “amhākaṃ ime”ti ñātakā. Na avajjāni anavajjāni, aninditāni agarahitānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti ayaṃ padavaṇṇanā.

7. Now, herein, regarding 'dānañca': 'That by which something is given' is 'dāna' (giving); this means that one's own property is presented to another. 'Conduct of the Dhamma' or 'conduct not apart from the Dhamma' is 'dhammacariyā' (righteous conduct). 'They are known as "these are ours"'—thus they are 'ñātaka' (relatives). 'Not blameworthy' is 'anavajjāni' (blameless); this means unreproached and unblamed. The remainder is in the manner already stated. This is the word-explanation.

Atthavaṇṇanā pana evaṃ veditabbā – dānaṃ nāma paraṃ uddissa subuddhipubbikā annādidasadānavatthupariccāgacetanā, taṃsampayutto vā alobho. Alobhena hi taṃ vatthuṃ parassa paṭipādeti, tena vuttaṃ “dīyate imināti dāna”nti. Taṃ bahujanapiyamanāpatādīnaṃ diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikānaṃ phalavisesānaṃ adhigamahetuto maṅgalanti vuccati. “Dāyako, sīha dānapati, bahuno janassa piyo hoti manāpo”ti evamādīni (a. ni. 5.34) cettha suttāni anussaritabbāni.

The explanation of the meaning, however, should be understood thus: 'Dāna' (giving) is the volition, preceded by wholesome wisdom, to relinquish the ten objects of giving, such as food, for the sake of another; or it is the non-greed associated with it. For it is through non-greed that one presents that object to another; therefore it is said, 'That by which one gives is dāna.' Because it is a cause for attaining special fruits—both in this life and in the hereafter—such as being dear and agreeable to many people, it is called a blessing. Herein, suttas such as the following should be recalled: 'O Sīha, a giver, a master of giving, becomes dear and agreeable to many people.'

Aparo [V 0.0113] nayo – dānaṃ nāma duvidhaṃ āmisadānaṃ, dhammadānañca, tattha āmisadānaṃ vuttappakārameva. Idhalokaparalokadukkhakkhayasukhāvahassa pana sammāsambuddhappaveditassa dhammassa paresaṃ hitakāmatāya desanā dhammadānaṃ [P 0.0141] , imesañca dvinnaṃ dānānaṃ etadeva aggaṃ. Yathāha –

Another method is as follows: 'Dāna' (giving) is twofold: material giving and the gift of the Dhamma. Therein, material giving is of the kind already described. However, the teaching of the Dhamma proclaimed by the Perfectly Enlightened One—which brings happiness through the destruction of suffering in this world and the next—out of a desire for the welfare of others, is called the gift of the Dhamma. And of these two kinds of giving, this one is indeed the highest. As it is said:

“Sabbadānaṃ dhammadānaṃ jināti,

Sabbarasaṃ dhammaraso jināti;

Sabbaratiṃ dhammarati jināti,

Taṇhakkhayo sabbadukkhaṃ jinātī”ti. (dha. pa. 354);

‘The gift of the Dhamma conquers all gifts; the taste of the Dhamma conquers all tastes; delight in the Dhamma conquers all delights; the destruction of craving conquers all suffering.’

Tattha āmisadānassa maṅgalattaṃ vuttameva. Dhammadānaṃ pana yasmā atthapaṭisaṃveditādīnaṃ guṇānaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ, tasmā maṅgalanti vuccati. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Therein, the nature of material giving as a blessing has already been stated. The gift of the Dhamma, however, is called a blessing because it is the proximate cause for qualities such as experiencing the meaning. For this was stated by the Blessed One:

“Yathā yathā, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ vitthārena paresaṃ deseti, tathā tathā so tasmiṃ dhamme atthapaṭisaṃvedī ca hoti dhammapaṭisaṃvedī cā”ti evamādi (a. ni. 5.26).

‘Monks, in whatever way a monk teaches the Dhamma to others in detail as he has heard it and learned it, in that same way he becomes one who experiences the meaning and one who experiences the Dhamma in that teaching.’ And so on.

Dhammacariyā nāma dasakusalakammapathacariyā. Yathāha – “tividhā kho gahapatayo kāyena dhammacariyā samacariyā hotī”ti evamādi. Sā panesā dhammacariyā saggalokūpapattihetuto maṅgalanti veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā – “dhammacariyāsamacariyāhetu kho gahapatayo evamidhekacce sattā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjantī”ti (ma. ni. 1.439).

'Dhammacariyā' (righteous conduct) is the practice of the ten wholesome courses of action. As it is said: ‘Householders, righteous conduct, good conduct, is threefold by way of the body,’ and so on. This righteous conduct should be known as a blessing because it is a cause for rebirth in a heavenly world. For this was stated by the Blessed One: ‘Householders, it is because of righteous conduct, because of good conduct, that some beings here, on the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.’

Ñātakā [M 0.0119] nāma mātito vā pitito vā yāva sattamā pitāmahayugā sambandhā. Tesaṃ bhogapārijuññena vā byādhipārijuññena vā abhihatānaṃ attano samīpaṃ āgatānaṃ yathābalaṃ ghāsacchādanadhanadhaññādīhi saṅgaho pasaṃsādīnaṃ diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ sugatigamanādīnañca samparāyikānaṃ visesādhigamānaṃ hetuto maṅgalanti vuccati.

'Relatives' are those connected from the mother's side or the father's side up to the seventh generation of ancestors. For those relatives who, afflicted by loss of wealth or by illness, have come near, supporting them according to one's ability with food, clothing, wealth, grain, and so on, is called a blessing. This is because it is a cause for the attainment of special advantages in this very life, such as praise, and for the attainment of special advantages in the hereafter, such as going to a good destination.

Anavajjāni kammāni nāma uposathaṅgasamādānaveyyāvaccakaraṇaārāmavanaropanasetukaraṇādīni kāyavacīmanosucaritakammāni. Tāni hi nānappakārahitasukhādhigamahetuto maṅgalanti vuccanti. “Ṭhānaṃ [P 0.0142] kho panetaṃ, visākhe, vijjati yaṃ idhekacco itthī vā puriso vā [V 0.0114] aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ uposathaṃ upavasitvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā cātumahārājikānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjeyyā”ti evamādīni cettha suttāni (a. ni. 8.43) anussaritabbāni.

'Blameless actions' are such things as undertaking the factors of the Uposatha, performing services, planting parks and groves, and building bridges—actions of good conduct by body, speech, and mind. These are called blessings because they are a cause for attaining various kinds of welfare and happiness. Herein, suttas such as the following should be recalled: ‘It is possible, Visākhā, that some woman or man here, having observed the Uposatha endowed with eight factors, on the breakup of the body, after death, might be reborn in the company of the devas of the Four Great Kings.’

Evaṃ imissā gāthāya dānañca, dhammacariyā ca, ñātakānañca saṅgaho, anavajjāni kammānīti cattāri maṅgalāni vuttāni. Maṅgalattañca nesaṃ tattha tattha vibhāvitamevāti.

Thus, in this verse, four blessings have been spoken of: giving, righteous conduct, the supporting of relatives, and blameless actions. And their nature as a blessing has been made clear in the respective places.

Niṭṭhitā dānañcāti imissā gāthāya atthavaṇṇanā.

The explanation of the meaning of the verse beginning with 'Dānañca' is concluded.

Āratītigāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Verse Beginning 'Āratī'

8. Idāni āratī viratīti ettha āratīti āramaṇaṃ, viratīti viramaṇaṃ, viramanti vā etāya sattāti virati. Pāpāti akusalā. Madanīyaṭṭhena majjaṃ, majjassa pānaṃ majjapānaṃ, tato majjapānā. Saṃyamanaṃ saṃyamo appamajjanaṃ appamādo. Dhammesūti kusalesu. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti ayaṃ padavaṇṇanā.

8. Now, in the phrase 'āratī virati,' the meaning should be understood thus: 'āratī' is refraining; 'virati' is special refraining. Or, because beings especially refrain by means of this, it is 'virati.' 'Pāpā' means from unwholesome states. In the sense of being intoxicating, it is 'majja'; the drinking of 'majja' is 'majjapāna'; hence, 'tato majjapānā' means from the drinking of intoxicants. 'Saṃyamanaṃ' is restraint; 'saṃyamo' is restraint. 'Appamajjanaṃ' is non-negligence; 'appamādo' is heedfulness. 'Dhammesu' means in wholesome states. The remainder is just as has been explained. This is the explanation of the words.

Atthavaṇṇanā pana evaṃ veditabbā – ārati nāma pāpe ādīnavadassāvino manasā eva anabhirati. Virati nāma kammadvāravasena kāyavācāhi viramaṇaṃ, sā cesā virati nāma sampattavirati, samādānavirati, samucchedaviratīti tividhā hoti, tattha yā kulaputtassa attano jātiṃ vā kulaṃ vā gottaṃ vā paṭicca “na me etaṃ patirūpaṃ, yvāhaṃ [M 0.0120] imaṃ pāṇaṃ haneyyaṃ, adinnaṃ ādiyeyya”ntiādinā nayena sampattavatthuto virati, ayaṃ sampattavirati nāma. Sikkhāpadasamādānavasena pavattā samādānavirati nāma, yassā pavattito pabhuti kulaputto pāṇātipātādīni na karoti. Ariyamaggasampayuttā samucchedavirati nāma, yassā pavattito pabhuti ariyasāvakassa pañca bhayāni verāni vūpasantāni honti. Pāpaṃ nāma yaṃ taṃ “pāṇātipāto kho, gahapatiputta, kammakileso, adinnādānaṃ…pe… kāmesumicchācāro…pe… musāvādo”ti evaṃ vitthāretvā –

The explanation of the meaning, however, should be understood thus: What is called 'ārati' is the mental non-delight in evil for one who is accustomed to seeing the danger in it. What is called 'virati' is refraining by way of the doors of kamma, through body and speech. And this 'virati' is threefold: sampattavirati (abstention on the occasion), samādānavirati (abstention by undertaking), and samucchedavirati (abstention by eradication). Among these, when a man of good family, reflecting on his own birth, clan, or lineage, thinks, 'It is not suitable for me that I should kill this living being or take what is not given,' and in this way refrains from the matter that has presented itself—this is called sampattavirati. The abstention that occurs by way of undertaking the training rules is called samādānavirati; from the moment it arises, the man of good family does not commit the killing of living beings and so on. The abstention associated with the Noble Path is called samucchedavirati; from the moment it arises, the five fears and enmities are calmed for the noble disciple. What is called evil is that which is to be elaborated thus: ‘The killing of living beings, O son of a householder, is a defilement of action; taking what is not given… sexual misconduct… false speech…’

“Pāṇātipāto [P 0.0143] adinnādānaṃ, musāvādo ca vuccati;

Paradāragamanañceva, nappasaṃsanti paṇḍitā”ti. (dī. ni. 3.245) –

‘The killing of living beings, taking what is not given, and false speech, and also going to another's wife—the wise do not praise.’

Evaṃ [V 0.0115] gāthāya saṅgahitaṃ kammakilesasaṅkhātaṃ catubbidhaṃ akusalaṃ, tato pāpā. Sabbāpesā ārati ca virati ca diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikabhayaverappahānādinānappakāravisesādhigamahetuto maṅgalanti vuccati. “Pāṇātipātā paṭivirato kho, gahapatiputta, ariyasāvako”tiādīni cettha suttāni anussaritabbāni.

From that evil—the fourfold unwholesome reckoned as action-defilements and summarized by the verse in this way—all this refraining (ārati) and abstention (virati) are called a blessing because they are a cause for attaining various special qualities, such as the abandoning of fear and enmity pertaining to the present life and future lives. Here, suttas such as, 'A noble disciple, O son of a householder, abstains from the killing of living beings,' and so forth should be recollected.

Majjapānā saṃyamo nāma pubbe vuttasurāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhānā veramaṇiyā evetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Yasmā pana majjapāyī atthaṃ na jānāti, dhammaṃ na jānāti, mātu antarāyaṃ karoti, pitu buddhapaccekabuddhatathāgatasāvakānampi antarāyaṃ karoti, diṭṭheva dhamme garahaṃ samparāye duggatiṃ aparāpariye ummādañca pāpuṇāti. Majjapānā pana saṃyamo tesaṃ dosānaṃ vūpasamaṃ tabbiparītaguṇasampadañca pāpuṇāti. Tasmā ayaṃ majjapānā saṃyamo maṅgalanti veditabbo.

Restraint from drinking intoxicants is simply another term for the abstinence from liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are a basis for heedlessness, spoken of before. For one who drinks intoxicants does not know what is beneficial, does not know the Dhamma, causes harm to his mother, to his father, and even to the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Tathāgata; in this very life he incurs blame, in the next life he reaches a bad destination, and in a future life, madness as well. But restraint from drinking intoxicants brings about the cessation of those faults and the attainment of the virtues contrary to them. Therefore, this restraint from drinking intoxicants should be understood as a blessing.

Kusalesu dhammesu appamādo nāma “kusalānaṃ vā dhammānaṃ bhāvanāya asakkaccakiriyatā, asātaccakiriyatā, anaṭṭhitakiriyatā, olīnavuttitā, nikkhittachandatā, nikkhittadhuratā, anāsevanā, abhāvanā, abahulīkammaṃ, anadhiṭṭhānaṃ, ananuyogo, pamādo. Yo evarūpo pamādo pamajjanā pamajjitattaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati pamādo”ti (vibha. 846). Ettha vuttassa pamādassa paṭipakkhavasena atthato kusalesu dhammesu satiyā avippavāso veditabbo. So nānappakārakusalādhigamahetuto amatādhigamahetuto ca maṅgalanti vuccati[M 0.0121]. Tattha [P 0.0144] “appamattassa ātāpino”ti ca (ma. ni. 2.18; a. ni. 5.26), “appamādo amataṃ pada”nti ca, evamādi (dha. pa. 21) satthu sāsanaṃ anussaritabbaṃ.

Heedfulness (`appamāda`) in wholesome states is as follows. Heedlessness (`pamāda`) is defined thus: 'Regarding the development of wholesome states, the lack of diligent performance, lack of continuous performance, lack of steadfast performance, sluggish conduct, the abandoning of desire, the abandoning of the burden, non-association, non-development, non-repetition, non-determination, non-application, is heedlessness. Whatever heedlessness of this kind, carelessness, or state of being heedless there is, this is called heedlessness' (Vibh. 846). By way of being the opposite of the heedlessness mentioned here, `appamāda` should be understood in meaning as the non-separation from mindfulness regarding wholesome states. It is called a blessing because it is a cause for attaining various kinds of wholesome qualities and for attaining the Deathless. In this regard, the Teacher's instruction should be recollected, such as: 'For the heedful and ardent one' (MN 2.18; AN 5.26), and 'Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless' (Dhp. 21), and so forth.

Evaṃ imissā gāthāya pāpā virati, majjapānā saṃyamo, kusalesu dhammesu appamādoti tīṇi maṅgalāni vuttāni. Maṅgalattañca nesaṃ tattha tattha vibhāvitamevāti.

Thus, in this verse, three blessings are stated: abstention from evil, restraint from drinking intoxicants, and heedfulness in wholesome states. And their nature as blessings has been clearly shown in the respective places.

Niṭṭhitā āratīti imissā gāthāya atthavaṇṇanā.

The explanation of the meaning of this verse beginning 'Āratī' is concluded.

Gāravocātigāthāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Verse beginning 'Gāravo ca'

9. Idāni gāravo cāti ettha gāravoti garubhāvo. Nivātoti nīcavuttitā. Santuṭṭhīti santoso[V 0.0116]. Katassa jānanatā kataññutā. Kālenāti khaṇena samayena. Dhammassa savanaṃ dhammassavanaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti ayaṃ padavaṇṇanā.

9. Now, in this phrase `gāravo ca`: `gāravo` (reverence) is the state of being respectful. `Nivāto` (humility) is humble conduct. `Santuṭṭhī` (contentment) is satisfaction. `Kataññutā` (gratitude) is the state of knowing what has been done. `Kālena` means at the right moment, at the right time. `Dhammassa savanaṃ` is the hearing of the Dhamma. The remainder is just as has been explained. This is the explanation of the words.

Atthavaṇṇanā pana evaṃ veditabbā – gāravo nāma garukārappayogārahesu buddhapaccekabuddhatathāgatasāvakaācariyupajjhāyamātāpitujeṭṭhakabhātikabhaginīādīsu yathānurūpaṃ garukāro garukaraṇaṃ sagāravatā. Sa cāyaṃ gāravo yasmā sugatigamanādīnaṃ hetu. Yathāha –

The explanation of the meaning, however, should be understood thus: What is called reverence is the appropriate showing of respect, the act of revering, and the state of being respectful towards those worthy of honor, such as Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, the Tathāgata's disciples, teachers, preceptors, mother, father, elder brothers, elder sisters, and so on. And this reverence is a cause for going to a good destination and so forth. As it is said:

“Garukātabbaṃ garuṃ karoti, mānetabbaṃ māneti, pūjetabbaṃ pūjeti. So tena kammena evaṃ samattena evaṃ samādinnena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati. No ce kāyassa…pe… upapajjati, sace manussattaṃ āgacchati, yattha yattha paccājāyati, uccākulīno hotī”ti (ma. ni. 3.295).

‘One reveres who should be revered, esteems who should be esteemed, and honors who should be honored. By that action, thus completed and thus undertaken, with the breaking up of the body, after death, one is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. If, with the breaking up of the body, after death, one is not reborn there, but instead comes to the human state, wherever one is reborn, one is of a high family.’

Yathā cāha – “sattime, bhikkhave, aparihāniyā dhammā. Katame satta? Satthugāravatā”tiādi (a. ni. 7.33), tasmā maṅgalanti vuccati.

And as it is said: ‘Monks, these are seven principles of non-decline. Which seven? Reverence for the Teacher,’ and so on. Therefore, it is called a blessing.

Nivāto nāma nīcamanatā nivātavuttitā, yāya samannāgato puggalo nihatamāno nihatadappo pādapuñchanakacoḷasadiso chinnavisāṇausabhasamo uddhaṭadāṭhasappasamo ca hutvā saṇho sakhilo sukhasambhāso [M 0.0122] hoti, ayaṃ nivāto. Svāyaṃ [P 0.0145] yasādiguṇappaṭilābhahetuto maṅgalanti vuccati. Āha ca “nivātavutti atthaddho, tādiso labhate yasa”nti evamādi (dī. ni. 3.273).

What is called humility (`nivāta`) is lowliness of mind and humble conduct. A person endowed with this, with conceit destroyed and pride eliminated, having become like a foot-wiping cloth, like a bull with broken horns, and like a snake with its fangs removed, is gentle, affable, and pleasant in speech. This is humility. And this humility is called a blessing because it is a cause for acquiring virtues such as fame. And it was said: ‘One of humble conduct, not rigid, such a one obtains fame,’ and so on.

Santuṭṭhi nāma itarītarapaccayasantoso, so dvādasavidho hoti. Seyyathidaṃ – cīvare yathālābhasantoso, yathābalasantoso, yathāsāruppasantosoti tividho. Evaṃ piṇḍapātādīsu.

What is called contentment (`santuṭṭhi`) is satisfaction with whatever requisites are obtained. It is of twelve kinds. Namely: regarding robes, it is threefold as contentment with whatever is obtained, contentment according to one's strength, and contentment according to suitability. Similarly, it is threefold regarding almsfood and so on.

Tassāyaṃ pabhedavaṇṇanā – idha bhikkhu cīvaraṃ labhati sundaraṃ vā asundaraṃ vā. So teneva yāpeti, aññaṃ na pattheti, labhantopi na gaṇhāti, ayamassa cīvare yathālābhasantoso. Atha pana bhikkhu ābādhiko hoti, garuṃ cīvaraṃ pārupanto oṇamati vā kilamati vā, so sabhāgena bhikkhunā saddhiṃ taṃ parivattetvā lahukena yāpentopi santuṭṭhova hoti, ayamassa cīvare yathābalasantoso. Aparo bhikkhu paṇītapaccayalābhī hoti, so paṭṭacīvarādīnaṃ aññataraṃ mahagghaṃ cīvaraṃ labhitvā “idaṃ therānaṃ cirapabbajitānaṃ bahussutānañca anurūpa”nti [V 0.0117] tesaṃ datvā attanā saṅkārakūṭā vā aññato vā kutoci nantakāni uccinitvā saṅghāṭiṃ karitvā dhārentopi santuṭṭhova hoti, ayamassa cīvare yathāsāruppasantoso.

This is the explanation of its divisions: Here, a monk obtains a robe, whether fine or coarse. He makes do with just that, does not desire another, and even if he obtains one, he does not accept it. This, for him, is contentment with robes according to what is obtained. Furthermore, a monk may be ill; when putting on a heavy robe, he stoops or becomes weary. Even if he exchanges that robe with a fellow monk and makes do with a light one, he is still content. This, for him, is contentment with robes according to his strength. Another monk may be a recipient of fine requisites. Having obtained a very valuable robe, he thinks, ‘This is suitable for the elders, for those long ordained, and for the very learned,’ and gives it to them. Then, having collected rags from a rubbish heap or elsewhere, made them into an outer robe, and wearing it, he is still content. This, for him, is contentment with robes according to suitability.

Idha pana bhikkhu piṇḍapātaṃ labhati lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā, so teneva yāpeti, aññaṃ na pattheti, labhantopi na gaṇhāti, ayamassa piṇḍapāte yathālābhasantoso. Atha pana bhikkhu ābādhiko hoti, lūkhaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ bhuñjitvā gāḷhaṃ rogātaṅkaṃ pāpuṇāti, so taṃ sabhāgassa bhikkhuno datvā tassa hatthato sappimadhukhīrādīni bhuñjitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karontopi santuṭṭhova hoti, ayamassa piṇḍapāte [P 0.0146] yathābalasantoso. Aparo bhikkhu paṇītaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ labhati, so “ayaṃ piṇḍapāto therānaṃ cirapabbajitānaṃ aññesañca paṇītapiṇḍapātaṃ vinā ayāpentānaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ anurūpo”ti tesaṃ datvā attanā piṇḍāya caritvā missakāhāraṃ bhuñjantopi santuṭṭhova hoti, ayamassa piṇḍapāte yathāsāruppasantoso.

Here, a monk obtains almsfood, whether coarse or refined. He sustains himself with just that, does not long for another, and even if he obtains it, he does not take it. This is his contentment with almsfood according to what is obtained. Then, if a monk is ill, and after eating coarse almsfood, he incurs a severe attack of illness, he gives it to a fellow monk and, eating ghee, honey, milk, and so forth from that monk’s hand, while still performing the ascetic duty, he remains content. This is his contentment with almsfood according to his strength. Another monk obtains refined almsfood and thinks, 'This almsfood is suitable for the elders who have long gone forth and for other fellow practitioners who cannot sustain themselves without refined almsfood.' Giving it to them, he himself goes for alms and eats mixed food, yet he remains content. This is his contentment with almsfood according to suitability.

Idha [M 0.0123] pana bhikkhuno senāsanaṃ pāpuṇāti. So teneva santussati, puna aññaṃ sundaratarampi pāpuṇantaṃ na gaṇhāti, ayamassa senāsane yathālābhasantoso. Atha pana bhikkhu ābādhiko hoti, nivātasenāsane vasanto ativiya pittarogādīhi āturīyati. So taṃ sabhāgassa bhikkhuno datvā tassa pāpuṇane savāte sītalasenāsane vasitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karontopi santuṭṭhova hoti, ayamassa senāsane yathābalasantoso. Aparo bhikkhu sundaraṃ senāsanaṃ pattampi na sampaṭicchati “sundarasenāsanaṃ pamādaṭṭhānaṃ, tatra nisinnassa thinamiddhaṃ okkamati, niddābhibhūtassa ca puna paṭibujjhato kāmavitakko samudācaratī”ti. So taṃ paṭikkhipitvā ajjhokāsarukkhamūlapaṇṇakuṭīsu yattha katthaci nivasantopi santuṭṭhova hoti, ayamassa senāsane yathāsāruppasantoso.

Here, a monk obtains a dwelling. He is content with just that, and does not take another, even if a more beautiful one becomes available. This is his contentment with lodging according to what is obtained. Then, if a monk is ill, and while dwelling in a sheltered dwelling, he suffers excessively from ailments like bile disorders, he gives that dwelling to a fellow monk and, dwelling in a breezy, cool dwelling that he obtains, he practices the ascetic duties while remaining content. This is his contentment with lodging according to his strength. Another monk, even having obtained a beautiful dwelling, does not accept it, thinking, 'A beautiful dwelling is a place of negligence. Sitting there, sloth and torpor overcome one, and when one wakes up after being overwhelmed by sleep, sensual thoughts arise.' Rejecting it, he dwells contentedly in the open air, at the foot of trees, or in leaf huts—wherever it may be. This is his contentment with lodging according to suitability.

Idha pana bhikkhu bhesajjaṃ labhati harītakaṃ vā āmalakaṃ vā. So teneva yāpeti, aññehi laddhasappimadhuphāṇitādimpi na pattheti, labhantopi na gaṇhāti, ayamassa gilānapaccaye yathālābhasantoso. Atha pana bhikkhu ābādhiko hoti, telenatthiko phāṇitaṃ labhati, so taṃ sabhāgassa bhikkhuno datvā tassa hatthato telena bhesajjaṃ katvā samaṇadhammaṃ karontopi santuṭṭhova hoti, ayamassa gilānapaccaye yathābalasantoso. Aparo bhikkhu ekasmiṃ [P 0.0147] bhājane pūtimuttaharītakaṃ ṭhapetvā ekasmiṃ catumadhuraṃ “gaṇhatha, bhante, yadicchasī”ti vuccamāno sacassa tesaṃ dvinnamaññatarenapi byādhi vūpasammati, atha “pūtimuttaharītakaṃ nāma buddhādīhi [V 0.0118] vaṇṇita”nti ca “pūtimuttabhesajjaṃ nissāya pabbajjā, tattha te yāvajīvaṃ ussāho karaṇīyoti vutta”nti (mahāva. 128) ca cintento catumadhurabhesajjaṃ paṭikkhipitvā pūtimuttaharītakena bhesajjaṃ karontopi paramasantuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa gilānapaccaye yathāsāruppasantoso.

Here, a monk obtains medicine—whether harītaka or āmalaka. He sustains himself with just that, and does not long for things such as ghee, honey, and molasses obtained by others, nor does he accept them even when he obtains them. This is his contentment with requisites for the sick according to what is obtained. Furthermore, if a monk is ill and needs oil but obtains molasses, he gives it to a fellow monk and, having made medicine with oil from that monk’s hand, still practices the ascetic's duties with contentment. This is his contentment with requisites for the sick according to his strength. Another monk, having placed harītaka soaked in putrid urine in one vessel and a fourfold sweet remedy in another, is told, 'Take, venerable one, whatever you wish.' If his illness would be cured by either of the two, he reflects: 'The medicine called harītaka soaked in putrid urine is praised by the Buddhas and so forth,' and 'It is said: "The going forth depends on the medicine of putrid urine; therein you should strive for as long as life lasts."' Thus, rejecting the fourfold sweet remedy and making medicine with harītaka soaked in putrid urine, he remains supremely content. This is his contentment with requisites for the sick according to suitability.

Evaṃpabhedo sabbopeso santoso santuṭṭhīti vuccati. Sā atricchatāmahicchatāpāpicchatādīnaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ pahānādhigamahetuto, sugatihetuto, ariyamaggasambhārabhāvato, cātuddisādibhāvahetuto ca maṅgalanti veditabbā. Āha ca –

All this contentment, thus classified, is called satisfaction. It should be understood as a blessing because it is a cause for achieving the abandonment of evil states such as excessive desire, great desire, and wicked desire; because it is a cause for a good destination; because it is a requisite for the Noble Path; and because it is a cause for being unobstructed in the four directions and so forth. And it is said:

“Cātuddiso [M 0.0124] appaṭigho ca hoti,

Santussamāno itarītarenā”ti. evamādi (su. ni. 42);

“Being content with whatever comes his way, he is of the four directions and without conflict.” Thus and so forth.

Kataññutā nāma appassa vā bahussa vā yena kenaci katassa upakārassa punappunaṃ anussaraṇabhāvena jānanatā. Apica nerayikādidukkhaparittāṇato puññāni eva pāṇīnaṃ bahūpakārāni, tato tesampi upakārānussaraṇatā kataññutāti veditabbā. Sā sappurisehi pasaṃsanīyādinānappakāravisesādhigamahetuto maṅgalanti vuccati. Āha ca “dveme, bhikkhave, puggalā dullabhā lokasmiṃ. Katame dve? Yo ca pubbakārī yo ca kataññū katavedī”ti (a. ni. 2.120).

Gratitude means the state of knowing, through repeated recollection, of a help that has been done, whether small or great, by anyone whatsoever. Moreover, because they protect from the suffering of hell and so forth, merits are indeed of great help to beings; therefore, the recollection of the help of those merits too should be known as gratitude. It is called a blessing since it is a cause for the acquisition of various kinds of special qualities, beginning with being praiseworthy by the virtuous. And He said: “Monks, these two persons are hard to find in the world. Which two? The one who helps first, and the one who is grateful and acknowledges what has been done.”

Kālena dhammassavanaṃ nāma yasmiṃ kāle uddhaccasahagataṃ cittaṃ hoti, kāmavitakkādīnaṃ vā aññatarena abhibhūtaṃ, tasmiṃ kāle tesaṃ vinodanatthaṃ dhammassavanaṃ. Apare āhu “pañcame pañcame divase dhammassavanaṃ kālena dhammassavanaṃ nāma. Yathāha āyasmā [P 0.0148] anuruddho ‘pañcāhikaṃ kho pana mayaṃ, bhante, sabbarattiṃ dhammiyā kathāya sannisīdāmā’”ti (ma. ni. 1.327; mahāva. 466).

Listening to the Dhamma at the proper time means: when the mind is accompanied by restlessness or is overcome by one or another of sensual thoughts and so forth, at that time, listening to the Dhamma is for the purpose of dispelling them. Other teachers say, “Listening to the Dhamma every fifth day is called listening to the Dhamma at the proper time.” As the Venerable Anuruddha said, “Indeed, venerable sir, every five days we sit together all night for a Dhamma talk.”

Apica yasmiṃ kāle kalyāṇamitte upasaṅkamitvā sakkā hoti attano kaṅkhāvinodakaṃ dhammaṃ sotuṃ, tasmiṃ kālepi dhammassavanaṃ kālena dhammassavananti veditabbaṃ. Yathāha “te kālena kālaṃ upasaṅkamitvā paripucchati paripañhatī”tiādi (dī. ni. 3.358). Tadetaṃ kālena dhammassavanaṃ nīvaraṇappahānacaturānisaṃsaāsavakkhayādinānappakāravisesādhigamahetuto maṅgalanti veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Furthermore, when it is possible to approach good friends and listen to the Dhamma that dispels one's own doubt, at that time too, listening to the Dhamma should be known as 'listening to the Dhamma at the proper time.' As it is said: “Approaching them from time to time, one asks questions, one discusses,” and so forth. This listening to the Dhamma at the proper time should be known as a blessing because it is a cause for the acquisition of various kinds of special qualities, such as the abandoning of the hindrances, the attainment of the four benefits, and the destruction of the taints. For this was said:

“Yasmiṃ[V 0.0119], bhikkhave, samaye ariyasāvako aṭṭhiṃ katvā manasi katvā sabbaṃ cetasā samannāharitvā ohitasoto dhammaṃ suṇāti, pañcassa nīvaraṇā tasmiṃ samaye na hontī”ti ca (saṃ. ni. 5.219).

“Bhikkhus, at the time when a noble disciple, having paid respect, having brought it to mind, having fully comprehended it with his whole mind, listens to the Dhamma with an attentive ear, for him the five hindrances are not present at that time.” And:

“Sotānugatānaṃ, bhikkhave, dhammānaṃ…pe… suppaṭividdhānaṃ cattāro ānisaṃsā pāṭikaṅkhā”ti ca (a. ni. 4.191).

“Bhikkhus, for those by whom the teachings that have reached the ear... are well penetrated, four benefits are to be expected.” And:

“Cattārome, bhikkhave, dhammā kālena kālaṃ sammā bhāviyamānā sammā anuparivattiyamānā anupubbena āsavānaṃ khayaṃ pāpenti. Katame cattāro? Kālena dhammassavana”nti ca evamādi (a. ni. 4.147).

“Bhikkhus, these four things, being rightly developed from time to time, being rightly practiced in sequence, gradually lead to the destruction of the taints. What four? Listening to the Dhamma at the proper time.” And so forth, it was said.

Evaṃ [M 0.0125] imissā gāthāya gāravo, nivāto, santuṭṭhi, kataññutā, kālena dhammassavananti pañca maṅgalāni vuttāni. Maṅgalattañca nesaṃ tattha tattha vibhāvitamevāti.

Thus, in this verse, five blessings are stated: reverence, humility, contentment, gratitude, and listening to the Dhamma at the proper time. And their nature as blessings has been made clear in their respective places.

Niṭṭhitā gāravo cāti imissā gāthāya atthavaṇṇanā.

The explanation of the meaning of this verse beginning “Gāravo ca” is finished.

Khantīcātigāthāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Verse Beginning 'Patience and So On'

10. Idāni khantī cāti ettha khamanaṃ khanti. Padakkhiṇaggāhitāya sukhaṃ vaco asminti suvaco, suvacassa kammaṃ sovacassaṃ, sovacassassa bhāvo sovacassatā. Kilesānaṃ samitattā samaṇā. Dassananti pekkhanaṃ. Dhammassa sākacchā dhammasākacchā. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti. Ayaṃ padavaṇṇanā.

10. Now, in this verse beginning 'Patience and so on,' endurance is patience (khanti). Because speech is easy for him due to his respectful reception, he is 'easy to admonish' (suvaco). The state of such a one is 'being easy to admonish' (sovacassaṃ), and the nature of that state is 'receptivity' (sovacassatā). Because their defilements are pacified, they are called 'ascetics' (samaṇā). 'Seeing' (dassana) means beholding. A discussion together of the Dhamma is 'Dhamma discussion' (dhammasākacchā). The remainder is just as has been stated. This is the explanation of the words.

Atthavaṇṇanā pana evaṃ veditabbā [P 0.0149] – khanti nāma adhivāsanakkhanti, tāya samannāgato bhikkhu dasahi akkosavatthūhi akkosante vadhabandhādīhi vā vihesante puggale asuṇanto viya apassanto viya ca nibbikāro hoti khantivādī viya. Yathāha –

The explanation of the meaning, however, should be known thus: What is called patience (khanti) is patience as endurance. A bhikkhu endowed with that patience remains unmoved—as if not hearing and not seeing—towards people who abuse him with the ten grounds for abuse or who harass him with killing, binding, and so on, just like the ascetic Khantivādī. As it is said:

“Ahu atītamaddhānaṃ, samaṇo khantidīpano;

Taṃ khantiyāyeva ṭhitaṃ, kāsirājā achedayī”ti. (jā. 1.4.51);

“In the long distant past, there was an ascetic, an exemplar of patience. The king of Kāsi cut him while he remained established only in patience.”

Bhadrakato [V 0.0120] vā manasi karoti tato uttari aparādhābhāvena āyasmā puṇṇatthero viya. Yathāha so –

Or, going even further, like the Venerable Elder Puṇṇa, he considers it a good thing by not seeing it as an offense. As he said:

“Sace maṃ, bhante, sunāparantakā manussā akkosissanti paribhāsissanti, tattha me evaṃ bhavissati ‘bhaddakā vatime sunāparantakā manussā, subhaddakā vatime sunāparantakā manussā, yaṃ me nayime pāṇinā pahāraṃ dentī’”tiādi (ma. ni. 3.396; saṃ. ni. 4.88).

“Venerable sir, if the people of Sunāparanta were to abuse and revile me, then this thought would occur to me: ‘Indeed, these people of Sunāparanta are good, indeed, these people of Sunāparanta are very good, in that they do not give me a blow with their hands!’” and so on.

Yāya ca samannāgato isīnampi pasaṃsanīyo hoti. Yathāha sarabhaṅgo isi –

And one who is endowed with this patience is worthy of praise even by the sages. As the sage Sarabhaṅga said:

“Kodhaṃ [M 0.0126] vadhitvā na kadāci socati,

Makkhappahānaṃ isayo vaṇṇayanti;

Sabbesaṃ vuttaṃ pharusaṃ khametha,

Etaṃ khantiṃ uttamamāhu santo”ti. (jā. 2.17.64);

“Having killed anger, one never grieves. The sages praise the abandoning of contempt. You should endure the harsh words spoken by all. The good say this patience is the highest.”

Devatānampi pasaṃsanīyo hoti. Yathāha sakko devānamindo –

He is worthy of praise even by the deities. As Sakka, the lord of the devas, said:

“Yo have balavā santo, dubbalassa titikkhati;

Tamāhu paramaṃ khantiṃ, niccaṃ khamati dubbalo”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.250-251);

“Whoever, being strong, endures the weak—that, the good say, is the supreme patience. The weak always endure.”

Buddhānampi pasaṃsanīyo hoti. Yathāha bhagavā –

He is worthy of praise even by the Buddhas. As the Blessed One said:

“Akkosaṃ vadhabandhañca, aduṭṭho yo titikkhati;

Khantībalaṃ balāṇīkaṃ, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇa”nti. (dha. pa. 399);

“Whoever, without ill will, endures abuse, killing, and binding—one whose strength is patience, whose army is strength—that one I call a brahmin.”

Sā [P 0.0150] panesā khanti etesañca idha vaṇṇitānaṃ aññesañca guṇānaṃ adhigamahetuto maṅgalanti veditabbā.

Now, this patience should be known as a blessing because it is the cause for the attainment of these qualities explained here and of other qualities as well.

Sovacassatā nāma sahadhammikaṃ vuccamāne vikkhepaṃ vā tuṇhībhāvaṃ vā guṇadosacintanaṃ vā [V 0.0121] anāpajjitvā ativiya ādarañca gāravañca nīcamanatañca purakkhatvā sādhūti vacanakaraṇatā. Sā sabrahmacārīnaṃ santikā ovādānusāsanippaṭilābhahetuto dosappahānaguṇādhigamahetuto ca maṅgalanti vuccati.

Receptivity (sovacassatā) is this: when being admonished by a companion in the Dhamma, without resorting to rejection, silence, or contemplating virtues and faults, but rather, having placed foremost extreme respect, reverence, and humility, one complies with the words, saying, 'Good.' This is called a blessing because it is a cause for receiving admonition and instruction from one's companions in the holy life, and because it is a cause for abandoning faults and attaining virtues.

Samaṇānaṃ dassanaṃ nāma upasamitakilesānaṃ bhāvitakāyavacīcittapaññānaṃ uttamadamathasamathasamannāgatānaṃ pabbajitānaṃ upasaṅkamanupaṭṭhānānussaraṇassavanadassanaṃ, sabbampi omakadesanāya dassananti vuttaṃ, taṃ maṅgalanti veditabbaṃ. Kasmā? Bahūpakārattā. Āha ca “dassanampahaṃ, bhikkhave, tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bahūpakāraṃ vadāmī”tiādi (itivu. 104). Yato hitakāmena kulaputtena sīlavante bhikkhū gharadvāraṃ sampatte disvā yadi deyyadhammo atthi, yathābalaṃ deyyadhammena patimānetabbā. Yadi natthi, pañcapatiṭṭhitaṃ katvā vanditabbā. Tasmimpi asampajjamāne añjaliṃ paggahetvā namassitabbā, tasmimpi asampajjamāne pasannacittena piyacakkhūhi sampassitabbā. Evaṃ dassanamūlakenapi hi puññena anekāni jātisahassāni cakkhumhi rogo vā dāho [M 0.0127] vā ussadā vā piḷakā vā na honti, vippasannapañcavaṇṇasassirikāni honti cakkhūni ratanavimāne ugghāṭitamaṇikavāṭasadisāni, satasahassakappamattaṃ devesu ca manussesu ca sampattīnaṃ lābhī hoti. Anacchariyañcetaṃ, yaṃ manussabhūto sappaññajātiko sammā pavattitena samaṇadassanamayena puññena evarūpaṃ vipākasampattiṃ anubhaveyya, yattha tiracchānagatānampi kevalaṃ saddhāmattakena katassa samaṇadassanassa evaṃ vipākasampattiṃ vaṇṇayanti.

What is called ‘seeing ascetics’ is the approaching, attending, recollecting, hearing, and seeing of renunciants who have pacified defilements, who have developed body, speech, mind, and wisdom, and who are endowed with supreme taming and tranquility. All of this is called ‘seeing’ by way of an elaborate teaching. That should be known as a blessing. Why? Because it is of great benefit. And it was said: ‘Bhikkhus, I say that seeing those bhikkhus is of great benefit,’ and so on. Therefore, when a person of good family who desires what is beneficial sees virtuous bhikkhus who have arrived at the door of the house, if there are alms to be given, they should be honored with those alms according to one’s ability. If there are not, they should be venerated by making the five-point prostration. If that is not accomplished, one should raise one’s joined hands and pay homage. If that is not accomplished, one should look upon them well with a confident mind and with loving eyes. For by the merit rooted in such seeing, for many thousands of births, no disease, burning, swelling, or boils arise in the eyes. The eyes become resplendent with the five pure colors, like opened doors of sapphire in a celestial mansion. For a hundred thousand eons, one obtains all accomplishments among devas and humans. And it is not surprising that a human being of a wise birth should experience such a fruition of accomplishment through the merit of seeing ascetics, properly undertaken, when they praise such a fruition of accomplishment for the seeing of ascetics done by animals with mere faith alone.

“Ulūko [P 0.0151] maṇḍalakkhiko, vediyake ciradīghavāsiko;

Sukhito vata kosiyo ayaṃ, kāluṭṭhitaṃ passati buddhavaraṃ.

“This owl with round eyes, a long-time dweller on Vedisaka, this one of the Kosiya clan is indeed happy; it sees the excellent Buddha who has risen in the morning.

“Mayi cittaṃ pasādetvā, bhikkhusaṅghe anuttare;

Kappānaṃ satasahassāni, duggateso na gacchati.

“Having made its mind confident in me and in the unsurpassed Saṅgha of bhikkhus, for a hundred thousand eons, it will not go to a bad destination.”

“Sa devalokā cavitvā, kusalakammena codito;

Bhavissati anantañāṇo, somanassoti vissuto”ti. (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.144);

Having passed away from the deva world, urged on by wholesome kamma, he will become a Paccekabuddha of infinite knowledge, renowned as Somanassa.

Kālena dhammasākacchā nāma padose vā paccūse vā dve suttantikā bhikkhū aññamaññaṃ suttantaṃ [V 0.0122] sākacchanti, vinayadharā vinayaṃ, ābhidhammikā abhidhammaṃ, jātakabhāṇakā jātakaṃ, aṭṭhakathikā aṭṭhakathaṃ, līnuddhatavicikicchāparetacittavisodhanatthaṃ vā tamhi tamhi kāle sākacchanti, ayaṃ kālena dhammasākacchā. Sā āgamabyattiādīnaṃ guṇānaṃ hetuto maṅgalanti vuccatīti.

What is called ‘Dhamma discussion at the proper time’ is when, in the evening or at dawn, two bhikkhus who are masters of the Suttas discuss the Suttas with each other; masters of the Vinaya discuss the Vinaya; masters of the Abhidhamma discuss the Abhidhamma; reciters of the Jātakas discuss the Jātakas; masters of the commentaries discuss the commentaries; or when they discuss at various times for the purpose of purifying a mind afflicted by sluggishness, restlessness, and doubt. This is ‘Dhamma discussion at the proper time.’ It is called a blessing because it is a cause for qualities such as proficiency in the scriptures.

Evaṃ imissā gāthāya khanti, sovacassatā, samaṇadassanaṃ, kālena dhammasākacchāti cattāri maṅgalāni vuttāni. Maṅgalattañca nesaṃ tattha tattha vibhāvitamevāti.

Thus, in this verse, four blessings have been stated: patience, receptivity, seeing ascetics, and Dhamma discussion at the proper time. And their nature as blessings has been made clear in their respective places.

Niṭṭhitā khantī cāti imissā gāthāya atthavaṇṇanā.

The explanation of the meaning of this verse beginning 'Patience and so on' is completed.

Tapocātigāthāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Verse 'Tapo ca'

11. Idāni [M 0.0128] tapo cāti ettha pāpake dhamme tapatīti tapo. Brahmaṃ cariyaṃ, brahmānaṃ vā cariyaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, seṭṭhacariyanti vuttaṃ hoti. Ariyasaccānaṃ dassanaṃ ariyasaccānadassanaṃ, ariyasaccāni dassanantipi eke, taṃ na sundaraṃ. Nikkhantaṃ vānatoti nibbānaṃ, sacchikaraṇaṃ sacchikiriyā, nibbānassa sacchikiriyā nibbānasacchikiriyā. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti ayaṃ padavaṇṇanā.

11. Now, in the phrase 'tapo ca,' 'tapo' is so called because it torments evil states. 'Brahmacariya' is the noble practice, or the practice of the noble ones; it is said to be the supreme practice. The seeing of the Noble Truths is 'ariyasaccānadassanaṃ.' Some recite it as 'ariyasaccāni dassanaṃ,' but that is not good. 'Nibbāna' is so called because it is the going forth from craving (vāna). Realization is 'sacchikiriyā.' The realization of Nibbāna is 'nibbānasacchikiriyā.' The remainder is just as has been explained. This is the explanation of the words.

Atthavaṇṇanā pana evaṃ veditabbā – tapo nāma abhijjhādomanassādīnaṃ tapanato indriyasaṃvaro[P 0.0152], kosajjassa vā tapanato vīriyaṃ, tehi samannāgato puggalo ātāpīti vuccati. Svāyaṃ abhijjhādippahānajhānādippaṭilābhahetuto maṅgalanti veditabbo.

The explanation of the meaning, however, should be understood thus: 'Tapo' by name is the restraint of the faculties, by way of tormenting covetousness, displeasure, and so on; or, it is energy, by way of tormenting laziness. A person endowed with these is called 'ātāpī' (ardent). This very 'tapa' should be understood as a blessing because it is the cause for abandoning covetousness and so on, and for attaining jhāna and so on.

Brahmacariyaṃ nāma methunaviratisamaṇadhammasāsanamaggānamadhivacanaṃ. Tathā hi “abrahmacariyaṃ pahāya brahmacārī hotī”ti evamādīsu (dī. ni. 1.194; ma. ni. 1.292) methunavirati brahmacariyanti vuccati. “Bhagavati no, āvuso, brahmacariyaṃ vussatīti? Evamāvuso”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 1.257) samaṇadhammo. “Na tāvāhaṃ, pāpima, parinibbāyissāmi, yāva me idaṃ brahmacariyaṃ na iddhañceva bhavissati phītañca vitthārikaṃ bāhujañña”nti evamādīsu (dī. ni. 2.168; saṃ. ni. 5.822; udā. 51) sāsanaṃ. “Ayameva kho, bhikkhu, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo brahmacariyaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ, sammādiṭṭhī”ti evamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.6) maggo. Idha pana ariyasaccadassanena parato maggassa [V 0.0123] saṅgahitattā avasesaṃ sabbampi vaṭṭati. Tañcetaṃ uparūpari nānappakāravisesādhigamahetuto maṅgalanti veditabbaṃ.

'Brahmacariya' is a designation for abstinence from sexual intercourse, the practice of recluses, the Teaching, and the Path. For instance, in passages such as, 'Having abandoned unchastity, one becomes one who lives the holy life,' abstinence from sexual intercourse is called 'brahmacariya.' In passages such as, 'Friend, is the holy life lived under the Blessed One?' the practice of recluses is meant. In passages such as, 'Evil One, I will not attain final Nibbāna so long as this holy life of mine has not become successful, prosperous, widespread, and known to many,' the Teaching is meant. In passages such as, 'Monks, this very Noble Eightfold Path is the holy life, that is: right view,' the Path is meant. Here, however, since the Path is included by the seeing of the Noble Truths, all the remaining meanings are also suitable. And this should be understood as a blessing because it is the cause for attaining various kinds of special qualities, higher and higher.

Ariyasaccāna dassanaṃ nāma kumārapañhe vuttānaṃ catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ abhisamayavasena maggadassanaṃ, taṃ saṃsāradukkhavītikkamahetuto maṅgalanti vuccati.

The 'seeing of the Noble Truths' by name is the seeing of the path by way of the realization of the four Noble Truths spoken of in the Kumārapañha. That is called a blessing because it is the cause for overcoming the suffering of saṃsāra.

Nibbānasacchikiriyā nāma idha arahattaphalaṃ nibbānanti adhippetaṃ. Tampi hi pañcagativānanena vānasaññitāya taṇhāya nikkhantattā nibbānanti vuccati. Tassa [M 0.0129] patti vā paccavekkhaṇā vā sacchikiriyāti vuccati. Itarassa pana nibbānassa ariyasaccānaṃ dassaneneva sacchikiriyā siddhā, tenetaṃ idha nādhippetaṃ. Evamesā nibbānasacchikiriyā [P 0.0153] diṭṭhadhammikasukhavihārādihetuto maṅgalanti veditabbā.

Here, by 'realization of Nibbāna,' the fruit of Arahantship is intended as Nibbāna. For that too is called Nibbāna because it is the going forth from craving—which is designated as 'vāna' and is established in the five destinations. Its attainment or its reviewing is called 'realization.' As for the other Nibbāna, its realization is accomplished by the very seeing of the Noble Truths; therefore, that is not intended here. Thus, this realization of Nibbāna should be understood as a blessing because it is a cause for pleasant abiding in the present life, and so on.

Evaṃ imissā gāthāya tapo brahmacariyaṃ, ariyasaccānaṃ dassanaṃ, nibbānasacchikiriyāti cattāri maṅgalāni vuttāni. Maṅgalattañca nesaṃ tattha tattha vibhāvitamevāti.

Thus, in this verse, four blessings are taught: ardency, the holy life, the seeing of the Noble Truths, and the realization of Nibbāna. And their nature as blessings has been made clear in each respective place.

Niṭṭhitā tapo cāti imissā gāthāya atthavaṇṇanā.

Here ends the explanation of the meaning of the verse beginning with 'Tapo ca'.

Phuṭṭhassalokadhammehītigāthāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Verse 'Phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehi'

12. Idāni phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehīti ettha phuṭṭhassāti phusitassa chupitassa sampattassa. Loke dhammā lokadhammā, yāva lokappavatti, tāva anivattakā dhammāti vuttaṃ hoti. Cittanti mano mānasaṃ. Yassāti navassa vā majjhimassa vā therassa vā. Na kampatīti na calati na vedhati. Asokanti nissokaṃ abbūḷhasokasallaṃ. Virajanti vigatarajaṃ viddhaṃsitarajaṃ. Khemanti abhayaṃ nirupaddavaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti ayaṃ padavaṇṇanā.

12. Now, in the phrase 'phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehi,' 'phuṭṭhassa' means contacted, touched, or reached. Phenomena that occur in the world are 'worldly phenomena' (lokadhammā); it is said that as long as the world's process exists, these phenomena are unavoidable. 'Cittaṃ' is the mind (mano, mānasaṃ). 'Yassa' (whose) refers to a junior, middle, or elder monk. 'Na kampati' (does not waver) means it does not shake, does not tremble. 'Asokaṃ' (sorrowless) means without sorrow, with the dart of sorrow pulled out. 'Virajaṃ' (stainless) means free from the dust of defilements, with the dust of defilements destroyed. 'Khemaṃ' (secure) means without fear, without affliction. The rest is just in the manner already stated. This is the explanation of the words.

Atthavaṇṇanā pana evaṃ veditabbā – phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehi cittaṃ yassa na kampati nāma yassa lābhālābhādīhi aṭṭhahi lokadhammehi phuṭṭhassa ajjhotthaṭassa cittaṃ na kampati na calati na vedhati, tassa taṃ cittaṃ kenaci akampanīyalokuttamabhāvāvahanato maṅgalanti veditabbaṃ.

The explanation of the meaning, however, should be known thus: 'Whose mind does not waver when touched by worldly conditions' means the mind of one who, when touched and overwhelmed by the eight worldly conditions beginning with gain and loss, does not waver, does not move, does not tremble. That mind should be known as a blessing because, being unshakable by anything, it brings about the supramundane state.

Kassa [V 0.0124] ca etehi phuṭṭhassa cittaṃ na kampatīti? Arahato khīṇāsavassa, na aññassa kassaci. Vuttañhetaṃ –

And whose mind, when touched by these, does not waver? It is that of an Arahant, one whose cankers are destroyed, and no one else's. For it has been said:

“Selo yathā ekagghano, vātena na samīrati;

Evaṃ rūpā rasā saddā, gandhā phassā ca kevalā.

“Just as a mountain of solid rock is not shaken by the wind; so too all forms, tastes, sounds, smells, and touches,

“Iṭṭhā dhammā aniṭṭhā ca, na pavedhenti tādino;

Ṭhitaṃ cittaṃ vippamuttaṃ, vayañcassānupassatī”ti. (mahāva. 244);

and desirable and undesirable mental objects, do not cause such a one to tremble. The mind is firm, liberated, and one sees their passing away.”

Asokaṃ [M 0.0130][P 0.0154] nāma khīṇāsavasseva cittaṃ. Tañhi yvāyaṃ “soko socanā socitattaṃ antosoko antoparisoko cetaso parinijjhāyitatta”ntiādinā (vibha. 237) nayena vuccati soko, tassa abhāvato asokaṃ. Keci nibbānaṃ vadanti, taṃ purimapadena nānusandhiyati. Yathā ca asokaṃ, evaṃ virajaṃ khemantipi khīṇāsavasseva cittaṃ. Tañhi rāgadosamoharajānaṃ vigatattā virajaṃ, catūhi ca yogehi khemattā khemaṃ, yato etaṃ tena tenākārena tamhi tamhi pavattikkhaṇe gahetvā niddiṭṭhavasena tividhampi appavattakkhandhatādilokuttamabhāvāvahanato āhuneyyādibhāvāvahanato ca maṅgalanti veditabbaṃ.

‘Asokaṃ’ (sorrowless) is the name for the mind of one whose cankers are destroyed. This is true. For that sorrow—which is spoken of by the method beginning with ‘grief, grieving, sorrowfulness, inner sorrow, inner deep sorrow, the mind’s being consumed’—is absent for that person; hence, the mind is called ‘asokaṃ’. Some teachers say it refers to Nibbāna, but that does not connect with the preceding phrase. And just as with ‘asokaṃ’, so too ‘virajaṃ’ (stainless) and ‘khemaṃ’ (secure) refer to the mind of one whose cankers are destroyed. This is true. That mind is called ‘virajaṃ’ because of the absence of the dust of greed, hatred, and delusion. It is called ‘khemaṃ’ because of its security from the four yokes. Therefore, this three-fold phrase—‘asokaṃ, virajaṃ, khemaṃ’—taken in that manner at each moment of occurrence as has been pointed out, should be known as a blessing because it brings about the supramundane state of non-occurring aggregates and so forth, and because it brings about the state of being worthy of offerings and so forth.

Evaṃ imissā gāthāya aṭṭhalokadhammehi akampitacittaṃ, asokacittaṃ, virajacittaṃ, khemacittanti cattāri maṅgalāni vuttāni. Maṅgalattañca nesaṃ tattha tattha vibhāvitamevāti.

Thus, in this verse, four blessings are spoken of: a mind unshaken by the eight worldly conditions, a sorrowless mind, a stainless mind, and a secure mind. And their nature as a blessing has been made clear in each respective case.

Niṭṭhitā phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehīti imissā gāthāya atthavaṇṇanā.

The explanation of the meaning of this verse, 'Phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehi,' is concluded.

Etādisānītigāthāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Verse 'Etādisāni'

13. Evaṃ bhagavā asevanā ca bālānantiādīhi dasahi gāthāhi aṭṭhatiṃsa mahāmaṅgalāni kathetvā idāni etāneva attanā vuttamaṅgalāni thunanto “etādisāni katvānā”ti avasānagāthamabhāsi.

13. Thus, the Blessed One, having taught the thirty-eight great blessings with ten verses beginning with 'Not associating with fools' (asevanā ca bālānaṃ), now, extolling those very blessings spoken by Himself, recited the concluding verse, 'Having done such things' (etādisāni katvāna).

Tassāyamatthavaṇṇanā – etādisānīti etāni īdisāni mayā vuttappakārāni bālānaṃ asevanādīni. Katvānāti katvā. Katvāna katvā karitvāti hi atthato anaññaṃ. Sabbatthamaparājitāti [V 0.0125] sabbattha khandhakilesābhisaṅkhāradevaputtamārappabhedesu [P 0.0155] catūsu paccatthikesu ekenāpi aparājitā hutvā, sayameva te cattāro māre parājetvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Makāro cettha padasandhikaramattoti viññātabbo.

This is the explanation of its meaning: 'Of such kind' (etādisāni) means these things of such a nature, of the kind spoken by me, beginning with the non-association with fools. 'Having done' (katvāna) means 'having done' (katvā). Indeed, 'katvāna,' 'katvā,' and 'karitvā' are not different in meaning. 'Unconquered in all respects' (sabbatthamaparājitā) means: having become unconquered by even one of the four adversaries in all respects—namely, the Māra of the aggregates, the Māra of defilements, the Māra of formations, and the Devaputta Māra—and having oneself defeated those four Māras. Thus it is meant. And here, the letter 'm' should be understood as merely for the purpose of euphonic conjunction of words.

Sabbattha sotthiṃ gacchantīti etādisāni maṅgalāni katvā catūhi mārehi aparājitā hutvā sabbattha idhalokaparalokesu ṭhānacaṅkamanādīsu ca sotthiṃ gacchanti, bālasevanādīhi ye uppajjeyyuṃ āsavā [M 0.0131] vighātapariḷāhā, tesaṃ abhāvā sotthiṃ gacchanti, anupaddutā anupasaṭṭhā khemino appaṭibhayā gacchantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Anunāsiko cettha gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ vuttoti veditabbo.

'They go in safety everywhere' (sabbattha sotthiṃ gacchanti) means: having performed such blessings, having become unconquered by the four Māras, they go in safety everywhere—in this world and the next, and in standing, walking, and so on. Whatever troubles, distress, and torments might arise from associating with fools and the like, due to their absence, they go in safety. They proceed free from calamity, free from reproach, secure, and fearless—thus it is meant. And here, the nasal sound (anunāsika) should be understood as spoken for the sake of ease in the verse composition.

Taṃ tesaṃ maṅgalamuttamanti iminā gāthāpadena bhagavā desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Kathaṃ? Evaṃ, devaputta, ye etādisāni karonti, te yasmā sabbattha sotthiṃ gacchanti, tasmā taṃ bālānaṃ asevanādiaṭṭhatiṃsavidhampi tesaṃ etādisakārakānaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ seṭṭhaṃ pavaranti gaṇhāhīti.

'That is their supreme blessing' (taṃ tesaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ)—with this line of verse, the Blessed One concluded the teaching. How? 'Thus, O devaputta, those who perform such things, because they go in safety everywhere, therefore, that blessing—which has thirty-eight aspects beginning with the non-association with fools—is the supreme, best, and foremost blessing for those who act in such a way. Thus you should understand it.'

Evañca bhagavatā niṭṭhāpitāya desanāya pariyosāne koṭisatasahassadevatāyo arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu, sotāpattisakadāgāmianāgāmiphalasampattānaṃ gaṇanā asaṅkhyeyyā ahosi. Atha bhagavā dutiyadivase ānandattheraṃ āmantesi – “imaṃ pana, ānanda, rattiṃ aññatarā devatā maṃ upasaṅkamitvā maṅgalapañhaṃ pucchi, athassāhaṃ aṭṭhatiṃsa maṅgalāni abhāsiṃ, uggaṇhāhi, ānanda, imaṃ maṅgalapariyāyaṃ, uggahetvā bhikkhū vācehī”ti. Thero uggahetvā bhikkhū vācesi. Tayidaṃ ācariyaparamparāya ābhataṃ yāvajjatanā pavattati, “evamidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ iddhañceva phītañca vitthārikaṃ bāhujaññaṃ puthubhūtaṃ [P 0.0156] yāva devamanussehi suppakāsita”nti veditabbaṃ.

And when the Blessed One had concluded the teaching in this way, at its end, a hundred thousand koṭis of devas attained Arahantship, and the number of those who attained the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, and non-returning was incalculable. Then, on the second day, the Blessed One addressed the Elder Ānanda: 'Ānanda, last night a certain deity approached me and asked the question on blessings. In response, I spoke the thirty-eight blessings to them. Learn, Ānanda, this discourse on blessings, and having learned it, teach it to the bhikkhus.' The Elder learned it and taught it to the bhikkhus. That Maṅgala Sutta, handed down through the lineage of teachers, continues to this day. Thus it should be understood: 'In this way this holy life is successful, prosperous, widespread, known to many, extensive, and well-proclaimed among devas and humans.'
