Idāni etesveva maṅgalesu ñāṇaparicayapāṭavatthaṃ ayamādito pabhuti yojanā – evamime idhalokaparalokalokuttarasukhakāmā sattā bālajanasevanaṃ pahāya, paṇḍite nissāya, pūjaneyye pūjetvā, patirūpadesavāsena pubbe ca katapuññatāya kusalappavattiyaṃ codiyamānā attānaṃ sammā paṇidhāya, bāhusaccasippavinayehi alaṅkatattabhāvā, vinayānurūpaṃ subhāsitaṃ bhāsamānā, yāva gihibhāvaṃ na vijahanti, tāva mātāpitūpaṭṭhānena porāṇaṃ iṇamūlaṃ visodhayamānā, puttadārasaṅgahena navaṃ iṇamūlaṃ payojayamānā, anākulakammantatāya dhanadhaññādisamiddhiṃ pāpuṇantā, dānena bhogasāraṃ dhammacariyāya jīvitasārañca gahetvā, ñātisaṅgahena sakajanahitaṃ anavajjakammantatāya [V 0.0126] parajanahitañca karontā, pāpaviratiyā parūpaghātaṃ majjapānasaṃyamena attūpaghātañca vivajjetvā, dhammesu appamādena kusalapakkhaṃ vaḍḍhetvā, vaḍḍhitakusalatāya gihibyañjanaṃ ohāya pabbajitabhāve ṭhitāpi buddhabuddhasāvakūpajjhāyācariyādīsu gāravena nivātena ca vattasampadaṃ ārādhetvā, santuṭṭhiyā [M 0.0132] paccayagedhaṃ pahāya, kataññutāya sappurisabhūmiyaṃ ṭhatvā, dhammassavanena cittalīnataṃ pahāya, khantiyā sabbaparissaye abhibhavitvā, sovacassatāya sanāthaṃ attānaṃ katvā, samaṇadassanena paṭipattipayogaṃ passantā, dhammasākacchāya kaṅkhāṭṭhāniyesu dhammesu kaṅkhaṃ vinodetvā, indriyasaṃvaratapena sīlavisuddhiṃ samaṇadhammabrahmacariyena cittavisuddhiṃ tato parā ca catasso visuddhiyo sampādentā[P 0.0157], imāya paṭipadāya ariyasaccadassanapariyāyaṃ ñāṇadassanavisuddhiṃ patvā arahattaphalasaṅkhyaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikaronti, yaṃ sacchikaritvā sinerupabbato viya vātavuṭṭhīhi aṭṭhahi lokadhammehi avikampamānacittā asokā virajā khemino honti. Ye ca khemino honti, te sabbattha ekenapi aparājitā honti, sabbattha sotthiṃ gacchanti. Tenāha bhagavā –

Now, for the sake of proficiency and familiarity with the knowledge of these very blessings, this is the syntactical analysis from the beginning: Thus, these beings, desiring happiness in this world, the next world, and the supramundane, having abandoned association with fools, relying on the wise, and honoring those worthy of honor; being urged toward wholesome activity by dwelling in a suitable place and by merit done in the past; having rightly established themselves; being adorned with much learning, skills, and discipline; speaking what is well-spoken in accordance with the discipline; for as long as they do not abandon the household life, they clear away the old root-debt by attending to their mother and father, and engage with a new root-debt by supporting their children and wife; by means of an untroubled occupation, they attain an abundance of wealth, grain, and so on; through giving, they take the essence of their possessions, and through righteous conduct, the essence of life; through supporting their relatives, they act for the welfare of their own people, and through blameless actions, for the welfare of others; by abstaining from evil, they avoid harming others, and by restraint from consuming intoxicants, they avoid harming themselves; through diligence in wholesome states, they increase the wholesome side. Due to their increased wholesomeness, having given up the appearance of a householder, even when established in the state of one gone forth, with reverence and humility toward the Buddha, the Buddha's disciples, preceptors, and teachers, they fulfill the accomplishment of conduct; through contentment, they abandon greed for requisites; through gratitude, they stand on the ground of good people; by listening to the Dhamma, they abandon sluggishness of mind; through patience, they overcome all adversities; by being easy to admonish, they make themselves have a protector; by seeing ascetics, they perceive the application of the practice; by discussion of the Dhamma, they dispel doubt regarding matters of uncertainty; through the austerity of sense restraint, they accomplish the purification of virtue; through the ascetic's practice and the holy life, they accomplish the purification of mind, and thereafter accomplish the four higher purifications. By this path, having reached the purification of knowledge and vision, which is the way to see the Noble Truths, they realize Nibbāna, which is designated as the fruit of Arahantship. Having realized it, like Mount Sineru unshaken by wind and rain, their minds are unshaken by the eight worldly conditions, and they become sorrowless, stainless, and secure. And those who are secure are unconquered by any single adversary anywhere, and they go in safety everywhere. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Etādisāni katvāna, sabbatthamaparājitā;

Sabbattha sotthiṃ gacchanti, taṃ tesaṃ maṅgalamuttama”nti.

Having performed such things, unvanquished everywhere, everywhere they go in safety—that is their supreme blessing.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha,

Maṅgalasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Maṅgala Sutta is concluded.

6. Ratanasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Ratana Sutta

Nikkhepappayojanaṃ

The Purpose of its Placement

Idāni [V 0.0127] yānīdha bhūtānītievamādinā maṅgalasuttānantaraṃ nikkhittassa ratanasuttassa atthavaṇṇanākkamo anuppatto. Tassa idha nikkhepappayojanaṃ vatvā tato paraṃ suparisuddhena titthena naditaḷākādīsu salilajjhogāhaṇamiva suparisuddhena nidānena imassa suttassa atthajjhogāhaṇaṃ dassetuṃ –

Now, the turn for the explanation of the meaning of the Ratana Sutta, placed immediately after the Maṅgala Sutta and beginning with 'yānīdha bhūtāni,' has arrived. Having stated the purpose of its placement here, thereafter, in order to show the immersion into the meaning of this sutta with a perfectly pure introduction—just as one plunges into the water in rivers, lakes, and so forth from a perfectly pure landing-place—

“Yena vuttaṃ yadā yattha, yasmā cetaṃ imaṃ nayaṃ;

Pakāsetvāna etassa, karissāmatthavaṇṇanaṃ”.

By whom it was spoken, when, where, and for what reason it was spoken—having explained this method, we will make a commentary on its meaning.

Tattha [M 0.0133] yasmā maṅgalasuttena attarakkhā akalyāṇakaraṇakalyāṇākaraṇapaccayānañca āsavānaṃ paṭighāto dassito, imañca suttaṃ parārakkhaṃ amanussādipaccayānañca āsavānaṃ paṭighātaṃ sādheti, tasmā tadanantaraṃ nikkhittaṃ siyāti.

Here, because the Maṅgala Sutta shows self-protection for those conditioned by doing the unwholesome and doing the wholesome, and it shows the warding off of the influxes; and this sutta accomplishes the protection of others for those subject to conditions such as non-human beings, and it accomplishes the warding off of the influxes; therefore, it should be placed immediately after that.

Idaṃ tāvassa idha nikkhepappayojanaṃ.

This, then, is the purpose of its placement here.

Vesālivatthu

The Story of Vesālī

Idāni “yena vuttaṃ yadā yattha, yasmā ceta”nti etthāha “kena panetaṃ suttaṃ vuttaṃ, kadā kattha, kasmā ca vutta”nti. Vuccate – idañhi bhagavatā eva vuttaṃ, na sāvakādīhi. Tañca yadā [P 0.0158] dubbhikkhādīhi upaddavehi upaddutāya vesāliyā licchavīhi rājagahato yācitvā bhagavā vesāliṃ ānīto, tadā vesāliyaṃ tesaṃ upaddavānaṃ paṭighātatthāya vuttanti. Ayaṃ tesaṃ pañhānaṃ saṅkhepavissajjanā. Vitthārato pana vesālivatthuto pabhuti porāṇehi vaṇṇīyati.

Now, regarding the phrase 'by whom it was spoken, when, where, and for what reason,' the question is asked: 'By whom, then, was this sutta spoken? When, where, and for what reason was it spoken?' It is said—indeed, this was spoken by the Blessed One alone, not by disciples or others. And it was spoken when the Blessed One was brought to Vesālī, having been invited from Rājagaha by the Licchavis of Vesālī, which was afflicted by calamities such as famine; it was spoken then in Vesālī for the purpose of counteracting those calamities. This is the summary answer to those questions. In detail, however, it is explained by the ancients, beginning with the story of Vesālī.

Tatrāyaṃ vaṇṇanā – bārāṇasirañño kira aggamahesiyā kucchimhi gabbho saṇṭhāsi, sā taṃ [V 0.0128] ñatvā rañño nivedesi, rājā gabbhaparihāraṃ adāsi. Sā sammā parihariyamānagabbhā gabbhaparipākakāle vijāyanagharaṃ pāvisi. Puññavatīnaṃ paccūsasamaye gabbhavuṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Sā ca tāsaṃ aññatarā, tena paccūsasamaye alattakapaṭalabandhujīvakapupphasadisaṃ maṃsapesiṃ vijāyi. Tato “aññā deviyo suvaṇṇabimbasadise putte vijāyanti, aggamahesī maṃsapesinti rañño purato mama avaṇṇo uppajjeyyā”ti cintetvā tena avaṇṇabhayena taṃ maṃsapesiṃ ekasmiṃ bhājane pakkhipitvā aññatarena paṭikujjitvā rājamuddikāya lañchitvā gaṅgāya sote pakkhipāpesi. Manussehi chaḍḍitamatte devatā ārakkhaṃ saṃvidahiṃsu. Suvaṇṇapaṭṭakañcettha jātihiṅgulakena “bārāṇasirañño aggamahesiyā pajā”ti likhitvā bandhiṃsu. Tato taṃ bhājanaṃ ūmibhayādīhi anupaddutaṃ gaṅgāsotena pāyāsi.

Here is the explanation: It is said that the chief queen of the king of Bārāṇasī conceived in her womb. Knowing this, she informed the king, who then provided care during her pregnancy. Being well cared for, she entered the delivery room when the pregnancy came to term. For women of great merit, delivery from the womb occurs at dawn. She, being one of them, gave birth at dawn to a lump of flesh resembling a bandhujīvaka flower the color of lac. Then she thought, 'Other queens give birth to sons like golden images, but if the chief queen gives birth to a lump of flesh, disgrace might befall me before the king.' Fearing this disgrace, she placed the lump of flesh in a vessel, covered it with another, sealed it with the royal seal, and had it cast into the current of the Ganges. As soon as it was discarded by the people, deities arranged for its protection. They wrote on a golden plate with vermilion, 'The offspring of the chief queen of the king of Bārāṇasī,' and fastened it to the vessel. Then, undisturbed by dangers such as waves, the vessel floated along the current of the Ganges.

Tena ca samayena aññataro tāpaso gopālakulaṃ nissāya gaṅgātīre viharati. So pātova gaṅgaṃ otaranto bhājanaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā [M 0.0134] paṃsukūlasaññāya aggahesi. Tato tattha taṃ akkharapaṭṭakaṃ rājamuddikālañchanañca disvā muñcitvā taṃ maṃsapesiṃ addasa[P 0.0159], disvānassa etadahosi “siyā gabbho, tathā hissa duggandhapūtibhāvo natthī”ti. Taṃ assamaṃ netvā suddhe okāse ṭhapesi. Atha aḍḍhamāsaccayena dve maṃsapesiyo ahesuṃ. Tāpaso disvā sādhutaraṃ ṭhapesi, tato puna aḍḍhamāsaccayena ekamekissā pesiyā hatthapādasīsānamatthāya pañca pañca piḷakā uṭṭhahiṃsu. Tāpaso disvā puna sādhutaraṃ ṭhapesi. Atha aḍḍhamāsaccayena ekā maṃsapesi suvaṇṇabimbasadiso dārako, ekā dārikā ahosi. Tesu tāpasassa puttasineho uppajji. Aṅguṭṭhakato cassa khīraṃ nibbatti. Tato pabhuti ca khīrabhattaṃ labhati, so bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā khīraṃ dārakānaṃ mukhe āsiñcati. Tesaṃ yaṃ yaṃ udaraṃ paviṭṭhaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ maṇibhājanagataṃ viya dissati. Evaṃ licchavī ahesuṃ. Apare panāhu “sibbetvā ṭhapitā viya nesaṃ aññamaññaṃ līnā chavi ahosī”ti. Evaṃ te nicchavitāya vā līnacchavitāya vā licchavīti paññāyiṃsu.

At that time, a certain ascetic lived on the bank of the Ganges, relying on a cowherd family for support. Early in the morning, while descending to the Ganges, he saw a vessel coming towards him and, perceiving it to be a dust-heap cloth, he took it. Then, noticing the inscribed plaque and the royal seal there, he opened it and saw the lump of flesh. Upon seeing it, this thought occurred to him: 'It might be a fetus, for indeed it has no foul or putrid quality.' He took it to his hermitage and placed it in a clean spot. After half a month, there were two lumps of flesh. The ascetic saw them and placed them even more carefully. Then, after another half-month, from each lump of flesh, five protrusions arose for the purpose of hands, feet, and a head. Seeing this, the ascetic again placed them even more carefully. After another half-month, one lump of flesh became a boy resembling a golden image, and the other became a girl. Affection for them as his own children arose in the ascetic. Milk issued forth from his thumb. From then on, he would receive milk-rice; having eaten the solid food, he would pour the milk into the children’s mouths. Whatever entered their stomachs was visible as if placed in a jeweled vessel. Thus they were without skin. Others, however, say, 'Their skin was clinging to each other as if sewn and placed.' Thus, they became known as the Licchavis—either because of having no skin (nicchavitāya) or because of having clinging skin (līnacchavitāya).

Tāpaso dārake posento ussūre gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisati, atidivā paṭikkamati. Tassa taṃ byāpāraṃ ñatvā gopālakā āhaṃsu, “bhante, pabbajitānaṃ dārakaposanaṃ palibodho, amhākaṃ dārake detha, mayaṃ posessāma, tumhe attano kammaṃ karothā”ti. Tāpaso “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇi. Gopālakā dutiyadivase maggaṃ samaṃ katvā pupphehi okiritvā dhajapaṭākaṃ ussāpetvā tūriyehi vajjamānehi assamaṃ āgatā. Tāpaso “mahāpuññā dārakā, appamādena vaḍḍhetha, vaḍḍhetvā ca aññamaññaṃ āvāhavivāhaṃ karotha, pañcagorasena rājānaṃ tosetvā bhūmibhāgaṃ gahetvā [V 0.0129] nagaraṃ māpetha, tattha kumāraṃ abhisiñcathā”ti vatvā dārake adāsi. Te “sādhū”ti [P 0.0160] paṭissuṇitvā dārake netvā posesuṃ.

The ascetic, while raising the children, entered the village for alms when the sun was high and returned very late in the day. Knowing his activity, the cowherds said to him, 'Venerable sir, raising children is an encumbrance for those who have gone forth. Give us the children; we will raise them, and you may attend to your own work.' The ascetic agreed, saying, 'Very well.' The next day, the cowherds leveled the path, scattered it with flowers, raised banners and flags, and, with musical instruments playing, came to the hermitage. The ascetic said, 'These children are of great merit. Raise them with diligence, and when they are grown, arrange marriages among them. Please the king with the five products of the cow, receive a portion of land, build a city, and consecrate a prince there.' Having said this, he gave them the children. They agreed, saying, 'Very well,' took the children, and raised them.

Dārakā vuḍḍhimanvāya kīḷantā vivādaṭṭhānesu aññe gopāladārake hatthenapi pādenapi paharanti, te rodanti. “Kissa rodathā”ti ca mātāpitūhi vuttā “ime nimmātāpitikā tāpasapositā amhe atīva paharantī”ti vadanti. Tato tesaṃ mātāpitaro “ime dārakā aññe dārake viheṭhenti dukkhāpenti, na ime saṅgahetabbā, vajjitabbā ime”ti āhaṃsu. Tato pabhuti kira so padeso “vajjī”ti [M 0.0135] vuccati, tiyojanasataṃ parimāṇena. Atha taṃ padesaṃ gopālakā rājānaṃ tosetvā aggahesuṃ. Tattheva nagaraṃ māpetvā soḷasavassuddesikaṃ kumāraṃ abhisiñcitvā rājānaṃ akaṃsu. Tāya cassa dārikāya saddhiṃ vāreyyaṃ katvā katikaṃ akaṃsu “na bāhirato dārikā ānetabbā, ito dārikā na kassaci dātabbā”ti. Tesaṃ paṭhamasaṃvāsena dve dārakā jātā dhītā ca putto ca, evaṃ soḷasakkhattuṃ dve dve jātā. Tato tesaṃ dārakānaṃ yathākkamaṃ vaḍḍhantānaṃ ārāmuyyānanivāsaṭṭhānaparivārasampattiṃ gahetuṃ appahontaṃ taṃ nagaraṃ tikkhattuṃ gāvutantarena gāvutantarena pākārena parikkhipiṃsu, tassa punappunaṃ visālīkatattā vesālītveva nāmaṃ jātaṃ. Idaṃ vesālivatthu.

As the children grew, while playing in places of dispute, they struck the other cowherd children with their hands and feet, and those children cried. When asked by their parents, “Why do you cry?” they said, “These motherless and fatherless children, raised by the ascetic, strike us excessively.” Then the parents of those other children said, “These children harass and cause suffering to other children; they should not be associated with, they should be avoided.” From that time onwards, it is said, that region, measuring three hundred yojanas, came to be called ‘Vajji’. Then the cowherds, having pleased the king, took possession of that region. There they had a city built, and having consecrated the sixteen-year-old prince, they made him king. They arranged a marriage for him with that girl and made an agreement: “A girl is not to be brought from outside, and a girl from here is not to be given to anyone.” By their first union two children were born, a daughter and a son; in this way, sixteen times, two children were born each time. Then, as their children grew in succession, the city being insufficient to hold the abundance of parks, gardens, dwelling places, and retinues, they enclosed that city with a wall three times, with an interval of a gāvuta between each enclosure. Because it was repeatedly made extensive (visālīkatattā), its name became Vesālī. This is the story of Vesālī.

Bhagavato nimantanaṃ

The Invitation to the Blessed One

Ayaṃ pana vesālī bhagavato uppannakāle iddhā vepullappattā ahosi. Tattha hi rājūnaṃyeva satta sahassāni satta satāni satta ca rājāno ahesuṃ. Tathā yuvarājasenāpatibhaṇḍāgārikappabhutīnaṃ[P 0.0161]. Yathāha –

Now this Vesālī, at the time of the Blessed One’s arising, was prosperous and had reached a state of abundance. For there, there were indeed seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven kings. Likewise, there were as many crown princes, generals, treasurers, and so forth. As it is said:

“Tena kho pana samayena vesālī iddhā ceva hoti phītā ca bahujanā ākiṇṇamanussā subhikkhā ca, satta ca pāsādasahassāni satta ca pāsādasatāni satta ca pāsādā, satta ca kūṭāgārasahassāni satta ca kūṭāgārasatāni satta ca kūṭāgārāni, satta ca ārāmasahassāni satta ca ārāmasatāni satta ca ārāmā, satta ca pokkharaṇisahassāni satta ca pokkharaṇisatāni satta ca pokkharaṇiyo”ti (mahāva. 326).

“At that time Vesālī was prosperous and flourishing, populous, crowded with people, and with abundant food. There were seven thousand palaces, seven hundred palaces, and seven palaces; seven thousand pinnacled houses, seven hundred pinnacled houses, and seven pinnacled houses; seven thousand parks, seven hundred parks, and seven parks; and seven thousand lotus ponds, seven hundred lotus ponds, and seven lotus ponds.”

Sā aparena samayena dubbhikkhā ahosi dubbuṭṭhikā dussassā. Paṭhamaṃ duggatamanussā maranti[V 0.0130], te bahiddhā chaḍḍenti. Matamanussānaṃ kuṇapagandhena amanussā nagaraṃ pavisiṃsu, tato bahutarā maranti. Tāya paṭikūlatāya sattānaṃ ahivātarogo uppajji. Iti tīhi dubbhikkhaamanussarogabhayehi upaddutā vesālinagaravāsino upasaṅkamitvā rājānaṃ āhaṃsu, “mahārāja, imasmiṃ nagare tividhaṃ bhayamuppannaṃ, ito pubbe yāva sattamā rājakulaparivaṭṭā evarūpaṃ anuppannapubbaṃ, tumhākaṃ maññe adhammikattena [M 0.0136] taṃ etarahi uppanna”nti. Rājā sabbe santhāgāre sannipātāpetvā “mayhaṃ adhammikabhāvaṃ vicinathā”ti āha. Te sabbaṃ paveṇiṃ vicinantā na kiñci addasaṃsu.

At a later time, that Vesālī was struck by famine, drought, and a poor harvest. First, the destitute people died, and they were discarded outside the city. Due to the stench of the corpses, non-human beings entered the city, and then many more people died. Because of that repulsiveness, a pestilence arose among beings. Thus, afflicted by the three dangers of famine, non-human beings, and disease, the city-dwellers of Vesālī approached the king and said, “Great king, in this city a threefold danger has arisen. Previously, for seven royal generations, such a thing has never occurred. We think it has now arisen due to your unrighteousness.” The king had everyone assemble in the assembly hall and said, “Investigate my unrighteousness.” While investigating the entire tradition, they saw no fault whatsoever.

Tato rañño dosamadisvā “idaṃ bhayaṃ amhākaṃ kathaṃ vūpasameyyā”ti cintesuṃ. Tattha ekacce cha satthāre apadisiṃsu “etehi okkantamatte vūpasamessatī”ti. Ekacce āhaṃsu – “buddho kira loke uppanno, so bhagavā sabbasattahitāya dhammaṃ deseti mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo, tena okkantamatte sabbabhayāni vūpasameyyu”nti. Tena te attamanā hutvā “kahaṃ pana so bhagavā etarahi viharati, amhehi pesito [P 0.0162] na āgaccheyyā”ti āhaṃsu. Athāpare āhaṃsu – “buddhā nāma anukampakā, kissa nāgaccheyyuṃ, so pana bhagavā etarahi rājagahe viharati, rājā bimbisāro taṃ upaṭṭhahati, so āgantuṃ na dadeyyā”ti. “Tena hi rājānaṃ saññāpetvā āneyyāmā”ti dve licchavirājāno mahatā balakāyena pahūtaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ datvā rañño santikaṃ pesiṃsu “bimbisāraṃ saññāpetvā bhagavantaṃ ānethā”ti. Te gantvā rañño paṇṇākāraṃ datvā taṃ pavattiṃ nivedetvā, “mahārāja, bhagavantaṃ amhākaṃ nagaraṃ pesehī”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā na sampaṭicchi, “tumheyeva jānāthā”ti āha. Te bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā evamāhaṃsu – “bhante, amhākaṃ nagare tīṇi bhayāni uppannāni, sace bhagavā āgaccheyya, sotthi no bhaveyyā”ti. Bhagavā āvajjetvā “vesāliyaṃ ratanasutte vutte sā rakkhā koṭisatasahassaṃ cakkavāḷānaṃ pharissati, suttapariyosāne caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo bhavissatī”ti adhivāsesi. Atha rājā bimbisāro bhagavato adhivāsanaṃ sutvā “bhagavatā vesāligamanaṃ adhivāsita”nti nagare ghosanaṃ kārāpetvā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā āha – “kiṃ, bhante, sampaṭicchatha vesāligamana”nti? Āma, mahārājāti. Tena hi, bhante, tāva āgametha, yāva maggaṃ paṭiyādemīti.

Then, not seeing any fault in the king, they thought, “How might this danger of ours be pacified?” There, some pointed to the six teachers, saying, “It will be pacified merely by their arrival.” Others said, “It is said that a Buddha has arisen in the world. That Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for the welfare of all beings; he is of great psychic power and great majesty. Merely by his arrival all dangers would be pacified.” Delighted by this, they said, “But where does that Blessed One now dwell? If sent for by us, he might not come.” Then others said, “Those called Buddhas are compassionate. Why would they not come? However, that Blessed One now dwells in Rājagaha, and King Bimbisāra attends upon him. He might not permit him to come.” Thinking, “In that case, let us inform the king and bring him,” they sent two Licchavi rulers with a great retinue and abundant gifts to the king, saying, “Inform King Bimbisāra and bring the Blessed One.” They went, gave the gifts to the king, related the matter, and said, “Great king, please send the Blessed One to our city.” The king did not consent, saying, “You yourselves should ask him.” They approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and said this: “Venerable sir, three dangers have arisen in our city. If the Blessed One were to come, there would be well-being for us.” The Blessed One reflected, “When the Ratana Sutta is spoken in Vesālī, its protection will pervade one hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems, and at the conclusion of the sutta, there will be a comprehension of the Dhamma for eighty-four thousand beings,” and he consented. Then King Bimbisāra, hearing of the Blessed One’s consent, had a proclamation made in the city: “The Blessed One has consented to go to Vesālī.” He approached the Blessed One and said, “Venerable sir, have you accepted the journey to Vesālī?” “Yes, great king.” “In that case, venerable sir, please wait until I have prepared the road.”

Atha kho rājā bimbisāro rājagahassa ca gaṅgāya ca antarā pañcayojanabhūmiṃ samaṃ katvā yojane yojane vihāraṃ māpetvā bhagavato gamanakālaṃ paṭivedesi. Bhagavā pañcahi bhikkhusatehi parivuto [M 0.0137] pāyāsi. Rājā pañcayojanaṃ maggaṃ pañcavaṇṇehi pupphehi jāṇumattaṃ okirāpetvā [V 0.0131] dhajapaṭākapuṇṇaghaṭakadaliādīni ussāpetvā [P 0.0163] bhagavato dve setacchattāni ekamekassa ca bhikkhussa ekamekaṃ ukkhipāpetvā saddhiṃ attano parivārena pupphagandhādīhi pūjaṃ karonto ekekasmiṃ vihāre bhagavantaṃ vasāpetvā mahādānāni datvā pañcahi divasehi gaṅgātīraṃ nesi. Tattha sabbālaṅkārehi nāvaṃ alaṅkaronto vesālikānaṃ sāsanaṃ pesesi “āgato bhagavā, maggaṃ paṭiyādetvā sabbe bhagavato paccuggamanaṃ karothā”ti. Te “diguṇaṃ pūjaṃ karissāmā”ti vesāliyā ca gaṅgāya ca antarā tiyojanabhūmiṃ samaṃ katvā bhagavato cattāri ekamekassa ca bhikkhussa dve dve setacchattāni sajjetvā pūjaṃ kurumānā gaṅgātīraṃ āgantvā aṭṭhaṃsu.

Then King Bimbisāra, having leveled the five-yojana stretch of land between Rājagaha and the Ganges, had a monastery built at every yojana and had the Blessed One informed of the time for his departure. The Blessed One set out, surrounded by five hundred monks. The king had the five-yojana road strewn knee-deep with flowers of five colors, had banners, flags, full water pots, plantain trees, and so forth erected, and had two white parasols held for the Blessed One and one for each and every monk. Together with his own retinue, making offerings with flowers, perfumes, and so forth, having the Blessed One reside in each and every monastery and giving great alms, in five days he led him to the bank of the Ganges. There, while adorning a boat with all ornaments, he sent a message to the people of Vesālī: “The Blessed One has arrived. Prepare the road and all of you come forth to meet the Blessed One.” They, thinking, “We will make offerings twofold,” leveled the three-yojana stretch of land between Vesālī and the Ganges, prepared four white parasols for the Blessed One and two white parasols for each and every monk, and, making offerings, they came to the bank of the Ganges and stood there.

Atha bimbisāro dve nāvāyo saṅghaṭetvā maṇḍapaṃ katvā pupphadāmādīhi alaṅkaritvā tattha sabbaratanamayaṃ buddhāsanaṃ paññapesi, bhagavā tattha nisīdi. Pañca satā bhikkhūpi nāvaṃ āruhitvā yathānurūpaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Rājā bhagavantaṃ anugacchanto galappamāṇaṃ udakaṃ ogāhetvā “yāva, bhante, bhagavā āgacchati, tāvāhaṃ idheva gaṅgātīre vasissāmī”ti vatvā nivatto. Upari devatā yāva akaniṭṭhabhavanā pūjaṃ akaṃsu. Heṭṭhāgaṅgānivāsino kambalassatarādayo nāgarājāno pūjaṃ akaṃsu. Evaṃ mahatiyā pūjāya bhagavā yojanamattaṃ addhānaṃ gaṅgāya gantvā vesālikānaṃ sīmantaraṃ paviṭṭho.

Then Bimbisāra, having joined two boats and made a pavilion, adorned it with flower garlands and so forth, and there he prepared a Buddha-seat made of all precious gems. The Blessed One sat there. Five hundred monks, having boarded the boat, sat down as was suitable. The king, escorting the Blessed One, entered the water up to the measure of his neck and, saying, “Venerable sir, until the Blessed One returns, I will remain right here on the bank of the Ganges,” he came up from the water. The deities above, up to the Akaniṭṭha realm, made offerings. The Nāga kings dwelling below the Ganges, such as Kambala and Assatara, also made offerings. Thus, with great veneration, the Blessed One, having traveled a distance of about one yojana in the Ganges, entered the territory of the people of Vesālī.

Tato licchavirājāno bimbisārena katapūjāya diguṇaṃ karontā galappamāṇe udake bhagavantaṃ paccuggacchiṃsu. Teneva khaṇena tena muhuttena vijjuppabhāvinaddhandhakāravisaṭakūṭo gaḷagaḷāyanto catūsu disāsu mahāmegho vuṭṭhāsi. Atha bhagavatā paṭhamapāde [P 0.0164] gaṅgātīre nikkhittamatte pokkharavassaṃ vassi. Ye temetukāmā, te eva tementi, atemetukāmā na tementi. Sabbattha jāṇumattaṃ ūrumattaṃ kaṭimattaṃ galappamāṇaṃ udakaṃ vahati, sabbakuṇapāni udakena gaṅgaṃ pavesitāni, parisuddho bhūmibhāgo ahosi.

Then the Licchavi kings, making their offerings twofold more than those made by Bimbisāra, went forth to meet the Blessed One in water up to the measure of their necks. At that very moment, at that instant, a great cloud with a peak of dark clouds dispelled by the light of lightning arose in the four directions, thundering. Then, as soon as the Blessed One placed his first foot on the bank of the Ganges, a lotus-rain fell. Those who wished to be wet were wet; those who did not wish to be wet were not wet. Everywhere, water flowed to the measure of the knee, the thigh, the waist, and the neck. All the corpses were carried into the Ganges by the current of water, and the surface of the land became pure.

Licchavirājāno bhagavantaṃ antarā yojane yojane vāsāpetvā mahādānāni datvā tīhi divasehi diguṇaṃ pūjaṃ karontā vesāliṃ nayiṃsu[M 0.0138]. Vesāliṃ sampatte bhagavati sakko devānamindo devasaṅghapurakkhato āgacchi. Mahesakkhānaṃ devatānaṃ sannipātena amanussā yebhuyyena palāyiṃsu. Bhagavā nagaradvāre ṭhatvā ānandattheraṃ āmantesi – “imaṃ, ānanda, ratanasuttaṃ uggahetvā balikammūpakaraṇāni gahetvā licchavirājakumārehi saddhiṃ vesāliyā tipākārantare vicaranto parittaṃ karohī”ti ratanasuttaṃ abhāsi. “Evaṃ kena panetaṃ suttaṃ vuttaṃ[V 0.0132], kadā, kattha, kasmā ca vutta”nti etesaṃ pañhānaṃ vissajjanā vitthārena vesālivatthuto pabhuti porāṇehi vaṇṇīyati.

The Licchavi kings, having the Blessed One reside at every yojana in the interval, gave great alms, and in three days, making twofold offerings, they led him to Vesālī. When the Blessed One arrived in Vesālī, Sakka, the lord of the devas, came, attended by the assembly of devas. Due to the gathering of deities of great power, the non-human beings, for the most part, fled. The Blessed One, standing at the city gate, addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, learn this Ratana Sutta, take the requisites for the ritual offering, and together with the Licchavi princes, walk within the three walls of Vesālī performing the protection.” Then he spoke the Ratana Sutta. The explanation for the questions, “By whom was this sutta spoken, when, where, and for what reason was it spoken?” is described at length by the ancients, beginning with the story of Vesālī.

Evaṃ bhagavato vesāliṃ anuppattadivaseyeva vesālinagaradvāre tesaṃ upaddavānaṃ paṭighātatthāya vuttamidaṃ ratanasuttaṃ uggahetvā āyasmā ānando parittatthāya bhāsamāno bhagavato pattena udakamādāya sabbanagaraṃ abbhukkiranto anuvicari. Yaṃ kiñcīti vuttamatte eva therena ye pubbe apalātā saṅkārakūṭabhittippadesādinissitā amanussā, te catūhi dvārehi palāyiṃsu, dvārāni anokāsāni ahesuṃ. Tato ekacce dvāresu okāsaṃ alabhamānā pākāraṃ bhinditvā palātā. Amanussesu gatamattesu manussānaṃ gattesu rogo vūpasanto. Te nikkhamitvā sabbapupphagandhādīhi theraṃ pūjesuṃ. Mahājano nagaramajjhe [P 0.0165] santhāgāraṃ sabbagandhehi limpitvā vitānaṃ katvā sabbālaṅkārehi alaṅkaritvā tattha buddhāsanaṃ paññapetvā bhagavantaṃ ānesi.

Thus, on the very day the Blessed One arrived in Vesālī, the Venerable Ānanda learned this Ratana Sutta, which had been spoken at the city gate of Vesālī to ward off those calamities. Taking water in the Blessed One's bowl, he walked about, sprinkling it throughout the entire city while reciting for protection. As soon as the Elder recited the words “Yaṃ kiñci,” the non-human beings who had not fled before and were clinging to places like rubbish heaps and wall areas fled through the four gates; the gates afforded no passage. Then some, unable to find an opportunity at the gates, broke through the city wall and fled. As soon as the non-human beings were gone, the disease in the bodies of the humans subsided. They came out and honored the Elder with all kinds of flowers, perfumes, and so forth. The great populace prepared the assembly hall in the middle of the city, anointing it with all perfumes, setting up a canopy, and decorating it with all ornaments. There they prepared the Buddha-seat and brought the Blessed One.

Bhagavā santhāgāraṃ pavisitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi. Bhikkhusaṅghopi kho rājāno manussā ca patirūpe patirūpe āsane nisīdiṃsu. Sakkopi devānamindo dvīsu devalokesu devaparisāya saddhiṃ upanisīdi aññe ca devā, ānandattheropi sabbaṃ vesāliṃ anuvicaranto rakkhaṃ katvā vesālinagaravāsīhi saddhiṃ āgantvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Tattha bhagavā sabbesaṃ tadeva ratanasuttaṃ abhāsīti.

The Blessed One entered the assembly hall and sat down on the prepared seat. The Saṅgha of monks, the kings, and the people also sat down in their respective suitable places. Sakka, the lord of the devas, together with the divine assembly from the two deva worlds, sat nearby. Other devas also sat down. The Venerable Ānanda, having walked about all of Vesālī and provided protection, came together with the inhabitants of the city of Vesālī and sat in a suitable place. There, the Blessed One taught that very Ratana Sutta to all of them.

Ettāvatā ca yā “yena vuttaṃ yadā yattha, yasmā cetaṃ imaṃ nayaṃ. Pakāsetvānā”ti mātikā nikkhittā, sā sabbappakārena vitthāritā hoti.

And by this much, the outline which was set down, stating, “By whom it was spoken, when, where, and for what reason this method was explained,” has been elaborated in all its aspects.

Yānīdhātigāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Verse Beginning 'Yānīdha'

1. Idāni [M 0.0139] “etassa karissāmatthavaṇṇana”nti vuttattā atthavaṇṇanā ārabbhate. Apare pana vadanti “ādito pañceva gāthā bhagavatā vuttā, sesā parittakaraṇasamaye ānandattherenā”ti. Yathā vā tathā vā hotu, kiṃ no imāya parikkhāya, sabbathāpi etassa ratanasuttassa karissāmatthavaṇṇanaṃ.

Now, since it was said, "We will make an explanation of the meaning of this," the explanation of the meaning begins. Others, however, say, "Only the first five verses were spoken by the Blessed One; the rest, by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of reciting the protective verses." Whether it is so or not, what is the use of this inquiry? In any case, we will make an explanation of the meaning of this Ratana Sutta.

Yānīdha bhūtānīti paṭhamagāthā. Tattha yānīti yādisāni appesakkhāni vā mahesakkhāni vā. Idhāti imasmiṃ padese, tasmiṃ khaṇe sannipātaṭṭhānaṃ sandhāyāha. Bhūtānīti kiñcāpi [V 0.0133] bhūtasaddo “bhūtasmiṃ pācittiya”nti evamādīsu (pāci. 69) vijjamāne. “Bhūtamidanti, bhikkhave[P 0.0166], samanupassathā”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 1.401) khandhapañcake. “Cattāro kho, bhikkhu, mahābhūtā hetū”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 3.86) catubbidhe pathavīdhātvādirūpe. “Yo ca kālaghaso bhūto”ti evamādīsu (jā. 1.2.190) khīṇāsave. “Sabbeva nikkhipissanti, bhūtā loke samussaya”nti evamādīsu (dī. ni. 2.220) sabbasatte. “Bhūtagāmapātabyatāyā”ti evamādīsu (pāci. 90) rukkhādike. “Bhūtaṃ bhūtato sañjānātī”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 1.3) cātumahārājikānaṃ heṭṭhā sattanikāyaṃ upādāya vattati. Idha pana avisesato amanussesu daṭṭhabbo.

1. "Whatever beings there are" is the first verse. Here, "whatever" refers to those that are of little power or of great power. "Here" means in this place, at this moment, referring to the place of assembly. "Beings"—though the term "bhūta" is found in contexts like "in a bhūta, a pācittiya offense" (Pāc. 69), referring to what is actual; or in phrases like "See this as a bhūta" (Ma. Ni. 1.401) referring to the five aggregates; or "Monk, the four great bhūtas are causes" (Ma. Ni. 3.86) referring to the fourfold elements such as the earth element; or "One who has become a time-eater" (Jā. 1.2.190), referring to an Arahant whose taints are destroyed; or "All bhūtas in the world will cast off their accumulation" (Dī. Ni. 2.220) referring to all beings; or "the destruction of a bhūta village" (Pāc. 90) referring to trees and the like; or "perceives a being as a being" (Ma. Ni. 1.3), which applies to the host of beings below the realm of the Four Great Kings—here, however, it should be understood without distinction as referring to non-human beings.

Samāgatānīti sannipatitāni. Bhummānīti bhūmiyaṃ nibbattāni. Vā-iti vikappane. Tena yānīdha bhummāni vā bhūtāni samāgatānīti imamekaṃ vikappaṃ katvā puna dutiyavikappaṃ kātuṃ “yāni va antalikkhe”ti āha. Antalikkhe vā yāni bhūtāni nibbattāni, tāni sabbāni idha samāgatānīti attho. Ettha ca yāmato yāva akaniṭṭhaṃ, tāva nibbattāni bhūtāni ākāse pātubhūtavimānesu nibbattattā “antalikkhe bhūtānī”ti veditabbāni. Tato heṭṭhā sineruto pabhuti yāva bhūmiyaṃ rukkhalatādīsu adhivatthāni pathaviyañca nibbattāni bhūtāni, tāni sabbāni bhūmiyaṃ bhūmipaṭibaddhesu ca rukkhalatāpabbatādīsu nibbattattā “bhummāni bhūtānī”ti veditabbāni.

"Samāgatānīti" means gathered together. "Bhummānīti" means those born on the ground. "Vā-iti" indicates an alternative. Therefore, having made one alternative here—"whatever beings here have gathered, whether born on the ground"—he then presents a second alternative by saying, "or whatever are in the sky." The meaning is: whatever beings are born in the sky, all of them have gathered here. In this context, beings born from the Yāma realm up to Akaniṭṭha should be understood as "beings in the sky," because they are born in celestial mansions manifesting in space. Below that, from Mount Sineru down to the ground, the beings dwelling in trees, vines, and so on, and those born on the earth—all of them should be understood as 'beings born on the ground' because they are born on the earth and in things connected to the earth, such as trees, vines, mountains, and the like.

Evaṃ [M 0.0140] bhagavā sabbāneva amanussabhūtāni “bhummāni vā yāni va antalikkhe”ti dvīhi padehi vikappetvā puna ekena padena pariggahetvā dassetuṃ “sabbeva bhūtā sumanā bhavantū”ti āha. Sabbeti anavasesā. Evāti avadhāraṇe, ekampi anapanetvāti adhippāyo. Bhūtāti amanussā. Sumanā bhavantūti sukhitamanā pītisomanassajātā bhavantu. Athopīti kiccantarasanniyojanatthaṃ vākyopādāne nipātadvayaṃ. Sakkacca suṇantu bhāsitanti aṭṭhiṃ [P 0.0167] katvā manasikatvā sabbaṃ cetasā samannāharitvā dibbasampattilokuttarasukhāvahaṃ mama desanaṃ suṇantu.

Thus, the Blessed One, having distinguished all non-human beings with the two phrases 'whether terrestrial or aerial,' and then encompassing them again with one phrase in order to teach them, declared, 'May all beings be of happy mind.' 'All' means without exception. The particle 'eva' is for emphasis, the intention being that not even one is excluded. 'Beings' refers to non-humans. 'May they be of happy mind' means may they be of joyful mind, born of gladness and delight. 'Moreover' is a pair of particles for connecting the sentence by introducing another purpose. 'Let them listen attentively to what is spoken' means let them listen with earnest attention, giving full mental application, to my teaching which brings divine attainments and supramundane happiness.

Evamettha bhagavā “yānīdha bhūtāni samāgatānī”ti aniyamitavacanena bhūtāni pariggahetvā puna “bhummāni vā yāni va antalikkhe”ti dvidhā vikappetvā tato “sabbeva bhūtā”ti puna ekajjhaṃ katvā “sumanā bhavantū”ti iminā vacanena āsayasampattiyaṃ niyojento “sakkacca suṇantu bhāsita”nti payogasampattiyaṃ, tathā yonisomanasikārasampattiyaṃ [V 0.0134] paratoghosasampattiyañca, tathā attasammāpaṇidhisappurisūpanissayasampattīsu samādhipaññāhetusampattīsu ca niyojento gāthaṃ samāpesi.

In this way, the Blessed One, having gathered the beings with the unrestricted phrase 'whatever beings are gathered here,' then differentiated them into two with 'whether on the ground or in the sky,' and then unified them again with 'all beings,' with the words 'may they be of joyful mind,' directed them towards the accomplishment of inclination (āsayasampatti). With 'let them listen attentively to what is spoken,' he directed them toward the accomplishment of effort (payogasampatti), and likewise, the accomplishment of wise reflection (yonisomanasikārasampatti) and the accomplishment of sound from another (paratoghosasampatti), as well as toward the accomplishments of self-directed right resolve, reliance on noble persons, and the accomplishments of the causes for concentration and wisdom. Thus, he concluded the verse.

Tasmā hītigāthāvaṇṇanā

The commentary on the verse beginning 'Tasmā hi'.

2. Tasmā hi bhūtāti dutiyagāthā. Tattha tasmāti kāraṇavacanaṃ. Bhūtāti āmantanavacanaṃ. Nisāmethāti suṇātha. Sabbeti anavasesā. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yasmā tumhe dibbaṭṭhānāni tattha upabhogaparibhogasampadañca pahāya dhammassavanatthaṃ idha samāgatā, na naṭanaccanādidassanatthaṃ, tasmā hi bhūtā nisāmetha sabbeti. Atha vā “sumanā bhavantu, sakkacca suṇantū”ti vacanena tesaṃ sumanabhāvaṃ sakkaccaṃ sotukamyatañca disvā āha “yasmā tumhe sumanabhāvena attasammāpaṇidhiyonisomanasikārāsayasuddhīhi sakkaccaṃ sotukamyatāya sappurisūpanissayaparatoghosapadaṭṭhānato payogasuddhīhi ca yuttā, tasmā hi bhūtā nisāmetha sabbe”ti. Atha vā yaṃ [M 0.0141] purimagāthāya ante “bhāsita”nti vuttaṃ, taṃ kāraṇabhāvena apadisanto āha “yasmā mama bhāsitaṃ nāma atidullabhaṃ aṭṭhakkhaṇaparivajjitassa khaṇassa dullabhattā, anekānisaṃsañca paññākaruṇāguṇena pavattattā, tañcāhaṃ vattukāmo ‘suṇantu bhāsita’nti avocaṃ, tasmā hi bhūtā nisāmetha sabbe”ti. Idaṃ iminā gāthāpadena vuttaṃ hoti.

2. “Tasmā hi bhūtā” (Therefore, O beings)—this is the second verse. Therein, “tasmā” (therefore) is a word indicating a reason. “Bhūtā” (O beings) is a word of address. “Nisāmetha” means “listen.” “Sabbe” (all) means “without remainder.” What is meant? “Because you have abandoned the divine abodes and the perfection of enjoyments therein, and have gathered here for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma—not for the purpose of seeing dancers, actors, and the like—for that very reason, O beings, all of you, listen.” Or else, having seen their joyful state and their desire to listen respectfully through the words, “May they be joyful, may they listen carefully,” he said: “Because you are endowed with a joyful state of mind—with the right establishment of self, proper attention, and purity of intention—and with the desire to listen respectfully—with purity of effort arising from the proximate causes of associating with good persons and the voice of another—for that very reason, O beings, all of you, listen.” Or else, pointing to what was said at the end of the previous verse—“bhāsitaṃ” (spoken)—as a reason, he said: “Because my spoken word is exceedingly difficult to obtain, due to the difficulty of obtaining the opportune moment that is free from the eight inopportune moments, and because it brings many benefits, being set forth through the quality of wisdom and compassion—and I wish to speak it, having said, ‘Let them listen to what is spoken’—for that very reason, O beings, all of you, listen.” This is what is said by this verse-line.

Evametaṃ kāraṇaṃ niropento attano bhāsitanisāmane niyojetvā nisāmetabbaṃ vattumāraddho [P 0.0168] “mettaṃ karotha mānusiyā pajāyā”ti. Tassattho – yāyaṃ tīhi upaddavehi upaddutā mānusī pajā, tassā mānusiyā pajāya mettaṃ mittabhāvaṃ hitajjhāsayataṃ paccupaṭṭhapethāti. Keci pana “mānusikaṃ paja”nti paṭhanti, taṃ bhummatthāsambhavā na yujjati. Yampi aññe atthaṃ vaṇṇayanti, sopi na yujjati. Adhippāyo panettha – nāhaṃ buddhoti issariyabalena vadāmi, api tu yaṃ tumhākañca imissā ca mānusiyā pajāya hitatthaṃ vadāmi “mettaṃ karotha mānusiyā pajāyā”ti. Ettha ca –

Thus, having established this reason and having urged them to heed what he had spoken, he began to say what should be heeded: “Cultivate loving-kindness for the human populace.” The meaning is this: For this human populace, which is afflicted by three calamities, you should establish loving-kindness, a state of friendliness, and a disposition of wishing for their welfare. Some teachers, however, read “mānusikaṃ pajaṃ” (the human-like populace), but that is not suitable as it is not possible in the terrestrial sense. And whatever other meaning other teachers explain, that too is not suitable. Here, however, the intention should be understood thus: “I do not speak as ‘the Buddha’ with the power of sovereignty; rather, I speak what is for the welfare of both you and this human populace: ‘Cultivate loving-kindness for the human populace.’” And here—

“Ye sattasaṇḍaṃ pathaviṃ vijetvā,

Rājisayo yajamānānupariyagā;

Assamedhaṃ purisamedhaṃ,

Sammāpāsaṃ vājapeyyaṃ niraggaḷaṃ.

“Those royal sages who, having conquered the host of enemies upon the earth, wandered about as sacrificers, having performed the horse sacrifice, the human sacrifice, the Sammāpāsa, the Vājapeyya, and the Niraggaḷa.”

“Mettassa [V 0.0135] cittassa subhāvitassa,

Kalampi te nānubhavanti soḷasiṃ;

Ekampi ce pāṇamaduṭṭhacitto,

Mettāyati kusalo tena hoti.

“Of a well-developed mind of loving-kindness, they do not experience even a sixteenth part. If, with a mind free from ill will, one extends loving-kindness towards even a single living being, by that one becomes meritorious.”

“Sabbe ca pāṇe manasānukampī, pahūtamariyo pakaroti puñña”nti. (itivu. 27; a. ni. 8.1) –

“Having compassion in mind for all beings, the noble one generates abundant merit.”

Evamādīnaṃ suttānaṃ ekādasānisaṃsānañca vasena ye mettaṃ karonti, etesaṃ mettā hitāti veditabbā.

It should be known that for those who cultivate loving-kindness by means of such suttas and the eleven benefits, loving-kindness is for their welfare.

“Devatānukampito poso, sadā bhadrāni passatī”ti. (udā. 76; mahāva. 286) –

“The person cherished by deities always sees auspicious things.”

Evamādīnaṃ [M 0.0142] suttānaṃ vasena yesu kayirati, tesampi hitāti veditabbā.

By means of such discourses, it should be understood that it is for the welfare of those also towards whom it is practiced.

Evaṃ ubhayesampi hitabhāvaṃ dassento “mettaṃ karotha mānusiyā”ti vatvā idāni upakārampi dassento āha [P 0.0169] “divā ca ratto ca haranti ye baliṃ, tasmā hi ne rakkhatha appamattā”ti. Tassattho – ye manussā cittakammakaṭṭhakammādīhipi devatā katvā cetiyarukkhādīni ca upasaṅkamitvā devatā uddissa divā baliṃ karonti, kālapakkhādīsu ca rattiṃ baliṃ karonti, salākabhattādīni vā datvā ārakkhadevatā upādāya yāva brahmadevatānaṃ pattidānaniyyātanena divā baliṃ karonti, chattāropanadīpamālāya sabbarattikadhammassavanādīni kārāpetvā pattidānaniyyātanena ca rattiṃ baliṃ karonti, te kathaṃ na rakkhitabbā? Yato evaṃ divā ca ratto ca tumhe uddissa karonti ye baliṃ, tasmā hi ne rakkhatha; tasmā balikammakaraṇāpi te manusse rakkhatha gopayatha, ahitaṃ nesaṃ apanetha, hitaṃ upanetha appamattā hutvā taṃ kataññubhāvaṃ hadaye katvā niccamanussarantāti.

Thus, wishing to show that it is for the welfare of both parties, having said, “Cultivate loving-kindness for the human populace,” he now, wishing also to show the service they render, said: “Those who bring offerings by day and by night, therefore, protect them heedfully.” The meaning is this: Those humans who, having made images of deities through painting, woodwork, and so on, and having approached shrines, trees, and the like, make offerings by day dedicated to the deities; and who make offerings at night during the dark fortnights and so on; or who, having given alms such as ticket-food, make offerings by day by dedicating the share of merit to the guardian deities up to the Brahma-devas; and who, having arranged for the raising of umbrellas, the lighting of lamps and garlands, the listening to the Dhamma all night, and so on, make offerings at night by dedicating the share of the gift—for what reason should they not be protected? Since they make offerings dedicated to you both day and night, for that very reason, protect them. Therefore, because of their making of offerings, protect and guard those humans. Remove what is not for their welfare. Being heedful, placing in your hearts the fact of gratitude for what they have done and constantly recollecting it, bring them what is for their welfare.

Yaṃkiñcītigāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Verse Beginning 'Yaṃkiñci'

3. Evaṃ devatāsu manussānaṃ upakārakabhāvaṃ dassetvā tesaṃ upaddavavūpasamanatthaṃ buddhādiguṇappakāsanena [V 0.0136] ca devamanussānaṃ dhammassavanatthaṃ “yaṃkiñci vitta”ntiādinā nayena saccavacanaṃ payuñjitumāraddho. Tattha yaṃkiñcīti aniyamitavasena anavasesaṃ pariyādiyati yaṃkiñci tattha tattha vohārūpagaṃ. Vittanti dhanaṃ. Tañhi vittiṃ janetīti vittaṃ. Idha vāti manussalokaṃ niddisati. Huraṃ vāti tato paraṃ avasesalokaṃ, tena ca ṭhapetvā manusse sabbalokaggahaṇe patte “saggesu vā”ti parato vuttattā ṭhapetvā manusse ca sagge ca avasesānaṃ nāgasupaṇṇādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ.

3. Having thus shown the helpful nature of humans towards deities, for the sake of pacifying the afflictions of those humans, and by proclaiming the virtues of the Buddha and others for the sake of gods and humans hearing the Dhamma, he began to employ a statement of truth by the method beginning with 'Whatever wealth...' Herein, by the word 'whatever' (yaṃkiñci), it is taken to encompass everything without remainder by way of being unrestricted—whatever in various places is suitable for trade. 'Wealth' (vittaṃ) means riches. For it generates delight (vittiṃ), therefore it is called 'wealth' (vittaṃ). 'Here' (idha vā) indicates the human world. 'Or beyond' (huraṃ vā) means the remaining world other than that. And by this, although the meaning of including all worlds, having excluded the human world, is arrived at, because 'or in the heavens' (saggesu vā) is stated later, it should be understood as the inclusion of the remaining beings such as nāgas, supaṇṇas, and so on, having excluded both humans and the heavens.

Evaṃ imehi dvīhi padehi yaṃ manussānaṃ vohārūpagaṃ alaṅkāraparibhogūpagañca jātarūparajatamuttāmaṇiveḷuriyapavāḷalohitaṅkamasāragallādikaṃ, yañca muttāmaṇivālukatthatāya bhūmiyā ratanamayavimānesu anekayojanasatavitthatesu [P 0.0170] bhavanesu uppannānaṃ nāgasupaṇṇādīnaṃ vittaṃ, taṃ niddiṭṭhaṃ hoti. Saggesu vāti kāmāvacararūpāvacaradevalokesu. Te [M 0.0143] hi sobhanena kammena ajīyantīti saggā. Suṭṭhu aggātipi saggā. Yanti yaṃ sasāmikaṃ vā asāmikaṃ vā. Ratananti ratiṃ nayati vahati janayati vaḍḍhetīti ratanaṃ. Yaṃkiñci cittīkataṃ mahagghaṃ atulaṃ dullabhadassanaṃ anomasattaparibhogañca, tassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Yathāha –

Thus, by these two terms ['here' and 'beyond'], whatever wealth of humans is suitable for trade, adornment, and use—such as gold, silver, pearls, gems, beryl, coral, rubies, spotted gems, and the like; and whatever wealth of nāgas, supaṇṇas, and others who have arisen in jeweled mansions stretching for many hundreds of yojanas, on ground layered with pearls and gems—all this is indicated. 'Or in the heavens' (saggesu vā) means in the sense-sphere and form-sphere celestial worlds. They are called 'heavens' (saggā) because they are brought into being by beautiful kamma. Alternatively, they are 'supremely excellent' (suṭṭhu aggā), thus they are also called 'heavens' (saggā). 'Whatever' (yaṃ) means that which is with an owner or without an owner. 'Jewel' (ratanaṃ) is so called because it leads to (nayati), carries (vahati), generates (janayati), or increases (vaḍḍheti) delight (ratiṃ). It is a designation for whatever is esteemed, of great price, incomparable, rare to see, and used by superior beings. As it is said:

“Cittīkataṃ mahagghañca, atulaṃ dullabhadassanaṃ;

Anomasattaparibhogaṃ, ratanaṃ tena vuccatī”ti.

That which is esteemed and of great price, incomparable and rare to see, and used by superior beings—therefore it is called a jewel.

Paṇītanti uttamaṃ seṭṭhaṃ atappakaṃ. Evaṃ iminā gāthāpadena yaṃ saggesu anekayojanasatappamāṇasabbaratanamayavimānasudhammavejayantappabhutīsu sasāmikaṃ, yañca buddhuppādavirahena apāyameva paripūrentesu sattesu suññavimānappaṭibaddhaṃ asāmikaṃ, yaṃ vā panaññampi pathavimahāsamuddahimavantādinissitamasāmikaṃ ratanaṃ, taṃ niddiṭṭhaṃ hoti.

'Excellent' (paṇītaṃ) means supreme, best, priceless. Thus, by this verse-phrase, it is indicated: whatever jewel in the heavens has an owner—in the Sudhammā, Vejayanta, and other celestial mansions made entirely of every kind of jewel and measuring many hundreds of yojanas; and whatever ownerless jewel is connected with empty mansions, because beings, in the absence of a Buddha's arising, are only filling the planes of misery; or whatever other ownerless jewel is dependent on the earth, the great ocean, the Himalayas, and so on—all this is indicated.

Na no samaṃ atthi tathāgatenāti na-iti paṭisedhe. No-iti avadhāraṇe. Samanti tulyaṃ. Atthīti vijjati. Tathāgatenāti buddhena. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yaṃ etaṃ vittañca ratanañca pakāsitaṃ, ettha ekampi buddharatanena sadisaṃ ratanaṃ nevatthi. Yampi hi taṃ cittīkataṭṭhena ratanaṃ, seyyathidaṃ – rañño cakkavattissa cakkaratanaṃ maṇiratanañca, yamhi uppanne mahājano na aññattha cittīkāraṃ karoti, na koci pupphagandhādīni gahetvā yakkhaṭṭhānaṃ vā bhūtaṭṭhānaṃ vā gacchati, sabbopi jano cakkaratanamaṇiratanameva cittīkāraṃ karoti pūjeti, taṃ taṃ varaṃ pattheti, patthitapatthitañcassa ekaccaṃ samijjhati, tampi ratanaṃ buddharatanena samaṃ natthi. Yadi hi [V 0.0137] cittīkataṭṭhena ratanaṃ, tathāgatova ratanaṃ. Tathāgate [P 0.0171] hi uppanne ye keci mahesakkhā devamanussā na te aññatra cittīkāraṃ karonti, na kañci aññaṃ pūjenti. Tathā hi brahmā sahampati sinerumattena ratanadāmena tathāgataṃ pūjesi, yathābalañca aññe devā manussā ca bimbisārakosalarājaanāthapiṇḍikādayo. Parinibbutampi bhagavantaṃ uddissa channavutikoṭidhanaṃ vissajjetvā asokamahārājā sakalajambudīpe caturāsīti vihārasahassāni patiṭṭhāpesi, ko pana vādo aññesaṃ cittīkārānaṃ. Apica kassaññassa parinibbutassāpi jātibodhidhammacakkappavattanaparinibbānaṭṭhānāni paṭimācetiyādīni vā uddissa evaṃ cittīkāragarukāro pavattati yathā bhagavato. Evaṃcittīkataṭṭhenāpi tathāgatasamaṃ ratanaṃ natthi.

'There is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata.' Here, 'na' is a particle of negation. 'No' is a particle of emphasis. 'Samaṃ' means equal. 'Atthi' means it exists. 'Tathāgatena' means with the Buddha. What is meant? Of that wealth and that jewel which have been declared, not even one jewel is similar to the Buddha-jewel. For even that which is a jewel in the sense of being esteemed—for instance, the wheel-jewel and the gem-jewel of a wheel-turning monarch. When these appear, the great populace does not pay reverence elsewhere; no one takes flowers, fragrances, and so on, and goes to a shrine of a yakkha or a spirit. The entire populace pays reverence only to the wheel-jewel and the gem-jewel; they worship them and ask for this or that boon, and for that person, some of what is wished for is fulfilled. Even that jewel is not equal to the Buddha-jewel. For if something is a jewel in the sense of being esteemed, then the Tathāgata alone is the jewel. When the Tathāgata appears, whatever powerful gods and humans there are, they do not pay reverence to another; they do not worship any other. Thus, Brahmā Sahampati worshipped the Tathāgata with a jeweled garland the size of Mount Sineru; and other gods, and humans such as King Bimbisāra, the King of Kosala, Anāthapiṇḍika, and others, did so according to their ability. Even with regard to the Blessed One after he had attained Parinibbāna, the great King Asoka, having given up wealth of ninety-six crores, established eighty-four thousand monasteries throughout all of Jambudīpa. What, then, can be said of the reverence of others? Furthermore, for which other person who has attained Parinibbāna does such reverence and respect arise in connection with the sites of their birth, enlightenment, the turning of the Dhamma-wheel, and Parinibbāna, or with regard to images, cetiyas, and so on, as it does for the Blessed One? Thus, even in the sense of being esteemed, there is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata.

Tathā [M 0.0144] yampi taṃ mahagghaṭṭhena ratanaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – kāsikaṃ vatthaṃ. Yathāha – “jiṇṇampi, bhikkhave, kāsikaṃ vatthaṃ vaṇṇavantañceva hoti sukhasamphassañca mahagghañcā”ti (a. ni. 3.100), tampi buddharatanena samaṃ natthi. Yadi hi mahagghaṭṭhena ratanaṃ, tathāgatova ratanaṃ. Tathāgato hi yesaṃ paṃsukampi paṭiggaṇhāti, tesaṃ taṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti mahānisaṃsaṃ seyyathāpi asokarañño, idamassa mahagghatāya. Evaṃ mahagghatāvacanena cettha dosābhāvasādhakaṃ idaṃ suttapadaṃ veditabbaṃ –

Likewise, there is that which is a jewel in the sense of being of great price. For instance, cloth from Kāsī. As it is said: 'Monks, even when old, cloth from Kāsī is beautiful, pleasant to the touch, and of great price.' Even that is not equal to the Buddha-jewel. For if something is a jewel in the sense of being of great price, then the Tathāgata alone is the jewel. For when the Tathāgata accepts even a handful of dust from someone, for them that gift becomes of great fruit and great benefit—as in the case of King Asoka. This is on account of the Buddha's great value. Thus, in connection with this statement about 'great value,' this following Sutta passage should be understood as establishing the absence of fault:

“Yesaṃ kho pana so paṭiggaṇhāti cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāraṃ, tesaṃ taṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti mahānisaṃsaṃ. Idamassa mahagghatāya vadāmi. Seyyathāpi taṃ, bhikkhave, kāsikaṃ vatthaṃ mahagghaṃ, tathūpamāhaṃ, bhikkhave, imaṃ puggalaṃ vadāmī”ti (a. ni. 3.100).

'From whomever he accepts the requisites of robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicines for the sick, for them that is of great fruit, of great benefit. This I say on account of his great value. Just as, monks, that cloth from Kāsī is of great price, so too, monks, do I declare this person to be of great price.'

Evaṃ mahagghaṭṭhenapi tathāgatasamaṃ ratanaṃ natthi.

Thus, even in the sense of being of great price, there is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata.

Tathā yampi taṃ atulaṭṭhena [P 0.0172] ratanaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – rañño cakkavattissa cakkaratanaṃ uppajjati indanīlamaṇimayanābhi sattaratanamayasahassāraṃ pavāḷamayanemi rattasuvaṇṇamayasandhi, yassa dasannaṃ dasannaṃ arānamupari ekaṃ muṇḍāraṃ hoti vātaṃ gahetvā saddakaraṇatthaṃ, yena kato saddo sukusalappatāḷitapañcaṅgikatūriyasaddo viya hoti, yassa nābhiyā ubhosu passesu dve sīhamukhāni honti, abbhantaraṃ sakaṭacakkasseva susiraṃ. Tassa kattā vā kāretā vā natthi, kammapaccayena ututo samuṭṭhāti. Yaṃ rājā dasavidhaṃ cakkavattivattaṃ pūretvā tadahuposathe puṇṇamadivase sīsaṃnhāto uposathiko uparipāsādavaragato sīlāni sodhento nisinno puṇṇacandaṃ [V 0.0138] viya sūriyaṃ viya ca uṭṭhentaṃ passati, yassa dvādasayojanato saddo suyyati, yojanato vaṇṇo dissati, yaṃ mahājanena “dutiyo maññe cando sūriyo vā uṭṭhito”ti ativiya kotūhalajātena dissamānaṃ nagarassa upari āgantvā rañño antepurassa pācīnapasse nātiuccaṃ nātinīcaṃ hutvā mahājanassa gandhapupphādīhi pūjetuṃ, yuttaṭṭhāne akkhāhataṃ viya tiṭṭhati.

Furthermore, whatever jewel there is, it is called a jewel because of its incomparable nature. To wit: the wheel-treasure of a wheel-turning king arises. It has a hub made of Indanīla jewel, a thousand spokes made of the seven kinds of jewels, a rim made of coral, and joints made of red gold. Above every ten of its spokes, there is a single bell for making a sound by catching the wind. The sound made by it is like the sound of a five-piece orchestra played by a very skilled musician. At its hub, on both sides, there are two lion's-mouth shapes, and the inside is hollow like a cartwheel. It has no maker, nor one who causes it to be made; it arises from the season, conditioned by kamma. The king, having fulfilled the tenfold duties of a wheel-turning monarch, on that Uposatha day, the day of the full moon, having bathed his head, observing the Uposatha, seated in the upper excellent palace purifying his precepts, sees it rising like the full moon and like the sun. Its sound is heard from twelve yojanas away, and its radiance is seen from one yojana. Being seen by the great multitude of people with exceedingly aroused curiosity, thinking, 'I believe a second moon or sun has risen!', it comes above the city and, at the eastern side of the king's inner palace, being not too high and not too low, it stands in a suitable place for the great multitude to honor with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as if with a broken axle.

Tadeva [M 0.0145] anubandhamānaṃ hatthiratanaṃ uppajjati, sabbaseto rattapādo sattappatiṭṭho iddhimā vehāsaṅgamo uposathakulā vā chaddantakulā vā āgacchati, uposathakulā ca āgacchanto sabbajeṭṭho āgacchati, chaddantakulā sabbakaniṭṭho sikkhitasikkho damathūpeto, so dvādasayojanaṃ parisaṃ gahetvā sakalajambudīpaṃ anusaṃyāyitvā purepātarāsameva sakaṃ rājadhāniṃ āgacchati.

Following that very wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure arises. It is completely white, with red feet, firmly established in seven places, endowed with psychic power, and able to travel through the sky. It comes from either the Uposatha clan or the Chaddanta clan. When coming from the Uposatha clan, the most senior of all comes. When coming from the Chaddanta clan, the youngest of all comes, with training perfected and endowed with discipline. Taking a retinue of twelve yojanas, it traverses the entire Jambudīpa and returns to its own royal capital before the morning meal.

Tampi anubandhamānaṃ assaratanaṃ uppajjati, sabbaseto rattapādo kāḷasīso muñjakeso valāhakassarājakulā āgacchati. Sesamettha hatthiratanasadisameva.

Following that also, the horse-treasure arises. It is completely white, with red feet and a black head, and has a mane like munja grass; it comes from the royal clan of Valāhaka horses. The rest in this matter is the same as for the elephant-treasure.

Tampi anubandhamānaṃ maṇiratanaṃ [P 0.0173] uppajjati. So hoti maṇi veḷuriyo subho jātimā aṭṭhaṃso suparikammakato āyāmato cakkanābhisadiso, vepullapabbatā āgacchati. So caturaṅgasamannāgatepi andhakāre rañño dhajaggaṃ gato yojanaṃ obhāseti, yassobhāsena manussā “divā”ti maññamānā kammante payojenti, antamaso kunthakipillikaṃ upādāya passanti.

Following that also, the gem-treasure arises. That gem is a beryl, beautiful, of noble origin, eight-faceted, and well-fashioned. In length, it is like the hub of a cartwheel, and it comes from Mount Vepulla. Even in the fourfold darkness, when placed at the tip of the king's banner, it illuminates for a yojana. By its radiance, people, thinking it is day, apply themselves to their work; they can see everything down to the last ant and small insect.

Tampi anubandhamānaṃ itthiratanaṃ uppajjati, pakatiaggamahesī vā hoti, uttarakuruto vā āgacchati maddarājakulato vā, atidīghatādichadosavivajjitā atikkantā mānusavaṇṇaṃ appattā dibbavaṇṇaṃ, yassā rañño sītakāle uṇhāni gattāni honti, uṇhakāle sītāni, satadhā phoṭita tūlapicuno viya samphasso hoti, kāyato candanagandho vāyati, mukhato uppalagandho, pubbuṭṭhāyinitādianekaguṇasamannāgatā ca hoti.

Following that also, the woman-treasure arises. She is either the natural chief queen, or she comes from Uttarakuru, or from the royal clan of Madda. She is devoid of the faults beginning with being too tall; she has surpassed the human complexion but has not attained the divine complexion. For the king, in the cold season her limbs are warm, and in the hot season they are cool. Her touch is like a ball of cotton carded a hundred times. From her body wafts the scent of sandalwood, and from her mouth the scent of the blue lotus. And she is endowed with many virtues, such as being the first to rise.

Tampi anubandhamānaṃ gahapatiratanaṃ uppajjati rañño pakatikammakāro seṭṭhi, yassa cakkaratane uppannamatte dibbaṃ cakkhu pātubhavati, yena samantato yojanamatte nidhiṃ passati asāmikampi sasāmikampi, so rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pavāreti “appossukko tvaṃ, deva, hohi, ahaṃ te dhanena dhanakaraṇīyaṃ karissāmī”ti.

Following that also, the householder-treasure arises. He is the king's regular steward, a setthi, in whom, as soon as the wheel-treasure has arisen, the divine eye manifests. With it, he sees treasure for a yojana all around, both that which is ownerless and that which has an owner. He approaches the king and offers, saying: 'Be without anxiety, Your Majesty. I will perform for you with wealth the duties that are to be done with wealth.'

Tampi [V 0.0139][M 0.0146] anubandhamānaṃ pariṇāyakaratanaṃ uppajjati rañño pakatijeṭṭhaputto. Cakkaratane uppannamatte atirekapaññāveyyattiyena samannāgato hoti, dvādasayojanāya parisāya cetasā cittaṃ parijānitvā niggahapaggahasamattho hoti, so rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pavāreti “appossukko tvaṃ, deva, hohi, ahaṃ te rajjaṃ anusāsissāmī”ti. Yaṃ vā panaññampi evarūpaṃ atulaṭṭhena ratanaṃ, yassa na sakkā tulayitvā tīrayitvā aggho kātuṃ “sataṃ vā sahassaṃ vā agghati koṭiṃ vā”ti. Tattha ekaratanampi buddharatanena samaṃ [P 0.0174] natthi. Yadi hi atulaṭṭhena ratanaṃ, tathāgatova ratanaṃ. Tathāgato hi na sakkā sīlato vā samādhito vā paññādīnaṃ vā aññatarato kenaci tulayitvā tīrayitvā “ettakaguṇo vā iminā samo vā sappaṭibhāgo vā”ti paricchindituṃ. Evaṃ atulaṭṭhenapi tathāgatasamaṃ ratanaṃ natthi.

Following that also, the counselor-treasure arises; he is the king's natural eldest son. As soon as the wheel-treasure has arisen, he becomes endowed with surpassing wisdom and discernment. He is capable of knowing with his own mind the minds of the twelve-yojana assembly and is able to restrain and encourage them. He approaches the king and offers, saying: 'Be without anxiety, Your Majesty. I will administer the kingdom for you.' Or whatever other such jewel there may be that is a jewel because of its incomparable nature, one whose value cannot be determined by weighing and assessing, saying, 'It is worth a hundred, or a thousand, or a koṭi.' Among them, not even one jewel is equal to the Buddha-treasure. For if there is a jewel because of its incomparable nature, the Tathāgata alone is that jewel. Indeed, the Tathāgata cannot be defined by anyone by weighing or assessing him in terms of virtue, or concentration, or any of the qualities beginning with wisdom, saying, 'He has such-and-such qualities,' or 'He is equal to this one,' or 'He has a counterpart.' Thus, even in terms of being incomparable, there is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata.

Tathā yampi taṃ dullabhadassanaṭṭhena ratanaṃ, seyyathidaṃ dullabhapātubhāvo rājā cakkavatti, cakkādīni ca tassa ratanāni, tampi buddharatanena samaṃ natthi. Yadi hi dullabhadassanaṭṭhena ratanaṃ, tathāgatova ratanaṃ, kuto cakkavattiādīnaṃ ratanattaṃ. Tāni hi ekasmiṃyeva kappe anekāni uppajjanti. Yasmā pana asaṅkhyeyyepi kappe tathāgatasuñño loko hoti, tasmā tathāgatova kadāci karahaci uppajjanato dullabhadassano. Vuttampi cetaṃ bhagavatā parinibbānasamaye –

Furthermore, whatever is a jewel because of its nature of being difficult to see—to wit, the wheel-turning king, whose appearance is rare, and his jewels beginning with the wheel-treasure—even that is not equal to the Buddha-treasure. For if there is a jewel because of its nature of being difficult to see, the Tathāgata alone is that jewel. How then could the wheel-turning king and the others have the state of being a jewel? For those arise many times in a single eon. But because the world is empty of a Tathāgata for even innumerable eons, therefore the Tathāgata alone, arising only sometime or other, is difficult to see. And this was also said by the Blessed One at the time of his final passing—

“Devatā, ānanda, ujjhāyanti ‘dūrā ca vatamha āgatā tathāgataṃ dassanāya, kadāci karahaci tathāgatā loke uppajjanti arahanto sammāsambuddhā, ajjeva rattiyā pacchime yāme tathāgatassa parinibbānaṃ bhavissati, ayañca mahesakkho bhikkhu bhagavato purato ṭhito ovārento, na mayaṃ labhāma pacchime kāle tathāgataṃ dassanāyā’”ti (dī. ni. 2.200).

“Ānanda, the deities are complaining: ‘Indeed, we have come from afar to see the Tathāgata, for only rarely do Tathāgatas, Arahants, Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones, arise in the world. And tonight, in the last watch of the night, the Tathāgata’s final passing away will occur. But this mighty monk is standing in front of the Blessed One, obstructing us, and we are unable to see the Tathāgata in this final moment!’”

Evaṃ dullabhadassanaṭṭhenāpi tathāgatasamaṃ ratanaṃ natthi.

Thus, even in the sense of being difficult to see, there is no gem equal to the Tathāgata.

Tathā yampi taṃ anomasattaparibhogaṭṭhena ratanaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – rañño cakkavattissa cakkaratanādi tañhi koṭisatasahassadhanānampi sattabhūmikapāsādavaratale [M 0.0147] vasantānampi caṇḍālavenanesādarathakārapukkusādīnaṃ nīcakulikānaṃ omakapurisānaṃ supinantepi [P 0.0175] paribhogatthāya na nibbattati. Ubhato sujātassa pana rañño khattiyasseva paripūritadasavidhacakkavattivattassa paribhogatthāya nibbattanato anomasattaparibhogaṃyeva hoti, tampi buddharatanasamaṃ natthi. Yadi hi anomasattaparibhogaṭṭhena [V 0.0140] ratanaṃ, tathāgatova ratanaṃ. Tathāgato hi loke omakasattasammatānaṃ anupanissayasampannānaṃ viparītadassanānaṃ pūraṇakassapādīnaṃ channaṃ satthārānaṃ aññesañca evarūpānaṃ supinantepi aparibhogo. Upanissayasampannānaṃ pana catuppadāyapi gāthāya pariyosāne arahattamadhigantuṃ samatthānaṃ nibbedhikañāṇadassanānaṃ bāhiyadārucīriyappabhutīnaṃ aññesañca mahākulappasutānaṃ mahāsāvakānaṃ paribhogo, te hi taṃ dassanānuttariyasavanānuttariyapāricariyānuttariyādīni sādhentā tathāgataṃ paribhuñjanti. Evaṃ anomasattaparibhogaṭṭhenāpi tathāgatasamaṃ ratanaṃ natthi.

Similarly, with regard to that which is a gem in the sense of being enjoyed by non-inferior beings. Namely, the wheel-gem of a wheel-turning monarch and so on. For that gem does not arise for the enjoyment, even in a dream, of outcastes, bamboo-workers, hunters, cartwrights, refuse-removers, and other low-born, inferior men, even if they possess wealth worth a hundred thousand crores and dwell in an excellent seven-storied palace. But it arises for the enjoyment of a king, a Khattiya, who is well-born on both sides and has fully accomplished the ten duties of a wheel-turning monarch; thus, it is indeed enjoyed by non-inferior beings. Yet even that is not equal to the Buddha-gem. For if there is a gem in the sense of being enjoyed by non-inferior beings, the Tathāgata alone is the gem. For the Tathāgata is not enjoyed even in dreams by those in the world who are considered lowly—the six teachers, such as Pūraṇa Kassapa, and others of that kind, who lack the supporting conditions and have perverse views. But he is enjoyed by those endowed with the supporting conditions, who are capable of attaining arahantship at the conclusion even of a four-line verse—those with penetrating knowledge and vision, like Bāhiya Dārucīriya and others, and other great disciples born into great families. For they enjoy the Tathāgata by accomplishing the unsurpassed sight, unsurpassed hearing, unsurpassed service, and so on. Thus, even in the sense of being enjoyed by non-inferior beings, there is no gem equal to the Tathāgata.

Yampi taṃ avisesato ratijananaṭṭhena ratanaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – rañño cakkavattissa cakkaratanaṃ. Tañhi disvāva rājā cakkavatti attamano hoti, evampi taṃ rañño ratiṃ janeti. Puna caparaṃ rājā cakkavatti vāmena hatthena suvaṇṇabhiṅkāraṃ gahetvā dakkhiṇena hatthena cakkaratanaṃ abbhukkirati “pavattatu bhavaṃ cakkaratanaṃ, abhivijinātu bhavaṃ cakkaratana”nti. Tato cakkaratanaṃ pañcaṅgikaṃ viya tūriyaṃ madhurassaraṃ niccharantaṃ ākāsena puratthimaṃ disaṃ gacchati[P 0.0176], anvadeva rājā, cakkavatti cakkānubhāvena dvādasayojanavitthiṇṇāya caturaṅginiyā senāya nātiuccaṃ nātinīcaṃ uccarukkhānaṃ heṭṭhābhāgena, nīcarukkhānaṃ uparibhāgena, rukkhesu pupphaphalapallavādipaṇṇākāraṃ gahetvā āgatānaṃ hatthato paṇṇākārañca gaṇhanto “ehi kho, mahārājā”ti evamādinā paramanipaccakārena āgate paṭirājāno “pāṇo na hantabbo”tiādinā nayena anusāsanto gacchati. Yattha pana rājā bhuñjitukāmo vā divāseyyaṃ vā kappetukāmo hoti, tattha cakkaratanaṃ ākāsā orohitvā udakādisabbakiccakkhame same bhūmibhāge akkhāhataṃ viya tiṭṭhati. Puna rañño gamanacitte uppanne purimanayeneva saddaṃ karontaṃ gacchati, taṃ sutvā dvādasayojanikāpi parisā ākāsena gacchati[M 0.0148]. Cakkaratanaṃ anupubbena puratthimaṃ samuddaṃ ajjhogāhati, tasmiṃ ajjhogāhante udakaṃ yojanappamāṇaṃ apagantvā bhittīkataṃ viya tiṭṭhati. Mahājano yathākāmaṃ satta ratanāni gaṇhāti. Puna rājā suvaṇṇabhiṅkāraṃ gahetvā “ito paṭṭhāya mama rajja”nti udakena abbhukkiritvā nivattati. Senā purato hoti, cakkaratanaṃ pacchato, rājā majjhe. Cakkaratanena osakkitosakkitaṭṭhānaṃ udakaṃ paripūrati. Eteneva upāyena dakkhiṇapacchimuttarepi samudde gacchati.

And there is that which is a gem in the sense of universally generating delight. Namely, the wheel-gem of a wheel-turning monarch. For upon seeing it, the wheel-turning monarch becomes delighted; thus, it generates delight for the king. Furthermore, the wheel-turning monarch takes a golden pitcher in his left hand and sprinkles the wheel-gem with his right hand, saying, ‘May the noble wheel-gem roll forth, may the noble wheel-gem conquer!’ Then the wheel-gem, emitting a sweet sound like a five-piece orchestra, moves through the sky toward the eastern direction. Following it, the wheel-turning king, by the wheel’s power, travels with his fourfold army—spanning twelve yojanas—neither too high nor too low, passing beneath the tall trees and above the short ones, receiving from the hands of those who have come the offerings of flowers, fruits, sprouts, and so on from the trees, and instructing the rival kings who have come with the utmost reverence, saying, ‘Come, great king,’ and so on, with principles such as ‘Living beings should not be killed.’ But wherever the king wishes to eat or to rest during the day, there the wheel-gem descends from the sky and stands on level ground suitable for all tasks such as fetching water, as if its axle were broken. Again, when the king’s mind turns to traveling, it goes, making a sound in the same manner as before. Hearing that, his twelve-yojana-wide retinue also travels through the sky. The wheel-gem gradually submerges into the eastern ocean, and as it submerges, the water recedes for a yojana, standing as if it were a wall. The great multitude takes the seven gems as they please. Again, the king takes the golden pitcher and, sprinkling water, declares, ‘From here onward, this is my kingdom,’ before turning back. The army is in front, the wheel-gem is behind, and the king is in the middle. The water fills back into the places from which the wheel-gem had retreated. In this same way, he travels to the southern, western, and northern oceans as well.

Evaṃ catuddisaṃ anusaṃyāyitvā cakkaratanaṃ tiyojanappamāṇaṃ ākāsaṃ ārohati. Tattha ṭhito rājā cakkaratanānubhāvena vijitavijayo pañcasataparittadīpapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ sattayojanasahassaparimaṇḍalaṃ [V 0.0141] pubbavidehaṃ, tathā aṭṭhayojanasahassaparimaṇḍalaṃ uttarakuruṃ, sattayojanasahassaparimaṇḍalaṃyeva [P 0.0177] aparagoyānaṃ, dasayojanasahassaparimaṇḍalaṃ jambudīpañcāti evaṃ catumahādīpadvisahassaparittadīpapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ ekaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ suphullapuṇḍarīkavanaṃ viya oloketi. Evaṃ olokayato cassa anappakā rati uppajjati. Evampi taṃ cakkaratanaṃ rañño ratiṃ janeti, tampi buddharatanasamaṃ natthi. Yadi hi ratijananaṭṭhena ratanaṃ, tathāgatova ratanaṃ, kiṃ karissati etaṃ cakkaratanaṃ? Tathāgato hi yassā dibbāya ratiyā cakkaratanādīhi sabbehipi janitā cakkavattirati saṅkhampi kalampi kalabhāgampi na upeti, tatopi ratito uttaritarañca paṇītatarañca attano ovādappaṭikarānaṃ asaṅkhyeyyānampi devamanussānaṃ paṭhamajjhānaratiṃ dutiyatatiyacatutthapañcamajjhānaratiṃ, ākāsānañcāyatanaratiṃ, viññāṇañcāyatanaākiñcaññāyatananevasaññānāsaññāyatanaratiṃ, sotāpattimaggaratiṃ, sotāpattiphalaratiṃ, sakadāgāmianāgāmiarahattamaggaphalaratiñca janeti. Evaṃ ratijananaṭṭhenāpi tathāgatasamaṃ ratanaṃ natthīti.

Having thus traveled around the four directions, the Wheel-jewel rises into the sky to a height of three hundred yojanas. Standing there, the king, victorious over the conquered by the power of the Wheel-jewel, surveys Pubbavideha, adorned with five hundred minor islands and measuring seven thousand yojanas in circumference; similarly, Uttarakuru, measuring eight thousand yojanas in circumference; Aparagoyāna, measuring seven thousand yojanas in circumference; and Jambudīpa, measuring ten thousand yojanas in circumference. Thus, he beholds this world-system, adorned with the four great continents and two thousand minor islands, like a fully bloomed lotus forest. As he gazes upon it, great joy arises in him. In this way, too, the Wheel-jewel generates joy for the king, yet it is not equal to the Buddha-jewel. For if a jewel is so called by reason of generating joy, then the Tathāgata alone is the jewel; what can this Wheel-jewel do? For the joy of a wheel-turning monarch, produced by all jewels beginning with the Wheel-jewel, does not amount to even a calculation, a part, or a fraction of that divine joy. And beyond that joy, the Tathāgata generates for countless devas and humans who follow his instruction a joy that is even higher and more sublime: the joy of the first jhāna, the second, third, fourth, and fifth jhānas; the joy of the base of boundless space, the base of boundless consciousness, the base of nothingness, and the base of neither perception nor non-perception; the joy of the path of stream-entry, the fruit of stream-entry, and the paths and fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship. Thus, even by reason of generating joy, there is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata.

Apica ratanaṃ nāmetaṃ duvidhaṃ hoti saviññāṇakamaviññāṇakañca. Tattha aviññāṇakaṃ cakkaratanaṃ maṇiratanañca, yaṃ vā panaññampi anindriyabaddhasuvaṇṇarajatādi, saviññāṇakaṃ hatthiratanādipariṇāyakaratanapariyosānaṃ, yaṃ vā panaññampi evarūpaṃ indriyabaddhaṃ. Evaṃ duvidhe cettha saviññāṇakaratanaṃ aggamakkhāyati[M 0.0149]. Kasmā? Yasmā aviññāṇakaṃ suvaṇṇarajatamaṇimuttādiratanaṃ saviññāṇakānaṃ hatthiratanādīnaṃ alaṅkāratthāya upanīyati.

Furthermore, this so-called jewel is of two kinds: conscious and unconscious. Among these, the unconscious are the Wheel-jewel and the Gem-jewel, or any other such as gold and silver not connected with faculties. The conscious are the jewels from the Elephant-jewel to the Counselor-jewel, or any other of such a kind that is connected with faculties. Of these two, the conscious jewel is declared supreme. Why? Because unconscious jewels such as gold, silver, gems, and pearls are brought for the purpose of adorning conscious jewels such as the Elephant-jewel and others.

Saviññāṇakaratanampi duvidhaṃ tiracchānagataratanaṃ, manussaratanañca. Tattha manussaratanaṃ aggamakkhāyati. Kasmā? Yasmā tiracchānagataratanaṃ manussaratanassa opavayhaṃ [P 0.0178] hoti. Manussaratanampi duvidhaṃ itthiratanaṃ, purisaratanañca. Tattha purisaratanaṃ aggamakkhāyati. Kasmā? Yasmā itthiratanaṃ purisaratanassa paricārikattaṃ āpajjati. Purisaratanampi duvidhaṃ agārikaratanaṃ, anagārikaratanañca. Tattha anagārikaratanaṃ aggamakkhāyati. Kasmā? Yasmā agārikaratanesu aggo cakkavattipi sīlādiguṇayuttaṃ anagārikaratanaṃ pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā upaṭṭhahitvā payirupāsitvā dibbamānusikā sampattiyo pāpuṇitvā ante nibbānasampattiṃ pāpuṇāti.

The conscious jewel is also of two kinds: the animal-jewel and the human-jewel. Among these, the human-jewel is declared supreme. Why? Because the animal-jewel serves as a vehicle for the human-jewel. The human-jewel is also twofold: the woman-jewel and the man-jewel. Among these, the man-jewel is declared supreme. Why? Because the woman-jewel attains the state of an attendant to the man-jewel. The man-jewel is also twofold: the householder-jewel and the homeless-jewel. Among these, the homeless-jewel is declared supreme. Why? Because even the foremost among householder-jewels, the wheel-turning monarch, after paying homage with the five-point prostration, attending upon, and revering the homeless-jewel who is endowed with virtues such as morality, attains divine and human prosperity, and in the end, attains the prosperity of Nibbāna.

Evaṃ anagārikaratanampi duvidhaṃ ariyaputhujjanavasena. Ariyaratanampi duvidhaṃ sekhāsekhavasena. Asekharatanampi duvidhaṃ sukkhavipassakasamathayānikavasena. Samathayānikaratanampi [V 0.0142] duvidhaṃ sāvakapāramippattamappattañca. Tattha sāvakapāramippattaṃ aggamakkhāyati. Kasmā? Guṇamahantatāya. Sāvakapāramippattaratanatopi paccekabuddharatanaṃ aggamakkhāyati. Kasmā? Guṇamahantatāya. Sāriputtamoggallānasadisāpi hi anekasatā sāvakā ekassa paccekabuddhassa guṇānaṃ satabhāgampi na upenti. Paccekabuddharatanatopi sammāsambuddharatanaṃ aggamakkhāyati. Kasmā? Guṇamahantatāya. Sakalampi hi jambudīpaṃ pūretvā pallaṅkena pallaṅkaṃ ghaṭentā nisinnā paccekabuddhā ekassa sammāsambuddhassa guṇānaṃ neva saṅkhaṃ na kalaṃ na kalabhāgaṃ upenti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā – “yāvatā, bhikkhave, sattā apadā vā…pe… tathāgato tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”tiādi (a. ni. 4.34; 5.32; itivu. 90). Evaṃ kenaci pariyāyena tathāgatasamaṃ ratanaṃ natthi. Tenāha bhagavā – “na no samaṃ atthi [P 0.0179] tathāgatenā”ti.

Thus, the homeless-jewel is also twofold, by way of noble ones and ordinary persons. The noble-jewel is also twofold, by way of trainees and those beyond training. The jewel of those beyond training is also twofold, by way of dry-insight practitioners and serenity-vehicle practitioners. The serenity-vehicle practitioner-jewel is also twofold: those who have attained the perfection of a disciple and those who have not. Among them, the one who has attained the perfection of a disciple is declared supreme. Why? By reason of the greatness of their qualities. The Paccekabuddha-jewel is declared supreme even over the jewel of one who has attained the perfection of a disciple. Why? By reason of the greatness of their qualities.
