For even many hundreds of disciples like Sāriputta and Moggallāna do not attain even a hundredth part of the qualities of a single Paccekabuddha. The Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha-jewel is declared supreme even over the Paccekabuddha-jewel. Why? By reason of the greatness of their qualities. For even if the entire Jambudīpa were filled with Paccekabuddhas sitting with cross-legged posture touching cross-legged posture, they would not attain a number, a fraction, or a fractional part of the qualities of a single Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha. This has been said by the Blessed One: 'Monks, as far as there are beings, whether footless or... the Tathāgata is declared supreme among them,' and so on. Thus, in no way is there a jewel equal to the Tathāgata. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'There is none equal to the Tathāgata.'

Evaṃ bhagavā buddharatanassa aññehi ratanehi asamataṃ vatvā idāni tesaṃ sattānaṃ uppannaupaddavavūpasamatthaṃ neva jātiṃ na gottaṃ na kolaputtiyaṃ na vaṇṇapokkharatādiṃ nissāya, apica kho avīcimupādāya bhavaggapariyante [M 0.0150] loke sīlasamādhikkhandhādīhi guṇehi buddharatanassa asadisabhāvaṃ nissāya saccavacanaṃ payuñjati “idampi buddhe ratanaṃ paṇītaṃ, etena saccena suvatthi hotū”ti.

Thus, having declared the Buddha-jewel's unequalledness with other jewels, the Blessed One now employs a statement of truth for the sake of pacifying the arisen dangers for those beings, relying not on birth, clan, family status, or perfection of complexion and the like, but rather, relying on the unequalled nature of the Buddha-jewel due to qualities such as the aggregates of morality and concentration in the world extending from Avīci up to the peak of existence: 'This, too, is an excellent jewel in the Buddha; by this truth, may there be well-being!'

Tassattho – idampi idha vā huraṃ vā saggesu vā yaṃkiñci atthi vittaṃ vā ratanaṃ vā, tena saddhiṃ tehi tehi guṇehi asamattā buddhe ratanaṃ paṇītaṃ. Yadi hi etaṃ saccaṃ, atha etena saccena imesaṃ pāṇīnaṃ suvatthi hotu, sobhanānaṃ atthitā hotu arogatā nirupaddavatāti. Ettha ca yathā “cakkhu kho, ānanda, suññaṃ attena vā attaniyena vā”ti evamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 4.85) attabhāvena vā attaniyabhāvena vāti attho. Itarathā hi cakkhu attā vā attaniyaṃ vāti appaṭisiddhameva siyā. Evaṃ ratanaṃ paṇītanti ratanattaṃ paṇītaṃ, ratanabhāvo paṇītoti ayamattho veditabbo. Itarathā hi buddho neva ratananti sijjheyya. Na hi yattha ratanaṃ atthi, taṃ ratananti na sijjhati. Yattha pana cittīkatādiatthasaṅkhātaṃ yena vā tena vā vidhinā sambandhagataṃ ratanaṃ atthi, yasmā taṃ ratanattamupādāya ratananti paññāpīyati, tasmā tassa ratanassa atthitāya ratananti sijjhati. Atha vā idampi buddhe ratananti imināpi pakārena buddhova ratananti evamattho veditabbo. Vuttamattāya ca bhagavatā imāya gāthāya rājakulassa sotthi jātā, bhayaṃ vūpasantaṃ. Imissā gāthāya āṇā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu amanussehi paṭiggahitāti.

The meaning of that verse should be known thus: Whatever wealth or jewel exists here in this human world, or in the realm of Nagas and Garudas, or in the celestial worlds, this jewel in the Buddha is excellent, being unequal to that worldly wealth on account of its various qualities. If this statement is true, then by this truth may there be well-being for these beings; may there be the existence of splendors, freedom from illness, and freedom from danger. And here, just as in such passages as, 'The eye, Ānanda, is empty of self or of what belongs to self,' the meaning should be understood as: it is empty of a self-entity or of what belongs to a self-entity. For otherwise, it would not have been refuted that the eye is self or belongs to self. Similarly, here in the phrase 'the jewel is excellent,' the meaning to be understood is: 'the state of being a jewel is excellent, the nature of a jewel is excellent.' For otherwise, it would not be established that the Buddha is a jewel. For surely, where a jewel exists, it is established as a jewel. But where there exists the state of being a jewel, which is connected by some means or other and is reckoned as having the meaning of being revered, etc., since it is designated a 'jewel' on account of that state of being a jewel, therefore, due to the existence of that state of being a jewel, it is established that the Buddha is a jewel. Alternatively, by this phrase 'this too is a jewel in the Buddha', the meaning should be understood thus: the Buddha himself is the jewel. And merely by this verse having been spoken by the Blessed One, well-being arose for the royal family, and fear was pacified. The command of this verse was accepted by non-human beings in a hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems.

Khayaṃ virāgantigāthāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Verse beginning 'Destruction, Dispassion'

4. Evaṃ [V 0.0143][P 0.0180] buddhaguṇena saccaṃ vatvā idāni nibbānadhammaguṇena vattumāraddho “khayaṃ virāga”nti. Tattha yasmā nibbānasacchikiriyāya rāgādayo khīṇā honti parikkhīṇā, yasmā vā taṃ tesaṃ anuppādanirodhakkhayamattaṃ, yasmā ca taṃ rāgādivippayuttaṃ sampayogato ca ārammaṇato ca, yasmā vā tamhi sacchikate rāgādayo accantaṃ virattā honti vigatā viddhastā, tasmā khayanti ca virāganti ca vuccati. Yasmā panassa na uppādo paññāyati, na vayo, na ṭhitassa aññathattaṃ tasmā taṃ na jāyati na jīyati na mīyatīti katvā amatanti vuccati. Uttamatthena pana atappakaṭṭhena ca paṇītanti. Yadajjhagāti yaṃ ajjhagā vindi paṭilabhi, attano ñāṇabalena sacchākāsi. Sakyamunīti [M 0.0151] sakyakulappasutattā sakyo, moneyyadhammasamannāgatattā muni, sakyo eva muni sakyamuni. Samāhitoti ariyamaggasamādhinā samāhitacitto. Na tena dhammena samatthi kiñcīti tena khayādināmakena sakyamuninā adhigatena dhammena samaṃ kiñci dhammajātaṃ natthi. Tasmā suttantarepi vuttaṃ – “yāvatā, bhikkhave, dhammā saṅkhatā vā asaṅkhatā vā, virāgo tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”tiādi (a. ni. 4.34; itivu. 90).

4. Having thus spoken the truth by means of the qualities of the Buddha, he now began to speak by means of the qualities of the Dhamma of Nibbāna, with the verse beginning 'Destruction, Dispassion.' Herein, because, through the realization of Nibbāna, lust and so forth are destroyed, completely destroyed; or because for the noble ones it has reached the state of destruction which is non-arising and cessation; and because it is dissociated from lust and so forth, both in terms of association and in terms of object; or because, when it is realized, lust and so forth become completely dispassionate, departed, and destroyed—therefore it is called 'Destruction' and 'Dispassion.' Moreover, because its arising is not apparent, nor its decay, nor any alteration of its state, therefore, thinking, 'It is not born, it does not age, it does not die,' it is called the 'Deathless.' And it is called 'excellent' in the sense of being supreme and in the sense of not causing torment. 'Which he attained' means: that which he attained, found, obtained; he realized it with the power of his own knowledge. 'The Sakyan Sage' means: a Sakyan because he was born in the Sakya clan, and a Muni because he was endowed with the practice of a sage; the Sakyan who is a Muni is the Sakyamuni. 'Concentrated' means: with a mind concentrated by the concentration of the noble path. 'There is nothing equal to that Dhamma' means: there is no kind of phenomenon whatsoever that is equal to that Dhamma, named 'Destruction' and so on, which was realized by the Sakyan Sage. Therefore, it is also said in another sutta: 'Monks, as far as conditioned or unconditioned phenomena go, dispassion is declared the highest among them,' and so on.

Evaṃ bhagavā nibbānadhammassa aññehi dhammehi asamataṃ vatvā idāni tesaṃ sattānaṃ uppannaupaddavavūpasamatthaṃ khayavirāgāmatapaṇītatāguṇehi nibbānadhammaratanassa asadisabhāvaṃ nissāya saccavacanaṃ payuñjati “idampi dhamme ratanaṃ paṇītaṃ, etena saccena suvatthi hotū”ti. Tassattho purimagāthāya vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Imissāpi gāthāya āṇā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu amanussehi paṭiggahitāti.

Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken of the inequality of the Dhamma of Nibbāna with other dhammas, now, for the pacification of the arisen dangers for those beings, employs a statement of truth, relying on the incomparable nature of the Dhamma-jewel with its qualities of being destruction, dispassion, deathless, and excellent: 'This too is an excellent jewel in the Dhamma. By this truth, may there be well-being.' Its meaning should be known in the very same way as stated in the preceding verse. The command of this verse too was accepted by non-human beings in a hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems.

Yaṃ buddhaseṭṭhotigāthāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Verse “What the Supreme Buddha...”

5. Evaṃ nibbānadhammaguṇena saccaṃ vatvā idāni maggadhammaguṇena vattumāraddho “yaṃ buddhaseṭṭho”ti. Tattha “bujjhitā saccānī”tiādinā nayena buddho[P 0.0181], uttamo pasaṃsanīyo cāti seṭṭho, buddho ca so seṭṭho cāti buddhaseṭṭho, anubuddhapaccekabuddhasutabuddhakhyesu vā buddhesu seṭṭhoti buddhaseṭṭho. So buddhaseṭṭho yaṃ parivaṇṇayī “aṭṭhaṅgikova maggānaṃ, khemaṃ nibbānapattiyā”ti (ma. ni. 2.215) ca “ariyaṃ vo, bhikkhave, sammāsamādhiṃ desissāmi saupanisaṃ saparikkhāra”nti (ma. ni. 3.136) ca evamādinā nayena tattha tattha [V 0.0144] pasaṃsi pakāsayi. Sucinti kilesamalasamucchedakaraṇato accantavodānaṃ. Samādhimānantarikaññamāhūti yañca attano pavattisamanantaraṃ niyameneva phalapadānato “ānantarikasamādhī”ti āhu. Na hi maggasamādhimhi uppanne tassa phaluppattinisedhako koci antarāyo atthi. Yathāha –

5. Having thus spoken the truth by means of the qualities of the Dhamma of Nibbāna, he now begins to speak by means of the qualities of the Dhamma of the path, with the verse beginning 'What the Supreme Buddha...'. Herein, by the method of 'having understood the truths,' etc., he is a Buddha. Because he is supreme and praiseworthy, he is 'seṭṭha'. He is a Buddha and he is 'seṭṭha', thus he is 'buddhaseṭṭha' (the Supreme Buddha). Or, among the Buddhas known as Anubuddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Sutabuddhas, he is supreme, thus he is 'buddhaseṭṭha'. That Supreme Buddha praised it, saying, “Of paths, the eightfold is for reaching Nibbāna, the secure,” and “Monks, I will teach you the noble right concentration with its supports and requisites,” and in this way praised and revealed it in various places. 'Pure' means utterly stainless because it cuts off the stain of defilements. And that which they call 'immediate concentration' is so called because it inevitably bestows its fruit immediately after its own arising. For when the path-concentration has arisen, there is no obstacle whatsoever that prevents the arising of its fruit. As it is said:

“Ayañca puggalo sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipanno assa, kappassa ca uḍḍayhanavelā assa, neva tāva kappo uḍḍayheyya, yāvāyaṃ puggalo na sotāpattiphalaṃ sacchikaroti, ayaṃ [M 0.0152] vuccati puggalo ṭhitakappī. Sabbepi maggasamaṅgino puggalā ṭhitakappino”ti (pu. pa. 17).

“And if this person is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, and it is the time for the burning up of an eon, the eon would not burn up so long as this person has not realized the fruit of stream-entry. This person is called one whose eon stands still. All persons endowed with the path are ones whose eon stands still.”

Samādhinā tena samo na vijjatīti tena buddhaseṭṭhaparivaṇṇitena sucinā ānantarikasamādhinā samo rūpāvacarasamādhi vā arūpāvacarasamādhi vā koci na vijjati. Kasmā? Tesaṃ bhāvitattā tattha tattha brahmaloke upapannassāpi puna nirayādīsupi upapattisambhavato, imassa ca arahattasamādhissa bhāvitattā ariyapuggalassa sabbūpapattisamugghātasambhavato. Tasmā suttantarepi vuttaṃ – “yāvatā, bhikkhave, dhammā [P 0.0182] saṅkhatā…pe… ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo, tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”tiādi (a. ni. 4.34; itivu. 90).

“There is no equal to that concentration” means that no concentration whatsoever, whether it be a concentration of the form realm or a concentration of the formless realm, is equal to that pure, immediate concentration which has been extolled by the Supreme Buddha. Why is this so? Because, through the development of those other concentrations, even one who has arisen in this or that Brahma world may still possibly arise again in the hells and other such states. However, through the development of this concentration of Arahantship, the complete uprooting of all future arising is possible for a noble individual. Therefore, it is also stated in another sutta: “Monks, inasmuch as there are conditioned phenomena... the Noble Eightfold Path is declared the foremost among them.”

Evaṃ bhagavā ānantarikasamādhissa aññehi samādhīhi asamataṃ vatvā idāni purimanayeneva maggadhammaratanassa asadisabhāvaṃ nissāya saccavacanaṃ payuñjati “idampi dhamme…pe… hotū”ti. Tassattho pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Imissāpi gāthāya āṇā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu amanussehi paṭiggahitāti.

Having thus spoken of the incomparability of the immediate concentration with other concentrations, the Blessed One now, in the same manner as before, employs a statement of truth based on the peerless nature of the Dhamma-jewel of the path, saying: “This too in the Dhamma... may there be well-being.” Its meaning should be understood in the same way as previously explained. The command of this verse was also accepted by non-human beings in one hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems.

Ye puggalātigāthāvaṇṇanā

The explanation of the verse beginning “Those Persons”

6. Evaṃ maggadhammaguṇenāpi saccaṃ vatvā idāni saṅghaguṇenāpi vattumāraddho “ye puggalā”ti. Tattha yeti aniyametvā uddeso. Puggalāti sattā. Aṭṭhāti tesaṃ gaṇanaparicchedo. Te hi cattāro ca paṭipannā cattāro ca phale ṭhitāti aṭṭha honti. Sataṃ pasatthāti sappurisehi buddhapaccekabuddhabuddhasāvakehi aññehi ca devamanussehi pasatthā. Kasmā? Sahajātasīlādiguṇayogā. Tesañhi campakavakulakusumādīnaṃ sahajātavaṇṇagandhādayo viya sahajātā sīlasamādhiādayo guṇā, tena te vaṇṇagandhādisampannāni viya pupphāni devamanussānaṃ [V 0.0145] sataṃ piyā manāpā pasaṃsanīyā ca honti. Tena vuttaṃ “ye puggalā aṭṭhasataṃ pasatthā”ti.

6. Having thus spoken a statement of truth by means of the qualities of the path-Dhamma, he now begins to speak also by means of the qualities of the Sangha with the verse beginning, “Those persons...” Therein, the word “those” (ye) is an indefinite indicator. “Persons” (puggalā) means beings. “Eight” (aṭṭha) is the enumeration of them. For they are four who are practicing the path and four who are established in the fruit; thus they are eight. “Praised by the good” (sataṃ pasatthā) means they are praised by the virtuous—by Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, the disciples of the Buddha, and by other devas and humans. Why is this so? Because of their connection with innate qualities such as virtue. For them, just as flowers like the campaka and bakula possess innate color and fragrance, so too are there innate qualities such as virtue, concentration, and so on. Therefore, like flowers endowed with color and fragrance, they are dear, pleasing, and praiseworthy to the good among devas and humans. For that reason it is said: “Those eight persons, praised by the good.”

Atha vā yeti aniyametvā uddeso. Puggalāti sattā. Aṭṭhasatanti tesaṃ gaṇanaparicchedo. Te hi ekabījī kolaṃkolo sattakkhattuparamoti tayo sotāpannā. Kāmarūpārūpabhavesu adhigataphalā [M 0.0153] tayo sakadāgāmino. Te sabbepi catunnaṃ paṭipadānaṃ vasena catuvīsati. Antarāparinibbāyī, upahaccaparinibbāyī, sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī, asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī, uddhaṃsoto, akaniṭṭhagāmīti avihesu pañca. Tathā atappasudassasudassīsu[P 0.0183]. Akaniṭṭhesu pana uddhaṃsotavajjā cattāroti catuvīsati anāgāmino. Sukkhavipassako samathayānikoti dve arahanto. Cattāro maggaṭṭhāti catupaññāsa. Te sabbepi saddhādhurapaññādhurānaṃ vasena diguṇā hutvā aṭṭhasataṃ honti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Alternatively, “those” (ye) is an indefinite indicator. “Persons” (puggalā) means beings. “One hundred and eight” (aṭṭhasataṃ) is the enumeration of them. For there are three types of stream-enterers: the one-seeder (ekabījī), the clan-to-clan (kolaṃkola), and the one with a maximum of seven rebirths (sattakkhattuparama). There are three types of once-returners who have attained the fruit in the desire, form, and formless realms. All of these, by way of the four modes of practice, become twenty-four. There are five types of non-returners in the Aviha realm: the one who attains Nibbāna in the interim (antarāparinibbāyī), the one who attains Nibbāna upon landing (upahaccaparinibbāyī), the one who attains Nibbāna with exertion (sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī), the one who attains Nibbāna without exertion (asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī), and the one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm (uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī). Likewise, there are five in the Atappa, Sudassa, and Sudassī realms. In the Akaniṭṭha realm, however, excluding the one who goes upstream, there are four. Thus, there are twenty-four types of non-returners. There are two types of Arahants: the dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka) and the one who follows the path of tranquility (samathayānika). And there are the four established on the paths. Thus, there are fifty-four. All of these, when doubled by way of being faith-led and wisdom-led, become one hundred and eight. The remainder should be understood in the way already stated.

Cattāri etāni yugāni hontīti te sabbepi aṭṭha vā aṭṭhasataṃ vāti vitthāravasena uddiṭṭhapuggalā saṅkhepavasena sotāpattimaggaṭṭho phalaṭṭhoti ekaṃ yugaṃ, evaṃ yāva arahattamaggaṭṭho phalaṭṭhoti ekaṃ yuganti cattāri yugāni honti. Te dakkhiṇeyyāti ettha teti pubbe aniyametvā uddiṭṭhānaṃ niyametvā niddeso. Ye puggalā vitthāravasena aṭṭha vā, aṭṭhasataṃ vā, saṅkhepavasena cattāri yugāni hontīti vuttā, sabbepi te dakkhiṇaṃ arahantīti dakkhiṇeyyā. Dakkhiṇā nāma kammañca kammavipākañca saddahitvā “esa me idaṃ vejjakammaṃ vā jaṅghapesanikaṃ vā karissatī”ti evamādīni anapekkhitvā diyyamāno deyyadhammo, taṃ arahanti nāma sīlādiguṇayuttā puggalā, ime ca tādisā, tena vuccanti “te dakkhiṇeyyā”ti.

Regarding the phrase, “These are the four pairs”: all those persons who were indicated in detail as eight or one hundred and eight are, in brief, taken as pairs. The one established on the path to stream-entry and the one established on its fruit are one pair; in this way, up to the one established on the path to Arahantship and the one established on its fruit as one pair, there are four pairs. In the phrase, “They are worthy of offerings” (te dakkhiṇeyyā), the word “they” (te) is a specific indicator, referring to those who were previously indicated indefinitely. The persons who were spoken of as eight or one hundred and eight in detail, or as four pairs in brief—all of them are worthy of an offering (dakkhiṇa), and are therefore called “worthy of offerings” (dakkhiṇeyyā). An “offering” refers to a gift given with faith in kamma and its result, without regard for such things as, “This person will perform medical services for me or run errands for me.” Persons endowed with qualities such as virtue are worthy of such a gift, and these individuals are of such a kind. Therefore, they are called “worthy of offerings.”

Sugatassa sāvakāti bhagavā sobhanena gamanena yuttattā, sobhanañca ṭhānaṃ gatattā, suṭṭhu ca gatattā, suṭṭhu eva ca gadattā sugato, tassa sugatassa. Sabbepi te vacanaṃ suṇantīti sāvakā. Kāmañca aññepi suṇanti, na pana sutvā kattabbakiccaṃ karonti, ime pana sutvā kattabbaṃ dhammānudhammappaṭipattiṃ katvā maggaphalāni pattā, tasmā “sāvakā”ti vuccanti. Etesu dinnāni mahapphalānīti etesu sugatasāvakesu appakānipi dānāni dinnāni paṭiggāhakato dakkhiṇāvisuddhibhāvaṃ upagatattā mahapphalāni honti. Tasmā suttantarepi vuttaṃ –

Regarding “disciples of the Well-Gone One” (sugatassa sāvakā): The Blessed One is called the “Well-Gone One” (sugato) because he is endowed with an excellent way of going, because he has gone to an excellent state, because he has gone well, and because he has spoken well. Of that Well-Gone One, all of these are “disciples” (sāvakā) because they listen (suṇanti) to his word. Although it is true that others also listen, they do not, after listening, perform the duty that ought to be done. These noble ones, however, after listening, undertake the practice in accordance with the Dhamma that ought to be done and thereby attain the paths and fruits. Therefore, they are called “disciples.” Regarding “Gifts given to these bear great fruit”: even small gifts, when given to these disciples of the Well-Gone One, become of great fruit because the offering attains a state of purity on account of the recipient. Therefore, it is also said in another sutta—

“Yāvatā[V 0.0146], bhikkhave[P 0.0184], saṅghā vā gaṇā vā tathāgatasāvakasaṅgho, tesaṃ aggamakkhāyati, yadidaṃ cattāri purisayugāni aṭṭha purisapuggalā, esa bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho…pe… aggo vipāko hotī”ti (a. ni. 4.34; 5.32; itivu. 90).

“Monks, inasmuch as there are communities or groups, the community of the Tathāgata’s disciples is declared the foremost among them—that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight individuals. This is the Blessed One’s community of disciples... the result is supreme.”

Evaṃ [M 0.0154] bhagavā sabbesampi maggaṭṭhaphalaṭṭhānaṃ vasena saṅgharatanassa guṇaṃ vatvā idāni tameva guṇaṃ nissāya saccavacanaṃ payuñjati “idampi saṅghe”ti. Tassattho pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Imissāpi gāthāya āṇā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu amanussehi paṭiggahitāti.

Thus the Blessed One, having spoken of the quality of the Sangha-jewel by way of all those established on the paths and the fruits, now, relying on that very quality, employs a statement of truth, saying: “This, too, in the Sangha...” Its meaning should be understood in the same way as previously stated. The command of this verse was also accepted by non-human beings in one hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems.

Ye suppayuttātigāthāvaṇṇanā

The explanation of the verse beginning “Those who are well-applied”

7. Evaṃ maggaṭṭhaphalaṭṭhānaṃ vasena saṅghaguṇena saccaṃ vatvā idāni tato ekaccānaṃ phalasamāpattisukhamanubhavantānaṃ khīṇāsavapuggalānaṃyeva guṇena vattumāraddho “ye suppayuttā”ti. Tattha yeti aniyamituddesavacanaṃ. Suppayuttāti suṭṭhu payuttā, anekavihitaṃ anesanaṃ pahāya suddhājīvitaṃ nissāya vipassanāya attānaṃ payuñjitumāraddhāti attho. Atha vā suppayuttāti suvisuddhakāyavacīpayogasamannāgatā, tena tesaṃ sīlakkhandhaṃ dasseti. Manasā daḷhenāti daḷhena manasā, thirasamādhiyuttena cetasāti attho. Tena tesaṃ samādhikkhandhaṃ dasseti. Nikkāminoti kāye ca jīvite ca anapekkhā hutvā paññādhurena vīriyena sabbakilesehi katanikkamanā. Tena tesaṃ vīriyasampannaṃ paññakkhandhaṃ dasseti.

7. Having thus spoken the truth by means of the quality of the Sangha, in terms of those established in the path and fruit, he now begins to speak by means of the quality of only those individuals who have destroyed the taints and are experiencing the bliss of fruition attainment, with the verse beginning, ‘Those who are well-applied.’ Herein, ‘those’ is a term of unspecified designation. ‘Well-applied’ means well applied—having abandoned various kinds of wrong livelihood, relying on a pure livelihood, they have begun to apply themselves to insight; this is the meaning. Alternatively, ‘well-applied’ means endowed with very pure bodily and verbal application; by this, he shows their aggregate of virtue. ‘With a steadfast mind’ means with a firm mind, with a mind endowed with stable concentration; this is the meaning. By this, he shows their aggregate of concentration. ‘Those who have gone forth’ means, being without longing for body and life, they have made an escape from all defilements with energy led by wisdom. By this, he shows their aggregate of wisdom endowed with energy.

Gotamasāsanamhīti gottato gotamassa tathāgatasseva sāsanamhi. Tena ito bahiddhā nānappakārampi amaratapaṃ karontānaṃ suppayogādiguṇābhāvato kilesehi nikkamanābhāvaṃ dasseti. Teti pubbe uddiṭṭhānaṃ niddesavacanaṃ. Pattipattāti ettha pattabbāti patti, pattabbā nāma pattuṃ arahā, yaṃ patvā accantayogakkhemino [P 0.0185] honti, arahattaphalassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, taṃ pattiṃ pattāti pattipattā. Amatanti nibbānaṃ. Vigayhāti ārammaṇavasena vigāhitvā. Laddhāti labhitvā. Mudhāti abyayena kākaṇikamattampi byayaṃ akatvā. Nibbutinti paṭippassaddhakilesadarathaṃ phalasamāpattiṃ. Bhuñjamānāti anubhavamānā. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Ye imasmiṃ gotamasāsanamhi sīlasampannattā suppayuttā, samādhisampannattā manasā daḷhena, paññāsampannattā nikkāmino[V 0.0147], te imāya sammāpaṭipadāya amataṃ vigayha mudhā laddhā phalasamāpattisaññitaṃ nibbutiṃ bhuñjamānā pattipattā nāma hontīti.

‘In the dispensation of Gotama’ means in the dispensation of the Tathāgata who is Gotama by clan. By this, he shows that those outside this dispensation who perform various kinds of practices that torment others are unable to escape from the defilements, due to their lack of qualities such as right application. The word ‘they’ is a term of reference for what was previously indicated. In ‘pattipattā,’ ‘patti’ means that which is to be attained. ‘That which is to be attained’ means that which is worthy of being attained; having attained it, they become completely secure from the yokes. This is a designation for the fruit of Arahantship. ‘Pattipattā’ means they have attained that attainment. ‘Amataṃ’ means Nibbāna. ‘Vigayha’ means having plunged into it by way of making it an object. ‘Laddhā’ means having obtained. ‘Mudhā’ means without cost, without incurring the expense of even a small coin. ‘Nibbutiṃ’ means the fruition attainment, which is the calming of the fever of the defilements. ‘Bhuñjamānā’ means experiencing. What is meant by this? Those who in this dispensation of Gotama are well-applied on account of being endowed with virtue, are of steadfast mind on account of being endowed with concentration, and are those who have gone forth on account of being endowed with wisdom—they, by this right practice, having plunged into the deathless as their object and obtained it without cost, while experiencing the peace designated as fruition attainment, are called ‘those who have attained the attainment.’

Evaṃ [M 0.0155] bhagavā phalasamāpattisukhamanubhavantānaṃ khīṇāsavapuggalānameva vasena saṅgharatanassa guṇaṃ vatvā idāni tameva guṇaṃ nissāya saccavacanaṃ payuñjati “idampi saṅghe”ti. Tassattho pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Imissāpi gāthāya āṇā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu amanussehi paṭiggahitāti.

Thus, the Blessed One, having described the quality of the Sangha Jewel by way of only those individuals who have destroyed the taints and experience the bliss of fruition attainment, now, relying on that very quality, employs a statement of truth, saying, “This too is in the Sangha.” Its meaning should be understood in the way previously stated. The command of this verse, too, was accepted by non-human beings in a hundred thousand koṭi of world-systems.

Yathindakhīlotigāthāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Verse 'Like an Indakhīla'

8. Evaṃ khīṇāsavapuggalānaṃ guṇena saṅghādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccaṃ vatvā idāni bahujanapaccakkhena sotāpannasseva guṇena vattumāraddho “yathindakhīlo”ti. Tattha yathāti upamāvacanaṃ. Indakhīloti nagaradvāravinivāraṇatthaṃ ummārabbhantare aṭṭha vā dasa vā hatthe pathaviṃ khaṇitvā ākoṭitassa sāradārumayathambhassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Pathavinti bhūmiṃ. Sitoti anto pavisitvā nissito. Siyāti bhaveyya. Catubbhi vātehīti catūhi disāhi āgatehi vātehi. Asampakampiyoti kampetuṃ vā cāletuṃ vā asakkuṇeyyo. Tathūpamanti tathāvidhaṃ. Sappurisanti uttamapurisaṃ. Vadāmīti bhaṇāmi. Yo ariyasaccāni avecca passatīti yo cattāri ariyasaccāni paññāya ajjhogāhetvā passati. Tattha ariyasaccāni kumārapañhe vuttanayeneva veditabbāni.

8. Having thus spoken the truth based on the Sangha by means of the quality of those individuals who have destroyed the taints, He now begins, with the verse starting ‘yathindakhīlo,’ to speak by means of the quality of the Stream-enterer alone, which is directly perceived by many people. Therein, ‘yathā’ is a word expressing a simile. ‘Indakhīla’ is a designation for a post made of heartwood, driven in after digging the earth eight or ten cubits within the threshold, for the purpose of securing the city gate. ‘Pathaviṃ’ means the earth. ‘Sito’ means having entered within, it is supported. ‘Siyā’ means ‘it would be.’ ‘Catubbhi vātehi’ means by the winds coming from the four directions. ‘Asampakampiyo’ means it cannot be made to tremble or to be moved. ‘Tathūpamaṃ’ means of such a kind. ‘Sappurisaṃ’ means an excellent person. ‘Vadāmi’ means I say. ‘Yo ariyasaccāni avecca passati’ means: one who, having penetrated with wisdom, sees the four Noble Truths. Therein, the Noble Truths should be understood in the way stated in the Kumārapañha.

Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho – yathā hi indakhīlo [P 0.0186] gambhīranematāya pathavissito catubbhi vātehi asampakampiyo siyā, imampi sappurisaṃ tathūpamameva vadāmi, yo ariyasaccāni avecca passati. Kasmā? Yasmā sopi indakhīlo viya catūhi vātehi sabbatitthiyavādavātehi asampakampiyo hoti, tamhā dassanā kenaci kampetuṃ vā cāletuṃ vā asakkuṇeyyo. Tasmā suttantarepi vuttaṃ –

This is the concise meaning here: Just as an indakhīla, due to its deep foundation and being established on the earth, would be unshakable by the four winds, I declare this good person, who sees the Noble Truths having understood them, to be of a similar comparison. Why? Because just as that indakhīla is unshakable by the four winds, so too is that person unshakable by the winds that are the doctrines of all sectarians. From that seeing, he cannot be made to tremble or be moved by anyone. Therefore, it is also stated in another sutta:

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, ayokhīlo vā indakhīlo vā gambhīranemo sunikhāto acalo asampakampī, puratthimāya cepi disāya āgaccheyya bhusā vātavuṭṭhi, neva naṃ saṅkampeyya na sampakampeyya na sampacāleyya. Pacchimāya…pe… dakkhiṇāya, uttarāyapi ce…pe… na sampacāleyya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Gambhīrattā, bhikkhave, nemassa[M 0.0156], sunikhātattā indakhīlassa. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, ye ca kho keci samaṇā vā [V 0.0148] brāhmaṇā vā ‘idaṃ dukkhanti…pe… paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti, te na aññassa samaṇassa vā brāhmaṇassa vā mukhaṃ olokenti ‘ayaṃ nūna bhavaṃ jānaṃ jānāti, passaṃ passatī’ti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Sudiṭṭhattā, bhikkhave, catunnaṃ ariyasaccāna”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.1109).

‘Just as, monks, an iron post or an indakhīla with a deep foundation, well-planted, immovable, and unshakable—even if a fierce wind and rain were to come from the eastern direction, it would not make it shake, tremble, or move. From the western... from the southern... from the northern direction... it would not make it move. For what reason? Because, monks, of the depth of the foundation and because the indakhīla is well-planted. In the same way, monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins know as it really is: ‘This is suffering… this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering,’ they do not look to the face of another ascetic or brahmin, thinking, ‘Surely this venerable one knows, knowing; sees, seeing.’ For what reason? Because, monks, the four Noble Truths have been well seen.’

Evaṃ bhagavā bahujanapaccakkhassa sotāpannasseva vasena saṅgharatanassa guṇaṃ vatvā idāni tameva guṇaṃ nissāya saccavacanaṃ payuñjati “idampi saṅghe”ti. Tassattho pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Imissāpi gāthāya āṇā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu amanussehi paṭiggahitāti.

Thus, the Blessed One, having described the quality of the Sangha Jewel by way of the Stream-enterer alone, who is directly perceived by many people, now, relying on that same quality, employs a statement of truth, saying, 'This too is in the Sangha.' Its meaning should be understood in the same way as stated before. The command of this verse was also accepted by non-human beings in a hundred thousand koṭi of world-systems.

Ye ariyasaccānītigāthāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Verse beginning 'Ye ariyasaccāni'

9. Evaṃ avisesato sotāpannassa guṇena saṅghādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccaṃ vatvā idāni ye te tayo sotāpannā ekabījī kolaṃkolo sattakkhattuparamoti. Yathāha –

9. Thus, having declared without specifying the truth that has the Saṅgha as its foundation by virtue of the qualities of a stream-enterer, now there are these three types of stream-enterers: the one-seeder, the family-to-family, and the seven-times-at-most. As it is said:

“Idhekacco puggalo tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā sotāpanno hoti…pe… so ekaṃyeva bhavaṃ nibbattitvā dukkhassantaṃ karoti, ayaṃ ekabījī. Tathā dve vā tīṇi vā kulāni sandhāvitvā [P 0.0187] saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karoti, ayaṃ kolaṃkolo. Tathā sattakkhattuṃ devesu ca manussesu ca sandhāvitvā saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karoti, ayaṃ sattakkhattuparamo”ti (pu. pa. 31-33).

“Here, a certain person, with the destruction of the three fetters, becomes a stream-enterer… having brought about only one more existence, he makes an end of suffering; this one is a one-seeder. Likewise, one who, having run through and wandered through two or three families, makes an end of suffering; this one is a family-to-family. Likewise, one who, having run through and wandered through among devas and humans for seven times at most, makes an end of suffering; this one is a seven-times-at-most.” (Pug. 31-33).

Tesaṃ sabbakaniṭṭhassa sattakkhattuparamassa guṇena vattumāraddho “ye ariyasaccānī”ti. Tattha ye ariyasaccānīti etaṃ vuttanayameva. Vibhāvayantīti paññāobhāsena saccappaṭicchādakaṃ kilesandhakāraṃ vidhamitvā attano pakāsāni pākaṭāni karonti. Gambhīrapaññenāti appameyyapaññatāya sadevakassa lokassa ñāṇena alabbhaneyyappatiṭṭhapaññena, sabbaññunāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sudesitānīti samāsabyāsasākalyavekalyādīhi tehi tehi nayehi suṭṭhu desitāni. Kiñcāpi te honti [M 0.0157] bhusaṃ pamattāti te vibhāvitaariyasaccā puggalā kiñcāpi devarajjacakkavattirajjādippamādaṭṭhānaṃ āgamma bhusaṃ pamattā honti, tathāpi sotāpattimaggañāṇena abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassa nirodhena ṭhapetvā satta bhave anamatagge saṃsāre ye uppajjeyyuṃ nāmañca rūpañca, tesaṃ niruddhattā atthaṅgatattā na aṭṭhamaṃ bhavaṃ ādiyanti, sattamabhave eva pana vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇanti.

He began to speak by virtue of the qualities of the lowest among them, the seven-times-at-most, with the verse 'Those Noble Truths.' Therein, 'Those Noble Truths' is as has been explained. 'They make clear' means: with the light of wisdom, having dispelled the darkness of defilements that obscures the truths, they make them manifest and clear. 'By one with profound wisdom' refers to the Omniscient One, so called because of His immeasurable wisdom, a wisdom whose foundation is unattainable by the knowledge of the world with its devas. 'Well-taught' means well-explained through various methods such as concise, detailed, complete, and incomplete. 'Though they may be greatly heedless' means: though those individuals who have realized the noble truths may be greatly heedless, having come to a cause for heedlessness such as the kingship of devas or universal monarchs, still, through the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, by the cessation of the consciousness born of formations, they do not take up an eighth existence; for whatever name-and-form might have arisen in the beginningless saṃsāra—apart from seven existences—has ceased and passed away. Rather, in the seventh existence itself, having undertaken insight, they attain Arahantship.

Evaṃ [V 0.0149] bhagavā sattakkhattuparamavasena saṅgharatanassa guṇaṃ vatvā idāni tameva guṇaṃ nissāya saccavacanaṃ payuñjati “idampi saṅghe”ti. Tassattho pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Imissāpi gāthāya āṇā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu amanussehi paṭiggahitāti.

Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken of the quality of the Saṅgha Jewel by way of the seven-times-at-most, now employs the statement of truth, 'This too is in the Saṅgha,' relying on that very quality. Its meaning should be understood in the same way as previously explained. The command of this verse was also received by non-human beings in a hundred thousand koṭi of world-systems.

Sahāvassātigāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Verse beginning 'Sahāvassa'

10. Evaṃ sattakkhattuparamassa aṭṭhamaṃ bhavaṃ anādiyanaguṇena saṅghādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccaṃ vatvā idāni tasseva satta bhave ādiyatopi aññehi appahīnabhavādānehi puggalehi visiṭṭhena guṇena vattumāraddho “sahāvassā”ti[P 0.0188]. Tattha sahāvāti saddhiṃyeva. Assāti “na te bhavaṃ aṭṭhamamādiyantī”ti vuttesu aññatarassa. Dassanasampadāyāti sotāpattimaggasampattiyā. Sotāpattimaggo hi nibbānaṃ disvā kattabbakiccasampadāya sabbapaṭhamaṃ nibbānadassanato “dassana”nti vuccati, tassa attani pātubhāvo dassanasampadā, tāya dassanasampadāya saha eva. Tayassu dhammā jahitā bhavantīti ettha assu-iti padapūraṇamatte nipāto “idaṃ su me, sāriputta, mahāvikaṭabhojanasmiṃ hotī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.156) viya. Yato sahāvassa dassanasampadāya tayo dhammā jahitā bhavanti pahīnā hontīti ayamettha attho.

10. Thus, having spoken the truth that has the Saṅgha as its foundation by the quality of the seven-times-at-most not taking up an eighth existence, He now began with 'Sahāvassa' in order to speak of that very one with a distinguished quality—even though he takes up seven existences—that is superior to other individuals who have not abandoned the taking up of existence. Therein, `sahāva` means 'together with.' `Assa` refers to one among those of whom it is said, 'They do not take up an eighth existence.' `Dassanasampadāya` means 'by the accomplishment of seeing,' that is, by the accomplishment of the stream-entry path. Indeed, the stream-entry path is called 'dassana' (seeing) because it sees Nibbāna, because of the accomplishment of the task to be done, and because it is the very first to see Nibbāna. The manifestation of that in oneself is `dassanasampadā`, the accomplishment of seeing. It means 'together with that accomplishment of seeing.' In 'Tayassu dhammā jahitā bhavanti,' the particle `ssu` is merely for filling out the verse, as in 'This, Sāriputta, is for me...' and so on. The meaning here is this: because, together with his accomplishment of seeing, three things are abandoned, are given up.

Idāni jahitadhammadassanatthamāha “sakkāyadiṭṭhī vicikicchitañca, sīlabbataṃ vāpi yadatthi kiñcī”ti. Tattha sati kāye vijjamāne upādānakkhandhapañcakākhye kāye vīsativatthukā diṭṭhi sakkāyadiṭṭhi, satī vā tattha kāye diṭṭhītipi sakkāyadiṭṭhi, yathāvuttappakāre kāye vijjamānā diṭṭhīti attho. Satiyeva vā kāye diṭṭhītipi sakkāyadiṭṭhi, yathāvuttappakāre kāye vijjamāne [M 0.0158] rūpādisaṅkhāto attāti evaṃ pavattā diṭṭhīti attho. Tassā ca pahīnattā sabbadiṭṭhigatāni pahīnāneva honti. Sā hi nesaṃ mūlaṃ. Sabbakilesabyādhivūpasamanato paññā“cikicchita”nti vuccati, taṃ paññācikicchitaṃ ito vigataṃ, tato vā paññācikicchitā idaṃ vigatanti vicikicchitaṃ. “Satthari kaṅkhatī”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1008; vibha. 915) nayena vuttāya aṭṭhavatthukāya vimatiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tassā pahīnattā sabbānipi vicikicchitāni pahīnāni honti. Tañhi nesaṃ mūlaṃ. “Ito bahiddhā samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ [P 0.0189] sīlena suddhi vatena suddhī”ti evamādīsu (dha. sa. 1222; vibha. 938) āgataṃ gosīlakukkurasīlādikaṃ sīlaṃ govatakukkuravatādikañca vataṃ sīlabbatanti vuccati, tassa pahīnattā sabbampi naggiyamuṇḍikādiamaratapaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti. Tañhi tassa mūlaṃ, teneva sabbāvasāne vuttaṃ “yadatthi kiñcī”ti. Dukkhadassanasampadāya cettha sakkāyadiṭṭhi [V 0.0150] samudayadassanasampadāya vicikicchitaṃ, maggadassananibbānadassanasampadāya sīlabbataṃ pahīyatīti viññātabbaṃ.

Now, to show the abandoned qualities, He said: 'Self-identity view and doubt, and whatever adherence to rules and observances there may be.' Therein, with regard to the existing body—the body designated as the five aggregates of clinging—the twenty-fold view is `sakkāyadiṭṭhi` (self-identity view). Or, it is `sakkāyadiṭṭhi` because it is a view regarding the existing body; the meaning is, it is a view existing in the body in the manner described. Or, it is `sakkāyadiṭṭhi` because it is a view regarding the truly existing body; the meaning is, it is a view that proceeds thus: 'The self is what is designated as form, etc., in the existing body in the manner described.' And because that is abandoned, all wrong views are abandoned, for it is their root. Wisdom, because it pacifies all the diseases of the defilements, is called `cikicchita` (that which cures). That which is devoid of this cure of wisdom, or the state of mind that is devoid of this cure of wisdom, is called `vicikicchita` (doubt). This is a designation for the eight-fold uncertainty spoken of in the manner of 'one doubts the Teacher,' etc. Because that is abandoned, all doubts are abandoned, for it is their root. The practice of cow-asceticism, dog-asceticism, etc., and the observance of cow-observances, dog-observances, etc., which appear in passages such as, 'Outside this Teaching, for ascetics and brahmins, purity is through practice, purity is through observance,' are called `sīlabbata` (adherence to rules and observances). Because that is abandoned, all austerities for immortality, such as nakedness and being shaven-headed, are also abandoned, for that is their root. Therefore, at the very end, it is said, 'whatever there may be.' And herein, it should be understood that self-identity view is abandoned by the accomplishment of seeing suffering, doubt by the accomplishment of seeing the origin, and adherence to rules and observances by the accomplishment of seeing the path and seeing Nibbāna.

Catūhapāyehītigāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Verse beginning 'Catūhapāyehi'

11. Evamassa kilesavaṭṭappahānaṃ dassetvā idāni tasmiṃ kilesavaṭṭe sati yena vipākavaṭṭena bhavitabbaṃ, tappahānā tassāpi pahānaṃ dīpento āha “catūhapāyehi ca vippamutto”ti. Tattha cattāro apāyā nāma nirayatiracchānapettivisayaasurakāyā. Tehi esa satta bhave ādiyantopi vippamuttoti attho.

11. Thus, having shown the abandonment of the cycle of defilements for him, now, showing that because of the abandonment of that cycle of defilements, the cycle of results that would have come to be is also abandoned, He said, 'and freed from the four states of woe.' Therein, the four states of woe are hell, the animal realm, the realm of ghosts, and the host of asuras. The meaning is that even though this one takes up seven existences, he is freed from these.

Evamassa vipākavaṭṭappahānaṃ dassetvā idāni yamassa vipākavaṭṭassa mūlabhūtaṃ kammavaṭṭaṃ, tassāpi pahānaṃ dassento āha “chaccābhiṭhānāni abhabba kātu”nti. Tattha abhiṭhānānīti oḷārikaṭṭhānāni, tāni esa cha abhabbo kātuṃ. Tāni ca “aṭṭhānametaṃ, bhikkhave, anavakāso, yaṃ diṭṭhisampanno puggalo mātaraṃ jīvitā voropeyyā”tiādinā (a. ni. 1.271; ma. ni. 3.128; vibha. 809) nayena ekakanipāte vuttāni mātughātapitughātaarahantaghātalohituppādasaṅghabhedaaññasatthāruddesakammānīti veditabbāni. Tāni hi kiñcāpi diṭṭhisampanno ariyasāvako kunthakipillikampi jīvitā na voropeti, apica [M 0.0159] kho pana puthujjanabhāvassa vigarahaṇatthaṃ vuttāni. Puthujjano hi adiṭṭhisampannattā evaṃmahāsāvajjāni abhiṭhānānipi karoti, dassanasampanno pana abhabbo tāni kātunti. Abhabbaggahaṇañcettha bhavantarepi akaraṇadassanatthaṃ. Bhavantarepi hi esa attano ariyasāvakabhāvaṃ ajānantopi dhammatāya eva etāni vā cha pakatipāṇātipātādīni [P 0.0190] vā pañca verāni aññasatthāruddesena saha cha ṭhānāni na karoti, yāni sandhāya ekacce “cha chābhiṭhānānī”tipi paṭhanti. Matamacchaggāhādayo cettha ariyasāvakagāmadārakānaṃ nidassanaṃ.

Having shown the abandonment of the cycle of results for him, now, showing the abandonment also of the cycle of kamma, which is the root of the cycle of results, He said: 'and is incapable of committing the six `abhiṭṭhānas`.' Therein, `abhiṭṭhānas` means gross offenses; this one is incapable of committing these six. And these should be understood as the actions stated in the Ekakanipāta in the manner of 'It is impossible, monks, it is not possible, that a person accomplished in view would deprive his mother of life,' etc., namely: matricide, patricide, the killing of an Arahant, the shedding of the Buddha’s blood, causing a schism in the Saṅgha, and taking another teacher. For although a noble disciple accomplished in view would not deprive even an ant or a termite of life, these are stated to censure the state of an ordinary person. For an ordinary person, being unaccomplished in view, commits even such highly blameworthy `abhiṭṭhānas`, but one accomplished in view is incapable of committing them. And the use of 'incapable' here is to show the non-commission even in another existence. For even in another existence, this one, though not knowing his own state as a noble disciple, by the nature of things does not commit these six offenses, nor the five enmities beginning with the killing of living beings, which together with taking another teacher make six positions, which some recite as 'the six `abhiṭṭhānas`.' Herein, the village girls who were noble disciples picking up dead fish are an example.

Evaṃ bhagavā satta bhave ādiyatopi ariyasāvakassa aññehi appahīnabhavādānehi puggalehi visiṭṭhaguṇavasena saṅgharatanassa guṇaṃ vatvā idāni tameva guṇaṃ nissāya saccavacanaṃ payuñjati “idampi saṅghe”ti. Tassattho pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Imissāpi gāthāya āṇā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu amanussehi paṭiggahitāti.

Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken of the virtue of the Saṅgha Jewel by way of the distinguished quality of the noble disciple—who, even though taking up seven more existences, is superior to other individuals who have not abandoned the taking up of existence—now, relying on that very virtue, utters the statement of truth: 'This too is in the Saṅgha.' Its meaning should be understood in the way previously stated. The efficacy of this verse was also received by non-human beings in one hundred thousand koṭi of world-systems.

Kiñcāpi sotigāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Verse Beginning 'Kiñcāpi so'

12. Evaṃ [V 0.0151] satta bhave ādiyatopi aññehi appahīnabhavādānehi puggalehi visiṭṭhaguṇena saṅghādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccaṃ vatvā idāni na kevalaṃ dassanasampanno cha abhiṭhānāni abhabbo kātuṃ, kintu appamattakampi pāpakammaṃ katvā tassa paṭicchādanāyapi abhabboti pamādavihārinopi dassanasampannassa katappaṭicchādanābhāvaguṇena vattumāraddho “kiñcāpi so kamma karoti pāpaka”nti.

Thus, having spoken the truth which has the Saṅgha as its foundation, distinguishing by a superior quality from other individuals who have not abandoned the taking up of existence, even though taking up existence for seven lives, now it is said that not only is one endowed with vision incapable of committing the six grave offenses, but even having committed some slight evil deed, he is incapable of concealing it. Thus, in order to speak of the quality of non-concealment of a deed that has been done, even for one endowed with vision who dwells heedlessly, the verse beginning 'Though he may commit an evil deed...' was introduced.

Tassattho – so dassanasampanno kiñcāpi satisammosena pamādavihāraṃ āgamma yaṃ taṃ bhagavatā lokavajjaṃ sañciccātikkamanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “yaṃ mayā sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, taṃ mama sāvakā jīvitahetupi nātikkamantī”ti (cūḷava. 385; udā. 45) taṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ kuṭikārasahaseyyādiṃ paṇṇattivajjavītikkamasaṅkhātaṃ buddhappatikuṭṭhaṃ kāyena pāpakammaṃ karoti, padasodhammauttarichappañcavācādhammadesanasamphappalāpapharusavacanādiṃ vā vācāya [P 0.0191], uda cetasā vā katthaci lobhadosuppādanaṃ jātarūpādisādiyanaṃ cīvarādiparibhogesu apaccavekkhaṇādiṃ vā pāpakammaṃ karoti. Abhabbo so tassa [M 0.0160] paṭicchadāya na so taṃ “idaṃ akappiyamakaraṇīya”nti jānitvā muhuttampi paṭicchādeti, taṃkhaṇaṃ eva pana satthari vā viññūsu vā sabrahmacārīsu āvi katvā yathādhammaṃ paṭikaroti, “na puna karissāmī”ti evaṃ saṃvaritabbaṃ vā saṃvarati. Kasmā? Yasmā abhabbatā diṭṭhapadassa vuttā, evarūpampi pāpakammaṃ katvā tassa paṭicchādāya diṭṭhanibbānapadassa dassanasampannassa puggalassa abhabbatā vuttāti attho.

12. The meaning of this is as follows: That person endowed with vision, although on account of a lapse of mindfulness, due to dwelling in heedlessness, may commit an evil deed—setting aside that which is blameworthy in the world, concerning which the Blessed One, referring to intentional transgression, said: 'Whatever training rule has been laid down by me for the disciples, my disciples do not transgress it even for the sake of their lives'—he may commit by body another evil deed condemned by the Buddha, reckoned as a transgression of what is blameworthy by convention, such as those concerning building a hut or lying down together; or he may commit by speech an evil deed such as [transgressing the rules regarding] teaching the Dhamma word-by-word, speaking more than six or five words, frivolous speech, or harsh speech; or else, he may commit by mind an evil deed such as, on some occasion, the arising of greed and aversion, delighting in gold and silver, or not reflecting when using robes and other requisites. However, he is incapable of concealing it. Knowing, 'This is improper, this should not be done,' he does not conceal it even for a moment. Instead, at that very moment, having revealed it to the Teacher or to wise fellow practitioners, he makes amends according to the Dhamma. He also undertakes the restraint that should be undertaken, thinking, 'I will not do it again.' Why? Because the state of being incapable has been spoken of for one who has seen the state [of Nibbāna]. Therefore, the meaning is that even having committed such an evil deed, the state of being incapable of concealing it has been spoken of for the person endowed with vision, who has seen the state of Nibbāna.

Kathaṃ?

How so?

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, daharo kumāro mando uttānaseyyako hatthena vā pādena vā aṅgāraṃ akkamitvā khippameva paṭisaṃharati, evameva kho, bhikkhave, dhammatā esā diṭṭhisampannassa puggalassa, kiñcāpi tathārūpiṃ āpattiṃ āpajjati, yathārūpāya āpattiyā vuṭṭhānaṃ paññāyati. Atha kho naṃ khippameva satthari vā viññūsu vā sabrahmacārīsu deseti vivarati uttānīkaroti, desetvā vivaritvā uttānīkatvā āyatiṃ saṃvaraṃ āpajjatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.496).

“Just as, monks, a young boy, of little intelligence, lying on his back, having touched a heap of embers with his hand or foot, quickly withdraws it; even so, monks, this is the nature of a person endowed with vision. Although he may fall into such an offense from which emergence is known, he then quickly confesses, discloses, and makes it open to the Teacher or to wise fellow practitioners. Having confessed, disclosed, and made it open, he enters upon restraint for the future.”

Evaṃ bhagavā pamādavihārinopi dassanasampannassa katappaṭicchādanābhāvaguṇena saṅgharatanassa guṇaṃ vatvā idāni tameva guṇaṃ nissāya saccavacanaṃ payuñjati “idampi saṅghe”ti. Tassattho pubbe [V 0.0152] vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Imissāpi gāthāya āṇā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu amanussehi paṭiggahitāti.

Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken of the quality of the Saṅgha Jewel—namely, the quality of non-concealment of a deed that has been done, even on the part of one endowed with vision who dwells heedlessly—now, relying on that very quality, utters the statement of truth: 'This too is in the Saṅgha...' The meaning of this should be understood in the same way as previously explained. The efficacy of this verse was also received by non-human beings in a hundred thousand koṭi of world-systems.

Vanappagumbetigāthāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Vanappagumbe Verse.

13. Evaṃ saṅghapariyāpannānaṃ puggalānaṃ tena tena guṇappakārena saṅghādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccaṃ vatvā idāni yvāyaṃ bhagavatā ratanattayaguṇaṃ dīpentena idha saṅkhepena aññatra ca vitthārena pariyattidhammo desito, tampi nissāya puna buddhādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccaṃ vattumāraddho “vanappagumbe yathā phussitagge”ti. Tattha āsannasannivesavavatthitānaṃ rukkhānaṃ samūho [P 0.0192] vanaṃ, mūlasārapheggutacasākhāpalāsehi pavuddho gumbo pagumbo, vanassa, vane vā pagumbo vanappagumbo. Svāyaṃ “vanappagumbe”ti vutto, evampi hi vattuṃ labbhati “atthi savitakkasavicāre[M 0.0161], atthi avitakkavicāramatte, sukhe dukkhe jīve”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.174; ma. ni. 2.228) viya. Yathāti upamāvacanaṃ. Phussitāni aggāni assāti phussitaggo, sabbasākhāpasākhāsu sañjātapupphoti attho. So pubbe vuttanayeneva “phussitagge”ti vutto. Gimhānamāse paṭhamasmiṃ gimheti ye cattāro gimhānaṃ māsā, tesaṃ catunnaṃ gimhamāsānaṃ ekasmiṃ māse. Katarasmiṃ māse iti ce? Paṭhamasmiṃ gimhe, citramāseti attho. So hi “paṭhamagimho”ti ca “bālavasanto”ti ca vuccati. Tato paraṃ padatthato pākaṭameva.

13. Thus, having spoken the truth founded on the Sangha by means of the various kinds of virtues of the individuals included in the Sangha, now, this Dhamma of the scriptures has been taught by the Blessed One, who illuminates the qualities of the Three Jewels here briefly and elsewhere in detail. Relying on that, he began again to speak the truth founded on the Buddha with the verse beginning, 'As in a woodland thicket with blossoming treetops.' Therein, 'vana' is a collection of trees that exist established nearby. A thicket that has grown with roots, heartwood, sapwood, bark, branches, and leaves is 'pagumba.' A thicket of a forest, or a thicket in a forest, is 'vanappagumbo.' This is called 'vanappagumbe.' For it is possible to say it thus, as in 'there is with thought and examination,' 'there is only with examination without thought,' 'in pleasure, in pain, in life,' and so on. 'Yathā' is a word of comparison. 'Phussitagga' is that which has blossoming treetops, meaning it has flowers that have appeared on all large and small branches. This is stated as 'phussitagge' in the same way as mentioned before. As for 'in the first month of the summer season': there are four summer months; this refers to one of those four summer months. If it is asked, 'In which month?' The meaning is: in the first summer month, the month of Citta. For it is called 'the first summer' and 'the young spring.' Beyond that, it is clear from the meaning of the words.

Ayaṃ panettha piṇḍattho – yathā paṭhamagimhanāmake bālavasante nānāvidharukkhagahane vane supupphitaggasākho taruṇarukkhagacchapariyāyanāmo pagumbo ativiya sassiriko hoti, evameva khandhāyatanādīhi satipaṭṭhānasammappadhānādīhi sīlasamādhikkhandhādīhi vā nānappakārehi atthappabhedapupphehi ativiya sassirikattā tathūpamaṃ nibbānagāmimaggadīpanato nibbānagāmiṃ pariyattidhammavaraṃ neva lābhahetu na sakkārādihetu, kevalantu mahākaruṇāya abbhussāhitahadayo sattānaṃ paramahitāya adesayīti. Paramaṃ hitāyāti ettha ca gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ anunāsiko. Ayaṃ panattho – paramahitāya nibbānāya adesayīti.

Herein, this is the summary meaning: Just as in the young spring named the 'first summer,' in a dense forest with various trees, a thicket named 'a collection of young trees and plants,' with well-blossomed treetops and branches, is exceedingly glorious; even so, the excellent Dhamma of the scriptures, which leads to Nibbāna because it illuminates the path leading to Nibbāna, is comparable to that, being exceedingly glorious due to the flowers which are the various kinds of meanings—such as the aggregates, sense bases, and so on; the foundations of mindfulness, right strivings, and so on; or the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and so on. He did not teach it for the sake of gain, nor for the sake of honor and so on; but solely, with a heart impelled by great compassion, He taught for the supreme welfare of beings. And here in 'Paramaṃ hitāya,' the nasal is for the ease of composing the verse. This, however, is the meaning: He taught for the supreme welfare, for Nibbāna.

Evaṃ bhagavā imaṃ supupphitaggavanappagumbasadisaṃ pariyattidhammaṃ vatvā idāni tameva nissāya buddhādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccavacanaṃ payuñjati “idampi buddhe”ti. Tassattho pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Kevalaṃ pana idampi yathāvuttapakārapariyattidhammasaṅkhātaṃ [P 0.0193] buddhe ratanaṃ paṇītanti evaṃ yojetabbaṃ[V 0.0153]. Imissāpi gāthāya āṇā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu amanussehi paṭiggahitāti.

Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken this Dhamma of the scriptures which is like a woodland thicket with well-blossomed treetops, now, relying on that very Dhamma, employs a statement of truth that has the Buddha as its foundation: 'This excellent jewel is in the Buddha...' Its meaning should be understood only in the way previously stated. However, it should be connected thus: This excellent jewel, known as the Dhamma of the scriptures of the kind described, is in the Buddha. The command of this verse, too, was accepted by non-human beings in one hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems.

Varo varaññūtigāthāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Verse 'The Best, the Knower of the Best'

14. Evaṃ bhagavā pariyattidhammena buddhādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccaṃ vatvā idāni lokuttaradhammena vattumāraddho “varo varaññū”ti. Tattha varoti paṇītādhimuttikehi icchito “aho vata mayampi evarūpā assāmā”ti, varaguṇayogato vā varo uttamo seṭṭhoti attho. Varaññūti [M 0.0162] nibbānaññū. Nibbānañhi sabbadhammānaṃ uttamaṭṭhena varaṃ, tañcesa bodhimūle sayaṃ paṭivijjhitvā aññāsi. Varadoti pañcavaggiyabhaddavaggiyajaṭilādīnaṃ aññesañca devamanussānaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyavāsanābhāgiyavaradhammadāyīti attho. Varāharoti varassa maggassa āhaṭattā varāharoti vuccati. So hi bhagavā dīpaṅkarato pabhuti samatiṃsa pāramiyo pūrento pubbakehi sammāsambuddhehi anuyātaṃ purāṇamaggavaramāhari, tena “varāharo”ti vuccati.

14. Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken the truth which has the Buddha as its foundation by means of the scriptural teaching, now began to speak by means of the supramundane teaching: “The Best, the Knower of the Best.” Herein, “the Best” (varo) means what is desired by those inclined toward excellence, thinking, “Oh, if only we too could be like this!” Or, it signifies the excellent, the supreme, due to its connection with excellent qualities. “The Knower of the Best” (varaññū) means the knower of Nibbāna. For Nibbāna is the best of all dhammas in the sense of being supreme, and he himself penetrated and knew it at the root of the Bodhi tree. “The Giver of the Best” (varado) means the giver of the excellent Dhamma, which is conducive to penetration and connected with the potential for liberation, to beings such as the group of five, the Bhaddavaggiyas, the matted-hair ascetics, and other devas and humans. “The Bearer of the Best” (varāharo) is so called because he brought the excellent path. For the Blessed One, fulfilling the thirty perfections from the time of Dīpaṅkara, brought forth the ancient, excellent path followed by previous Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones. Therefore, he is called “the Bearer of the Best.”

Apica sabbaññutaññāṇappaṭilābhena varo, nibbānasacchikiriyāya varaññū, sattānaṃ vimuttisukhadānena varado, uttamapaṭipadāharaṇena varāharo. Etehi lokuttaraguṇehi adhikassa kassaci guṇassa abhāvato anuttaro.

Furthermore, he is the Best through the attainment of omniscient knowledge. He is the Knower of the Best through the realization of Nibbāna. He is the Giver of the Best through giving the happiness of liberation to beings. He is the Bearer of the Best through bringing the highest practice. Because there is no quality in anyone higher than these supramundane qualities, he is unsurpassed.

Aparo nayo – varo upasamādhiṭṭhānaparipūraṇena, varaññū paññādhiṭṭhānaparipūraṇena, varado cāgādhiṭṭhānaparipūraṇena, varāharo saccādhiṭṭhānaparipūraṇena, varaṃ maggasaccamāharīti. Tathā varo puññussayena, varaññū paññussayena, varado buddhabhāvatthikānaṃ tadupāyasampadānena, varāharo paccekabuddhabhāvatthikānaṃ tadupāyāharaṇena, anuttaro tattha tattha asadisatāya, attanā vā anācariyako hutvā paresaṃ ācariyabhāvena, dhammavaraṃ adesayi sāvakabhāvatthikānaṃ tadatthāya svākkhātatādiguṇayuttassa dhammavarassa desanato. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

Another method: He is the Best by fulfilling the foundation of serenity; the Knower of the Best by fulfilling the foundation of wisdom; the Giver of the Best by fulfilling the foundation of generosity; the Bearer of the Best by fulfilling the foundation of truth, in that he brought the supreme truth of the path. Similarly, he is the Best by the abundance of merit; the Knower of the Best by the abundance of wisdom; the Giver of the Best by providing the means for those aspiring to Buddhahood; the Bearer of the Best by bringing the means for those aspiring to Paccekabuddhahood. He is the Unsurpassed One by being unequalled in these various respects, or by being himself without a teacher while being a teacher to others. He taught the excellent Dhamma to those aspiring to discipleship for their benefit, by teaching the excellent Dhamma endowed with qualities such as being well-proclaimed. The rest is as explained before.

Evaṃ bhagavā navavidhena lokuttaradhammena attano guṇaṃ vatvā idāni tameva [P 0.0194] guṇaṃ nissāya buddhādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccavacanaṃ payuñjati “idampi buddhe”ti. Tassattho pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Kevalaṃ pana yaṃ varaṃ lokuttaradhammaṃ esa aññāsi, yañca adāsi, yañca āhari, yañca desesi, idampi buddhe ratanaṃ paṇītanti evaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Imissāpi gāthāya āṇā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu amanussehi paṭiggahitāti.

Thus, having proclaimed his own virtues by means of the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, the Blessed One now, relying on those very virtues, utters a statement of truth founded on the Buddha: 'This excellent jewel is in the Buddha...' Its meaning should be understood in the way previously stated. However, it should be connected thus: that excellent supramundane Dhamma which he knew, which he gave, which he brought, and which he taught—this too is the precious, excellent jewel in the Buddha. Regarding this verse too, the command was received by non-human beings in one hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems.

Khīṇantigāthāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Verse beginning 'Khīṇaṃ'

15. Evaṃ [V 0.0154] bhagavā pariyattidhammañca navalokuttaradhammañca nissāya dvīhi gāthāhi buddhādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccaṃ vatvā idāni ye taṃ pariyattidhammaṃ assosuṃ, sutānusārena [M 0.0163] ca paṭipajjitvā navappakārampi lokuttaradhammaṃ adhigamiṃsu, tesaṃ anupādisesanibbānapattiguṇaṃ nissāya puna saṅghādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccaṃ vattumāraddho “khīṇaṃ purāṇa”nti. Tattha khīṇanti samucchinnaṃ. Purāṇanti purātanaṃ. Navanti sampati vattamānaṃ. Natthi sambhavanti avijjamānapātubhāvaṃ. Virattacittāti vītarāgacittā. Āyatike bhavasminti anāgatamaddhānaṃ punabbhave. Teti yesaṃ khīṇaṃ purāṇaṃ navaṃ natthi sambhavaṃ, ye ca āyatike bhavasmiṃ virattacittā, te khīṇāsavā bhikkhū. Khīṇabījāti ucchinnabījā. Avirūḷhichandāti virūḷhichandavirahitā. Nibbantīti vijjhāyanti. Dhīrāti dhitisampannā. Yathāyaṃ padīpoti ayaṃ padīpo viya.

15. Thus, the Blessed One, relying on the Dhamma of learning and the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, having spoken in two verses the truth established in the Buddha, now began to speak the truth established in the Saṅgha with the words, “The old is exhausted.” He did so relying on the quality of attaining Nibbāna without remaining kamma-born aggregates, with regard to those who heard that Dhamma of learning and, having practiced in accordance with what was heard, attained the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. Therein, “exhausted” means completely eradicated. “The old” means the old kamma. “New” means the presently occurring kamma. “There is no arising” means it does not cause rebirth to manifest. “With minds detached” means with minds free from craving for new existence. “In future existence” means in a future time, in a new existence. “They” refers to those for whom the old is exhausted, for whom there is no new arising, and who are detached in mind from future existence—they are the monks whose taints are destroyed. “With seeds destroyed” means with seeds cut off. “Without desire for growth” means devoid of the desire to grow. “They are extinguished” means they are quenched. “The wise” means those endowed with wisdom. “Just as this lamp” means like this lamp.

Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yaṃ taṃ sattānaṃ uppajjitvā niruddhampi purāṇaṃ atītakālikaṃ kammaṃ taṇhāsinehassa appahīnattā paṭisandhiāharaṇasamatthatāya akhīṇaṃyeva hoti, taṃ purāṇaṃ kammaṃ yesaṃ arahattamaggena taṇhāsinehassa sositattā agginā daḍḍhabījamiva āyatiṃ vipākadānāsamatthatāya khīṇaṃ. Yañca nesaṃ buddhapūjādivasena idāni pavattamānaṃ kammaṃ navanti vuccati, tañca taṇhāpahāneneva chinnamūlapādapapupphamiva āyatiṃ phaladānāsamatthatāya yesaṃ natthi sambhavaṃ, ye ca taṇhāpahāneneva āyatike bhavasmiṃ virattacittā, te khīṇāsavā bhikkhū “kammaṃ [P 0.0195] khettaṃ viññāṇaṃ bīja”nti (a. ni. 3.77) ettha vuttassa paṭisandhiviññāṇassa kammakkhayeneva khīṇattā khīṇabījā. Yopi pubbe punabbhavasaṅkhātāya virūḷhiyā chando ahosi. Tassapi samudayappahāneneva pahīnattā pubbe viya cutikāle asambhavena avirūḷhichandā dhitisampannattā dhīrā carimaviññāṇanirodhena yathāyaṃ padīpo nibbuto, evaṃ nibbanti, puna “rūpino vā arūpino vā”ti evamādiṃ paññattipathaṃ accentīti. Tasmiṃ kira samaye nagaradevatānaṃ pūjanatthāya jālitesu padīpesu eko padīpo vijjhāyi, taṃ dassento āha “yathāyaṃ padīpo”ti.

What is meant by this? For beings, that old kamma associated with the past, though it has arisen and ceased, is not yet exhausted because the adhesive of craving has not been abandoned, and thus it is capable of bringing about rebirth-linking. For those, however, by whom the adhesive of craving has been dried up by the path of Arahantship, that old kamma is exhausted, incapable of giving its fruit in the future, like a seed scorched by fire. And whatever kamma is presently occurring for them, by way of honoring the Buddha and so on, is called ‘new.’ That too, due to the very abandonment of craving, is incapable of giving fruit in the future, like a flower on a tree with its root cut; for them there is no arising of a new existence. And those who, through the very abandonment of craving, have minds detached from future existence—they are the monks whose taints are destroyed. In the statement, “Kamma is the field, consciousness the seed,” because the rebirth-linking consciousness spoken of is exhausted through the exhaustion of kamma, they are called ‘those with destroyed seeds.’ And whatever desire there was previously for growth, known as renewed existence, that desire too, having been abandoned through the abandonment of its origin, they are without desire for growth, as there is no arising at the time of death as there was before. Because they are endowed with wisdom, they are wise. Through the cessation of the final consciousness, they are extinguished just as this lamp is extinguished. They transcend the path of designation such as ‘those with form’ or ‘those without form.’ It is said that at that time, among the lamps lit to honor the city deities, one lamp was extinguished. Pointing to it, he said, “Just as this lamp…”

Evaṃ bhagavā ye taṃ purimāhi dvīhi gāthāhi vuttaṃ pariyattidhammaṃ assosuṃ, sutānusārena ca paṭipajjitvā navappakārampi lokuttaradhammaṃ adhigamiṃsu, tesaṃ anupādisesanibbānapattiguṇaṃ vatvā idāni tameva guṇaṃ nissāya saṅghādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccavacanaṃ payuñjanto desanaṃ samāpesi “idampi saṅghe”ti. Tassattho [M 0.0164] pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Kevalaṃ pana idampi yathāvuttena pakārena [V 0.0155] khīṇāsavabhikkhūnaṃ nibbānasaṅkhātaṃ saṅghe ratanaṃ paṇītanti evaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Imissāpi gāthāya āṇā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu amanussehi paṭiggahitāti.

Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken of the quality of attaining Nibbāna without remaining kamma-born aggregates for those who heard the Dhamma of learning spoken in the two previous verses and, having practiced in accordance with what was heard, attained the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, now, relying on that very quality, concluded the teaching by employing a statement of truth established in the Saṅgha: “This too is in the Saṅgha.” Its meaning should be understood in the same way as previously explained. However, it should be construed thus: This excellent jewel, known as Nibbāna, is in the Saṅgha of monks whose taints are destroyed in the aforesaid manner. Regarding this verse too, its command was received by non-human beings in a hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems.

Desanāpariyosāne rājakulassa sotthi ahosi, sabbūpaddavā vūpasamiṃsu, caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi.

At the conclusion of the teaching, there was well-being for the royal family. All misfortunes subsided. There was an attainment of the Dhamma for eighty-four thousand beings.

Yānīdhātigāthāttayavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Three Verses Beginning 'Yānīdha'

16. Atha sakko devānamindo “bhagavatā ratanattayaguṇaṃ nissāya saccavacanaṃ payuñjamānena nāgarassa sotthi katā, mayāpi nāgarassa sotthitthaṃ ratanattayaguṇaṃ nissāya kiñci vattabba”nti cintetvā avasāne gāthāttayaṃ abhāsi “yānīdha bhūtānī”ti tattha yasmā buddho yathā lokahitatthāya ussukkaṃ āpannehi āgantabbaṃ[P 0.0196], tathā āgatato yathā ca tehi gantabbaṃ, tathā gatato yathā ca tehi ājānitabbaṃ, tathā ājānanato, yathā ca jānitabbaṃ, tathā jānanato, yañca tatheva hoti, tassa gadanato ca “tathāgato”ti vuccati. Yasmā ca so devamanussehi pupphagandhādinā bahi nibbattena upakārakena, dhammānudhammapaṭipattādinā ca attani nibbattena ativiya pūjito, tasmā sakko devānamindo sabbaṃ devaparisaṃ attanā saddhiṃ sampiṇḍetvā āha “tathāgataṃ devamanussapūjitaṃ, buddhaṃ namassāma suvatthi hotū”ti.

16. Then Sakka, the lord of the devas, thought, 'The Blessed One, relying on the virtues of the Triple Gem and uttering words of truth, has brought about well-being for the city. I too, for the well-being of the city, relying on the virtues of the Triple Gem, should say something.' Having thought thus, at the conclusion, he spoke a group of three verses beginning, 'Whatever beings are here.' Therein, because the Buddha has come in such a way as he should have come for those who have undertaken the effort for the welfare of the world; and has gone in such a way as they should have gone; and has understood in such a way as they should have understood; and knows in such a way as one should know; and because he speaks of that which is just so, he is called 'Tathāgata.' And because he is exceedingly honored by devas and humans with external requisites such as flowers and scents, and with internal practice such as the practice in conformity with the Dhamma, therefore Sakka, the lord of the devas, gathering the entire assembly of devas together with himself, said, 'We pay homage to the Tathāgata, the Buddha, honored by devas and humans—may there be well-being!'

17. Yasmā pana dhamme maggadhammo yathā yuganaddhasamathavipassanābalena gantabbaṃ kilesapakkhaṃ samucchindantena, tathā gatoti tathāgato. Nibbānadhammopi yathā gato paññāya paṭividdho sabbadukkhappaṭivighātāya sampajjati, buddhādīhi tathā avagato, tasmā “tathāgato”tveva vuccati. Yasmā ca saṅghopi yathā attahitāya paṭipannehi gantabbaṃ tena tena maggena, tathā gatoti “tathāgato”tveva vuccati. Tasmā avasesagāthādvayepi tathāgataṃ dhammaṃ namassāma suvatthi hotu, tathāgataṃ saṅghaṃ namassāma suvatthi hotūti vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

17. Furthermore, because in the Dhamma, the path-Dhamma is gone to (`gata`) in such a way (`tathā`) as it should be by one who, with the power of serenity and insight yoked together, has thoroughly cut off the faction of defilements, it is called 'Tathāgata.' The Nibbāna-Dhamma, too, is penetrated by wisdom as it truly is; it conduces to the removal of all suffering; it is gone to without deviation (`tathā avagato`) by the Buddhas and other noble ones; therefore, it is called 'Tathāgata.' And because the Saṅgha also goes without deviation (`tathā gato`) by this or that path, in such a way as it should be gone to by persons practicing for their own welfare, it is called 'Tathāgata.' Therefore, in the remaining two verses, it is said: 'We pay homage to the Dhamma, which has been arrived at without deviation (`tathāgataṃ`)—may there be well-being! We pay homage to the Saṅgha, which has been arrived at without deviation (`tathāgataṃ`)—may there be well-being!' The rest is in the manner already stated.

Evaṃ [M 0.0165] sakko devānamindo imaṃ gāthāttayaṃ bhāsitvā bhagavantaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā devapurameva gato saddhiṃ devaparisāya. Bhagavā pana tadeva ratanasuttaṃ dutiyadivasepi desesi, puna caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi, evaṃ yāva sattamadivasaṃ desesi, divase divase tatheva dhammābhisamayo ahosi. Bhagavā aḍḍhamāsameva vesāliyaṃ viharitvā rājūnaṃ “gacchāmā”ti paṭivedesi. Tato rājāno diguṇena sakkārena [P 0.0197] puna tīhi divasehi bhagavantaṃ [V 0.0156] gaṅgātīraṃ nayiṃsu. Gaṅgāya nibbattā nāgarājāno cintesuṃ “manussā tathāgatassa sakkāraṃ karonti, mayaṃ kiṃ na karissāmā”ti suvaṇṇarajatamaṇimayā nāvāyo māpetvā suvaṇṇarajatamaṇimaye eva pallaṅke paññapetvā pañcavaṇṇapadumasañchannaṃ udakaṃ karitvā “amhākaṃ anuggahaṃ karothā”ti bhagavantaṃ yāciṃsu. Bhagavā adhivāsetvā ratananāvamārūḷho, pañca ca bhikkhusatāni pañcasataṃ nāvāyo abhirūḷhā. Nāgarājāno bhagavantaṃ saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena nāgabhavanaṃ pavesesuṃ. Tatra sudaṃ bhagavā sabbarattiṃ nāgaparisāya dhammaṃ desesi. Dutiyadivase dibbehi khādanīyabhojanīyehi mahādānaṃ akaṃsu, bhagavā anumoditvā nāgabhavanā nikkhami.

Thus Sakka, the lord of the devas, having spoken this group of three verses and having circumambulated the Blessed One keeping him to the right, went to the deva world itself together with the assembly of devas. The Blessed One, for his part, taught that same Ratanasutta on the second day as well, and again, for eighty-four thousand living beings, there was the realization of the Dhamma. In this way, he taught for up to seven days, and on each day, there was the realization of the Dhamma in the same way. The Blessed One, having dwelt in Vesālī for half a month, informed the kings, 'We shall go.' Then the kings, with twofold honor, in three days led the Blessed One to the bank of the Ganges. The nāga kings who had arisen in the Ganges thought, 'Humans are making offerings to the Tathāgata, why should we not do so?' Having created boats made of gold, silver, and gems, and having prepared couches made of gold, silver, and gems, and having covered the water with five-colored lotuses, they requested the Blessed One, saying, 'Grant us your favor.' The Blessed One, having consented, boarded the jeweled boat, and five hundred bhikkhus boarded five hundred boats. The nāga kings led the Blessed One together with the Sangha of bhikkhus into the nāga abode. There, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma to the assembly of nāgas throughout the whole night. On the second day, they made a great offering with divine foods, hard and soft. The Blessed One, having given the anumodanā, departed from the nāga abode.

Bhūmaṭṭhā devā “manussā ca nāgā ca tathāgatassa sakkāraṃ karonti, mayaṃ kiṃ na karissāmā”ti cintetvā vanappagumbarukkhapabbatādīsu chattātichattāni ukkhipiṃsu. Eteneva upāyena yāva akaniṭṭhabrahmabhavanaṃ, tāva mahāsakkāraviseso nibbatti. Bimbisāropi licchavīhi āgatakāle katasakkārato diguṇamakāsi. Pubbe vuttanayeneva pañcahi divasehi bhagavantaṃ rājagahaṃ ānesi.

The earth-dwelling devas, thinking, 'Humans and nāgas are making offerings to the Tathāgata, why should we not do so?' raised canopies upon canopies over the forests, thickets, trees, mountains, and so on. By this same method, an extraordinary great offering came to be, extending as far as the Akaniṭṭha Brahma world. King Bimbisāra also made an offering twofold greater than the offering made by the Licchavis at the time of their arrival. In the same manner as stated before, in five days he brought the Blessed One to Rājagaha.

Rājagahamanuppatte bhagavati pacchābhattaṃ maṇḍalamāḷe sannipatitānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ayamantarakathā udapādi “aho buddhassa bhagavato ānubhāvo, yaṃ uddissa gaṅgāya orato ca pārato ca aṭṭhayojano bhūmibhāgo ninnañca thalañca samaṃ katvā vālukāya okiritvā pupphehi sañchanno, yojanappamāṇaṃ gaṅgāya udakaṃ nānāvaṇṇehi padumehi sañchannaṃ, yāva akaniṭṭhabhavanaṃ, tāva chattātichattāni ussitānī”ti. Bhagavā taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā gandhakuṭito nikkhamitvā taṅkhaṇānurūpena pāṭihāriyena gantvā maṇḍalamāḷe paññattavarabuddhāsane [P 0.0198] nisīdi. Nisajja kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti. Bhikkhū sabbaṃ [M 0.0166] ārocesuṃ bhagavā etadavoca – “na, bhikkhave, ayaṃ pūjāviseso mayhaṃ buddhānubhāvena nibbatto, na nāgadevabrahmānubhāvena, apica kho pubbe appamattakapariccāgānubhāvena nibbatto”ti. Bhikkhū āhaṃsu “na mayaṃ, bhante, taṃ appamattakaṃ pariccāgaṃ jānāma, sādhu no bhagavā tathā kathetu, yathā mayaṃ taṃ jāneyyāmā”ti.

When the Blessed One had arrived at Rājagaha, after the meal, this conversation arose among the bhikkhus who had assembled in the circular hall: 'Oh, the spiritual power of the Blessed One, the Buddha! On his account, an area of land of eight yojanas on this side and the far side of the Ganges—both the low-lying and high ground—was made level, strewn with sand, and covered with flowers. The water of the Ganges for a measure of one yojana was covered with lotuses of various colors, and canopies upon canopies were raised as far as the Akaniṭṭha abode.' The Blessed One, knowing of that event, departed from the Perfumed Chamber and, having gone with a miracle appropriate for that moment, sat down in the circular hall on the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: 'Bhikkhus, for the sake of what talk are you now sitting together?' The bhikkhus related everything. The Blessed One said this: 'Bhikkhus, this extraordinary offering did not come to be through my power as a Buddha, nor through the power of nāgas, devas, or Brahmās. But rather, it came to be through the power of a small act of giving in the past.' The bhikkhus said, 'Venerable sir, we do not know of that small act of giving. It would be good, venerable sir. May the Blessed One so explain it to us that we may know it.'

Bhagavā āha – bhūtapubbaṃ, bhikkhave, takkasilāyaṃ saṅkho nāma brāhmaṇo ahosi. Tassa putto susīmo nāma māṇavo soḷasavassuddesiko vayena. So ekadivasaṃ pitaraṃ upasaṅkamitvā abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Atha taṃ pitā āha “kiṃ, tāta, susīmā”ti? So āha “icchāmahaṃ, tāta, bārāṇasiṃ gantvā sippaṃ uggahetu”nti. “Tena hi[V 0.0157], tāta, susīma, asuko nāma brāhmaṇo mama sahāyako, tassa santikaṃ gantvā uggaṇhāhī”ti kahāpaṇasahassaṃ adāsi. So taṃ gahetvā mātāpitaro abhivādetvā anupubbena bārāṇasiṃ gantvā upacārayuttena vidhinā ācariyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā abhivādetvā attānaṃ nivedesi. Ācariyo “mama sahāyakassa putto”ti māṇavaṃ sampaṭicchitvā sabbaṃ pāhuneyyavattamakāsi. So addhānakilamathaṃ vinodetvā taṃ kahāpaṇasahassaṃ ācariyassa pādamūle ṭhapetvā sippaṃ uggahetuṃ okāsaṃ yāci. Ācariyo okāsaṃ katvā uggaṇhāpesi.

The Blessed One said: 'Once upon a time, monks, in Takkasilā there was a brahmin named Saṅkha. He had a son, a young man named Susīma, who was sixteen years of age. One day, he approached his father, paid homage, and stood in a suitable place. Then his father said to him, 'What is it, dear Susīma?' He replied, 'Father, I wish to go to Bārāṇasī to learn the art.' 'In that case, dear Susīma, a certain brahmin is a friend of mine. Go to him and learn.' He gave him a thousand kahāpaṇas. Taking them, Susīma paid homage to his parents and, in due course, went to Bārāṇasī. Following the proper procedure, he approached the teacher, paid homage, and presented himself. The teacher, thinking, 'He is the son of my friend,' accepted the young man and performed all the duties of hospitality for him. After recovering from the fatigue of the journey, Susīma placed the thousand kahāpaṇas at the teacher's feet and requested the opportunity to learn the art. The teacher granted the opportunity and had him taught.'

So lahuñca gaṇhanto, bahuñca gaṇhanto, gahitagahitañca suvaṇṇabhājane pakkhittatelamiva avinassamānaṃ dhārento, dvādasavassikaṃ sippaṃ katipayamāseneva pariyosāpesi. So sajjhāyaṃ karonto ādimajjhaṃyeva passati, no pariyosānaṃ. Atha ācariyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā āha “imassa sippassa [P 0.0199] ādimajjhameva passāmi, no pariyosāna”nti. Ācariyo āha “ahampi, tāta, evamevā”ti. Atha ko, ācariya, imassa sippassa pariyosānaṃ jānātīti? Isipatane, tāta, isayo atthi, te jāneyyunti. Te upasaṅkamitvā pucchāmi, ācariyāti?
