Puccha, tāta, yathāsukhanti. So isipatanaṃ gantvā paccekabuddhe upasaṅkamitvā pucchi “api, bhante, pariyosānaṃ jānāthā”ti? Āma, āvuso, jānāmāti. Taṃ mampi sikkhāpethāti. Tena hāvuso, pabbajāhi, na sakkā apabbajitena sikkhāpetunti. Sādhu, bhante, pabbājetha vā maṃ, yaṃ vā icchatha, taṃ katvā pariyosānaṃ [M 0.0167] jānāpethāti. Te taṃ pabbājetvā kammaṭṭhāne niyojetuṃ asamatthā “evaṃ te nivāsetabbaṃ, evaṃ pārupitabba”ntiādinā nayena ābhisamācārikaṃ sikkhāpesuṃ. So tattha sikkhanto upanissayasampannattā na cireneva paccekabodhiṃ abhisambujjhi. Sakalabārāṇasiyaṃ “susīmapaccekabuddho”ti pākaṭo ahosi lābhaggayasaggappatto sampannaparivāro. So appāyukasaṃvattanikassa kammassa katattā na cireneva parinibbāyi. Tassa paccekabuddhā ca mahājanakāyo ca sarīrakiccaṃ katvā dhātuyo gahetvā nagaradvāre thūpaṃ patiṭṭhāpesuṃ.

Learning both quickly and much, and retaining what he had learned so that it would not perish, like oil poured into a golden vessel, he completed in just a few months the art that takes twelve years. While reciting, he saw only the beginning and the middle, but not the end. Then he approached his teacher and said, 'Of this art, I see only the beginning and the middle, not the end.' The teacher replied, 'For me too, dear one, it is the same.' 'Then, teacher, who knows the end of this art?' 'At Isipatana, dear one, there are seers; they would know.' 'Shall I approach them and ask, teacher?' 'Ask, dear one, as you please.' So he went to Isipatana, approached the Paccekabuddhas, and asked, 'Venerable sirs, do you know the end?' 'Yes, friend, we know.' 'Then please teach me also.' 'In that case, friend, you must go forth; it is not possible to teach one who has not gone forth.' 'Very well, venerable sirs, ordain me, or do whatever you wish, and make known to me the end.' They ordained him, but being unable to engage him in meditation subjects, they taught him the rules of proper conduct, in the manner of 'Thus should you wear your lower robe, thus should you wear your upper robe,' and so on. While practicing there, due to being endowed with the supporting conditions, he very soon awakened to Paccekabodhi. Throughout all of Bārāṇasī, he became famous as 'Susīma the Paccekabuddha,' having reached the peak of gain and fame, and endowed with a retinue. Because he had performed a kamma that conduced to a short lifespan, he attained Parinibbāna not long after. The Paccekabuddhas and a great multitude of people performed his funeral rites, took his relics, and established a stupa at the city gate.

Atha kho saṅkho brāhmaṇo “putto me ciragato, na cassa pavattiṃ jānāmī”ti puttaṃ daṭṭhukāmo takkasilāya nikkhamitvā anupubbena bārāṇasiṃ gantvā mahājanakāyaṃ sannipatitaṃ disvā “addhā bahūsu ekopi me puttassa pavattiṃ jānissatī”ti cintento upasaṅkamitvā pucchi “susīmo nāma māṇavo idha āgato atthi, api nu tassa pavattiṃ jānāthā”ti? Te “āma, brāhmaṇa, jānāma, imasmiṃ nagare brāhmaṇassa santike tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū hutvā paccekabuddhānaṃ santike pabbajitvā paccekabuddho hutvā anupādisesāya [P 0.0200] nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyi, ayamassa thūpo patiṭṭhāpito”ti āhaṃsu. So bhūmiṃ hatthena paharitvā roditvā ca paridevitvā ca [V 0.0158] taṃ cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ gantvā tiṇāni uddharitvā uttarasāṭakena vālukaṃ ānetvā paccekabuddhacetiyaṅgaṇe okiritvā kamaṇḍaluto udakena samantato bhūmiṃ paripphositvā vanapupphehi pūjaṃ katvā uttarasāṭakena paṭākaṃ āropetvā thūpassa upari attano chattaṃ bandhitvā pakkāmīti.

Then the brahmin Saṅkha, thinking, 'My son has been gone a long time, and I have no news of him,' and desiring to see his son, set out from Takkasilā and, in due course, went to Bārāṇasī. Seeing a great multitude of people gathered, he thought, 'Surely, among so many, at least one will know what has become of my son.' Approaching them, he asked, 'Is there a young man named Susīma who has come here? Do you have any news of him?' They replied, 'Yes, brahmin, we know. In this city, having become a master of the three Vedas in the presence of a brahmin, he went forth in the presence of the Paccekabuddhas, became a Paccekabuddha, and attained Parinibbāna with the Nibbāna-element that is without remaining residue. This is his stupa, which has been established.' Striking the ground with his hand, weeping and lamenting, he went to that stupa enclosure, pulled out the grass, and brought sand in his upper garment, which he scattered in the Paccekabuddha's stupa enclosure. He sprinkled the ground all around with water from his water pot, made an offering with forest flowers, raised a banner with his upper garment, tied his own parasol above the stupa, and departed.

Evaṃ atītaṃ desetvā jātakaṃ paccuppannena anusandhento bhikkhūnaṃ dhammakathaṃ kathesi. “Siyā kho pana vo, bhikkhave, evamassa ‘añño nūna tena samayena saṅkho brāhmaṇo ahosī’ti, na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, ahaṃ tena samayena saṅkho brāhmaṇo ahosiṃ, mayā susīmassa paccekabuddhassa cetiyaṅgaṇe tiṇāni uddhaṭāni, tassa me kammassa nissandena aṭṭhayojanamaggaṃ vigatakhāṇukaṇṭakaṃ katvā samaṃ suddhamakaṃsu. Mayā tattha vālukā okiṇṇā, tassa me nissandena aṭṭhayojanamagge vālukaṃ okiriṃsu. Mayā tattha vanakusumehi pūjā katā, tassa me nissandena navayojane magge thale ca udake ca nānāpupphehi [M 0.0168] pupphasantharamakaṃsu. Mayā tattha kamaṇḍaludakena bhūmi paripphositā, tassa me nissandena vesāliyaṃ pokkharavassaṃ vassi. Mayā tasmiṃ cetiye paṭākā āropitā, chattañca baddhaṃ, tassa me nissandena yāva akaniṭṭhabhavanā paṭākā ca āropitā, chattātichattāni ca ussitāni. Iti kho, bhikkhave, ayaṃ mayhaṃ pūjāviseso neva buddhānubhāvena nibbatto[P 0.0201], na nāgadevabrahmānubhāvena, apica kho appamattakapariccāgānubhāvena nibbatto”ti. Dhammakathāpariyosāne imaṃ gāthamabhāsi –

Having thus recounted the past, connecting the jātaka to the present, he gave a Dhamma talk to the monks. 'Monks, you might think, “Surely, someone else was the brahmin Saṅkha at that time.” But you should not see it thus. I myself was the brahmin Saṅkha at that time. I removed the grass from the courtyard of the shrine of the Paccekabuddha Susīma. As a result of that deed, they made an eight-yojana road free of stumps and thorns, smooth and clear. I scattered sand there. As a result of that deed, they scattered sand along the eight-yojana road. I made offerings of forest flowers there. As a result of that deed, they spread a carpet of various flowers along a nine-yojana road, both on land and in water. I sprinkled the ground with water from my water pot. As a result of that deed, a rain of lotuses fell upon Vesālī. I raised a banner at that shrine and set up a parasol. As a result of that deed, banners were raised up to the Akaniṭṭha realm, and parasols upon parasols were erected. Thus, monks, this special honor of mine was not produced by the power of a Buddha, nor by the power of nāgas, devas, or Brahmā, but rather by the power of a small relinquishment.' At the conclusion of the Dhamma talk, he spoke this verse:

“Mattāsukhapariccāgā, passe ce vipulaṃ sukhaṃ;

Caje mattāsukhaṃ dhīro, sampassaṃ vipulaṃ sukha”nti. (dha. pa. 290);

If, by giving up a limited happiness, one might see an abundant happiness, the wise one, seeing the abundant happiness, should give up the limited happiness.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha:

Ratanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Ratana Sutta is concluded.

7. Tirokuṭṭasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta

Nikkhepappayojanaṃ

The Purpose of its Placement

Idāni [V 0.0159] “tirokuṭṭesu tiṭṭhantī”tiādinā ratanasuttānantaraṃ nikkhittassa tirokuṭṭasuttassa atthavaṇṇanākkamo anuppatto, tassa idha nikkhepappayojanaṃ vatvā atthavaṇṇanaṃ karissāma.

Now, the turn for explaining the meaning of the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta, which was placed after the Ratana Sutta and begins with “standing outside the walls,” has arrived. Here, having stated the purpose of its placement, we will explain its meaning.

Tattha idañhi tirokuṭṭaṃ iminā anukkamena bhagavatā avuttampi yāyaṃ ito pubbe nānappakārena kusalakammapaṭipatti dassitā, tattha pamādaṃ āpajjamāno nirayatiracchānayonīhi visiṭṭhatarepi ṭhāne uppajjamāno yasmā evarūpesu petesu uppajjati, tasmā na ettha pamādo karaṇīyoti dassanatthaṃ, yehi ca bhūtehi upaddutāya vesāliyā upaddavavūpasamanatthaṃ ratanasuttaṃ vuttaṃ, tesu ekaccāni evarūpānīti dassanatthaṃ vā vuttanti.

In this regard, although this Tirokuṭṭa Sutta was not spoken by the Blessed One in this sequence, it was included for the purpose of showing this: since a person who falls into negligence regarding the practice of wholesome kamma, which was taught previously in various ways, is reborn among such petas—even when reborn in a state more distinguished than the hells and the animal realm—therefore, negligence should not be practiced in this matter. Or, it was spoken for the purpose of showing that some of those beings by whom Vesālī was afflicted, for the pacification of which affliction the Ratana Sutta was spoken, were of this very kind.

Idamassa idha nikkhepappayojanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

This should be understood as the purpose for its placement here.

Anumodanākathā

Discourse on Rejoicing

Yasmā [M 0.0169] panassa atthavaṇṇanā –

Now, as for the explanation of its meaning—

“Yena yattha yadā yasmā, tirokuṭṭaṃ pakāsitaṃ;

Pakāsetvāna taṃ sabbaṃ, kayiramānā yathākkamaṃ;

Sukatā hoti tasmāhaṃ, karissāmi tatheva taṃ”.

By whom, where, when, and for what reason the Tirokuṭṭa was taught; since explaining all that in due order is a good telling, therefore I shall do it just so.

Kena panetaṃ pakāsitaṃ, kattha kadā kasmā cāti? Vuccate – bhagavatā pakāsitaṃ, taṃ kho pana rājagahe dutiyadivase [P 0.0202] rañño māgadhassa anumodanatthaṃ. Imassa catthassa vibhāvanatthaṃ ayamettha vitthārakathā kathetabbā –

By whom was this taught, where, when, and for what reason? It is said—it was taught by the Blessed One. Moreover, it was spoken at Rājagaha, on the second day, as a blessing for the king of Magadha. To make the meaning of this clear, this detailed story should be told here—

Ito [V 0.0160] dvānavutikappe kāsi nāma nagaraṃ ahosi. Tattha jayaseno nāma rājā. Tassa sirimā nāma devī, tassā kucchiyaṃ phusso nāma bodhisatto nibbattitvā anupubbena sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjhi. Jayaseno rājā “mama putto abhinikkhamitvā buddho jāto, mayhameva buddho, mayhaṃ dhammo, mayhaṃ saṅgho”ti mamattaṃ uppādetvā sabbakālaṃ sayameva upaṭṭhahati, na aññesaṃ okāsaṃ deti.

Ninety-two aeons from this one, there was a city named Kāsi. There, there was a king named Jayasena. He had a queen named Sirimā. In her womb, the Bodhisatta named Phussa arose and, in due course, fully awakened to perfect enlightenment. King Jayasena, having generated possessiveness, thinking, "My son, having gone forth, has become a Buddha. The Buddha is mine alone, the Dhamma is mine, the Sangha is mine," attended to him himself at all times and did not give an opportunity to others.

Bhagavato kaniṭṭhabhātaro vemātikā tayo bhātaro cintesuṃ – “buddhā nāma sabbalokahitāya uppajjanti, na cekassevatthāya, amhākañca pitā aññesaṃ okāsaṃ na deti, kathaṃ nu mayaṃ labheyyāma bhagavantaṃ upaṭṭhātu”nti. Tesaṃ etadahosi – “handa mayaṃ kiñci upāyaṃ karomā”ti. Te paccantaṃ kupitaṃ viya kārāpesuṃ. Tato rājā “paccanto kupito”ti sutvā tayopi putte paccantavūpasamanatthaṃ pesesi. Te vūpasametvā āgatā, rājā tuṭṭho varaṃ adāsi “yaṃ icchatha, taṃ gaṇhathā”ti. Te “mayaṃ bhagavantaṃ upaṭṭhātuṃ icchāmā”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā “etaṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ gaṇhathā”ti āha. Te “mayaṃ aññena anatthikā”ti āhaṃsu. Tena hi paricchedaṃ katvā gaṇhathāti. Te satta vassāni yāciṃsu, rājā na adāsi. Evaṃ cha, pañca, cattāri, tīṇi, dve, ekaṃ, satta māsāni, cha, pañca, cattārīti yāva temāsaṃ yāciṃsu. Rājā “gaṇhathā”ti adāsi.

The Blessed One's three younger brothers of a different mother thought: "Buddhas arise for the welfare of the whole world, not for the benefit of one alone, and our father does not give an opportunity to others. How then might we get to attend upon the Blessed One?" It occurred to them: "Come, let us devise some stratagem." They caused the border region to appear as if it were in revolt. Then the king, hearing that "the border is in revolt," sent the three sons to pacify the border region. Having pacified it, they returned. The king, pleased, gave them a boon: "Take whatever you wish." They said, "We wish to attend upon the Blessed One." The king said, "Putting that aside, take something else." They said, "We have no need of anything else." When he said, "In that case, having set a limit, take it," they requested seven years, but the king did not grant it. In this way, they requested for six, five, four, three, two, and one year; for seven, six, five, and four months, down to three months. The king granted three months, saying, "Take it."

Te varaṃ labhitvā paramatuṭṭhā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā āhaṃsu – “icchāma mayaṃ, bhante, bhagavantaṃ temāsaṃ upaṭṭhātuṃ, adhivāsetu no, bhante[M 0.0170], bhagavā imaṃ temāsaṃ vassāvāsa”nti. Adhivāsesi bhagavā tuṇhībhāvena. Tato te attano janapade niyuttakapurisassa [P 0.0203] lekhaṃ pesesuṃ “imaṃ temāsaṃ amhehi bhagavā upaṭṭhātabbo, vihāraṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbaṃ bhagavato upaṭṭhānasambhāraṃ karohī”ti. So taṃ sabbaṃ sampādetvā paṭinivedesi. Te kāsāyavatthanivatthā hutvā aḍḍhateyyehi purisasahassehi veyyāvaccakarehi bhagavantaṃ sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhahamānā janapadaṃ netvā vihāraṃ niyyātetvā vasāpesuṃ.

Having received the boon, they were exceedingly pleased. They approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and said: "Venerable sir, we wish to attend upon the Blessed One for three months. Venerable sir, may the Blessed One consent to this three-month rains-residence for us." The Blessed One consented by means of silence. Then they sent a letter to an appointed man in their own country: "For these three months, the Blessed One is to be attended upon by us. Starting with the monastery, prepare all the requisites for attending on the Blessed One." That man, having prepared all that, informed them in return. They, having become clad in ochre robes, while respectfully attending upon the Blessed One with two and a half thousand men as attendants, led him to their country, and having dedicated the monastery, had him dwell there.

Tesaṃ bhaṇḍāgāriko eko gahapatiputto sapajāpatiko saddho ahosi pasanno. So buddhappamukhassa saṅghassa dānavattaṃ sakkaccaṃ adāsi. Janapade niyuttakapuriso taṃ gahetvā jānapadehi ekādasamattehi purisasahassehi saddhiṃ sakkaccameva dānaṃ pavattāpesi. Tattha keci jānapadā paṭihatacittā ahesuṃ. Te dānassa antarāyaṃ katvā deyyadhamme attanā khādiṃsu, bhattasālañca agginā dahiṃsu. Pavārite rājaputtā bhagavato mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ katvā bhagavantaṃ purakkhatvā [V 0.0161] pituno sakāsameva agamaṃsu. Tattha gantvā eva bhagavā parinibbāyi. Rājā ca rājaputtā ca janapade niyuttakapuriso ca bhaṇḍāgāriko ca anupubbena kālaṃ katvā saddhiṃ parisāya sagge uppajjiṃsu, paṭihatacittajanā nirayesu nibbattiṃsu. Evaṃ tesaṃ dvinnaṃ gaṇānaṃ saggato saggaṃ, nirayato nirayaṃ upapajjantānaṃ dvānavutikappā vītivattā.

Among them, a treasurer, a householder's son, together with his wife, was faithful and devout. He respectfully gave the regular alms to the Sangha with the Buddha at its head. The man appointed in the country, taking him, together with about eleven thousand men from the country, caused the alms-giving to proceed with respect. There, some of the country people were of hostile minds. They, having created an obstruction to the alms, consumed the alms-gifts themselves and burned down the food-hall with fire. When the Pavāraṇā was completed, the princes, having paid great honor to the Blessed One and placing the Blessed One in front, went to their father's presence. Having gone there, the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna. The king and the princes, the man appointed in the country, and the treasurer, in due course, passed away and, together with their retinue, were reborn in heaven. The people with hostile minds were born in the hells. Thus, for those two groups, being reborn from heaven to heaven and from hell to hell, ninety-two eons passed by.

Atha imasmiṃ bhaddakappe kassapabuddhassa kāle te paṭihatacittajanā petesu uppannā. Tadā manussā attano ñātakānaṃ petānaṃ atthāya dānaṃ datvā uddisanti “idaṃ amhākaṃ ñātīnaṃ hotū”ti. Te sampattiṃ labhanti. Atha imepi petā taṃ disvā bhagavantaṃ kassapaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pucchiṃsu – “kiṃ nu kho, bhante, mayampi evarūpaṃ sampattiṃ labheyyāmā”ti? Bhagavā āha – “idāni na labhatha[P 0.0204], apica anāgate gotamo nāma buddho bhavissati, tassa bhagavato kāle bimbisāro nāma rājā bhavissati, so tumhākaṃ ito dvānavutikappe ñāti ahosi, so buddhassa dānaṃ datvā tumhākaṃ uddisissati, tadā labhissathā”ti. Evaṃ vutte kira tesaṃ petānaṃ taṃ vacanaṃ “sve labhissathā”ti vuttaṃ viya ahosi.

Then, in this fortunate aeon, during the time of the Buddha Kassapa, those people with hostile minds were born among the petas. At that time, humans would give alms for the benefit of their peta relatives and dedicate it, saying, "May this be for our relatives." They would obtain good fortune. Then, these petas too, seeing that, approached the Blessed One Kassapa and asked, "Venerable sir, how might we too obtain such good fortune?" The Blessed One said: "Now you will not obtain it. But in the future, there will be a Buddha named Gotama. In that Blessed One's time, there will be a king named Bimbisāra, who was your relative ninety-two aeons ago from this one. He, having given alms to the Buddha, will dedicate it to you. Then you will obtain it." When this was said, it is said that to those petas, that word was as if it had been said, "Tomorrow you will obtain it."

Atha ekasmiṃ buddhantare vītivatte amhākaṃ bhagavā loke uppajji. Tepi tayo rājaputtā tehi aḍḍhateyyehi purisasahassehi saddhiṃ [M 0.0171] devalokā cavitvā magadharaṭṭhe brāhmaṇakule uppajjitvā anupubbena isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā gayāsīse tayo jaṭilā ahesuṃ, janapade niyuttakapuriso, rājā ahosi bimbisāro, bhaṇḍāgāriko, gahapati visākho nāma mahāseṭṭhi ahosi, tassa pajāpati dhammadinnā nāma seṭṭhidhītā ahosi. Evaṃ sabbāpi avasesā parisā rañño eva parivārā hutvā nibbattā.

Then, after one Buddha-interval had passed, our Blessed One arose in the world. Those three princes, together with those two thousand five hundred men, having passed away from the deva world, were reborn in the country of Magadha in a brahmin family. In due course, having gone forth into the ascetic life, they became three matted-hair ascetics at Gayāsīsa. The man appointed in the countryside became King Bimbisāra. The treasurer became the great merchant and householder named Visākha. His wife was the merchant's daughter named Dhammadinnā. Thus, all the remaining assembly, having become the king's retinue, were reborn.

Amhākaṃ bhagavā loke uppajjitvā sattasattāhaṃ atikkamitvā anupubbena bārāṇasiṃ āgamma dhammacakkaṃ pavattetvā pañcavaggiye ādiṃ katvā yāva aḍḍhateyyasahassaparivāre tayo jaṭile vinetvā rājagahaṃ agamāsi. Tattha ca tadahupasaṅkamantaṃyeva rājānaṃ bimbisāraṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāpesi ekādasanavutehi māgadhakehi brāhmaṇagahapatikehi saddhiṃ. Atha raññā svātanāya bhattena nimantito bhagavā adhivāsetvā dutiyadivase sakkena devānamindena purato purato gacchantena –

Our Blessed One, having arisen in the world and passed forty-nine days, in due course arrived at Bārāṇasī, set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, and, beginning with the group of five monks, having disciplined the three matted-hair ascetics with their retinue of two thousand five hundred, he went to Rājagaha. And there, he established King Bimbisāra, who had approached on that very day, in the fruit of stream-entry, together with one hundred and ten thousand Magadhan brahmins and householders. Then, having been invited by the king for a meal on the morrow, the Blessed One consented. On the second day, with Sakka, the lord of devas, going before him—

“Danto dantehi saha purāṇajaṭilehi, vippamutto vippamuttehi;

Siṅgīnikkhasavaṇṇo, rājagahaṃ pāvisi bhagavā”ti. (mahāva. 58) –

The tamed, the liberated, the one with a complexion like Siṅgī gold, the Blessed One, entered Rājagaha together with the former matted-hair ascetics who were tamed and liberated.

Evamādīhi [V 0.0162] gāthāhi abhitthaviyamāno rājagahaṃ pavisitvā rañño nivesane mahādānaṃ sampaṭicchi. Te petā “idāni rājā [P 0.0205] amhākaṃ dānaṃ uddisissati, idāni uddisissatī”ti āsāya parivāretvā aṭṭhaṃsu.

Being praised with such verses, he entered Rājagaha and received the great offering at the king's residence. Those petas, with the hope, "Now the king will dedicate the offering to us, now he will dedicate it!", surrounded the residence and stood.

Rājā dānaṃ datvā “kattha nu kho bhagavā vihareyyā”ti bhagavato vihāraṭṭhānameva cintesi, na taṃ dānaṃ kassaci uddisi. Petā chinnāsā hutvā rattiṃ rañño nivesane ativiya bhiṃsanakaṃ vissaramakaṃsu. Rājā bhayasaṃvegasantāsamāpajji, tato pabhātāya rattiyā bhagavato ārocesi – “evarūpaṃ saddamassosiṃ, kiṃ nu kho me, bhante, bhavissatī”ti. Bhagavā āha – “mā bhāyi, mahārāja, na te kiñci pāpakaṃ bhavissati, apica kho te purāṇañātakā petesu uppannā santi, te ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ tameva paccāsīsamānā vicaranti ‘buddhassa dānaṃ datvā amhākaṃ uddisissatī’ti[M 0.0172], na tesaṃ tvaṃ hiyyo uddisi, te chinnāsā tathārūpaṃ vissaramakaṃsū”ti.

The king, having given the offering, thought only of a dwelling place for the Blessed One, "Where, indeed, might the Blessed One dwell?", and did not dedicate that offering to anyone. The petas, their hopes cut off, made an exceedingly terrifying noise at night in the king's residence. The king experienced fear, agitation, and terror. Then, when the night had dawned, he reported to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I heard such a sound. What, indeed, will become of me?" The Blessed One said: "Do not fear, great king. No evil will befall you. However, your former relatives have been reborn among the petas. For one whole Buddha-interval, they have been wandering, expecting you alone, thinking, 'Having given an offering to the Buddha, he will dedicate it to us.' Yesterday, you did not dedicate it to them. Their hopes being cut off, they made such a noise."

So āha “idāni pana, bhante, dinne labheyyu”nti? “Āma, mahārājā”ti. “Tena hi me, bhante, adhivāsetu bhagavā ajjatanāya dānaṃ, tesaṃ uddisissāmī”ti? Bhagavā adhivāsesi. Rājā nivesanaṃ gantvā mahādānaṃ paṭiyādetvā bhagavato kālaṃ ārocāpesi. Bhagavā rājantepuraṃ gantvā paññatte āsane nisīdi saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena. Tepi kho petā “api nāma ajja labheyyāmā”ti gantvā tirokuṭṭādīsu aṭṭhaṃsu. Bhagavā tathā akāsi, yathā te sabbeva rañño pākaṭā ahesuṃ. Rājā dakkhiṇodakaṃ dento “idaṃ me ñātīnaṃ hotū”ti uddisi, taṅkhaṇaññeva tesaṃ petānaṃ padumasañchannā pokkharaṇiyo nibbattiṃsu. Te tattha nhatvā ca pivitvā ca paṭippassaddhadarathakilamathapipāsā suvaṇṇavaṇṇā ahesuṃ. Rājā yāgukhajjakabhojanāni datvā uddisi, taṅkhaṇaññeva tesaṃ dibbayāgukhajjakabhojanāni nibbattiṃsu. Te tāni paribhuñjitvā pīṇindriyā ahesuṃ. Atha vatthasenāsanāni datvā uddisi. Tesaṃ [P 0.0206] dibbavatthadibbayānadibbapāsādadibbapaccattharaṇadibbaseyyādialaṅkāravidhayo nibbattiṃsu. Sāpi tesaṃ sampatti yathā sabbāva pākaṭā hoti, tathā bhagavā adhiṭṭhāsi. Rājā ativiya attamano ahosi. Tato bhagavā bhuttāvī pavārito rañño māgadhassa anumodanatthaṃ “tirokuṭṭesu tiṭṭhantī”ti imā gāthā abhāsi.

He said: "But now, Venerable Sir, if an offering is given, would they receive it?" "Yes, great king." "In that case, Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One consent to my offering for today; I will dedicate it to them." The Blessed One consented. The king, going to his residence, prepared a great offering and had the time announced to the Blessed One. The Blessed One went to the king's inner palace and sat down on the prepared seat together with the Sangha of monks. Those petas also, thinking, "Perhaps today we might receive!", went and stood behind the walls and other such places. The Blessed One acted in such a way that all of them became visible to the king. The king, while giving the dedication water, dedicated it, saying: "May this be for my relatives." In that very moment, lotus-covered ponds arose for those petas. Having bathed and drunk there, their distress, fatigue, and thirst were allayed, and they became golden in complexion. The king gave and dedicated rice-gruel, hard food, and soft food. In that very moment, divine rice-gruel, hard food, and soft food arose for them. Having consumed these, their faculties were gratified. Then he gave and dedicated robes and lodgings. For them arose various kinds of divine adornments, such as divine robes, divine vehicles, divine palaces, divine coverings, and divine beds. The Blessed One resolved that all this prosperity of theirs should become visible. The king was exceedingly joyful. Then the Blessed One, having finished his meal and indicated he was satisfied, for the rejoicing of the king of Magadha, spoke these verses beginning with: "They stand outside the walls..."

Ettāvatā ca “yena yattha yadā yasmā, tirokuṭṭaṃ pakāsitaṃ, pakāsetvāna taṃ sabba”nti ayaṃ mātikā saṅkhepato vitthārato ca vibhattā hoti.

And by this much, this mātikā—"By whom, where, when, from what, the Tirokuṭṭa was explained; having explained all that"—has been analyzed in brief and in detail.

Paṭhamagāthāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the First Verse.

1. Idāni [V 0.0163] imassa tirokuṭṭassa yathākkamaṃ atthavaṇṇanaṃ karissāma. Seyyathidaṃ – paṭhamagāthāya tāva tirokuṭṭāti kuṭṭānaṃ parabhāgā vuccanti. Tiṭṭhantīti nisajjādippaṭikkhepato ṭhānakappanavacanametaṃ. Tena yathā pākāraparabhāgaṃ pabbataparabhāgañca gacchantaṃ “tiropākāraṃ tiropabbataṃ asajjamāno gacchatī”ti vadanti, evamidhāpi kuṭṭassa parabhāgesu tiṭṭhante “tirokuṭṭesu [M 0.0173] tiṭṭhantī”ti āha. Sandhisiṅghāṭakesu cāti ettha sandhiyoti catukkoṇaracchā vuccanti gharasandhibhittisandhiālokasandhiyo cāpi. Siṅghāṭakāti tikoṇaracchā vuccanti, tadekajjhaṃ katvā purimena saddhiṃ saṅghaṭento “sandhisiṅghāṭakesu cā”ti āha. Dvārabāhāsu tiṭṭhantīti nagaradvāragharadvārānaṃ bāhā nissāya tiṭṭhanti. Āgantvāna sakaṃ gharanti ettha sakaṃ gharaṃ nāma pubbañātigharampi attanā sāmikabhāvena ajjhāvutthapubbagharampi. Tadubhayampi yasmā te sakagharasaññāya āgacchanti, tasmā “āgantvāna sakaṃ ghara”nti āha.

1. Now, we shall provide the explanation of the meaning of this Tirokuṭṭa Sutta in due order. It is as follows: Regarding the first verse, firstly, as for `tirokuṭṭa`, the regions beyond the walls are so called. The term `tiṭṭhanti` is a statement indicating the act of standing, by way of excluding sitting and so on. Therefore, just as one who goes to the other side of a rampart or the other side of a mountain is said to go 'beyond the rampart' or 'beyond the mountain' unhindered, so too here, regarding those who stand in the regions beyond a wall, He said, 'they stand beyond the walls' (`tirokuṭṭesu tiṭṭhanti`). In the phrase `sandhisiṅghāṭakesu ca`, `sandhiyo` are said to be four-cornered crossroads, and also junctions of houses, junctions of walls, and junctions of open spaces. `Siṅghāṭakā` are said to be three-cornered crossroads. Combining these into one and joining it with the preceding, He said, `sandhisiṅghāṭakesu ca`. As for `dvārabāhāsu tiṭṭhanti`, it means they stand relying on the posts of city gates and house doors. In the phrase `āgantvāna sakaṃ gharaṃ`, 'one's own house' refers to the house of relatives from a previous life as well as a house where one had previously lived as its owner. Because they come to both of these with the perception of it being 'their own house', He said, `āgantvāna sakaṃ gharaṃ`.

Dutiyagāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Second Verse.

2. Evaṃ bhagavā pubbe anajjhāvutthapubbampi pubbañātigharaṃ bimbisāranivesanaṃ sakagharasaññāya āgantvā tirokuṭṭasandhisiṅghāṭakadvārabāhāsu ṭhite issāmacchariyaphalaṃ anubhavante, appekacce dīghamassukesavikāradhare [P 0.0207] andhakāramukhe sithilabandhanavilambamānakisapharusakāḷakaṅgapaccaṅge tattha tattha ṭhitavanadāhadaḍḍhatālarukkhasadise, appekacce jighacchāpipāsāraṇinimmathanena udarato uṭṭhāya mukhato viniccharantāya aggijālāya pariḍayhamānasarīre, appekacce sūcichiddāṇumattakaṇṭhabilatāya pabbatākārakucchitāya ca laddhampi pānabhojanaṃ yāvadatthaṃ bhuñjituṃ asamatthatāya khuppipāsāparete aññaṃ rasamavindamāne, appekacce aññamaññassa aññesaṃ vā sattānaṃ pabhinnagaṇḍapiḷakamukhā paggharitarudhirapubbalasikādiṃ laddhā amatamiva sāyamāne ativiya duddasikavirūpabhayānakasarīre bahū pete rañño nidassento –

2. Thus the Blessed One, wishing to point out to the king many petas—who, with the perception of it being their own home, had come to the residence of Bimbisāra, a home of their relatives from a previous life though they had not lived there before, and were standing beyond the walls, at junctions, at crossroads, and at doorposts, experiencing the fruit of envy and stinginess; some of whom had long beards, deformed appearances, and dark faces, with loosely-jointed and dangling, emaciated, rough, and black major and minor limbs, like palm trees standing here and there that had been scorched in a forest fire; some of whom were being churned by hunger and thirst, with bodies being burned by a flame that, having arisen from the belly, issued forth from the mouth; some of whom, due to having a throat-opening the size of a needle's eye and a belly the size of a mountain, were unable to eat their fill of the drink and food they obtained and, being overcome by hunger and thirst, found no other taste; and some of whom, having obtained the blood, pus, fluid, and so on, that oozed from the burst boils and sores of one another or of other beings, were licking it as if it were ambrosia, and who had bodies that were extremely repulsive, deformed, and frightening—

“Tirokuṭṭesu tiṭṭhanti, sandhisiṅghāṭakesu ca;

Dvārabāhāsu tiṭṭhanti, āgantvāna sakaṃ ghara”nti. –

‘They stand beyond the walls, and at junctions and crossroads; they stand at the doorposts, having come to their own home.’

Vatvā puna tehi katassa kammassa dāruṇabhāvaṃ dassento “pahūte annapānamhī”ti dutiyagāthamāha.

Having spoken thus, and then wishing to show the harsh nature of the kamma done by them, He spoke the second verse, beginning: ‘When there is abundant food and drink….’

Tattha [V 0.0164] pahūteti anappake bahumhi, yāvadatthiketi vuttaṃ hoti. Bha-kārassa hi ha-kāro labbhati “pahu santo na bharatī”tiādīsu (su. ni. 98) viya. Keci pana “bahūte” iti ca “bahūke” iti ca paṭhanti. Pamādapāṭhā ete[M 0.0174]. Anne ca pānamhi ca annapānamhi. Khajje ca bhojje ca khajjabhojje, etena asitapītakhāyitasāyitavasena catubbidhaṃ āhāraṃ dasseti. Upaṭṭhiteti upagamma ṭhite, sajjite paṭiyatte samohiteti vuttaṃ hoti. Na tesaṃ koci sarati, sattānanti tesaṃ pettivisaye uppannānaṃ sattānaṃ koci mātā vā pitā vā putto vā na sarati. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Kammapaccayā, attanā katassa adānadānappaṭisedhanādibhedassa kadariyakammassa [P 0.0208] paccayā. Tañhi tesaṃ kammaṃ ñātīnaṃ sarituṃ na deti.

Therein, `pahūte` means 'not a little', 'much'; it is said to mean 'as much as is desired'. For the letter `ha` is found in place of the letter `bha`, as in `pahu santo na bharatī` and so on. Some, however, recite it as `bahūte` and `bahūke`. These are readings due to negligence. `Annapānamhi` is from `anne ca pānamhi ca` (in food and in drink). `Khajjabhojje` is from `khajje ca bhojje ca` (in hard food and in soft food); by this, He shows the four kinds of nutriments, namely what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and savored. `Upaṭṭhite` means 'having approached and been placed', 'arranged', 'prepared', 'gathered'. `Na tesaṃ koci sarati, sattānaṃ` means: of those beings who have been reborn in the peta-realm, no one—be it mother, father, or son—remembers them. For what reason? Because of the condition of their kamma; because of the condition of the stingy kamma they themselves performed, of the nature of not giving, preventing others from giving, and so on. For that kamma of theirs does not allow their relatives to remember.

Tatiyagāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Third Verse.

3. Evaṃ bhagavā anappakepi annapānādimhi paccupaṭṭhite “api nāma amhe uddissa kiñci dadeyyu”nti ñātī paccāsīsantānaṃ vicarataṃ tesaṃ petānaṃ tehi katassa atikaṭukavipākakarassa kammassa paccayena kassaci ñātino anussaraṇamattābhāvaṃ dassento –

3. Thus, when much food and drink, etc., was set before them, the Blessed One, wishing to show the state of not even being remembered by any relative whatsoever—due to the cause of the kamma done by them, which has an extremely harsh result—for those petas who were wandering about, hoping from their relatives, ‘Perhaps they might give something, intending it for us,’—

“Pahūte annapānamhi, khajjabhojje upaṭṭhite;

Na tesaṃ koci sarati, sattānaṃ kammapaccayā”ti. –

‘When abundant food and drink are available, with solid and soft food prepared, no one remembers them, those beings, due to the cause of their kamma.’

Vatvā puna rañño pettivisayūpapanne ñātake uddissa dinnaṃ dānaṃ pasaṃsanto “evaṃ dadanti ñātīna”nti tatiyagāthamāha.

Having spoken thus, then, wishing to praise the gift given by the king, intending it for his relatives who had arisen in the peta-realm, He spoke the third verse beginning, ‘evaṃ dadanti ñātīnaṃ’.

Tattha evanti upamāvacanaṃ. Tassa dvidhā sambandho – tesaṃ sattānaṃ kammapaccayā asarantepi kismiñci dadanti, ñātīnaṃ, ye evaṃ anukampakā hontīti ca yathā tayā, mahārāja, dinnaṃ, evaṃ suciṃ paṇītaṃ kālena kappiyaṃ pānabhojanaṃ dadanti ñātīnaṃ, ye honti anukampakāti ca. Dadantīti denti uddisanti niyyātenti. Ñātīnanti mātito ca pitito ca sambandhānaṃ. Yeti ye keci puttā vā dhītaro vā bhātaro vā hontīti bhavanti. Anukampakāti atthakāmā hitesino. Sucinti vimalaṃ dassaneyyaṃ manoramaṃ dhammikaṃ dhammaladdhaṃ. Paṇītanti uttamaṃ seṭṭhaṃ. Kālenāti ñātipetānaṃ tirokuṭṭādīsu āgantvā ṭhitakālena. Kappiyanti anucchavikaṃ patirūpaṃ ariyānaṃ paribhogārahaṃ. Pānabhojananti pānañca bhojanañca. Idha pānabhojanamukhena sabbopi deyyadhammo adhippeto.

Therein, `evaṃ` is a word of comparison. Its connection should be understood in two ways. Firstly: Although they do not remember those beings due to the cause of their kamma, those relatives who are thus compassionate towards their peta-relatives give a gift for some reason. Secondly: O great king, just as was given by you, so too, those relatives who are compassionate towards their peta-relatives give pure, excellent, suitable drink and food at the proper time. `Dadanti` means they give, they intend, they dedicate. `Ñātīnaṃ` means of those connected through the mother and through the father. `Ye` means whoever—sons, daughters, or brothers. `Honti` means they are. `Anukampakā` means desiring their benefit, seeking their welfare. `Suciṃ` means stainless, lovely to see, delightful to the mind, righteous, and righteously acquired. `Paṇītaṃ` means supreme, excellent. `Kālena` means at the time when the peta-relatives have come and are standing outside the walls, etc. `Kappiyaṃ` means suitable, appropriate, worthy of being used by the noble ones. `Pānabhojanaṃ` means drink and food. Here, by means of drink and food, every kind of gift-object is intended.

Catutthagāthāpubbaddhavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the First Half of the Fourth Verse.

4. Evaṃ [V 0.0165][M 0.0175] bhagavā raññā māgadhena petabhūtānaṃ ñātīnaṃ anukampāya dinnaṃ pānabhojanaṃ pasaṃsanto –

4. Thus the Blessed One, wishing to praise the drink and food given by the Magadhan king out of compassion for his relatives who had become petas—

“Evaṃ dadanti ñātīnaṃ, ye honti anukampakā;

Suciṃ paṇītaṃ kālena, kappiyaṃ pānabhojana”nti. –

Thus do they give to relatives, those who are compassionate: pure, excellent, timely, and suitable drink and food.

Vatvā puna yena pakārena dinnaṃ tesaṃ hoti, taṃ dassento “idaṃ vo ñātīnaṃ hotū”ti catutthagāthāya pubbaddhamāha taṃ tatiyagāthāya pubbaddhena sambandhitabbaṃ –

Having spoken thus, and again, wishing to show the manner in which what is given is for them, He spoke the first half of the fourth verse, 'idaṃ vo ñātīnaṃ hotu,' which should be connected with the first half of the third verse—

“Evaṃ dadanti ñātīnaṃ, ye honti anukampakā[P 0.0209];

Idaṃ vo ñātīnaṃ hotu, sukhitā hontu ñātayo”ti.

Those relatives who are compassionate give to their relatives in this manner: 'May this be for the relatives, may the relatives be happy!'

Tena “idaṃ vo ñātīnaṃ hotūti evaṃ dadanti, no aññathā”ti ettha ākāratthena evaṃsaddena dātabbākāranidassanaṃ kataṃ hoti.

By that, with the phrase, 'May this be for the relatives,' it is meant 'thus they give, and not otherwise.' Here, by the word 'evaṃ', which has the meaning of 'manner', the indication of the manner of giving is made.

Tattha idanti deyyadhammanidassanaṃ. Voti “kacci pana vo anuruddhā samaggā sammodamānā”ti ca (ma. ni. 1.326; mahāva. 466), “yehi vo ariyā”ti ca evamādīsu viya kevalaṃ nipātamattaṃ, na sāmivacanaṃ. Ñātīnaṃ hotūti pettivisaye uppannānaṃ ñātakānaṃ hotu. Sukhitā hontu ñātayoti te pettivisayūpapannā ñātayo idaṃ paccanubhavantā sukhitā hontūti.

Therein, 'idaṃ' is the indication of the gift-object. 'Vo' is merely a particle, not a possessive term, as in such phrases as 'I hope, Anuruddhas, that you are living in harmony and mutual joy' and 'by whom your noble ones...' and so on. 'Ñātīnaṃ hotu' means 'may it be for the relatives who have arisen in the peta-realm.' 'Sukhitā hontu ñātayo' means 'may those relatives who have arisen in the peta-realm, experiencing this, be happy.'

Catutthagāthāparaddhapañcamagāthāpubbaddhavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Latter Half of the Fourth Verse and the First Half of the Fifth Verse.

4-5. Evaṃ bhagavā yena pakārena pettivisayūpapannānaṃ ñātīnaṃ dātabbaṃ, taṃ dassento “idaṃ vo ñātīnaṃ hotu, sukhitā hontu ñātayo”ti vatvā puna yasmā “idaṃ vo ñātīnaṃ hotū”ti vuttepi na aññena kataṃ kammaṃ aññassa phaladaṃ hoti, kevalantu tathā uddissa diyyamānaṃ taṃ vatthu ñātīnaṃ kusalakammassa paccayo hoti. Tasmā yathā tesaṃ tasmiṃyeva vatthusmiṃ taṅkhaṇe phalanibbattakaṃ kusalakammaṃ hoti, taṃ dassento “te ca tatthā”ti catutthagāthāya pacchimaddhaṃ “pahūte annapānamhī”ti pañcamagāthāya pubbaddhañca āha.

4-5. Thus the Blessed One, showing the manner in which it should be given to relatives who have arisen in the peta-realm, having said, 'May this be for the relatives; may the relatives be happy!', then spoke further. Since, even when it is said, 'May this be for the relatives,' an action done by one does not become fruit-bearing for another—but rather, that gift-object, being dedicated in such a way, becomes a condition for the relatives' wholesome kamma—therefore, to show how, for them, on account of that very gift-object, wholesome kamma productive of fruit arises at that very moment, He spoke the latter half of the fourth verse, 'And they there...' and the first half of the fifth verse, 'When there is abundant food and drink...'

Tesaṃ [V 0.0166][M 0.0176] attho – te ñātipetā yattha taṃ dānaṃ dīyati, tattha samantato āgantvā samāgantvā, samodhāya vā ekajjhaṃ hutvāti vuttaṃ hoti, sammā āgatā samāgatā “ime no ñātayo amhākaṃ atthāya dānaṃ uddisissantī”ti etadatthaṃ sammā āgatā hutvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Pahūte annapānamhīti tasmiṃ attano uddissamāne pahūte annapānamhi. Sakkaccaṃ anumodareti abhisaddahantā kammaphalaṃ avijahantā cittīkāraṃ avikkhittacittā hutvā “idaṃ no dānaṃ hitāya sukhāya hotū”ti modanti anumodanti, pītisomanassajātā hontīti.

The meaning of these is: those departed relatives, in whatever place that offering is given, having come there from all around, having assembled together, or having united and become as one—this is the meaning. 'Well-assembled' means having come together properly for this purpose: 'These relatives of ours will dedicate an offering for our benefit'—this is the meaning. 'When there is abundant food and drink' means when abundant food and drink is being dedicated to oneself. 'They rejoice reverently' means, having great faith, not abandoning the fruit of kamma, paying respect, and becoming undistracted in mind, they think, 'May this offering be for our welfare and happiness,' and thus they rejoice and rejoice approvingly; they become filled with joy and gladness.

Pañcamagāthāparaddhachaṭṭhagāthāpubbaddhavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Latter Half of the Fifth Verse and the First Half of the Sixth Verse.

5-6. Evaṃ [P 0.0210] bhagavā yathā pettivisayūpapannānaṃ taṅkhaṇe phalanibbattakaṃ kusalaṃ kammaṃ hoti, taṃ dassento –

5-6. Thus the Blessed One, showing how, for those who have arisen in the peta-realm, wholesome kamma productive of fruit arises at that very moment:

“Te ca tattha samāgantvā, ñātipetā samāgatā;

Pahūte annapānamhi, sakkaccaṃ anumodare”ti. –

“And they, the departed relatives, having gathered there, having assembled; in the abundant food and drink, they reverently rejoice.”

Vatvā puna ñātake nissāya nibbattakusalakammaphalaṃ paccanubhontānaṃ tesaṃ ñātī ārabbha thomanākāraṃ dassento “ciraṃ jīvantū”ti pañcamagāthāya pacchimaddhaṃ “amhākañca katā pūjā”ti chaṭṭhagāthāya pubbaddhañca āha.

Having spoken thus, and again, to show the manner of praise concerning those relatives who experience the fruit of wholesome kamma that has arisen depending on their living relatives, He spoke the latter half of the fifth verse, 'May they live long...' and the first half of the sixth verse, 'And for us, worship has been done...'

Tesaṃ attho – ciraṃ jīvantūti cirajīvino dīghāyukā hontu. No ñātīti amhākaṃ ñātakā. Yesaṃ hetūti ye nissāya yesaṃ kāraṇā. Labhāmaseti labhāma. Attanā taṅkhaṇaṃ paṭiladdhasampattiṃ apadisantā bhaṇanti. Petānañhi attano anumodanena, dāyakānaṃ uddesena, dakkhiṇeyyasampadāya cāti tīhi aṅgehi dakkhiṇā samijjhati, taṅkhaṇe phalanibbattikā hoti. Tattha dāyakā visesahetu. Tenāhaṃsu “yesaṃ hetu labhāmase”ti. Amhākañca katā pūjāti “idaṃ vo ñātīnaṃ hotū”ti evaṃ imaṃ dānaṃ uddisantehi amhākañca pūjā katā. Dāyakā ca anipphalāti yamhi santāne pariccāgamayaṃ kammaṃ kataṃ, tassa tattheva phaladānato dāyakā ca anipphalāti.

The meaning of these is: 'May they live long' means may they be long-lived, having long lives. 'Our relatives' means our relatives. 'Because of whom' means depending on whom, by cause of whom. 'We receive' means we obtain. Pointing to the prosperity they themselves have obtained at that moment, they speak. Indeed, for the petas, the offering succeeds through three factors: by their own rejoicing, by the dedication of the donors, and by the accomplishment of the worthy recipient. It becomes productive of fruit at that moment. Therein, the donors are a special cause. Therefore, the petas said, 'Because of whom we receive.' 'And worship has been done for us' means: by those dedicating this gift thus, 'May this be for the relatives,' worship has been done for us also. 'And the donors are not without fruit' means: because the kamma of relinquishment, performed in a certain continuity of existence, gives its fruit right there to that being, the donors are also not without fruit.

Etthāha [M 0.0177] – “kiṃ pana pettivisayūpapannā eva ñātayo labhanti, udāhu aññepi labhantī”ti[V 0.0167]? Vuccate – bhagavatā evetaṃ byākataṃ jāṇussoṇinā brāhmaṇena puṭṭhena, kimettha amhehi vattabbaṃ atthi. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ –

Here it is asked: “Do only relatives who have arisen in the peta-realm receive, or do others also receive?” It is answered: This was explained by the Blessed One himself when questioned by the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi; what is there for us to say in this matter? For it has been said:

“Mayamassu, bho gotama, brāhmaṇā nāma dānāni dema, saddhāni karoma ‘idaṃ dānaṃ petānaṃ ñātisālohitānaṃ upakappatu, idaṃ dānaṃ petā ñātisālohitā paribhuñjantū’ti, kacci taṃ, bho gotama, dānaṃ petānaṃ ñātisālohitānaṃ upakappati, kacci te petā ñātisālohitā taṃ dānaṃ paribhuñjantīti. Ṭhāne kho, brāhmaṇa, upakappati, no aṭṭhāneti.

“Indeed, Master Gotama, we who are called brahmins give gifts and perform funeral rites, saying, ‘May this gift benefit our departed relatives and blood-kin; may our departed relatives and blood-kin enjoy this gift.’ Master Gotama, does that gift truly benefit our departed relatives and blood-kin? Do those departed relatives and blood-kin enjoy that gift?” “In a possible case, Brahmin, it benefits; in an impossible case, it does not.”

“Katamaṃ pana taṃ, bho gotama, ṭhānaṃ, katamaṃ aṭṭhānanti? Idha, brāhmaṇa, ekacco pāṇātipātī hoti…pe… micchādiṭṭhiko hoti, so [P 0.0211] kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā nirayaṃ upapajjati. Yo nerayikānaṃ sattānaṃ āhāro, tena so tattha yāpeti, tena so tattha tiṭṭhati. Idaṃ kho, brāhmaṇa, aṭṭhānaṃ, yattha ṭhitassa taṃ dānaṃ na upakappati.

“What then, Master Gotama, is the possible case, and what is the impossible case?” “Here, Brahmin, a certain person destroys life... holds wrong view. With the breakup of the body, after death, he arises in hell. Whatever is the food of beings in hell, with that he sustains himself there, with that he remains there. This, Brahmin, is an impossible case, wherein for one established there, that gift does not benefit.”

“Idha pana, brāhmaṇa, ekacco pāṇātipātī hoti…pe… micchādiṭṭhiko hoti, so kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā tiracchānayoniṃ upapajjati. Yo tiracchānayonikānaṃ sattānaṃ āhāro, tena so tattha yāpeti, tena so tattha tiṭṭhati. Idampi kho, brāhmaṇa, aṭṭhānaṃ, yattha ṭhitassa taṃ dānaṃ na upakappati.

“Here, Brahmin, a certain person destroys life… holds wrong view. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the animal realm. Whatever is the food of beings in the animal realm, with that he sustains himself there, with that he remains there. This also, Brahmin, is an impossible case, wherein for one established there, that gift does not benefit him.

“Idha pana, brāhmaṇa, ekacco pāṇātipātā paṭivirato hoti…pe… sammādiṭṭhiko hoti, so kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā manussānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjati…pe… devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjati. Yo devānaṃ āhāro, tena so tattha yāpeti, tena so tattha tiṭṭhati. Idampi kho, brāhmaṇa, aṭṭhānaṃ, yattha ṭhitassa taṃ dānaṃ na upakappati.

“Here, Brahmin, a certain person abstains from destroying life… holds right view. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in companionship with humans… he is reborn in companionship with devas. Whatever is the food of the devas, with that he sustains himself there, with that he remains there. This also, Brahmin, is an impossible case, wherein for one established there, that gift does not benefit him.

“Idha pana, brāhmaṇa, ekacco pāṇātipātī hoti…pe… micchādiṭṭhiko hoti, so kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā pettivisayaṃ upapajjati. Yo pettivesayikānaṃ sattānaṃ āhāro, tena [M 0.0178] so tattha yāpeti, tena so tattha tiṭṭhati. Yaṃ vā panassa ito anupavecchanti [V 0.0168] mittāmaccā vā ñātisālohitā vā, tena so tattha yāpeti, tena so tattha tiṭṭhati. Idaṃ kho, brāhmaṇa, ṭhānaṃ, yattha ṭhitassa taṃ dānaṃ upakappatīti.

“Here, Brahmin, a certain person destroys life… holds wrong view. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the peta-realm. Whatever is the food of beings in the peta-realm, with that he sustains himself there, with that he remains there. Or, with whatever his friends, associates, or kinsmen and blood-relatives dedicate to him from here, with that he sustains himself there, with that he remains there. This, Brahmin, is the possible case, wherein for one established there, that gift benefits him.”

“Sace pana, bho gotama, so peto ñātisālohito taṃ ṭhānaṃ anupapanno hoti, ko taṃ dānaṃ paribhuñjatīti? Aññepissa, brāhmaṇa, petā ñātisālohitā taṃ ṭhānaṃ upapannā honti, te taṃ dānaṃ paribhuñjantīti.

“But if, Master Gotama, that departed kinsman and blood-relative is not reborn in that state, who enjoys that gift?” “Other departed kinsmen and blood-relatives of his, Brahmin, who are reborn in that state enjoy that gift.”

“Sace pana, bho gotama, so ceva peto ñātisālohito taṃ ṭhānaṃ anupapanno hoti, aññepissa petā ñātisālohitā taṃ ṭhānaṃ anupapannā honti, ko taṃ dānaṃ paribhuñjatīti? Aṭṭhānaṃ kho etaṃ brāhmaṇa anavakāso, yaṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ vivittaṃ assa iminā dīghena addhunā yadidaṃ petehi ñātisālohitehi. Apica brāhmaṇa dāyakopi anipphalo”ti (a. ni. 10.177).

“But if, Master Gotama, that very departed kinsman and blood-relative is not reborn in that state, and other departed kinsmen and blood-relatives of his are also not reborn in that state, who then enjoys that gift?” “Brahmin, it is impossible, there is no chance, that this state would be devoid of departed kinsmen and blood-relatives for such a long time. Moreover, Brahmin, the giver too is not without fruit.”

Chaṭṭhagāthāparaddhasattamagāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Latter Half of the Sixth Verse and the Seventh Verse

6-7. Evaṃ [P 0.0212] bhagavā rañño māgadhassa pettivisayūpapannānaṃ pubbañātīnaṃ sampattiṃ nissāya thomento “ete te, mahārāja, ñātī imāya dānasampadāya attamanā evaṃ thomentī”ti dassento –

6–7. Thus the Blessed One, with reference to the prosperity of the former kinsmen of the king of Magadha who had been reborn in the peta-realm, wishing to praise them and to show, “These kinsmen of yours, great king, being delighted by this accomplishment of giving, praise thus,” said:

“Ciraṃ jīvantu no ñātī, yesaṃ hetu labhāmase;

Amhākañca katā pūjā, dāyakā ca anipphalā”ti. –

“Long live our kinsmen, on whose account we receive this. For us an offering has been made, and the givers are not without fruit.”

Vatvā puna tesaṃ pettivisayūpapannānaṃ aññassa kasigorakkhādino sampattipaṭilābhakāraṇassa abhāvaṃ ito dinnena yāpanabhāvañca dassento “na hi tattha kasī atthī”ti chaṭṭhagāthāya pacchimaddhaṃ “vaṇijjā tādisī”ti imaṃ sattamagāthañca āha.

Having said this, wishing to show further to those reborn in the peta-realm the absence of any other cause for obtaining prosperity, such as agriculture and cattle-herding, and the fact that they subsist on what is given from here, he spoke the latter half of the sixth verse, “For there is no agriculture there,” and this seventh verse, “Nor is there such trade.”

Tatrāyaṃ atthavaṇṇanā – na hi, mahārāja, tattha pettivisaye kasi atthi, yaṃ nissāya te petā sampattiṃ paṭilabheyyuṃ. Gorakkhettha na vijjatīti na kevalaṃ kasi eva, gorakkhāpi ettha pettivisaye na vijjati, yaṃ [M 0.0179] nissāya te sampattiṃ paṭilabheyyuṃ. Vaṇijjā tādisī natthīti vāṇijjāpi tādisī natthi, yā tesaṃ sampattipaṭilābhahetu bhaveyya. Hiraññena kayākayanti [V 0.0169] hiraññena kayavikkayampi tattha tādisaṃ natthi, yaṃ tesaṃ sampattipaṭilābhahetu bhaveyya. Ito dinnena yāpenti, petā kālagatā tahinti kevalaṃ pana ito ñātīhi vā mittāmaccehi vā dinnena yāpenti, attabhāvaṃ gamenti. Petāti pettivisayūpapannā sattā. Kālagatāti attano maraṇakālena gatā, “kālakatā”ti vā pāṭho, katakālā katamaraṇāti attho. Tahinti tasmiṃ pettivisaye.

Therein, this is the explanation of the meaning: Indeed, great king, in that peta-realm there is no agriculture, by relying on which those petas might obtain prosperity. ‘Cattle-herding is not found there’ means not only agriculture, but cattle-herding is also not found here in this peta-realm, by relying on which they might obtain prosperity. ‘Nor is there such trade’ means trade of such a kind also does not exist, which could be a cause for them to obtain prosperity. ‘Nor buying and selling with gold’ means buying and selling with gold of such a kind also does not exist there, which could be a cause for them to obtain prosperity. ‘They subsist on what is given from here, the petas who have passed on there’ means they subsist only on what is given from here by kinsmen or by friends and associates; they maintain their existence. ‘Petas’ means beings reborn in the peta-realm. ‘Passed on’ (kālagatā) means gone at the time of their own death; or the reading is ‘kālakatā’ (time-done), the meaning of which is ‘their time is done,’ ‘their death has occurred.’ ‘There’ means in that peta-realm.

Aṭṭhamanavamagāthādvayavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Pair of the Eighth and Ninth Verses

8-9. Evaṃ “ito dinnena yāpenti, petā kālagatā tahi”nti vatvā idāni upamāhi tamatthaṃ pakāsento “unname udakaṃ vuṭṭha”nti idaṃ gāthādvayamāha.

8–9. Having thus said, “The departed who have passed away are sustained there by what is given from here,” now, wishing to reveal that meaning with similes, he spoke this pair of verses beginning, “As water rained upon a height…”

Tassattho – yathā unnate thale ussāde bhūmibhāge meghehi abhivuṭṭhaṃ udakaṃ ninnaṃ pavattati, yo yo bhūmibhāgo ninno oṇato, taṃ taṃ pavattati gacchati pāpuṇāti, evameva [P 0.0213] ito dinnaṃ dānaṃ petānaṃ upakappati nibbattati, pātubhavatīti attho. Ninnamiva hi udakappavattiyā ṭhānaṃ petaloko dānupakappanāya. Yathāha – “idaṃ kho, brāhmaṇa, ṭhānaṃ, yattha ṭhitassa taṃ dānaṃ upakappatī”ti (a. ni. 10.177). Yathā ca kandarapadarasākhāpasākhakusobbhamahāsobbhasannipātehi vārivahā mahānajjo pūrā hutvā sāgaraṃ paripūrenti, evampi ito dinnadānaṃ pubbe vuttanayeneva petānaṃ upakappatīti.

Its meaning is: just as water rained down by clouds on a high, elevated area of land flows to a low place—whichever area of land is low and hollow, to that it flows, goes, and reaches—in the same way, a gift given from here benefits the departed, is accomplished, and becomes manifest. This is the meaning. Indeed, the peta-world should be understood as the place for the benefit of giving, just as a low place is for the flowing of water. As it is said: “This, Brahmin, is the place where, when one is established, that gift becomes beneficial” (AN 10.177). And just as the great rivers that carry water, having become full from the confluence of mountain-clefts, chasms, major channels, minor channels, small streams, and great streams, fill the ocean, so too a gift given from here benefits the departed in the manner already stated.

Dasamagāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Tenth Verse

10. Evaṃ bhagavā “ito dinnena yāpenti, petā kālagatā tahi”nti imaṃ atthaṃ upamāhi pakāsetvā puna yasmā te petā “ito kiñci lacchāmā”ti āsābhibhūtā ñātigharaṃ āgantvāpi “idaṃ nāma no dethā”ti yācituṃ asamatthā, tasmā tesaṃ imāni anussaraṇavatthūni anussaranto [M 0.0180] kulaputto dakkhiṇaṃ dajjāti dassento “adāsi me”ti imaṃ gāthamāha.

Thus the Blessed One, having explained with similes this meaning—“The departed who have passed away are sustained there by what is given from here”—spoke this verse, “He gave to me,” to show that, since those petas, overwhelmed by desire and thinking, “May we receive something from here,” are unable, even after coming to their relatives’ house, to ask, “Give us this,” therefore a clansman, recollecting these grounds for recollection for them, should give an offering.

Tassattho – “idaṃ nāma me dhanaṃ vā dhaññaṃ vā adāsī”ti ca, “idaṃ nāma me kiccaṃ attanā uyyogamāpajjanto akāsī”ti ca, “amu me mātito vā pitito vā sambandhattā ñātī”ti ca sinehavasena tāṇasamatthatāya “mittā”ti ca, “asuko me saha paṃsukīḷako sakhā”ti [V 0.0170] ca evaṃ sabbamanussaranto petānaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ dajjā, dānaṃ niyyāteyyāti. Aparo pāṭho “petānaṃ dakkhiṇā dajjā”ti. Tassattho – dātabbāti dajjā. Kā sā? Petānaṃ dakkhiṇā, teneva “adāsi me”tiādinā nayena pubbe katamanussaraṃ anussaratāti vuttaṃ hoti. Karaṇavacanappasaṅge paccattavacanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Its meaning is: “He gave me such-and-such wealth or grain,” and “He performed such-and-such a duty for me, exerting himself,” and “This person is my relative through connection to my mother or father,” and “This person is a friend, capable of being a refuge due to affection,” and “So-and-so is my companion, who played in the dust together with me.” Thus, recollecting all this, one should give an offering to the departed; one should dedicate the gift. Another reading is “petānaṃ dakkhiṇā dajjā.” Its meaning is: “dajjā” means “it should be given.” What is that? An offering for the departed. Therefore, it is said that one recollects, repeatedly recollecting what was done before in the manner of “He gave to me,” etc. Where the instrumental case is indicated, the nominative case should be understood.

Ekādasamagāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Eleventh Verse

11. Evaṃ bhagavā petānaṃ dakkhiṇāniyyātane kāraṇabhūtāni anussaraṇavatthūni dassento –

11. Thus, the Blessed One, wishing to show the grounds for recollection that are the cause for the dedication of an offering to the departed:

“Adāsi me akāsi me, ñātimittā sakhā ca me;

Petānaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ dajjā, pubbe katamanussara”nti. –

“‘He gave to me, he acted for me; they were my kinsmen, friends, and companions.’ Remembering what was done in the past, one should give an offering for the departed.”

Vatvā [P 0.0214] puna ye ñātimaraṇena ruṇṇasokādiparā eva hutvā tiṭṭhanti, na tesaṃ atthāya kiñci denti, tesaṃ taṃ ruṇṇasokādi kevalaṃ attaparitāpanameva hoti, na petānaṃ kiñci atthaṃ nipphādetīti dassento “na hi ruṇṇaṃ vā”ti imaṃ gāthamāha.

Having spoken thus, again, wishing to show that for those who, due to the death of relatives, remain overcome by weeping, sorrow, and so on, and give nothing for their benefit, that weeping, sorrow, and so on is merely self-torment and accomplishes no benefit for the departed, He spoke this verse beginning with, “For not by weeping…”

Tattha ruṇṇanti rodanā roditattaṃ assupātanaṃ, etena kāyaparissamaṃ dasseti. Sokoti socanā socitattaṃ, etena cittaparissamaṃ dasseti. Yā caññāti yā ca ruṇṇasokehi aññā. Paridevanāti ñātibyasanena phuṭṭhassa lālappanā, “kahaṃ ekaputtaka piya manāpā”ti evamādinā nayena guṇasaṃvaṇṇanā, etena vacīparissamaṃ dasseti.

Therein, ‘ruṇṇaṃ’ is weeping, the state of weeping, the shedding of tears; by this, He shows bodily exertion. ‘Soko’ is sorrowing, the state of sorrowing; by this, He shows mental exertion. ‘Yā caññā’ is whatever is other than weeping and sorrow. ‘Paridevanā’ is the lamentation of one afflicted by the destruction of relatives, praising their qualities by way of such as, “Where are you, my only son, beloved and pleasing?”; by this, He shows verbal exertion.

Dvādasamagāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Twelfth Verse

12. Evaṃ [M 0.0181] bhagavā “ruṇṇaṃ vā soko vā yā caññā paridevanā, sabbampi taṃ petānaṃ atthāya na hoti, kevalantu attānaṃ paritāpanamattameva, evaṃ tiṭṭhanti ñātayo”ti ruṇṇādīnaṃ niratthakabhāvaṃ dassetvā puna māgadharājena yā dakkhiṇā dinnā, tassā sātthakabhāvaṃ dassento “ayañca kho dakkhiṇā”ti imaṃ gāthamāha.

12. Thus the Blessed One, having shown the fruitlessness of weeping and so on with the words, “Whatever weeping or sorrow or other lamentation there is, all of that is not for the benefit of the departed; it is merely self-torment. Thus the relatives stand,” again, wishing to show the beneficial nature of the offering given by the king of Magadha, spoke this verse beginning with, “And this offering indeed…”

Tassattho – ayañca kho, mahārāja, dakkhiṇā tayā ajja attano ñātigaṇaṃ uddissa dinnā[V 0.0171], sā yasmā saṅgho anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassa, tasmā saṅghamhi suppatiṭṭhitā assa petajanassa dīgharattaṃ hitāya upakappati sampajjati phalatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Upakappatīti ca ṭhānaso upakappati, taṃkhaṇaṃyeva upakappati, na cirena. Yathā hi taṃkhaṇaññeva paṭibhantaṃ “ṭhānasovetaṃ tathāgataṃ paṭibhātī”ti vuccati, evamidhāpi taṃkhaṇaṃyeva upakappantā “ṭhānaso upakappatī”ti vuttā. Yaṃ vā taṃ “idaṃ kho, brāhmaṇa, ṭhānaṃ, yattha ṭhitassa taṃ dānaṃ upakappatī”ti (a. ni. 10.177) vuttaṃ, tattha khuppipāsikavantāsaparadattūpajīvinijjhāmataṇhikādibhedabhinne ṭhāne upakappatīti vuttaṃ yathā kahāpaṇaṃ dento “kahāpaṇaso detī”ti [P 0.0215] loke vuccati. Imasmiñca atthavikappe upakappatīti pātubhavati, nibbattatīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Its meaning is this: O great king, this offering given by you today, dedicated to your group of relatives—because the Saṅgha is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world, it is therefore well-established in the Saṅgha. For the departed beings, it serves their welfare for a long time, is accomplished, and bears fruit; this is the meaning. And ‘it serves’ (upakappati) means it serves instantly (ṭhānaso), it serves at that very moment, not after a long time. For just as something that occurs at that very moment is said to ‘occur to the Tathāgata instantly,’ so too here, serving at that very moment is spoken of as ‘serving instantly.’ Or, as it was said, “This, brahmin, is the condition (ṭhānaṃ) where, for one established therein, that gift serves” (A.N. 10.177), it is meant that it serves in that condition (ṭhāne) which is differentiated by the various kinds such as those afflicted by hunger and thirst, those who eat what is vomited, those living on what is given by others, and those consumed by burning thirst. This is like how in the world one who gives a kahāpaṇa is said to ‘give by the kahāpaṇa’ (kahāpaṇaso). And in this alternative interpretation of the meaning, ‘it serves’ (upakappati) means it becomes manifest, it comes into being; this is the meaning.

Terasamagāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Thirteenth Verse

13. Evaṃ bhagavā raññā dinnāya dakkhiṇāya sātthakabhāvaṃ dassento –

13. Thus, the Blessed One, wishing to show the fruitfulness of the offering given by the king—

“Ayañca kho dakkhiṇā dinnā, saṅghamhi suppatiṭṭhitā;

Dīgharattaṃ hitāyassa, ṭhānaso upakappatī”ti. –

“This offering, given and well-established in the Saṅgha, serves his welfare for a long time, taking effect instantly.”

Vatvā puna yasmā imaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ dentena ñātīnaṃ ñātīhi kattabbakiccakaraṇavasena ñātidhammo nidassito, bahujanassa pākaṭīkato, nidassanaṃ vā kato, tumhehipi ñātīnaṃ evameva ñātīhi kattabbakiccakaraṇavasena ñātidhammo paripūretabbo, na niratthakehi ruṇṇādīhi attā paritāpetabboti ca pete dibbasampattiṃ adhigamentena petānaṃ pūjā katā uḷārā, buddhappamukhañca bhikkhusaṅghaṃ annapānādīhi santappentena bhikkhūnaṃ balaṃ anupadinnaṃ, anukampādiguṇaparivārañca cāgacetanaṃ nibbattentena anappakaṃ puññaṃ [M 0.0182] pasutaṃ, tasmā bhagavā imehi yathābhuccaguṇehi rājānaṃ sampahaṃsento –

Having spoken thus, again: because by giving this offering for the sake of relatives, the duty of relatives to be performed by living relatives was pointed out and made manifest to the multitude, or a demonstration was made; and because you too should fulfill this duty for your relatives in the same way, by performing the necessary actions, and not torment yourself with useless weeping and the like; and because, desiring the departed to attain divine fortune, a sublime offering was made for them; and by satisfying the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha with food and drink, strength was given to the monks; and by generating a volition of generosity accompanied by qualities such as compassion, immeasurable merit was produced—therefore, the Blessed One, praising the king with these true qualities,

“So ñātidhammo ca ayaṃ nidassito,

Petāna pūjā ca katā uḷārā;

Balañca bhikkhūnamanuppadinnaṃ,

Tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappaka”nti. –

“This duty of relatives has thus been shown, and a sublime offering made to the departed; strength, too, has been given to the monks, and by you immeasurable merit has been generated.”

Imāya gāthāya desanaṃ pariyosāpeti.

With this verse, he concluded the discourse.

Atha [V 0.0172] vā “so ñātidhammo ca ayaṃ nidassito”ti iminā gāthāpadena bhagavā rājānaṃ dhammiyā kathāya sandasseti. Ñātidhammanidassanameva hi ettha sandassanaṃ petāna pūjā ca katā uḷārāti iminā samādapeti. Uḷārāti pasaṃsanameva hi ettha punappunaṃ pūjākaraṇe samādapanaṃ. Balañca bhikkhūnamanuppadinnanti iminā samuttejeti. Balānuppadānameva hi ettha evaṃ dānaṃ, balānuppadānatāti tassa ussāhavaḍḍhanena samuttejanaṃ. Tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappakanti iminā sampahaṃseti. Puññappasutakittanameva hi ettha tassa yathābhuccaguṇasaṃvaṇṇanabhāvena sampahaṃsanajananato [P 0.0216] sampahaṃsananti veditabbaṃ.

Alternatively, with the verse line, “This duty of relatives has thus been shown,” the Blessed One instructs the king with a Dhamma talk. Indeed, here the instruction is the pointing out of the duty of relatives. With, “And a sublime offering made to the departed,” he encourages. For `uḷārā` (sublime) is here simply praise, and it is an encouragement to make offerings again and again. With, “And strength has been given to the monks,” he rouses. For here, such a gift is indeed the giving of strength; 'the giving of strength' means rousing by increasing his enthusiasm. With, “By you immeasurable merit has been generated,” he gladdens. For here, the proclaiming of the generated merit, by being an extolling of his qualities in accordance with reality, generates gladness; therefore, it should be known as 'gladdening'.

Desanāpariyosāne ca pettivisayūpapattiādīnavasaṃvaṇṇanena saṃviggānaṃ yoniso padahataṃ caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi. Dutiyadivasepi bhagavā devamanussānaṃ idameva tirokuṭṭaṃ desesi, evaṃ yāva sattamadivasā tādiso eva dhammābhisamayo ahosīti.

And at the conclusion of the discourse, eighty-four thousand living beings, who were stirred with urgency by the description of the dangers of arising in the realm of the departed spirits and were striving with wise attention, attained comprehension of the Dhamma. On the second day also, the Blessed One taught this very Tirokuṭṭa Sutta to devas and humans. In this way, up to the seventh day, a similar comprehension of the Dhamma occurred.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Khuddakapāṭha Commentary named the Paramatthajotikā,

Tirokuṭṭasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta is concluded.

8. Nidhikaṇḍasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta

Nikkhepakāraṇaṃ

The Reason for the Placement

Idāni [V 0.0173] yadidaṃ tirokuṭṭānantaraṃ “nidhiṃ nidheti puriso”tiādinā nidhikaṇḍaṃ nikkhittaṃ, tassa –

Now, concerning this Nidhikaṇḍa which has been placed immediately after the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta, beginning with 'A person lays down a treasure,' etc.—

“Bhāsitvā [M 0.0183] nidhikaṇḍassa, idha nikkhepakāraṇaṃ;

Aṭṭhuppattiñca dīpetvā, karissāmatthavaṇṇanaṃ”.

Having explained the reason for the placement of the Nidhikaṇḍa here, and having elucidated its origin story, we shall provide an explanation of its meaning.

Tattha idha nikkhepakāraṇaṃ tāvassa evaṃ veditabbaṃ. Idañhi nidhikaṇḍaṃ bhagavatā iminā anukkamena avuttampi yasmā anumodanavasena vuttassa tirokuṭṭassa mithunabhūtaṃ, tasmā idha nikkhittaṃ. Tirokuṭṭena vā puññavirahitānaṃ vipattiṃ dassetvā iminā katapuññānaṃ sampattidassanatthampi idaṃ idha nikkhittanti veditabbaṃ. Idamassa idha nikkhepakāraṇaṃ.

Therein, the reason for its placement here should first be understood thus. Although this Nidhikaṇḍa was not spoken by the Blessed One in this sequence, because it forms a pair with the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta, which was spoken by way of appreciation, it is therefore placed here. Or, it should be understood that after showing the misfortune of those devoid of merit through the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta, this is placed here by means of this Sutta for the purpose of also showing the accomplishment of those who have made merit. This is the reason for its placement here.

Suttaṭṭhuppatti

The Origin Story of the Sutta

Aṭṭhuppatti panassa – sāvatthiyaṃ kira aññataro kuṭumbiko aḍḍho mahaddhano mahābhogo. So ca saddho hoti pasanno, vigatamalamaccherena cetasā agāraṃ ajjhāvasati. So ekasmiṃ divase buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa dānaṃ deti. Tena ca samayena rājā dhanatthiko hoti, so tassa santike purisaṃ pesesi “gaccha, bhaṇe, itthannāmaṃ kuṭumbikaṃ ānehī”ti. So gantvā taṃ kuṭumbikaṃ āha “rājā taṃ gahapati āmantetī”ti. Kuṭumbiko saddhādiguṇasamannāgatena [P 0.0217] cetasā buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ parivisanto āha “gaccha, bho purisa, pacchā āgamissāmi, idāni tāvamhi nidhiṃ nidhento ṭhito”ti. Atha bhagavā bhuttāvī pavārito tameva puññasampadaṃ paramatthato nidhīti dassetuṃ tassa kuṭumbikassa anumodanatthaṃ “nidhiṃ nidheti puriso”ti imā gāthāyo abhāsi. Ayamassa aṭṭhuppatti.

Now, its origin story is as follows: In Sāvatthī, it is said, there was a certain householder who was prosperous, of great wealth, and of great possessions. And he was faithful and devoted, dwelling at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess. One day, he gave a gift to the community of monks with the Buddha at its head. At that time, the king was in need of wealth, and he sent a man to the householder, saying, 'Go, friend, and bring the householder of such-and-such a name.' That man went and said to the householder, 'Householder, the king summons you.' The householder, with a mind endowed with faith and other virtues, while serving the community of monks with the Buddha at its head, replied, 'Go, good man, I will come later; for now, I am engaged in laying down a treasure.' Then the Blessed One, having finished his meal and indicated he was satisfied, in order to show that this very accomplishment of merit is, in the ultimate sense, a treasure, and for the appreciation of that householder, spoke these verses beginning, 'A person lays down a treasure…' This is its origin story.

Evamassa [V 0.0174] –

Thus, concerning this—

“Bhāsitvā nidhikaṇḍassa, idha nikkhepakāraṇaṃ;

Aṭṭhuppattiñca dīpetvā, karissāmatthavaṇṇanaṃ”.

Having explained the reason for the placement of the Nidhikaṇḍa here, and having elucidated its origin story, we shall now provide an explanation of its meaning.

Paṭhamagāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the First Verse

1. Tattha nidhiṃ nidheti purisoti nidhīyatīti nidhi, ṭhapīyati rakkhīyati gopīyatīti attho. So catubbidho thāvaro, jaṅgamo, aṅgasamo, anugāmikoti. Tattha thāvaro nāma bhūmigataṃ vā vehāsaṭṭhaṃ vā hiraññaṃ vā [M 0.0184] suvaṇṇaṃ vā khettaṃ vā vatthu vā, yaṃ vā panaññampi evarūpaṃ iriyāpathavirahitaṃ, ayaṃ thāvaro nidhi. Jaṅgamo nāma dāsidāsaṃ hatthigavassavaḷavaṃ ajeḷakaṃ kukkuṭasūkaraṃ yaṃ vā panaññampi evarūpaṃ iriyāpathapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ. Ayaṃ jaṅgamo nidhi aṅgasamo nāma kammāyatanaṃ, sippāyatanaṃ, vijjāṭṭhānaṃ, bāhusaccaṃ, yaṃ vā panaññampi evarūpaṃ sikkhitvā gahitaṃ aṅgapaccaṅgamiva attabhāvappaṭibaddhaṃ, ayaṃ aṅgasamo nidhi. Anugāmiko nāma dānamayaṃ puññaṃ sīlamayaṃ bhāvanāmayaṃ dhammassavanamayaṃ dhammadesanāmayaṃ, yaṃ vā panaññampi evarūpaṃ puññaṃ tattha tattha anugantvā viya iṭṭhaphalamanuppadeti, ayaṃ anugāmiko nidhi. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne thāvaro adhippeto.

1. Therein, regarding 'A person lays down a treasure': 'nidhi' is so called because it is laid down (nidhīyati); the meaning is that it is placed, protected, and guarded. It is of four kinds: immovable, movable, limb-like, and consequential. Therein, 'immovable treasure' refers to silver or gold, a field or land, whether gone into the earth or standing in the air, or any other such thing devoid of movement. This is the immovable treasure. 'Movable treasure' refers to female and male slaves, elephants, cattle, horses, and mares, goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, or any other such thing connected with movement. This is the movable treasure. 'Limb-like treasure' refers to a field of work, a craft, a branch of knowledge, great learning, or any other such thing that, having been learned and grasped, is connected to one's individual existence like a limb. This is the limb-like treasure. 'Consequential treasure' refers to merit consisting of giving, merit consisting of virtue, merit consisting of meditation, merit consisting of listening to the Dhamma, merit consisting of teaching the Dhamma, or any other such merit that, as if following one, produces a desired result in various existences. This is the consequential treasure. In this context, however, the immovable treasure is intended.

Nidhetīti ṭhapeti paṭisāmeti gopeti. Purisoti manusso. Kāmañca purisopi itthīpi paṇḍakopi nidhiṃ nidheti, idha pana purisasīsena desanā katā, atthato pana tesampi idha samodhānaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Gambhīre odakantiketi ogāhetabbaṭṭhena gambhīraṃ, udakassa antikabhāvena odakantikaṃ. Atthi gambhīraṃ na odakantikaṃ jaṅgale bhūmibhāge satikaporiso āvāṭo viya, atthi odakantikaṃ na gambhīraṃ ninne pallale ekadvividatthiko āvāṭo viya, atthi gambhīrañceva odakantikañca [P 0.0218] jaṅgale bhūmibhāge yāva idāni udakaṃ āgamissatīti, tāva khato āvāṭo viya. Taṃ sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ “gambhīre odakantike”ti. Atthe kicce samuppanneti atthā anapetanti atthaṃ, atthāvahaṃ hitāvahanti vuttaṃ hoti. Kātabbanti kiccaṃ, kiñcideva karaṇīyanti vuttaṃ hoti. Uppannaṃ eva samuppannaṃ, kattabbabhāvena upaṭṭhitanti vuttaṃ hoti. Tasmiṃ atthe kicce samuppanne. Atthāya me bhavissatīti nidhānappayojananidassanametaṃ. Etadatthañhi so nidheti “atthāvahe kismiñcideva karaṇīye samuppanne atthāya me bhavissati, tassa me kiccassa nipphattiyā bhavissatī”ti. Kiccanipphattiyeva hi tassa kicce samuppanne atthoti veditabbo.

'He lays it down' means he places it, stores it away, guards it. 'A person' means a human. Although a man, a woman, or a paṇḍaka may lay down a treasure, here the teaching is given with a man as the principal subject; however, in terms of meaning, their inclusion should be understood here. 'In a deep place, near the water': 'deep' (gambhīra) in the sense that one must enter it; 'near the water' (odakantika) due to being in the vicinity of water. There is a place that is deep but not near water, like a pit more than a man's height on high ground in a forest. There is a place that is near water but not deep, like a pit of one or two spans in a low-lying marsh. There is a place that is both deep and near water, like a pit on high ground in a forest dug down to where water will come. It is with reference to this that 'in a deep place, near the water' was said. 'When a need and a task have arisen': 'need' (attha) is so called because it is not separate from benefit (atthā anapeta); it is said to mean 'bringing benefit, bringing welfare.' 'Task' (kicca) is so called because it is something to be done (kātabba); it is said to mean 'some matter to be attended to.' 'Arisen' (samuppanna) is simply what has arisen (uppanna); it is said to mean 'what has presented itself as needing to be done.' This is when that need and task have arisen. 'It will be for my benefit': this shows the purpose of laying down the treasure. For it is for this purpose that one lays it down: 'When some beneficial matter to be attended to has arisen, it will be for my benefit; it will be for the completion of that task of mine.' For the completion of the task itself, when a task has arisen, should be understood as the benefit for that person.

Dutiyagāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Second Verse

Evaṃ [V 0.0175] nidhānappayojanaṃ dassento atthādhigamādhippāyaṃ dassetvā idāni anatthāpagamādhippāyaṃ dassetumāha –

Thus, the Blessed One, wishing to show the purpose of burying a treasure, having shown the intention regarding the attainment of benefit, now, in order to show the intention regarding freedom from misfortune, spoke:

2. “Rājato [M 0.0185] vā duruttassa, corato pīḷitassa vā.

2. “From a king, when one is spoken ill of, or from a thief, when one is oppressed,

Iṇassa vā pamokkhāya, dubbhikkhe āpadāsu vā”ti.

For release from debt, or in famine and calamities.”

Tassattho “atthāya me bhavissatī”ti ca “iṇassa vā pamokkhāyā”ti ca ettha vuttehi dvīhi bhavissatipamokkhāya-padehi saddhiṃ yathāsambhavaṃ yojetvā veditabbo.

Its meaning should be understood by connecting it, as is appropriate, with the two words `bhavissati` and `pamokkhāya` mentioned herein, which are taken from the phrases 'it will be for my benefit' and 'or for release from debt'.

Tatthāyaṃ yojanā – na kevalaṃ atthāya me bhavissatīti eva puriso nidhiṃ nidheti, kintu “ayaṃ coro”ti vā “pāradāriko”ti vā “suṅkaghātako”ti vā evamādinā nayena paccatthikehi paccāmittehi duruttassa me sato rājato vā pamokkhāya bhavissati, sandhicchedādīhi dhanaharaṇena vā, “ettakaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ dehī”ti jīvaggāhena vā corehi me pīḷitassa sato corato vā pamokkhāya bhavissati. Santi me iṇāyikā, te maṃ “iṇaṃ dehī”ti codessanti, tehi me codiyamānassa iṇassa vā pamokkhāya bhavissati. Hoti so samayo, yaṃ dubbhikkhaṃ hoti dussassaṃ dullabhapiṇḍaṃ, tattha na sukaraṃ appadhanena yāpetuṃ, tathāvidhe āgate dubbhikkhe vā me bhavissati[P 0.0219]. Yathārūpā āpadā uppajjanti aggito vā udakato vā appiyadāyādato vā, tathārūpāsu vā uppannāsu āpadāsu me bhavissatītipi puriso nidhiṃ nidhetīti.

Here is the explanation: A person does not bury a treasure merely thinking, "It will be for my benefit," but also considering, "If I am spoken ill of by enemies or adversaries in such a way as 'This one is a thief,' or 'an adulterer,' or 'a tax evader,' then this treasure will be for my release from the king. Or, if I am oppressed by robbers, by their taking my wealth through housebreaking and so forth, or by seizing me alive and demanding, 'Give so much gold and silver,' then this treasure will be for my release from robbers. I have creditors; they will press me, saying, 'Give the debt.' When I am thus pressed by them, this treasure will be for my release from debt. There comes a time when there is famine, when food is scarce and alms-food is hard to obtain, where it is not easy to survive with little wealth. In such a famine, this treasure will be for me. Or, if calamities arise, such as from fire, or from water, or from unloved heirs, then in such arisen calamities, this treasure will be for me." Thus, a person buries a treasure.

Evaṃ atthādhigamādhippāyaṃ anatthāpagamādhippāyañcāti dvīhi gāthāhi duvidhaṃ nidhānappayojanaṃ dassetvā idāni tameva duvidhaṃ payojanaṃ nigamento āha –

Thus, the Blessed One, having shown with two stanzas the twofold purpose of burying a treasure—namely, the intention regarding the attainment of benefit and the intention regarding freedom from misfortune—now, concluding that same twofold purpose, spoke:

“Etadatthāya lokasmiṃ, nidhi nāma nidhīyatī”ti.

"For this purpose in the world is a treasure deposited."

Tassattho – yvāyaṃ “atthāya me bhavissatī”ti ca “rājato vā duruttassā”ti evamādīhi ca atthādhigamo anatthāpagamo ca dassito. Etadatthāya etesaṃ nipphādanatthāya imasmiṃ [V 0.0176] okāsaloke yo koci hiraññasuvaṇṇādibhedo nidhi nāma nidhīyati ṭhapīyati paṭisāmīyatīti.

Its meaning is this: That which was shown by such phrases as 'it will be for my benefit' and 'from the king, when one is spoken ill of,' and so forth, is the attainment of benefit and freedom from misfortune. For this purpose, for the accomplishment of these, in this world of space, whatever is known as a treasure, differentiated as gold, silver, and so on, is buried, placed, and stored away.

Tatiyagāthāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Third Stanza

Idāni [M 0.0186] yasmā evaṃ nihitopi so nidhi puññavataṃyeva adhippetatthasādhako hoti, na aññesaṃ, tasmā tamatthaṃ dīpento āha –

Now, since even when a treasure is hidden in this way, it fulfills its intended purpose only for the meritorious, and not for others, therefore, illuminating that meaning, he says:

3. “Tāvassunihito santo, gambhīre odakantike.

3. “Even though it is well-hidden, in the deep, near the water's edge,

Na sabbo sabbadā eva, tassa taṃ upakappatī”ti.

Not all of it is always available for that person.”

Tassattho – so nidhi tāva sunihito santo, tāva suṭṭhu nikhaṇitvā ṭhapito samānoti vuttaṃ hoti. Kīva suṭṭhūti? Gambhīre odakantike, yāva gambhīre odakantike nihitoti saṅkhaṃ gacchati, tāva suṭṭhūti vuttaṃ hoti. Na sabbo sabbadā eva, tassa taṃ upakappatīti yena purisena nihito, tassa sabbopi sabbakālaṃ na upakappati na sampajjati, yathāvuttakiccakaraṇasamattho na hotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Kintu kocideva kadācideva upakappati, neva vā upakappatīti. Ettha ca nti padapūraṇamatte nipāto daṭṭhabbo “yathā taṃ appamattassa ātāpino”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 2.18-19; 3.154) viya. Liṅgabhedaṃ vā katvā “so”ti vattabbe “ta”nti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ hi vuccamāne so attho sukhaṃ bujjhatīti.

Its meaning is this: That treasure, being well-hidden in the first place, means it is well buried and placed, so it is said. How well? To the extent that it is buried deep near the water, to that extent it is considered well-hidden, so it is said. 'Not all of it is always available for that person' means that for the person by whom it was hidden, not all of the treasure is available or successful at all times; he is not capable of accomplishing the task as stated, is what is meant. Rather, only some of it may be available only at some time, or it may not be available at all.
