And here, the particle 'taṃ' should be understood as merely a verse-filler, just as in phrases like 'as it is for one who is diligent and ardent,' and so on. Alternatively, having made a change of gender, 'taṃ' is said where 'so' should be said. For when explained thus, that meaning is easily understood.

Catutthapañcamagāthāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Fourth and Fifth Stanzas

Evaṃ [P 0.0220] “na sabbo sabbadā eva, tassa taṃ upakappatī”ti vatvā idāni yehi kāraṇehi na upakappati, tāni dassento āha –

Thus, having said, 'Not all of it is always available for that person,' now, showing the reasons why it is not available, he says:

4. “Nidhi vā ṭhānā cavati, saññā vāssa vimuyhati.

4. “Either the treasure departs from its place, or his perception is confused.

Nāgā vā apanāmenti, yasmā vāpi haranti naṃ.

Or nāgas may remove it, or yakkhas may carry it away.

5. “Appiyā vāpi dāyādā, uddharanti apassato”ti.

5. Or unloved heirs may unearth it, unseen by him.”

Tassattho [V 0.0177] – yasmiṃ ṭhāne sunihito hoti nidhi, so vā nidhi tamhā ṭhānā cavati apeti vigacchati, acetanopi samāno puññakkhayavasena aññaṃ ṭhānaṃ gacchati. Saññā vā assa vimuyhati, yasmiṃ ṭhāne nihito nidhi, taṃ na jānāti, assa puññakkhayacoditā nāgā vā taṃ nidhiṃ apanāmenti aññaṃ ṭhānaṃ gamenti. Yakkhā vāpi haranti yenicchakaṃ ādāya [M 0.0187] gacchanti. Apassato vā assa appiyā vā dāyādā bhūmiṃ khaṇitvā taṃ nidhiṃ uddharanti. Evamassa etehi ṭhānā cavanādīhi kāraṇehi so nidhi na upakappatīti.

Its meaning is: the treasure that is well-hidden in a certain place, that treasure may move, depart, or vanish from that spot. Even though it is inanimate, due to the exhaustion of merit, it goes to another place. Or, his perception may become confused, and he may not know the place where the treasure was hidden. Urged on by the exhaustion of his merit, nāgas may remove that treasure and take it to another place. Or, yakkhas may also carry it away, taking it and going wherever they wish. Or, unseen by him, his unloved heirs may dig up the ground and unearth that treasure. Thus, for him, due to these reasons—such as its moving from its place and so on—that treasure is of no use.

Evaṃ ṭhānā cavanādīni lokasammatāni anupakappanakāraṇāni vatvā idāni yaṃ taṃ etesampi kāraṇānaṃ mūlabhūtaṃ ekaññeva puññakkhayasaññitaṃ kāraṇaṃ, taṃ dassento āha –

Thus, having stated that moving from its place and so on are worldly-accepted causes for it not being available, now, showing that which is the root cause of even these causes, the single cause known as the exhaustion of merit, he says:

“Yadā puññakkhayo hoti, sabbametaṃ vinassatī”ti.

“When the exhaustion of merit occurs, all this is destroyed.”

Tassattho – yasmiṃ samaye bhogasampattinipphādakassa puññassa khayo hoti, bhogapārijuññasaṃvattanikamapuññamokāsaṃ katvā ṭhitaṃ hoti, atha yaṃ nidhiṃ nidhentena nihitaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇādidhanajātaṃ, sabbametaṃ vinassatīti.

Its meaning is: at the time when the merit that produces wealth and prosperity is exhausted, and demerit conducive to the decline of wealth has gained an opportunity and is established, then whatever store of wealth—such as gold, silver, and other valuables—was deposited by the one who hid the treasure, all of it will perish.

Chaṭṭhagāthāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Sixth Stanza

Evaṃ bhagavā tena tena adhippāyena nihitampi yathādhippāyaṃ anupakappantaṃ nānappakārehi nassanadhammaṃ lokasammataṃ nidhiṃ vatvā idāni yaṃ puññasampadaṃ paramatthato nidhīti dassetuṃ tassa kuṭumbikassa anumodanatthamidaṃ nidhikaṇḍamāraddhaṃ, taṃ dassento āha –

Thus the Blessed One, having spoken of the worldly-accepted treasure—which, though laid down with this or that intention, does not conform to one's wish and is, in various ways, of a nature to be destroyed—now, in order to show that the accomplishment of merit is the treasure in the ultimate sense, and for the sake of that householder's rejoicing, this Section on Treasure was begun. Showing that treasure, he said:

6. “Yassa dānena sīlena, saṃyamena damena ca.

6. “For whom, through giving, virtue, restraint, and self-control,

Nidhī sunihito hoti, itthiyā purisassa vā”ti.

a treasure is well-laid-down, whether for a woman or a man.”

Tattha [P 0.0221] dānanti “dānañca dhammacariyā cā”ti ettha vuttanayeneva gahetabbaṃ. Sīlanti kāyikavācasiko avītikkamo. Pañcaṅgadasaṅgapātimokkhasaṃvarādi vā sabbampi sīlaṃ idha sīlanti adhippetaṃ. Saṃyamoti saṃyamanaṃ saṃyamo, cetaso nānārammaṇagatinivāraṇanti vuttaṃ hoti, samādhissetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Yena saṃyamena samannāgato “hatthasaṃyato, pādasaṃyato, vācāsaṃyato, saṃyatuttamo”ti ettha saṃyatuttamoti vutto. Apare āhu “saṃyamanaṃ saṃyamo, saṃvaraṇanti [V 0.0178] vuttaṃ hoti, indriyasaṃvarassetaṃ adhivacana”nti. Damoti damanaṃ, kilesūpasamananti vuttaṃ hoti, paññāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Paññā hi katthaci paññātveva [M 0.0188] vuccati “sussūsā labhate pañña”nti evamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.246; su. ni. 188). Katthaci dhammoti “saccaṃ dhammo dhiti cāgo”ti evamādīsu. Katthaci damoti “yadi saccā damā cāgā, khantyā bhiyyo na vijjatī”tiādīsu.

Therein, dāna (giving) should be understood in the very way stated in the passage, “giving and righteous conduct.” Sīla (virtue) is non-transgression by way of body and speech. Or, all virtue—such as the fivefold, eightfold, tenfold, and the Pātimokkha restraint—is intended here as sīla. Saṃyama (restraint) means restraining; it is said to be the prevention of the mind’s going to various objects. This is a designation for concentration (samādhi). Endowed with this restraint, one is called “supremely restrained” in the passage, “restrained in hand, restrained in foot, restrained in speech, supremely restrained.” Other teachers say: “Restraint means guarding; it is a designation for sense restraint.” Dama (taming) means subduing; it is said to be the pacification of defilements. This is a designation for wisdom (paññā). Indeed, wisdom is in some places called paññā, as in “one who is attentive gains wisdom.” In some places, it is called dhamma, as in “truth, dhamma, steadfastness, and generosity.” In some places, it is called dama, as in “if there are truth, taming, and generosity, there is nothing greater than patience.”

Evaṃ dānādīni ñatvā idāni evaṃ imissā gāthāya sampiṇḍetvā attho veditabbo – yassa itthiyā vā purisassa vā dānena sīlena saṃyamena damena cāti imehi catūhi dhammehi yathā hiraññena suvaṇṇena muttāya maṇinā vā dhanamayo nidhi tesaṃ suvaṇṇādīnaṃ ekattha pakkhipanena nidhīyati, evaṃ puññamayo nidhi tesaṃ dānādīnaṃ ekacittasantāne cetiyādimhi vā vatthumhi suṭṭhu karaṇena sunihito hotīti.

Thus, having understood giving and so on, the meaning of this verse should now be understood in summary as follows: For whichever woman or man, by these four qualities—giving, virtue, restraint, and self-control—just as a treasure made of wealth, such as silver, gold, pearls, or gems, is laid down by placing that gold and so on together in one place, so too a treasure made of merit is well-laid-down by properly performing those acts of giving and so on in a single continuum of consciousness or in a basis such as a shrine.

Sattamagāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Seventh Verse

Evaṃ bhagavā “yassa dānenā”ti imāya gāthāya puññasampadāya paramatthato nidhibhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni yattha nihito, so nidhi sunihito hoti, taṃ vatthuṃ dassento āha –

Thus, having shown by this verse beginning “Yassa dānena” that the accomplishment of merit is in the ultimate sense a treasure, the Blessed One, now wishing to show the object wherein that treasure, being deposited, is well-deposited, said:

7. “Cetiyamhi ca saṅghe vā, puggale atithīsu vā.

7. “At a shrine or in the Saṅgha, to an individual or to guests,

Mātari pitari cāpi, atho jeṭṭhamhi bhātarī”ti.

to mother or to father also, and furthermore to an elder brother.”

Tattha cayitabbanti cetiyaṃ, pūjetabbanti vuttaṃ hoti, citattā vā cetiyaṃ. Taṃ panetaṃ cetiyaṃ tividhaṃ hoti paribhogacetiyaṃ[P 0.0222], uddissakacetiyaṃ, dhātukacetiyanti. Tattha bodhirukkho paribhogacetiyaṃ, buddhapaṭimā uddissakacetiyaṃ, dhātugabbhathūpā sadhātukā dhātukacetiyaṃ. Saṅghoti buddhappamukhādīsu yo koci. Puggaloti gahaṭṭhapabbajitesu yo koci. Natthi assa tithi, yamhi vā tamhi divase āgacchatīti atithi. Taṅkhaṇe āgatapāhunakassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Therein, it is a cetiya because it is to be revered (cayitabba); it is said to be worthy of worship (pūjetabba). Or, it is a cetiya because it is constructed (cita). That cetiya is of three kinds: a cetiya of use (paribhogacetiya), a cetiya of dedication (uddisakacetiya), and a cetiya with relics (dhātukacetiya). Among these, the Bodhi tree is a cetiya of use; a Buddha image is a cetiya of dedication; a stūpa with a relic chamber containing relics is a cetiya with relics. Saṅgha means any Saṅgha whatsoever among those beginning with the one headed by the Buddha. Individual means any person whatsoever among householders and renunciants. An atithi (guest) is so called because 'for him there is no fixed date (tithi); he comes on any day whatsoever.' This is a designation for a visitor who arrives at that moment. The rest is in the manner already stated.

Evaṃ cetiyādīni ñatvā idāni evaṃ imissā gāthāya sampiṇḍetvā attho veditabbo – yo so nidhi “sunihito hotī”ti vutto, so imesu vatthūsu sunihito hoti. Kasmā? Dīgharattaṃ [V 0.0179] iṭṭhaphalānuppadānasamatthatāya. Tathā hi appakampi cetiyamhi datvā dīgharattaṃ iṭṭhaphalalābhino honti. Yathāha –

Thus, having understood about cetiyas and the like, now the meaning of this verse should be understood in summary: that treasure which was spoken of as 'is well-deposited,' is well-deposited in these objects. Why? Because of its ability to continuously produce the desired fruit for a long time. For, having given even a little to a cetiya, people become receivers of the desired fruit for a long time. As it was said:

“Ekapupphaṃ [M 0.0189] yajitvāna, asītikappakoṭiyo;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, pupphadānassidaṃ phala”nti ca.

“Having made an offering of a single flower, for eighty crores of eons I have not known a bad destination; this is the fruit of offering a flower.” And,

“Mattāsukhapariccāgā, passe ce vipulaṃ sukha”nti ca. (dha. pa. 290);

“If by giving up a small happiness, one might see an abundant happiness.” (Dhp. 290)

Evaṃ dakkhiṇāvisuddhivelāmasuttādīsu vuttanayena saṅghādivatthūsupi dānaphalavibhāgo veditabbo. Yathā ca cetiyādīsu dānassa pavatti phalavibhūti ca dassitā, evaṃ yathāyogaṃ sabbattha taṃ taṃ ārabhitvā cārittavārittavasena sīlassa, buddhānussativasena saṃyamassa, tabbatthukavipassanāmanasikārapaccavekkhaṇavasena damassa ca pavatti tassa tassa phalavibhūti ca veditabbā.

Thus, in the manner stated in the Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta, the Velāma Sutta, and others, the division of the fruit of giving should also be understood in regard to objects such as the Saṅgha. And just as the practice of giving and the manifestation of its fruit are shown in relation to cetiyas and other objects, so too, as is suitable in every case, one should understand the practice and the manifestation of the respective fruits of each of these, having undertaken them: of virtue, by way of conduct to be performed and conduct to be avoided; of restraint, by way of recollection of the Buddha; and of taming, by way of insight, attention, and reviewing based on those objects.

Aṭṭhamagāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Eighth Verse

Evaṃ bhagavā dānādīhi nidhīyamānassa puññamayanidhino cetiyādibhedaṃ vatthuṃ dassetvā idāni etesu vatthūsu sunihitassa tassa nidhino gambhīre odakantike nihitanidhito visesaṃ dassento āha –

Thus, having shown the various types of objects, such as shrines and so forth, for the treasure of merit being stored up through generosity and other virtues, the Blessed One, now wishing to show the special distinction of that well-deposited treasure in those objects over a treasure buried near deep water, said:

8. “Eso [P 0.0223] nidhi sunihito, ajeyyo anugāmiko.

8. “This treasure is well-deposited, unconquerable, an accompanier.

Pahāya gamanīyesu, etaṃ ādāya gacchatī”ti.

Among things that are to be abandoned and gone from, one takes this and goes.”

Tattha pubbapadena taṃ dānādīhi sunihitanidhiṃ niddisati “eso nidhi sunihito”ti. Ajeyyoti parehi jetvā gahetuṃ na sakkā, acceyyotipi pāṭho, tassa accitabbo accanāraho hitasukhatthikena upacitabboti attho. Etasmiñca pāṭhe eso nidhi acceyyoti sambandhitvā puna “kasmā”ti anuyogaṃ dassetvā “yasmā sunihito anugāmiko”ti sambandhitabbaṃ. Itarathā hi sunihitassa acceyyattaṃ vuttaṃ bhaveyya, na ca sunihito accanīyo. Accito eva hi soti. Anugacchatīti anugāmiko, paralokaṃ gacchantampi tattha tattha phaladānena na vijahatīti attho.

Here, by the preceding phrase, “this treasure is well-deposited,” he indicates that treasure well-deposited through generosity and so forth. “Unconquerable” (ajeyya) means it cannot be conquered and taken by others. There is also the reading “to be cultivated” (acceyya); its meaning is that it should be cultivated, is worthy of cultivation, and should be accumulated by one who desires welfare and happiness. And in this reading, having connected it as “this treasure is to be cultivated,” and then showing the question “why?,” it should be connected thus: “because, being well-deposited, it is an accompanier.” Otherwise, it would be said that what is well-deposited is something to be cultivated; but what is well-deposited is not something to be cultivated, for it has indeed already been cultivated. “It accompanies” (anugacchati), thus it is an “accompanier” (anugāmiko); the meaning is that even when one goes to the next world, it does not abandon them, by giving its fruit in various existences.

Pahāya [V 0.0180] gamanīyesu etaṃ ādāya gacchatīti maraṇakāle paccupaṭṭhite sabbabhogesu pahāya gamanīyesu etaṃ nidhiṃ ādāya paralokaṃ gacchatīti ayaṃ kira etassa attho. So pana na yujjati. Kasmā? Bhogānaṃ [M 0.0190] agamanīyato. Pahātabbā eva hi te te bhogā, na gamanīyā, gamanīyā pana te te gativisesā. Yato yadi esa attho siyā, pahāya bhoge gamanīyesu gativisesesu iti vadeyya. Tasmā evamettha attho veditabbo – “nidhi vā ṭhānā cavatī”ti evamādinā pakārena pahāya maccaṃ bhogesu gacchantesu etaṃ ādāya gacchatīti. Eso hi anugāmikattā taṃ nappajahatīti.

“Among things that are to be abandoned and gone from, one takes this and goes”—this, it is said, is its meaning: when the time of death is at hand, among all possessions that are to be abandoned and gone from, one takes this treasure and goes to the next world. But that is not suitable. Why? Because possessions are not things that accompany one. For those possessions must indeed be abandoned, not gone with; but the various destinations are what are to be gone to. Therefore, if this were the meaning, it would say, “having abandoned possessions, in the various destinations that are to be gone to.” Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: in the manner of “the treasure is removed from its place” and so forth, when possessions, having abandoned the mortal, are departing, one takes this and goes. For this, being an accompanier, does not abandon him.

Tattha siyā “gamanīyesūti ettha gantabbesūti attho, na gacchantesū”ti. Taṃ na ekaṃsato gahetabbaṃ. Yathā hi “ariyā niyyānikā”ti (dī. ni. 2.141) ettha niyyantāti attho, na niyyātabbāti, evamidhāpi gacchantesūti attho, na gantabbesūti.

Here, an objection might arise: “In ‘gamanīyesu,’ the meaning is ‘what is to be gone to,’ not ‘among those that are going.’” That should not be taken absolutely. Just as in “the noble ones are guides to deliverance,” the meaning is “they lead out,” not “they are to be led out,” so here too, the meaning is “among those that are going,” not “among what is to be gone to.”

Atha vā yasmā esa maraṇakāle kassaci dātukāmo bhoge āmasitumpi na labhati, tasmā tena te bhogā pubbaṃ kāyena [P 0.0224] pahātabbā, pacchā vihatāsena cetasā gantabbā, atikkamitabbāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tasmā pubbaṃ kāyena pahāya pacchā cetasā gamanīyesu bhogesūti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Purimasmiṃ atthe niddhāraṇe bhummavacanaṃ, pahāya gamanīyesu bhogesu ekamevetaṃ puññanidhivibhavaṃ tato nīharitvā ādāya gacchatīti. Pacchime atthe bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇe bhummavacanaṃ. Bhogānañhi gamanīyabhāvena etassa nidhissa ādāya gamanīyabhāvo lakkhīyatīti.

Alternatively, because at the time of death one who wishes to give is unable even to touch their wealth, therefore it is said that those possessions must first be abandoned by the body, and afterwards be gone from or transcended with a mind free from attachment. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: among possessions that are to be gone from, having first abandoned them with the body and afterwards with the mind. In the former meaning, the locative case is for specification: among possessions that are to be abandoned and gone from, one takes only this single treasure of merit and prosperity, having extracted it from there, and goes. In the latter meaning, the locative case is for indicating one state by means of another. For by the state of possessions being something to be gone from, the state of this treasure being something that can be taken along is indicated.

Navamagāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Ninth Verse

Evaṃ bhagavā imassa puññanidhino gambhīre odakantike nihitanidhito visesaṃ dassetvā puna attano bhaṇḍaguṇasaṃvaṇṇanena kayajanassa ussāhaṃ janento uḷārabhaṇḍavāṇijo viya attanā desitapuññanidhiguṇasaṃvaṇṇanena tasmiṃ puññanidhimhi devamanussānaṃ ussāhaṃ janento āha –

Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the distinction of this treasure of merit from a treasure buried deep near water, then, like a merchant of excellent goods arousing enthusiasm in a potential buyer by praising the qualities of his own goods, wishing to arouse enthusiasm in gods and humans for that treasure of merit by praising the qualities of the treasure of merit taught by Himself, said:

9. “Asādhāraṇamaññesaṃ, acorāharaṇo nidhi.

9. “A treasure not shared with others, a treasure that cannot be taken by thieves.

Kayirātha dhīro puññāni, yo nidhi anugāmiko”ti.

Let the wise person perform meritorious deeds, which is a treasure that follows one.”

Tattha [M 0.0191] asādhāraṇamaññesanti asādhāraṇo aññesaṃ, makāro padasandhikaro “adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya [V 0.0181] sampayuttā”tiādīsu viya. Na corehi āharaṇo acorāharaṇo, corehi ādātabbo na hotīti attho. Nidhātabboti nidhi. Evaṃ dvīhi padehi puññanidhiguṇaṃ saṃvaṇṇetvā tato dvīhi tattha ussāhaṃ janeti “kayirātha dhīro puññāni, yo nidhi anugāmiko”ti. Tassattho – yasmā puññāni nāma asādhāraṇo aññesaṃ, acorāharaṇo ca nidhi hoti. Na kevalañca asādhāraṇo acorāharaṇo ca nidhi, atha kho pana “eso nidhi sunihito, ajeyyo anugāmiko”ti ettha vutto yo nidhi anugāmiko. So ca yasmā puññāniyeva, tasmā kayirātha kareyya dhīro buddhisampanno dhitisampanno ca puggalo puññānīti.

Therein, as for asādhāraṇamaññesaṃ, it means asādhāraṇo aññesaṃ (not shared with others); the letter 'm' is for euphonic conjunction, as in passages such as adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā. Acorāharaṇo means 'not to be carried away by thieves' (na corehi āharaṇo); the meaning is that it is not to be taken by thieves. Because it is to be laid down (nidhātabbo), it is a treasure (nidhi). Thus, having praised the quality of the treasure of merit with two phrases, He then arouses enthusiasm for it with two phrases: 'Let the wise person perform meritorious deeds, which is a treasure that follows one.' Its meaning is this: Because meritorious deeds are a treasure that is not shared with others and cannot be carried away by thieves. And it is not merely a treasure that is not shared and cannot be carried away by thieves, but furthermore, as stated in the passage, 'This treasure is well-laid down, unconquerable, and follows along,' it is a treasure that follows. And since that is indeed merit itself, therefore, a wise person, one endowed with wisdom and steadfastness, should perform meritorious deeds.

Dasamagāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Tenth Verse

Evaṃ bhagavā guṇasaṃvaṇṇanena puññanidhimhi devamanussānaṃ ussāhaṃ janetvā idāni ye ussahitvā puññanidhikiriyāya sampādenti, tesaṃ so yaṃ phalaṃ deti, taṃ saṅkhepato dassento āha –

Thus, the Blessed One, having aroused enthusiasm in gods and humans for the treasure of merit by praising its qualities, now, wishing to show in brief what fruit it gives to those who, having striven, accomplish the making of the treasure of merit, said:

10.

10.

“Esa devamanussānaṃ, sabbakāmadado nidhī”ti.

“This treasure is for gods and humans, the giver of all desires.”

Idāni [P 0.0225] yasmā patthanāya paṭibandhitassa sabbakāmadadattaṃ, na vinā patthanaṃ hoti. Yathāha –

Now, since the state of being a giver of all desires is connected with aspiration, it does not occur without aspiration. As it is said:

“Ākaṅkheyya ce gahapatayo dhammacārī samacārī ‘aho vatāhaṃ kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā khattiyamahāsālānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjeyya’nti, ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjati yaṃ so kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā khattiyamahāsālānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjeyya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tathā hi so dhammacārī samacārī” (ma. ni. 1.442).

“If, householders, one who practices the Dhamma, who lives righteously, should wish: ‘Oh, that I, on the breaking up of the body, after death, might be reborn in the company of wealthy khattiyas!’—this is a possible condition, that on the breaking up of the body, after death, they would be reborn in the company of wealthy khattiyas. For what reason? Because they are one who practices the Dhamma, who lives righteously.”

Evaṃ “anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihareyya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tathā hi so dhammacārī samacārī”ti (ma. ni. 1.442).

Thus: “…they would dwell having realized for themselves through direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having attained them. For what reason? Because they are one who practices the Dhamma, who lives righteously.”

Tathā [M 0.0192] cāha –

And thus He said:

“Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu saddhāya samannāgato hoti, sīlena, sutena, cāgena, paññāya samannāgato hoti, tassa evaṃ hoti ‘aho vatāhaṃ kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā khattiyamahāsālānaṃ [V 0.0182] sahabyataṃ upapajjeyya’nti. So taṃ cittaṃ padahati, taṃ cittaṃ adhiṭṭhāti, taṃ cittaṃ bhāveti. Tassa te saṅkhārā ca vihārā ca evaṃ bhāvitā evaṃ bahulīkatā tatrūpapattiyā saṃvattantī”ti (ma. ni. 3.161) evamādi.

“Here, monks, a monk is endowed with faith, with virtue, with learning, with generosity, and with wisdom. It occurs to him thus: ‘Oh, that on the breaking up of the body, after death, I might be reborn in the company of wealthy khattiyas!’ He applies that mind, he resolves on that mind, he develops that mind. For him, those formations and abidings, being thus developed and made much of, conduce to rebirth there,” and so on.

Tasmā taṃ tathā tathā ākaṅkhapariyāyaṃ cittapadahanādhiṭṭhānabhāvanāparikkhāraṃ patthanaṃ tassa sabbakāmadadatte hetuṃ dassento āha –

Therefore, wishing to show that such aspiration—in its various modes as taught in the discourse on aspirations, and equipped with application, resolution, and development of mind—is the cause for its being a giver of all desires, He said:

“Yaṃ yadevābhipatthenti, sabbametena labbhatī”ti.

“Whatever they might aspire to, all that is obtained through this.”

Ekādasamagāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Eleventh Verse

11. Idāni yaṃ taṃ sabbaṃ etena labbhati, taṃ odhiso odhiso dassento “suvaṇṇatā susaratā”ti evamādigāthāyo āha.

11. Now, wishing to show in detail all that is obtained by this [treasure of merit], He spoke the verses beginning, 'A golden hue, a sweet voice,' and so on.

Tattha paṭhamagāthāya tāva suvaṇṇatā nāma sundaracchavivaṇṇatā kañcanasannibhattacatā, sāpi etena puññanidhinā labbhati. Yathāha –

Therein, in the first verse, firstly: what is called 'a golden hue' is the state of having a beautiful skin color, the state of having skin like the color of gold. That too is obtained by this treasure of merit. As it is said:

“Yampi, bhikkhave, tathāgato purimaṃ jātiṃ…pe… pubbe manussabhūto samāno akkodhano ahosi anupāyāsabahulo, bahumpi vutto samāno nābhisajji [P 0.0226] na kuppi na byāpajji na patitthīyi, na kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātvākāsi, dātā ca ahosi sukhumānaṃ mudukānaṃ attharaṇānaṃ pāvuraṇānaṃ khomasukhumānaṃ kappāsika…pe… koseyya…pe… kambalasukhumānaṃ. So tassa kammassa katattā upacitattā…pe… itthattaṃ āgato samāno imaṃ mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ paṭilabhati. Suvaṇṇavaṇṇo hoti kañcanasannibhattaco”ti (dī. ni. 3.218).

Monks, the Tathāgata, in a previous existence... formerly, having become a human being, was without anger and was not given to much despair. Even when much was said to him, he was not resentful, did not become angry, did not act maliciously, and did not harbor resentment; he did not manifest anger, ill will, or displeasure. He was a giver of fine and soft spreads and coverings: fine linen, fine cotton... silk... fine woolen blankets. He, because that kamma was done and accumulated... having come to this state, obtains this mark of a great man: he has a golden hue and skin resembling gold.

Susaratā nāma brahmassaratā karavīkabhāṇitā, sāpi etena labbhati. Yathāha –

What is called 'a sweet voice' is the state of having a voice like a Brahmā and speaking like a karavīka bird. That too is obtained by this [treasure of merit]. As it is said:

“Yampi[M 0.0193], bhikkhave, tathāgato purimaṃ jātiṃ…pe… pharusaṃ vācaṃ pahāya pharusāya vācāya paṭivirato ahosi, yā sā vācā nelā kaṇṇasukhā…pe… tathārūpiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā ahosi. So tassa kammassa katattā upacitattā…pe… itthattaṃ [V 0.0183] āgato samāno imāni dve mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni paṭilabhati. Pahutajivho ca hoti brahmassaro ca karavīkabhāṇī”ti (dī. ni. 3.236).

Monks, the Tathāgata, in a previous existence... having abandoned harsh speech, abstained from harsh speech. That speech which is faultless, pleasant to the ear... he was one who spoke such speech. He, because that kamma was done and accumulated... having come to this state, obtains these two marks of a great man: he has a long tongue, a voice like a Brahmā, and speaks like a karavīka bird.

Susaṇṭhānāti suṭṭhu saṇṭhānatā, samacitavaṭṭitayuttaṭṭhānesu aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ samacitavaṭṭitabhāvena sannivesoti vuttaṃ hoti. Sāpi etena labbhati. Yathāha –

'Good proportion' means well-proportionedness. It is said to be the well-composed arrangement of the major and minor limbs, by their state of being even and round in places where it is suitable for them to be even and round. That too is obtained by this [treasure of merit]. As it is said:

“Yampi, bhikkhave, tathāgato purimaṃ jātiṃ…pe… pubbe manussabhūto samāno bahujanassa atthakāmo ahosi hitakāmo phāsukāmo yogakkhemakāmo ‘kinti me saddhāya vaḍḍheyyuṃ, sīlena sutena cāgena paññāya dhanadhaññena khettavatthunā dvipadacatuppadehi puttadārehi dāsakammakaraporisehi ñātīhi mittehi bandhavehi vaḍḍheyyu’nti, so tassa kammassa…pe… samāno imāni tīṇi mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni paṭilabhati, sīhapubbaḍḍhakāyo ca hoti citantaraṃso ca samavaṭṭakkhandho [P 0.0227] cā”ti (dī. ni. 3.224) evamādi.

Monks, the Tathāgata, in a previous existence... formerly, having become a human being, was desirous of the welfare of many people, desirous of their benefit, desirous of their comfort, and desirous of their security from the yokes, thinking: 'How might these people increase in faith, in virtue, in learning, in generosity, in wisdom, in wealth and grain, in fields and land, with two-footed and four-footed creatures, with children and wives, with slaves, workers, and servants, with relatives, with friends, and with kinsmen?' He, because of that kamma... having come to this state, obtains these three marks of a great man: his torso is like the front half of a lion, the space between his shoulders is filled out, and he has evenly rounded shoulders.

Iminā nayena ito paresampi iminā puññanidhinā paṭilābhasādhakāni suttapadāni tato tato ānetvā vattabbāni. Ativitthārabhayena tu saṃkhittaṃ, idāni avasesapadānaṃ vaṇṇanaṃ karissāmi.

In this way, for the other characteristics as well, sutta passages that demonstrate their attainment through this treasure of merit should be brought from various suttas and spoken. However, for fear of excessive elaboration, this is abbreviated. Now I will provide the commentary on the remaining terms.

Surūpatāti ettha sakalasarīraṃ rūpanti veditabbaṃ “ākāso parivārito rūpaṃtveva saṅkhaṃ gacchatī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.306) viya, tassa rūpassa sundaratā surūpatā nātidīghatā nātirassatā nātikisatā nātithūlatā nātikāḷatā naccodātatāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ādhipaccanti adhipatibhāvo, khattiyamahāsālādibhāvena sāmikabhāvoti attho. Parivāroti agārikānaṃ sajanaparijanasampatti, anagārikānaṃ parisasampatti, ādhipaccañca [M 0.0194] parivāro ca ādhipaccaparivāro. Ettha ca suvaṇṇatādīhi sarīrasampatti, ādhipaccena bhogasampatti, parivārena sajanaparijanasampatti vuttāti veditabbā. Sabbametena labbhatīti yaṃ taṃ “yaṃ yadevābhipatthenti, sabbametena labbhatī”ti vuttaṃ, tattha idampi tāva paṭhamaṃ odhiso vuttasuvaṇṇatādi sabbametena labbhatīti veditabbanti dasseti.

Regarding 'beauty of form' (surūpatā), here the entire body should be understood as 'form' (rūpa), as in passages such as, 'Enclosed space is designated as form.' The beauty of that form is surūpatā, meaning it is not too tall, not too short, not too thin, not too stout, not too dark, and not excessively white. 'Sovereignty' (ādhipacca) is the state of being a master; the meaning is the state of lordship through being a Khattiya Mahāsāla and so on. 'Retinue' (parivāra) for householders is accomplishment in one's own people and attendants; for the homeless, it is accomplishment in an assembly. Sovereignty and retinue are ādhipaccaparivāra. And here, it should be understood that by 'golden hue' and so on, perfection of body is stated; by 'sovereignty,' perfection of wealth is stated; by 'retinue,' accomplishment in one's own people and attendants is stated. As for the statement, 'All this is obtained by this,' which refers to the verse, 'Whatever they might wish for, all that is obtained by this,' it shows that it should be known thus: here, firstly, as a specific part, this too—all that was said, beginning with 'a golden hue'—is obtained by this [treasure of merit].

Dvādasamagāthāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Twelfth Verse

12. Evamimāya [V 0.0184] gāthāya puññānubhāvena labhitabbaṃ rajjasampattito oraṃ devamanussasampattiṃ dassetvā idāni tadubhayarajjasampattiṃ dassento “padesarajja”nti imaṃ gāthamāha.

Thus, by this verse, having shown the prosperity of devas and humans obtainable through the power of merit, which is preliminary to the prosperity of kingship, now, wishing to show the prosperity of both divine and human kingship, he spoke this verse beginning 'padesarajjaṃ'.

Tattha padesarajjanti ekadīpampi sakalaṃ apāpuṇitvā pathaviyā ekamekasmiṃ padese rajjaṃ. Issarabhāvo issariyaṃ, iminā dīpacakkavattirajjaṃ dasseti. Cakkavattisukhaṃ piyanti iṭṭhaṃ kantaṃ manāpaṃ cakkavattisukhaṃ. Iminā cāturantacakkavattirajjaṃ dasseti. Devesu rajjaṃ devarajjaṃ, etena mandhātādīnampi manussānaṃ devarajjaṃ dassitaṃ hoti. Api dibbesūti iminā ye te divi bhavattā “dibbā”ti vuccanti, tesu dibbesu kāyesu uppannānampi devarajjaṃ dasseti. Sabbametena labbhatīti yaṃ taṃ “yaṃ yadevābhipatthenti, sabbametena labbhatī”ti [P 0.0228] vuttaṃ, tattha idampi dutiyaṃ odhiso padesarajjādi sabbametena labbhatīti veditabbanti dasseti.

12. Therein, 'regional kingship' (padesarajjaṃ) means kingship in a single region of the earth, without having attained the whole of even one continent. 'Sovereignty' (issariyaṃ) is the state of being a ruler; by this is shown the kingship of a continent-wheel-turning monarch. 'Dear' (piyaṃ) means desired (iṭṭhaṃ), lovely (kantaṃ), and pleasing (manāpaṃ). By this is shown the kingship of a wheel-turning monarch of the four continents. 'Kingship among the devas' (devesu rajjaṃ) is devarajjaṃ; by this is shown the kingship among devas even of humans such as Mandhātu and others. By 'even among the divine' (api dibbesu) is shown the kingship among devas even for those who have arisen in divine bodies, who are called 'divine' because of their existence in a divine realm. As for 'all this is obtained by this' (sabbametena labbhati), regarding what was said—'Whatever they desire, all that is obtained by this'—it shows that it should be known thus: Herein, this second time, as a specific part, all this beginning with regional kingship is obtained by this.

Terasamagāthāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Thirteenth Verse

13. Evamimāya gāthāya puññānubhāvena labhitabbaṃ devamanussarajjasampattiṃ dassetvā idāni dvīhi gāthāhi vuttaṃ sampattiṃ samāsato purakkhatvā nibbānasampattiṃ dassento “mānussikā ca sampattī”ti imaṃ gāthamāha.

Thus, by this verse, having shown the attainment of the sovereignty of devas and humans obtainable through the power of merit, now, having concisely set forth the attainment spoken of in the two verses, and wishing to show the attainment of Nibbāna, he spoke this verse beginning 'mānusikā ca sampattī'.

Tassāyaṃ padavaṇṇanā – manussānaṃ ayanti mānussī, mānussī eva mānussikā. Sampajjanaṃ sampatti. Devānaṃ loko devaloko. Tasmiṃ devaloke. Yāti anavasesapariyādānaṃ, ramanti etāya ajjhattaṃ uppannāya bahiddhā vā upakaraṇabhūtāyāti rati, sukhassa sukhavatthuno cetaṃ [M 0.0195] adhivacanaṃ. Yāti aniyatavacanaṃ casaddo pubbasampattiyā saha sampiṇḍanattho. Nibbānaṃyeva nibbānasampatti.

This is its explanation of terms: 'Offspring of humans' (manussānaṃ apaccaṃ), hence mānussī; mānussī itself is mānussikā. Accomplishing (sampajjanaṃ) is attainment (sampatti). The world of devas (devānaṃ loko) is devaloko. 'And in that devaloka' (tasmiṃ devaloke ca). 'Whatever delight' (yā rati): 'delight' (rati) is so called because they delight (ramanti) in this (etāya), whether it has arisen internally or is an external requisite. This is a term for both happiness and the basis of happiness. The word yā is an indefinite term. The word ca has the meaning of combining with the previously mentioned attainment. Nibbāna itself is the attainment of Nibbāna (nibbānasampatti).

Ayaṃ pana atthavaṇṇanā – yā esā “suvaṇṇatā”tiādīhi padehi mānussikā ca sampatti devaloke ca yā rati vuttā, sā ca sabbā, yā cāyamaparā saddhānusāribhāvādivasena pattabbā nibbānasampatti, sā cāti idaṃ tatiyampi odhiso sabbametena labbhatīti.

This, however, is the explanation of the meaning: Whatever human attainment and whatever delight in the devaloka is spoken of by terms such as 'golden complexion,' etc.—all that; and also this other attainment of Nibbāna to be reached by means of the state of a faith-follower and so on—all this, for the third time, as a specific part, is obtained by this.

Atha [V 0.0185] vā yā pubbe suvaṇṇatādīhi avuttā “sūrā satimanto idha brahmacariyavāso”ti evamādinā (a. ni. 9.21) nayena niddiṭṭhā paññāveyyattiyādibhedā ca mānussikā sampatti, aparā devaloke ca yā jhānādirati, yā ca yathāvuttappakārā nibbānasampatti cāti idampi tatiyaṃ odhiso sabbametena labbhatīti. Evampettha atthavaṇṇanā veditabbā.

Or alternatively: that human attainment not previously spoken of with terms such as 'golden complexion,' etc., but which is indicated by the method beginning 'Heroic, mindful, here is the holy life...' and is distinguished by wisdom, cleverness, and so on; and the other delight in the devaloka, such as the delight of jhāna, etc.; and the attainment of Nibbāna of the kind already described—this too, for the third time, as a specific part, is all obtained by this. In this way, the explanation of the meaning here should be understood.

Cuddasamagāthāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Fourteenth Verse.

14. Evamimāya gāthāya puññānubhāvena labhitabbaṃ saddhānusārībhāvādivasena pattabbaṃ nibbānasampattimpi dassetvā idāni tevijjaubhatobhāgavimuttabhāvavasenapi pattabbaṃ tameva tassa upāyañca dassento “mittasampadamāgammā”ti imaṃ gāthamāha.

14. Thus, having shown by this verse the attainment of Nibbāna—obtainable through the power of merit and to be reached through the state of a faith-follower and so forth—He now speaks this verse, ‘Having relied on the accomplishment of a friend…’, wishing to show that this same attainment is also to be reached through the state of one with the three knowledges and liberated in both ways, and the means for that person.

Tassāyaṃ padavaṇṇanā – sampajjati etāya guṇavibhūtiṃ pāpuṇātīti sampadā, mitto eva sampadā mittasampadā, taṃ mittasampadaṃ[P 0.0229]. Āgammāti nissāya. Yonisoti upāyena. Payuñjatoti yogānuṭṭhānaṃ karoto. Vijānāti etāyāti vijjā, vimuccati etāya, sayaṃ vā vimuccatīti vimutti, vijjā ca vimutti ca vijjāvimuttiyo, vijjāvimuttīsu vasībhāvo vijjāvimuttivasībhāvo.

This is the explanation of the terms: 'Sampadā' is so called because by it one accomplishes (sampajjati), one attains (pāpuṇāti) the excellence of virtues. A friend (mitto) itself (eva) is an accomplishment (sampadā), hence 'mittasampadā'. 'Āgamma' means relying upon (nissāya). 'Yoniso' means by means (upāyena). 'Payuñjato' means for one who makes effort (yogānuṭṭhānaṃ karoto). 'Vijjā' (knowledge) is so called because one knows (vijānāti) by it (etāya). 'Vimutti' (liberation) is so called because one is liberated (vimuccati) by it (etāya), or one is liberated (vimuttā) oneself (sayaṃ). Knowledge (vijjā) and liberation (vimutti) are 'vijjāvimuttiyo'. Mastery (vasībhāvo) in knowledge and liberation (vijjāvimuttīsu) is 'vijjāvimuttivasībhāvo'.

Ayaṃ pana atthavaṇṇanā – yvāyaṃ mittasampadamāgamma satthāraṃ vā aññataraṃ vā garuṭṭhāniyaṃ sabrahmacāriṃ nissāya tato ovādañca anusāsaniñca gahetvā yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipattiyā yoniso payuñjato pubbenivāsādīsu tīsu vijjāsu “tattha katamā vimutti? Cittassa ca adhimutti nibbānañcā”ti (dha. sa. 1381) evaṃ āgatāya aṭṭhasamāpattinibbānabhedāya vimuttiyā ca tathā tathā adandhāyitattena [M 0.0196] vasībhāvo, idampi catutthaṃ odhiso sabbametena labbhatīti.

This, however, is the explanation of the meaning: For a person who, having relied on the accomplishment of a friend, depends on the Teacher or another venerable fellow practitioner, and having received advice and instruction from them, strives in practice as instructed and by proper means, there is mastery—through non-sluggishness in their various aspects—over the three knowledges beginning with the recollection of past lives, and over the liberation which is divided into the eight attainments and Nibbāna, as stated: 'What is liberation there? The mind’s resolution and Nibbāna' (Dhs. 1381). This fourth item, as a category, is also entirely obtained by this.

Pannarasamagāthāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Fifteenth Verse.

15. Evamimāya gāthāya pubbe kathitavijjāvimuttivasībhāvabhāgiyapuññānubhāvena labhitabbaṃ tevijjaubhatobhāgavimuttabhāvavasenapi pattabbaṃ nibbānasampattiṃ dassetvā idāni yasmā vijjāvimuttivasībhāvappattā tevijjā ubhatobhāgavimuttāpi sabbe paṭisambhidādiguṇavibhūtiṃ labhanti, imāya puññasampadāya ca tassā guṇavibhūtiyā padaṭṭhānavasena [V 0.0186] tathā tathā sāpi labbhati, tasmā tampi dassento “paṭisambhidā vimokkhā cā”ti imaṃ gāthamāha.

15. Thus, having shown by this verse the attainment of Nibbāna—to be gained by the power of merit pertaining to the mastery of knowledge and liberation mentioned previously, and also by means of the state of being one with the three knowledges and liberated in both ways—now, since all those who have attained mastery of knowledge and liberation, those with the three knowledges, and those liberated in both ways, obtain the splendor of qualities such as the analytical knowledges, and since that splendor of qualities is also obtained in various ways with this accomplishment of merit as its proximate cause, therefore, wishing to show that as well, He spoke this verse: 'The analytical knowledges and the liberations too...'

“Yato sammā katena yā cāyaṃ dhammatthaniruttipaṭibhānesu pabhedagatā paññā paṭisambhidā”ti vuccati, ye cime “rūpī rūpāni passatī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.129; 3.339) nayena aṭṭha vimokkhā, yā cāyaṃ bhagavato sāvakehi pattabbā sāvakasampattisādhikā sāvakapāramī, yā ca sayambhubhāvasādhikā paccekabodhi, yā ca sabbasattuttamabhāvasādhikā buddhabhūmi, idampi pañcamaṃ odhiso sabbametena labbhatīti veditabbaṃ.

Because from what is rightly done, that wisdom which is differentiated in regard to Dhamma, meaning, language, and ready wit is called 'analytical knowledge'; and these eight liberations, in the manner beginning with 'One with form sees forms' (DN 2.129; 3.339); and this perfection of a disciple, to be attained by the Blessed One's disciples, which brings about the accomplishment of a disciple; and the solitary enlightenment, which brings about the state of a self-enlightened one; and the Buddha-stage, which brings about the state of being supreme among all beings—this fifth item, as a category, is also entirely to be understood as obtainable through this.

Soḷasamagāthāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Sixteenth Verse.

16. Evaṃ bhagavā yaṃ taṃ “yaṃ yadevābhipatthenti, sabbametena labbhatī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ imāhi pañcahi gāthāhi odhiso odhiso dassetvā [P 0.0230] idāni sabbamevidaṃ sabbakāmadadanidhisaññitaṃ puññasampadaṃ pasaṃsanto “evaṃ mahatthikā esā”ti imāya gāthāya desanaṃ niṭṭhapesi.

16. Thus, the Blessed One, having shown section by section with these five verses what was stated as, “Whatever they desire, all that is obtained by this,” now, praising this entire accomplishment of merit, which is designated as a treasure granting all wishes, concluded the teaching with this verse: “Thus, this is of great benefit.”

Tassāyaṃ padavaṇṇanā – evanti atītatthanidassanaṃ. Mahanto attho assāti mahatthikā, mahato atthāya saṃvattatīti vuttaṃ hoti, mahiddhikātipi pāṭho. Esāti uddesavacanaṃ, tena “yassa dānena sīlenā”ti ito pabhuti yāva “kayirātha dhīro puññānī”ti vuttaṃ puññasampadaṃ uddisati. Yadidanti abhimukhakaraṇatthe nipāto, tena esāti uddiṭṭhaṃ niddisituṃ yā esāti abhimukhaṃ karoti. Puññānaṃ sampadā puññasampadā[M 0.0197]. Tasmāti kāraṇavacanaṃ. Dhīrāti dhitimanto. Pasaṃsantīti vaṇṇayanti. Paṇḍitāti paññāsampannā. Katapuññatanti katapuññabhāvaṃ.

This is the word-by-word explanation. The word `evaṃ` is indicative of what has gone before. `Mahatthikā` means 'it has a great benefit'; that is to say, 'it conduces to a great benefit.' There is also the reading `mahiddhikā` (of great power). `Esā` is a demonstrative word. By it, the accomplishment of merit stated from “By one's giving and virtue” up to “the wise one should do meritorious deeds” is indicated. `Yadidaṃ` is a particle used for direct presentation; by it, what was indicated by `esā` is presented directly as `yā esā`. The accomplishment of merits is `puññasampadā`. `Tasmā` is a causal word. `Dhīrā` means those possessed of resolve. `Pasaṃsanti` means they praise. `Paṇḍitā` means those endowed with wisdom. `Katapuññataṃ` means the state of having done merit.

Ayaṃ pana atthavaṇṇanā – iti bhagavā suvaṇṇatādiṃ buddhabhūmipariyosānaṃ puññasampadānubhāvena adhigantabbamatthaṃ vaṇṇayitvā idāni tamevatthaṃ sampiṇḍetvā dassento tenevatthena yathāvuttappakārāya puññasampadāya mahatthikattaṃ thunanto āha – evaṃ mahato atthassa āvahanena mahatthikā esā, yadidaṃ mayā “yassa dānena sīlenā”tiādinā nayena desitā puññasampadā, tasmā mādisā sattānaṃ hitasukhāvahāya dhammadesanāya akilāsutāya yathābhūtaguṇena ca dhīrā paṇḍitā “asādhāraṇamaññesaṃ, acorāharaṇo nidhī”tiādīhi idha vuttehi [V 0.0187] ca, avuttehi ca “mā, bhikkhave, puññānaṃ bhāyittha, sukhassetaṃ, bhikkhave, adhivacanaṃ, yadidaṃ puññānī”tiādīhi (a. ni. 7.62; itivu. 22; netti. 121) vacanehi anekākāravokāraṃ katapuññataṃ pasaṃsanti, na pakkhapātenāti.

This, however, is the explanation of the meaning. Thus, the Blessed One, having extolled the goal to be attained through the power of the accomplishment of merit—culminating in the stage of Buddhahood, beginning with a golden complexion and so forth—now, summarizing and showing that very meaning, and by that same meaning extolling the great benefit of the accomplishment of merit of the kind described, spoke thus: This accomplishment of merit, which I have taught in the way beginning with ‘By one's giving and virtue,’ is of great benefit, for it brings about a great benefit. Therefore, the steadfast and wise, like myself, untiring in teaching the Dhamma for the welfare and happiness of beings, and by its true quality, praise the state of having performed merit in its many aspects and reasons, with statements mentioned here, such as, ‘It is a treasure not shared by others, not carried off by thieves,’ and with statements not mentioned here, such as, ‘Monks, do not fear meritorious deeds; this, monks, is a term for happiness, namely, meritorious deeds’ (AN 7.62; Itivuttaka 22; Netti 121). They do not praise it out of partiality.

Desanāpariyosāne so upāsako bahujanena saddhiṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi, rañño ca pasenadikosalassa santikaṃ gantvā etamatthaṃ ārocesi, rājā ativiya tuṭṭho hutvā “sādhu, gahapati, sādhu kho tvaṃ[P 0.0231], gahapati, mādisehipi anāharaṇīyaṃ nidhiṃ nidhesī”ti saṃrādhetvā mahatiṃ pūjamakāsīti.

At the end of the discourse, that lay follower, together with many people, was established in the fruit of stream-entry. He then went to King Pasenadi of Kosala and informed him of this matter. The king, being exceedingly pleased, gratified him, saying, “Good, householder! Good indeed are you, householder! You have laid up a treasure that cannot be carried off even by those like me,” and made a great offering.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha,

Nidhikaṇḍasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta is finished.

9. Mettasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Mettā Sutta

Nikkhepappayojanaṃ

The Purpose of Its Inclusion

Idāni [V 0.0188] nidhikaṇḍānantaraṃ nikkhittassa mettasuttassa vaṇṇanākkamo anuppatto. Tassa idha nikkhepappayojanaṃ vatvā tato paraṃ –

Now, immediately after the Nidhikaṇḍa, the turn for the commentary on the Mettā Sutta that was placed there has arrived. Having first stated here the purpose of its inclusion, thereafter—

“Yena vuttaṃ yadā yattha, yasmā cetesa dīpanā;

Nidānaṃ sodhayitvāssa, karissāmatthavaṇṇanaṃ”.

“By whom it was spoken, when, and where; and for what reason—elucidating these, and having clarified its occasion, we shall make a commentary on the meaning.”

Tattha [M 0.0198] yasmā nidhikaṇḍena dānasīlādipuññasampadā vuttā, sā ca sattesu mettāya katāya mahapphalā hoti yāva buddhabhūmiṃ pāpetuṃ samatthā, tasmā tassā puññasampadāya upakāradassanatthaṃ, yasmā vā saraṇehi sāsane otaritvā sikkhāpadehi sīle patiṭṭhitānaṃ dvattiṃsākārena rāgappahānasamatthaṃ, kumārapañhena mohappahānasamatthañca kammaṭṭhānaṃ dassetvā, maṅgalasuttena tassa pavattiyā maṅgalabhāvo attarakkhā ca, ratanasuttena tassānurūpā pararakkhā, tirokuṭṭena rattanasutte vuttabhūtesu ekaccabhūtadassanaṃ vuttappakārāya puññasampattiyā pamajjantānaṃ vipatti ca, nidhikaṇḍena tirokuṭṭe vuttavipattipaṭipakkhabhūtā sampatti ca dassitā, dosappahānasamatthaṃ pana kammaṭṭhānaṃ adassitameva, tasmā taṃ dosappahānasamatthaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ dassetuṃ idaṃ mettasuttaṃ idha nikkhittaṃ. Evañhi suparipūro hoti khuddakapāṭhoti idamassa idha nikkhepappayojanaṃ.

In this context, because the Nidhikaṇḍa has described the accomplishment of merit such as generosity and virtue, and that accomplishment, when loving-kindness is developed towards beings, becomes of great fruit and is capable of leading one even to the state of a Buddha, it is included therefore to show its supportive nature for that accomplishment of merit. Or else, because for those who have entered the Dispensation through the refuges and are established in virtue through the training rules, a meditation subject capable of abandoning lust by means of the thirty-two parts of the body and a meditation subject capable of abandoning delusion by means of the Kumārapañha have been shown; and by the Maṅgala Sutta, the state of being a blessing for one's conduct and self-protection are shown; by the Ratana Sutta, the suitable protection of others is shown; by the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta, the appearance of certain beings among those mentioned in the Ratana Sutta and the downfall for those who are heedless of the aforesaid accomplishment of merit are shown; and by the Nidhikaṇḍa, the success which is the opposite of the downfall mentioned in the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta is shown. However, a meditation subject capable of abandoning aversion has not yet been shown. Therefore, to show that meditation subject capable of abandoning aversion, this Mettā Sutta is placed here. For in this way, the Khuddakapāṭha becomes fully complete. This is the purpose of its inclusion here.

Nidānasodhanaṃ

Clarification of the Occasion

Idāni yāyaṃ –

Now, regarding this:

“Yena vuttaṃ yadā yattha, yasmā cetesa dīpanā;

Nidānaṃ sodhayitvāssa, karissāmatthavaṇṇana”nti. –

“By whom it was spoken, when, and where; and for what reason—elucidating these, and having clarified its occasion, we shall make a commentary on the meaning.”

Mātikā [V 0.0189] nikkhittā, tattha idaṃ [P 0.0232] mettasuttaṃ bhagavatāva vuttaṃ, na sāvakādīhi, tañca pana yadā himavantapassato devatāhi ubbāḷhā bhikkhū bhagavato santikaṃ āgatā, tadā sāvatthiyaṃ tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ parittatthāya kammaṭṭhānatthāya ca vuttanti evaṃ tāva saṅkhepato etesaṃ padānaṃ dīpanā nidānasodhanā veditabbā.

The mātikā has been set down. Therein, this Mettā Sutta was spoken by the Blessed One himself, not by disciples or others. And it was spoken when monks, harassed by deities on a slope of the Himālaya, came to the presence of the Blessed One; at that time, it was spoken in Sāvatthī for the protection of those monks and as a meditation subject. Thus, for now, the elucidation of these terms should be understood in brief as the clarification of the occasion.

Vitthārato pana evaṃ veditabbā – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati upakaṭṭhāya vassūpanāyikāya, tena kho pana samayena sambahulā nānāverajjakā bhikkhū bhagavato santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā tattha tattha vassaṃ upagantukāmā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamanti. Tatra sudaṃ bhagavā rāgacaritānaṃ saviññāṇakaaviññāṇakavasena ekādasavidhaṃ asubhakammaṭṭhānaṃ, dosacaritānaṃ catubbidhaṃ mettādikammaṭṭhānaṃ, mohacaritānaṃ maraṇassatikammaṭṭhānādīni, vitakkacaritānaṃ ānāpānassatipathavīkasiṇādīni, saddhācaritānaṃ buddhānussatikammaṭṭhānādīni, buddhicaritānaṃ catudhātuvavatthānādīnīti [M 0.0199] iminā nayena caturāsītisahassappabhedacaritānukūlāni kammaṭṭhānāni katheti.

But in detail, it should be understood thus: At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling in Sāvatthī as the rains-residence was approaching. At that time, many monks from various regions, having received a meditation subject from the Blessed One, approached the Blessed One, desiring to enter the rains-residence in various places. There, the Blessed One taught meditation subjects suitable for the eighty-four thousand types of temperaments in this way: for those of lustful temperament, the eleven kinds of meditation on foulness, by way of objects with and without consciousness; for those of aversive temperament, the fourfold meditation subject beginning with loving-kindness; for those of deluded temperament, meditation subjects such as mindfulness of death; for those of discursive temperament, meditation subjects such as mindfulness of breathing and the earth kasiṇa; for those of faithful temperament, meditation subjects such as the recollection of the Buddha; for those of intelligent temperament, meditation subjects such as the analysis of the four elements.

Atha kho pañcamattāni bhikkhusatāni bhagavato santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggahetvā sappāyasenāsanañca gocaragāmañca pariyesamānāni anupubbena gantvā paccante himavantena saddhiṃ ekābaddhaṃ nīlakācamaṇisannibhasilātalaṃ sītalaghanacchāyanīlavanasaṇḍamaṇḍitaṃ muttājālarajatapaṭṭasadisavālukākiṇṇabhūmibhāgaṃ sucisātasītalajalāsayaparivāritaṃ pabbatamaddasaṃsu. Atha te bhikkhū tatthekarattiṃ vasitvā pabhātāya rattiyā sarīraparikammaṃ katvā tassa avidūre aññataraṃ gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisiṃsu. Gāmo ghananivesanasanniviṭṭhakulasahassayutto, manussā cettha [P 0.0233] saddhā pasannā te paccante pabbajitadassanassa dullabhatāya bhikkhū disvā eva pītisomanassajātā hutvā te bhikkhū bhojetvā “idheva, bhante, temāsaṃ vasathā”ti yācitvā pañca padhānakuṭisatāni kāretvā tattha mañcapīṭhapānīyaparibhojanīyaghaṭādīni sabbūpakaraṇāni paṭiyādesuṃ.

Then, five hundred monks, having taken up the meditation subject in the presence of the Blessed One and searching for a suitable dwelling and a village for alms-food, journeying in due course, saw a mountain in a border region, contiguous with the Himālaya. It had a rock surface like blue crystal, was adorned with groves of dark forest, cool with dense shade, had a ground portion strewn with sand like a surface of pearls or a silver sheet, and was surrounded by reservoirs of pure, pleasant, cool water. Then those monks, having stayed there for one night, when the night had dawned, performed their bodily duties and entered a certain village not far from there for alms-food. The village was endowed with a thousand families living in dense dwellings, and the people there were faithful and devoted. Because of the rarity of seeing monastics in the border region, upon seeing the monks they became filled with joy and gladness. Having fed the monks, they requested, 'Venerable sirs, please dwell right here for the three months of the rains-residence.' They had five hundred meditation huts made and prepared there all the requisites, such as beds, seats, and pots for drinking water and water for use.

Bhikkhū dutiyadivase aññaṃ gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisiṃsu. Tatthapi manussā tatheva upaṭṭhahitvā vassāvāsaṃ yāciṃsu. Bhikkhū “asati antarāye”ti adhivāsetvā taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ pavisitvā sabbarattindivaṃ āraddhavīriyā yāmaghaṇḍikaṃ koṭṭetvā yonisomanasikārabahulā viharantā rukkhamūlāni upagantvā nisīdiṃsu. Sīlavantānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ tejena vihatatejā rukkhadevatā attano attano vimānā oruyha dārake gahetvā ito cito vicaranti. Seyyathāpi [V 0.0190] nāma rājūhi vā rājamahāmattehi vā gāmakāvāsaṃ gatehi gāmavāsīnaṃ gharesu okāse gahite gharamanussakā gharā nikkhamitvā aññatra vasantā “kadā nu gamissantī”ti dūratova olokenti, evameva devatā attano attano vimānāni chaḍḍetvā ito cito ca vicarantiyo dūratova olokenti “kadā nu bhadantā gamissantī”ti. Tato evaṃ samacintesuṃ “paṭhamavassūpagatā bhikkhū avassaṃ temāsaṃ vasissanti, mayaṃ pana tāva ciraṃ dārake gahetvā okkamma vasituṃ na sakkoma, handa mayaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bhayānakaṃ ārammaṇaṃ dassemā”ti. Tā rattiṃ bhikkhūnaṃ samaṇadhammakaraṇavelāya bhiṃsanakāni yakkharūpāni nimminitvā purato [M 0.0200] purato tiṭṭhanti, bheravasaddañca karonti. Bhikkhūnaṃ tāni rūpāni disvā tañca saddaṃ sutvā hadayaṃ phandi, dubbaṇṇā [P 0.0234] ca ahesuṃ uppaṇḍuppaṇḍukajātā. Tena te bhikkhū cittaṃ ekaggaṃ kātuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu, tesaṃ anekaggacittānaṃ bhayena ca punappunaṃ saṃviggānaṃ sati sammussi, tato tesaṃ muṭṭhasatīnaṃ duggandhāni ārammaṇāni payojesuṃ, tesaṃ tena duggandhena nimmathiyamānamiva matthaluṅgaṃ ahosi, gāḷhā sīsavedanā uppajjiṃsu, na ca taṃ pavattiṃ aññamaññassa ārocesuṃ.

The monks entered another village for alms on the second day. There too, the people similarly attended to them and requested them to spend the rains-residence. The monks, saying, “If there are no obstacles,” agreed and entered that grove. Exerting themselves diligently day and night, striking the watch-bell, and dwelling with abundant wise attention, they approached the roots of trees and sat down. The tree deities, their power overcome by the power of the virtuous monks, descended from their respective celestial mansions, taking their children, and wandered here and there. Just as when kings or royal ministers go to reside in a village, and the villagers, their houses occupied, leave their homes and dwell elsewhere, watching from afar, thinking, “When will they go?”—so too the deities, abandoning their mansions, wandered here and there, watching from afar, thinking, “When will the venerable ones leave?” Then they reflected thus: “The monks who have undertaken the first rains-residence will surely stay for three months. But we cannot dwell long with our children displaced. Come, let us show the monks a frightening object.” At night, when the monks were engaged in their monastic practice, they created terrifying demonic forms and stood before them, making dreadful sounds. Seeing those forms and hearing those sounds, the monks’ hearts trembled, their complexions became discolored, and they became pale and jaundiced. Unable to concentrate their minds, their scattered thoughts and repeated fright caused their mindfulness to lapse. Then, with their mindfulness lost, they were assailed by foul smells. Overwhelmed by the stench, it was as if their brains were being crushed. Severe headaches arose, yet they did not inform one another of what was happening.

Athekadivasaṃ saṅghattherassa upaṭṭhānakāle sabbesu sannipatitesu saṅghatthero pucchi “tumhākaṃ, āvuso, imaṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ paviṭṭhānaṃ katipāhaṃ ativiya parisuddho chavivaṇṇo ahosi pariyodāto, vippasannāni ca indriyāni, etarahi panattha kisā dubbaṇṇā uppaṇḍuppaṇḍukajātā, kiṃ vo idha asappāya”nti. Tato eko bhikkhu āha – “ahaṃ, bhante, rattiṃ īdisañca īdisañca bheravārammaṇaṃ passāmi ca suṇāmi ca, īdisañca gandhaṃ ghāyāmi, tena me cittaṃ na samādhiyatī”ti, eteneva upāyena sabbeva te taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesuṃ. Saṅghatthero āha – “bhagavatā, āvuso, dve vassūpanāyikā paññattā, amhākañca idaṃ senāsanaṃ asappāyaṃ, āyāmāvuso, bhagavato santikaṃ gantvā aññaṃ sappāyasenāsanaṃ pucchāmā”ti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti te bhikkhū therassa paṭissuṇitvā sabbeva senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā pattacīvaramādāya anupalittattā kulesu kañci anāmantetvā eva yena sāvatthi tena cārikaṃ pakkamiṃsu. Anupubbena sāvatthiṃ gantvā bhagavato santikaṃ āgamiṃsu.

Then one day, at the time of attending to the Sangha elder, when all had assembled, the Sangha elder asked, “Friends, for some days after you entered this forest grove, your complexion was exceedingly pure and bright, and your faculties were serene. But now you are thin, of poor complexion, and have become pale and jaundiced. What is unsuitable for you here?” Then one monk said, “Venerable sir, at night I see and hear such and such a terrifying object, and I smell such and such an odor, so my mind does not become concentrated.” In this same way, all of them related that occurrence. The Sangha elder said, “Friends, the Blessed One has laid down two periods for entering the rains-residence. And for us, this lodging is unsuitable. Come, friends, let us go to the Blessed One and ask for another suitable lodging.” “Very well, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the elder. Then, all of them, having put their lodging in order and taken their bowls and robes, due to being unattached, without taking leave of anyone among the supporter families, set out on a journey in the direction of Sāvatthī. Traveling in stages, they went to Sāvatthī and approached the Blessed One.

Bhagavā te bhikkhū disvā etadavoca – “na, bhikkhave, antovassaṃ cārikā caritabbāti mayā sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, kissa tumhe [P 0.0235] cārikaṃ carathā”ti. Te bhagavato sabbamārocesuṃ. Bhagavā āvajjento sakalajambudīpe antamaso catupādapīṭhakaṭṭhānamattampi tesaṃ sappāyasenāsanaṃ nāddasa. Atha te bhikkhū āha – “na, bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ aññaṃ sappāyasenāsanaṃ atthi, tattheva tumhe viharantā āsavakkhayaṃ pāpuṇissatha, gacchatha, bhikkhave, tameva [V 0.0191] senāsanaṃ upanissāya viharatha, sace pana devatāhi abhayaṃ icchatha, imaṃ parittaṃ uggaṇhatha. Etañhi vo parittañca kammaṭṭhānañca bhavissatī”ti idaṃ suttamabhāsi.

Seeing those monks, the Blessed One said this: “Monks, the training rule ‘one should not go on a journey during the rains-residence’ was laid down by me. Why do you go on a journey?” They told the Blessed One everything. The Blessed One, reflecting, did not see a suitable lodging for them in the whole of Jambudīpa, not even so much as a place for a four-legged stool. Then he said to those monks: “Monks, there is no other suitable lodging for you. Dwelling right there, you will reach the destruction of the cankers. Go, monks, dwell relying on that very lodging. But if you desire safety from the deities, learn this protection. For this will be both your protection and your meditation subject.” Having said this, he spoke this discourse.

Apare [M 0.0201] panāhu – “gacchatha, bhikkhave, tameva senāsanaṃ upanissāya viharathā”ti idañca vatvā bhagavā āha – “apica kho āraññakena pariharaṇaṃ ñātabbaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – sāyaṃ pātaṃ karaṇavasena dve mettā dve parittā dve asubhā dve maraṇassatī aṭṭhamahāsaṃvegavatthusamāvajjanañca, aṭṭha mahāsaṃvegavatthūni nāma jātijarābyādhimaraṇaṃ cattāri apāyadukkhānīti, atha vā jātijarābyādhimaraṇāni cattāri, apāyadukkhaṃ pañcamaṃ, atīte vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, anāgate vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, paccuppanne āhārapariyeṭṭhimūlakaṃ dukkha”nti. Evaṃ bhagavā pariharaṇaṃ ācikkhitvā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ mettatthañca parittatthañca vipassanāpādakajjhānatthañca idaṃ suttamabhāsīti. Evaṃ vitthāratopi “yena vuttaṃ yadā yattha, yasmā ce”ti etesaṃ padānaṃ dīpanā nidānasodhanā veditabbā.

But other teachers say: Having said, “Go, monks, dwell relying on that very lodging,” the Blessed One also said: “Moreover, a forest-dweller should know the proper practice. That is to say: by way of practice in the evening and morning, two mettās, two parittas, two asubhas, two maraṇassatis, and the contemplation of the eight great grounds for spiritual urgency. The eight great grounds for spiritual urgency are: birth, aging, sickness, death, and the four kinds of suffering in the woeful states. Or alternatively: the four which are birth, aging, sickness, and death; fifth, the suffering of the woeful states; suffering rooted in the round of existence in the past; suffering rooted in the round of existence in the future; and suffering in the present rooted in the search for food.” Thus, they say, the Blessed One, having explained the practice, taught this discourse to those monks for the purpose of mettā, for the purpose of protection, and for the purpose of the jhāna that is the basis for insight. Thus, even in detail, the clarification of these words—‘by whom it was said, when, where, and why’—should be understood as the purification of the introduction.

Ettāvatā ca yā sā “yena vuttaṃ yadā yattha, yasmā cetesa dīpanā. Nidānaṃ sodhayitvā”ti mātikā ṭhapitā, sā [P 0.0236] sabbākārena vitthāritā hoti.

And by this much, that mātikā which was set down—“By whom it was said, when, where, and why, the clarification of these, having purified the Nidāna”—has been explained in detail in all aspects.

Paṭhamagāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the First Verse

1. Idāni “assa karissāmatthavaṇṇana”nti vuttattā evaṃ katanidānasodhanassa assa suttassa atthavaṇṇanā ārabbhate. Tattha karaṇīyamatthakusalenāti imissā paṭhamagāthāya tāva ayaṃ padavaṇṇanā – karaṇīyanti kātabbaṃ, karaṇārahanti attho. Atthoti paṭipadā, yaṃ vā kiñci attano hitaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ araṇīyato atthoti vuccati, araṇīyato nāma upagantabbato. Atthe kusalena atthakusalena atthachekenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Yanti aniyamitapaccattaṃ. Nti niyamitaupayogaṃ, ubhayampi vā yaṃ tanti paccattavacanaṃ. Santaṃ padanti upayogavacanaṃ, tattha lakkhaṇato santaṃ, pattabbato padaṃ, nibbānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Abhisameccāti abhisamāgantvā. Sakkotīti sakko, samattho paṭibaloti vuttaṃ hoti. Ujūti ajjavayutto. Suṭṭhu ujūti suhuju. Sukhaṃ vaco tasminti suvaco. Assāti bhaveyya. Mudūti maddavayutto. Na atimānīti anatimāni.

1. Now, since it was said, “We shall explain its meaning,” the explanation of the meaning of this sutta, which has had its introduction thus purified, is begun. Therein, regarding the first verse, karaṇīyamatthakusalena, this, first of all, is the explanation of the words: Karaṇīyaṃ means ‘what should be done,’ ‘what is worthy of being done.’ Attho means the practice; or, whatever is for one’s own welfare, all that is called attha because it is to be approached (araṇīyato), that is, because it is to be gone to. By atthe kusalena is meant atthakusalena, ‘skilled in the goal,’ or atthachekena, ‘adept in the goal’; thus it is said. The word yaṃ is an unspecified nominative term; the word taṃ is a specified accusative term. Alternatively, both yaṃ and taṃ are nominative terms, while santaṃ padaṃ is an accusative term. Therein, it is santaṃ (peaceful) by its characteristic, and padaṃ (state) because it is to be attained; this is a designation for Nibbāna. Abhisamecca means having fully realized. Sakkoti means he is able, therefore he is sakko, capable, competent; thus it is said. Ujū means endowed with uprightness. Suṭṭhu ujū means excellently upright, hence suhuju. One is suvaco because one is easy to speak to. Assa means ‘he should be.’ Mudū means endowed with gentleness. Anatimāni means not conceited.

Ayaṃ panettha atthavaṇṇanā – karaṇīyamatthakusalena, yantaṃ santaṃ padaṃ abhisameccāti ettha tāva [V 0.0192] atthi karaṇīyaṃ, atthi akaraṇīyaṃ. Tattha saṅkhepato [M 0.0202] sikkhattayaṃ karaṇīyaṃ. Sīlavipatti, diṭṭhivipatti, ācāravipatti, ājīvavipattīti evamādi akaraṇīyaṃ. Tathā atthi atthakusalo, atthi anatthakusalo. Tattha yo imasmiṃ sāsane pabbajitvā na attānaṃ sammā payojeti, khaṇḍasīlo hoti, ekavīsatividhaṃ anesanaṃ nissāya jīvikaṃ kappeti. Seyyathidaṃ – veḷudānaṃ pattadānaṃ pupphadānaṃ phaladānaṃ dantakaṭṭhadānaṃ mukhodakadānaṃ sinānadānaṃ cuṇṇadānaṃ mattikādānaṃ cāṭukamyataṃ muggasūpyataṃ pāribhaṭayataṃ jaṅghapesanikaṃ vejjakammaṃ dūtakammaṃ pahiṇagamanaṃ piṇḍapaṭipiṇḍaṃ [P 0.0237] dānānuppadānaṃ vatthuvijjaṃ nakkhattavijjaṃ aṅgavijjanti. Chabbidhe ca agocare carati. Seyyathidaṃ – vesiyāgocare vidhavathullakumārikapaṇḍakabhikkhunīpānāgāragocareti. Saṃsaṭṭho ca viharati rājūhi rājamahāmattehi titthiyehi titthiyasāvakehi ananulomikena gihisaṃsaggena, yāni vā pana tāni kulāni assaddhāni appasannāni anopānabhūtāni akkosakaparibhāsakāni anatthakāmāni ahitaaphāsukayogakkhemakāmāni bhikkhūnaṃ…pe… upāsikānaṃ, tathārūpāni kulāni sevati bhajati payirupāsati. Ayaṃ anatthakusalo.

This is the explanation of the meaning herein: In the phrase karaṇīyamatthakusalena, yantaṃ santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca (‘What is to be done by one skilled in the goal, having realized the peaceful state’), first, there is what is to be done and what is not to be done. In brief, the threefold training is what is to be done. Corruption of virtue, corruption of view, corruption of conduct, corruption of livelihood, and so forth, are what is not to be done. Likewise, there is one who is skilled in the goal and one who is unskilled in the goal. Therein, one who, having gone forth in this Dispensation, does not apply himself correctly, is of broken virtue, and makes a living by relying on the twenty-one kinds of improper search. Namely: giving bamboo, giving leaves, giving flowers, giving fruit, giving tooth-sticks, giving water for washing the face, giving bathing powder, giving cosmetic powder, giving clay, flattery, acting like mung bean soup, acting as a children's nurse, acting as a leg-messenger, medical practice, acting as a messenger, going on errands, giving alms in return for alms, giving gifts in return for gifts, site-lore, star-lore, and limb-lore. And he wanders in the six kinds of improper resorts. Namely: the resort of prostitutes; the resort of widows, spinsters, eunuchs, bhikkhunīs, and taverns. He dwells associated with kings, royal ministers, sectarians, and the disciples of sectarians, with inappropriate association with householders. Or he resorts to, associates with, and serves those families that are faithless, displeased, unwelcoming, abusive, and reviling towards bhikkhus… up to… laywomen, wishing them no benefit, welfare, comfort, or release from bonds. This one is unskilled in the goal.

Yo pana imasmiṃ sāsane pabbajitvā attānaṃ sammā payojeti, anesanaṃ pahāya catupārisuddhisīle patiṭṭhātukāmo saddhāsīsena pātimokkhasaṃvaraṃ satisīsena indriyasaṃvaraṃ vīriyasīsena ājīvapārisuddhiṃ, paññāsīsena paccayapaṭisevanaṃ pūreti. Ayaṃ atthakusalo.

But one who, having gone forth in this Dispensation, applies himself correctly, abandoning improper search and desiring to be established in the fourfold purity of virtue, fulfills: the Pātimokkha restraint with faith as its head, the sense restraint with mindfulness as its head, the purity of livelihood with energy as its head, and the use of requisites with wisdom as its head. This one is skilled in the goal.

Yo vā sattāpattikkhandhasodhanavasena pātimokkhasaṃvaraṃ, chadvāre ghaṭṭitārammaṇesu abhijjhādīnaṃ anuppattivasena indrisaṃvaraṃ, anesanaparivajjanavasena viññuppasatthabuddhabuddhasāvakavaṇṇitapaccayapaṭisevanena ca ājīvapārisuddhiṃ, yathāvuttapaccavekkhaṇavasena paccayapaṭisevanaṃ, catuiriyāpathaparivattane sātthakatādipaccavekkhaṇavasena sampajaññañca sodheti. Ayampi atthakusalo.

Alternatively, one who purifies the Pātimokkha restraint by means of purifying the seven classes of offenses; who purifies the sense restraint by means of the non-arising of covetousness and so on towards objects that impinge on the six doors; who purifies the purity of livelihood by means of avoiding improper search and by using requisites praised by the wise, the Buddha, and the disciples of the Buddha; who purifies the use of requisites by means of reflecting as has been stated; and who purifies clear comprehension by means of reflecting on the purposefulness and so on when changing the four postures. This one, too, is skilled in the goal.

Yo vā yathā ūsodakaṃ paṭicca saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ vatthaṃ pariyodāpayati, chārikaṃ paṭicca ādāso, ukkāmukhaṃ paṭicca jātarūpaṃ, tathā ñāṇaṃ paṭicca sīlaṃ vodāyatīti ñatvā ñāṇodakena dhovanto sīlaṃ pariyodāpeti. Yathā ca kikī sakuṇikā aṇḍaṃ, camarī migo vāladhiṃ, ekaputtikā nārī [M 0.0203] piyaṃ ekaputtakaṃ, ekanayano puriso taṃ ekanayanañca rakkhati, tathā ativiya appamatto attano sīlakkhandhaṃ rakkhati, sāyaṃ [P 0.0238] pātaṃ paccavekkhamāno aṇumattampi vajjaṃ na passati. Ayampi atthakusalo.

Alternatively, just as one purifies a stained cloth by means of alkaline water, a mirror by means of ash, or gold by means of a furnace, so too, knowing that ‘one purifies virtue by means of wisdom,’ one purifies virtue by washing it with the water of wisdom. And just as a jay guards her egg, a camarī deer its tail, a woman with only one son her beloved only son, and a one-eyed man his single eye, so too, being extremely heedful, one guards one's own aggregate of virtue. Reflecting morning and evening, one does not see even a minute fault. This one, too, is skilled in the goal.

Yo [V 0.0193] vā pana avippaṭisārakare sīle patiṭṭhāya kilesavikkhambhanapaṭipadaṃ paggaṇhāti, taṃ paggaṇhitvā kasiṇaparikammaṃ karoti, kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā samāpattiyo nibbatteti. Ayampi atthakusalo.

Alternatively, one who, established in virtue that leads to no remorse, undertakes the practice for the suppression of defilements; having undertaken it, performs the kasiṇa preliminary work; and having performed the kasiṇa preliminary work, generates the meditative attainments. This one, too, is skilled in the goal.

Yo vā pana samāpattito vuṭṭhāya saṅkhāre sammasitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, ayaṃ atthakusalānaṃ aggo. Tattha ye ime yāva avippaṭisārakare sīle patiṭṭhānena yāva vā kilesavikkhambhanapaṭipadāyapaggahaṇena vaṇṇitā atthakusalā, te imasmiṃ atthe atthakusalāti adhippetā. Tathā vidhā ca te bhikkhū. Tena bhagavā te bhikkhū sandhāya ekapuggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya “karaṇīyamatthakusalenā”ti āha.

Alternatively, one who, having arisen from meditative attainment, contemplates the formations and attains Arahantship—this one is the foremost among those skilled in the goal. Therein, those who have been praised as skilled in the goal—from establishing oneself in virtue that leads to no remorse up to undertaking the practice for the suppression of defilements—are intended by ‘skilled in the goal’ in this context. And those bhikkhus were of such a kind. Therefore the Blessed One, with reference to those bhikkhus, spoke with a discourse established on a single individual, saying, ‘karaṇīyamatthakusalena’.

Tato “kiṃ karaṇīya”nti tesaṃ sañjātakaṅkhānaṃ āha “yantaṃ santaṃ padaṃ abhisameccā”ti. Ayamettha adhippāyo – taṃ buddhānubuddhehi vaṇṇitaṃ santaṃ nibbānapadaṃ paṭivedhavasena abhisamecca viharitukāmena yaṃ karaṇīyanti. Ettha ca yanti imassa gāthāpadassa ādito vuttameva karaṇīyanti adhikārato anuvattati, taṃ santaṃ padaṃ abhisameccāti. Ayaṃ pana yasmā sāvasesapāṭho attho, tasmā viharitukāmenāti vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Then, to those in whom doubt had arisen as to 'What is to be done?', He said: 'Having realized that peaceful state.' Herein, this is the intended meaning: What is to be done by one who wishes to dwell, having realized by way of penetration that peaceful state of Nibbāna praised by the Buddhas and their disciples? And here, the word 'what' (yaṃ), which was stated at the beginning of this verse, follows by its governing connection to 'is to be done' (karaṇīyaṃ). As for 'having realized that peaceful state,' because this is an elliptical text, it should be understood that 'by one who wishes to dwell' is stated.

Atha vā santaṃ padaṃ abhisameccāti anussavādivasena lokiyapaññāya nibbānapadaṃ “santa”nti ñatvā taṃ adhigantukāmena yantaṃ karaṇīyanti adhikārato anuvattati, taṃ karaṇīyamatthakusalenāti evampettha adhippāyo veditabbo. Atha vā “karaṇīyamatthakusalenā”ti vutte “ki”nti cintentānaṃ āha “yantaṃ santaṃ padaṃ abhisameccā”ti. Tassevaṃ adhippāyo veditabbo – lokiyapaññāya santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca yaṃ karaṇīyaṃ kātabbaṃ, taṃ karaṇīyaṃ, karaṇārahameva tanti vuttaṃ hoti.

Alternatively, 'having realized the peaceful state' means: having known the state of Nibbāna as 'peaceful' with worldly wisdom by way of hearsay and so forth, for one who wishes to attain it, 'what is to be done' follows by its governing connection, meaning that which is to be done by one skilled in the goal. In this way, too, the meaning should be understood here. Alternatively, when 'to be done by one skilled in the goal' was said, to those who were thinking 'What?', He said: 'Having realized that peaceful state.' Its meaning should be understood thus: having realized the peaceful state with worldly wisdom, what is to be done (yaṃ karaṇīyaṃ) is what should be performed (kātabbaṃ); that (taṃ) is to be done (karaṇīyaṃ); it is only worthy of being done—this is what is meant.

Kiṃ pana tanti[P 0.0239]? Kimaññaṃ siyā aññatra tadadhigamupāyato, kāmañcetaṃ karaṇārahaṭṭhena sikkhattayadīpakena ādipadeneva vuttaṃ. Tathā hi tassa atthavaṇṇanāyaṃ avocumhā “atthi karaṇīyaṃ, atthi akaraṇīyaṃ. Tattha [M 0.0204] saṅkhepato sikkhattayaṃ karaṇīya”nti. Atisaṅkhepena desitattā pana tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ kehici viññātaṃ, kehici na viññātaṃ. Tato yehi na viññātaṃ, tesaṃ viññāpanatthaṃ yaṃ visesato āraññakena bhikkhunā kātabbaṃ, taṃ vitthārento “sakko ujū ca suhujū ca, suvaco cassa mudu anatimānī”ti imaṃ tāva upaḍḍhagāthamāha.

But what is that (taṃ)? What else could it be other than the means for its attainment? And indeed, this was stated by the very first word, which indicates the threefold training by its meaning of 'being worthy of being done.' For so, in the explanation of its meaning, we said: 'There is what is to be done, and there is what is not to be done. Therein, in brief, the threefold training is what is to be done.' However, because it was taught very concisely, it was understood by some of those bhikkhus, but not understood by others. Therefore, for the purpose of making it known to those by whom it was not understood, elaborating on what is to be done especially by a forest-dwelling bhikkhu, He first spoke this half-verse: 'He should be capable, upright and very upright, easy to speak to, gentle, and without conceit.'

Kiṃ [V 0.0194] vuttaṃ hoti? Santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca viharitukāmo, lokiyapaññāya vā taṃ abhisamecca tadadhigamāya paṭipajjamāno āraññako bhikkhu dutiyacatutthapadhāniyaṅgasamannāgamena kāye ca jīvite ca anapekkho hutvā saccappaṭivedhāya paṭipajjituṃ sakko assa, tathā kasiṇaparikammavattasamādānādīsu attano pattacīvarappaṭisaṅkharaṇādīsu ca yāni tāni sabrahmacārīnaṃ uccāvacāni kiṃ karaṇīyāni, tesu aññesu ca evarūpesu sakko assa dakkho analaso samattho. Sakko hontopi ca tatiyapadhāniyaṅgasamannāgamena uju assa. Uju hontopi ca sakiṃ ujubhāvena daharakāle vā ujubhāvena santosaṃ anāpajjitvā yāvajīvaṃ punappunaṃ asithilakaraṇena suṭṭhutaraṃ uju assa. Asaṭhatāya vā uju, amāyāvitāya suhuju. Kāyavacīvaṅkappahānena vā uju, manovaṅkappahānena suhuju. Asantaguṇassa vā anāvikaraṇena uju, asantaguṇena uppannassa lābhassa anadhivāsanena suhuju. Evaṃ ārammaṇalakkhaṇūpanijjhānehi purimadvayatatiyasikkhāhi payogāsayasuddhīhi ca uju ca suhuju ca assa.

What is meant? A forest-dwelling bhikkhu who wishes to realize the peaceful state and dwell therein—or who, having realized it with worldly wisdom, is practicing for its attainment—should, being endowed with the second and third factors of striving, and being unconcerned with body and life, be capable (sakko) of practicing for the penetration of the truths. Likewise, in such tasks as the preliminary work for the kasiṇas, undertaking duties, repairing his own bowl and robes, and in whatever other high and low duties there are for his companions in the holy life that are to be done, and in other such matters, he should be capable (sakko), skilled, not lazy, and competent. And though being capable, he should, being endowed with the third factor of striving, be upright (uju). And though being upright, not becoming content with a single instance of uprightness or with uprightness in his youth, he should, by not slackening throughout his life, again and again, be exceedingly upright. Alternatively, one is upright (uju) through non-deceitfulness, and very upright (suhuju) through not being guileful. Or, one is upright by abandoning the crookedness of body and speech, and very upright by abandoning the crookedness of mind. Or, one is upright by not revealing a non-existent quality, and very upright by not tolerating gain that has arisen from a non-existent quality. Thus, by the close contemplation of the object and its characteristics, by the first two trainings and the third training, and by purity of effort and intention, he should be both upright and very upright.

Na kevalañca uju ca suhuju ca, apica pana suvaco ca assa. Yo hi puggalo “idaṃ na kattabba”nti vutto “kiṃ te diṭṭhaṃ, kiṃ te sutaṃ, ko me sutvā vadasi, kiṃ upajjhāyo ācariyo sandiṭṭho sambhatto vā”ti vadeti, tuṇhībhāvena vā taṃ viheseti, sampaṭicchitvā vā na tathā karoti, so visesādhigamassa dūre hoti. Yo pana ovadiyamāno “sādhu, bhante suṭṭhu vuttaṃ, attano vajjaṃ nāma [P 0.0240] duddasaṃ hoti, punapi maṃ evarūpaṃ disvā vadeyyātha anukampaṃ upādāya, cirassaṃ me tumhākaṃ santikā ovādo laddho”ti vadati, yathānusiṭṭhañca paṭipajjati, so visesādhigamassa avidūre hoti. Tasmā evaṃ parassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā karonto suvaco ca assa.

And not only should he be upright and very upright, but he should also be easy to admonish. For a person who, when told, 'This should not be done,' retorts, 'What have you seen? What have you heard? Who are you to speak to me? Are you my preceptor? My teacher? A close acquaintance or a companion?'—or who vexes that person by remaining silent, or who, having accepted the advice, does not act accordingly—such a one is far from the attainment of distinction. But one who, when being admonished, says, 'Good, venerable sir, it is well said. One's own fault is indeed hard to see. Again, upon seeing such a thing, please speak out of compassion. It has been long since I received an admonition from you,' and who practices as instructed—such a one is not far from the attainment of distinction. Therefore, by thus accepting another's words and acting upon them, he should be easy to admonish.

Yathā [M 0.0205] ca suvaco, evaṃ mudu assa.
