Mudūti gahaṭṭhehi dūtagamanapahiṇagamanādīsu niyujjamāno tattha mudubhāvaṃ akatvā thaddho hutvā vattapaṭipattiyaṃ sakalabrahmacariye ca mudu assa suparikammakatasuvaṇṇaṃ viya tattha tattha viniyogakkhamo. Atha vā mudūti abhākuṭiko uttānamukho sukhasambhāso paṭisanthāravutti sutitthaṃ viya sukhāvagāho assa. Na kevalañca mudu, apica pana anatimānī assa, jātigottādīhi atimānavatthūhi pare nātimaññeyya, sāriputtatthero viya caṇḍālakumārakasamena cetasā vihareyyāti.

And just as he is easy to admonish, so should he be gentle. 'Gentle' (mudu) means: when engaged by householders in such tasks as going as a messenger or on errands, not being gentle there but being firm, he should be gentle in his duties and practice and in the entire holy life, fit to be employed in this or that way like well-refined gold. Alternatively, 'gentle' means he should be without a frown, with an open face, pleasant in conversation, of a welcoming disposition, and easy to approach like a good ford. And not only should he be gentle, but he should also be without conceit (anatimānī). He should not despise others based on grounds for conceit such as birth, clan, and so forth. Like the Elder Sāriputta, he should dwell with a mind like that of a young outcaste boy.

Dutiyagāthāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Second Stanza

2. Evaṃ [V 0.0195] bhagavā santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca viharitukāmassa tadadhigamāya vā paṭipajjamānassa visesato āraññakassa bhikkhuno ekaccaṃ karaṇīyaṃ vatvā puna tatuttaripi vattukāmo “santussako cā”ti dutiyagāthamāha.

2. Thus, the Blessed One, having thoroughly understood the peaceful state, and having stated the duty to be performed collectively for a forest-dwelling monk who desires to dwell therein or, alternatively, is especially practicing for its attainment, again, being desirous of teaching even beyond that, spoke the second stanza beginning with 'santussako ca'.

Tattha “santuṭṭhī ca kataññutā”ti ettha vuttappabhedena dvādasavidhena santosena santussatīti santussako. Atha vā tussatīti tussako, sakena tussako, santena tussako, samena tussakoti santussako. Tattha sakaṃ nāma “piṇḍiyālopabhojanaṃ nissāyā”ti evaṃ upasampadamaṇḍale uddiṭṭhaṃ attanā ca sampaṭicchitaṃ catupaccayajātaṃ, tena sundarena vā asundarena vā sakkaccaṃ vā asakkaccaṃ vā dinnena paṭiggahaṇakāle paribhogakāle ca vikāraṃ adassetvā yāpento “sakena tussako”ti vuccati. Santaṃ nāma yaṃ laddhaṃ hoti attano ‘vijjamānaṃ[P 0.0241], tena santeneva tussanto tato paraṃ na patthento atricchataṃ pajahanto “santena tussako”ti vuccati. Samaṃ nāma iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu anunayapaṭighappahānaṃ, tena samena sabbārammaṇesu tussanto “samena tussako”ti vuccati.

Herein, regarding the phrase 'contentment and gratitude,' one is called 'santussako' because one is content with the twelve kinds of contentment as previously described. Alternatively, one is called 'tussako' because one is pleased; one is 'santussako' because one is pleased with what is one's own, pleased with what is available, and pleased in a balanced way. Herein, 'one's own' (sakaṃ) refers to the four kinds of requisites which were specified in the ordination ceremony, as in 'relying on alms-food gathered,' and which have been accepted by oneself. One who maintains oneself with what is given, whether it is fine or not fine, given respectfully or disrespectfully, without showing any change at the time of receiving and at the time of using, is called 'one pleased with what is one's own.' 'What is available' (santaṃ) refers to what has been received, what is existing in one's presence. Being pleased with just that which is available, not longing for anything beyond it and abandoning excessive desire—such a one is called 'one pleased with what is available.' 'Balanced' (samaṃ) refers to the abandonment of attraction and aversion towards the desirable and undesirable. Being pleased with all sense-objects in that balanced way—such a one is called 'one pleased in a balanced way.'

Sukhena bharīyatīti subharo, suposoti vuttaṃ hoti. Yo hi bhikkhu manussehi sālimaṃsodanādīnaṃ patte pūretvā dinnepi dummukhabhāvaṃ anattamanabhāvameva ca dasseti, tesaṃ vā sammukhāva taṃ piṇḍapātaṃ “kiṃ tumhehi dinna”nti apasādento sāmaṇeragahaṭṭhādīnaṃ deti, esa dubbharo. Etaṃ disvā manussā dūratova parivajjenti “dubbharo bhikkhu na sakkā posetu”nti[M 0.0206]. Yo pana yaṃ kiñci lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā labhitvā attamano vippasannamukho hutvā yāpeti, esa subharo. Etaṃ disvā manussā ativiya vissatthā honti, “amhākaṃ bhadanto subharo, thokathokenāpi tussati, mayameva naṃ posessāmā”ti paṭiññaṃ katvā posenti. Evarūpo idha subharoti adhippeto.

He is called 'subharo' (easy to support) because he is supported with ease; this means he is easily nourished. Indeed, a monk who, even when people fill his bowl with offerings like rice with meat, displays a displeased expression and an unhappy demeanor, or who, right in front of them, disparages the alms-food by saying, 'What is this you have given?' and then gives it to novices or laypeople—such a one is 'dubbharo' (difficult to support). Seeing this, people avoid him from afar, thinking, 'This monk is difficult to support; it is not possible to provide for him.' But one who, upon receiving anything—whether coarse or fine, little or much—maintains himself with a pleased mind and a bright face, such a one is 'subharo.' Seeing this, people become very free from aversion, and making a promise, they support him, saying, 'Our venerable sir is easy to support; he is satisfied even with a little. We ourselves will support him.' Such a one is intended here by the term 'subharo.'

Appaṃ kiccamassāti appakicco, na kammārāmatābhassārāmatāsaṅgaṇikārāmatādianekakiccabyāvaṭo, atha vā sakalavihāre navakammasaṅghaparibhogasāmaṇeraārāmikavosāsanādikiccavirahito, attano kesanakhacchedanapattacīvarakammādiṃ katvā samaṇadhammakiccaparo hotīti vuttaṃ hoti.

'He has few duties,' thus he is called 'appakicco'; he is not occupied with many duties such as delighting in work, delighting in talk, or delighting in company. Alternatively, being free from duties in the entire monastery—such as new construction, matters of the Sangha, the group, novices, supporting monastery attendants, and so forth—and having done his own tasks like cutting his hair, trimming his nails, and tending to his bowl and robes, he is devoted to the duty of a recluse's practice. This is the meaning.

Sallahukā [V 0.0196] vutti assāti sallahukavutti. Yathā ekacco bahubhaṇḍo bhikkhu disāpakkamanakāle bahuṃ pattacīvarapaccattharaṇatelaguḷādiṃ mahājanena sīsabhārakaṭibhārādīhi ubbahāpetvā pakkamati, evaṃ ahutvā yo appaparikkhāro hoti, pattacīvarādiaṭṭhasamaṇaparikkhāramattameva pariharati, disāpakkamanakāle pakkhī sakuṇo viya samādāyeva pakkamati[P 0.0242], evarūpo idha sallahukavuttīti adhippeto. Santāni indriyāni assāti santindriyo, iṭṭhārammaṇādīsu rāgādivasena anuddhatindriyoti vuttaṃ hoti. Nipakoti viññū vibhāvī paññavā, sīlānurakkhaṇapaññāya cīvarādivicāraṇapaññāya āvāsādisattasappāyaparijānanapaññāya ca samannāgatoti adhippāyo.

'He has a light livelihood,' thus he is called 'sallahukavutti.' Just as a certain monk with many possessions, when departing for another region, has a great number of people carry his many bowls, robes, bedding, oil, jaggery, and so on, as head-loads, waist-loads, and the like; not being like that, one who has few requisites, who carries only the eight requisites of a recluse such as a bowl and robes, and who, when departing for another region, goes taking them up just as a winged bird flies off—such a one is intended here by 'sallahukavutti.' 'He has tranquil faculties,' thus he is called 'santindriyo'; this means that his faculties are not agitated by lust and so forth in regard to desirable objects. 'Nipako' means one who is discerning, discriminating, and endowed with wisdom; the intention is that one is endowed with the wisdom to protect one's virtue, the wisdom to manage one's robes and so forth, and the wisdom to discern the seven suitable conditions, such as a dwelling place.

Na pagabbhoti appagabbho, aṭṭhaṭṭhānena kāyapāgabbhiyena catuṭṭhānena vacīpāgabbhiyena anekena ṭhānena manopāgabbhiyena ca virahitoti attho.

'Not impudent,' thus 'appagabbho'; the meaning is that one is devoid of bodily impudence on eight grounds, verbal impudence on four grounds, and mental impudence on many grounds.

Aṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ kāyapāgabbhiyaṃ (mahāni. 87) nāma saṅghagaṇapuggalabhojanasālājantāgharanhānatitthabhikkhācāramaggaantaragharappavesanesu kāyena appatirūpakaraṇaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – idhekacco saṅghamajjhe pallatthikāya vā nisīdati pāde pādamodahitvā vāti evamādi. Tathā gaṇamajjhe catuparisasannipāte, tathā vuḍḍhatare puggale. Bhojanasālāyaṃ pana vuḍḍhānaṃ āsanaṃ [M 0.0207] na deti, navānaṃ āsanaṃ paṭibāhati. Tathā jantāghare, vuḍḍhe cettha anāpucchā aggijālanādīni karoti. Nhānatitthe ca yadidaṃ “daharo vuḍḍhoti pamāṇaṃ akatvā āgatapaṭipāṭiyā nhāyitabba”nti vuttaṃ, tampi anādiyanto pacchā āgantvā udakaṃ otaritvā vuḍḍhe ca nave ca bādheti. Bhikkhācāramagge pana aggāsanaaggodakaaggapiṇḍatthaṃ vuḍḍhānaṃ purato purato yāti, bāhāya bāhaṃ paharanto. Antaragharappavesane vuḍḍhānaṃ paṭhamataraṃ pavisati, daharehi kāyakīḷanaṃ karotīti evamādi.

Bodily impudence on eight grounds is improper bodily conduct in the midst of the Sangha, a group, towards an individual, in a dining hall, a fire-hall, at a bathing place, on the alms-round path, and when entering a house. For instance: here a certain monk in the midst of the Sangha sits with his arms crossed or with one foot placed on the other, and so on. Likewise in the midst of a group, a gathering of three or four persons, and likewise towards a more senior individual. In the dining hall, he does not give a seat to the seniors and prevents the junior monks from taking a seat. Likewise in the fire-hall; and there, without asking the seniors, he does things like lighting the fire. And at the bathing place, not taking to heart the rule spoken by the Blessed One, 'One should bathe in the order of arrival, without making a distinction between junior and senior,' he comes later, gets into the water, and obstructs both the seniors and the juniors. On the alms-round path, for the sake of the first seat, the first water, and the first alms-food, he walks right in front of the seniors, striking them arm to arm. When entering a house, he enters before the seniors. He engages in physical play with the junior monks, and so on.

Catuṭṭhānaṃ vacīpāgabbhiyaṃ (mahāni. 87) nāma saṅghagaṇapuggalaantaragharesu appatirūpavācānicchāraṇaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – idhekacco saṅghamajjhe anāpucchā dhammaṃ bhāsati, tathā pubbe vuttappakāre gaṇe [P 0.0243] vuḍḍhatare puggale ca, tattha manussehi pañhaṃ puṭṭho vuḍḍhataraṃ anāpucchā vissajjeti, antaraghare pana “itthannāme kiṃ atthi, kiṃ yāgu udāhu khādanīyaṃ vā bhojanīyaṃ vā, kiṃ me dassasi, kiṃ ajja khādissāmi, kiṃ bhuñjissāmi, kiṃ pivissāmī”ti evamādiṃ bhāsati.

Verbal impudence on four grounds is the uttering of unsuitable speech in the midst of the Sangha, a group, towards an individual, and within houses. For instance: here a certain monk, without asking permission, speaks the Dhamma in the midst of the Sangha; likewise in a group or towards a more senior person, as described before. There, when asked a question by people, he answers without asking the more senior monk. Within a house, he says such things as: 'What is there, so-and-so? Is there gruel, or is there hard food or soft food? What will you give me? What will I eat today? What will I consume? What will I drink?'

Anekaṭṭhānaṃ [V 0.0197] manopāgabbhiyaṃ (mahāni. 87) nāma tesu tesu ṭhānesu kāyavācāhi ajjhācāraṃ anāpajjitvāpi manasā eva kāmavitakkādinānappakāraṃ appatirūpavitakkanaṃ.

Mental impudence, which occurs on many grounds, is this: even without having committed a transgression with body and speech in those various instances, it is the thinking, with the mind alone, of various kinds of improper thoughts, such as sensual thoughts.

Kulesvananugiddhoti yāni tāni kulāni upasaṅkamati, tesu paccayataṇhāya vā ananulomikagihisaṃsaggavasena vā ananugiddho, na sahasokī, na sahanandī, na sukhitesu sukhito, na dukkhitesu dukkhito, na uppannesu kiccakaraṇīyesu attanā vā uyyogamāpajjitāti vuttaṃ hoti. Imissāya ca gāthāya yaṃ “suvaco cassā”ti ettha vuttaṃ assāti vacanaṃ, taṃ sabbapadehi saddhiṃ santussako ca assa, subharo ca assāti evaṃ yojetabbaṃ.

As for 'not greedy among families': whatever families he approaches, among them he should be not greedy, either through craving for requisites or through the influence of unsuitable association with householders. He is not sorrowful together with them, not joyful together with them; he is not happy among the happy, nor is he sorrowful among the sorrowful; he does not personally apply himself to tasks and duties that have arisen. Thus is the meaning. And in this stanza, the word 'assa' (should be), which is stated here in 'suvaco c'assa' (and he should be easy to admonish), should be connected with all the terms, thus: 'he should be easily contented,' and 'he should be easy to support.'

Tatiyagāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Third Stanza.

3. Evaṃ bhagavā santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca viharitukāmassa tadadhigamāya vā paṭipajjitukāmassa visesato āraññakassa bhikkhuno taduttaripi karaṇīyaṃ ācikkhitvā idāni akaraṇīyampi ācikkhitukāmo “na ca khuddamācare kiñci, yena viññū pare upavadeyyu”nti imaṃ upaḍḍhagāthamāha.

3. Thus the Blessed One, for a bhikkhu—especially a forest-dweller—who wishes to dwell having thoroughly realized the peaceful state, or who wishes to practice for its attainment, having taught what is to be done beyond that, now, wishing to teach also what is not to be done, spoke this half-stanza: 'And he should not practice any slight thing for which other wise ones might censure him.'

Tassattho [M 0.0208] – evamimaṃ karaṇīyaṃ karonto yaṃ taṃ kāyavacīmanoduccaritaṃ khuddaṃ lāmakanti vuccati, taṃ na ca khuddaṃ samācare, asamācaranto ca na kevalaṃ oḷārikaṃ, kintu kiñci na samācare, appamattakampi aṇumattakampi na samācareti vuttaṃ hoti.

Its meaning is this: While performing this duty, he should not practice that slight thing, that is, the bodily, verbal, and mental misconduct which is called 'slight' and 'base'. And in not practicing, it is not only the gross, but rather he should not practice anything whatsoever; he should not practice even a trifle, even an atom's worth. Thus is the meaning.

Tato tassa samācāre sandiṭṭhikamevādīnavaṃ dasseti “yena viññū pare upavadeyyu”nti. Ettha ca yasmā aviññū pare appamāṇaṃ. Te hi anavajjaṃ vā sāvajjaṃ karonti, appasāvajjaṃ vā mahāsāvajjaṃ. Viññū eva pana pamāṇaṃ. Te hi anuvicca pariyogāhetvā avaṇṇārahassa [P 0.0244] avaṇṇaṃ bhāsanti, vaṇṇārahassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsanti. Tasmā “viññū pare”ti vuttaṃ.

Then, He points out the immediately visible danger in such conduct with the words: 'for which other wise ones might censure him.' And here, it is because other unwise ones are not the standard. For they make what is blameless blameworthy, or what has a small fault into what has a great fault. But only the wise are the standard. For they, having investigated and comprehended, speak dispraise of one who deserves dispraise and praise of one who deserves praise. Therefore, 'other wise ones' was said.

Evaṃ bhagavā imāhi aḍḍhateyyāhi gāthāhi santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca viharitukāmassa tadadhigamāya vā paṭipajjitukāmassa visesato āraññakassa, āraññakasīsena ca sabbesampi kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā viharitukāmānaṃ karaṇīyākaraṇīyabhedaṃ kammaṭṭhānūpacāraṃ vatvā idāni tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ tassa devatābhayassa paṭighātāya parittatthaṃ vipassanāpādakajjhānavasena kammaṭṭhānatthañca “sukhinova khemino hontū”tiādinā nayena mettakathaṃ kathetumāraddho.

Thus the Blessed One, with these two and a half stanzas, having spoken on the preliminary practice for the meditation subject, with its distinction between what should and should not be done—especially for the forest-dweller who wishes to dwell having thoroughly realized the peaceful state, or who wishes to practice for its attainment, and, with the forest-dweller as the principal example, for all who wish to dwell having taken up a meditation subject—now, for those bhikkhus, for the warding off of that fear from deities, for the sake of protection, and for the purpose of the meditation subject by means of the jhāna that is the basis for insight, began to teach loving-kindness with the method beginning, 'May they be happy and secure.'

Tattha [V 0.0198] sukhinoti sukhasampannā. Kheminoti khemavanto, abhayā nirupaddavāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sabbeti anavasesā. Sattāti pāṇino. Sukhitattāti sukhitacittā. Ettha ca kāyikena sukhena sukhino, mānasena sukhitattā, tadubhayenāpi sabbabhayupaddavavigamena vā kheminoti veditabbo. Kasmā pana evaṃ vuttaṃ? Mettābhāvanākāradassanatthaṃ. Evañhi mettā bhāvetabbā “sabbe sattā sukhino hontū”ti vā, “khemino hontū”ti vā, “sukhitattā hontū”ti vā.

Herein, 'sukhino' means endowed with happiness. 'Khemino' means secure, fearless, and without danger; thus is the meaning. 'Sabbe' means all, without remainder. 'Sattā' means living beings. 'Sukhitattā' means with happy minds. And here, it should be understood that with bodily happiness they are 'sukhino'; with mental happiness they are 'sukhitattā'; and with both of these, or by the removal of all fear and danger, they are 'khemino'. But why was it said thus? For the purpose of showing the mode of developing loving-kindness. For loving-kindness should be developed thus: 'May all beings be happy,' or 'May they be secure,' or 'May they be happy-minded.'

Catutthagāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Fourth Stanza.

4. Evaṃ yāva upacārato appanākoṭi, tāva saṅkhepena mettābhāvanaṃ dassetvā idāni vitthāratopi taṃ dassetuṃ “ye kecī”ti gāthādvayamāha. Atha vā yasmā puthuttārammaṇe paricitaṃ cittaṃ na ādikeneva ekatte saṇṭhāti ārammaṇappabhedaṃ pana anugantvā anugantvā kamena [M 0.0209] saṇṭhāti, tasmā tassa tasathāvarādidukatikappabhede ārammaṇe anugantvā anugantvā saṇṭhānatthampi “ye kecī”ti gāthādvayamāha. Atha vā yasmā yassa yaṃ ārammaṇaṃ vibhūtaṃ hoti, tassa tattha cittaṃ sukhaṃ [P 0.0245] tiṭṭhati, tasmā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ yassa yaṃ vibhūtaṃ ārammaṇaṃ, tassa tattha cittaṃ saṇṭhāpetukāmo tasathāvarādidukatikārammaṇabhedadīpakaṃ “ye kecī”ti imaṃ gāthādvayamāha.

4. Thus, having shown the development of loving-kindness concisely up to the culmination of access and absorption, He now spoke the pair of verses beginning 'ye keci' in order to show it in detail. Or alternatively, because the mind, practiced in a wide range of objects, does not settle on a single individual right from the start, but settles down in sequence by following after the distinctions of the object again and again, therefore, He also spoke the pair of verses beginning 'ye keci' for the purpose of establishing the mind by following again and again the object which has the distinctions of the dyads and triads beginning with 'moving' and 'unmoving'. Or alternatively, because for whichever monk a particular object is distinct, wishing to establish his mind in that distinct object, He spoke this pair of verses beginning with 'ye keci,' which shows the distinctions of the objects of the dyads and triads beginning with 'moving' and 'unmoving'.

Ettha hi tasathāvaradukaṃ diṭṭhādiṭṭhadukaṃ dūrasantikadukaṃ bhūtasambhavesidukanti cattāro duke, dīghādīhi ca chahi padehi majjhimapadassa tīsu aṇukapadassa ca dvīsu tikesu atthasambhavato dīgharassamajjhimatikaṃ mahantāṇukamajjhimatikaṃ thūlāṇukamajjhimatikanti tayo tike ca dīpeti. Tattha ye kecīti anavasesavacanaṃ. Pāṇā eva bhūtā pāṇabhūtā. Atha vā pāṇantīti pāṇā, etena assāsapassāsappaṭibaddhe pañcavokārasatte gaṇhāti. Bhavantīti bhūtā, etena ekavokāracatuvokārasatte gaṇhāti. Atthīti santi saṃvijjanti.

Herein, it shows four dyads: the moving and unmoving dyad, the seen and unseen dyad, the far and near dyad, and the born and seeking-birth dyad. And with the six terms beginning with 'long', because the meaning of the 'middle' term is applicable in three triads and the 'minute' term in two, it also explains three triads: the long-short-middle triad, the large-minute-middle triad, and the coarse-minute-middle triad. Therein, 'ye keci' is a term for 'without remainder.' Beings that breathe (pāṇā) are beings (bhūtā); thus pāṇabhūtā. Or alternatively, they are called 'pāṇā' because they breathe; by this are included the five-constituent beings connected with in-breathing and out-breathing. They are called 'bhūtā' because they come to be; by this are included the one-constituent and four-constituent beings. 'Atthi' means 'they are,' 'they exist.'

Evaṃ “ye keci pāṇabhūtatthī”ti iminā vacanena dukatikehi saṅgahetabbe sabbasatte ekato dassetvā idāni sabbepi te tasā vā thāvarā va navasesāti iminā dukena saṅgahetvā dasseti.

Thus, with the phrase “whatever living beings exist,” having shown collectively all beings that are to be included by the dyads, he now shows all of them included by this dyad: “moving or unmoving, without exception.”

Tattha tasantīti tasā, sataṇhānaṃ sabhayānañcetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tiṭṭhantīti thāvarā, pahīnataṇhābhayānaṃ arahataṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Natthi tesaṃ avasesanti anavasesā, sabbepīti vuttaṃ [V 0.0199] hoti. Yañca dutiyagāthāya ante vuttaṃ, taṃ sabbadukatikehi sambandhitabbaṃ “ye keci pāṇabhūtatthi tasā vā thāvarā vā anavasesā, imepi sabbe sattā bhavantu sukhitattā. Evaṃ yāva bhūtā vā sambhavesī vā, imepi sabbe sattā bhavantu sukhitattā”ti.

Therein, ‘moving’ (tasā) are so called because they tremble (tasanti); this is a designation for those with craving and fear. ‘Unmoving’ (thāvarā) are so called because they are stable (tiṭṭhanti); this is a designation for the arahants who have abandoned craving and fear. ‘Without exception’ (anavasesā) means for them there is no remainder (natthi tesaṃ avasesa); it is said to mean ‘all beings.’ And what was stated at the end of the second verse should be connected with all the dyads and triads: “Whatever living beings exist, moving or unmoving, without exception, may all these beings be happy-minded. Thus, up to ‘those who are born or are seeking to be born, may all these beings be happy-minded.’”

Idāni dīgharassamajjhimāditikattayadīpakesu dīghā vātiādīsu chasu padesu dīghāti dīghattabhāvā nāgamacchagodhādayo. Anekabyāmasatappamāṇāpi hi mahāsamudde nāgānaṃ attabhāvā anekayojanappamāṇā ca macchagodhādīnaṃ attabhāvā honti. Mahantāti mahantattabhāvā jale macchakacchapādayo, thale [P 0.0246] hatthināgādayo, amanussesu dānavādayo[M 0.0210]. Āha ca “rāhuggaṃ attabhāvīna”nti (a. ni. 4.15). Tassa hi attabhāvo ubbedhena cattāri yojanasahassāni aṭṭha ca yojanasatāni, bāhū dvādasayojanasataparimāṇā, paññāsayojanaṃ bhamukantaraṃ, tathā aṅgulantarikā, hatthatalāni dve yojanasatānīti. Majjhimāti assagoṇamahiṃsasūkarādīnaṃ attabhāvā. Rassakāti tāsu tāsu jātīsu vāmanādayo dīghamajjhimehi omakappamāṇā sattā. Aṇukāti maṃsacakkhussa agocarā dibbacakkhuvisayā udakādīsu nibbattā sukhumattabhāvā sattā ūkādayo vā. Apica ye tāsu tāsu jātīsu mahantamajjhimehi thūlamajjhimehi ca omakappamāṇā sattā, te aṇukāti veditabbā. Thūlāti parimaṇḍalattabhāvā sippikasambukādayo sattā.

Now, in the six terms that illuminate the three triads of long, short, and medium, beginning with “long” and so on: “Long” refers to beings with long bodies like nāgas, fish, and monitor lizards. For in the great ocean, the bodies of nāgas are of a measure of many hundreds of fathoms, and the bodies of fish, monitor lizards, and so on are of a measure of many leagues. “Large” refers to beings with large bodies: in water, fish, turtles, and so on; on land, elephants, nāgas, and so on; among non-humans, dānavas and so on. And it was said: “Rāhu has an immense body.” For his body is four thousand and eight hundred leagues in height; his arms measure one hundred and twenty leagues; the space between his eyebrows is fifty leagues, likewise the space between his fingers; the palms of his hands are two hundred leagues. “Medium” refers to the bodies of horses, cattle, buffaloes, pigs, and so on. “Short” refers to beings in those various species, such as dwarfs, who are of a lesser measure than the long and medium. “Minute” refers to beings with subtle bodies not in the range of the physical eye but the domain of the divine eye; or those born in water and so on; or lice and so on. Furthermore, those beings in various species that are of a lesser measure than the large and medium, and the coarse and medium, should be understood as “minute.” “Coarse” refers to beings with round bodies, such as fish, turtles, oysters, conches, and so on.

Pañcamagāthāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Fifth Verse

5. Evaṃ tīhi tikehi anavasesato satte dassetvā idāni “diṭṭhā vā ye va adiṭṭhā”tiādīhi tīhi dukehipi te saṅgahetvā dasseti.

Thus, having shown beings completely by the three triads, he now also shows them included by the three dyads beginning with ‘those seen or unseen.’

Tattha diṭṭhāti ye attano cakkhussa āpāthamāgatavasena diṭṭhapubbā. Adiṭṭhāti ye parasamuddaparaselaparacakkavāḷādīsu ṭhitā. “Ye vā dūre vasanti avidūre”ti iminā pana dukena attano attabhāvassa dūre ca avidūre ca vasante satte dasseti, te apadadvipadavasena veditabbā. Attano hi kāye vasantā sattā avidūre, bahikāye vasantā sattā dūre. Tathā antoupacāre vasantā avidūre, bahiupacāre vasantā dūre. Attano vihāre gāme janapade dīpe cakkavāḷe vasantā avidūre, paracakkavāḷe vasantā dūre vasantīti vuccanti.

5. Therein, ‘seen’ refers to those who have been previously seen by means of coming within the range of one’s own eye. ‘Unseen’ refers to those who are established in other oceans, other mountains, other world-systems, and so forth. Furthermore, by this dyad, ‘those who dwell far or near,’ he shows beings dwelling far and near in relation to one’s own existence; they are to be understood by way of the footless and the two-footed. For beings dwelling in one’s own body are nearby; beings dwelling outside the body are far away. Likewise, beings dwelling within one’s vicinity are nearby; beings dwelling outside the vicinity are far away. Beings dwelling in one’s monastery, alms-round village, country, island, or world-system are nearby; beings dwelling in another world-system are said to dwell far away.

Bhūtāti jātā abhinibbattā. Ye bhūtā eva, na puna bhavissantīti saṅkhyaṃ gacchanti, tesaṃ [V 0.0200] khīṇāsavānaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sambhavamesantīti sambhavesī. Appahīnabhavasaṃyojanattā āyatimpi [P 0.0247] sambhavaṃ esantānaṃ sekhaputhujjanānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Atha vā catūsu yonīsu aṇḍajajalābujā sattā yāva aṇḍakosaṃ vatthikosañca na bhindanti, tāva sambhavesī nāma, aṇḍakosaṃ vatthikosañca bhinditvā bahi nikkhantā bhūtā nāma[M 0.0211]. Saṃsedajā opapātikā ca paṭhamacittakkhaṇe sambhavesī nāma, dutiyacittakkhaṇato pabhuti bhūtā nāma. Yena vā iriyāpathena jāyanti, yāva tato aññaṃ na pāpuṇanti, tāva sambhavesī nāma, tato paraṃ bhūtāti.

‘Born’ (bhūtā) means born (jātā), come into being (abhinibbattā). This is a designation for those destroyers of the taints who are indeed ‘born’ and reach the state of ‘they will not become again.’ ‘Seeking to be born’ (sambhavesī) means those who seek becoming (sambhavaṃ esanti). This is a designation for trainees and worldlings who, because the fetter of becoming is not yet abandoned, seek a new existence also in the future. Alternatively, among the four kinds of birth, egg-born and womb-born beings are called ‘seeking to be born’ for as long as they do not break the eggshell and the womb; having broken the eggshell and the womb and come out, they are called ‘born.’ Moisture-born and spontaneous-born beings are called ‘seeking to be born’ at the first moment of consciousness; from the second moment of consciousness onwards, they are called ‘born.’ Or, by whatever posture they are born, for as long as they do not attain another, they are called ‘seeking to be born’; thereafter, they are called ‘born.’

Chaṭṭhagāthāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Sixth Verse

6. Evaṃ bhagavā “sukhino vā”tiādīhi aḍḍhateyyāhi gāthāhi nānappakārato tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ hitasukhāgamapatthanāvasena sattesu mettābhāvanaṃ dassetvā idāni ahitadukkhānāgamapatthanāvasenāpi taṃ dassento āha “na paro paraṃ nikubbethā”ti. Esa porāṇo pāṭho, idāni pana “paraṃ hī”tipi paṭhanti, ayaṃ na sobhano.

Thus, the Blessed One, through two and a half verses beginning with ‘May they be happy,’ having shown the cultivation of loving-kindness towards beings for those bhikkhus in various ways by means of wishing for the attainment of their welfare and happiness, now, wishing to show it also by means of wishing for the non-arrival of harm and suffering, said, ‘Let no one deceive another.’ This is the ancient reading. But now, some also recite it as ‘paraṃ hi’; this is not proper.

Tattha paroti parajano. Paranti parajanaṃ. Na nikubbethāti na vañceyya. Nātimaññethāti na atikkamitvā maññeyya. Katthacīti katthaci okāse, gāme vā gāmakhette vā ñātimajjhe vā pūgamajjhe vātiādi. Nanti etaṃ. Kañcīti yaṃ kañci khattiyaṃ vā brāhmaṇaṃ vā gahaṭṭhaṃ vā pabbajitaṃ vā sukhitaṃ vā dukkhitaṃ vātiādi. Byārosanā paṭighasaññāti kāyavacīvikārehi byārosanāya ca manovikārena paṭighasaññāya ca. “Byārosanāya paṭighasaññāyā”ti hi vattabbe “byārosanā paṭighasaññā”ti vuccati, yathā “sammadaññāya vimuttā”ti vattabbe “sammadaññā vimuttā”ti, yathā ca “anupubbasikkhāya anupubbakiriyāya anupubbapaṭipadāyā”ti vattabbe “anupubbasikkhā anupubbakiriyā anupubbapaṭipadā”ti. Nāññamaññassa dukkhamiccheyyāti aññamaññassa dukkhaṃ na iccheyya[P 0.0248]. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Na kevalaṃ “sukhino vā khemino vā hontū”tiādimanasikāravaseneva mettaṃ bhāveyya, kintu “ahovata yo koci parapuggalo yaṃ kañci parapuggalaṃ vañcanādīhi nikatīhi na nikubbetha, jātiādīhi ca navahi mānavatthūhi katthaci padese kañci parapuggalaṃ nātimaññeyya, aññamaññassa ca byārosanāya vā paṭighasaññāya vā dukkhaṃ na iccheyyā”ti evampi manasikaronto bhāveyyāti.

Therein, 'paro' means another person. 'Paraṃ' means another person. 'Na nikubbetha' means one should not cheat. 'Nātimaññetha' means one should not, having overpowered them, think contemptuously of them. 'Katthaci' means in any place, such as in a village, a field, in the midst of relatives, or in the midst of an association, and so on. 'Naṃ' means that person. 'Kañci' means anyone at all, whether a noble, a brahmin, a householder, a renunciate, one who is happy, or one who is suffering, and so on. 'Byārosanā paṭighasaññā' means by oppression through deviation of body and speech, and by the perception of conflict through deviation of mind. For when it should be said 'byārosanāya paṭighasaññāya', it is said 'byārosanā paṭighasaññā,' just as when it should be said 'sammadaññāya vimuttā', it is said 'sammadaññā vimuttā,' and just as when it should be said 'anupubbasikkhāya anupubbakiriyāya anupubbapaṭipadāya', it is said 'anupubbasikkhā anupubbakiriyā anupubbapaṭipadā.' 'Nāññamaññassa dukkhamiccheyya' means one should not desire suffering for each other. What is meant? One should not cultivate loving-kindness merely by way of attention such as, 'May they be happy, may they be secure.' Rather, one should cultivate it while attending thus: 'Oh, may it be that any person would not deceive any other person with deceptions and cunning! Oh, may it be that in any place, no one would despise any other person through the nine bases of conceit beginning with birth! And oh, may it be that they would not wish suffering for one another through oppression or the perception of conflict!'

Sattamagāthāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Seventh Stanza

7. Evaṃ [V 0.0201][M 0.0212] ahitadukkhānāgamapatthanāvasena atthato mettābhāvanaṃ dassetvā idāni tameva upamāya dassento āha “mātā yathā niyaṃputta”nti.

7. Having thus shown in meaning the cultivation of loving-kindness by way of wishing for the non-arrival of what is unbeneficial and suffering, now, wishing to show that very thing with a simile, He said: 'mātā yathā niyaṃ puttaṃ'.

Tassattho – yathā mātā niyaṃ puttaṃ attani jātaṃ orasaṃ puttaṃ, tañca ekaputtameva āyusā anurakkhe, tassa dukkhāgamappaṭibāhanatthaṃ attano āyumpi cajitvā taṃ anurakkhe, evampi sabbabhūtesu idaṃ mettākhyaṃ mānasaṃ bhāvaye, punappunaṃ janaye vaḍḍhaye, tañca aparimāṇasattārammaṇavasena ekasmiṃ vā satte anavasesapharaṇavasena aparimāṇaṃ bhāvayeti.

The meaning of this is: Just as a mother would protect with her life her own son, born of herself, the son of her breast, and that son being her only son; just as she would protect that one son, having given up even her own life for the sake of warding off the arrival of suffering for him, so too, towards all beings, one should cultivate this mind called loving-kindness. One should generate and increase it again and again. And one should cultivate it as limitless, either by way of having limitless beings as its object, or by way of pervading a single being without remainder.

Aṭṭhamagāthāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Eighth Stanza

8. Evaṃ sabbākārena mettābhāvanaṃ dassetvā idāni tasseva vaḍḍhanaṃ dassento āha “mettañca sabbalokasmī”ti.

8. Having thus shown in all aspects the cultivation of loving-kindness, now, wishing to show the increase of that very thing, He said: 'mettañca sabbalokasmiṃ'.

Tattha mijjati tāyati cāti mitto, hitajjhāsayatāya siniyhati, ahitāgamato rakkhati cāti attho. Mittassa bhāvo mettaṃ. Sabbalokasmīti anavasese sattaloke. Manasi bhavanti mānasaṃ. Tañhi cittasampayuttattā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Bhāvayeti vaḍḍhaye. Na assa parimāṇanti aparimāṇaṃ, appamāṇasattārammaṇatāya evaṃ vuttaṃ. Uddhanti upari, tena arūpabhavaṃ gaṇhāti. Adhoti heṭṭhā, tena kāmabhavaṃ gaṇhāti. Tiriyanti vemajjhaṃ, tena rūpabhavaṃ gaṇhāti. Asambādhanti sambādhavirahitaṃ, bhinnasīmanti vuttaṃ hoti. Sīmā nāma paccatthiko vuccati, tasmimpi pavattanti attho. Averanti veravirahitaṃ[P 0.0249], antarantarāpi veracetanāpātubhāvavirahitanti attho. Asapattanti vigatapaccatthikaṃ. Mettāvihārī hi puggalo manussānaṃ piyo hoti, amanussānaṃ piyo hoti, nāssa koci paccatthiko hoti, tenassa taṃ mānasaṃ vigatapaccatthikattā asapattanti vuccati. Pariyāyavacanañhi etaṃ, yadidaṃ paccatthiko sapattoti. Ayaṃ anupadato atthavaṇṇanā.

Herein, a 'friend' is so called because one is affectionate and one protects. The meaning is that because of a disposition for what is beneficial, one is affectionate; and one protects from the arrival of what is unbeneficial. The state of a friend is loving-kindness. 'In all the world' means in the entire world of beings without remainder. That which arises in the mind is 'mānasaṃ'. Indeed, it is said thus because it is associated with a wholesome mind. 'One should cultivate' means one should increase. That which has no measure is 'immeasurable'; it is said thus because of having limitless beings as its object. 'Above' means up; by this, one takes the formless existence. 'Below' means down; by this, one takes the sense-sphere existence. 'Across' means the middle; by this, one takes the form existence. 'Unrestricted' means free from constriction; it is said to mean 'with boundaries broken'. A 'boundary' is called an enemy; the meaning is that the mind of loving-kindness arises even towards that one. 'Without enmity' means free from enmity; the meaning is being free from the arising of a hostile volition, even intermittently. 'Without rivals' means with enemies gone. Indeed, a person who dwells in loving-kindness is dear to humans and dear to non-humans; they have no enemy whatsoever. Therefore, that mind of theirs is called 'without rivals' because of being free from enemies. For 'paccatthiko' and 'sapatto' are synonymous terms. This is the word-by-word explanation of the meaning.

Ayaṃ [M 0.0213] panettha adhippetatthadīpanā – yadidaṃ “evampi sabbabhūtesu mānasaṃ bhāvaye aparimāṇa”nti vuttaṃ, tañcetaṃ aparimāṇaṃ mettaṃ mānasaṃ sabbalokasmiṃ bhāvaye vaḍḍhaye, vuḍḍhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ gamaye pāpaye. Kathaṃ? Uddhaṃ adho ca tiriyañca, uddhaṃ yāva bhavaggā, adho [V 0.0202] yāva avīcito, tiriyaṃ yāva avasesadisā. Uddhaṃ vā āruppaṃ, adho kāmadhātuṃ, tiriyaṃ rūpadhātuṃ anavasesaṃ pharanto. Evaṃ bhāventopi ca taṃ yathā asambādhaṃ averaṃ asapattañca hoti, tathā sambādhaverasapattānaṃ abhāvaṃ karonto bhāvaye. Yaṃ vā taṃ bhāvanāsampadaṃ pattaṃ sabbattha okāsalokavasena asambādhaṃ, attano paresu āghātappaṭivinayanena averaṃ, attani ca paresaṃ āghātavinayanena asapattaṃ hoti. Taṃ asambādhamaveramasapattaṃ aparimāṇaṃ mettaṃ mānasaṃ uddhaṃ adho tiriyañcāti tividhaparicchede sabbalokasmiṃ bhāvaye vaḍḍhayeti.

This, however, is the explanation of the intended meaning here. That which was said: 'So too, towards all beings, one should cultivate a limitless mind,' this immeasurable mind of loving-kindness one should cultivate and increase in the entire world; one should bring it to growth, development, and abundance. How? Above, below, and across. Above, up to the peak of existence; below, down to the Avīci hell; and across, as far as the remaining directions. Or: above, to the formless realm; below, to the sense-sphere realm; across, to the form-sphere realm, pervading without remainder. And one should cultivate it in such a way that it becomes unrestricted, without enmity, and without rivals, thus bringing about the absence of restriction, enmity, and rivalry. Alternatively, that which has reached the accomplishment of cultivation is unrestricted everywhere by way of the spatial world; it is without enmity through the removal of one's own resentment towards others; and it is without rivals through the removal of others' resentment towards oneself. That unrestricted, enmity-free, rival-free, immeasurable mind of loving-kindness, one should cultivate and increase it in the entire world in its threefold division: above, below, and across.

Navamagāthāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Ninth Stanza

9. Evaṃ mettābhāvanāya vaḍḍhanaṃ dassetvā idāni taṃ bhāvanamanuyuttassa viharato iriyāpathaniyamābhāvaṃ dassento āha “tiṭṭhaṃ caraṃ…pe… adhiṭṭheyyā”ti.

9. Having thus shown the growth in the cultivation of loving-kindness, now, indicating the absence of a fixed rule for posture for one dwelling devoted to that cultivation, He says: 'Whether standing, walking... one should resolve.'

Tassattho – evametaṃ mettaṃ mānasaṃ bhāvento so “nisīdati [P 0.0250] pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāyā”tiādīsu viya iriyāpathaniyamaṃ akatvā yathāsukhaṃ aññataraññatarairiyāpathabādhanavinodanaṃ karonto tiṭṭhaṃ vā caraṃ vā nisinno vā sayāno vā yāvatā vigatamiddho assa, atha etaṃ mettājhānasatiṃ adhiṭṭheyya.

The meaning of this is: While cultivating this loving mind in such a way—without making a fixed rule for posture, as in 'he sits, having folded his legs crosswise, having set his body erect,' and so on, but dispelling the pain of one or another posture as is comfortable—whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, for as long as one might be free from drowsiness, one should then establish this mindfulness present in the loving-kindness jhāna.

Atha vā evaṃ mettābhāvanāya vaḍḍhanaṃ dassetvā idāni vasībhāvaṃ dassento āha “tiṭṭhaṃ cara”nti. Vasippatto hi tiṭṭhaṃ vā caraṃ vā nisinno vā sayāno vā yāvatā iriyāpathena etaṃ mettājhānasatiṃ adhiṭṭhātukāmo hoti, atha vā tiṭṭhaṃ vā caraṃ vā…pe… sayāno vāti na tassa ṭhānādīni antarāyakarāni honti, apica kho yāvatā etaṃ mettājhānasatiṃ adhiṭṭhātukāmo hoti, tāvatā vigatamiddho hutvā adhiṭṭhāti, natthi tassa tattha dandhāyitattaṃ. Tenāha “tiṭṭhaṃ caraṃ nisinno va, sayāno yāvatāssa vitamiddho. Etaṃ satiṃ adhiṭṭheyyā”ti.

Alternatively, having thus shown the growth through the development of loving-kindness, now, wishing to show mastery, He said: 'Standing, walking...' For one who has attained mastery, whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down—in whatever posture he wishes to establish this mindfulness of loving-kindness jhāna—then, whether standing, walking... or lying down, these postures such as standing do not become obstacles for him. Moreover, to whatever extent he wishes to establish this mindfulness of loving-kindness jhāna, to that extent, being free from drowsiness, he establishes it. There is no slowness for him in that. Therefore, He said: 'Whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, for as long as he is free from drowsiness, he should establish this mindfulness.'

Tassāyamadhippāyo [M 0.0214] – yaṃ taṃ “mettañca sabbalokasmi, mānasaṃ bhāvaye”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ yathā bhāveyya, yathā ṭhānādīsu yāvatā iriyāpathena ṭhānādīni vā anādiyitvā yāvatā etaṃ mettājhānasatiṃ adhiṭṭhātukāmo assa, tāvatā vigatamiddhova hutvā etaṃ satiṃ adhiṭṭheyyāti.

This is its intention: Regarding what was said, 'One should develop a mind of loving-kindness toward the entire world,' one should develop it in such a way that, in whatever posture among standing and so forth, without giving consideration to standing and so forth, to whatever extent one might wish to establish this mindfulness of loving-kindness jhāna, to that extent, being free from drowsiness, one should establish this mindfulness.

Evaṃ mettābhāvanāya vasībhāvaṃ dassento “etaṃ satiṃ adhiṭṭheyyā”ti tasmiṃ mettāvihāre niyojetvā idāni taṃ vihāraṃ thunanto āha “brahmametaṃ vihāramidhamāhū”ti.

Thus, while showing mastery in the development of loving-kindness, having enjoined one in that abiding in loving-kindness with the words, 'one should establish this mindfulness,' now, praising that abiding, He said: 'This they call a Brahma-abiding here.'

Tassattho [V 0.0203] – yvāyaṃ “sukhino vā khemino vā hontū”tiādi katvā yāva “etaṃ satiṃ adhiṭṭheyyā”ti vaṇṇito mettāvihāro. Etaṃ catūsu dibbabrahmaariyairiyāpathavihāresu niddosattā attanopi paresampi atthakarattā ca idha ariyassa dhammavinaye brahmavihāramāhu [P 0.0251] seṭṭhavihāramāhūti, yato satataṃ samitaṃ abbokiṇṇaṃ tiṭṭhaṃ caraṃ nisinno vā sayāno vā yāvatāssa vigatamiddho, etaṃ satiṃ adhiṭṭheyyāti.

Its meaning is as follows: This abiding in loving-kindness, which is described from 'May they be happy and secure...' up to '...one should establish this mindfulness,' is called a Brahma-abiding—a supreme abiding—here in this Dhamma and Vinaya of the noble one. This is because, among the four abidings—the divine, the Brahma, the noble, and the postural—it is faultless and beneficial to both oneself and others. And it is so called because one should establish this mindfulness continuously, constantly, and without interruption, whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, for as long as one is free from drowsiness.

Dasamagāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Tenth Verse

10. Evaṃ bhagavā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ nānappakārato mettābhāvanaṃ dassetvā idāni yasmā mettā sattārammaṇattā attadiṭṭhiyā āsannā hoti, tasmā diṭṭhigahananisedhanamukhena tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ tadeva mettājhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā ariyabhūmippattiṃ dassento “diṭṭhiñca anupaggammā”ti imāya gāthāya desanaṃ samāpesi.

10. Thus, having shown those monks the development of loving-kindness in various ways, the Blessed One now—because loving-kindness, having beings as its object, is proximate to the view of self—wishing to show them the attainment of the noble plane by way of prohibiting the grasping of views and making that very loving-kindness jhāna the basis, concluded the teaching with this verse: 'And not approaching a view...'

Tassattho – yvāyaṃ “brahmametaṃ vihāramidhamāhū”ti saṃvaṇṇito mettājhānavihāro, tato vuṭṭhāya ye tattha vitakkavicārādayo dhammā, te tesañca vatthādianusārena rūpadhamme pariggahetvā iminā nāmarūpaparicchedena “suddhasaṅkhārapuñjoyaṃ, nayidha sattūpalabbhatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.171; mahāni. 186) evaṃ diṭṭhiñca anupaggamma anupubbena lokuttarasīlena sīlavā hutvā lokuttarasīlasampayutteneva sotāpattimaggasammādiṭṭhisaññitena dassanena sampanno, tato paraṃ yopāyaṃ vatthukāmesu gedho kilesakāmo appahīno hoti, tampi sakadāgāmianāgāmimaggehi tanubhāvena anavasesappahānena [M 0.0215] ca kāmesu gedhaṃ vineyya vinayitvā vūpasametvā na hi jātu gabbhaseyyaṃ puna reti ekaṃseneva puna gabbhaseyyaṃ na eti. Suddhāvāsesu nibbattitvā tattheva arahattaṃ pāpuṇitvā parinibbātīti.

Its meaning is this: Having arisen from that abiding in the jhāna of loving-kindness which was praised as, 'This, they say, is a Brahma-abiding here,' and having comprehended those mental phenomena present there, such as initial and sustained thought, and also the material phenomena according to their basis and so on, through this discernment of mentality-materiality, one understands: 'This is a mere heap of formations; no being is found herein.' Thus, not approaching any view, and having, in due course, become virtuous with supramundane virtue, one is endowed with the vision—associated with that very supramundane virtue—designated as the right view of the stream-entry path. Thereafter, whatever greed for sensual objects, that defilement of sensual desire, remains unabandoned, that too—having made it attenuated through the path of the once-returner and abandoned it without remainder through the path of the non-returner—and having thus removed and pacified the greed for sensual pleasures, one 'surely never again comes to lie in a womb.' One definitely does not come to lie in a womb again. Being reborn in the Pure Abodes, and having attained Arahantship right there, one attains final Parinibbāna.

Evaṃ bhagavā desanaṃ samāpetvā te bhikkhū āha – “gacchatha, bhikkhave, tasmiṃyeva vanasaṇḍe viharatha, imañca suttaṃ māsassa aṭṭhasu dhammassavanadivasesu ghaṇḍiṃ ākoṭetvā ussāretha, dhammakathaṃ karotha sākacchatha anumodatha, idameva kammaṭṭhānaṃ āsevatha bhāvetha [P 0.0252] bahulīkarotha, tepi vo amanussā taṃ bheravārammaṇaṃ na dassessanti, aññadatthu atthakāmā hitakāmā bhavissantī”ti. Te “sādhū”ti bhagavato paṭissuṇitvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā tattha gantvā tathā akaṃsu. Devatāyo ca “bhadantā amhākaṃ atthakāmā hitakāmā”ti pītisomanassajātā hutvā sayameva senāsanaṃ sammajjanti, uṇhodakaṃ paṭiyādenti[V 0.0204], piṭṭhiparikammaṃ pādaparikammaṃ karonti, ārakkhaṃ saṃvidahanti. Tepi bhikkhū tameva mettaṃ bhāvetvā tameva ca pādakaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā sabbe tasmiṃyeva antotemāse aggaphalaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇitvā mahāpavāraṇāya visuddhipavāraṇaṃ pavāresunti.

Having thus concluded the teaching, the Blessed One said to those monks: 'Go, monks, dwell in that very forest grove. And on the eight days of the month for hearing the Dhamma, having struck the gong, you should recite this sutta. Give Dhamma talks, discuss them, and express appreciation; practice this very meditation subject, develop it, and make much of it. Those non-human beings will not show you that terrifying object; on the contrary, they will desire your benefit and welfare.' They, having assented to the Blessed One's words with 'Very well, venerable sir,' rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him respectfully, went there, and did as instructed. And the deities, filled with joy and happiness, thinking, 'The venerable ones desire our benefit and welfare,' of their own accord swept the lodging places, prepared warm water, performed massages for the back and feet, and arranged for protection. Those monks too, having developed that very loving-kindness and having made it the basis, undertook insight meditation. All of them, within that very three-month period, attained the supreme fruit, Arahantship, and on the day of the great Pavāraṇā, they performed the Pavāraṇā of purity.

Evampi atthakusalena tathāgatena,

Dhammissarena kathitaṃ karaṇīyamatthaṃ;

Katvānubhuyya paramaṃ hadayassa santiṃ,

Santaṃ padaṃ abhisamenti samattapaññā.

Thus, having performed the beneficial task that should be done, as taught by the Tathāgata, who is skilled in what is beneficial and is Lord of the Dhamma, and having experienced the supreme peace of heart, those of perfected wisdom realize the peaceful state.

Tasmā hi taṃ amatamabbhutamariyakantaṃ,

Santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca viharitukāmo;

Viññū jano vimalasīlasamādhipaññā-

Bhedaṃ kareyya satataṃ karaṇīyamatthanti.

Therefore, a wise person who desires to dwell having realized that deathless, unassailable, beloved of the noble ones, peaceful state, should constantly perform the beneficial task that is to be done, distinguished by stainless virtue, concentration, and wisdom.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha.

Mettasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mettasutta is concluded.

Nigamanakathā

Concluding Words

Ettāvatā [M 0.0216] ca yaṃ vuttaṃ –

And thus far, what was stated:

“Uttamaṃ vandaneyyānaṃ, vanditvā ratanattayaṃ;

Khuddakānaṃ karissāmi, kesañci atthavaṇṇana”nti.

“Having venerated the Triple Gem, supreme among those worthy of veneration, I shall compose an explanation of the meaning of some of the Minor Texts.”

Tattha saraṇasikkhāpadadvattiṃsākārakumārapañhamaṅgalasuttaratanasuttatirokuṭṭanidhikaṇḍamettasuttavasena navappabhedassa khuddakapāṭhassa tāva atthavaṇṇanā katā hoti. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Herein, the commentary on the meaning of the Khuddakapāṭha, which has nine divisions—namely, the Refuges, the Precepts, the Thirty-Two Parts, the Youth's Questions, the Maṅgala Sutta, the Ratana Sutta, the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta, the Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta, and the Mettā Sutta—has thus been completed.

“Imaṃ [V 0.0205][P 0.0253] khuddakapāṭhassa, karontenatthavaṇṇanaṃ;

Saddhammaṭṭhitikāmena, yaṃ pattaṃ kusalaṃ mayā.

Tassānubhāvato khippaṃ, dhamme ariyappavedite;

Vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ, pāpuṇātu ayaṃ jano”ti.

By me, composing this commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha with a desire for the stability of the True Dhamma, whatever merit has been attained—through the power of that, may this multitude of beings quickly attain growth, increase, and fullness in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble Ones.

Paramavisuddhasaddhābuddhivīriyaguṇappaṭimaṇḍitena sīlācārajjavamaddavādiguṇasamudayasamuditena sakasamayasamayantaragahanajjhogāhaṇasamatthena paññāveyyattiyasamannāgatena tipiṭakapariyattidhammappabhede sāṭṭhakathe satthusāsane appaṭihatañāṇappabhāvena chamahāveyyākaraṇenachamahāveyyākaraṇena karaṇasampattijanitasukhaviniggatamadhurodāravacanalāvaṇṇayuttena yuttamuttavādinā vādīvarena mahākavinā chaḷabhiññāpaṭisambhidādippabhedaguṇappaṭimaṇḍite uttarimanussadhamme suppatiṭṭhitabuddhīnaṃ theravaṃsappadīpānaṃ therānaṃ mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ vaṃsālaṅkārabhūtena vipulavisuddhabuddhinā buddhaghosoti garūhi gahitanāmadheyyena therena katā ayaṃ paramatthajotikā nāma khuddakapāṭhavaṇṇanā –

This commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha, called Paramatthajotikā, was composed by the elder whose name, Buddhaghosa, was given by his revered teachers—he who is adorned with the supremely pure virtues of faith, wisdom, and energy; endowed with an accumulation of virtues such as morality, conduct, uprightness, and gentleness; capable of plunging into the depths of his own doctrine and that of others; possessed of sagacity; with unobstructed knowledge in the Teacher's Dispensation with its commentaries, in the divisions of the Tipiṭaka scriptural learning; a great grammarian; endowed with the charm of sweet and noble speech, uttered with ease, born of accomplishment in execution; a speaker of what is fit and proper; a foremost speaker; a great sage; an ornament to the lineage of the elders residing at the Great Monastery, who are lamps unto the lineage of the elders, with well-established wisdom in the higher human states adorned with virtues such as the six supernormal knowledges and the four analytical knowledges; and who possesses vast and pure wisdom.

Tāva tiṭṭhatu lokasmiṃ, lokanittharaṇesinaṃ;

Dassentī kulaputtānaṃ, nayaṃ sīlādisuddhiyā.

May it remain long in the world, showing to sons of good family who seek to cross over the world the method for purity beginning with virtue.

Yāva buddhoti nāmampi, suddhacittassa tādino;

Lokamhi lokajeṭṭhassa, pavattati mahesinoti.

May it do so for as long as even the name ‘Buddha’—of the Great Seer who is pure-minded, steadfast, and foremost in the world—prevails in the world.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

Of the Paramatthajotikā, the commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha.

Khuddakapāṭhavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha is concluded.
